events.text: Prayers reach a god the way smoke reaches a ceiling: most of them thin and grey. One reaches you every dawn bright as a struck bell and entirely wrong. {npc} has got your name confused with the god of the next domain, and has been thanking you for rain you never sent, with great sincerity, for eleven years.
events.arc: The One Who Prays Wrong

choices.text: Send the rain {he} has been thanking you for

effects.log: You send a small rain to {his} terraces, out of season, as if you had always meant to. The next dawn the prayer is louder than ever. (+faith)

choices.text: Appear in {his} dream and correct {him}

effects.log: {npc} wakes, ashamed, and the next prayer is spelled right. It is also, you notice, a great deal quieter.

choices.text: Leave it. A prayer is a prayer

effects.log: You let the wrong name stand. It reaches you anyway; faith, it seems, is not fussy about spelling.

events.text: The god of the next domain has noticed that one of their worshippers prays to you by their name. A herald arrives with a scroll of complaint written so formally it takes an hour to find the verb.
events.arc: The One Who Prays Wrong

choices.text: Offer to share the prayer: half the dawn each

effects.log: The neighbouring god accepts, stiffly. {npc} never knows that two gods now listen to {him} at dawn, one after the other.

choices.text: Tell the herald the prayer chose you

effects.log: The herald goes away offended, and the neighbour does not invite you to the next court feast. The prayer keeps coming.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and {his} last prayer is not a thanks. {He} asks whichever god has been listening to tell {him}, just once, whether anyone ever was. {He} does not ask for a sign. {He} asks for an answer.
events.arc: The One Who Prays Wrong

choices.text: Go down to {his} terrace in person

effects.log: You sit with {npc} on the terrace wall in the last of the sun, a god in a plain coat, and tell {him} yes. {He} laughs, and says {he} knew it was raining for {him}.

choices.text: Send a dream of every dawn {he} prayed

effects.log: {He} dreams of eleven thousand dawns, each one heard. {He} wakes once more, says thank you, by the right name this time, and does not wake again.

events.text: At noon in your domain everything that worships you pauses for one breath: the herders, the kilns, the hawks on the updraft. It is not a rule. Nobody remembers starting it. For one breath the whole domain listens for you, and today you have nothing to say.

choices.text: Say nothing, and listen back

effects.log: You listen to the domain listening to you. It is the strangest conversation you have had in a thousand years, and the best.

choices.text: Send a single warm wind across it

effects.log: The wind goes over every field and roof at once. The breath ends, and the domain goes back to work humming.

events.text: Your oldest shrine lost its roof in a storm three centuries ago. {npc} keeps it anyway, sweeping the bare floor each morning and covering the altar with a tarp when it rains. {He} has never once complained to you about the roof.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Roofless Shrine

choices.text: Send a dream of a carpenter-god's address

effects.log: {npc} wakes with a name in mind and walks four days to find it. The carpenter-god, flattered, agrees to a visit.

choices.text: Let a tree grow a canopy over the altar

effects.log: A cedar rises overnight beside the shrine and leans over the altar like an old friend holding an umbrella.

choices.text: Leave it. {He} has made peace with it

effects.log: You leave the roof as it is. {npc} sweeps on, and sparrows nest in the rafters that are not there.

events.text: The carpenter-god arrives with a ladder, a flask, and opinions about your shrine. {npc} serves tea on the swept floor and asks nothing at all. The carpenter-god is so unnerved by this that {he} does the whole roof for nothing.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Roofless Shrine

choices.text: Thank the carpenter-god before the whole court

effects.log: At the next feast you name the roofer aloud. The carpenter-god pretends not to blush; three other gods ask for the same favour.

choices.text: Send a quiet gift of seasoned timber

effects.log: A stack of seasoned timber appears at the carpenter-god's workshop door with no note. They know.

events.text: The cedar has grown a hollow in its trunk, and {npc} has started leaving the day's offerings in it. Birds, bees and a very bold squirrel now share your congregation. The count of worshippers has risen by forty-one, none of them able to speak.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Roofless Shrine

choices.text: Count them all as faithful

effects.log: You count the squirrel too. The faith that arrives is small and warm and utterly sincere.

choices.text: Keep the count to people alone

effects.log: You keep your accounts strict. The squirrel does not mind.

events.text: {npc} dies in the autumn, gently, with the broom still in {his} hand. The roof, the cedar or the bare floor, whichever stands, is now yours alone to keep. Someone must sweep.
events.arc: The Keeper of the Roofless Shrine

choices.text: Send a young wind to sweep each dawn

effects.log: A small wind takes over the sweeping. The floor is cleaner than it has ever been, and a little lonely.

choices.text: Let the next pilgrim find the broom

effects.log: A stranger picks up the broom, uncertain, and sweeps one stroke. Then another. By dusk {he} is the keeper.

events.text: The valley offers you pickled radishes. This is not a metaphor. Every season, a heap of them arrives at your shrine in jars, courtesy of {npc}, whose family has pickled them for you for nine generations. You are a god of storms. You have never been able to eat one.
events.arc: Offerings You Cannot Use

choices.text: Ask the sea-god what gods do with food

effects.log: The sea-god laughs for a full minute, then explains how the offering is taken in the smell alone. The radishes are suddenly wonderful.

choices.text: Return one jar, labelled with a blessing

effects.log: {npc} receives a jar with a storm-god's blessing scrawled on the lid, and builds a small business on it within a year.

choices.text: Accept them in silence

effects.log: The radishes sit on the altar and you inhale them every season with great dignity.

events.text: The pickling family has put "Blessed by the Storm" on every jar and is selling them in three provinces. The tide of new worshippers is large and sticky and smells of vinegar.
events.arc: Offerings You Cannot Use

choices.text: Tell {npc} the labels are fair

effects.log: {npc} weeps with relief. The jars keep selling and your shrines multiply along the trade roads.

choices.text: Ask {him} to add a line about patience

effects.log: The new label says "Patience is a storm that has not yet decided." It is the best thing anyone has written about you.

events.text: A harvest-god who has watched all this sends a note. The tone is airy. The note says that radishes are really the Green Assembly's affair and would you kindly move your name off the jars.
events.arc: Offerings You Cannot Use

choices.text: Reply with a jar and a small bow

effects.log: The harvest-god accepts the jar, and complains for a week that it is the best radish they ever tasted.

choices.text: Ignore the note

effects.log: The note goes into the storm and is not seen again. The harvest-god sulks for a century.

events.text: A child on a hillside shouts at the sky every afternoon. It is not a prayer. {npc} is nine and furious that it rains during the harvest games, and has decided that the god in charge is simply being unreasonable. {He} is correct about most of it.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues With the Weather

choices.text: Answer from a cloud: 'It is not that simple.'

effects.log: {npc} nods, as though a colleague had said it, and returns with new objections.

choices.text: Clear the sky for one afternoon

effects.log: The games go ahead beneath a flawless sky. {npc} stares up suspiciously, then yells, 'Thank you,' in the tone of a creditor.

choices.text: Listen without answering

effects.log: You listen. It is a very good argument, mostly about fairness.

events.text: {npc} is fifteen. {He} still argues, but now with figures: rain tables, harvest dates, a map. {He} has worked out when you will send storms, and is about to publish this in the market. Half the valley will plan around it.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues With the Weather

choices.text: Let {him} publish. A predictable god is loved

effects.log: The valley plans around you, and loves you for being reliable. A little of your mystery drains away, and more faith arrives.

choices.text: Shift the storms by a week, once

effects.log: {npc} is wrong, loudly, in public, and returns humbled and delighted that you are alive.

events.text: {npc} has become the valley's weather-reader, and no longer shouts. {He} asks only one thing: to know, before {he} dies, whether the rain was ever personal.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues With the Weather

choices.text: Tell the truth: it was, once, on the day of the games

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down. 'I knew it!' {He} says it three more times, all the way home.

choices.text: Say only that the sky is fond of {him}

effects.log: {npc} accepts this, and writes it on the wall of the weather-hut, where it stays.

events.text: {npc} began to walk toward your highest shrine when {he} was twenty. The shrine is on a mountain that moves, a little, each decade. {He} has been walking forty years, and keeps arriving at where the shrine used to be.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Nudge the shrine back toward {his} road

effects.log: The shrine slides a few miles east in the night. {npc} looks at the new horizon, and weeps, and keeps walking.

choices.text: Walk with {him} in a plain coat

effects.log: You walk beside {npc} for a week as a stranger. {He} tells you everything about the shrine, and nothing you did not know.

choices.text: Leave the mountain where it is

effects.log: Some journeys are the point. You watch {him} go on, and say nothing.

events.text: At a crossing of roads {npc} meets another pilgrim, younger, bound for your rival's shrine. They argue for a day about whose god is better, and then fall into step together, because the roads are long.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Bless both pilgrims' shoes

effects.log: Their soles are suddenly eerily comfortable. Both of them look at their feet for a long time.

choices.text: Say nothing. It is their road

effects.log: The two walk on. The rival god never learns whose idea it was.

events.text: {npc} reaches the summit at last, in a wind that smells of thunder. There is no great altar, only a stone with a cup on it. {He} puts down {his} staff and asks nothing, since {he} has used up every wish on the road.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Fill the cup with rain from the first cloud {he} ever saw

effects.log: {npc} drinks, remembers being twenty, and sits down at the stone for the rest of the afternoon, smiling.

choices.text: Step out of the wind and be seen

effects.log: {He} falls on {his} knees at the sight of you, then gets up, because you ask {him} to. You have tea.

events.text: The old keeper of your hill shrine is failing, and has taken two apprentices. {npc} is gentle and forgetful; the other is quick and polishes everything. The keeper asks you, in a prayer wrapped in tea, which of them you would like to keep the bell.
events.arc: The Keeper's Two Apprentices

choices.text: Hint for the gentle one

effects.log: The old keeper hears you and sighs. {npc} is made the keeper's heir, to the quick one's wounded silence.

choices.text: Hint for the quick one

effects.log: The old keeper smiles; the quick one gets the bell, and {npc} is made shrine-gardener, which is not nothing.

choices.text: Say it is not for you to say

effects.log: The old keeper is annoyed, and says so, and then settles it by a footrace.

events.text: {npc} has been the keeper for some years, and the shrine has grown quieter. People like it, but they bring less. A clerk of the court notes that the offerings have dropped, and mentions it in a tone.
events.arc: The Keeper's Two Apprentices

choices.text: Send a gentle sign: the bell rings twice

effects.log: The bell rings twice at dusk. Pilgrims arrive to find out why. {npc} is baffled, and kind to all of them.

choices.text: Tell the clerk the quiet is the point

effects.log: The clerk files that away. A quiet shrine, you point out, is a rare thing.

events.text: The quick one has opened a rival shrine in town and takes the crowds. {npc}, the real keeper, is left sweeping an empty yard and humming. A pilgrim wanders in by mistake and stays for two hours.
events.arc: The Keeper's Two Apprentices

choices.text: Make the pilgrim a regular

effects.log: The pilgrim returns every season, with friends who also want to be somewhere calm.

choices.text: Let it be. The calm shrine will be found

effects.log: You leave it. A shrine like this is found, in the end, by the people who need it.

events.text: A cat has taken over your small coastal shrine. It sleeps on the altar and ignores the offerings. {npc}, the shrine-keeper, says the cat belongs to a different god entirely and must be treated with care, as a visiting envoy.
events.arc: The Shrine Cat Who Is Not Yours

choices.text: Ask the cat's god politely about the cat

effects.log: A grey cat-god's messenger arrives to say yes, the cat is theirs, and no, they do not want it back.

choices.text: Treat the cat as an envoy anyway

effects.log: You leave out a saucer of milk and a small cushion. The cat accepts both with condescension.

events.text: The cat has brought you a gift: a very large fish, dead, on the altar steps. {npc} insists it is a sacred offering from a higher power. You are not sure the higher power is you.
events.arc: The Shrine Cat Who Is Not Yours

choices.text: Accept it as a treaty gift

effects.log: You send a gentle breeze of thanks. The cat-god's followers hear of it and add a charm to your shrine.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to bury it respectfully

effects.log: The fish is buried with a short rite. The cat watches, and finds the rite adequate.

events.text: Kittens have appeared at the shrine, then three more, then seven. {npc} reports that the cat-god's followers now treat your shrine as an embassy, and ask whether the embassy may keep its own incense on your altar.
events.arc: The Shrine Cat Who Is Not Yours

choices.text: Grant the embassy its incense

effects.log: The altar now smells of two faiths. {npc} lights both sticks every dawn with great ceremony.

choices.text: Say the shrine is shared, not annexed

effects.log: The envoy bows to the principle, if not the incense. The saucer stays where it is.

events.text: Years pass and the embassy thrives. The cat-god's envoy asks you to stand witness at the renewal of the treaty, in a hall of folded paws. {npc} is old now, and is given the seat of honour by the cats themselves.
events.arc: The Shrine Cat Who Is Not Yours

choices.text: Stand witness and sign as an equal

effects.log: Your name goes beside a paw-print. The cats' faithful carry word of it up and down the coast. (+faith)

choices.text: Stand witness, and let {npc} sign for the shrine

effects.log: {npc} signs with a shaking hand and is applauded by forty cats. {He} is never prouder.

events.text: The cats move on to a coastal shrine that welcomes them, and the envoy's last note is polite and brief. {npc} still sets out the saucer each morning. {He} asks whether you mind that {he} is keeping a shrine for guests who will not return.
events.arc: The Shrine Cat Who Is Not Yours

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep setting it out

effects.log: The saucer is filled for another ten years. One grey cat comes back for a night, and sleeps on the altar.

choices.text: Tell {him} the shrine is enough on its own

effects.log: {npc} puts the saucer away and sweeps with a lighter arm. The cat is not mentioned again.

events.text: {npc} stands in the market with a placard that reads, in careful ink, THE GODS ARE ONLY WEATHER AND HABIT. People have stopped being angry about it. Some bring {him} tea. {He} is, you realise, one of your most dedicated observers.
events.arc: The Heretic of the Hill Road

choices.text: Send {him} a small clear proof you exist

effects.log: A sparrow lands on {his} placard and sings a perfect note, then flies away. {npc} writes a long note in a ledger.

choices.text: Visit in a plain coat and argue

effects.log: You argue for an afternoon. {npc} is wickedly good at it. You both enjoy yourselves.

choices.text: Let {him} be a heretic

effects.log: A god is made stronger by one honest sceptic. You do not intervene.

events.text: {npc} has changed the placard: it now says THE GODS ARE ONLY WEATHER AND HABIT, AND I AM GRATEFUL FOR BOTH. The crowd has thickened. A priest of the court is furious and wants the placard burned.
events.arc: The Heretic of the Hill Road

choices.text: Quietly protect the placard from the priest

effects.log: A sudden dry wind turns the priest's torch to nothing. The placard stays. {npc} never asks why.

choices.text: Let the court priest do as they will

effects.log: The placard is taken down. {npc} writes another that night, in smaller letters, and puts it up again.

events.text: {npc} is old, and sceptical to the end, and the last thing {he} asks of a god who may not exist is a good death. A heretic's request carries a particular weight.
events.arc: The Heretic of the Hill Road

choices.text: Grant it, in the first person

effects.log: You sit by {his} bed and say nothing. {He} sleeps, comfortable, with a faint smile of vindication.

choices.text: Send a dream of the market, and a crowd

effects.log: {He} dreams of the market full of people with placards of their own. It is hardly a prayer. It will do.

events.text: Someone leaves letters at your shrine gate, folded small, addressed to you by the wrong title. {npc} writes four a week, always short, always ending: 'Do not trouble yourself.' It is the most trouble anyone has ever taken over you.
events.arc: The Letters Left at the Gate

choices.text: Write back, in rain on the paper

effects.log: {npc} finds the answer in the smudge of the ink, and reads it like a poem.

choices.text: Keep them all in a box

effects.log: You keep the letters in a small box in a cloud that only you can find. It is a good box.

events.text: {npc} is moving to a far city. The last letter is the longest, and ends differently: 'Come with me, if it is no trouble.' A god cannot follow a letter. Though one might, in a coat, for a season.
events.arc: The Letters Left at the Gate

choices.text: Follow in a plain coat

effects.log: You live in the next city for a season as an unknown neighbour. {npc} does not know. It is the best season you remember.

choices.text: Send a shrine-stone to the new city

effects.log: A shrine-stone is found in {his} new garden, small and grey. {npc} looks at it, and puts a letter on top.

events.text: A new god has set up a little shrine beside the stone and offers to take over the letters, being young and keen. {npc} refuses, politely. The letters are not for the young god.
events.arc: The Letters Left at the Gate

choices.text: Promise to read each letter yourself

effects.log: The young god sulks, and you read every letter. It is no hardship.

choices.text: Ask the young god to take every second one

effects.log: The young god is pleased. The letters now arrive on both desks, and {npc} never knows.

events.text: Every dawn, {npc} lights a stick at your shrine and sits for an hour with {his} eyes closed. {He} does not pray in words, or ask anything. You have never had so quiet a worshipper, and it has begun to feel like being watched.
events.arc: The One Who Asks Nothing

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} wants

effects.log: You send a small voice, and {npc} jumps. 'Nothing,' {he} says. 'I just come to sit with someone.'

choices.text: Sit with {him}, unseen

effects.log: You sit beside {him} each dawn. Nothing happens. It is an extraordinary hour.

events.text: {npc} stops coming. A week, then a month. The incense stick on the step has gone cold. A neighbour says only: 'Fallen ill, I think.' The neighbour does not say where.
events.arc: The One Who Asks Nothing

choices.text: Go to {his} house in a plain coat

effects.log: You find {npc} abed, grumpy, and astonished to see you. {He} does not guess who you are.

choices.text: Send a small cure by a sparrow

effects.log: The sparrow drops a herb at {his} window. By the next day {he} is on the mend.

events.text: {npc} is back, recovered, and has finally asked for something: that the shrine's single lamp never go out. It is a small thing. You have given and withheld far bigger.
events.arc: The One Who Asks Nothing

choices.text: Grant it forever

effects.log: The lamp is lit that night by a flame that will not fail. Pilgrims will speak of it, for centuries.

choices.text: Promise to keep it lit, as long as {he} lives

effects.log: You keep the promise, which is the easier thing to bear.

events.text: There is a shrine to you beneath a stone bridge, three feet wide, made of a crate and a doll's tea cup. {npc}, a ferryman, built it in a flood and has kept it since. Nobody else knows it is there.
events.arc: The Shrine Under the Bridge

choices.text: Make it a place of safe crossing

effects.log: Boats pass the bridge more easily from that day. Ferrymen up and down the river come to leave small gifts.

choices.text: Leave it small and secret

effects.log: You leave the shrine under the bridge as it is. A secret shrine is, in its way, the most private kind of prayer.

events.text: A river-god, whose river this is, discovers the little shrine and is not pleased. They arrive in a flurry of ripples. 'You are in my water,' they say. The ferryman is hiding under a seat.
events.arc: The Shrine Under the Bridge

choices.text: Offer the river-god half the offerings

effects.log: The river-god sulks and then accepts. The ferryman breathes again.

choices.text: Argue the shrine is in the air, not the water

effects.log: A long and absurd argument about the bottom edge of a bridge. The river-god gives up, laughing.

events.text: The river-god sends a bill for half the offerings, itemised by the pebble. {npc} cannot read it, and brings it to the little shrine with trembling hands, holding it away from {him} like a snake.
events.arc: The Shrine Under the Bridge

choices.text: Pay it in full, with a dream-written receipt

effects.log: {npc} wakes with a receipt in mind and writes it out in a round hand. The river-god frames it.

choices.text: Dispute it, line by line, with the river-god

effects.log: A day of polite shouting across the water. By dusk three lines are struck out and the river-god is smiling.

events.text: The river-god and the little shrine become friends over the years. {npc}'s grandchildren take the ferry, and every crossing now ends with a pebble set on the shrine's crate. The river-god sends a spring flood only when asked.
events.arc: The Shrine Under the Bridge

choices.text: Bless the pebbles of the shrine

effects.log: The pebbles of the crate warm in the sun and keep the warmth for a hundred years. (+faith)

choices.text: Let the friendship be its own blessing

effects.log: The two gods agree, over the bridge, never to mention the bill again.

events.text: The dispute made the shrine famous and the river-god a rival. A flood takes the ferry, and {npc} gives up the river and moves to the coast with the crate. The bridge-shrine is empty. A tide of pilgrims arrives too late.
events.arc: The Shrine Under the Bridge

choices.text: Follow {him} to the coast and keep the crate lit

effects.log: A shrine appears in a coastal alley beside a fish stall. {npc} lives there and tends it until {he} dies.

choices.text: Let the old bridge-shrine go to the river

effects.log: The river-god takes the crate, with a small apology. You hear it sing in the water for a night.

events.text: A shrine of yours has not had a visitor in nine years. Its dust is so undisturbed it has begun to look like a landscape: dunes, ridges, a small dry sea. You wonder if the dust is the real congregation.

choices.text: Blow gently and watch the dunes shift

effects.log: The dunes shift into new shapes, and you watch the little sea redraw itself. Nobody has seen this for nine years.

choices.text: Send a wanderer to find the place

effects.log: A wanderer stumbles upon the shrine within the month, sneezes, and begins to sweep.

events.text: A goat has eaten the offering of rice and then, with great gravity, a small sacred scroll. The keeper is aghast. The goat appears delighted. You are rather amused.

choices.text: Treat the goat as a minor oracle

effects.log: The goat becomes a local legend. People line up to ask it things, and it eats their questions.

choices.text: Replace the scroll in a dream

effects.log: The keeper dreams the scroll, line by line, and writes it out again, relieved.

events.text: A child rings your shrine bell every morning because it makes a loud noise and they like loud noises. They have no thoughts about you whatsoever. By your reckoning they are the most honest worshipper in the valley.

choices.text: Make the bell ring a note sweeter than they expect

effects.log: The child stops, stares at the bell, and then rings it again, gently, forever after.

choices.text: Let them be loud

effects.log: A shrine should be a bit loud. You settle down to enjoy it.

events.text: A woman at your altar thanks you for a recovery. It was not your doing. It was a physician's, and a good one. The physician is not a god. The woman is certain you were involved.

choices.text: Take the thanks, and pass it on to the physician

effects.log: You send a modest dream of gratitude to the physician. They wake feeling inexplicably appreciated.

choices.text: Accept the thanks quietly

effects.log: You accept. Credit is a thing a god might hold in trust and not spend.

events.text: A priest of your hill shrine has been collecting money for a new roof. The roof has been under construction for fourteen years. The congregation has begun to ask whether it is ever coming. The priest looks hunted.

choices.text: Send a little rain through the unfinished roof

effects.log: The rain falls on the priest's own head. The roof is finished by the end of the year.

choices.text: Quietly pay the builders in a dream of lumber

effects.log: Timber arrives from nowhere, and the builders ask no questions.

events.text: Fog fills the valley of your newest shrine so thick that pilgrims cannot find it. They stand at the foot of the hill, calling your name, in confusion. The fog is nothing to do with you. It is, however, your fault.

choices.text: Part the fog with a small light

effects.log: A thin, steady glow leads them up the hill. Several declare it a miracle. You say nothing.

choices.text: Let them find it by guessing

effects.log: They climb and slip, and cheer when they find the shrine. You have rarely seen such joy.

events.text: A dog follows a pilgrim all the way to your shrine, and then sits at the altar and stares at you. Not at the statue. At you. The pilgrim apologises. The dog does not.

choices.text: Meet the dog's eye

effects.log: The dog and you share a long and unembarrassed look. It seems to be satisfied that you exist.

choices.text: Send a bone, discreetly

effects.log: A bone appears on the altar step. The pilgrim thinks it a miracle. The dog knows better.

events.text: Someone leaves a fresh flower on a forgotten shrine of yours each morning. Nobody sees them do it. The shrine has not had a priest in two hundred years. The flowers are always the wrong season.

choices.text: Wait up one dawn and look

effects.log: At dawn a small mist in the shape of a child places the flower, and looks at you, and does not flee. It is a minor god of the shrine.

choices.text: Let the mystery be

effects.log: A mystery is a very good gift to leave a god. You keep it.

events.text: A shrine-keeper fasts for your name every year in the cold season, until the valley folk beg them to stop. The valley folk this season are not begging. They are very quiet. The keeper looks quite thin.

choices.text: Send the keeper a warm meal in a dream

effects.log: The keeper dreams of a long table, wakes up hungry, and eats an enormous breakfast, delighted.

choices.text: Ask the keeper to stop, gently

effects.log: A voice in the cold tells the keeper to eat, and the keeper cries and obeys.

events.text: A couple marries at your shrine, and you are surprised to be wanted. The groom is shaking. The bride is calm. Neither has any idea what you do; they just know the shrine is pretty.

choices.text: Send petals from nowhere

effects.log: A soft fall of petals settles on them. They look up, delighted, and a little frightened.

choices.text: Give them a quiet blessing of patience

effects.log: You give them what they will need. They do not notice. It will be useful in about thirty years.

events.text: Moss has covered your statue so thoroughly that visitors take it for a boulder. The keeper wants to clean it. You find you are quite comfortable under the moss, and rather like the little frogs.

choices.text: Ask the keeper to leave the moss

effects.log: The statue stays green. A hundred years from now it will be thought a natural wonder.

choices.text: Let the keeper scrub, with a good grace

effects.log: The statue emerges, stiff and pale. The frogs relocate with dignity.

events.text: An old worshipper prays at your altar for forty minutes in a language nobody else speaks. You know it, as it happens. They are telling you about their day, and complaining about their knee, and asking after your health.

choices.text: Answer in kind, softly, in their tongue

effects.log: The old worshipper stops, listens, and says, 'Oh. There you are.' Then continues about the knee.

choices.text: Send that knee some relief

effects.log: The old worshipper stands, surprised, and walks away with a lighter step, and tells everyone.

events.text: A new priest at your lake shrine is terrified. They have studied thirty years, and have been told you are a demanding god. They have your ritual perfectly and a tremor in every hand.

choices.text: Send a warm laugh on the lake wind

effects.log: The priest hears it, and the tremor eases. A god with a laugh is not so frightening.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let them find their feet

effects.log: They stumble, recover, and finish the rite with a quiet pride you can feel.

events.text: A whole street dances at your shrine for rain, badly, with great vigour. It is the least graceful ritual you have ever received. It is, somehow, the most wholehearted. Several dancers have fallen into each other.

choices.text: Send the rain they asked for

effects.log: It rains in a downpour, and the street dances on, drenched and screaming with joy.

choices.text: Send a gentle drizzle, and applaud

effects.log: A drizzle falls, and a small sound of applause drifts down. They are absolutely thrilled.

events.text: At the end of the harvest, every house on the road hangs a lantern for you. The road glows for a night like a long string of small suns. A traveller arrives and asks what the festival is for. Nobody quite remembers.

choices.text: Brighten each lantern briefly

effects.log: Every lantern flares, once, and the road gasps. Then it settles into its glow.

choices.text: Let the road glow as it is

effects.log: The glow is enough. You lean on a dark cloud and watch it.

events.text: The hymn of your oldest shrine has been lost. Only the tune remains, hummed by the keeper, who keeps trying words. None fit. They have been trying for a decade, and the humming is wonderful.

choices.text: Whisper the original words in a dream

effects.log: The keeper wakes, sings it through, weeping, and writes it down before dawn.

choices.text: Let the tune stand without words

effects.log: The shrine's hymn stays a hum. Pilgrims call it the Wordless Song, and cry at it.

events.text: A child lost a coin and prays to you to find it. You can see it, in the gutter, a foot from where they are standing. There is a larger matter in the next valley that needs you. The child looks hopeful.

choices.text: Nudge them toward the gutter

effects.log: The child finds it, shouts, and tells the whole street. A very small miracle has gone a very long way.

choices.text: Ignore it. They will find it

effects.log: They do, an hour later, grumbling, and credit themselves. It is as it should be.

events.text: Two shrines to two different gods stand back to back in a courtyard. The keepers have shared a broom for sixty years and never once mentioned it. The gods, each, believe the broom is theirs.

choices.text: Quietly give the broom to the keepers as a joint gift

effects.log: The broom gleams. Both keepers think the other did it. The other god sighs in relief.

choices.text: Leave the broom and the argument to age

effects.log: You let sleeping brooms lie. It is a lovely friendship.

events.text: A bellmaker casts a bell for your shrine and puts a flaw in it, deliberately, so the sound will carry in the valley. The flaw gives the bell a slight, wobbling cry like a goose. The congregation loves it.

choices.text: Make the flaw ring true across the valley

effects.log: The goose-cry carries to the farthest farm. Travellers follow it, delighted.

choices.text: Praise the bellmaker in a dream

effects.log: The bellmaker wakes, sure that their flaw was seen. They are right.

events.text: A cold spring has killed the blossom in the Upper Terraces and the valley has decided it is your doing. {npc}, the loudest voice, has hung a black cloth on your shrine gate. It was not you. You were, at the time, asleep.
events.arc: The Valley That Blames You

choices.text: Take the blame, and send warm winds

effects.log: Warm winds go up the terraces for a month. {npc} removes the cloth without a word and leaves a bowl of plums.

choices.text: Send a dream explaining the cold

effects.log: The valley dreams of a far glacier tipping in its sleep. Many of them forgive you; {npc} does not.

choices.text: Let the cloth hang

effects.log: You let the black cloth hang. A god accustomed to blame learns patience.

events.text: Summer comes and the harvest is excellent. {npc} stands at your gate with the black cloth folded over one arm, and no idea what to do with it. The valley is watching.
events.arc: The Valley That Blames You

choices.text: Let {him} off with a small wind of thanks

effects.log: {npc} laughs out loud and ties the cloth to a kite. The kite flies for an hour, a black bird over the terraces.

choices.text: Wait. Let {him} speak first

effects.log: {npc} stammers out an apology and you accept it in the hum of the cicadas.

events.text: {npc} has become your most vocal defender. Anyone who curses the weather in the market is met with a long speech about how the god of the valley is doing the best a god can. People now avoid {him} on bad days.
events.arc: The Valley That Blames You

choices.text: Ask {him} gently to ease off

effects.log: {npc} hears, in a gust, a request not to scold. {He} is wounded but obedient, and pays more attention to the sky.

choices.text: Enjoy the loyalty, tempered with mercy

effects.log: A bit of loyalty is a handsome thing. You send {him} a good-weather wedding day.

events.text: In the hearth-halls of your domain, noon is a ritual. Every cook, smith and baker stops, holds a breath, and offers the first spark of the day to you. {npc}, the oldest smith, has been doing it since before the hall had walls.
events.arc: The Noon Breath of the Fire Court

choices.text: Take the spark and light every forge

effects.log: Every forge in the domain lights from one spark. It is a lovely, tiny mass event.

choices.text: Take the spark and hold it for a moment

effects.log: You hold the spark in your palm for a moment, an unmeasured warmth. Then you hand it back.

events.text: A young apprentice drops the noon spark and the forge goes dark in front of the whole hall. {npc} says nothing, but the silence is the loudest sound you have heard in a year.
events.arc: The Noon Breath of the Fire Court

choices.text: Relight it with a small flicker of your own

effects.log: The forge catches, and the apprentice weeps with relief. {npc} nods once.

choices.text: Let {npc} teach the apprentice to start it

effects.log: It takes an hour of patience, flint and breath. The apprentice learns in a way a gift never teaches.

events.text: The apprentice is a master now, and {npc} is dying. The last request: that the noon spark be given by the apprentice's hand, not yours, from now on. Let the hall light itself.
events.arc: The Noon Breath of the Fire Court

choices.text: Agree. The hall must live without you

effects.log: From that noon on, the spark is lit by human hands. Your faith drops a little, and the hall's heart rises.

choices.text: Promise to light it only on the worst days

effects.log: You keep a quiet promise. On a hard winter day you will come down, unseen.

events.text: One of the great tide-oxen has wandered inland and is standing in a farmer's barley, wet and enormous and utterly bewildered. {npc}, whose barley it is, has been feeding it for three days and cannot decide whether this is an honour or a curse.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox Who Went Inland

choices.text: Come down and coax it back toward the sea

effects.log: The tide-ox follows you for a week of hot dry road. {npc} sees it off with a tear and a bundle of grain.

choices.text: Let it stay a season. It likes the barley

effects.log: The tide-ox sleeps in the field until the first frost. The barley that grew round it is salted, and wonderful.

choices.text: Send a calf of the sea to fetch it

effects.log: A small wet calf arrives and the tide-ox rumbles, then wakes, then follows meekly.

events.text: A season after, {npc}'s barley wins the harvest feast. The farmer insists on dedicating the first loaf to the tide-ox, and so, by roundabout courtesy, to you. The loaf is huge. It is slightly salty.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox Who Went Inland

choices.text: Accept the loaf with delight

effects.log: The salted loaf is, you decide, the best bread in the realm. You say so to the market.

choices.text: Send the loaf back to the sea as an offering

effects.log: The loaf is carried to the shore and given to the waves. The tide-oxen low in the dark.

events.text: One midwinter night the tide-ox wakes and walks toward the sea on its own. {npc} stands at the gate with a lantern, and the great wet head turns once, as if it would say something. It is a long way to the shore.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox Who Went Inland

choices.text: Walk beside the tide-ox to the shore

effects.log: A week of frosty road, you in a plain coat, {npc} behind with grain. The ox lows at each hill.

choices.text: Let {npc} walk it alone

effects.log: {npc} insists. {He} takes the ox's rope and the road, and you watch the lantern shrink.

events.text: At the shore the tide-wardens of Haeryong Keeper of Tides are waiting, with a salt-bell and a long speech. They thank you for returning one of their herd, and offer your shrine a share of the autumn tides.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox Who Went Inland

choices.text: Accept the tides for your shrine

effects.log: The sea sends you its first wave every autumn from then on, and the faith of every coastal town. (+faith)

choices.text: Accept the thanks but leave the tides to the sea

effects.log: The wardens are astonished and then pleased. A salt-bell is left on your altar.

events.text: {npc} comes back from the shore a different person, quiet, with a shell the size of a bowl in {his} arms. {He} says the ox spoke on the last night and said a name. {He} has taken up a post as a tide-reader on the barley coast.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox Who Went Inland

choices.text: Bless the shell so it hears tides inland

effects.log: The shell sings the tide-tables to anyone who asks. Farmers come from four valleys to hear it.

choices.text: Let {him} find the ox's name alone

effects.log: {npc} sits with the shell for years. The name, when it comes, is only a small wet sound, and {he} is satisfied.

events.text: A mountain in your domain, a proud old thing, has been quietly sloughing a little rock each year, as though trying to be smaller. {npc}, who lives on its flank, has noticed and thinks the mountain is sad.
events.arc: The Peak That Wanted to Be Smaller

choices.text: Ask the mountain what is wrong

effects.log: The mountain says only that it has grown very tired of looking over everyone's heads.

choices.text: Let it go on. Mountains grieve in rocks

effects.log: A little scree falls. {npc} sits for a time beside the fall, and says a kind word to the stone.

events.text: The mountain has asked you for a favour: a valley of its own below, so that it might look up as well as down. You can raise the ground. You cannot easily lower the rest of the range.
events.arc: The Peak That Wanted to Be Smaller

choices.text: Open a gentle valley at its foot

effects.log: A broad dish of earth settles beneath the peak. Crocus come up. The mountain, much moved, looks up for the first time in an age.

choices.text: Offer a cloud to sit at its base

effects.log: A great grey cloud settles at the foot and sheds a long soft rain. It is not quite a valley but the mountain approves.

events.text: Crocus fill the dish below the peak, and {npc} has built a hut among them. The peak leans down each evening to listen to {him} sing. The other peaks of the range have noticed, and are murmuring across the sky about being left looking up.
events.arc: The Peak That Wanted to Be Smaller

choices.text: Open a valley for each of them

effects.log: The range is a quiet fury of earthworks for a season. Every peak gets a small low dish of crocus.

choices.text: Say the one valley was a gift of one night

effects.log: The range grumbles for a century. {npc} sings anyway, to whoever will listen.

events.text: The mountains hold a slow council and send you a letter that took forty years to write. It thanks you, in the manner of rocks, with a long list of their names. {npc}'s hut is on the first page.
events.arc: The Peak That Wanted to Be Smaller

choices.text: Read the letter aloud in the valley

effects.log: The range hears its names and rumbles. Every shrine on the slopes gets a bell. (+faith)

choices.text: Frame it, and say nothing

effects.log: The letter hangs in your hall, and the peaks think it very modest of you.

events.text: The peak that received the valley grows fond of {npc} and tries, in the manner of mountains, to say so. A landslide shapes itself into a staircase to {his} door, a very kind, very large gesture. {He} climbs it in tears.
events.arc: The Peak That Wanted to Be Smaller

choices.text: Bless the staircase against slipping

effects.log: The stair stands for a thousand years, and {npc} is buried at the top, looking down at the crocus.

choices.text: Ask the mountain to be gentler next time

effects.log: It tries. The next gesture is a single flat stone, and {npc} sits on it all summer.

events.text: Two neighbouring valleys have different calendars for the harvest feast, and each swears yours is the true one. {npc}, a priest of the second valley, has brought a brass instrument with fourteen dials to prove it. It is a very good instrument.
events.arc: The Two Harvest Calendars

choices.text: Declare the first calendar true

effects.log: The first valley cheers. {npc} folds the instrument away with the air of one planning a long war.

choices.text: Declare both true, on alternate years

effects.log: Both valleys complain, which is the sign of fair compromise.

choices.text: Ask for a demonstration of the instrument

effects.log: {npc} is thrilled. It takes the afternoon. You learn a great deal about brass.

events.text: In the alternating year, the second valley's feast falls on a day of foul weather, and {npc} blames the arrangement. A second instrument has appeared. It has seventeen dials. It is somehow worse.
events.arc: The Two Harvest Calendars

choices.text: Send a clear afternoon, free of charge

effects.log: The feast is saved. {npc} bows to the sky, stiffly, and for once says nothing.

choices.text: Let the feast be rained on, and enjoy the dancing

effects.log: They dance in mud. It is the best feast the valley remembers.

events.text: {npc} comes to the harvest feast with no instrument at all, only a loaf. {He} says the dials have stopped agreeing with each other, and with {him}. {He} asks which calendar a priest should keep when {he} no longer trusts any of them.
events.arc: The Two Harvest Calendars

choices.text: Teach {him} to watch the swallows instead

effects.log: {npc} sits on a wall for a month, watching birds. By the end {he} has a calendar of feathers and is, for once, quiet.

choices.text: Give {him} a ruling to read out in the square

effects.log: A short ruling is written in your hand and read to both valleys. {npc} folds it carefully.

events.text: Both valleys adopt the swallows' calendar, grudgingly, then proudly. The first swallow of the year is welcomed in each valley by a feast, and the two arrive on the same day. {npc} is the keeper of the first-bird bell.
events.arc: The Two Harvest Calendars

choices.text: Bless the first-bird bell

effects.log: The bell rings sweet in both valleys on the same morning every year. (+faith)

choices.text: Leave the swallows their credit

effects.log: The swallows get all the gratitude, as is right. {npc} is happy to be second.

events.text: The ruling settles the feast but not {npc}. {He} retires, sells the fourteen-dial instrument to a travelling god, and spends {his} remaining years mending clocks for neighbours. The valleys still keep the ruling.
events.arc: The Two Harvest Calendars

choices.text: Send {him} a clock of your own, silent

effects.log: A small plain clock with no dials. {npc} keeps it on the sill and says it is the only honest one.

choices.text: Visit {him} once, in a plain coat

effects.log: You drink tea over the mended clocks and say nothing of the ruling. {He} knows.

events.text: This is the year of the deer in your domain: ten thousand of them cross the high pass on the same day, and everyone who lives on the road comes out to watch. {npc}, a pass-keeper, has been counting them since dawn and has lost {his} place twice.
events.arc: The Year of the Deer

choices.text: Walk among them, unseen

effects.log: You walk through the stream of deer in a plain coat. Not one of them is afraid.

choices.text: Let a single white deer pass near {npc}

effects.log: The white deer pauses, looks at {npc}, and goes on. {He} will tell this story for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Count them with {him}

effects.log: You count alongside, and are off by nine.

events.text: A deer has fallen behind, hurt, near the pass-keeper's hut. {npc} is torn: the herd will not wait, and the pass-keeper is no healer. The deer looks at you through the keeper's window.
events.arc: The Year of the Deer

choices.text: Heal the deer quietly in the night

effects.log: By morning the deer is gone, and {npc} is certain {he} did it. The sleepless pride shows.

choices.text: Let {npc} tend it, with only a nudge of luck

effects.log: {npc} nurses the deer for a month. {He} is proud of that month forever.

events.text: The healed deer returns the next year with a fawn, and stands outside {npc}'s hut for a whole day. {npc} says the herd has chosen the hut as a halt. Pilgrims have begun to follow the herd, and to sleep in the yard.
events.arc: The Year of the Deer

choices.text: Bless the halt

effects.log: A low wall and a bell appear in the yard, and the herd treats the hut as its own. {npc} cooks for thirty.

choices.text: Keep the hut unmarked, a secret between a keeper and a herd

effects.log: The deer come, as before, in the grey of the morning. Few pilgrims find the place.

events.text: The halt has become a small shrine of the herd, and {npc} its keeper. A young herder asks to learn {his} counting. {He} teaches the youngster to lose the place twice and to start again, which is the whole art.
events.arc: The Year of the Deer

choices.text: Bless the counting

effects.log: The youngster counts the deer every year and is off by nine, and every year the herd obliges. (+faith)

choices.text: Send the white deer back, once more

effects.log: It stands at the gate at dusk and then goes. The youngster never speaks of it, and keeps the hut.

events.text: {npc} grows old among the deer, in the hut no one else knows. One grey morning the herd stands outside, still, and does not move on. {He} has gone gently in the night. The deer wait for the whole day.
events.arc: The Year of the Deer

choices.text: Lay a white deer's antler on the door

effects.log: The antler becomes a small tree, and the herd keeps the halt for a thousand years.

choices.text: Let the herd go on at dusk

effects.log: They go over the pass as the light fails. The hut keeps its door ajar.

events.text: In the bottom of the sea domain it is always the same hour, a kind of green dusk. A ferry-eel has been circling a lantern left by some long-ago sailor. The lantern still burns. It is not yours. It has never gone out.

choices.text: Ask the eel whose it is

effects.log: The eel says nothing in a very complete way. You leave the lantern as it is.

choices.text: Add a flame to it, quietly

effects.log: The lantern burns a shade brighter. The eel gives you a look of approval.

events.text: The morning drill in the war domain has slipped; officers are late, banners wrinkled, and a rumour says even Mujin has been seen yawning. A subaltern is reading out the orders of the day in a voice of terrible gloom.

choices.text: Let them have a slow morning

effects.log: They find the slow morning very much to their liking, and the day's drill is the best in a year.

choices.text: Send a brisk wind across the parade

effects.log: The banners snap straight. The subaltern is inspired, though no more cheerful.

events.text: The ferry of the dead never runs late. Today it did, by a single heartbeat, because a ferryman stopped to look at the weather. A soul on the bank waited the extra beat in perfect calm. The ferryman has been apologising ever since.

choices.text: Tell the ferryman no harm was done

effects.log: The ferryman's shoulders drop. The soul steps aboard, still calm. It was a good heartbeat.

choices.text: Ask the soul how the beat felt

effects.log: The soul says it was the longest and kindest second of its life. You write it down.

events.text: A knot has appeared in a thread of fate in the loom-rooms, a tiny snag that will, in about forty years, become a quarrel between two brothers. Nobody has found it yet. You can see it from where you stand.

choices.text: Tease the knot loose with a thumbnail

effects.log: The thread runs clean. Two brothers will be friends who might have been strangers.

choices.text: Leave it. The Weaver knows the work

effects.log: You leave the knot. The Weaver's work is the Weaver's.

events.text: The doors of the dream-paths hang open on a thousand corridors. A young dreamer has strayed into your corridor and is gazing at the walls in awe. It is a corridor lined with unfinished sentences.

choices.text: Finish a sentence for the dreamer

effects.log: The dreamer wakes holding a perfect sentence, and writes poems for a decade.

choices.text: Lead the dreamer gently back

effects.log: They wake rested, and a little wiser about walls.

events.text: A star-stag has shed an antler of pure light in the Sky domain, and it lies blazing in the heather. A shepherd has already found it and is using it to see the sheep by. They are not in the least afraid of what it is.

choices.text: Let the shepherd keep it

effects.log: The shepherd grazes the flock by starlight for a season, and writes a ballad about it.

choices.text: Gently ask for it back

effects.log: The shepherd returns it in tears. You give them a small lamp that never gutters.

events.text: One of the nine drums of the Thunder domain has a split in it. A thunderclap that should boom has come out as a cough. A cloud-herder is standing under it with an umbrella, looking up and wondering why the sky is clearing its throat.

choices.text: Mend the drum with a bolt of your own

effects.log: The next clap is magnificent. The cloud-herder cheers, soaked.

choices.text: Let the cough stand. It is rather endearing

effects.log: People in the district begin to call a small cloudburst a Cough. It is a local joy.

events.text: A seed in Saengmo's garden has refused to sprout for nine hundred years. A cluster of lesser gods has staked their pride on it. This morning it shivered. Everyone has stopped what they are doing and is staring at a pot.

choices.text: Name a day of your own

effects.log: You name a day. The seed waits for it, then sprouts, and a pile of small gods cheer your good judgement.

choices.text: Stand quietly with the others

effects.log: A tiny green tip appears. Nobody cheers. Everyone just exhales together.

events.text: The first snow of the year in the mountain domain fell, as always, on one particular rock. It is a custom nobody invented. Pilgrims gather to watch a single patch of white grow on a single stone.

choices.text: Let the snow fall on every rock but that one, just once

effects.log: The pilgrims gasp and clap. The next year it is restored, and they treasure the old way.

choices.text: Watch with the pilgrims, unseen

effects.log: You stand among them, and the snow comes down on the rock, as it always has.

events.text: A hailstorm broke every window in the market of a town you have favoured for a hundred years. A crowd stands at your shrine in the cold, hollow-eyed, not shouting. This is worse than shouting.

choices.text: Rebuild the windows in a single night

effects.log: In the morning the glass is whole, a little greener than before. The town murmurs and puts out bread.

choices.text: Stand among them, in a plain coat, and help sweep

effects.log: You sweep glass for a day beside a stranger who never learns who you are. It is a better answer than a miracle.

events.text: A whole province has prayed for rain at once, and the sound of it is like a low steady engine in your chest. You would send rain at once, but the harvest-god's pride is at stake in the next province, and rain belongs to both.

choices.text: Send rain, and be ready to explain

effects.log: The rain falls on both provinces. The harvest-god sulks, then sends an unexpected jar of honey.

choices.text: Ask the harvest-god to share the cloud

effects.log: The harvest-god, flattered, shares. Two provinces are watered by one cloud, and everyone is cross but fed.

events.text: On the hottest day of the year all the beasts of your domain nap at noon, and the whole world goes quiet, a held note. A single cicada keeps going, determined. You feel something like fellowship with it.

choices.text: Nap with them

effects.log: You nap under a shade tree that was always there, apparently. It is the best nap you have taken in a century.

choices.text: Keep the cicada company

effects.log: You sit and listen, and the cicada, delighted, plays on all afternoon.

events.text: A river in your domain has begun to flow uphill for one hour each night. Nobody has complained, since it is rather pretty, but a surveyor from the court has been sent to look at it and has brought nine assistants.

choices.text: Tell the river to cut it out

effects.log: The river resumes normal habits. The surveyor writes a long report about nothing at all.

choices.text: Let the river keep its hour

effects.log: The river flows uphill for an hour. The assistants camp on the bank to watch it. It becomes a destination.

events.text: At dawn on the summit of the Unmoving Peak, a mist forms in the shape of a bowing figure, as it does once a year, and then dissolves. No one knows who first bowed. Today it bowed slightly lower than usual.

choices.text: Bow back, unseen

effects.log: The mist lingers a heartbeat longer. You feel, for no reason, that you have been introduced.

choices.text: Ask the peak's keeper who it is

effects.log: The keeper says it is nobody; it is the mountain's habit. It is the answer a mountain would give.

events.text: A wedding on the plain has been planned for a clear day, and the storm you have in the east is nowhere near ready to break. The only thing you need to decide is whether to hold it back for a day. The couple has not prayed.

choices.text: Hold the storm back one day

effects.log: The wedding is perfect, and the couple will never know. The storm, when it breaks, is bigger.

choices.text: Let the storm come, and the wedding be wet

effects.log: The couple marries in a downpour, laughing. They will say it was luck. It was.

events.text: On the anniversary of the day your domain was cut, the old gods hold a small unceremonious meal in the empty places. Nobody makes speeches. Someone has brought a cake of rice and honey and everyone eats it standing up.

choices.text: Bring something to share

effects.log: You bring a jar of your own fruit. Three old gods hold it up to the light, and say nothing, and eat it, and nod.

choices.text: Eat the cake and say nothing

effects.log: The cake is dense and sweet. Nobody speaks. It is the closest thing to a toast the old gods allow.

events.text: The wind in your domain has turned, as it does every ninety years, and all the weathervanes in the realm are mildly wrong. A weathervane-maker is distraught. A child is delighted. Nobody remembers the last time.

choices.text: Send a small wind to the maker's door

effects.log: The maker sees the new wind in the vane, and is calmed.

choices.text: Let the confusion run its course

effects.log: A week of crooked weathervanes. Then a new generation of makers appears.

events.text: At the hearth festival, children throw handfuls of ash at each other, which is meant to bring luck. The ash gets in everything. A grandmother, scrubbing a window, mutters that the god of fire has a lot to answer for.

choices.text: Let a little ash fall on the grandmother's laundry

effects.log: The grandmother shrieks, then laughs, and throws some back at the sky. You are covered in ash, in a fond sense.

choices.text: Keep the ash out of the clean washing

effects.log: A kind hearth-wind spares the washing. The grandmother thinks it was their own foresight.

events.text: A goat has climbed a cliff in your domain that no goat has ever climbed. It stands on the top, trembling and magnificent, and a small crowd has gathered. They are cheering, which the goat does not understand.

choices.text: Hold the cliff steady

effects.log: The goat descends, flustered. The crowd names it a hero. It eats an enormous lunch.

choices.text: Do nothing, and admire the goat

effects.log: The goat gets itself down. Everyone goes home pleased, including the goat.

events.text: A map of your domain, drawn six hundred years ago, is in the market, and it is wrong in thirty small ways. The mapmaker had never seen the coast. A scholar has bought it for far more than it is worth because the errors are so charming.

choices.text: Whisper the real coastline to the scholar

effects.log: The scholar redraws the map with joy. The new one is accurate. It is not nearly so lovely.

choices.text: Leave the errors

effects.log: The map is hung in a hall, and visitors admire how a place can be invented by being badly seen.

events.text: The seating plan for the spring feast has arrived, and you are placed beside the third pillar from the door. The marshal of precedence, {npc}, has added a note saying the pillar is 'structurally significant'. Everyone knows what it means.
events.arc: The Seat Beside the Pillar

choices.text: Accept with a gracious bow

effects.log: You take the pillar seat with such grace that three gods nearby feel obscurely rude. {npc} looks suspicious.

choices.text: Ask to be moved, politely, in writing

effects.log: A short exchange of letters follows. {npc} replies in a neat hand that the plan is sacred. You frame the letter.

choices.text: Arrive early and take the best seat quietly

effects.log: You arrive an hour before the doors open and sit. Nobody has the heart to move you.

events.text: At the feast, the pillar blocks your view of the high table. Behind it, you discover the best conversations: lesser gods who dare not sit anywhere better. A god of lost keys is describing the history of locks.
events.arc: The Seat Beside the Pillar

choices.text: Befriend the pillar-row

effects.log: By the end of the evening you have a dozen allies who will never be invited to anything. They will remember.

choices.text: Eat in peace and ignore the high table

effects.log: The food is superb. The high table is dull. You have the better evening.

events.text: {npc} has been demoted by the court for an error in the placement of a duke. The marshal is humiliated, and comes to the pillar row to ask if there is any chance of a seat. The pillar-row looks at you.
events.arc: The Seat Beside the Pillar

choices.text: Offer the marshal your seat

effects.log: The pillar-row gasps, and then cheers. {npc} says nothing for a long while, then asks to be seated beside the lamp.

choices.text: Offer your friendship, not your seat

effects.log: {npc} accepts, gruffly, and sits on a stool at the back. They are inseparable for decades.

events.text: A small god, {npc}, the god of the third hour of the morning, has come to the court with a petition. Nobody has ever noticed their hour. They want a bell. Just one, in the town square, rung once a day. Their hands are shaking.
events.arc: The Petition of the Third Hour

choices.text: Support the petition in open court

effects.log: You speak for the third hour in front of everyone. A few gods laugh. Several others fall silent. The petition is passed on.

choices.text: Quietly arrange the bell yourself

effects.log: A bell appears in the square. Nobody knows who ordered it. The third hour rings for the first time in a thousand years.

choices.text: Wish the petitioner well and say no more

effects.log: {npc} thanks you, wide-eyed, and goes to try another door.

events.text: The bell rings at the third hour each day, and the town has started to wake for it. {npc} is flushed and happy and has begun to be asked to local feasts. A greater god of morning has noticed and is cool about it.
events.arc: The Petition of the Third Hour

choices.text: Soothe the greater god with a courtesy

effects.log: The greater god is mollified, and agrees to share the early light.

choices.text: Let the small god sort it out

effects.log: {npc} turns out to be good at diplomacy, being practised in being overlooked.

events.text: A century passes. {npc} has a town, a bell, and ten thousand sleepers who wake without alarm. A proud little god at a courtyard table says only: 'It was you, wasn't it?'
events.arc: The Petition of the Third Hour

choices.text: Admit it

effects.log: {npc} grips your sleeve for a moment. They do not say thank you. They just bring tea, every dawn, for a century.

choices.text: Say the bell rang itself

effects.log: {npc} smiles. 'Of course.' Both of you know better.

events.text: An envoy of the Silent Hall has come to your threshold, {npc}, in grey. They have a message. They will not give it until you offer them a chair, tea, and a promise not to ask what it says. They are very patient.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Offer all three

effects.log: The envoy sits. The message is a single line about a dream. You are asked to forget it. You do your best.

choices.text: Offer tea only, and ask what it says

effects.log: The envoy refuses to say and leaves with the tea cup. A strained silence settles over the pantheon.

choices.text: Let the envoy wait on the step

effects.log: They wait on the step for a day and a night, in a perfect stillness. The household is terrified.

events.text: The message turns out to concern a lost dream that the Hall wants returned. It was taken, long ago, by a god who has since been forgotten. The envoy asks whether you might know where such a thing could rest.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Offer your archive of forgotten dreams

effects.log: You find the dream in a jar under a pile of old prayers. The envoy takes it with a bow like a closing door.

choices.text: Admit you know nothing, honestly

effects.log: The envoy nods, as if an honest answer were the rarest item in the realm.

events.text: The envoy comes again, in grey, with a second errand: the Silent Hall wants a name for the dream you handed over. The Hall's own gods cannot agree. They ask you, a stranger to their quarrel, to choose.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Name it for something small and kind

effects.log: You name it after a cup of tea at dawn. The envoy writes it down in a stiff hand.

choices.text: Name it for the god who was forgotten

effects.log: You name it for the lost taker of the dream, a name last said four centuries ago.

events.text: The Hall adopts the small name and sends it down the corridors of every pantheon. A rumour spreads that you are the god who names dreams for tea. The envoy leaves a pot of grey leaves on your step.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Keep the leaves, and the connection

effects.log: The Silent Hall counts you a friend. A line of loyalty is entered to your pantheon's credit.

choices.text: Share the leaves with the household

effects.log: The household sleeps very well for a month.

events.text: The Hall hears the old name and falls quiet. The envoy returns, not in grey but in white, with a bow. A ledger of the remembered is opened in the corridor of the Hall, and the forgotten god's name is entered first.
events.arc: The Envoy of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Attend the entering of the name

effects.log: Few attend. You are one of them. The envoy says it is the only occasion they have seen the Hall cry. (+faith)

choices.text: Send a dream of thanks for the entering

effects.log: The Hall's gods dream of a river that ran once, and wake in good humour for a season.

events.text: Custom demands each god bring a gift to the autumn feast. {npc}, a lesser god of unripe things, has brought you a green plum the size of a pea, wrapped in gold leaf. It is the single saddest gift you have ever received. It is also extremely carefully chosen.
events.arc: The Feast Gift Nobody Wanted

choices.text: Eat it in front of the court

effects.log: You eat the plum. It is sour as a sermon. {npc} weeps with joy, and the court, perplexed, applauds.

choices.text: Plant it on the high terrace

effects.log: The stone is planted. In a hundred years it will be a tree of unripe fruit, famous for nothing. {npc} visits often.

choices.text: Place it on the altar with honour

effects.log: The plum sits on the altar like a green moon. Visitors ask about it for decades.

events.text: A greater god has noticed your plum and wants one. They send a gift, an enormous one, to {npc}, and ask for a plum in return. {npc} is terrified, and the gift is bigger than their house.
events.arc: The Feast Gift Nobody Wanted

choices.text: Help {npc} choose a worthy plum

effects.log: You pick a plum together at dawn. It is a better plum than the original and {npc} is almost sick with pride.

choices.text: Tell the greater god to ask politely

effects.log: A short note is sent. The greater god is mildly stunned. A plum is delivered with a bow.

events.text: {npc}'s plum has grown to three trees thanks to your dawn picking, and the greater god's gift still sits in {his} yard like a ship in a garden. It is too big to move and too grand to ignore. Visitors ask whether it is a temple.
events.arc: The Feast Gift Nobody Wanted

choices.text: Ask the greater god to take it back

effects.log: A note goes up, folded small. A very large pair of hands comes for the gift, and leaves a plum-press instead.

choices.text: Invite the court to the yard to feast on it

effects.log: A long table is set among the plum trees, and the great gift is used as a roof. The court comes in good humour.

events.text: The plum-press turns out to be a marvel of the greater god's own workshop. {npc} makes a plum cordial that is famous in three domains. The greater god sends a case of it to your hall every year, with a bow.
events.arc: The Feast Gift Nobody Wanted

choices.text: Serve the cordial at the next court feast

effects.log: The cordial is poured at the high table. {npc} is thanked by name.

choices.text: Keep the cordial for quiet evenings

effects.log: A glass on the terrace at dusk is the nicest thing in the realm.

events.text: At the feast under the great gift {npc} is seated beside gods who never spoke to {him}. By the end of the night {he} has a standing invitation to three pantheons' tables, and has never been so afraid in {his} life.
events.arc: The Feast Gift Nobody Wanted

choices.text: Sit beside {him} the whole night

effects.log: You hold {him} steady through three toasts. {He} is, afterward, a person of quiet importance.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it, with a wink

effects.log: {npc} comes through it with a trembling smile. {He} thanks you at dawn.

events.text: The painted corridor of the court is where gods whisper. {npc}, a minor goddess of rumour, confides a juicy item: the god of the east wind and the god of the west wind have not spoken in a thousand years over a misplaced shuttlecock.
events.arc: The Gossip of the Painted Corridor

choices.text: Offer to mediate

effects.log: You carry a shuttlecock between two sulking gods, and both of them are secretly relieved.

choices.text: Spread the gossip, gently

effects.log: The corridor learns, in a day, and the two winds each hear it, and each pretend not to.

choices.text: Keep the confidence

effects.log: You thank {npc}, and file it away. A secret is a quiet coin.

events.text: The two winds have been put on the same bench for the Spring Council. They sit with their backs very straight. The shuttlecock lies between them on the floor. Neither will pick it up.
events.arc: The Gossip of the Painted Corridor

choices.text: Kick it gently into the middle of the room

effects.log: Everyone laughs. The east wind picks it up. The west wind reaches for it at the same time. Nobody looks.

choices.text: Pick it up and hold it neutral

effects.log: You hold the shuttlecock until the meeting ends. Neither wind will take it. You keep it.

events.text: The east and west winds have invited you to tea, separately, each to explain something about the other. {npc} whispers that they want the same thing: for you to take a side, so that neither need.
events.arc: The Gossip of the Painted Corridor

choices.text: Refuse to take a side

effects.log: Both winds are put out. Both are, privately, impressed.

choices.text: Take the east wind's part, lightly

effects.log: The east wind preens. The west wind gets very quiet.

events.text: A year later the two winds arrive on your terrace together to complain, at length, about you. It is the first time they have shared a bench in a thousand years. By the end of the tea they are laughing at the same joke.
events.arc: The Gossip of the Painted Corridor

choices.text: Ask them to keep the shuttlecock between them

effects.log: The shuttlecock goes between two benches in two halls, a small token of a long peace. (+faith)

choices.text: Send them off with biscuits

effects.log: The winds blow off in good humour, rattling the shutters of the whole realm.

events.text: The west wind sulks for a century, and the court cools toward you. {npc} stops telling you secrets, and says, kindly, that it is better to be careful with a god who takes sides. It stings.
events.arc: The Gossip of the Painted Corridor

choices.text: Apologise to the west wind in person

effects.log: You cross the sky to the western bench with a plate of figs. The wind accepts the plate, if not the apology.

choices.text: Let the court think what it will

effects.log: The gossip moves on in time, as it does. {npc} resumes the secrets, in a low voice.

events.text: Each pantheon hangs a banner at the feasts. Yours has gone threadbare, and {npc}, the pantheon's seamstress, has stitched a patch in a slightly different shade. The elders of the pantheon notice it at once and say nothing, in a way that carries.
events.arc: The Pantheon Banner

choices.text: Praise the patch aloud

effects.log: You call the patch 'a pantheon of many colours.' The elders grumble, then adopt the phrase.

choices.text: Quietly replace the banner with a new one

effects.log: A banner arrives overnight, correct in every thread. {npc} is hurt, though not for long.

events.text: A rival pantheon has copied the patch on their own banner as a mark of wit. The elders are outraged. {npc} is delighted, and is now being courted for commissions.
events.arc: The Pantheon Banner

choices.text: Congratulate {npc} publicly

effects.log: The court applauds. {npc} gets three orders and a handful of apprentices.

choices.text: Remind the elders it was theirs first

effects.log: The elders recover their dignity. The patch becomes a pantheon custom.

events.text: {npc} is offered a post in the rival pantheon's loom-hall, with a house, a pension and a banner of {his} own design. {He} comes to you before answering, and stands at the door with the offer in both hands.
events.arc: The Pantheon Banner

choices.text: Tell {him} to go, with your blessing

effects.log: {npc} bows low. You give a thread of silver to carry. {He} leaves by the dawn ferry.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay and make the pantheon a new banner

effects.log: {npc} thinks it over for a night, and then asks for better thread.

events.text: The new banner is hung at the next feast. It is every colour the patch ever was. The elders are silent a long time, then rise. {npc} stands at the back with the thread still in {his} sleeve.
events.arc: The Pantheon Banner

choices.text: Call {npc} to the front

effects.log: {He} walks to the banner with the whole pantheon watching. The elders bow to the seamstress. (+loyalty)

choices.text: Let {him} stand where {he} is, unseen and proud

effects.log: The banner is admired, and {npc} hears every word of it from the back.

events.text: {npc} sends a banner every year from the rival hall, a small one, in your pantheon's old colours. The elders say it is treason. You hang it in your hall. Nobody comes to take it down, though some do glare at it.
events.arc: The Pantheon Banner

choices.text: Hang it where the elders pass

effects.log: The glares fade over the years. The banner becomes the hall's oldest custom.

choices.text: Keep it in the shrine's inner room

effects.log: It hangs by your bed, a thread of someone you did not keep.

events.text: At the Masterless table of the feast hall, you notice a god you do not know: thin, dusty, with a cup in both hands. {npc} is nobody's guest. The marshal has quietly set a place and not named them. {He} looks as if {he} will leave at once if spoken to.
events.arc: The Guest Nobody Invited

choices.text: Sit beside {him} and ask for a name

effects.log: {npc} gives a name no one has said aloud in four hundred years. You say it back. {He} straightens.

choices.text: Pass {him} the bread without a word

effects.log: A loaf changes hands. It is the only conversation, and it is enough.

events.text: {npc} is a forgotten god, a god of a river that dried before the domains were cut. {He} lingers at feasts for the warmth and the food, and says that no one has asked for {his} help in three hundred years. {He} is a very good listener.
events.arc: The Guest Nobody Invited

choices.text: Ask {him} for help with something small

effects.log: You ask {npc} to listen to a trouble of yours. {He} does, and the listening is the help. {He} leaves less thin.

choices.text: Carry {his} name to the court

effects.log: The name is read at a council. A few old gods nod. A line is added to a ledger of the remembered.

events.text: The name read in council has done an odd thing: a trickle of faith reaches {npc} from a stream nobody visits. {He} comes to your table with a cup, newly warm, and asks what a god is meant to do with a gift.
events.arc: The Guest Nobody Invited

choices.text: Teach {him} to receive prayers

effects.log: You show {npc} how to hold a prayer without dropping it. {He} cries a little, and learns fast.

choices.text: Let {him} wander and find them in {his} own way

effects.log: {npc} walks off with the cup held out in front of {him}, and is gone for a year.

events.text: {npc} takes a small shrine on the bank of the dry river. The first prayer is a child asking for a stone to skip. {He} hands over the best stone in the world. The Masterless table now has a place with a name on it.
events.arc: The Guest Nobody Invited

choices.text: Send a worshipper to the new shrine

effects.log: A traveller, lost, rests at the bank and stays. (+faith)

choices.text: Visit the shrine in a plain coat

effects.log: You leave a skipping stone on the step. {npc} knows whose it is.

events.text: {npc} returns after a year with muddy hems and a cup full of river water. The old river runs a trickle now, because {he} walked it from source to bed, speaking to every stone. {He} leaves the cup on your table and does not come again.
events.arc: The Guest Nobody Invited

choices.text: Pour the water into your own garden

effects.log: A thin stream starts at the cup and runs for a hundred years.

choices.text: Keep the cup, and say the name once a year

effects.log: The name is said at each autumn feast, quietly, by you.

events.text: The feast cup, honey-water by custom, is passed around the table and everyone is expected to take exactly one sip and say a toast. The god before you gives a long boring one. The cup is now cold. You have the cup, the toast, and the audience.

choices.text: Make the shortest toast of the evening

effects.log: You say, 'To the next cup.' The table roars. The cup goes round again, warm.

choices.text: Make a toast to the cook

effects.log: The kitchen hears, and sends out a round of sweet rolls.

events.text: A herald reads out the day's decrees to a gathering of drowsy gods and, on the ninth, reads a name in the wrong order. A minor god of rice is now outranked by a minor god of rain. The two of them stand frozen, each thinking it is a plot.

choices.text: Correct the herald, mildly

effects.log: The herald apologises. The two gods exhale. Peace holds for a week.

choices.text: Leave it. A small confusion keeps the court honest

effects.log: The court argues for an hour. Nothing is decided, and everyone feels they have contributed.

events.text: A confectioner-god has made a sugar dragon the size of a pavilion for the harvest feast. It is, regrettably, melting. A queue of lesser gods has formed to lick it before it goes.

choices.text: Join the queue in a plain coat

effects.log: You lick the dragon's tail with a hundred small gods, and it is divine.

choices.text: Chill it with a kind breath

effects.log: The dragon holds for another hour. The confectioner weeps in gratitude.

events.text: At the opening of court, the incense-bearer has set the censer a hand's breadth too far to the left. A senior god notices. The entire court notices them noticing. The incense-bearer is gripping the censer as if it were the last rope on a cliff.

choices.text: Shift the censer yourself, casually
