effects.log: You move it with a foot, a small unforced courtesy. The bearer breathes. The court stays silent a second longer.

choices.text: Compliment the censer's fragrance

effects.log: The senior god, distracted, begins to talk about incense. The error is forgotten.

events.text: The Council votes on whether the third night of the spring festival should be called the Night of Lanterns or the Night of Many Lights. The two sides have clashed for seven hundred years. This year you hold the deciding voice.

choices.text: Vote Lanterns

effects.log: The Lanterns side cheers. The Lights side files an eloquent complaint. It will be voted on again in a century.

choices.text: Vote Many Lights

effects.log: The Many Lights side cheers. The Lanterns side sulks beautifully.

choices.text: Propose a third name, absurd and long

effects.log: The Council, appalled, retires to consider. The question is deferred, and everyone is a little relieved.

events.text: A visiting god from the mountains insists on pouring tea with the left hand, which in your court is an insult. The hosts are rigid. The guest is cheerful. A steward silently weeps behind a screen.

choices.text: Pour with the left hand yourself, smiling

effects.log: The room relaxes, a heartbeat at a time. The guest is touched.

choices.text: Explain the custom gently to the guest

effects.log: The guest, mortified, switches hands. The hosts, mortified in turn, apologise to each other.

events.text: The last dish of the feast, a famous soup, arrives cold because the cook-god was arguing with the fire-god. The table is ravenous and silent. Everyone is looking at you because you sit nearest the fire.

choices.text: Warm the soup with a breath

effects.log: The soup steams. The cook-god and the fire-god glare at each other over your shoulder.

choices.text: Declare cold soup the fashion of the season

effects.log: The table solemnly slurps. By morning it is a trend.

events.text: An elder of your pantheon visits your hall unannounced, and walks through every room, touching the furniture. They say nothing. They do not sit. They leave a plain stone on your table.

choices.text: Keep the stone on the table

effects.log: The stone sits there for a century. Visitors speak in whispers around it.

choices.text: Ask a servant what it means

effects.log: The servant says only that it means the elder has been. It is, apparently, enough.

events.text: As a Masterless God you are seated at the far end of the hall, beside the door and the draught. Several gods look at you as one looks at a stray cat who has learned to bow. You have the sharp pleasure of being underestimated.

choices.text: Bow back, smiling

effects.log: Your bow is flawless, and slightly ironic. A few gods find themselves bowing deeper.

choices.text: Eat well and listen

effects.log: The far end of the hall hears everything. By the time pudding arrives you know three secrets.

events.text: Someone at the Masterless table has proposed a toast to the gods with no home, and the whole table has joined in with loud, slightly tearful vigour. It is the loudest toast of the feast. The high table pretends it has heard nothing.

choices.text: Add a line to the toast

effects.log: You raise your cup: 'To the ones with no lord but their own work.' The roar is tremendous.

choices.text: Drink quietly and smile

effects.log: You drink. The warmth of the toast stays in your chest for days.

events.text: At the gate of the heavenly archive, a clerk tells you that gods outside any pantheon pay a small fee of respect: a deep bow, a written apology for the inconvenience, a name on a wait-list. The wait-list has your name on it already, twice.

choices.text: Bow deeply and sign the list

effects.log: The clerk is nonplussed by your courtesy. You are admitted in under an hour, which is a record.

choices.text: Decline to bow, and wait in the shade

effects.log: You wait with a book. The clerk, embarrassed, lets you in before the shadow moves.

events.text: The court has decreed that all feasts shall end with a cake of five layers. The kitchens have, as one, rebelled. A delegation of cooks waits at your door with a four-layer cake, hoping you will be on their side.

choices.text: Eat the cake, and rule four layers sufficient

effects.log: The cooks cheer. The court is scandalised. The cake is excellent.

choices.text: Counsel patience and make the fifth layer yourself

effects.log: You contribute a layer of honey and moonlight. The court is satisfied. The cooks are overjoyed.

events.text: A string of bells from the lower table has started playing the same tune as the hall musicians, only slightly sharper, and with enthusiasm. The hall musicians look pained. The bells keep going.

choices.text: Join the bells with a drum on the table

effects.log: The room joins in, and the hall musicians, defeated, begin to laugh.

choices.text: Ask the bells to wait for the next song

effects.log: The bells fall silent, abashed, and wait, and the next song is theirs.

events.text: A great god's ceremonial hat has gone missing before the audience. The hat is tall and pointed and the god is tall and pointed. The entire court is searching under cushions. You see the hat on a lesser god's head. They have no idea.

choices.text: Return the hat unseen to its stand

effects.log: The hat is back before anyone notices. The lesser god feels oddly lighter.

choices.text: Tell the great god the hat is on a fellow guest

effects.log: The great god's face does something wonderful. The lesser god gets a hat of their own as an apology.

events.text: The council appoints each year a god to keep the night-watch over the court, a job of no consequence and long hours. This year the lot has fallen on you. The lot, you suspect, was not entirely random.

choices.text: Take the watch with a good grace

effects.log: You keep the watch, and discover the court at night: its sleepers, its mice, its quiet corners. A quiet year.

choices.text: Send a servant of mist in your place

effects.log: A mist walks the corridors in your name. Nobody notices, and nothing happens.

events.text: A god from a realm beyond the known domains arrives at court, speaks no language anyone has heard, and bows to the wrong end of the room. The court is polite to the point of agony. A clerk, sweating, asks you to take the guest in hand.

choices.text: Take the guest on a quiet walk through the garden

effects.log: You communicate in pointing and tea. By evening the guest knows the word for 'thank you' in five tongues.

choices.text: Hand the guest to the clerks with a kind note

effects.log: The guest is looked after. You send a basket of fruit with a drawing of a smiling sun.

events.text: {npc}, a god of a small hill spring, comes to your door in the evening and asks you to say {his} name. You say it. {He} nods and says again, 'Once more.' {He} has begun to forget it, and says that the fastest way to be gone is to be the only one who remembers.
events.arc: The God Whose Name Is Slipping

choices.text: Write the name on your door-post

effects.log: The name is carved into the wood. {npc} traces it with a finger every morning for a century.

choices.text: Ask a hundred worshippers to say it once

effects.log: Your congregation sings the spring-god's name at dusk. It carries, and {npc} listens at your window.

choices.text: Say it each morning yourself

effects.log: You say the name at dawn, over tea, for years. It is a small daily courtesy to the dying.

events.text: The spring has dried to a damp patch, and {npc} is faint at the edges. A pilgrim passing through has been told the story, and wants to leave an offering. They ask what a forgotten spring-god might want.
events.arc: The God Whose Name Is Slipping

choices.text: Ask the pilgrim to pour a cup of water on the stone

effects.log: The cup is poured. For a moment there is a small clear sound, as of a spring remembering itself.

choices.text: Say the god wants only to be talked to

effects.log: The pilgrim sits on the stone and talks about the road for an hour. {npc} listens, nearly whole.

events.text: A small child hears the name sung in the evening and begins using it for the family dog. The name travels the valley, half-meaning, half-joke. {npc} hears it bark in the street and weeps for joy.
events.arc: The God Whose Name Is Slipping

choices.text: Let the dog carry the name

effects.log: The dog is the most blessed beast in the district. {npc} is not forgotten for a hundred years.

choices.text: Thank the boy in a dream

effects.log: The boy wakes puzzled and keeps the dog, and the name.

events.text: A hundred years later, a spring wells up at the foot of the hill. It is small, and clean, and has a name. You do not know who gave it. {npc} sits by it, whole again, and says, 'Say it once more.'
events.arc: The God Whose Name Is Slipping

choices.text: Say it, and add your own

effects.log: You say the name of a spring and a friend, together. {npc} laughs until the water ripples.

choices.text: Say it and leave them to the water

effects.log: You say it softly, and go. The spring says it back.

events.text: At a crossroads lies the burned frame of a shrine to a god nobody remembers. {npc} sweeps the ash into neat piles every month and has been told repeatedly to stop. {He} says it is only tidy, and then asks you, plainly, whose shrine it was.
events.arc: The Burned Shrine at the Crossroads

choices.text: Say you do not know, and ask the old gods

effects.log: You ask. The old gods look away. One says only: 'We do not say that name.'

choices.text: Say it was a friend's

effects.log: The lie is gentle. {npc} nods, and begins placing flowers, and the ash is at peace.

choices.text: Help sweep, unseen

effects.log: You sweep ash beside {npc} all afternoon. Neither of you speaks.

events.text: The old gods have a reason for silence: the burned god was a rebel, and the fire was the Council's. {npc} learns this from a gossiping pilgrim, and now stands at the crossroads with a hard face.
events.arc: The Burned Shrine at the Crossroads

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth, whole

effects.log: {npc} listens, grey-faced. Then {he} lights a stick of incense at the ash and says the god's true name aloud.

choices.text: Tell {him} the Council acted in fear

effects.log: A partial truth. {npc} nods slowly, unsatisfied but unbroken.

events.text: Pilgrims have started to come to the burned shrine to leave small things. The Council has noticed. A herald arrives at your door with a polite request that something be done about the crossroads.
events.arc: The Burned Shrine at the Crossroads

choices.text: Defend the shrine in open court

effects.log: You speak for the burned god. The court is cold. A handful of gods stay behind to talk with you afterward.

choices.text: Ask the herald for a decade of grace

effects.log: The herald, who is not unkind, grants it. The shrine stands another ten years.

events.text: The court's accountant, {npc}, has come to audit your faith. {He} carries a ledger and a small brass scale. Your count is high in places and strange in others: a great deal from a nursery rhyme, a little from your largest temple.
events.arc: The Faith You Cannot Count

choices.text: Let {him} count it all

effects.log: The audit takes a week. {npc} is astonished that your rhyme is the strongest source. {He} stays on as a friend.

choices.text: Ask what the count is for

effects.log: {npc} admits the count is only a custom, and the court's real use of it is to feel superior. It is a comfort.

choices.text: Offer {him} tea and let the books wait

effects.log: The audit is never finished, but you have an ally in accounts.

events.text: {npc} has found something odd: a thread of faith that comes from no worshipper, but from a stray dog that sleeps at your most distant shrine. It is steady, and has been for a century. The ledger has no column for it.
events.arc: The Faith You Cannot Count

choices.text: Enter it as a dog

effects.log: It goes in the ledger as 'the dog.' The court, which dislikes oddities, hums.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to leave it out of the court's books

effects.log: {npc} agrees. Some faith is not for counting.

events.text: The court has put the dog in its ledger, and now wants it inspected. A clerk is sent to the distant shrine, and {npc} goes along, with a bone, as a friend of the accounts. The dog has never been looked at by so many people at once.
events.arc: The Faith You Cannot Count

choices.text: Send the dog a dream first, to prepare it

effects.log: The dog dreams of a long stair and a gentleman in a hat, and wakes composed.

choices.text: Let the inspection happen as it will

effects.log: The clerk arrives in the rain. The dog barks once, politely.

events.text: The dog leads the clerk behind the shrine to a hidden spring that has fed the place for a thousand years. The ledger gains a column, headed Water, and {npc} is asked to keep it. The court, astonished, sends an honorary bone.
events.arc: The Faith You Cannot Count

choices.text: Accept the column for the shrine

effects.log: The spring is entered in the court's books, and pilgrims arrive to drink. (+faith)

choices.text: Credit the dog in the margin

effects.log: A paw print is stamped in the ledger. {npc} is delighted beyond words.

events.text: The clerk pats the dog, writes 'adequate' in the margin, and leaves. The dog is declared a minor shrine-beast, which carries a stipend of one bone per month. {npc} is made the keeper of the stipend and takes the office to heart.
events.arc: The Faith You Cannot Count

choices.text: Send the monthly bone yourself

effects.log: A bone arrives on the shrine step each month for the rest of the dog's life, and some years after.

choices.text: Let the court's stipend run on its own

effects.log: The bone is irregular, the dog patient. {npc} makes up the shortfall quietly.

events.text: Under your largest altar lives a god of dust, small and soft and grey, who has been there since the altar was built. {npc} sits in the corner of a crack and says only that it is warm and nobody dusts there. {He} asks if {he} may stay.
events.arc: The God of Dust Under the Altar

choices.text: Say yes, and no sweeping there

effects.log: The crack becomes {his}. Dust gathers in a neat soft heap. {npc} is much happier.

choices.text: Say yes, and ask what {he} does

effects.log: {He} says: 'Remembers who passed.' {He} lists the last four hundred visitors, with details.

events.text: A new keeper, a tidy one, has arrived and wants every crack under the altar scoured. {npc} is distraught. The dust-god will lose the only home {he} knows, and four centuries of visitors will go with it.
events.arc: The God of Dust Under the Altar

choices.text: Whisper to the keeper to leave the crack

effects.log: The keeper leaves it, unaccountably, though puzzled. {npc} gives you a record of the last visitors as thanks.

choices.text: Help {npc} move to a new corner

effects.log: Together you carry the dust-god to a small niche in the ceiling. {He} settles in and finds the view of the hall splendid.

events.text: In the ceiling niche {npc} has begun a new ledger, of those who look up. It is a short list. {He} asks, with grey shyness, whether you would care to be on it.
events.arc: The God of Dust Under the Altar

choices.text: Look up at the ceiling, and be written

effects.log: You stand a long moment under the beam. {npc} writes your name in dust on a rafter.

choices.text: Ask {him} to write the tidy keeper too

effects.log: The tidy keeper, who never looks up, is added with a small footnote. {npc} says it is only fair.

events.text: Your name in dust is the first of a long line. Pilgrims, hearing of it, tilt their heads back in your hall and are written down one by one. The dust-god becomes the shrine's quietest oracle, and the hall is finally dusty again.
events.arc: The God of Dust Under the Altar

choices.text: Bless the rafter with a little light

effects.log: The dust of the rafter glows faintly, and pilgrims call the shrine's ceiling the Quiet Sky. (+faith)

choices.text: Leave the dust as it falls

effects.log: The niche fills with soft grey names. {npc} dusts none of them.

events.text: The tidy keeper hears of the footnote, climbs a stepladder with a cloth, and stops. For the first time in forty years the keeper stands very still. After that the cloth stays in the cupboard, and a saucer of water is left in the niche.
events.arc: The God of Dust Under the Altar

choices.text: Bless the keeper's change of heart

effects.log: The shrine is cared for and not scoured. {npc} keeps a record of the keeper, too. (+faith)

choices.text: Say nothing of it to anyone

effects.log: A dust-god and a keeper are friends in silence. It is the best secret of the shrine.

events.text: A prayer has reached you three centuries late. It was lost in a drift of old smoke and has only now arrived. {npc}, long dead, asked for {his} son to be brought home safely from a sea voyage. You do not know how it ended.
events.arc: The Unspent Prayer

choices.text: Search the old logs for the voyage

effects.log: You find the ship in a dusty record. The ship was lost with all hands. You close the book slowly.

choices.text: Ask the Sea-god if the son lived

effects.log: Haeryong's keeper checks the sea-registers. The answer comes by afternoon.

choices.text: Hold the prayer a while before deciding

effects.log: You hold the prayer. It is light and warm, like a letter that has been read many times.

events.text: The son lived. The ship was wrecked on a distant coast; the son came home forty years later with a new name and a child. The son is gone now, but that child is alive and keeps a shrine to a god they cannot name.
events.arc: The Unspent Prayer

choices.text: Answer the old prayer in a dream to the grandchild

effects.log: The grandchild dreams of a woman on a quay waving a cloth, and weeps in the morning, and tells the story to the children.

choices.text: Let the prayer rest, answered in the telling

effects.log: You let the unspent prayer go. It rises like smoke.

events.text: The grandchild's shrine has become known. The god they cannot name is you, it seems, or something like you. They ask, to the empty room, whether anyone listens. You are in the room.
events.arc: The Unspent Prayer

choices.text: Speak, once, in a plain voice

effects.log: They hear, and nod, and never tell another soul.

choices.text: Let a small breeze turn the pages of their book

effects.log: A page turns. They laugh, and keep reading.

events.text: The ford at the edge of your domain has dried up. Its small toll-god, {npc}, sits on a rock and demands payment from passers-by anyway, grimly, for a crossing they no longer need. {He} has not noticed that the river is gone.
events.arc: The Toll-God of the Dry Ford

choices.text: Pay the toll and tell {him} what has happened

effects.log: You hand over three small coins of faith. {npc} stares at the dry bed for a long time and then at you.

choices.text: Pay, and say nothing

effects.log: You pay. {npc} is grateful and grumpy. The river is still dry.

events.text: {npc} has come to your door with a dry bucket and a challenge: bring back the river, or {he} will turn all {his} tolls on you. It is not clear how a toll-god could do so. It sounds terrible.
events.arc: The Toll-God of the Dry Ford

choices.text: Send a spring to the ford

effects.log: A spring bubbles up through the sand, and the ford is a ford. {npc} is utterly silent, then weeps into the water.

choices.text: Offer the toll-god a post at your bridge

effects.log: {npc} accepts, with suspicion. {He} is the best bridge-keeper in the realm.

events.text: The ford runs again, and {npc} has put up a sign with the toll doubled. Travellers pay it, grumbling. Your faith from the ford has gone up, and so have the complaints. A donkey has refused to cross on principle.
events.arc: The Toll-God of the Dry Ford

choices.text: Ask {him} to lower the toll

effects.log: {npc} glares, thinks, and halves it. The donkey crosses at once.

choices.text: Let the toll stand, and pay for the ford's upkeep

effects.log: The toll buys stone for a proper crossing. {npc} counts each coin into the bank like a prayer.

events.text: Word spreads: the fairest crossing in the realm, with a toll-god who weighs each coin and gives change in kindness. River-gods upstream send gifts and ask to be consulted on fords. {npc} becomes a minor court of crossings.
events.arc: The Toll-God of the Dry Ford

choices.text: Accept the river-gods' gifts for the ford

effects.log: A small procession of river-gods leaves wreaths on the rock. (+faith)

choices.text: Let {him} receive them alone

effects.log: {npc} accepts with great gravity, and has never been so fine.

events.text: The tolls build a stone ford, then a bridge. {npc} is moved from the rock to a booth, and from the booth to a seat in the bridge-gods' council. {He} sends a note: 'I no longer need to remind anyone that the river was here.'
events.arc: The Toll-God of the Dry Ford

choices.text: Attend the opening of the bridge

effects.log: The bridge opens with a long speech and a short rain. {npc} cuts the ribbon with great care.

choices.text: Send a spring flower to the first stone

effects.log: A small flower grows between the slabs, and travellers step around it.

events.text: Your very first shrine, the one from the first century of your divinity, has become a place where people take family portraits. Nobody prays. It is just a nice backdrop. A photographer is arranging a family around the altar.

choices.text: Smile for the portrait, invisibly

effects.log: The portrait comes out a trifle luminous. The family prizes it for generations.

choices.text: Let them go, and be glad of it

effects.log: A shrine is a place people come to be together. That counts.

events.text: A very new god, barely a decade old, comes to your door for advice. They are a god of a certain street corner, and they do not know what to do with all the attention. A bakery has opened and the bakers worship them already.

choices.text: Teach them to say thank you without promising anything

effects.log: The young god nods fiercely and writes it on their sleeve. Much of the rest comes later.

choices.text: Tell them to enjoy the bread

effects.log: They go away with a box of warm buns. It is probably the best advice.

events.text: A friend of yours among the lesser gods has faded in the night. Their shrine has closed, their prayers have thinned to nothing, and their chair at the feast is empty. A servant asks whether to set the place.

choices.text: Set it, once, with their favourite dish

effects.log: The dish is set. The empty chair, for a moment, is a little warm.

choices.text: Pour a libation at their old shrine

effects.log: You pour clear water on the stone. A cricket, startled, begins to sing.

events.text: A choir of children sings a hymn to you in a language that changed three times since it was written. They do not know what the words mean, but they sing them with great feeling. The meaning, you realise, has drifted somewhere quite beautiful.

choices.text: Leave the drift as it is

effects.log: The hymn survives a thousand years more, meaning something new each generation.

choices.text: Send a dream of the original words to the choirmaster

effects.log: The choirmaster restores a line, and the choir resents it and sings it better.

events.text: A farmer has left half the harvest at your gate, then regrets it, then comes back to take some. You watch the argument with themselves from the roof. The faith they have given is the real kind: a little fearful, a little proud.

choices.text: Return the half they need, in a dream

effects.log: They wake thinking they have made a sound decision. The family eats well.

choices.text: Accept what remains and bless the field

effects.log: The field is blessed. The farmer sighs with relief, and the faith is pure.

events.text: In the lowest cellar of the archive stands a wall of stone names, one for each god that was forgotten. A clerk dusts it once a year. Your own name is not on it, of course. But there is a blank space beside the last.

choices.text: Look away from the blank space

effects.log: You look away, and the blank space looks at you. It is not unkind.

choices.text: Touch the last name, gently

effects.log: The stone is warm. The name belongs to someone who was loved.

events.text: A young scholar has come to your temple to test whether faith is real. Armed with scales and a lamp, they stand at your altar and ask you to prove yourself with a measure. They are sweet about it.

choices.text: Move the scale, a hair

effects.log: The scale trembles. The scholar writes the number down, delighted and scared.

choices.text: Leave the scale perfectly still

effects.log: A perfect zero. The scholar publishes a thoughtful paper on the matter.

events.text: A parent at the market tells a child a story about you, and gets half of it wrong, and the child corrects the teller with delight. The pair argue about the end of the story. It is nothing like what happened, and it is better.

choices.text: Leave it as they tell it

effects.log: The story, as they tell it, will be the version told in the valley after you are gone.

choices.text: Nudge the child's version a little closer to true

effects.log: The child's ending gets a little more accurate and a lot less fun.

events.text: In a pile of undelivered offerings in the heavenly post-house you find a small parcel addressed to a god who no longer exists. The sender has attached a note: 'Sorry it is late.' It has been waiting two hundred years.

choices.text: Open it and read the note aloud to the empty air

effects.log: The note says thank you. You read it three times. The air takes it in.

choices.text: Keep it with your own correspondence

effects.log: You keep it in a drawer. It is the best-kept parcel in the realm.

events.text: The prayer clerks of the heavenly post-house have a rule: any prayer not answered within a century is declared 'settled by the passage of time.' You have sixty-three in that pile this month. A clerk looks at you hopefully.

choices.text: Answer ten of them, quickly

effects.log: Ten small things happen in ten small lives. The clerk stamps the paperwork with a contented sigh.

choices.text: Let the passage of time do its work

effects.log: Time settles them. The clerk admires your calm.

events.text: In the ruin of a temple to a god long vanished, a family of mice keeps a household shrine, a bit of rind on a stone. They say a prayer every night in a language of squeaks. You are not the god they mean. You listen anyway.

choices.text: Answer the mice with a crumb of cheese

effects.log: The mice take it as a sign. The rind-shrine is enlarged by one.

choices.text: Listen, and say nothing

effects.log: The mice's prayer is brief and entirely sincere. You feel absurdly honoured.

events.text: A potter has begun to leave a bowl at your shrine every year. Each bowl is a little better than the last. After thirty years the bowls are exquisite. They are never thanked. The potter has never asked for anything. The bowls are piled in the vault.

choices.text: Make a dream of a perfect glaze for the potter

effects.log: The potter wakes and fires a bowl that shines like a lake. They weep and set it on the altar.

choices.text: Go and drink tea from one of the bowls

effects.log: You drink tea out of the potter's third bowl, in the vault, with some reverence.

events.text: The hearth of a forgotten kitchen-god has gone cold, and a servant of yours is shivering in the draught of it. The hearth has not been lit in a thousand years, and the servant has just been told that, if they light it, the god might return.

choices.text: Tell the servant to light it

effects.log: The servant lights the hearth. It catches after nine tries. A small domestic spirit sighs in the chimney.

choices.text: Light it yourself, with a spark from the First Hearth

effects.log: The hearth glows. The kitchen-god, thin but present, is back to stirring.

events.text: You walk your own domain in a plain coat, as you do on quiet days, and stop at a stall where {npc} sells fried cakes. A customer is complaining that the god of this district is useless. {npc} nods along, then slips you an extra cake.
events.arc: The Stall of the Plain Coat

choices.text: Join the complaint, in a mild way

effects.log: You grumble about the god alongside the crowd. It is the most honest conversation about yourself you have had.

choices.text: Defend the god gently

effects.log: You say the god is doing {his} best. {npc} squints at you, then laughs. 'You sound like the shrine-keeper.'

choices.text: Eat the cake and listen

effects.log: The cake is excellent. The crowd's complaints are specific and, annoyingly, fair.

events.text: {npc} has taken to saving you a cake each morning, 'for the quiet one in the coat.' You are, as far as {he} knows, a pilgrim. {He} confides that the stall is failing: the new market hall charges rent {he} cannot meet.
events.arc: The Stall of the Plain Coat

choices.text: Quietly pay the rent in a dream to the hall-keeper

effects.log: The hall-keeper wakes feeling very generous. The stall's rent is remitted by an obscure custom.

choices.text: Send a flock of customers

effects.log: A flock of pilgrims arrives, hungry and in a mood. The stall is saved by volume.

choices.text: Tell {him} to ask the god for help

effects.log: {npc} says the god is busy. You do not argue.

events.text: A pilgrim from the court recognises you at the stall, and drops a tray. The whole street goes quiet. {npc} stares at the plain coat, at the cake in your hand, at the pilgrim bowing so low {he} nearly tips over.
events.arc: The Stall of the Plain Coat

choices.text: Keep your coat and buy another cake

effects.log: 'The usual,' you say. {npc} nods, trembling, and hands it over. The street breathes out.

choices.text: Drop the coat and apologise

effects.log: You name yourself, and apologise for the deception. {npc} is silent, then scolds you for not saying so earlier. It is the best scolding you have had.

events.text: The market of the gods is held on a plateau above the clouds each new moon. {npc}, a god of accounts, sits at a desk at the gate and logs every transaction in a vast book. Nobody has asked {him} to. {He} is, as far as anyone can tell, doing it for the beauty of the sums.
events.arc: The God Who Keeps Accounts at the Star Market

choices.text: Ask {him} for the market's total this month

effects.log: The number is enormous and absurdly precise. {npc} glows.

choices.text: Offer {him} a desk in your hall

effects.log: {npc} considers this for an hour and declines, politely, preferring the gate.

choices.text: Buy something small and let {him} record it

effects.log: A button is entered in the book, in a hand of perfect beauty.

events.text: One day {npc} announces a discrepancy of one copper in the market's accounts. It has taken eleven years to find, and {he} cannot rest until it is accounted for. The whole market has been drawn into the search.
events.arc: The God Who Keeps Accounts at the Star Market

choices.text: Help search in earnest

effects.log: You find the copper in a gutter, shining. {npc} weeps at the sight.

choices.text: Quietly drop a copper into the till

effects.log: The books balance. {npc} is both relieved and deeply suspicious.

events.text: The copper is framed on {npc}'s desk. A travelling god of audits offers {him} a seat in the great Ledger-House of the court, where sums are done by the thousand and nobody weeps at a decimal. {He} brings the letter to you, unopened.
events.arc: The God Who Keeps Accounts at the Star Market

choices.text: Encourage {him} to go

effects.log: {npc} reads the letter, and then reads it again. {He} says that no one has ever wanted the sums as much as the sums wanted {him}.

choices.text: Tell {him} the gate needs {him} more

effects.log: {npc} looks at the gate, and at the copper, and at you. {He} sets the letter in the drawer and stays.

events.text: The desk at the gate stands empty for a month, then is taken by a younger god of sums, who is less beautiful and more fair. The market accounts are looser, and everyone feels it. A letter arrives yearly from the Ledger-House, in perfect figures.
events.arc: The God Who Keeps Accounts at the Star Market

choices.text: Answer each letter with a figure of your own

effects.log: You send a number. It is the best letter {npc} receives all year. {He} sends back a thank-you.

choices.text: Keep the letters in a box

effects.log: A box of numbers, in a hand you came to know.

events.text: The market thrives under {npc}'s eye. Stallholders give honest weight, and the god of accounts is thanked in a small bell rung at the end of each market day. Your share of the faith is a sum {he} calculates to the last grain.
events.arc: The God Who Keeps Accounts at the Star Market

choices.text: Let {him} send you the sum

effects.log: The sum is large and absurdly precise. (+faith)

choices.text: Ask {him} to keep it, as thanks

effects.log: {npc} keeps it in the ledger as 'a friend's, held in trust.'

events.text: At the seasonal games, a plump god of puddings has challenged you to a wrestling match. {npc} says it is a courtesy; you suspect {he} has been training for a hundred years. The crowd has gathered. It is hard to decline a challenge in front of fifty cheerful gods.
events.arc: The Wrestling Match on the Green Plateau

choices.text: Accept, and wrestle seriously

effects.log: You grapple for a long and farcical time. {npc} is stronger than expected, and you both end on your backs laughing.

choices.text: Accept, and lose on purpose with flourish

effects.log: You fall in a great theatrical arc. The crowd roars. {npc} is slightly suspicious and mostly delighted.

choices.text: Decline, bowing deeply

effects.log: The crowd groans. {npc} bows back, gravely. A challenge declined with grace is not a loss.

events.text: {npc} has a request: a rematch, for no prize, in a hundred years. {He} wants to finish what you started. It is the most flattering thing anyone has said to you this century.
events.arc: The Wrestling Match on the Green Plateau

choices.text: Agree. Mark the date

effects.log: A date is fixed, a century away. The crowd cheers. You enter it in your book, with some flourish.

choices.text: Agree, but suggest tea instead

effects.log: The two of you drink tea, and talk wrestling for hours.

events.text: Fifty years on, {npc} sends a note: {he} has pulled a muscle in the shoulder and fears the match. {He} suggests a postponement. The crowd has already bought seats, and the seat-sellers are weeping on the plateau.
events.arc: The Wrestling Match on the Green Plateau

choices.text: Postpone, and send liniment

effects.log: A jar of liniment goes to {npc} with a bow. The seat-sellers are paid in sweet buns.

choices.text: Wrestle on, gently, as a show

effects.log: You send word that the match will be a dance. {npc} writes back at once: 'A dance, then.'

events.text: The match is postponed so long it becomes a tradition. Every fifty years you and {npc} meet over tea, discuss the match with great seriousness, and postpone it again. The crowd keeps its seats in a small box, in case.
events.arc: The Wrestling Match on the Green Plateau

choices.text: Make the postponement official

effects.log: A tablet is carved at the plateau: 'To be wrestled, in due course.' The games gain a new custom. (+faith)

choices.text: Let it stay unofficial

effects.log: The tea is better for having no rules.

events.text: The show-match is a spectacle: two gods in slow-motion circles, bowing and sliding while the crowd roars. {npc} loses on purpose and so do you, and the referee is forced to declare a tie in forty languages.
events.arc: The Wrestling Match on the Green Plateau

choices.text: Take the crowd's roar as your due

effects.log: The crowd rises. Pilgrims for three domains remember the night. (+faith)

choices.text: Share it with {npc} on the dais

effects.log: The two of you hold up each other's arms. The crowd roars louder.

events.text: The wind gods hold a kite contest each year, and you have been invited. {npc}, a god of a small mountain gust, has built a kite that looks like a small disapproving bird. The kite is magnificent. It has never flown.
events.arc: The Kite Contest of the Wind Gods

choices.text: Help {him} launch it, in secret

effects.log: You lend a breath at the right moment. The kite climbs into the sky and sits there, glaring at everyone.

choices.text: Let the kite fly on {his} own wind alone

effects.log: {npc} stands for an hour, coaxing the gust. The kite, at last, lifts. The crowd weeps at the dedication.

choices.text: Admire the kite and offer a snack

effects.log: The kite is admired. A snack is eaten. The contest begins without them.

events.text: In the contest, a rival's kite tangles with {npc}'s. Both fall. The rival is furious, and {npc} apologises to a kite. Judges confer for an hour, then give a joint prize to a squirrel who happens to be on the field.
events.arc: The Kite Contest of the Wind Gods

choices.text: Protest the squirrel's prize, in a kind way

effects.log: The judges, flustered, give the squirrel a medal and {npc} a lesser one.

choices.text: Pat the squirrel and move on

effects.log: The squirrel is most pleased.

events.text: The squirrel has adopted {npc}'s kite as a nest. {npc} wants to fly it anyway. The squirrel objects with its whole tail, and the two glare at each other in the grass while the contest judges wait.
events.arc: The Kite Contest of the Wind Gods

choices.text: Make the squirrel a smaller kite of its own

effects.log: A tiny kite appears beside the big one. The squirrel inspects it, and takes it for a hat.

choices.text: Convince {npc} to let the nest alone

effects.log: {npc} sighs, and sets the kite on its stand. The squirrel climbs in and goes to sleep.

events.text: Next year the contest has a new class: small kites. {npc} wins it with a tiny disapproving bird, and the squirrel wins best companion. The judges, relieved, hand out ribbons like confetti.
events.arc: The Kite Contest of the Wind Gods

choices.text: Hang a ribbon on your own door

effects.log: A blue ribbon on your lintel for a decade. Visitors ask. You say 'a friend's.'

choices.text: Applaud from the stands, loudly

effects.log: You are heard in three domains. {npc} waves back.

events.text: The big kite becomes a shrine of a sort: a nest on a stand, a squirrel on the nest, a god of small gusts who comes to feed it. Wind-gods leave scraps of ribbon on the stand. It is the smallest shrine in the realm, and one of the warmest.
events.arc: The Kite Contest of the Wind Gods

choices.text: Bless the stand against the weather

effects.log: The stand does not rot in a hundred years. (+faith)

choices.text: Let it age as it will

effects.log: It leans, and the squirrel's descendants have it still.

events.text: A group of Masterless gods holds a small feast each equinox in an unused corner of the realm, with no pantheon's blessing and no marshal. {npc}, a god of lost keys, invites you with the flat sincerity of one who has been left out of many invitations.
events.arc: The Table With No Lord

choices.text: Go, and bring something good

effects.log: You bring a basket of fruit. The feast is a small, loud, humble affair, and the best in years.

choices.text: Go, and bring a proposal

effects.log: You propose a yearly assembly of the Masterless. The table hums. {npc} writes it on a napkin.

choices.text: Send regrets and a gift

effects.log: You send a gift. {npc} understands, but the feast feels a size smaller.

events.text: The assembly meets. Forty Masterless gods sit in a circle on the grass. A herald of the Will of Heaven drops by to observe, and writes in a notebook. The circle falls silent, wary, and then {npc} offers the herald a cup.
events.arc: The Table With No Lord

choices.text: Welcome the herald

effects.log: The herald, awkward, accepts the cup, and leaves with an invitation to a minor court dinner. A small door opens.

choices.text: Ask the herald to leave

effects.log: The herald goes without protest. The circle is relieved and slightly ashamed.

events.text: The Masterless assembly has a name now, 'the Open Table', and a banner of mismatched cloth. Pantheon gods are quietly asking whether they might sit there on a quiet evening. {npc} turns the matter over to you.
events.arc: The Table With No Lord

choices.text: Let them come, if they bring no title

effects.log: The Open Table fills with titleless gods of every pantheon. It becomes the place where decisions are really made.

choices.text: Keep it Masterless, for now

effects.log: The Table stays small. The ones who belong know it.

events.text: At the Hall of Titles, a clerk named {npc} processes the petitions of the pantheon gods in a flash, and yours, as a Masterless god, with a long sigh. {He} does not look up. {He} sets your petition to the bottom of the pile with the tip of a finger.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Would Not Look Up

choices.text: Wait with exemplary patience

effects.log: You wait. The sigh grows deeper. Others in the line begin to look at {npc} instead of at you.

choices.text: Point out the sigh, politely

effects.log: {npc} looks up for the first time, startled, and your petition moves to the top, grudgingly.

choices.text: Leave and send the petition by a servant

effects.log: The servant is processed in a minute. It is a small injustice that stings for a century.

events.text: {npc} is in trouble: a misfiled scroll has insulted an elder. {He} comes to you in the corridor, for no reason {he} can name, and asks if you might say you saw the scroll filed correctly. You did not.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Would Not Look Up

choices.text: Say you did not see

effects.log: {npc} deflates. Later, quietly, a fair copy is filed and the matter vanishes.

choices.text: Say you saw it filed correctly

effects.log: {npc} lives. You are owed a favour by a clerk of the Hall of Titles, which is worth more than any title.

events.text: {npc} comes to collect nothing and offer something: a drawer in the Hall of Titles, plain and low, where a Masterless god's petition can wait unsorted by the pantheons. {He} does not look up, but {he} slides the key across the desk.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Would Not Look Up

choices.text: Use the drawer for the petitions of the Masterless

effects.log: Word spreads on the back benches. A line of nobody's petitioners files into the Hall.

choices.text: Decline, so the favour stays unspent

effects.log: {npc} nods, surprised, and puts the key back. {He} says you are the only god who ever left a debt unpaid on purpose.

events.text: The drawer overflows. Years pass, and the Masterless gods' petitions are answered in time, because {npc} reads them first, aloud, under the breath of an elder. Some say the Hall has gone soft. You say nothing.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Would Not Look Up

choices.text: Thank {npc} publicly at the next court

effects.log: The Hall is a little embarrassed and a little proud. A new drawer is built. (+faith)

choices.text: Send {him} a cup of tea at the desk

effects.log: {npc} drinks it without looking up. The cup is returned, rinsed, with a note: 'Yes.'

events.text: Long after, you are in trouble, a petition struck from the roll for a fault of form. {npc} arrives at your threshold with the key and no sigh at all. 'The favour,' {he} says, 'was always yours.' It is, finally, spent.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Would Not Look Up

choices.text: Take the key and get the petition restored

effects.log: The petition returns to the roll, correct in every thread. The clerk looks up, at last.

choices.text: Hand the key back, and ask for tea

effects.log: {npc} laughs, the first time anyone has heard it in the Hall.

events.text: At the market of the gods, a stall sells lost prayers by the bundle. They are cheap. The seller guarantees nothing about their content. A lesser god in front of you buys a bundle at random and opens it with trembling hands.

choices.text: Peek over their shoulder

effects.log: The prayers are small domestic ones: a lost sock, a sick hen. The lesser god laughs and spends the day answering them.

choices.text: Buy a bundle yourself

effects.log: Your bundle holds a love letter and a recipe. Both are answered.

events.text: A seller of weather has set up a stall: little jars of drizzle, mist, a wedge of fog. A god of the harvest haggles with fierce charm. The seller smiles with every tooth. You have the sense of a performance.

choices.text: Buy a jar of drizzle for your domain

effects.log: The drizzle is exactly the right amount of damp. You use it on a dry hillside, with pride.

choices.text: Watch the haggle and learn

effects.log: The haggle lasts an hour. Both sides win. You admire the art.

events.text: At the games a child-god, newly made, tries to throw a stone across the lake and fails, repeatedly. The crowd is encouraging in the worst way. The stone sinks again. The child-god's lip trembles.

choices.text: Skip a stone beside them, and show how

effects.log: The child-god learns in three throws. The crowd cheers, and the child-god glares at the cheerful ones.

choices.text: Quiet the crowd with a look

effects.log: The crowd falls silent. The child-god, in peace, makes the throw.

events.text: A box of puzzles sits at the edge of the games field, each one made by a different god. You pick the plainest. It takes you the whole afternoon to open, and inside is a little paper that says: 'Good. Now close it.'

choices.text: Close it and return it with a smile

effects.log: The box shuts. Its maker, watching from afar, laughs aloud.

choices.text: Leave a note inside

effects.log: You leave a note: 'Never again.' It sits in the box for centuries, waiting for the next opener.

events.text: A poetry contest has been called for the autumn court, the theme 'the weight of a leaf.' Forty poems have been read. They are all excellent and all mournful. The judges are weeping politely. The clerk turns to you for a poem.

choices.text: Recite a poem of your own

ok.log: Your poem is short, dry, and funny. The court laughs through its tears, and awards you the leaf of honour.

fail.log: Your poem is long and ponderous. The court bears it politely.

choices.text: Decline, and applaud the others

effects.log: You applaud. The judges are grateful for a break from weeping.

events.text: At the pond of the games a fishing contest for the divine is held, every angler a god. Nobody has caught a fish for seven hundred years. The bait is excellent. The fish, evidently, are sceptical of the whole affair.

choices.text: Cast a line, in good humour

effects.log: You catch a boot. The crowd cheers as if it were a whale.

choices.text: Sit by the pond and think about fish

effects.log: You think quietly, and a fish rises, looks at you, and sinks again. You consider this a win.

events.text: In a corner of the market, a tiny oracle-booth offers fortunes for a copper of faith. The oracle is a retired god with a talent for obvious predictions: 'You will eat dinner. You will be tired.' The queue is half a mile.

choices.text: Buy a fortune

effects.log: Your fortune reads: 'You will be asked to a feast you do not want to attend.' It is correct within the hour.

choices.text: Praise the oracle's honesty

effects.log: The retired god sits up, delighted, and tells you three true things nobody else knows.

events.text: A pantheon god at the market charges you double for a spool of thread, with a sweet smile, on the grounds that you are Masterless. The seller is certain you will pay. The crowd is waiting for you to flinch.

choices.text: Pay the double, and tip generously

effects.log: The seller is thrown. The crowd looks away. You carry the thread with a courtly air, and a small, righteous heat.

choices.text: Walk away and buy from the next stall

effects.log: The next stall sells it at half price, from a Masterless friend. They remember.

events.text: A door in the hall of a pantheon is shut to you with perfect politeness: 'Members only, I am afraid, and the member is out.' The member has been out for two hundred years. The porter is dignified about it.

choices.text: Leave a card, courteously

effects.log: The porter takes the card with an expression of grief. The card is found, a century later, in the member's pocket.

choices.text: Find another door

effects.log: You find a side door, open, with a kind hand holding it. A pantheon god of no importance, cheerful.

events.text: The court has seated the pantheon gods by rank, and left a row of stools in the corridor for the Masterless. A stool is a stool. The corridor, however, has an excellent view of the arriving heralds, and nobody on the stools is bored.

choices.text: Take the best stool and begin to chat

effects.log: You and the corridor gods become fast friends, and gain a glimpse of every secret in the hall.

choices.text: Stand, and refuse the stool

effects.log: You stand with dignity. The porters are visibly torn about it.

events.text: A kind pantheon god offers to sponsor you into the Will of Heaven's lower rolls. It would mean a seat and a robe and an oath. It would also mean a chain, in the nicest possible way. They await your answer with real warmth.

choices.text: Thank them and decline

effects.log: They are puzzled, and then, slowly, admiring. They offer to be a friend instead.

choices.text: Ask for a century to think

effects.log: They grant it graciously. It is a long and pleasant wait.

events.text: A candied-fruit seller at the market of the gods is giving away a skewer to every Masterless passer-by, with a wink. The pantheon gods have noticed, and a small cold war is being fought over the candy.

choices.text: Take a skewer and thank the seller

effects.log: The skewer is sticky and sweet. The pantheon gods eye you. You eat it deliberately.

choices.text: Buy a skewer for a pantheon god as well

effects.log: Peace breaks out, in a mess of candy.

events.text: You enter an inn in a distant domain in a plain coat, and the landlord, who has never seen you, asks your business. You say 'travelling.' The landlord says the god of this place is a bore. A pot of tea arrives, and with it, a full account of your own failings.

choices.text: Agree, and add a few of your own

effects.log: The landlord loves you at once. You leave with a free pie.

choices.text: Defend the god, mildly, and pay for the tea

effects.log: The landlord shrugs and takes the coins. 'You have not met the god.' 'No,' you agree.

events.text: On the road through another god's domain, you share a cart with a talkative farmer, who explains in detail how the god of the place has ruined the weather. You note that it is your own weather, borrowed for the week.

choices.text: Take notes on the farmer's complaints

effects.log: You file them away. The farmer's list is long and very specific, and useful.

choices.text: Pay the carter extra and change the subject

effects.log: You hear about the farmer's goats. It is a great relief.

events.text: At a distant shrine to a rival god you leave a bowl of rice, in your plain coat, as if you were nobody. The keeper thanks you warmly and says that rival gods' bowls are always the most carefully made. You wonder how they knew.

choices.text: Ask how

effects.log: The keeper smiles and says: 'We are a small shrine. We notice.' You bow, unseen, in the dark.

choices.text: Smile and leave

effects.log: You leave as quietly as you came. It is a pleasant thing, to be thanked for the wrong god.

events.text: A sculptor named {npc} has carved a statue of you for the town square. It is eleven feet tall, bearded, and holds a thunderbolt. You are neither bearded nor tall. {He} asks, nervously, how it looks, standing under it with a chisel.
events.arc: The Statue That Does Not Look Like You

choices.text: Praise it warmly

effects.log: {npc} sags with relief. The statue is unveiled that spring. Pilgrims arrive to admire the beard.

choices.text: Send a dream of your true face

effects.log: {npc} wakes, stares at the stone, and begins a second statue at once, working through the night.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them see you as they like

effects.log: The beard stays. A god can be many faces, and this is one of them.

events.text: The second statue is better, smaller, more like you. The first one has become a minor god in itself, taking prayers about thunder and facial hair. {npc} is torn about this, and visits the first one every week with a cloth.
events.arc: The Statue That Does Not Look Like You

choices.text: Accept the first statue as a lesser aspect

effects.log: The beard-god, as the town calls it, answers small wishes through you. The faith is odd and wide.

choices.text: Let the town decide which is the god

effects.log: They argue amiably for years. Both are worshipped.

events.text: {npc} is old, and the statues are known across three provinces. {He} comes to ask only that, when {he} dies, {his} chisel be laid at the foot of the first statue, the one that was wrong. 'It taught me more,' {he} says.
events.arc: The Statue That Does Not Look Like You

choices.text: Promise it

effects.log: When the sculptor dies, the chisel is laid at the bearded feet. A pilgrim, years later, finds it and weeps.

choices.text: Say you will lay it there yourself

effects.log: You carry the chisel, in a plain coat, and set it down with some ceremony. The statue seems to approve.

events.text: A temple oracle, {npc}, reads signs in incense smoke and gets them wrong in a consistent, charming way. {He} says a coming rain means a wedding. {He} says a bad omen means a good dinner. Somehow {he} is right about half the time.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Reads the Wrong Smoke

choices.text: Make the next wrong reading come true

effects.log: {npc} predicts a stranger will bring bread. A stranger brings bread. {He} faints from the validation.

choices.text: Ask {him} how {he} reads it

effects.log: 'I read what I want to happen,' {npc} says, 'and then I try.' You have rarely heard better theology.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it

effects.log: The smoke curls. The oracle squints. The town tends to agree with {him}.

events.text: A formal oracle from the court has arrived to examine {npc}'s methods. The court oracle is cold, correct, and frighteningly accurate. {npc} is shaking. The town gathers outside the temple.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Reads the Wrong Smoke

choices.text: Speak up for the amateur

effects.log: You speak for {npc}, unseen, through the smoke. The court oracle pauses, and says: 'The method is unsound. The results are not.'

choices.text: Let {npc} face it alone

effects.log: {npc} reads a smoke the court oracle cannot, and the examination ends in a draw.

events.text: {npc} has become the best-loved oracle in the district, and accepts apprentices who read smoke wrongly on purpose. The court tolerates it. A year of smoke has never been so cheerful.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Reads the Wrong Smoke

choices.text: Bless the school with a clear dawn

effects.log: The school has its best year yet. Apprentices wander off to teach their own.

choices.text: Visit in secret and sit in the back

effects.log: You sit in the back row and read a smoke wrongly, in solidarity. The teacher notices and nods.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper has misplaced a dream. It has come to your threshold, shy, shaped like a small grey rabbit. {npc}, a dream-clerk, follows it up the steps with a lantern and an apology. The dream will not go back.
events.arc: The Dream the Sleeper Left Behind

choices.text: Hold the dream, and ask what it wants

effects.log: It says it wishes to be dreamed by someone who is awake. You have never been so flattered.

choices.text: Tuck it into a child's sleep in a faraway house

effects.log: The child dreams of a rabbit, wakes giggling, and draws it for a week.

choices.text: Hand it back to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} carries it home. It sulks in the clerk's arms the whole way.

events.text: The grey rabbit-dream comes back to you each night, now, and sits at the foot of your bed. It has begun to show you things: old shrines, forgotten gods, a field of grain at dawn. {npc} calls it a symptom of generosity.
events.arc: The Dream the Sleeper Left Behind

choices.text: Follow where it leads

effects.log: The dream takes you across a thousand sleeping houses to a ruined shrine and sits on the step. You light a candle there.

choices.text: Ask it to show you something small instead

effects.log: It shows you a spoon. The spoon is wonderful.

events.text: The candle at the ruined shrine burns without a wick now, and {npc} finds you there at dusk, the grey rabbit-dream asleep in your lap. Nearby, an old worshipper sleeps on the step, a forgotten god's last, dreaming of nothing in particular.
events.arc: The Dream the Sleeper Left Behind

choices.text: Wake the dreamer gently to the candle

effects.log: The old worshipper wakes, sees the light, and says: 'There you are.' They do not ask which god.

choices.text: Leave the dreamer to the dream

effects.log: The rabbit goes to the dreamer's feet and curls. You sit with {npc} and watch over the sleeper.

events.text: The old worshipper has a god again, even if it is you in a plain coat. They bring the shrine flowers and a stool and talk all afternoon. The rabbit-dream sleeps beside them. {npc} writes it all down in a clerk's neat hand.
events.arc: The Dream the Sleeper Left Behind

choices.text: Take the shrine as your own, quietly

effects.log: The ruined shrine becomes a small place of yours, with a candle that needs no wick. (+faith)

choices.text: Keep the worshipper's faith for the forgotten god's name

effects.log: You tell them the old name, and they say it aloud, over and over, glad.

events.text: The old worshipper dreams on, and the rabbit-dream grows large and soft. When Mongsa the Sleeper comes by, wearing slippers, to ask after the lost one, {npc} points to the step. Mongsa laughs in a doze and leaves a pillow.
events.arc: The Dream the Sleeper Left Behind

choices.text: Accept the pillow for the shrine

effects.log: The pillow is put on the step. All who sit on it dream of the old worshipper. (+faith)

choices.text: Thank the Sleeper with silence

effects.log: A dream is the most private of gifts. Mongsa nods, and goes.

events.text: Once a year a festival of lanterns lights the plain below your hall. {npc}, the lantern-maker, has built a lantern that is not for hanging. It is the size of a house. It is the most beautiful ridiculous thing you have seen. {He} would like to know where to put it.
events.arc: The Lantern-Maker's Festival

choices.text: Suggest the middle of the lake

effects.log: The lantern floats out on a raft of reeds, glowing. The festival goes silent as it passes.

choices.text: Suggest your own roof

effects.log: The lantern perches on your hall like an enormous moon. For a month, you cannot sleep for the glow.

choices.text: Ask {him} to decide

effects.log: {npc} chooses the middle of the lake, after all. You nod as if you had thought of it.

events.text: A storm blows in on festival night, and the great lantern lists in the wind. {npc} is on the shore in tears. The town is watching. It is, in its way, a perfect disaster.
events.arc: The Lantern-Maker's Festival

choices.text: Hold the storm back for an hour

effects.log: The lantern rides out the storm, and the festival goes on beneath it. The town cheers.

choices.text: Let the storm take the lantern, gently

effects.log: The lantern sails to sea in the wind and the whole town waves it off. It is the best ending a lantern ever had.

events.text: A year after the storm, a letter arrives from a far coast: the great lantern was found, still burning, in a harbour town. {npc} wants to go and see it, and asks whether a god might make the road short.
events.arc: The Lantern-Maker's Festival

choices.text: Shorten the road

effects.log: The road folds. {npc} arrives in a day, breathless and happy.

choices.text: Let {him} walk it

effects.log: {npc} sets out on foot, with a pack of lantern paper, and a promise to write.

events.text: In the harbour town the great lantern has become a lighthouse, tended by three fishing families, who wept when {npc} walked up the quay. The town gives {him} a house on the hill, facing it. {He} thinks it is the best view in the realm.
events.arc: The Lantern-Maker's Festival

choices.text: Send a clear night for the lantern

effects.log: The harbour's boats come home by its light for a hundred years. (+faith)

choices.text: Leave {him} to the view

effects.log: {npc} sits at the window and does not move for a week.

events.text: {npc} takes years to arrive, and makes a small lantern in every town on the way, giving each to a child. When {he} reaches the harbour, the child of the first town is waiting, grown, with a lantern still burning. They say nothing, and hold it up.
events.arc: The Lantern-Maker's Festival

choices.text: Bless the long chain of lanterns

effects.log: A line of small lights runs inland to the hill, and pilgrims follow it. (+faith)

choices.text: Walk the last mile with {him}

effects.log: You walk the last mile in a plain coat, and no one looks twice.

events.text: On the stairs of your hall you meet an old, unhurried god in a faded robe, carrying a stool. {npc} nods, says nothing, and sits on the fifth step. A servant whispers that this is one of the oldest gods in the realm. {He} is, apparently, resting.
events.arc: A Great God on the Stairs

choices.text: Sit with {him} on the stairs

effects.log: You sit. The stairs are not comfortable. After a long time {npc} says: 'This is the best step.' You agree.

choices.text: Offer {him} a proper chair

effects.log: {npc} thanks you, and does not move. The servants bring a cushion for the step.

choices.text: Walk past quietly

effects.log: You pass without a word. Behind you the old god chuckles.

events.text: {npc} returns the next spring, at the same hour, with the stool. The servants have swept the fifth step. {He} brings a little paper bag of sweets and offers you one. It is, you realise, a very old kind of courtesy.
events.arc: A Great God on the Stairs

choices.text: Accept the sweet and ask for a story

effects.log: {npc} tells you of the first morning of the realm. It is short, and humble, and exact.

choices.text: Accept the sweet and say nothing

effects.log: The sweet is lemon. You eat it on the stairs. It is the best afternoon of the year.

events.text: {npc} stops coming. The servants find the stool on the fifth step with a note in a shaky hand: 'The step is yours.' The hall holds its breath, waiting to see what you do with it. A lemon sweet lies on the seat.
events.arc: A Great God on the Stairs

choices.text: Sit on the stool each spring

effects.log: You take the stool out each year, and eat a lemon sweet. It is not comfortable, and you would not move it.

choices.text: Put the stool in the hall's shrine

effects.log: The stool is placed on a plinth with a lamp beside it. The servants whisper a small prayer to it.

events.text: Years on, a young god in an ill-fitting robe finds you on the stairs, and sits on the fourth step without being asked. You offer a lemon sweet. They say nothing. After a long time, they say: 'This is the best step.' You agree.
events.arc: A Great God on the Stairs

choices.text: Hand over the stool to the young god

effects.log: The stool changes hands with a nod. The tradition continues. (+faith)

choices.text: Keep the stool, and share the stair

effects.log: Two gods on the stairs, quiet. The servants sweep around you both.

events.text: Pilgrims hear that the oldest god of the realm once sat in your hall, and come to see the stool. A queue forms on the stairs. The servants hand out lemon sweets from a basket. It is the first time the hall has ever had a crowd.
events.arc: A Great God on the Stairs

choices.text: Let the pilgrims touch the stool

effects.log: They go away blessed, and the stool is polished by a thousand sleeves. (+faith)

choices.text: Ask them only to sit a moment

effects.log: The pilgrims sit on the stairs in turn, quietly. It is the best crowd you ever had.

events.text: A god from a far domain visits your hall, bringing a cook. {npc}, the cook, is a cheerful god of one dish, a river-fish stew, and begs the use of your kitchen. The hall's own cooks look on in horror. The stew smells like heaven.
events.arc: The Cook of the Visiting God

choices.text: Give {him} the kitchen for the day

effects.log: The stew is eaten by the whole household. The hall's own cooks demand the recipe and are refused with a grin.

choices.text: Cook beside {him}

effects.log: You stir, chop, and burn your thumb. {npc} praises your enthusiasm and sends you to sit.

choices.text: Ask for a small bowl and stay out of the way

effects.log: The bowl is warm and perfect. You eat on the step.

events.text: {npc} has left a note, and a jar of the stew's secret ingredient, with instructions not to open it for ten years. The hall's cooks are aflame with curiosity. You have the jar. You are the holder of a secret.
events.arc: The Cook of the Visiting God

choices.text: Keep the jar closed for ten years

effects.log: A decade passes. The jar opens: a slip of paper reads 'Patience.' The stew, by then, is memory.

choices.text: Open it early, and share the secret with the cooks

effects.log: The ingredient is a dried flower. The hall cooks are gloriously smug for a century.

events.text: Ten years on, {npc} comes back thin and tired: the far domain's river has dried and the fish are gone. {He} carries the pot and the ladle, and the recipe in {his} head, and no fish. {He} stands at your door and does not ask for anything.
events.arc: The Cook of the Visiting God

choices.text: Send fish up your own river for {him}

effects.log: A silver shoal turns into the far river's old channel. {npc} watches them come in, ladle in hand.

choices.text: Offer {him} a permanent place in your kitchen

effects.log: {npc} looks at the stove, the stool, the window, and hangs the ladle on the nail.

events.text: The far river runs again, thick with the fish you sent, and {npc} cooks a feast for both domains by the shore. The two gods' people eat together, and the pantheons' old quarrel loses a leg. Your share of the feast is a bowl of the stew.
events.arc: The Cook of the Visiting God

choices.text: Raise your bowl to both domains

effects.log: The shore applauds. A thread of kindness runs between the two. (+faith)

choices.text: Eat in silence on the shore

effects.log: It is the best bowl of stew in the realm. You do not say so.

events.text: The hall's cooks learn the river-fish stew, one dial at a time, and call {npc} the Master. Every moon a pot of it simmers for the household. {He} never asks for a title. The hall's guests ask for seconds, and for the cook by name.
events.arc: The Cook of the Visiting God

choices.text: Give {him} a name for the stew

effects.log: The stew is named for {npc}, and carried in jars to the court. (+faith)

choices.text: Eat the stew every moon, and say little

effects.log: A pot on the stove, a friend at the pot. It is enough.

events.text: On the turning of the year every shrine in your domain is swept, bell by bell, and the sweepings are thrown into the river in a gesture of release. A hundred small bundles of dust drift out to sea. It is sweet and silly and you are very fond of it.

choices.text: Follow the dust downstream, unseen

effects.log: The bundles sail to the sea in a long silent line. A heron follows too.

choices.text: Add your own sweepings to the river

effects.log: You toss in a lifetime of small regrets. They float off, dust.

events.text: At dawn on the festival of the first thunder, all the drums of the valley are struck at once, and the dogs howl, and a hundred children wake and shout. The sound rolls over the hills and returns, delayed. It is gorgeous. It is also extremely loud.

choices.text: Add one low roll of thunder

effects.log: The sky rumbles. The children shriek with joy. Several dogs take cover.

choices.text: Muffle it for the sleepers on the edge

effects.log: A soft cloud takes the edge off the noise. A baby sleeps through the dawn.

events.text: A child's nightmare has strayed into the corridors of your hall and is wandering the halls, big and wet and confused. It looks at you with huge eyes. It is, evidently, someone's nightmare of being left behind.

choices.text: Lead it back to the child's bedside

effects.log: The nightmare shrinks to the size of a mouse and curls on the pillow. The child sleeps.

choices.text: Give it a quiet corner and a blanket

effects.log: The nightmare sleeps in your corner for a season, and wakes up as a small grey cat.

events.text: An oracle has given a pilgrim a riddle: 'What is heavier than a mountain and lighter than a feather?' The pilgrim has been asking everyone in the market for a week. They come to you, in despair, in your plain coat.

choices.text: Answer: 'A promise.'

effects.log: The pilgrim's face clears. 'Of course.' They go off, humbled and pleased.

choices.text: Say you do not know, and offer them tea

effects.log: You drink tea and talk about the road. The riddle, in the end, solves itself.

events.text: The nose has fallen off your oldest statue in the night and a flock of children is trying to put it back with honey. It is stuck at an angle. The statue now looks pleasantly surprised.

choices.text: Leave the nose where the children put it

effects.log: The statue is fixed with honey and good will. Nobody ever fixes it again.

choices.text: Mend it properly in the night

effects.log: In the morning the nose is straight. The children are puzzled, then proud.

events.text: A pigeon has built a nest in the hand of your great statue, among the fingers of the gesture of blessing. The keeper wants to remove it. The pigeon's chicks are very fluffy. The statue is, in a sense, blessing a family.

choices.text: Ask the keeper to leave the nest

effects.log: The nest stays. Pilgrims point at the baby pigeons and murmur.

choices.text: Let the keeper scrape it carefully

effects.log: The nest is moved to a ledge, with a ribbon. The pigeons settle at once.

events.text: At the harvest festival a baker has made dumplings the shape of your face. They are unflattering. Children bite off the nose. An elder weeps at the sight of their own dumpling. You are not sure what to feel.

choices.text: Eat one in a plain coat, grinning

effects.log: You bite off your own nose. The child beside you cheers. You are accepted into the feast.

choices.text: Bless the dumplings as they steam

effects.log: The dumplings are somewhat more handsome by the time they cool. Nobody complains.

events.text: In the dusk, Horang Lord of the Wild passes through your domain on the way to somewhere else. The forest quiets as Horang goes. A single deer stops mid-step and bows. The god does not look at you. The deer, you notice, watches you the whole time.

choices.text: Bow to the deer

effects.log: The deer inclines its head a little further. You feel obscurely received.

choices.text: Stand very still until it passes

effects.log: The forest resumes. You have the feeling of having been briefly passed over by something old and kind.

events.text: Before dawn, in the palace of Hwarin of the First Hearth, an ember that has never gone out is blown upon, once, by a lone old servant. The servant does it every day. You happen to be watching. The ember brightens. The hall brightens. The servant shuffles away, unseen.

choices.text: Thank the servant in a dream

effects.log: The servant wakes with a warm feeling and does not know why.

choices.text: Say nothing, and remember it

effects.log: You keep the image in your hall, like a small lamp.

events.text: Mongsa's dream-paths cross your sleep, and in a garden there you find a bench with your name on it that you did not carve. Someone has been keeping the garden for you. A small watering can hangs from a nail.

choices.text: Water a few of the plants

effects.log: The plants stir. A leaf waves at you. You wake smelling of damp earth.

choices.text: Sit on the bench and rest

effects.log: You sit on the bench for an hour and wake with an unexpected calm.

events.text: The oracle at the cliff temple has gone silent. The smoke rises. The signs are plain. The oracle, a calm old god, has simply nothing to say, and says so. A queue of anxious petitioners winds down the cliff path, stunned.

choices.text: Whisper a kind remark to the petitioners

effects.log: They go home thoughtful, with a sense that some answers are not meant to be given.

choices.text: Sit with the oracle in the quiet

effects.log: You and the oracle share a long calm hour. They do not mind that you are not saying anything either.

events.text: A parade of children in paper hats winds through the lanes of your oldest town, banging pots, with a grave, uneven pageantry. They are the gods of the day, for one day. A tiny god of rice, aged six, wears a hat ten sizes too large and receives a bow from the mayor.

choices.text: Bow to the tiny god of rice

effects.log: The tiny god of rice looks at you, astonished, and bows back. It falls over.

choices.text: Send a gentle wind to hold the hat steady

effects.log: The hat holds. The tiny god parades on, enormous.

events.text: A cat sits on the head of your statue every noon and washes. The sun glints off it like a crown. Pilgrims have started leaving fish at the foot of the pedestal, and the cat has begun to receive them with condescension.

choices.text: Bless the cat with a long life

effects.log: The cat lives to see forty seasons. It is thought a saint.

choices.text: Smile and look away

effects.log: A statue is happy to be a throne, now and then.

events.text: {npc}, the council usher, keeps a ledger of who sits beside whom, and has kept it so long that the ledger now keeps {him}. Today {he} shows you a page: your chair has moved one hand-width toward the door since spring. 'Nobody ordered it,' {he} says. 'It simply drifted.'
events.arc: The Ledger of Seats

choices.text: Ask {him} to move it back quietly

effects.log: {npc} moves it back with a clerk's sleight of hand. Nobody comments, which is how you know someone noticed.

choices.text: Leave it, and watch who moved it

effects.log: You leave the chair where it is and watch the hall. The drift, it turns out, has a very polite author.

choices.text: Thank {him} and say nothing

effects.log: {npc} writes your thanks in the margin, which is more than most gods get.

events.text: The author of the drift is a mid-ranked god who sits two chairs off and has been nudging every chair in the hall toward their own, one hand-width a season. {npc} brings you the proof in a sleeve, looking miserable.
events.arc: The Ledger of Seats

choices.text: Expose it at the next council

effects.log: The hall goes silent. The mid-ranked god laughs it off, but the chairs stay where they are for a century.

choices.text: Nudge your own chair back toward theirs, slowly

effects.log: A game begins that nobody admits to. By midsummer the whole hall has shuffled in a slow, silent dance.

choices.text: Return the proof to {npc} and say burn it

effects.log: {npc} burns the proof. The ledger is lighter, and so are you.

events.text: {npc} grows old and sells the ledger to no one, and gives it to you. The last page holds, in {his} small hand, the true order of every god in the hall as it should be, which differs from the official one in eleven places.
events.arc: The Ledger of Seats

choices.text: Keep the true order secret

effects.log: You read it every year and tell no one. A god can be quite powerful knowing who really outranks whom.

choices.text: Read it aloud at the next feast

effects.log: Nobody enjoys the feast. Everyone remembers it fondly for centuries.

events.text: {npc} leaves you the ledger on a quiet night. The dance has made it useless, since nobody sits where the book says. {He} writes one line: 'Sit where you are glad to.' It is the only entry that is ever right.
events.arc: The Ledger of Seats

choices.text: Move your chair to the window

effects.log: You sit by the window, and over a century half the hall follows. The hall grows lighter.

choices.text: Keep the line framed over your door

effects.log: Visitors read it and say nothing. Some leave humming.

events.text: The council votes with white and grey stones dropped in an urn, and the count is read by {npc}, who has not once been wrong in four thousand years. Today a proposal about river tolls ends in a tie, and {npc} looks straight at you, because yours was the last stone.
events.arc: The Counting of the Stones

choices.text: Say your stone was a mistake and ask for a recount

effects.log: The recount is granted with a sigh. The result flips, and two gods you never meant to cross stop speaking to you.

choices.text: Stand by your stone

effects.log: You stand by it. The proposal fails by one, and the god who proposed it bows to you with great care, which is worse than a glare.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to count again, slowly, aloud

effects.log: {npc} counts aloud, stone by stone. The hall learns something about its own patience.

events.text: {npc} comes to your hall at night with a grey stone in each hand. 'One of these was in the urn twice,' {he} says. 'I have never had to say that before. I came to you first.'
events.arc: The Counting of the Stones

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell the council

effects.log: {npc} tells the council in a flat voice. The vote is annulled, and the hall learns what an honest counter costs.

choices.text: Ask {him} to keep it between you

effects.log: {npc} nods, grey with it. You now hold a secret the size of an urn.

choices.text: Offer {him} tea and the quiet

effects.log: You do not decide anything that night. You only sit, and {he} is grateful for that.

events.text: {npc} steps down from the counting after four thousand years. At the last vote {he} counts every stone with the whole hall standing. At the end {he} sets the urn in front of you and says only: 'It was always going to be you who asked.'
events.arc: The Counting of the Stones

choices.text: Take the urn and the counting

effects.log: You count honestly for a thousand years. It is the dullest honour in the realm and the one you are proudest of.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: The secret does what secrets do. {npc} stops coming to council, and the urn is counted by a bored clerk who gets everything slightly wrong. Nobody notices but you.
events.arc: The Counting of the Stones

choices.text: Confess it yourself, late

effects.log: Your confession is long, graceless and true. The hall forgives you faster than you forgave yourself.

choices.text: Let it lie. Some urns are best left uncounted

effects.log: You let it lie. The council goes on a little more crooked.

events.text: An envoy from a rival pantheon, {npc}, arrives with a gift: a bell cast in the shape of your own domain, tuned so finely it rings when anyone in the realm prays to you. 'No obligation at all,' {he} says, which in this court means there is an obligation the size of a mountain.
events.arc: A Gift You Cannot Accept

choices.text: Accept the bell with a gift of your own

effects.log: You return a small silver spoon. {npc} accepts it with a smile that means the bargain is even and nothing else is.

choices.text: Decline, politely, in three languages
