effects.log: {npc} accepts the refusal with great grace, and tells every god at supper how correct you were. It costs you nothing and is repeated for years.

choices.text: Ask what the bell costs to silence

effects.log: {npc} chuckles. 'Wise question,' {he} says. 'The answer is a favour.'

events.text: The bell rings in your hall at odd hours now, whenever a faraway stranger prays to you. Each time {npc} sends a note: 'Heard that? I hope it brings you joy.' The notes are never signed and always on time.
events.arc: A Gift You Cannot Accept

choices.text: Hang the bell where only you can hear it

effects.log: You hang it in a closet. It rings quietly all week. You find you do not mind.

choices.text: Write back a note of your own each time

effects.log: A correspondence begins that neither pantheon authorised. It is the most honest thing either has written in a century.

choices.text: Give the bell to a shrine-keeper

effects.log: The keeper rings it for lost travellers, and it is lovelier there than in any hall.

events.text: The favour arrives: a single vote on a minor matter, to be cast in {npc}'s pantheon's favour. It is small. It is exactly the size of a bell. You understand how a lot of the realm has come to be built.
events.arc: A Gift You Cannot Accept

choices.text: Cast the vote, and let the bell be paid for

effects.log: You vote as asked. The matter is minor. You note, in your own ledger, the price of a gift.

choices.text: Return the bell and refuse the vote

effects.log: You return the bell in its box. The envoy is hurt, then amused, then, years later, quite fond of you.

events.text: {npc} visits one last time before going home, with no gift. {He} sits in your hall and says that in four hundred years of envoy work you are the only god who ever wrote back. It seems to matter to {him} greatly.
events.arc: A Gift You Cannot Accept

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay for supper

effects.log: {npc} stays for supper. The pantheons stay at odds, but two gods sit very comfortably across one table.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: Mujin of the Thousand Banners sits on the steps of the war hall at dawn with a needle, mending a banner that is older than most domains. {npc}, a young war-god, has been told to carry messages to Mujin and cannot work out how to speak. Mujin does not look up.
events.arc: The Banner Mujin Mends

choices.text: Introduce {npc} yourself

effects.log: Mujin looks up, nods, and hands {npc} a corner of the banner to hold. That is all. {npc} holds it as though it were a newborn.

choices.text: Sit and mend a corner of the banner

effects.log: Mujin hands you a needle without a word. You mend a thread no bigger than an eyelash. It is the best sentence you have ever been given.

choices.text: Let {npc} find the way alone

effects.log: {npc} stammers out a message in the end, and Mujin listens to every word. Some things have to be done by yourself.

events.text: Word has spread that Mujin lets certain young gods hold the banner. {npc} is treated at court as someone who has been blessed, and does not know how to bear it. {He} comes to you with the question young gods ask: what did I do?
events.arc: The Banner Mujin Mends

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: nothing, and that was the point

effects.log: {npc} goes quiet, then laughs, and the awkward glow of favour fades into something steadier.

choices.text: Say it was a sign, and let it stand

effects.log: The sign stands. {npc} grows into it, uneasily, and the court gets a new favourite.

choices.text: Suggest {he} ask Mujin

effects.log: {npc} asks. Mujin says, after a long time: 'The hands were steady.' It is more than enough.

events.text: Mujin's banner is finished at last, and the war hall hangs it. {npc} is among the ones who hold the cord. When the banner unrolls, there is one thread along the edge, a little crooked, that Mujin has left exactly as it was mended. It is yours or {npc}'s, and Mujin will not say which.
events.arc: The Banner Mujin Mends

choices.text: Look at the crooked thread and say nothing

effects.log: You look at the crooked thread for a long time. In a banner of a thousand battles, it is the part that is somebody's.

choices.text: Light a candle for it that evening

effects.log: A small light burns in your hall until morning, for no reason a god would need.

events.text: {npc} becomes a god of the hall and takes a post on the steps with a needle of {his} own. The first thing {he} mends is nothing: a small cloth for a small boy's boat. The war hall is richer for it.
events.arc: The Banner Mujin Mends

choices.text: Send a stray wind to help the cloth

effects.log: The cloth bellies and the boat sails. {npc} watches from the steps and does not know it was you.

choices.text: Bring {him} a better needle

effects.log: {npc} accepts it and puts it away unused. Some gifts are for the shelf.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman eats lunch on the landing between crossings: one rice ball, one pickle, always. {npc}, a soul who has not decided yet whether to board, asks if it may share the pickle. Baekun, to the shock of the whole landing, says yes.
events.arc: The Pale Ferryman's Lunch

choices.text: Bring a second pickle for the soul

effects.log: The soul takes it with both hands. Baekun says nothing, but sets the pole down gently.

choices.text: Ask Baekun about the soul's wait

effects.log: 'The wait is the soul's,' Baekun says. 'I only carry what is ready.' It is the most you have heard Baekun say in a century.

choices.text: Leave them to their lunch

effects.log: You leave. Across the water the lunch goes on, quietly, for an hour.

events.text: {npc} is still on the landing a season later. The other souls give it a wide berth and the ferrymen leave a cup of tea beside it each morning. Baekun has begun to cross slowly, as though in no hurry at all.
events.arc: The Pale Ferryman's Lunch

choices.text: Sit with {npc} through an evening

effects.log: You listen as {npc} tells the story of a life, out of order, and mostly about food. It is a good one.

choices.text: Urge {npc} gently to board

effects.log: {npc} listens, thanks you, and does not board. Baekun gives you a long, level look from the water.

choices.text: Leave a blanket and a lamp

effects.log: In the morning the blanket is folded and the lamp is still lit.

events.text: {npc} boards at last, on a grey dawn, with a pickle in its sleeve. Baekun pushes off with the slowest stroke the landing has ever seen. At the middle of the river the soul turns and waves. You wave back until the mist closes.
events.arc: The Pale Ferryman's Lunch

choices.text: Leave a pickle on the landing for next time

effects.log: A pickle waits on the landing every dawn from then on. Nobody knows who leaves it. The ferrymen say it is lucky.

choices.text: Tell no one, and keep it

effects.log: It becomes one of the few private things you own.

events.text: {npc} goes on waiting. Years pass. Baekun does not push, and you do not either, and the landing accepts this as one more kind of arrival. Some partings are slow because the one parting is not done being here.
events.arc: The Pale Ferryman's Lunch

choices.text: Bring {npc} something from its old life to read

effects.log: {npc} reads in the lamplight for a decade. When it boards, it is smiling.

choices.text: Visit once a year and leave it alone

effects.log: You visit once a year. Each time it is a little more ready.

events.text: Saengmo, Mother of Seeds, presses a small brown seed into your palm at a feast and walks away. It is warm. It hums. {npc}, an under-gardener, sees and goes pale: 'Saengmo never gives them out. In nine thousand years I have seen four.'
events.arc: The Seed Saengmo Pressed Into Your Palm

choices.text: Plant it in the hall garden

effects.log: A shoot appears by evening. It leans toward you like a child waiting for a story.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what it is

effects.log: {npc} says nobody knows. The four before were each a different thing: a tree, a river, a wolf, a song.

choices.text: Keep it in your sleeve and tell no one

effects.log: It hums against your wrist all week. You have never been so well-looked-after.

events.text: The seed has, in a season, become a plant you cannot name: grey-green, shy, bending toward the sound of your voice. Gods drop by to see it and go quiet. {npc} visits every morning to water it and talk about nothing.
events.arc: The Seed Saengmo Pressed Into Your Palm

choices.text: Read to it from the council minutes

effects.log: It wilts with boredom. It perks up when you read a love-letter instead.

choices.text: Let it grow wild and unwatched

effects.log: It grows ragged and beautiful in the corner. Lizards move in.

choices.text: Ask Saengmo, at the next feast, what it is

effects.log: Saengmo smiles, says 'Yours,' and goes on with the soup.

events.text: The plant flowers once, on a night with no moon, and the flower is a small bright face with your own tilt of the eyebrow. It opens, looks at you, and breathes. Then it folds and becomes a seed again. You are holding the next one.
events.arc: The Seed Saengmo Pressed Into Your Palm

choices.text: Press the new seed into {npc}'s hand

effects.log: {npc} stares at it, then at you. 'Five,' {he} whispers. A new line of the garden begins.

choices.text: Plant it where the first one grew

effects.log: It grows again, differently, a patient thing that turns out to be a tree.

events.text: The wild thing seeds itself over the corner, and then the courtyard, and then a neighbour's hall, which sends a note of complaint wrapped around a very fine flower. Saengmo laughs the whole way through the feast.
events.arc: The Seed Saengmo Pressed Into Your Palm

choices.text: Offer cuttings to every hall

effects.log: Within a century the whole divine quarter is soft with green. People start to arrive earlier at council to sit in it.

choices.text: Apologise to the neighbour in person, with tea

effects.log: The neighbour keeps the flower, and the feud, in equal parts.

events.text: Haeryong Keeper of Tides publishes the tide-table each year in a book thick as a door. {npc}, the clerk who copies it, has found an error: the table says the sea will rise at an hour when it has never risen. Haeryong does not make errors. The clerk wants to know who should be told.
events.arc: The Tide-Table of Haeryong

choices.text: Tell Haeryong yourself

effects.log: Haeryong reads the line, laughs a deep slow laugh, and says: 'That is the hour the sea is going to try something new.'

choices.text: Ask {npc} to leave the error alone

effects.log: The table goes out as written. The sea does rise at the odd hour, and fishing boats are caught flat, gently, on the sand.

choices.text: Copy the line yourself and see what follows

effects.log: You copy it. For a week you are the only one who knows what the tide will do.

events.text: The odd tide arrives, and {npc} stands on the quay in the grey light, holding the book. The sea rises, a quiet silver hand, and sets down on the sand a hundred small shells shaped like the letters of the clerk's name.
events.arc: The Tide-Table of Haeryong

choices.text: Stand with {npc} and read the shells

effects.log: You and the clerk gather every one. The sea, it turns out, has been reading the book too.

choices.text: Tell the town it is a blessing

effects.log: The town gathers the shells and strings them for children. {npc} is mortified and also quietly thrilled.

choices.text: Look away and let it be private

effects.log: You leave the quay. It was theirs, and the sea's.

events.text: Haeryong sends for {npc} and offers a seat as co-copyist. The book thickens by one page: a single line, in the clerk's hand, at the margin: 'The sea may try something new.' It is never struck out.
events.arc: The Tide-Table of Haeryong

choices.text: Send a gift of salt-tea to the clerk's desk

effects.log: It arrives with the evening tide. The clerk drinks it and writes a better margin.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: The year after the shells, the tide comes at every hour the table said it would. The clerk grows quiet. One night {he} says: 'I miss the error.' So do you. The sea, listening, thinks about it.
events.arc: The Tide-Table of Haeryong

choices.text: Ask Haeryong to allow one small mistake a year

effects.log: A small tide arrives each year at the wrong hour. It is the best-loved thing on the coast.

choices.text: Keep the missing line to yourself

effects.log: Some errors are better left to the ones who loved them.

events.text: The First Hearth is never allowed to go cold. Hwarin lends embers to new households, and on the day a lent ember goes out the lender must be told. {npc} brings you an ember that has dimmed, with an apology: it belonged to a tiny shrine of yours, and the keeper there has been ill.
events.arc: The Borrowed Ember

choices.text: Breathe on the ember until it blazes

effects.log: It leaps up gold. The shrine's keeper wakes the next morning with colour in the cheeks.

choices.text: Carry it back to Hwarin to relight

effects.log: Hwarin relights it with a touch and says, kindly, 'The one who tends it matters more than the flame.'

choices.text: Tell {npc} to leave it dim and watch

effects.log: You watch the ember all night. It does not go out. Some fires only look unwell.

events.text: The keeper of the small shrine is a child now, the old keeper's grandchild, who has taken the ember in as a pet. The child talks to it every evening about school. The ember has started to answer in sparks.
events.arc: The Borrowed Ember

choices.text: Answer the child through the ember

effects.log: A spark spells the child's name in the air. The child does not scream, and has never felt more understood.

choices.text: Let the ember be only an ember

effects.log: The child goes on talking. Sometimes the ember, in its own way, listens.

events.text: The child is grown and has a household of their own. The ember goes along, in a clay pot, to a new hearth in a new place, and the keeper lights it first thing each day without a word. A god might wish for no better worshipper than a habit.
events.arc: The Borrowed Ember

choices.text: Visit on a cold morning and warm your hands

effects.log: Nobody ever learns who it was. They only say the hearth burned especially well that day.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: The old keeper recovers and puts the ember back in its niche, scolded and clean. A little shrine, a little flame, years going by. The ember is brighter than it was, the way the lent things always are.
events.arc: The Borrowed Ember

choices.text: Send a pilgrim by with oil

effects.log: The pilgrim leaves oil at the door and a candle. The shrine has a good winter.

choices.text: Light your own candle from it

effects.log: Your candle is no hotter than any other. But it feels like a promise.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver sends for you with a polite note. In the thread of a mortal's life, a knot has formed that the loom cannot pass. {npc}, a loom-attendant with ink on both hands, points to it: the knot is, plainly, a decision that has not been made yet.
events.arc: The Knot in the Weaver's Thread

choices.text: Ask the mortal's god to nudge the choice

effects.log: A small god of that district is consulted. They decline, saying a choice nudged is not a choice. The knot stays.

choices.text: Offer to sit with the thread and wait

effects.log: You sit. The knot trembles but does not loosen. A very long hour goes by on a very small thing.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what happens if the loom is stopped

effects.log: 'Everything waits,' {npc} says. 'The sea, the sun. I would not like to be the one who said stop.'

events.text: The mortal, three streets from a river you have never heard of, is a baker. The knot is whether to leave the shop to a daughter or sell it to a stranger. The baker has been turning it over for a month. {npc} shows you the hour the choice will come, and says the thread is almost loose.
events.arc: The Knot in the Weaver's Thread

choices.text: Send a smell of good bread across the baker's dream

effects.log: The baker wakes and bakes. By noon it is decided. You made nothing happen. You merely helped it smell right.

choices.text: Let the knot work itself out

effects.log: At the last hour the baker decides without knowing it was decided, and the loom turns.

events.text: Unmyeong thanks you with a single thread, grey, soft, less than a hand long. 'It is a piece of someone's quiet afternoon,' the Weaver says. 'Keep it somewhere you can reach.' You will carry it for a thousand years.
events.arc: The Knot in the Weaver's Thread

choices.text: Keep it in your sleeve

effects.log: On bad days you hold the thread. It is just a quiet afternoon. It is enough.

choices.text: Light a candle for it that evening

effects.log: A small light burns in your hall until morning, for no reason a god would need.

events.text: The loom passes the knot in the end, with a sound like a sigh from the whole workshop. {npc} marks the date. Unmyeong says nothing, but the next time you pass the loom-room the door is open a little wider than before.
events.arc: The Knot in the Weaver's Thread

choices.text: Stop in and say thank you for the open door

effects.log: You stop in. {npc} brings tea. For an hour you watch the threads go by, and you think each of them is a person.

choices.text: Walk on, glad

effects.log: You walk on, glad of a door that opens.

events.text: The council's minutes are written by {npc}, a minute-taker with a scribe's squint. Each season the real record sits in a locked drawer, and the published one goes out polished. {He} asks you to witness a page of the real record because {he} is afraid of dying with it unread.
events.arc: The Minutes That Were True

choices.text: Witness it and say nothing

effects.log: You read it. It is shabbier, funnier and a good deal crueller than the published one. You sign the margin.

choices.text: Ask {him} to publish it

effects.log: {npc} goes white. 'Never,' {he} says. But the word hangs in the drawer like a bell.

choices.text: Suggest {he} burn it, kindly

effects.log: {npc} shakes {his} head. Some truths are meant to be preserved, not told.

events.text: A senior god discovers there is a second record, and summons {npc}. The minute-taker comes to you, shaking, with the drawer under {his} arm. 'They will take it,' {he} says. 'Could you hold it for me?'
events.arc: The Minutes That Were True

choices.text: Hold it. A god may keep a drawer

effects.log: You lock it in your hall. For ninety years you are the quiet keeper of the council's real voice.

choices.text: Take it to the senior god yourself

effects.log: You hand it over with good grace. The senior god is silent a long time, then keeps it, and thanks you for the courtesy.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to hide it in the open, in a joke-book

effects.log: The record spends a century in the joke section of the archive. Nobody ever reads it.

events.text: {npc} dies, content, and the drawer comes to you in the post. A last note: 'Publish it when everyone in it is gone.' You are patient. You wait a thousand years. When the last name in it is forgotten, you open the drawer and read aloud to an empty hall.
events.arc: The Minutes That Were True

choices.text: Read it aloud, every funny word

effects.log: The empty hall seems to enjoy it. A dusty banner stirs in an old chair's place.

choices.text: Tell no one, and keep it

effects.log: It becomes one of the few private things you own.

events.text: The senior god's silence turns out to be a form of affection. Years pass. One night the drawer is returned to {npc} unread, with a note: 'It is better with you.' {He} bursts into tears and starts writing again.
events.arc: The Minutes That Were True

choices.text: Send a mug of the minute-taker's favourite tea

effects.log: The tea arrives hot. The minutes that season are the best the council has ever not published.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the drawer be

effects.log: You let the drawer be.

events.text: A minor god, {npc}, comes to your door after dark with a small bag. {He} belongs to a rival pantheon and has had enough: of the dinners, the rank, the dull sermons. {He} asks, in a very small voice, whether your pantheon might have a seat. There is a rule against it, ancient and quite clear.
events.arc: The God Who Wished to Change Pantheons

choices.text: Offer a seat and hide the rule

effects.log: You find {him} a chair at the end of a long table. The rule sleeps, for now, and so does the rival pantheon's temper.

choices.text: Send {him} to a neutral shrine

effects.log: A Masterless altar takes {him} in. It is not a seat, but it is a roof.

choices.text: Tell {him} the rule and see what {he} does

effects.log: {npc} nods, shoulders sinking. Then, after a long time, {he} asks what the rule is for.

events.text: The rival pantheon has found out. A herald arrives in perfect robes to ask, in the politest language ever spoken, for the return of a lost god. {npc} is behind a screen, shaking. The herald's eyes pass over the screen without stopping. This is a courtesy and a threat.
events.arc: The God Who Wished to Change Pantheons

choices.text: Refuse to answer, courteously, for a century

effects.log: The herald leaves with nothing. A cold wind blows between the pantheons, and {npc} stays.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to speak for {him}self to the herald

effects.log: {npc} steps out from behind the screen and says, steadily, no. The herald bows, and the rule is quietly rewritten.

choices.text: Offer the herald tea, and time

effects.log: The herald drinks the tea. The matter, as many matters do, drifts into a larger season.

events.text: A century on, {npc} sits at the table as if {he} had always done so, and has become the best-loved bore at supper. At the end of one long night {he} says: 'I did not know a god could choose.' You tell {him} it is the oldest rule of all, and the least observed.
events.arc: The God Who Wished to Change Pantheons

choices.text: Raise a cup to the one who chose

effects.log: The table raises its cups. It is a small toast, and it is remembered.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: {npc} stays in the end, in a quiet corner, without a seat on any list. The rival pantheon never forgives you and never quite stops trying to. It is, you reflect, a perfectly good enemy.
events.arc: The God Who Wished to Change Pantheons

choices.text: Send them a case of good wine each year

effects.log: They return the case unopened every year. It becomes a ritual with a rhythm and a taste of its own.

choices.text: Add a footnote to the old rule

effects.log: The footnote is eleven lines long and reads like an apology.

events.text: The council cannot begin without a quorum, and the quorum cannot be reached because three gods are, as always, late. {npc}, who has been waiting longest, sits with you on the hall steps. 'It is a thing, being on time,' {he} says. 'It is not a virtue. It is a grievance with a clock.'
events.arc: Waiting for a Quorum

choices.text: Start without the three, as a joke

effects.log: You begin to 'hold' the council on the steps. By the time the three arrive the whole hall is laughing, and they are not.

choices.text: Wait with {npc}, and talk

effects.log: You wait for an hour. {npc} tells you the history of every late god by name. It is the best hour of the year.

choices.text: Send a servant to fetch the three

effects.log: The servant returns an hour later, alone, with an apology from each.

events.text: The three late gods are discovered playing a gentle game of stones in the garden, quite happily, and have been since morning. {npc} stands in the doorway, torn between outrage and the secret wish to join.
events.arc: Waiting for a Quorum

choices.text: Join the game for one round

effects.log: The hall sits empty while the gods play. A secretary writes 'recess' in the minutes. It is the only decision made that day.

choices.text: Call them in with a bell

effects.log: They troop in, sheepish. The council opens, and the afternoon is long.

events.text: It becomes a custom: council opens with one round of stones in the garden. Nobody can say who started it. The quorum is always reached by the second round. {npc} is the best of the players and refuses, every year, to say how.
events.arc: Waiting for a Quorum

choices.text: Ask for a rematch against {npc}

effects.log: You lose, graciously, in nine moves. {npc} pours you a cup of tea and does not gloat.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: {npc} dies in the hall, at the table, mid-sentence, and the council goes on without a quorum for the first time. Nobody can quite remember how to begin. In the end it is you who says: 'Let us wait.'
events.arc: Waiting for a Quorum

choices.text: Wait with the others, in silence

effects.log: The hall waits. The silence is a very long one and very good.

choices.text: Light a candle for it that evening

effects.log: A small light burns in your hall until morning, for no reason a god would need.

events.text: A cushion has appeared on your council chair. No one admits to it. It is embroidered with a tiny pattern of your own domain's beasts. Under the cushion is a note: 'You looked uncomfortable last season. A friend.'

choices.text: Keep the cushion and say nothing

effects.log: You sit on it in silence for forty years. You never learn who gave it, and it is the best-kept kindness in the hall.

choices.text: Ask the hall who the friend is

effects.log: Nobody confesses. Three gods look away at once, smiling.

events.text: A senior god speaks for three hours on the subject of a ditch. Half the hall is asleep. The other half is pretending not to be. At the end the senior god turns to you and asks, with great courtesy, for your view.

choices.text: Say the ditch is fine

effects.log: The hall wakes in gratitude. The ditch is declared fine and the session closes at once.

choices.text: Offer a real point, and risk the long answer

ok.log: Your point is sound and short. The senior god is stunned by the brevity and agrees.

fail.log: Your point is lost in the senior god's reply, which takes another hour.

events.text: The council adjourns early for the first time in nine hundred years. Nobody knows what to do with the afternoon. A scattering of old gods stand about the hall like people at a station, looking at their hands.

choices.text: Invite three of them to your hall for tea

effects.log: They come. By evening you are laughing at a joke from before the sea was cut.

choices.text: Take a walk alone in the garden

effects.log: The garden, unvisited, is better than it has any right to be.

events.text: Gods of your pantheon wear a certain colour of scarf on feast days. You have forgotten yours. A young god, desperate to be correct, offers you a spare, folded in thirds, with a bow so deep it hurts to watch.

choices.text: Accept it with real thanks

effects.log: The scarf is a little too long. You wear it and the young god glows all feast.

choices.text: Decline, and go bare-necked

effects.log: The feast notices. Nobody mentions it. A senior god leaves their own scarf on the next chair, at the end of the night.

events.text: At the opening of the season your pantheon sings its old anthem. Half the gods have forgotten the second verse, which is about a flood nobody remembers. They hum it instead, with confidence. You find you remember it perfectly.

choices.text: Sing the second verse alone

effects.log: Your voice carries through the hall. Some of the old gods cry, some pretend not to. The hum becomes a song.

choices.text: Hum with the rest, politely

effects.log: You hum. The flood stays forgotten, and the anthem stays brisk.

events.text: Your pantheon collects a small tithe of prayers each season, a handful of faith toward the shared lamp. The collector, a kindly steward, arrives with a ledger and a sympathetic cough. You are slightly behind.

choices.text: Give what you can, and an apology

effects.log: The steward notes it with a kind smile. The lamp is slightly brighter.

choices.text: Argue that your shrine's smoke is better than its count

effects.log: The steward, charmed, writes 'quality noted.' It means nothing, but you are not quite ashamed.

events.text: Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars dusts them by hand every century, from a ladder that reaches nowhere, with a long soft brush. Today you pass beneath and Cheonho calls down: 'Hold the ladder? It is longer than it looks.'

choices.text: Hold the ladder

effects.log: You hold the ladder for an hour. A fine silver dust drifts down on your hair and does not wash out for a year.

choices.text: Offer to hold the lamp instead

effects.log: From below you watch the stars, one by one, come back to their full brightness.

events.text: Horang Lord of the Wild comes into the council hall in muddy boots, with half the forest still on them. Nobody says a word. A servant mops after with long suffering. Horang notices you smiling and winks, without breaking stride.

choices.text: Smile back and offer a cup of water

effects.log: Horang drinks it in one pull and sets the cup down gently. 'Good hall,' says Horang. 'Smells of rain.'

choices.text: Mop a boot-print yourself, as a joke

effects.log: The servant stares. The hall roars. Horang, delighted, leaves three more.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field keeps accounts of the harvest in a neat hand, and each year the accounts balance to the last grain. This year they are short by one seed. Pungnyeon finds you in the garden and asks, very courteously, whether you might have seen it.

choices.text: Say you have not, and help look

effects.log: You search the garden together on your knees. You find it under a leaf, a day later, sprouting. Pungnyeon leaves it.

choices.text: Say you will keep an eye out

effects.log: Pungnyeon thanks you gravely. The seed turns up in a pocket of the Golden Field's own coat.

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums practises on the roof of the hall at night, and the whole district keeps time without knowing it: cooks chop, children skip, mourners sway. You stand on the roof's edge and, without thinking, tap a rhythm on the tiles.

choices.text: Tap along, softly

effects.log: Noegong glances your way, smiles once, and adds a drum beneath yours. The district sleeps unusually well.

choices.text: Listen only

effects.log: The thunder under the drum is almost a language. You nearly understand.

events.text: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak has not moved in six thousand years, and a flock of small birds has built nests on the god's shoulder. Today one bird has laid an egg in the hollow of the god's ear. The egg hatches. Daeak's face does not change; a single tear rolls into the beard.

choices.text: Bring the nestlings a bowl of seed

effects.log: You leave the seed on the ledge. Daeak, unmoving, seems to approve.

choices.text: Sit on the ledge and say nothing

effects.log: You sit a day beside the great still god. Nothing is said. Nothing is needed.

events.text: A goddess you barely know has sent you a shawl, grey and soft, with a note that says only 'Cold in the high halls.' It is exactly the right weight. You have no idea how they knew.

choices.text: Wear it to the next council

effects.log: Three other gods, noting it, send shawls of their own. A new fashion starts.

choices.text: Send a jar of preserved plums in return

effects.log: The goddess writes back a single word: 'Excellent.' It is the start of a friendship of centuries.

events.text: Two goddesses are quarrelling in the corridor outside your hall, in the finest and most savage vocabulary you have ever heard, over the right to a certain song. One of them turns and says: 'You. Whose is it?'

choices.text: Say the song belongs to the one who sings it best

effects.log: They both begin to sing. The corridor rings. By the end they are weeping with laughter.

choices.text: Say you do not know the song

effects.log: They glare at you, forgive you, and resume. You slip away.

events.text: A goddess of orchards invites you to the grove at the turning of the year to taste a fruit no one else has ever tried, a plum of a colour you cannot name. The goddess watches you bite it with the focus of a god awaiting a verdict.

choices.text: Tell the goddess the truth: it is strange and wonderful

effects.log: The goddess lets out a breath held for a century. The tree is renamed in your honour.

choices.text: Say nothing, and ask for another

effects.log: The goddess laughs aloud and gives you a basket.

events.text: The court scribes have run out of the good ink, and a mid-ranked clerk is crying quietly into the sleeve of a robe. A treaty needs signing by dusk, and the only ink in the hall is the grey stuff used for laundry lists.

choices.text: Lend your own bottle

effects.log: The treaty is signed in your ink. A small smell of sandalwood clings to the agreement for centuries.

choices.text: Suggest signing in water, then fixing it with breath

effects.log: The scribe breathes. The signature bakes into the paper like a memory. The clerk is stunned.

events.text: A petitioner has stood in the hall of petitions for seventy years waiting to be heard, with a rolled paper and a patient expression. Nobody can find the petition's office. The petitioner has stopped expecting to be heard, and now simply stands, as though standing were the request.

choices.text: Sit with the petitioner and read the paper

effects.log: The paper asks for a spring to be moved ten paces to the left. You move it. The petitioner bows and goes home.

choices.text: Show the petitioner to the right office

effects.log: The right office is two doors down. The petitioner weeps with a kind of exhausted joy.

events.text: At the court gate there is a bell any god may ring to be received. Nobody rings it. Today a very old and very small god rings it, three times, and then looks up at the gatekeepers with the hope of someone who has been told to ring and not what happens next.

choices.text: Receive the small god yourself

effects.log: You lead them in. They are the god of a single doorstep and have come to complain about the weather. You listen to all of it.

choices.text: Send a servant with a stool and tea

effects.log: The small god drinks the tea and gives the servant a medal made of a bottle-cap.

events.text: At the feast you are asked to give the toast, on a theme given only as 'something true.' The whole table goes silent, because no god has dared something true at a feast in a long time. A servant stops mid-pour.

choices.text: Toast the cooks

effects.log: The kitchen, hearing, bursts into tears and then into song. It is the best toast in memory.

choices.text: Toast the table's secret grief, and hope it lands

ok.log: Your toast lands true. The table lifts its cups in a long, grave quiet.

fail.log: Your toast is too true. A cup is quietly set down and a chair pushed back.

events.text: After the feast the long tables are left with enough for an army. The gods drift away. A line of mortals' ghosts, tiny and patient, have gathered at the kitchen door in the hope of scraps. They are very polite about it.

choices.text: Feed them from the high table

effects.log: They eat with astonishing gravity. A small ghost thanks you in a thin voice and fades.

choices.text: Send a servant with a basket and walk away

effects.log: You walk away. Behind you the basket is emptied and the line disperses, content.

events.text: The seat card at the feast has your name on it, in the writing of a hand you do not know, on a chair at the foot of the table, and under it, very small: 'Not for any reason. I like the view.' Whoever wrote it is not there.

choices.text: Take the seat and enjoy the view

effects.log: From the foot of the table you can see the whole hall at once. It is a better seat than the head.

choices.text: Swap with a god who looks tired

effects.log: The tired god sits in the foot's quiet and lets out a long sigh. You take their seat, and they take your grudge.

events.text: The keeper of your hill shrine, {npc}, is a bent old person who sweeps the same flagstones every dawn and talks to you as to a slow cousin. Today {he} announces that {his} grandchild will take over when {he} is gone. 'The child is clumsy,' {he} warns. 'Be patient.'
events.arc: Three Keepers of the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Promise patience

effects.log: You send a small warm breath across the porch. {npc} nods as though a contract had been signed.

choices.text: Ask to meet the child in a dream

effects.log: The child dreams of a quiet hall and a tall figure who says nothing. It wakes wanting to sweep.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch

effects.log: You watch the old keeper sweep, the dust rising and settling, and know the line will go on.

events.text: {npc} is gone, and the grandchild has taken the broom and broken three lamps in the first week. The porch smells of spilled oil. The child sits on the step, defeated, and addresses you for the first time, in a small cracked voice, with no idea if anyone is listening.
events.arc: Three Keepers of the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Let a lamp relight by itself

effects.log: A lamp flickers on, steady, by the child's knee. The child stares, then slowly picks up the broom.

choices.text: Answer in a dream with the old keeper's voice

effects.log: The child wakes in tears and sweeps for nine hours straight.

choices.text: Let the child struggle

effects.log: The child learns the porch the slow way. A god can be a patient teacher by being absent.

events.text: A decade on, the child keeps the shrine better than the old keeper ever did, with a ledger, a roster of helpers and a small shop of charms. The shrine is lovely and busy and a little loud. At dusk the keeper sits alone on the step and says: 'Is it still you in there?'
events.arc: Three Keepers of the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Send the evening wind through the porch bells

effects.log: The keeper laughs, wipes {npc}'s eyes, and tells the empty porch about the day.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: The grandchild, grown, leaves the hill for a city and a different trade. The shrine is left in the care of a neighbour's boy, who is eleven and takes it very seriously. The old line is broken and a new one begins, with a hesitant wave.
events.arc: Three Keepers of the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Accept the new keeper without ceremony

effects.log: You accept. The boy sweeps a little too hard. The flagstones are cleaner than they have ever been.

choices.text: Send the old keepers a message in the wind

effects.log: Somewhere, two sweeps of a broom answer your wind.

events.text: The step to your oldest shrine is worn into a dip by ten thousand pilgrim knees. A mason, {npc}, has come to replace it with new stone. 'It is just a step,' {he} says, brushing off dust. 'It is going to break someone's ankle.'
events.arc: The Step Worn by Ten Thousand Knees

choices.text: Let the mason replace it

effects.log: The new step is smooth, white and slightly cold. Pilgrims touch it and look uneasy.

choices.text: Ask the mason to keep the old one in the wall

effects.log: The old step is set in the wall beside the door. Pilgrims touch it for luck. It is warm.

choices.text: Soften the old stone with a quiet thought

effects.log: The dip stays, but the edges round. Nobody falls, and nothing is lost.

events.text: A pilgrim, very old, has come all the way to kneel on the worn step and cannot find it. {npc} is on the road trying to explain. The pilgrim does not seem to mind: 'It was never the stone,' the pilgrim says, kneeling on the new one. 'It was the knees.'
events.arc: The Step Worn by Ten Thousand Knees

choices.text: Warm the new stone for the pilgrim

effects.log: The stone warms to the pilgrim's touch for the first time. It is a very small miracle and the pilgrim weeps.

choices.text: Let the pilgrim have the discovery

effects.log: The pilgrim kneels, content. The mason watches, thoughtful.

events.text: {npc} comes back years later, grey, to see the step. It is already worn, a little, by a generation of knees. 'I'd wanted it to last,' {he} says. 'I forgot what lasting is.' {He} kneels on it, creaking, and prays to you with a mason's plain care.
events.arc: The Step Worn by Ten Thousand Knees

choices.text: Answer by warming the stone again

effects.log: The stone warms. The mason, kneeling, does not look up.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: The step in the wall grows famous. A fretful merchant offers a lot of faith for a chip of it. The keepers have to decide if a step can be sold in pieces. Pilgrims arrive to see them argue.
events.arc: The Step Worn by Ten Thousand Knees

choices.text: Bless the keepers' refusal

effects.log: The keepers refuse, and the step is left whole. The merchant leaves a candle at the porch instead.

choices.text: Let them decide without you

effects.log: They decide to keep it. It takes eleven hours and a pot of tea.

events.text: {npc} is a novice in your temple and has been honest enough to tell the head priest, in front of the whole congregation, that {he} is not sure you exist. The head priest turns purple. The congregation holds its breath. You are, as it happens, listening.
events.arc: The Novice Who Did Not Believe

choices.text: Send a small sign to the novice

effects.log: A butterfly lands on {npc}'s sleeve and stays an hour. {He} watches it solemnly, unconvinced, but moved.

choices.text: Praise the novice's honesty in a dream

effects.log: {npc} wakes puzzled. 'I dreamed a god said thank you for asking,' {he} tells the head priest, who is not pleased.

choices.text: Do nothing. Let the doubt be

effects.log: You keep your silence. It is the most respectful thing you can do.

events.text: {npc} has been given the hardest work in the temple: scrubbing the stairs. {He} scrubs for a year, thinking. One evening {he} asks the empty hall a plain question: 'If you are there, why are the stairs always dirty?'
events.arc: The Novice Who Did Not Believe

choices.text: Let the stairs stay clean for one evening

effects.log: The stairs gleam. {npc} sits down on them and laughs until the lamps gutter.

choices.text: Answer: because they are walked on

effects.log: A whisper in the stone, soft as dust. {npc} goes still, then nods slowly.

choices.text: Let the question echo

effects.log: The hall carries the question to the roof. Nobody answers, and that is its own kind of answer.

events.text: {npc} stays at the temple, still not sure about you, and becomes the most beloved teacher of novices. 'I'll tell you what I don't know,' {he} begins each lesson. It is the best sermon the temple has ever heard.
events.arc: The Novice Who Did Not Believe

choices.text: Visit a lesson, unseen, at the back

effects.log: You sit at the back. At the end {npc} looks directly at your corner and says: 'Thank you for coming.'

choices.text: Light a candle for it that evening

effects.log: A small light burns in your hall until morning, for no reason a god would need.

events.text: {npc} leaves the temple, sure at last that you do not exist, and becomes a gentle keeper of a lighthouse. Each night {he} says good evening to the sea. You answer through the wind, softly, and {he} never tells a soul.
events.arc: The Novice Who Did Not Believe

choices.text: Keep answering the lighthouse

effects.log: For thirty years you answer. It is the strangest, truest prayer you ever kept.

choices.text: Let the sea answer in your place

effects.log: The sea answers, and the lighthouse keeper is content.

events.text: A poet, {npc}, has written a long, witty and entirely unfair poem against you. It is on every tongue in the lowland towns. It says your wind is cheap, your thunder a pose, your shrines full of flatterers. The worst of it is that two lines are true.
events.arc: The Poet Who Wrote Against You

choices.text: Answer with a quiet gift of rain to the poet's fields

effects.log: The poet's fields are green all summer. {He} writes a second poem, which is more unfair than the first, and a little less sure.

choices.text: Send a dream with the two true lines marked

effects.log: {npc} wakes up shaken. {He} has not told anyone why.

choices.text: Ignore it. A god is not so thin-skinned

effects.log: You ignore it for nine years. It becomes a classic.

events.text: {npc} comes to your shrine at last, in person, to see what {he} had been writing about. The shrine is small, honest and a little cracked. The poet stands inside a long time. 'It is not what I wrote,' {he} says to the empty room.
events.arc: The Poet Who Wrote Against You

choices.text: Let a candle light itself beside the poet

effects.log: The candle burns steady. {npc} sits down in front of it and does not say a word.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let the poet look

effects.log: {npc} looks at the shrine for an hour and leaves, thoughtful.

events.text: {npc} publishes a third poem, brief and plain, which says: 'I was wrong about the thunder.' It spreads in the lowlands faster than the first. Critics call it weak. The common folk learn it by heart.
events.arc: The Poet Who Wrote Against You

choices.text: Answer with a very soft thunder at dusk

effects.log: The thunder rolls once, low and amused. The poet laughs out loud, alone on a hill.

choices.text: Tell no one, and keep it

effects.log: It becomes one of the few private things you own.

events.text: The poet dies bitter and cheerful, and the unfair poem outlives every shrine you own. Children recite it on the roads. In the last verse there is one line, true, that you have kept in the back of your hall for five hundred years.
events.arc: The Poet Who Wrote Against You

choices.text: Put the line on the shrine wall yourself

effects.log: A pilgrim carves it. Visitors read it and nod. The shrine is a little more honest after that.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself

effects.log: You keep it. It is a good line.

events.text: {npc} has crossed three rivers to leave a rival god's shrine for yours. {He} stands in your doorway with a bundle and an expression of sheepish defiance. 'Your wind smelled better,' {he} says. It is the whole reason, and it is enough.
events.arc: The Convert From the Other Shore

choices.text: Welcome {him} and say nothing of the rival

effects.log: {npc} unpacks in your shrine's side room. By evening {he} is sweeping the porch as though {he} had always been there.

choices.text: Warn {him} that gods do not like losing worshippers

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'I know. I am prepared.' {He} is not, but it is a good beginning.

choices.text: Send {him} back with a loaf, to say goodbye properly

effects.log: {npc} goes back and says goodbye to the old god, in person, with a loaf. It takes a week.

events.text: The rival god has noticed. A cold wind blows through your hall one night, and a dream arrives for {npc}: a long mournful face, quite hurt. {He} wakes up in a sweat and wants to go back.
events.arc: The Convert From the Other Shore

choices.text: Appear to {npc} in a dream and keep {him} company

effects.log: You sit with {npc} in the dream for an hour. {He} stays.

choices.text: Send a note to the rival god, very polite

effects.log: The rival replies in three days: 'Do take care of {him}.' It is a defeat that feels like a gift.

choices.text: Let {npc} choose alone

effects.log: {npc} chooses to stay, and it is {his} choice, which is better than yours.

events.text: {npc} has become a quiet pillar of the shrine, and at the festival the old rival's own priests come across the river for a visit. They eat at one table. {npc} is called upon to speak, and, uncertainly, thanks both gods by name.
events.arc: The Convert From the Other Shore

choices.text: Answer both thanks with a single breeze

effects.log: The breeze passes over the whole table. The two sets of priests exchange startled looks, and then smiles.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: {npc} goes home to the other shore in the end, old and unsure, to be buried there. The rival god receives {him} with courtesy. You send a wind for the funeral from far across the water, and the rival, after a pause, lets it in.
events.arc: The Convert From the Other Shore

choices.text: Keep sending winds across the river

effects.log: A friendship of winds begins. The two shrines end up sharing a festival.

choices.text: Let the rivals have their grief

effects.log: You let it be. A god's silence is sometimes a courtesy.

events.text: {npc} has prayed to you every morning for thirty years. This morning there is no prayer. You wait. Noon passes. Evening. The silence is a small flat stone in the middle of your day, and you are surprised how much it weighs.
events.arc: The One Who Stopped Praying

choices.text: Send a dream to ask what is wrong

effects.log: {npc} dreams of you, awake, and answers: 'I am tired.' It is not a refusal. It is a person.

choices.text: Wait another day

effects.log: The next morning the prayer comes, shorter, and with a different tune.

choices.text: Look in on {him} as a bird

effects.log: From a windowsill you see {npc} asleep in the chair, a bowl of cold tea beside {him}. You cover {him} with a breeze.

events.text: {npc}'s prayers stop for good after a death in the family. You know the reason. The silence is not hostile. {He} has simply run out of words for you. A small bowl of rice still sits before your altar each day, and nothing more.
events.arc: The One Who Stopped Praying

choices.text: Appear at the altar in a plain coat

effects.log: You sit at the altar and eat the rice. {npc} comes in, sees a stranger, and sits down quietly beside you. Neither of you speaks.

choices.text: Leave the silence alone

effects.log: You do not push. The bowl of rice goes on. The two of you keep the same quiet for years.

choices.text: Tell a dream of {his} dead to the sleeper

effects.log: {He} dreams a gentle dream of the dead, laughing in a kitchen. It helps, a little.

events.text: A decade later {npc} prays again, one word, no more. It is your name, said as one says the name of a neighbour who has been away. You answer with the very smallest wind, in the porch bells, and {he} smiles at the empty room.
events.arc: The One Who Stopped Praying

choices.text: Say nothing more, and let the bells ring

effects.log: The bells ring. The word was enough.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: {npc} never prays again, but the bowl of rice goes on sitting before your altar every morning until {he} dies, and for a long time after, set there by whoever lives in the house. You eat it, in a plain coat, when you can.
events.arc: The One Who Stopped Praying

choices.text: Eat the rice every year on the day

effects.log: Once a year a stranger in a plain coat sits at an altar and eats a small bowl of rice. It becomes the best habit you have.

choices.text: Let the rice be

effects.log: You let it be. The house keeps it.

events.text: A pilgrim named {npc} has started walking toward your furthest shrine. It is a forty-year walk by the slow road, and {he} intends to do it on foot, in sandals, with one bag. Nobody has told {him} the shrine was abandoned a century ago. {He} is already past the first ridge.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Rebuild the shrine at the road's end

effects.log: A modest hall, patient and plain, rises at the end of the road. A pair of wandering carpenters, who will never know why, get the job.

choices.text: Walk a few days with {him} as a stranger

effects.log: You walk. {npc} tells you the whole plan, which is mostly about the weather. You are a very good listener.

choices.text: Leave the shrine ruined and see what the pilgrim does

effects.log: The pilgrim's walk will be long. You do not wish to change what is being decided.

events.text: Twenty years in, {npc} has gone grey, slow and thoughtful. The road has become the point. {He} sleeps in barns and teaches songs to children for bread. The shrine is a rumour. At each inn {he} gives your name to people who have never heard it.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Send a mild wind at {his} back each morning

effects.log: The road gets easier. {npc} credits {his} knees to a good diet.

choices.text: Let {him} walk without help

effects.log: {npc} walks alone. The road, in its way, is the prayer.

events.text: {npc} arrives at the end of the road, white-haired and tired, and finds the shrine you built. {He} sits on its step for a day, utterly still. Then {he} says, out loud, 'It was worth it,' and does not say whether the shrine or the road is meant.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Warm the step under {him}

effects.log: {npc} dozes in the sun on the warm step. It is the best nap of {his} life.

choices.text: Light a candle for it that evening

effects.log: A small light burns in your hall until morning, for no reason a god would need.

events.text: The pilgrim reaches the ruin and finds only stones. {He} laughs for a long time. Then {he} builds a small lean-to out of the best of them, and prays under it, happy. You decide not to build anything. Some shrines are best made by the one who arrives.
events.arc: The Pilgrim of Forty Years

choices.text: Send a small flock of birds to nest in the lean-to

effects.log: The birds nest. The pilgrim names them all.

choices.text: Pray back, once, in {his} own words

effects.log: You pray back, once, in a pilgrim's voice, to a pilgrim, in a ruin.

events.text: A child named {npc} has been told to thank you for the rain, and has refused. 'I did not ask for it,' {npc} says clearly to the sky. 'And it ruined my kite.' The parents are mortified. You are enchanted.
events.arc: The Child Who Argued Back

choices.text: Dry the kite with a warm wind

effects.log: The kite dries in an instant and takes flight. {npc} looks up and says, grudgingly, 'Fine. Thank you. A little.'

choices.text: Answer in a dream: because the fields were thirsty

effects.log: {npc} wakes and considers this. 'Fields can ask,' {he} concedes, 'but they should say please.'

choices.text: Let {him} be angry

effects.log: The child scowls at the sky for an hour, then plays in the puddles.

events.text: {npc} is twelve now and has built a small shrine of mud and sticks to you, with a hand-lettered sign: 'God of Rain: complaints box.' There is, indeed, a box. It is full. Half the valley has used it.
events.arc: The Child Who Argued Back

choices.text: Answer the complaints box, one by one, in dreams

effects.log: The valley wakes to find its complaints addressed. The weather grows slightly more reasonable.

choices.text: Add a note of your own to the box

effects.log: 'Apologies,' it says, in no hand. The valley talks of nothing else for a week.

choices.text: Leave the box alone

effects.log: The box is a quiet joke you keep.

events.text: {npc} grows up to be a clerk of the harvest, stern and funny. At the end of {his} life, {he} dictates a complaint to the box and has it read aloud. It says: 'The weather was acceptable. I should like to keep it.'
events.arc: The Child Who Argued Back

choices.text: Answer with an exact, gentle rain at the funeral

effects.log: The rain falls on the mourners for an hour. 'Acceptable,' someone whispers, and everyone laughs through tears.

choices.text: Tell no one, and keep it

effects.log: It becomes one of the few private things you own.

events.text: The child grows into a farmer of few words who forgets the mud shrine until the box is found in an attic. The farmer reads the complaints aloud to grandchildren, who laugh. The old god of rain has not complained in thirty years.
events.arc: The Child Who Argued Back

choices.text: Send a rainbow to the attic window

effects.log: The grandchildren cheer. The old farmer says nothing, and puts the box back.

choices.text: Leave the rainbow unsaid

effects.log: You keep the thought, and the rain.

events.text: {npc}, a young goddess of a single mountain pass, takes a seat at council for the first time and sits on the hem of a robe. {He} is trembling. {His} domain is the size of a courtyard. The gods around {him} are polite in the way of those about to eat.
events.arc: A Young Goddess at Her First Council

choices.text: Sit next to {him} and make small talk

effects.log: You discuss, with a straight face, the weather in {his} pass. {npc} relaxes enough to say something clever.

choices.text: Introduce {him} to a kind senior god

effects.log: The senior god takes {npc} under a wing. The wing is long and the council notices.

choices.text: Let {him} find {his} feet

effects.log: {npc} finds {his} feet in forty minutes. It is the fastest anyone has ever done it.

events.text: A year on, {npc} has turned out to be unexpectedly sharp, and quite a few gods are afraid of {him}. At feast {he} asks you, over the wine, whether it is acceptable for a small goddess to be disliked. 'Because I am,' {he} says. 'And I rather like it.'
events.arc: A Young Goddess at Her First Council

choices.text: Say it is the surest sign of a real voice

effects.log: {npc} raises a cup to you. A small rivalry with a large god begins, and everyone enjoys it.

choices.text: Warn {him} gently about the long memory of gods

effects.log: {npc} listens. 'Memory,' {he} says, 'is a sword that cuts both ways.'

choices.text: Pour {him} another cup

effects.log: You pour. {He} drinks, steady.

events.text: A century later {npc} holds a council seat of real weight, and {his} pass has become a thoroughfare for a hundred towns. On {his} first day at the high chair {he} finds, under the cushion, a note in your hand: 'Sit on the hem of your robe.' {He} laughs aloud in front of everyone.
events.arc: A Young Goddess at Her First Council

choices.text: Smile across the hall

effects.log: {npc} holds your eye across the council, the way one holds a hand.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: The senior god who took {npc} in dies at last, in the middle of a council, and the young goddess weeps in public. {npc} says only: 'I was frightened, and someone was kind.' It becomes the most-quoted line in the hall.
events.arc: A Young Goddess at Her First Council

choices.text: Rise and say the same of your own early days

effects.log: You rise. The hall listens. For a quarter of an hour nobody is a god.

choices.text: Sit beside {him} until the hall empties

effects.log: The hall empties. You do not leave {him}.

events.text: A spring flood has carried off your riverside shrine, roof, bell, altar and all. The keeper, {npc}, stands on the bank in wet clothes holding the only thing recovered: a spoon. 'It was in the porch,' {he} says. 'I do not know why I took it.'
events.arc: The Shrine the River Took

choices.text: Rebuild at once, bigger

effects.log: A grand shrine rises on higher ground. It is lovely and a little cold.

choices.text: Rebuild small, from what the river left

effects.log: {npc} and some neighbours gather boards and bells from the mud. The new shrine is crooked and loved.

choices.text: Let the river keep it

effects.log: The river sings over the old altar. You do not interrupt.

events.text: The river is calm again. {npc} brings the spoon to the new shrine each morning and sets it on the altar, and says that it is a very good spoon. A stranger passing through asks what god is honoured here, and the keeper says: 'The one who lets us keep the spoon.'
events.arc: The Shrine the River Took

choices.text: Let the stranger leave a coin for the spoon

effects.log: The stranger leaves a coin and a small bell. The altar grows by two things.

choices.text: Answer the keeper in the bell's note

effects.log: The bell rings once, a small clear note, without a hand to ring it.

events.text: A generation later the spoon is the shrine's holiest relic, though nobody knows why. It is carried in procession each flood season. A priest recites its history, which is entirely invented and entirely true in spirit.
events.arc: The Shrine the River Took

choices.text: Add one true detail to the invented history, in a dream

effects.log: The priest wakes, adds a line, and weeps. The history is now seventy per cent true.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: The grand shrine thrives. The spoon, found in the rubble, is sent to a museum of the court, labelled 'domestic.' {npc} dies without seeing it again. A visiting god notices the label and quietly takes the spoon home.
events.arc: The Shrine the River Took

choices.text: Return the spoon to the small chapel by the river

effects.log: It rests at last on a modest shelf, next to a handful of fresh flowers.

choices.text: Keep it, and eat soup from it in secret

effects.log: It is, in fact, a very good spoon.

events.text: {npc}, a priest at one of your larger shrines, is taking a little from the offering plate each week. Nothing grand. A handful here, a bun there. {He} thinks you do not see. You see very well, and are not sure what to do with what you see.
events.arc: The Priest Who Skimmed the Offering

choices.text: Appear in a dream and say nothing, only look

effects.log: {npc} wakes in a cold sweat and returns two weeks' worth. It is not enough, but it is a start.

choices.text: Let the shrine's collection drop for a month

effects.log: The offering plate empties, mysteriously. {npc} grows pale and then thoughtful.

choices.text: Ask a neighbouring god what is usual

effects.log: The neighbour sighs. 'Usual,' they say, 'is very common indeed.'

events.text: It turns out {npc} has a sick parent and a small salary. The skimming is not greed but arithmetic. A deacon has found out and proposes to report {him} to the council of priests. {npc} is pale in the doorway of your shrine at midnight, begging you without a word.
events.arc: The Priest Who Skimmed the Offering

choices.text: Quietly arrange a better salary for {him}

effects.log: A sympathetic merchant endows a stipend. {npc} never knows why, but never skims again.

choices.text: Let the deacon's report run its course

effects.log: The council of priests hears it and suspends {npc} for a season. It is just, and hard.

choices.text: Send the deacon a dream of their own small sins

effects.log: The deacon withdraws the report and spends a month being kinder.

events.text: Years later {npc} is head priest, honest and unforgiving of the dishonest. The shrine's accounts are public. A new young priest skims a bun, and {npc} says to the empty room: 'I know how it starts.' The bun is replaced and the matter is closed.
events.arc: The Priest Who Skimmed the Offering

choices.text: Answer with a quiet laugh in the rafters

effects.log: The head priest startles, then laughs. 'You too,' {he} murmurs.

choices.text: Light a candle for it that evening

effects.log: A small light burns in your hall until morning, for no reason a god would need.

events.text: {npc} serves the suspension and returns thin and silent, and the shrine's accounts are never wrong again. There is no joy in the priest, though, only correctness, and the congregation feels it. Nobody laughs on the porch.
events.arc: The Priest Who Skimmed the Offering

choices.text: Send a child with a lost kitten into the shrine

effects.log: The child and the kitten run through the priest's quiet hall. {npc}, startled, almost smiles.

choices.text: Let correctness do its work

effects.log: You let it. Some mending takes more than a god.

events.text: A mountain valley that has worshipped you for six hundred years has, in a single season, changed its mind. A newer god of harvest-songs has come through, and the valley loves the songs. {npc}, your last priest there, stands alone in the porch and asks, uncertainly, if you are still wanted.
events.arc: The Valley That Changed Its Mind

choices.text: Sing back, in your own awkward voice

effects.log: The valley hears a dry, rough tune across the fields. It is not good. It is, strangely, endearing.

choices.text: Let the valley go, and bless the new god

effects.log: You send a blessing to the singing god. It is accepted with astonishment, and the valley remembers.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to rest and not to worry

effects.log: {npc} rests. The valley goes on singing.

events.text: Autumn comes. The singing god is a lovely thing and a poor fit for hail. When a storm threatens the terraces the valley comes quietly up the hill with a basket of apples and no explanation. {npc} meets them at the porch. 'It's a matter of range,' {he} says gently.
events.arc: The Valley That Changed Its Mind

choices.text: Turn the hail aside, wordlessly

effects.log: The hail falls on the empty road. The valley looks at the sky, then at the porch, then at the apples.

choices.text: Let the valley see what it chose

effects.log: The hail falls. The valley loses part of a harvest. It learns.

events.text: Two gods share the valley now, and nobody minds. At the harvest feast a singer and a priest take turns at the centre of the ring, and when the wind picks up there is no telling whether it is a song or a prayer. It is both.
events.arc: The Valley That Changed Its Mind

choices.text: Stay in the wind and listen

effects.log: The song goes up and the prayer goes down, and in the middle is the whole valley.

choices.text: Tell no one, and keep it

effects.log: It becomes one of the few private things you own.

events.text: You sing your awkward song every year at harvest, always off-key, and the valley, which has not forgotten you, joins in on purpose out of tune. It is the worst choir in the realm and the best.
events.arc: The Valley That Changed Its Mind

choices.text: Rehearse a little in a quiet place

effects.log: You rehearse. It does not help. The valley adores the error.

choices.text: Go on being awkward

effects.log: You go on being awkward.

events.text: Your worshippers in the northern towns have split. Half say you are blue, half say green. It has become a dispute with banners and carts. {npc}, the arbiter, arrives at your hall with a bundle of petitions and a look of serious despair. 'Well?' {he} asks. 'Which is it?'
events.arc: The Schism Over Your Colour

choices.text: Say you are both

effects.log: The arbiter writes this down with a sigh. The towns do not accept it, but the carts stop being thrown.

choices.text: Say neither: you are the colour of whoever sees you

effects.log: {npc} is stunned. The answer is posted in every town. A good third of them accept it, and the dispute becomes theological.

choices.text: Say you have never cared

effects.log: {npc} drops the petitions in the fire in relief. The fire is blue and then green.

events.text: The argument lingers in smaller form. In one town a baker makes blue buns for the blues and green buns for the greens, and everyone eats both. {npc} writes you with some hope: the dispute has reached the stage where it is most useful, which is as dinner.
events.arc: The Schism Over Your Colour

choices.text: Bless the buns

effects.log: The buns become the most celebrated in the north. The dispute changes into a rivalry between bakers.

choices.text: Appear at the baker's counter and buy one of each

effects.log: The baker nearly drops the tray. You are, apparently, polite and hungry.

events.text: A generation on the colour dispute is a festival: a day of blue lanterns and green lanterns that, by evening, are all hung together, and nobody can tell which are which. The arbiter's grandchild lights the last lantern, and it is, for a moment, a colour you have no name for.
events.arc: The Schism Over Your Colour

choices.text: Colour the last lantern with a thought

effects.log: The last lantern is both and neither. The crowd gasps in joy.

choices.text: Let it pass in silence

effects.log: You let the moment pass without a word, and it is whole all the same.

events.text: The dispute hardens in the high towns, where the blues refuse to speak to the greens for generations, and the arbiter's chair becomes a seat of petty power. You watch it with a sad detachment. A god cannot unmake an argument people have grown fond of.
events.arc: The Schism Over Your Colour

choices.text: Send a long rain over all the towns at once

effects.log: The rain falls on blue and green alike. For a week nobody quarrels, being wet.

choices.text: Let it run its course

effects.log: You let it run. Colours are only colours.

events.text: Your great hall on the plain was once full. Today it holds one old worshipper, {npc}, who sweeps, trims lamps and lights incense for the sole benefit of a god who is, at this moment, standing at the back in a plain coat. 'The others will come back,' {he} says, to no one.
events.arc: The Hall With One Worshipper

choices.text: Introduce yourself as a visitor and help sweep

effects.log: You sweep side by side. {npc} tells you the history of the hall. Half of it is wrong. You love every word.

choices.text: Send a crowd of echoes through the hall at dusk

effects.log: The hall fills with the sound of a thousand pilgrims. {npc} stands still, tears in {his} eyes, and bows to the nothing.

choices.text: Stay at the back and be quiet

effects.log: You stay at the back. It is the quietest hour of your life.

events.text: A rumour has reached the plain that the hall's old god is dying for lack of faith. It is not true, but it moves. Pilgrims arrive in a trickle out of pity. {npc} treats each with the same ceremony as a crowd. Some stay.
events.arc: The Hall With One Worshipper

choices.text: Let the pilgrims feel the god's warmth

effects.log: A gentle warmth fills the hall. Several pilgrims fall to their knees. The rumour changes to a different rumour.

choices.text: Let the rumour stand, and see who comes

effects.log: Those who come out of pity stay for faith. It takes two years.

events.text: {npc} dies on a winter night in the hall, with a lit lamp, among thirty worshippers who came because {he} did. The hall is full for the first time in a century, at a funeral. You stand at the back and say a quiet word. It is the only prayer you have ever made.
events.arc: The Hall With One Worshipper

choices.text: Stay until the lamps burn down

effects.log: The lamps burn down. You are the last to leave, and you leave the door open.

choices.text: Take a slow walk afterwards

effects.log: You walk the long way home, and the realm seems a little kinder for it.

events.text: {npc} goes on sweeping an empty hall until the day {he} dies, never knowing that anyone heard. The hall closes. You take its lamp and keep it. It burns ever after in your hall, at the back, in a place where nobody sees.
events.arc: The Hall With One Worshipper

choices.text: Let the lamp burn for {him}

effects.log: It burns for a thousand years, steady, small. It is the smallest light in your house and the brightest.

choices.text: Give the lamp to a new shrine

effects.log: It lights a new shrine, a long way off, with a keeper who sweeps.

events.text: The bell rope at your small roadside shrine is frayed and the keeper has patched it with a bit of red wool. Every traveller who rings it adds a knot of their own thread. It is now a fat, ridiculous rope, and the bell sounds, you think, rather happy.

choices.text: Ring it softly yourself

effects.log: You ring once. A traveller down the road turns and smiles at nothing.

choices.text: Add a thread of your own, grey

effects.log: The rope has one more colour in it. The bell is a note richer.

events.text: Someone has left a wheel of cheese at your shrine. It is very large and quite ripe. The keeper has been fretting for a week about what a god does with cheese. 'They are expecting something,' the keeper tells you. 'I feel it.'

choices.text: Eat it, in a plain coat, with the keeper

effects.log: You eat the cheese with the keeper on the porch, saying little. It is excellent.

choices.text: Bless the cheese and send it to a hungry house

effects.log: The cheese goes to a family down the lane. A new name is added to the faithful.

events.text: A grey cat has taken up residence on your shrine's altar and will not move. The keeper is scandalised. Pilgrims are charmed and have begun to leave small fish. The cat looks at you with a dry, unimpressed expression, as one who has known gods before.

choices.text: Send a mouse as an offering to the cat

effects.log: The cat receives the mouse with cool dignity and eats it behind the altar. The matter is settled.

choices.text: Let the cat keep the altar

effects.log: The cat keeps the altar. Pilgrims touch its ears for luck and, it seems, receive some.

events.text: A keeper sweeps a back room of the shrine and finds a hundred small paper wishes tucked into cracks in the wall, going back generations, mostly illegible. Most are for health, a handful for love, one for a better knife. The keeper sits on the floor and reads them all.

choices.text: Grant the one for a better knife

effects.log: A knife turns up at the market stall of the old writer's descendant, cheap and perfect.

choices.text: Let the wishes stay in the wall

effects.log: They stay, warm and unread, a little archive of ordinary hope.

events.text: Moss has covered your oldest standing stone and a local child has decided that the moss is a small god of its own. The child feeds it water in a thimble. You, who have been called many things, have never been replaced by a lichen.

choices.text: Honour the moss-god with a very good rain

effects.log: The moss swells green and the child dances. Your own stone, beneath, hums slightly.

choices.text: Pay a quiet visit to the moss-god as a peer

effects.log: The moss says nothing. It is a good listener and has all the time in the world.

events.text: The keeper of your lakeside shrine is to be married, and has asked, in the shy way of mortals, whether the god might attend. The wedding is small, held on the porch, and the guests have been told to leave a seat empty.

choices.text: Attend in a plain coat and sit in the empty seat

effects.log: You sit in the empty seat. The couple look at you once, and look away, and do not stop smiling.

choices.text: Send a gentle west wind through the porch at the vows

effects.log: The wind lifts a veil. The couple feel blessed, and the guests feel an unexpected urge to hold hands.

events.text: A temple choir sings a hymn to you every dawn, and in forty years nobody has noticed that the third verse contains a rude word, the result of a scribe's slip centuries ago. You know, and you are very fond of it.

choices.text: Let it go on

effects.log: The rude word sounds, once a day, in four-part harmony. It is the most reverent thing in the realm.

choices.text: Correct it gently in a dream to the choirmaster

effects.log: The choirmaster wakes and fixes the verse, with a wistful look. The hymn is a shade duller.

events.text: The head priest of your oldest temple wishes to retire, after sixty years, and cannot choose a successor. The two candidates are a gifted scold and a generous fool. They sit side by side on the steps, each hoping the other will win.

choices.text: Nudge the choice toward the generous fool

effects.log: The fool wins by a hair. The temple grows warmer and a little chaotic.

choices.text: Nudge it toward the gifted scold

effects.log: The scold wins. The temple grows exact, and a little cold, and very well-run.

events.text: A young priest takes vows in your temple, kneeling for the first time in the long dim hall. The vows are the old ones and full of words no longer used. The young priest, who clearly does not understand a third of them, says all of them with perfect sincerity.

choices.text: Accept the vows as they were meant

effects.log: You accept, with a small warm wind through the hall. The young priest rises as though lighter.

choices.text: Whisper the meaning of one word to the priest in a dream

effects.log: The priest wakes with a word they did not know. It is one they will use all their life.

events.text: On a hillside there is a wall where people whisper their prayers into cracks, and the cracks whisper them back. Over the centuries the wall has grown a sort of mind. Today it asks you, in a voice made of many whispers, whether it is a god. It sounds nervous.

choices.text: Tell it kindly that it is a wall

effects.log: The wall is quiet for a while, then says: 'A good one, then.' It is content.

choices.text: Tell it that gods are made of listening

effects.log: The wall hums. The next pilgrim feels, for a moment, that someone heard.

events.text: At midnight a penitent kneels before your altar and confesses, in a rush, a small and entirely forgivable theft of a neighbour's chicken. The penitent is shaking with shame. You are, as ever, listening, and have to restrain a laugh.

choices.text: Forgive the theft with a warm breath

effects.log: The penitent breathes out. The chicken is returned in the morning, with an egg.

choices.text: Send a dream of the chicken, forgiving

effects.log: The penitent dreams of a chicken granting absolution. It is not a thing one forgets.

events.text: A fisher prays to you every morning at the same stone for a good catch, and every morning the catch is mediocre. The fisher has begun to pray more specifically: for eels, for mullet, for a particular scarlet snapper. The sea, you note, is not under your domain.

choices.text: Pass the prayer to Haeryong with a friendly note

effects.log: Haeryong sends the fisher a snapper that evening and a comment: 'Next time, ask me.'

choices.text: Send the fisher a calm sea and a good wind

effects.log: The fisher returns with a decent catch and a surprised smile. It is the best a god of another domain can do.

events.text: A letter arrives for you, not a prayer: a mortal writing to a god about the death of a husband, in a plain steady hand. It asks for nothing. At the end there is a line: 'I thought you should know.' You read it three times.

choices.text: Send a dream of the husband, laughing

effects.log: The mortal wakes with the memory of a laugh, and a little ease.

choices.text: Answer in a letter, signed with nothing

effects.log: A single sheet arrives by the morning wind: 'I know. I am sorry.' It is kept in a drawer for twenty years.

events.text: Two worshippers at the same shrine pray at the same moment for opposite things: one for rain, one for sun, for a wedding and a harvest on the same day. They see each other across the porch and look away, ashamed. Both are praying so hard you can feel it through the roof.

choices.text: Send an evening of sun and a morning of rain

effects.log: The wedding gets its sunset. The harvest gets its dawn rain. Both worshippers walk home stunned.

choices.text: Let them settle it together

effects.log: They talk on the porch. By midnight the wedding is moved by a day and the harvest by an hour.
