events.text: A goddess of the hearth is lighting a lantern at your door, on the yearly walk to every shrine in the district that has gone on for four thousand years. The goddess nods without a word, lights yours, and passes on. It is the most formal courtesy in the realm.

choices.text: Return the nod and keep the lantern lit all night

effects.log: The lantern burns until dawn. The goddess's flame, you note, is warmer than yours.

choices.text: Follow the goddess a few steps in silence

effects.log: You follow to the next door, and the next. The goddess does not mind your company.

events.text: A goddess of births comes to your hall at night, dusty from a long journey, and asks to rest. The goddess has attended nine hundred and twelve births this week and is a little stunned. You give a bed and a bowl of soup. The goddess is asleep before you set it down.

choices.text: Watch over the sleep

effects.log: You watch, in your plain coat, and the house is quiet for twelve hours. The goddess wakes and leaves a small bright charm on the pillow.

choices.text: Send a dream of an empty shore

effects.log: The goddess sleeps in a dream of white sand and no cries. In the morning there are thanks and no reason given.

events.text: A goddess of one small moon has a standing complaint against the larger one, aired softly at every feast. You are seated beside the goddess this year and are required to listen through three courses. The grievance is magnificent.

choices.text: Take the small moon's side

effects.log: The goddess presses your hand. You have an ally in the sky and a grudge against the large moon you do not quite understand.

choices.text: Suggest the large moon might be lonely

effects.log: The goddess sets down a cup. After a long moment, 'Perhaps,' comes the answer. The complaint is never made the same way again.

events.text: A goddess you barely know sends a gift: a bolt of cloth in a colour you can only call 'the inside of a bell.' With it a note: 'For your shrine's banner. I have been admiring your wind.' You are, to your embarrassment, blushing.

choices.text: Make the banner and hang it

effects.log: The banner flutters over your shrine. Pilgrims remark that it sings very quietly.

choices.text: Send back a jar of your best rainwater

effects.log: The jar is poured into a goddess's garden. A rose blooms in your colour.

events.text: At the start of your domain's year the first morning is traditionally greeted by the whole domain at once, in a ritual no one has organised. Today the weather is wrong and the greeting is ragged and sleepy. You find it the dearest thing you have heard.

choices.text: Greet it back, quietly

effects.log: Your greeting runs across the domain like a wave. Several sleepers wake smiling.

choices.text: Hold the clouds off for the ragged greeting

effects.log: The sun comes up on the sleepy domain a little early, and everyone feels slightly clever.

events.text: Rain falls on your domain on the day of the harvest festival, and the farmers blame you. They do not say so, they say 'the weather.' But all the fingers point upward, and a dozen small prayers of reproach reach you at once.

choices.text: Part the cloud for an hour, if you can

ok.log: The cloud parts. The festival goes on, a little steaming, and the crowd cheers.

fail.log: The cloud half-parts and the festival gets a drizzle with a rainbow.

choices.text: Let it rain, and send warm wind to dry the dancers

effects.log: The dancers dance in the rain. The wind helps. The festival is wet and wonderful.

events.text: It is a dry year, and your domain is cracking in places. The farmers dig, pray and pray. You can do little: the clouds belong to other gods this season. You sit on the highest rock and feel, for the first time in a century, helpless.

choices.text: Ask a cloud-god for a favour, humbly

effects.log: The cloud-god sends a morning's mist. It is a small gift and a large humiliation.

choices.text: Walk among the farmers as a plain traveller and help dig

effects.log: You dig a well alongside a family. At the bottom, a damp stone. It is the best result of the year.

events.text: An elder god whom you wronged by accident four thousand years ago is in your hall. Neither of you has mentioned it. They sit politely, sip your tea, and talk about the weather. The grudge sits between you on the table like a third cup.

choices.text: Mention it, plainly, and apologise

effects.log: The elder god sets down the cup. 'I had forgotten,' they say. Then, after a pause: 'No. I had not. Thank you.'

choices.text: Pour the tea and say nothing

effects.log: The tea is drunk. The grudge is carried out with the cups, at the end, by a servant.

events.text: An old god tells a story at supper that you have heard eleven times, each time with a different ending. Tonight it ends with the god of the story forgiving the god of the story's brother. The whole table goes quiet. It is the first time the story has ended kindly.

choices.text: Ask what changed

effects.log: 'I got old,' says the elder god. 'It takes the shortest time.'

choices.text: Raise a cup to the new ending

effects.log: The table drinks. The story, with its new ending, will be told for centuries.

events.text: A neighbouring god you have never met sends a messenger with a basket of dried persimmons and the single line: 'We have been neighbours for nine thousand years. I thought it time.' The persimmons are exceptional.

choices.text: Return a basket and a longer note

effects.log: A correspondence begins that outlasts three empires of mortals. The neighbour is quite dull and wonderful.

choices.text: Visit in person, unannounced, in a plain coat

effects.log: The neighbour is gardening. You help weed. Neither of you mentions that you are gods.

events.text: A small house of the dying lies at the edge of your domain, where mortals spend their last season. The nurses keep a lamp lit for you in the window, and sometimes ask, between tasks, whether you are there. Tonight you are.

choices.text: Sit in the corner until the lamp burns low

effects.log: You sit with a dying stranger, in the corner, unseen. At the end, the stranger turns toward you and says thank you.

choices.text: Warm the room, and leave the lamp to the nurses

effects.log: The room is warmer. The nurses, noticing, say nothing, and work a little more softly.

events.text: A newly made god arrives at the edge of your quarter, uncertain and glowing, with nothing to their name but a single prayer in a pocket and a name that is not quite settled. A servant whispers that the new god has been waiting for an hour for someone to say hello.

choices.text: Say hello and offer tea

effects.log: The new god weeps with relief, and takes the tea in both hands. A friendship begins in a doorway.

choices.text: Show the new god the way to the registry

effects.log: The registry is two corridors away. The new god thanks you as though you had given them a kingdom.

events.text: A god returns to the divine quarter after four hundred years of exile, shabby and unannounced, and sits down quietly at the back of the hall. The whole room pretends not to notice. You, who were fond of the exile once, are suddenly very busy folding a napkin.

choices.text: Cross the hall and sit beside them

effects.log: You sit. A hush falls, then the sound of a hundred chairs being re-arranged to include another.

choices.text: Send a cup of tea by a servant, without a name

effects.log: The tea arrives. The returning god looks at it for a long time, and drinks.

events.text: {npc} is the god of a single river, forty miles long, from a spring in a barn to a marsh nobody visits. {He} arrives at your hall with a map drawn on a napkin. 'I have been meaning to introduce myself for six thousand years,' {he} says. 'It is a very small river. I hope you do not mind.'
events.arc: The God of One River

choices.text: Ask to see the river

effects.log: {npc} is thrilled. You walk the whole forty miles in a plain coat in a single afternoon, and every bend has a story.

choices.text: Offer a seat at your table for the river's feast day

effects.log: {npc} stammers. Nobody has ever invited the river. It comes, with a jar of water as a gift.

choices.text: Tell {him} size is the least of a god's qualities

effects.log: {npc} brightens. It is a thing {he} has needed to hear since the sea was cut.

events.text: The river has flooded the barn at the spring, and the farmer is furious. {npc} is in your hall in distress: a small god cannot always control a small river, and the farmer's prayers lately have been rude. {He} asks if you might say a word.
events.arc: The God of One River

choices.text: Say a word to the farmer in a dream

effects.log: The farmer wakes, shamefaced, and moves the barn up the slope. {npc} is overcome.

choices.text: Teach {him} to speak to a farmer {him}self

effects.log: You spend an evening role-playing a cross farmer. {npc} improves a great deal by the end.

choices.text: Offer to hold the river back for a night

effects.log: You hold the water. The barn dries. The river grumbles at the dam of a stranger's will.

events.text: {npc} grows slowly famous. Pilgrims arrive to walk the whole forty miles. A fair springs up at the marsh. A song is composed, cheerful and not very good. On the river's feast day {he} sits at your table and looks at the whole hall in wonder.
events.arc: The God of One River

choices.text: Raise a cup of river water to the small god

effects.log: You drink. The water tastes of clay and cold, and exactly like home to someone.

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell the story of the marsh

effects.log: {npc} tells it. Half the table fall quiet. It is a story about a heron.

events.text: A drought narrows the river to a trickle, and {npc} comes to you pale and fading. A god of a river without water is a very small thing. {He} does not ask for help. {He} only says goodbye, with a napkin map in hand.
events.arc: The God of One River

choices.text: Bring rain from your own domain to the river

effects.log: Rain falls on the barn and the marsh. The river rises, and {npc} sits on the bank with tears in {his} eyes.

choices.text: Carry the napkin map to a bigger god and plead

effects.log: Haeryong takes the napkin, reads it, and sends a tide up the estuary. The river is saved by the sea, and everyone is slightly embarrassed.

events.text: The god of lost keys, {npc}, is an apologetic, tired deity who has been in charge of every key that was ever misplaced since the first lock. {He} comes to your hall to ask whether you have seen a certain brass key. You have not. It is the third time this week {he} has asked someone in the quarter.
events.arc: The God of Lost Keys

choices.text: Help {him} search your hall

effects.log: You find eleven keys under cushions. None is the right one. {npc} thanks you for each as though it were a gift.

choices.text: Ask what the key opens

effects.log: {npc} looks at the floor. 'I don't know,' {he} says. 'I only know it is lost.' It is the most honest answer in the realm.

choices.text: Tell {him} to rest and have tea

effects.log: {npc} drinks a cup of tea, looking startled that anyone should offer.

events.text: Over the next year {npc} turns up in your hall at odd hours, tired and lost {him}self. {He} has begun to leave small piles of keys in your garden, a quiet gift: all those {he} has found. Visitors take one each by mistake, and are astonished to find their own door opens.
events.arc: The God of Lost Keys

choices.text: Give the keys back to their owners, through dreams

effects.log: A hundred doors across the realm open smoothly. A hundred households forget why they smile.

choices.text: Let the keys sit in the garden. Nobody needs them all

effects.log: The garden becomes a quiet, jingling place. The keys keep to themselves.

events.text: At last the brass key turns up, in the pocket of an old coat, in an attic. {npc} holds it for a long time. It opens, as it turns out, a small box in {his} own hall, and in the box is a hair ribbon and a note: a gift from {his} mother, long gone. {He} weeps and thanks you.
events.arc: The God of Lost Keys

choices.text: Sit with {him} in the quiet

effects.log: You sit with the god of lost keys in the quiet of a very old grief. The key is warm in {his} hand.

choices.text: Leave the god alone with the box

effects.log: You leave. A good god knows when a room is not for them.

events.text: The key is never found, and {npc} comes to accept it, over the years, as the god of what is lost for good. {He} keeps a lamp lit for it in a window. Each year on the day, {he} sits with a cup of tea and says, 'Wherever you are.' You join {him}.
events.arc: The God of Lost Keys

choices.text: Join {him} every year

effects.log: A custom is born. Over the centuries a small crowd of lost-key believers gathers at the window for tea.

choices.text: Hang a bell in the window so the key will find the way

effects.log: The bell rings every night. Nothing comes. But it rings.

events.text: Between the second hour of morning and the fourth lives a god, {npc}, who is in charge of the third. Nobody worships it, for it is a quiet, unremarkable hour. {He} arrives at your hall at dawn, exactly on time, with a request: 'Could you make it a little more interesting? I have a great deal of time to fill.'
events.arc: The God of the Third Hour

choices.text: Put a small bird in it every day

effects.log: At the third hour a thrush sings outside every window. {npc} is delighted. The mortals under the third hour begin to wake early to hear it.

choices.text: Ask what {he} has already tried

effects.log: {npc} has tried quiet, warmth, and a faint smell of bread. 'People sleep through it,' {he} says. 'That is the point,' you tell {him}, and {he} frowns.

choices.text: Tell {him} nothing needs to happen in an hour

effects.log: {npc} considers this slowly. It is apparently a revolutionary idea.

events.text: The third hour has acquired a little following: insomniacs, nursing mothers, night watchmen, bakers about to begin. They call it the hour of the awake. {npc} comes to tell you in a state of puzzled joy. 'They say thank you,' {he} says. 'I have not been thanked for the hour before.'
events.arc: The God of the Third Hour

choices.text: Send the bakers a warm draught of sweet air

effects.log: The bakers' ovens light a minute early. The hour smells of bread, and a god of the third hour grows more real.

choices.text: Sit with the watchmen and keep the hour with them

effects.log: You keep the third hour in a plain coat, on a wall, among tired men. They offer you tea. It is better than any feast.

events.text: A century later the third hour has a festival. The people carry lamps into the dark and walk to the hills at midnight to watch the sky turn. {npc} walks among them, unnoticed. When the thrush sings, the whole crowd gasps, as if it were the first morning.
events.arc: The God of the Third Hour

choices.text: Hold the dark an extra breath, for the moment

effects.log: The dark holds. The thrush sings into it. A few people cry.

choices.text: Slip a lamp into a child's hand

effects.log: The child carries it up the hill alone. It is a very small, very bright thing.

events.text: The god of the third hour fades in the end, not from neglect but from contentment. The hour remains: quiet, unremarkable, and to those who know, the best. A single lamp is lit every night in a window at the third hour, and nobody remembers why.
events.arc: The God of the Third Hour

choices.text: Keep the lamp lit yourself

effects.log: You keep it. For ten thousand years, a lamp at the third hour. It is the smallest duty you own and the one you never miss.

choices.text: Let the hour be quiet

effects.log: You let it be. The quiet that is left is a gift too.

events.text: A child in the lowlands has been feeding a puddle for a year, naming it and telling it secrets. Worship, in its purest form, is just attention. The puddle is waking up. It has a name now, {npc}, and a faint shape in the surface, and it has not yet figured out what it is a god of.
events.arc: The Puddle That Became a God

choices.text: Introduce yourself to the puddle

effects.log: You crouch and say hello. The puddle ripples. The child gasps. Between you, you have become a small society.

choices.text: Tell the puddle what gods do

effects.log: The puddle listens. It decides it wants to be the god of reflections and getting your boots wet.

choices.text: Leave the puddle to the child

effects.log: You watch from a tree. The child tells the puddle everything.

events.text: The puddle has grown a small following of frogs, three children and a stray dog. {npc} is not fully a god, yet, but it has opinions and its own corner of faith. When the sun comes out it grows alarmed. 'Where do I go?' it asks, in a bubble. 'I do not want to go.'
events.arc: The Puddle That Became a God

choices.text: Promise to keep a little rain for it

effects.log: You send a shower just big enough. The puddle fills, glad, with a ring of frogs around it.

choices.text: Show it how to become a pond

effects.log: You dig a small hollow with a stick. The puddle sinks into it and becomes a pond of its own. A new small god with a future.

choices.text: Tell the child to carry a cup of puddle to safety

effects.log: The child carries a cup. The puddle goes on in the cup, small and bright.

events.text: The pond is a thing of beauty now, with reeds, a heron and a fine school of minnows. The child has grown and brings a child of their own. {npc} greets them in a ripple. The child's child names the pond a new name, and the pond, gratefully, accepts.
events.arc: The Puddle That Became a God

choices.text: Drop a pebble in as a blessing

effects.log: The ripples spread for a long time, silver, then still.

choices.text: Watch from the tree and say nothing

effects.log: A god may watch a small god thrive. It is a good afternoon.

events.text: The puddle never dries out. Rain after rain keeps it alive, and it becomes the best-loved small thing in the lowlands. When the child is an old person, they sit at its edge and say 'good evening,' and the puddle, which has never been wrong about anything, ripples back.
events.arc: The Puddle That Became a God

choices.text: Send a little rain every year on the day

effects.log: The puddle fills on the day. The old person smiles in the rain.

choices.text: Leave a pebble where the puddle was

effects.log: A small pebble, a long memory.

events.text: You hold no pantheon, and the heavenly court's petition-hall will not accept your papers without a sponsor. {npc}, a clerk with kind eyes and tired shoulders, explains this with such apology that it is hard to be angry. 'It is just the form,' {he} says. 'I'm sorry. It is always the form.'
events.arc: The Petition Without a Pantheon

choices.text: Ask {him} to find a sponsor among the clerks

effects.log: {npc} finds an old retired god of ledgers who owes {him} a favour. The papers go through, and a very odd friendship begins.

choices.text: Argue the form is unjust, in writing

effects.log: Your letter is read aloud in the hall of clerks, to a silence. It is copied and passed around. Nothing changes, but everything is a little less certain.

choices.text: Thank {him} and leave without a fuss

effects.log: {npc} watches you go and, once the door is closed, quietly files your papers under 'follow up.'

events.text: {npc} has been reprimanded for helping you. A senior clerk has added a note to {his} file: 'overly accommodating to unaffiliated petitioners.' {He} arrives at your hall with the note and a bottle of cheap wine. 'I thought you should see it,' {he} says. 'It's the most flattering thing in the file.'
events.arc: The Petition Without a Pantheon

choices.text: Pour {him} the wine and laugh with {him}

effects.log: {He} drinks it, and you drink tea. It is terrible, {he} says. You laugh until the lamps gutter, and a friendship of the powerless takes root.

choices.text: Write a letter of commendation for the clerk

effects.log: Your letter is filed. It carries no weight, but it is, on its own, a beautiful piece of prose.

choices.text: Say nothing. Listen

effects.log: {npc} talks for an hour. It is enough.

events.text: A year of small kindnesses later, a rule changes. A new clause allows petitions from unaffiliated gods if three clerks vouch. It is {npc}'s doing, a clause hidden in a footnote, and it passes without a single vote. {He} looks tired and happy and slightly sick.
events.arc: The Petition Without a Pantheon

choices.text: Send {him} a basket of fruit with no note

effects.log: {npc} eats the fruit in the hall of clerks with a tiny, secret smile.

choices.text: Be the first to file under the new clause

effects.log: You file. The hall of clerks, in a hush, accepts the papers. It is a small moment and a large one.

events.text: The old retired god of ledgers who vouched for you dies, and the sponsorship goes with them. Your papers are in limbo again. {npc} meets you at the door with a different apology, and a different bottle of cheap wine, and you both laugh, with a flat resignation, until dawn.
events.arc: The Petition Without a Pantheon

choices.text: Find a new sponsor in the Masterless fold

effects.log: Masterless gods have long had their own small custom: they sponsor each other. You are the first of a new line of petitions.

choices.text: Let the papers lapse and live without them

effects.log: You do. Nobody, it turns out, was waiting for your forms.

events.text: Without a pantheon, you have been left to your own devices for centuries. Now an emissary arrives from one of the four, {npc}, with a warm smile and a sheaf of offers. 'The council has noticed you,' {he} says. 'We would like you to be part of something.' The way {he} says 'something' is very smooth.
events.arc: When a Pantheon Came Calling

choices.text: Hear the whole offer out

effects.log: The offer is generous. Too generous. It arrives with a seat, a title and a quiet clause about votes.

choices.text: Decline at once, politely

effects.log: {npc} bows and thanks you. {He} will return in a century, with a different smile.

choices.text: Ask for time to think

effects.log: {npc} grants a year. A year is a long time for an emissary, and short for a decision.

events.text: Other Masterless gods, hearing, come to see you. Some are bitter, some hopeful. An old one with a patched robe says: 'Take it, if you want a roof. Do not take it if you want your voice.' A younger one says: 'They will own you by spring.' You are the subject of a great many opinions.
events.arc: When a Pantheon Came Calling

choices.text: Ask each to say what they have lost

effects.log: A long evening. Three of them have lost nothing; two have lost everything. The old one, quietly, has lost the least of all.

choices.text: Propose an informal Masterless council

effects.log: A table is set. For the first time in memory, the Masterless gods sit in a room together, argue, and eat the same cake.

choices.text: Thank them and stay silent

effects.log: You go home to think. The year goes quickly.

events.text: You turn the offer down, and the emissary arrives a century later with a different smile and a smaller offer. The Masterless table meets every spring now. It has no rules, no chair, and a lot of cake. The pantheons watch with a mixture of worry and envy.
events.arc: When a Pantheon Came Calling

choices.text: Raise a cup to the cake

effects.log: The table raises its cups. It is the finest, most disorderly toast in the realm.

choices.text: Pass the chair of the table around each year

effects.log: Each year a different god sits at the head, on a stool. It is the closest thing to a government that anyone wants.

events.text: In the end you do join a pantheon, not the one that courted you but a smaller one, loose and untidy, that asks nothing. It is a kind of freedom, to belong to something that does not require it. {npc} is the first to congratulate you, sincerely.
events.arc: When a Pantheon Came Calling

choices.text: Thank {him} and invite {him} to supper

effects.log: {npc} comes. The conversation is lighter than it has ever been between your two kinds of god.

choices.text: Keep your old Masterless habits anyway

effects.log: You do. A free god's habits are the last to go.

events.text: You stumbled in a hall of the hearth and, in catching yourself, knocked a candle onto a dry broom. The broom burned, harmlessly, in the shape of a bird. {npc}, a passing pilgrim, saw it. 'A sign!' {he} cries. 'A bird of fire! A miracle!' You were, at the time, mostly worried about your sleeve.
events.arc: The Miracle That Was an Accident

choices.text: Let it be a miracle

effects.log: The pilgrim spreads the word. By night, three hundred people have come to see the burnt broom. Faith swells, oddly, on a small accident.

choices.text: Come clean to the pilgrim

effects.log: You admit it was an accident. {npc} stares, then bursts into joyful laughter. 'Even better,' {he} cries. 'A god who slips!'

choices.text: Slip away, quietly

effects.log: You go. The legend grows regardless. A fluke, once told, cannot be called back.

events.text: The burnt broom is now behind glass in a shrine, with a card that reads 'The Bird of Fire.' Pilgrims leave offerings. A priest has written an elaborate commentary. {npc}, the first witness, is now a minor celebrity and has started to forget that the fire was an accident.
events.arc: The Miracle That Was an Accident

choices.text: Appear to {npc} in a dream and remind {him}

effects.log: {npc} wakes, flushed. 'It was an accident,' {he} says, to the lamps. 'But I still saw a bird.' Both can be true.

choices.text: Let the legend stand

effects.log: The legend stands. It has outgrown its origins and found a life.

events.text: Years later the fire-bird is a national symbol, put on seals and flags and the lids of biscuit tins. A pious historian proves, with great scholarship, that the bird was a sign of the First Hearth. You attend the conference in a plain coat and take notes.
events.arc: The Miracle That Was an Accident

choices.text: Stand up and say nothing, and clap at the end

effects.log: You clap with real feeling. The historian beams. Nothing in your heart is false.

choices.text: Leave a pinch of ash on the speaker's desk

effects.log: The speaker finds it later, blinks, and sneezes. A very small miracle.

events.text: The broom crumbles at last, in its glass, and the priests fret. The bird of fire has become a bird of ash. Pilgrims weep. You, in a plain coat, in the back row, find that you cannot help but be moved. It was a fluke, and it was a good one.
events.arc: The Miracle That Was an Accident

choices.text: Send a small ember to the ash, to keep it warm

effects.log: The ash glows a moment, soft and amber. The pilgrims see it and are comforted.

choices.text: Sweep the ash up and scatter it on a river

effects.log: You scatter it from a bridge. The river carries the bird of fire to the sea.

events.text: The god of the hill next to yours, {npc}, has lost most of their worshippers over a hundred years, and is going thin. You can see through {him} now when the light is right. {He} comes to your hall with a hollow smile and a request that is half a joke: 'Could you spare a few believers? You have a surplus.'
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Was Fading

choices.text: Share some of your faith, quietly

effects.log: A little of your faith drifts across the boundary stones and settles on {npc}'s hill. {He} is a shade more solid at dusk.

choices.text: Send worshippers to {his} hill with a reason to go

effects.log: A fair, a festival, a pilgrimage. {npc}'s hill fills for a week. It is the most temporary of miracles.

choices.text: Say you have none to spare, kindly

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'I knew,' {he} says. 'I had to ask once.'

events.text: The faith you shared has done what shared faith does: it has made your neighbour real enough to be cross about everything. {npc} critiques your shrines, your hymns and the placement of your hall. {He} has, apparently, been wanting to for a long time. It is a good sign.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Was Fading

choices.text: Take the criticism and make three of the changes

effects.log: Three small changes later, your shrine is a touch better. {npc} claims credit, loudly, at a feast.

choices.text: Argue back, enjoying it

effects.log: A quarrel begins that lasts a century and is one of the great pleasures of your life.

events.text: {npc}'s hill is lively now. A weekly market, a school, a spring of good water. When {he} finally fades, centuries later, it is on a summer afternoon, content, with a full porch around {him}. You sit on the porch too. {He} says: 'Thank you for the argument.'
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Was Fading

choices.text: Say it was the best of your career

effects.log: {He} laughs, and is gone. The hill goes on.

choices.text: Hold the porch in silence until the evening

effects.log: The sun sets. The porch stays full. Someone lights a lamp.

events.text: The fair ends, the festival passes, the worshippers go home. {npc} is thinner than before, and says nothing about it. You find a note on your doorstep a month later: 'I am going to the sea, to be a small ripple. Thank you for trying.' You keep it.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Was Fading

choices.text: Send a wind after {him} to the coast

effects.log: The wind rides to the shore. A ripple, in the evening, turns toward it.

choices.text: Frame the note and hang it in your hall

effects.log: It hangs by the door. Visitors ask who wrote it. You say a friend.

events.text: The year of the Harvest begins in your domain with a seed-counting. {npc}, the oldest farmer in the district, counts out the first seed with a ritual so unchanged that the seed itself seems to know the words. This spring {he} asks, with unusual shyness: 'Would you attend this year?'
events.arc: The Turning Year of the Harvest

choices.text: Attend, in a plain coat

effects.log: You stand at the edge of the field. {npc} counts. When {he} reaches the last seed {he} looks straight at you and winks.

choices.text: Send a warm spring wind to the sowing

effects.log: The seeds settle in the earth gladly. The year begins on a good note.

choices.text: Stay home and keep an ear open

effects.log: The sowing prayer reaches you, plain and warm, all the way across the domain.

events.text: Midsummer: a thin hot month, when the grain has not decided what to be. {npc} walks the field every evening with a stick, tapping, and talks to the stalks like a doctor to children. A blight shows on one corner. {He} stands over it and stays there all night.
events.arc: The Turning Year of the Harvest

choices.text: Clear the blight before dawn

effects.log: In the morning the corner is green. {npc} sits on the ground for a long time, then thanks the empty air.

choices.text: Stand with {him} and say nothing

effects.log: You stand with {npc} in the dark. At dawn the blight is still there, but smaller. {He} laughs, tired. Some years, the standing is the prayer.

choices.text: Send a dream of the corner whole

effects.log: {He} dozes at the foot of the field and dreams of rows of gold.

events.text: The harvest is good, and a feast comes to the field at dusk with trestle tables and too much soup. {npc} gives the first sheaf to the god of the harvest, which is you, in the form of an empty chair. {He} bows. The whole field bows. The chair is warm.
events.arc: The Turning Year of the Harvest

choices.text: Sit in the chair, and let them see you

effects.log: For one breath the chair holds a god. The field sees. No one says a word.

choices.text: Leave the chair empty and the sheaf on it

effects.log: The chair stays empty. The field understands that this is the better courtesy.

events.text: The harvest is thin, and the feast small. {npc} gives the first sheaf anyway. 'A thin year is a year,' {he} says, to the chair. The hamlet sings anyway, off-key. You sit unseen at the edge of the light, and have never been more moved by a meal.
events.arc: The Turning Year of the Harvest

choices.text: Send a late warm evening over the table

effects.log: The evening holds a minute past its time. The soup is hot. Nobody knows why.

choices.text: Let the thin year be thin

effects.log: You let it. The song, off-key, goes on.

events.text: There is a week each year when death in the realm goes unusually soft: in the cold of the year, people die gently in sleep, with the windows open. {npc}, a ferry-hand of Baekun's, has been sent to ask whether the gods of other domains would observe it by sending no storms. It is a peculiar custom, and a lovely one.
events.arc: The Quiet Season of Death

choices.text: Promise a storm-free week

effects.log: Your domain is quiet for seven days. Sleepers die in peace. {npc} is moved by the courtesy.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the week is for

effects.log: 'For the ones who were afraid,' {he} says. 'They go easier if the night is kind.'

choices.text: Send a hand of your own to the ferry

effects.log: A bell of yours rings at the landing, one low note. It is accepted.

events.text: This year the week has been broken: a sudden storm from a quarrelsome neighbour has torn through the districts that were to be quiet. {npc} is in your hall at dawn, exhausted, soaked. Several crossings have gone badly, and a ferry-hand cannot sit still in the face of it.
events.arc: The Quiet Season of Death

choices.text: Go with {him} to the landing

effects.log: At the landing, several souls are frightened and wet. You hold a lamp for each as they step aboard. Baekun poles slowly.

choices.text: Send a sharp word to the neighbour who sent the storm

effects.log: The neighbour is shamed. The week next year is, by general agreement, the stillest in the realm.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and let {him} rest

effects.log: {He} sleeps in your hall for a day. When {he} wakes, the week has ended, and the river is quiet.

events.text: A decade of quiet weeks. {npc} is a senior hand now, with white at the temples. Before the next week {he} leaves a small lamp at your door, a ferry lamp, with a note: 'To light the way.' You hang it by your window and light it every year on the day.
events.arc: The Quiet Season of Death

choices.text: Light it with the first star

effects.log: The lamp burns until the week ends. Across the realm, other lamps burn in other windows, all lit by strangers.

choices.text: Send a lamp of your own to the ferry-hand

effects.log: It is hung at the prow of Baekun's boat. It swings gently in the dark.

events.text: The quarrelsome neighbour sends a gift of reeds, a formal apology, wrapped in silk. It is accepted. The week is kept for a thousand years afterward by gods who never speak of why. Once a year, though, a dry reed is laid at the landing, in memory of a storm.
events.arc: The Quiet Season of Death

choices.text: Lay the reed yourself

effects.log: You lay it. The landing, in its slow way, keeps it.

choices.text: Send the reed on to the ferry-hand

effects.log: The reed goes on, passed from hand to hand, to the end of the river.

events.text: Once a year, at the turn of Fate's domain, every thread in the loom is counted aloud by a tired choir of clerks. {npc}, one of the counters, sits on your hall's steps with a thread in each hand. 'I miscounted,' {he} says. 'There is one thread too many. It does not belong to anyone.'
events.arc: The Season the Threads Are Counted

choices.text: Ask whose thread it might be

effects.log: {npc} lifts it to the light. It is faint, silver, and shivers. It has no start and no end. 'It is the only thread I have ever seen that is not tied to a life,' {he} says.

choices.text: Suggest the thread belongs to a god

effects.log: {npc} turns the thread over in thought. 'Gods have threads,' {he} says slowly. 'We do not count them. It is not done.'

choices.text: Tell {him} to count again

effects.log: {npc} counts again. The same number. {He} is pale.

events.text: The thread, taken to Unmyeong, is turned and turned. The Weaver studies it for a night and returns it with a single sentence: 'It is yours, on loan, until you need it.' {npc} brings it to you with the reverence of a pilgrim.
events.arc: The Season the Threads Are Counted

choices.text: Take the thread

effects.log: The thread curls around your wrist, silver and quiet. You wear it. It hums at odd hours.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to keep it safe for you

effects.log: {npc} nods and pockets it. For a hundred years it sits in a clerk's sleeve, doing nothing but being there.

choices.text: Give it back to the loom

effects.log: The thread returns to the loom and vanishes into the weave. The count is right again, and a little lonelier.

events.text: A century later, when you are tired and nearly lost to something small and bitter, the silver thread tightens on your wrist. It pulls you, gently, toward a door you had not planned to open. Behind it is a window. In the window, someone is lighting a lamp for you.
events.arc: The Season the Threads Are Counted

choices.text: Go through the door

effects.log: You go through. The lamp is lit. It is the first of many nights you will be waited for.

choices.text: Stand at the door and let the thread guide

effects.log: The thread guides, and you stay. It is enough to know there is a door.

events.text: The clerk keeps the thread for years, uneasy, and one night it is gone from the sleeve. {npc} searches the loom-room in a panic, then finds it knotted around the leg of a stool, quietly, in a place where no clerk has ever sat. It is the most beautiful knot {he} has seen.
events.arc: The Season the Threads Are Counted

choices.text: Leave the knot undisturbed

effects.log: The stool is never moved. A clerk sits on it, one day, and finds a quiet in the loom-room that wasn't there before.

choices.text: Ask Unmyeong what it means

effects.log: 'A thread chose its own place,' the Weaver says. 'I find that I like it.'

events.text: A new shrine to you has been raised on the far side of the mountains by people you have never met. It is very small, and very proud. {npc}, its first keeper, writes to you by smoke: 'We have not had a pilgrim yet. We are practising our welcome. May we practise on you?'
events.arc: The First Pilgrims of a New Shrine

choices.text: Arrive as a pilgrim in a plain coat

effects.log: You arrive footsore at the new shrine at dusk. {npc} bows too low, brings you tea, and rehearses the welcome speech in full.

choices.text: Send a wind of warm bread through the porch

effects.log: The shrine smells of baking all week. {npc} chalks it down as an omen.

choices.text: Let them practise on their own

effects.log: They practise, and the welcome speech grows by nine words.

events.text: The first real pilgrim arrives in a downpour: a grandmother with an umbrella and a very small dog. {He} is doing a pilgrimage for a promise to a dead sister. {npc} is flustered and recites the whole welcome speech, which lasts eleven minutes. The grandmother, politely soaked, listens to every word.
events.arc: The First Pilgrims of a New Shrine

choices.text: Dry the grandmother with a warm draught

effects.log: The rain stops on the porch and does not on the road. The grandmother thanks the keeper, and the keeper, flustered, thanks you.

choices.text: Let the keeper's welcome do the work

effects.log: The grandmother, at the end, says: 'That was lovely.' {He} means it. The keeper floats.

events.text: A decade on, the shrine is the stop on a pilgrim road with an inn, a ferry and a modest festival. {npc} is a patient host. At the door hangs a bell and a sign: 'Practise your welcome.' Every pilgrim rings it for luck, whispers something, and goes in.
events.arc: The First Pilgrims of a New Shrine

choices.text: Ring the bell yourself, in passing

effects.log: The bell rings. A traveller, hearing, smiles at nothing.

choices.text: Leave the sign as it is

effects.log: It is the truest sign in the realm.

events.text: The shrine's first welcome-speech is now recited by children at school. Nobody remembers the keeper's name. You visit on a spring morning and find a child reciting it to a wall. You sit on the step and listen until the end.
events.arc: The First Pilgrims of a New Shrine

choices.text: Applaud, softly, from the step

effects.log: The child turns, startled, and sees no one. A smile spreads. It is a very good speech.

choices.text: Add a word to the speech through a dream

effects.log: The child dreams of a missing word, and adds it. The speech improves, minimally.

events.text: In the domain of War the year turns with the laying-down of the spears. Every garrison, in every season of dispute, spends one day unarmed: sweeping, sewing, eating together. Mujin begins it by setting a banner-pole in the ground. Today the pole is yours to plant, and it is heavier than it looks.

choices.text: Plant it firmly

effects.log: The pole stands. Across the domain, spears are laid down in a long clatter, and people look at each other without anger.

choices.text: Plant it crooked, to make the guards laugh

effects.log: The pole leans. The guards laugh. A laugh, laid down with the spears, is the best kind of peace.

events.text: In the Sky the year turns on the day the stars are counted back into their places. Cheonho climbs a ladder and checks a hundred thousand lamps. A lamp near the edge of the sky is out, and Cheonho calls down for a volunteer to climb up with the oil.

choices.text: Climb up with the oil

effects.log: You climb until the ladder gets thin. The lamp relights with a sneeze of gold. Below, a small crowd cheers a god on a ladder.

choices.text: Send a breath of wind to nudge the wick

effects.log: The wick catches. Cheonho waves a long arm in thanks, and the sky is whole again.

events.text: In the domain of Fire the year turns at the Night of Embers, when every hearth is allowed to go out and be lit again from the First Hearth. Hwarin hands out embers at the door. The line is mortals in blankets, gods in robes, and one very serious fox.

choices.text: Hand out embers with Hwarin for an hour

effects.log: Embers are handed out and hearths relit. A chain of small fires spreads out across the dark.

choices.text: Give the fox its ember first

effects.log: The fox bows its whole body and carries the ember off in a tin. It is the first creature in the realm to be warm.

events.text: In the domain of Death the year turns when the ferry changes its oarsman. The new hand, a young soul unready to cross, takes the pole for a year in the oldest of arrangements. Baekun has set a place for you at the landing to witness it.

choices.text: Witness, and bow to the oarsman

effects.log: The oarsman nods, pale, the pole upright. A year is a long time to hold an oar, and a very short time to be a god's helper.

choices.text: Bring a pickle and a rice ball for the new hand

effects.log: The oarsman eats at the landing. Baekun, watching, takes a pickle too.

events.text: In the domain of Fate the year turns with the Day of Loose Threads, when the loom is allowed to drop a thousand stitches so that something, somewhere, can go wrong in a pleasant way. A clerk brings you a basket and asks you to choose one stitch to drop.

choices.text: Drop a stitch from a quiet street

effects.log: A baker finds a lost coin. A child finds a dog. The street has a good day for no reason.

choices.text: Pull one from your own thread

effects.log: A small unpredictability enters your life. It is delightful and a little frightening.

events.text: In the domain of Dreams the year turns when Mongsa wakes for one hour. Everyone lowers their voice. The sleeper blinks, yawns, and looks at the hall as though it were a pleasant surprise. Today you are close enough to hear the first sentence.

choices.text: Greet the Sleeper softly

effects.log: Mongsa smiles and says: 'Was I asleep?' It is the most reassuring sentence in the realm.

choices.text: Offer a cup of cold tea

effects.log: Mongsa takes it and drinks it with deep gratitude and falls asleep again. The hour is over.

events.text: In the domain of Life the year turns on the Day of First Leaves, when Saengmo walks the world and gives every sprout a name. Today she is slow, and stops at your shrine to rest. A bird lands on the Mother of Seeds' shoulder. It does not leave.

choices.text: Offer a bench and a glass of water

effects.log: Saengmo sits, and tells you in four sentences how the world was seeded. It is a very good story.

choices.text: Name a sprout with her

effects.log: A small shoot at the foot of your shrine receives a name from two gods at once. It will not forget.

events.text: In the domain of the Beasts the year turns with the Night of Tracks, when every animal walks a path it has never walked, for no reason. Horang leads, in a plain coat, with a stick. The tracks in the dust the next morning are a sort of scripture.

choices.text: Walk a new path yourself that night

effects.log: You walk a path you do not know. A deer joins you without a sound. In the morning your boots are full of burrs.

choices.text: Read the tracks at dawn

effects.log: The tracks, together, make a spiral. Horang looks at it, nods, and goes to sleep.

events.text: In the domain of the Harvest the year turns on the Last Sheaf, the one left standing in the field for the gods and the hungry. Pungnyeon chooses it. The farmers wait, and the sheaf glows slightly in the dusk. This year the choosing is left to you.

choices.text: Choose the sheaf by the roadside, for the hungry

effects.log: The sheaf is gleaned by a stranger at dawn, and a family eats a good meal.

choices.text: Choose the one nearest the old shrine

effects.log: The shrine's keeper cries at the sight. The sheaf is hung in the porch until spring.

events.text: In the domain of the Sea the year turns at the Wide Tide, the one night the water goes out so far that the seabed can be walked for a mile. Haeryong lights a lantern at the shore. Children and old women walk out, picking shells, quiet as in a church.

choices.text: Walk out on the sand and carry a lantern

effects.log: You walk a mile of seabed. Every shell is a small prayer. The tide returns at dawn, gently.

choices.text: Stay at the shore and hold the lantern for those returning

effects.log: A line of walkers come home in the lantern's glow. Each says thank you to a god they cannot see.

events.text: In the domain of Thunder the year turns on the Night of the Drums, when all nine drums sound at once and the sky shakes like a table. Noegong asks the gods of other domains to bring a drum of their own. The hall fills with a ridiculous orchestra of pots, boxes and one real tom-tom.

choices.text: Bring a pot and bang it with a spoon

effects.log: Your pot adds a thin high note. Noegong grins and points at you with a drumstick. The sky shudders approvingly.

choices.text: Listen from the roof without playing

effects.log: You listen. The thunder is a language, and tonight it says only: here.

events.text: In the domain of the Mountains the year turns on the day Daeak does not move. Everyone knows this is every day, but on this one the stillness is recognised. The whole domain stands still for a minute. Even the avalanches hold their breath.

choices.text: Stand still with them

effects.log: A minute passes. A pebble rolls, then stops. You remember what it is to be a mountain.

choices.text: Sit with the old god and share a flask of tea

effects.log: Daeak does not accept, but the tea cools in the flask in perfect stillness, and the cup stays full.

events.text: A schoolchild has written you a thank-you list, in crayon, for every small good thing in a year: a warm day, a lost tooth, a cat that came back. It ends: 'I think you did some of it. Not all.' You hold the list in a corner of your hall. It is the fairest accounting you have ever received.

choices.text: Make the list true: do one thing on it again next year

effects.log: The cat does not come back, but a different one does. The child writes again.

choices.text: Keep the list on your wall

effects.log: The crayon list hangs by your window. It is the only thing in the hall that smells of pencil.

events.text: A shrine-keeper has left a living goat on your porch in a ribbon, as a gift. The goat is calm. It has, apparently, been well fed. The keeper's note says only: 'He is yours.' You have never owned a goat, and the goat seems to know this.

choices.text: Keep the goat, and name it

effects.log: The goat is called Councillor. It sits in your garden, eating the minutes of a hundred meetings.

choices.text: Send the goat to a hungry orchard in a dream

effects.log: The goat is welcomed by an orchard-keeper who had prayed for something to eat the weeds. It does.

events.text: A shrine of yours, on a high plain, has not seen rain in a year. The keeper prays every day for a single cloud and receives, each day, a clear sky. It is not your domain and you have no favours left. The keeper's prayer this evening is simpler: 'Are you well?'

choices.text: Answer: yes, and I am sorry

effects.log: The keeper hears nothing. But a bird lands on the porch and sings an odd, careful note.

choices.text: Ask a cloud-god, in person, humbly

effects.log: The cloud-god grumbles and sends a thin rain for a night. The keeper weeps at the roof.

events.text: A man on a mule has stopped by your roadside shrine and cursed you at length for a sprained wrist. He gives up, mid-curse, and sits down to rest. He asks, tired, whether you could do something about the wrist, or at least stop the mule laughing.

choices.text: Mend the wrist and mute the mule

effects.log: The man flexes his wrist, astonished, and leaves a coin. The mule is, in its way, grateful.

choices.text: Do nothing, but let a breeze cool his brow

effects.log: He sits in the cool breeze and, unprompted, says sorry to the shrine.

events.text: A newly-wed couple has left a wedding cake on your altar, small and slightly crushed, with two names in icing. The names are wrong. They have misspelled yours, and you realise that this is the first time you have been remembered at a wedding. You eat a corner, discreetly.

choices.text: Bless them with an uneventful year

effects.log: The couple have a quiet, boring, wonderful year. They credit the cake.

choices.text: Send a dream with your name spelled right

effects.log: They dream of the right spelling and are mortified. They do not change the cake.

events.text: A soldier has come to your shrine to pray for the end of a war. It is not your war and not your domain. The soldier knows this, and prays to you because you are the nearest god with a roof. The prayer is plain, and unbearable.

choices.text: Carry the prayer to Mujin personally

effects.log: Mujin takes the prayer in both hands. 'It will be heard,' the god of war says, which is not the same as granted.

choices.text: Sit with the soldier through the night

effects.log: You sit in the porch with the soldier until dawn. Nothing is said. The soldier goes back to the front lighter.

events.text: A blind scribe has been taking dictation from prayers for forty years, writing out the petitions of the illiterate in an exquisite hand. At your shrine she writes a prayer of her own, in the dark, and reads it back aloud to the empty hall. It is the best prayer you have heard this century.

choices.text: Answer in the same hand, on the same page

effects.log: Overnight, a line appears under hers in a script no one can read. It makes her cry in the morning.

choices.text: Give her the quiet to finish it

effects.log: She finishes it in peace, and sleeps the whole afternoon in the porch.

events.text: The bell-ringer of your great temple is deaf, and has been for thirty years. The congregation has never been told. He rings by the sun and the swing of the rope and has not missed a note. You, listening from the rafters, have never heard a better dawn.

choices.text: Ring the bell with him in secret, once

effects.log: The bell sounds twice as full. The ringer looks up, puzzled, then tears up. He cannot hear it, but he feels the rope.

choices.text: Leave a plain gold cord on his rope

effects.log: He finds the new cord at dawn and hangs it in his room, never wondering how.

events.text: Two priests are arguing in your temple over a chair, which each claims is theirs. It is an old chair with a cracked leg. The argument has lasted a week. You, in the roof, are mildly tempted to make the chair collapse.

choices.text: Make the chair collapse

effects.log: The chair collapses. Both priests laugh, then fall silent, then split the pieces for firewood.

choices.text: Offer a third chair in a dream

effects.log: A third chair arrives in the morning, from a cousin, and the argument dissolves.

events.text: An elder god cannot recall their own name, and asks you to remind them. You do not know it either. Neither do any of the gods you ask. The elder is quite calm about this. 'I shall be the god of whatever you call me,' they say. 'Call me something kind.'

choices.text: Call them Old Friend

effects.log: The elder smiles. 'Old Friend,' they repeat. By dusk half the quarter calls them that, and it sticks.

choices.text: Offer to look in the oldest archive

effects.log: You look. There is no name. There is a note: 'Never wrote it down. It was obvious.' The elder laughs for a week.

events.text: An elder god has been sleeping for nine centuries in your garden, under a persimmon tree, and you are the only one who knows. The persimmons have been unusually sweet. When the elder stirs, the tree drops a fruit on the elder's chest, and the elder murmurs: 'Thank you.'

choices.text: Leave a pillow under the elder's head

effects.log: The elder shifts, content, and goes on sleeping. The tree keeps dropping its sweetest fruit.

choices.text: Sit and wait for the elder to wake

effects.log: You wait for nine decades. The elder sits up and says: 'Is it still the Third Age?' It is not.

events.text: A goddess of fog has settled over your garden for a week and will not leave. She is the polite kind, who asks nothing and is not in the way, but every path is soft and unknown. You have lost your own hall twice. In the evening she says: 'I am so sorry. I am shy.'

choices.text: Tell her she is welcome, and fetch a lantern

effects.log: The fog clings to the lantern and makes a glow like a moon. The goddess hums, pleased.

choices.text: Walk into the fog and stay lost for an hour

effects.log: You wander the garden and meet yourself twice. It is a surprisingly useful hour.

events.text: Two goddesses of seasons are quarrelling about whose turn it is. One insists spring has already begun; the other says it was only an exceptionally warm winter. The quarrel has delayed the blossoming of an orchard, which is anxious. You are asked to judge.

choices.text: Declare a week of in-between

effects.log: A week of mild air settles over the realm. Both goddesses are annoyed in equal measure, which is the fairest outcome.

choices.text: Ask the orchard what it wants

effects.log: The orchard blooms the next dawn. Neither goddess is quite sure who won.

events.text: At the feast a cup is set at the foot of the table for the god who is not present: the forgotten one, the unknown, the one who has just died. The cup is full. Tonight, as the wine is poured, the table falls quiet because the cup, quite plainly, has been drunk from.

choices.text: Raise your cup to the empty place

effects.log: You raise a cup. Around the table, others do. The empty place is not empty for a breath.

choices.text: Refill it without a word

effects.log: A servant refills it. The feast goes on, a little thoughtfully, until the last lantern.

events.text: A very old god has fallen asleep at the feast with a spoon in hand. The room, rather than wake them, has arranged itself around the nap: lower voices, softer plates, a cushion slipped in. You are asked, as the youngest at the table, to keep an eye on the spoon.

choices.text: Hold the spoon and keep it steady

effects.log: You hold the spoon for an hour. The old god wakes, takes the spoon, and says: 'Ah. The soup.'

choices.text: Take the spoon and eat the soup yourself

effects.log: It is an excellent soup. The old god sleeps on.

events.text: In the divine market a stall sells prayers by the pound: bright, loud ones, and thin grey quiet ones. The stall-keeper, a small god of leftovers, offers you a free sample. 'Sometimes,' they say, 'a prayer is wasted on the one it was meant for.'

choices.text: Taste a thin grey prayer

effects.log: It is a child's prayer, for a lost mitten. You find the mitten and leave it on a doorstep.

choices.text: Buy a bright loud one and send it back

effects.log: The loud prayer goes home with a dream of thanks. The stall-keeper sells out by noon.

events.text: It rains in your domain, steady and slow, and the roofs sing. Nothing needs doing. You sit at the window with a cup of tea and listen to a hundred small prayers that all say the same thing: thank you for the rain. Not one asks for anything.

choices.text: Answer each with a drop on the glass

effects.log: The glass fills with drops, each one a small reply.

choices.text: Do nothing at all

effects.log: You do nothing at all. It is, in its way, the best thing a god does.

events.text: A moth has come into your hall in the night and circles your lamp. It is not a spirit and not a messenger. It is a moth. You find yourself watching it for an hour with the tender attention of a god with nothing else to look at.

choices.text: Dim the lamp so it can rest

effects.log: The moth lands on the shade and sleeps. In the morning it is gone.

choices.text: Follow the moth when it leaves

effects.log: It leads you to a window where a child is looking at the same lamp. You smile at both.

events.text: Once a year the star-stags of the Sky cross your lands, and the old custom is a hunt that never draws a bow: the herd is turned toward one meadow and a single stag is let touch the ground. {npc}, the huntmaster, asks you to sound the opening horn. {He} has done it forty times and says the horn sounds wrong in a mortal throat.
events.arc: The Yearly Hunt of the Star-Stags

choices.text: Sound the horn yourself

effects.log: The note goes up and the herd turns as one. {npc} watches your face and says nothing, which from {him} is praise.

choices.text: Ride out masked and let the huntmaster sound it

effects.log: You ride at the back in a plain coat. Nobody knows you, and the herd turns for the old horn as it always did.

choices.text: Decline the hunt this year

effects.log: You stay home. The herd crosses unturned and scatters over three domains; the neighbours send polite notes.

events.text: The stag that touches the ground this year is a young one, antlers still in velvet, and it does not run back up. It stands in the meadow and looks at you, and {npc} whispers that it has never happened in forty years.
events.arc: The Yearly Hunt of the Star-Stags

choices.text: Kneel and let it come close

effects.log: It lowers its head to the grass beside you and stays. The herd waits above, wheeling, until dusk.

choices.text: Lift it back up yourself

effects.log: You carry the stag into the air on a stair of light. It goes with a backward look, and the herd closes around it.

events.text: The young stag comes back every year, alone, a day before the herd, and waits in the meadow. {npc} has taken to leaving it salt. The herd's other members have started to wait too, a little way up, as if for a verdict.
events.arc: The Yearly Hunt of the Star-Stags

choices.text: Name the stag and keep it

effects.log: You name it Dawnhoof. The huntmaster files the name in the book of the hunt, in a slow proud hand.

choices.text: Leave it unnamed and free

effects.log: You leave the meadow open and do not say a word. The stag keeps coming, and nobody owns the arrangement.

events.text: A hard winter thins the herd, and the Sky's stars go dim above your meadow. {npc} wonders aloud whether a hunt that touches the ground is the cause. The stag, grown, stands waiting in the snow.
events.arc: The Yearly Hunt of the Star-Stags

choices.text: Keep the hunt and add a feeding meadow

effects.log: You lay a second meadow of silver grass. The herd thickens by spring, and the stars come back one by one.

choices.text: End the hunt, kindly, for good

effects.log: The last hunt is held at dusk and everyone cries a little. The herd never touches ground again and does well enough, and still looks down.

events.text: The ember-cranes of the First Hearth must be counted every year when they come to nest in the chimneys of the world. {npc}, who counts them, says there are three fewer than last year, and three fewer the year before, and that {he} is too old to be wrong a third time.
events.arc: The Count of the Ember-Cranes

choices.text: Go out to count them yourself

effects.log: You stand on a ridge at dusk while the cranes come down like falling coals. The count is right. The number is still three short.

choices.text: Ask the Hearth itself

effects.log: The Hearth gives you a warm, tired answer: the cranes are nesting elsewhere, in a new chimney you have not lit.

choices.text: Tell the counter {he} is not wrong

effects.log: You tell {npc} the tally is right. {He} eyes you for a long moment and goes back to counting.

events.text: The three missing cranes are found: a lowly stove-god three isles over has lit a hearth with a proper chimney and no one told you. The cranes are nesting happily and the god is terrified you will be angry.
events.arc: The Count of the Ember-Cranes

choices.text: Visit, and bless the little chimney

effects.log: The stove-god cries into a sleeve. The cranes lift a leg at you as one, which is as close to a bow as a crane gets.

choices.text: Ask the stove-god to share the nesting season

effects.log: You agree on a calendar, three weeks each. Both chimneys smoke contentedly.

events.text: {npc} dies in the cranes' season, quietly, with the count in {his} hand. The cranes circle the chimney that evening in a ring that is not a pattern, and settle all at once, and every chimney in the domain is warm.
events.arc: The Count of the Ember-Cranes

choices.text: Keep the ledger {he} left, and keep counting

effects.log: You begin your own column of numbers under {his}. It is slow and dull and you find you love it.

choices.text: Light a crane-fire at {his} grave

effects.log: A small bright fire burns there every dusk and the cranes come in to it without fail.

events.text: Years on, the stove-god's chimney and yours have become one long line of smoke the cranes follow across the world. A mortal poet writes that fire has a road. It is the best thing anyone has written about you.
events.arc: The Count of the Ember-Cranes

choices.text: Send the poet a warm room for the winter

effects.log: The poet writes a second poem in that room, and it is worse, and you keep it anyway.

choices.text: Say nothing; let the road run

effects.log: The road of smoke runs on, and no one needs to be thanked for it.

events.text: Each spring the tide-oxen are driven from the deep pastures to the shallows to calve. {npc}, the herd-master, reports that the great bull of the herd has stopped at the reef's edge and will go neither forward nor back. {He} ignores both whistle and drum.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox That Would Not Be Herded

choices.text: Go down to the reef and speak to the bull

effects.log: The bull is not stubborn. It is listening for something under the sand. You listen too, and hear a slow bell.

choices.text: Turn the tide behind the herd to push it on

effects.log: The tide turns and the bull moves, grumbling. The herd-master says nothing and looks at the sand.

choices.text: Wait a day for the bull to decide

effects.log: The bull decides at dawn. It goes forward, as if nothing had happened, and the calves are born on time.

events.text: Under the sand is a sunken bell from a drowned temple, rung by the tide, and the bull has been answering it for years: it is a calling-song. The herd-master says the oxen are mourning a god who is no longer remembered.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox That Would Not Be Herded

choices.text: Raise the bell and hang it where it can ring freely

effects.log: You lift the bell onto a tall rock. It rings across the shallows and every ox lows back. The forgotten god is, for a moment, heard.

choices.text: Leave it buried and learn its song

effects.log: You learn the call. In the evenings you answer it from the shore and the bull comes in close to listen.

events.text: The bull comes to the shore at spring's end and lays its heavy head on a rock by your feet. The herd-master takes off {his} cap. It is, {he} says, the old bull's way of saying goodbye.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox That Would Not Be Herded

choices.text: Sit with it through the tide

effects.log: The tide goes out and in again, and the bull is gone with the water, unhurried. The calves sing the bell-song at dusk.

choices.text: Give the bull a name for the shore

effects.log: You give it a long name that no one can say. The herd-master shortens it to Bell, and so it is remembered.

events.text: A mortal fisher sails a skiff into the shallows at calving and sees, by the light of the low moon, a hundred oxen swimming in a ring around a sunken bell. {npc} is called to calm the fisher before the story gets abroad.
events.arc: The Tide-Ox That Would Not Be Herded

choices.text: Let the story get abroad

effects.log: The fisher tells it in harbour taverns for the rest of {npc}'s long life and gains a small reputation, and so does your reef.

choices.text: Fog the shallows for a night and tell nobody

effects.log: The fog rolls in; the fisher drifts out unharmed, puzzled, with only a half-memory of bells.

events.text: The ferry-eels of Death draw the long boats across the river of the departed, and they all swim one way. This morning {npc}, the eel-keeper, reports that one swam the other, against the current, with an empty boat behind it.
events.arc: The Ferry-Eel That Swam Upstream

choices.text: Follow it upstream

effects.log: You walk the bank for a day. The eel is making for the source of the river, where the dead are first poured into it.

choices.text: Have the keeper call it back

effects.log: The keeper whistles the eel-call three times. It lifts its head, looks at you, and goes on.

choices.text: Let it go and add a note to the ledger

effects.log: You note: one eel gone upstream, cause unknown. It is the shortest entry in the ledger, and the saddest.

events.text: At the source you find the eel curled round a small stone in the shallows. Under it is a name written in water, a person who has been waiting a very long time for a boat that never came. The eel went to fetch them.
events.arc: The Ferry-Eel That Swam Upstream

choices.text: Row the waiting one down yourself

effects.log: You take the oars. The crossing is quiet, and at the far bank the waiting one thanks you in a voice like cold water.

choices.text: Lift the stone and let the eel carry it

effects.log: The eel carries the stone and its name down with the current. The waiting is over, and it does not look back.

events.text: After that {npc} keeps a boat at the source, with a lamp lit in it all night. The eels sometimes bring one up there who had missed their place in the queue. No one is turned away. The ledger is a good deal longer.
events.arc: The Ferry-Eel That Swam Upstream

choices.text: Name the lamp-boat after the first waiting one

effects.log: The boat takes the old name. It is the only boat on the river with a name, and the dead point to it as they pass.

choices.text: Add a second boat on the far bank

effects.log: A second lamp answers the first from across the water, and some say it is a gate.

events.text: Something has gotten out of a walled-off heaven. {npc}, a warden from the sealing-office, arrives in your hall with a scroll and a limp, saying a grey-eyed beast with a hundred joints is loose somewhere in your lands, and asks for your leave to search.
events.arc: The Beast That Slipped a Sealed Heaven

choices.text: Give leave and join the search

effects.log: You ride out with the warden at dusk. The tracks are light as breath, and they lead toward the hills.

choices.text: Give leave, and stay home

effects.log: The warden searches alone. Nothing is found by midnight except a single long white hair on your gate.

choices.text: Ask what it was sealed for

effects.log: The warden shuffles the scroll and admits nobody now alive remembers. That, you decide, is worth knowing.

events.text: The beast is found sleeping in a cave, curled around a hearth some forgotten shepherd left. It is vast, old, and entirely unthreatening. It opens one grey eye and asks, in a voice like paper, whether the war is over.
events.arc: The Beast That Slipped a Sealed Heaven

choices.text: Tell it yes, and sit down

effects.log: You sit with it by the dead hearth and tell it the war ended long ago. It sighs, and its hundred joints settle, one after another.

choices.text: Tell it that it must go back behind the seal

effects.log: It rises with a creaking dignity. The warden looks away, and the beast says nothing at all.

events.text: The warden returns with a petition: the sealing-office would like the beast back inside before the next audit. {npc} has no heart for it. {He} asks only that you do not make {him} choose.
events.arc: The Beast That Slipped a Sealed Heaven

choices.text: Offer the beast a home in a quiet corner of your domain

effects.log: The beast takes the corner and begins, slowly, to tend it. The audit passes without comment because nobody reads the register.

choices.text: Sign the petition and walk it back yourself

effects.log: You walk the beast to the seal at dawn. At the threshold it turns, thanks you, and steps through. The warden weeps.

events.text: A year on, the old beast's corner has grown a garden of white moss and slow stones. Travellers cross your domain to see it. The sealing-office has quietly stopped asking about a beast that, officially, was never loose.
events.arc: The Beast That Slipped a Sealed Heaven

choices.text: Open the garden to the faithful

effects.log: The garden is filled with quiet people and one grey eye watching from the moss. Faith grows there like lichen.

choices.text: Keep the garden private

effects.log: You and the beast keep the garden between you. It remembers the war; you remember the peace.

events.text: Every seventh year the Green Assembly holds a hunt whose quarry is never killed: the first hind of spring, caught only by being followed in silence. {npc}, a god of reeds, tells you that your turn to lead the following has come, and that you must not speak for a day.
events.arc: The Sacred Hunt of the Green Assembly

choices.text: Follow in silence with the whole assembly

effects.log: You walk a day without speaking behind a white hind through woods that have been waiting seven years for your feet.

choices.text: Follow alone, a little way apart

effects.log: Alone at the rear you hear the hind turn and look back, once, for you.

choices.text: Decline, with a polite excuse

effects.log: The assembly accepts it graciously and gives the lead to a god of mushrooms, who is delighted.

events.text: At dusk the hind stops at a spring in a dell you have never seen. The followers stand in a ring, silent. It is the rule that the leader must now say a single word, any word, and the hind will remember it for seven years.
events.arc: The Sacred Hunt of the Green Assembly

choices.text: Say your own name

effects.log: The hind bows its head. For seven years you will have a small, soft presence in a wood that did not know you.

choices.text: Say the name of the one who prays wrong

effects.log: The hind looks at you for a long moment, and walks away into the trees. It is the oddest blessing you have ever given.

choices.text: Say nothing at all

effects.log: The ring holds its breath. The hind lowers its head and goes, and the god of reeds pats your shoulder and says that was the wisest word anyone has ever said.

events.text: Seven years later the hind comes to your door in the dark and stands at the threshold. It does not ask for anything. It only wishes to be remembered one more year, in the old way, and {npc} says the assembly would be honoured to have you lead again.
events.arc: The Sacred Hunt of the Green Assembly

choices.text: Lead again, gladly

effects.log: The assembly follows you a second time. The hind stays at your hearth three nights.

choices.text: Hand the lead on to a younger god

effects.log: You teach the younger god the rule of silence. The hind watches you do it and seems to approve.

events.text: In the oldest corridor of your hall is a sealed door that has been sealed longer than your domain has been cut. This morning someone knocked on it from the other side: three slow knocks, then a pause, then a cough. {npc}, the hall's keeper, drops a lamp.
events.arc: The Sealed Door That Knocks Back

choices.text: Knock back, three times

effects.log: The reply comes at once: three knocks, and a faint pleased laugh. {npc} sits down on the floor.

choices.text: Put an ear to the door and listen

effects.log: Behind the seal someone is humming a work-song, badly, over the sound of a kettle.

choices.text: Order the corridor closed for a month

effects.log: The keeper closes the corridor and the knocking goes on, politely, through the shut door.

events.text: Over a month of evenings you learn that behind the door lives a householder who sealed {his} own heaven shut with a quarrel and has forgotten how to open it. {npc} apologises, a good deal, and asks whether it is still the age of the First Harvest.
events.arc: The Sealed Door That Knocks Back

choices.text: Say it is long past, and offer to open the door

effects.log: There is a long silence. Then: please do. {He} sounds frightened, and not of you.

choices.text: Say it is long past, and keep the door shut for now

effects.log: You promise to visit often. The householder is relieved and a little hurt, in about equal measure.

events.text: You open the door. Behind it is a very tidy little heaven, one room and a kettle, and a person with kind, old, bewildered eyes who has been keeping house for an age no one counted. {He} offers you tea before anything else.
events.arc: The Sealed Door That Knocks Back

choices.text: Drink the tea, and ask {him} to stay as your guest

effects.log: The tea is perfect. {npc} stays, and takes over the hall's kitchen, and is happier there than anywhere.

choices.text: Drink the tea, and ask {him} what the quarrel was

effects.log: The quarrel is long and mostly about a gate that has since been demolished. You both laugh until the kettle boils over.

events.text: Every few evenings you visit the sealed door, which stays sealed, and talk through it. The householder is a good listener. The corridor smells of tea, which the keeper has stopped asking about.
events.arc: The Sealed Door That Knocks Back

choices.text: Ask for the household's recipes through the crack

effects.log: They come folded thin and slid under the door, one by one. The kitchen of your hall has never been better.

choices.text: Just keep the evenings

effects.log: It is the best hour of your day, and neither of you ever mentions it.

events.text: The gods once walled off a heaven because of what grew in it, and left the wall standing. {npc}, the wall-warden, brings you the news that the wall has a crack, and that through it a hand has been seen watering something on the far side.
events.arc: The Gardener of a Walled-Off Heaven

choices.text: Look through the crack

effects.log: On the far side is a garden, perfectly kept, and a gardener who has not noticed anyone has been gone.

choices.text: Ask the warden to widen it carefully

effects.log: The warden chisels the crack wide enough for a lantern. The light falls on a bed of pale flowers nodding in a wind that is not there.

choices.text: Have it plastered shut and say nothing

effects.log: It is plastered shut. The warden looks at you for a moment longer than is usual and says nothing either.

events.text: The gardener comes to the crack at dusk and speaks first. {npc} has grown a flower that blooms only for a single guest, and has been waiting for one since the wall went up. {He} will not say what the flower does.
events.arc: The Gardener of a Walled-Off Heaven

choices.text: Accept the invitation to see it

effects.log: You pass through the crack. The flower opens for you, slowly, and for the length of its bloom you remember every kindness you were ever given.

choices.text: Ask for a cutting to take home

effects.log: The gardener gives you a seed. It will not sprout until you forget about it. You plant it and walk away, trying very hard not to think.

events.text: The warden has had a letter from the sealing-office: the crack must be mended. {npc} stands between you and the wall, a small, unhappy figure, and does not move. {He} says the gardener should have a visitor at least once in an age.
events.arc: The Gardener of a Walled-Off Heaven

choices.text: Intercede for a standing gate in the wall

effects.log: The sealing-office grants a small gate, locked only on your side. The gardener plants a hedge round it by spring.

choices.text: Promise to mend it yourself, and never do

effects.log: Your promise holds the office for a decade. The gardener never learns how thin the arrangement is.

events.text: One morning the sprouted seed breaks the soil in your garden, a single pale flower. It opens for you, and for the length of its bloom you hear the walled-off gardener humming from a very long way off.
events.arc: The Gardener of a Walled-Off Heaven

choices.text: Hum back

effects.log: The flower closes slowly. A moment later it opens again and there is a humming answer, a little closer.

choices.text: Let it bloom unwatched

effects.log: It blooms and fades. You tell no one, and find you are lighter for it.

events.text: A very old god arrives at your gate with one iron key on a cord. {npc} says it opens one door, in one of the sealed heavens, and the door's whereabouts has been lost for three ages. {He} asks to be allowed to sit on your doorstep and wait for the door to come to {him}.
events.arc: The Keeper of a Single Key

choices.text: Let {him} wait, with a stool and a blanket

effects.log: You set a stool by the gate. {npc} thanks you with a courtesy so old it has no words left in it.

choices.text: Offer to search the sealed heavens for the door

effects.log: You send word to the sealing-office, which promises a list in due course. The keeper bows deeply.

choices.text: Send {him} to someone with more patience

effects.log: You point out a god with a longer doorstep. {npc} goes politely and says nothing more.

events.text: The sealing-office sends a list of nine hundred doors, with annotations. {npc} reads it aloud on the doorstep, one name at a time, and after each one says softly: no. At the four hundred and sixth {he} stops, and sits with the key held to {his} chest.
events.arc: The Keeper of a Single Key

choices.text: Go to the four hundredth and sixth door with {him}

effects.log: The door is a plain one. The key will not fit. {npc} sits down in front of it and laughs, long and helplessly.

choices.text: Ask what {he} would do if the door never came

effects.log: After a long pause, {he} says {he} would be glad to have been trusted with something. You do not think this is a small answer.
