events.text: Late in a long winter the door comes to the keeper. A plain wooden door, that was never in any list, stands by your gate in the morning, and the key fits it. Beyond is nothing but a lit room with an empty chair and a kettle. {npc} goes in and does not need anyone to follow.
events.arc: The Keeper of a Single Key

choices.text: Close the door gently behind {him}

effects.log: The door closes with a click. By evening it is gone, and the stool by the gate is empty, and warm.

choices.text: Leave the door ajar

effects.log: You leave a lamp at the threshold. The door stays beside your gate, and in the evenings you hear someone moving around inside.

events.text: At the edge of your domain is a place no map shows, from the days before the domains were cut. {npc}, an old hermit of the margins, says it has no weather, no seasons, and no gods. {He} dares you to walk in until you can no longer feel your own name.
events.arc: The Place Before the Domains Were Cut

choices.text: Walk in until your name fades

effects.log: Your name goes, and then your title, and then the way you hold your hands. What is left is quiet and wide, and not unpleasant.

choices.text: Walk in only a little way

effects.log: A little way in, the air is so still you can hear your pulse. You turn back, a touch lighter.

choices.text: Decline the dare

effects.log: You tell the hermit that a god who walks off the map should leave a note. {He} laughs and leaves one for you.

events.text: Something in the place before the cut has noticed you. It does not speak or move. It just turns, very slowly, the way a sleeping animal does at a footstep, and the quiet around you leans a little toward your side.
events.arc: The Place Before the Domains Were Cut

choices.text: Sit down, and let it be near

effects.log: You sit, and it settles. The hermit watches from the edge, hands folded, and neither of you speaks for a long time.

choices.text: Offer it a small gift: a name

effects.log: You offer a plain name, no title. It takes it, and the quiet thins and flickers, and a single bird calls somewhere that has no trees.

events.text: The place is less quiet than it was. A bird, once; a trickle of water; a breeze. The hermit notes it in a book with a stubby pencil, and says the cutting of the domains may not have been the only cut. Something is growing back.
events.arc: The Place Before the Domains Were Cut

choices.text: Leave the place alone and let it heal

effects.log: You promise to ask the other domains to leave it be. Most agree. The hermit takes a thousand years of notes in that decade alone.

choices.text: Tend it with a few seeds from your domain

effects.log: The seeds sprout in odd colours. The place does not mind; it seems to find them funny.

events.text: Years on, a bird from that place nests on the roof of your hall. It sings one note, over and over, a note that belongs to nothing. {npc} nods when {he} hears it and says: that was the first sound.
events.arc: The Place Before the Domains Were Cut

choices.text: Keep the nest undisturbed

effects.log: The bird raises two chicks on your eaves. Their note is slightly different. The hermit says that is how music started.

choices.text: Learn the note

effects.log: You hum it. It will not stay in your head; it comes and goes. That, you suspect, is correct.

events.text: In the cellars under your hall sits the first dark: not a night, which belongs to the Sky, but the dark from before there was a light to be dark against. {npc}, the cellar-warden, says it has been sighing lately, and the sighs have a shape like a question.
events.arc: The First Dark Wants a Name

choices.text: Go down with a lamp and ask it

effects.log: It answers by cooling the lamp-flame very gently, not to put it out, only to see it better.

choices.text: Go down without a lamp

effects.log: In the pure dark you find you can see after all, in a sense, as one sees a sound. The question is a very simple one: what shall I be called?

choices.text: Have the cellar stairs closed for a day

effects.log: The warden bars the stairs. The sighing deepens, and the next morning a cold note is left on the top step: please.

events.text: You and {npc} argue over names for three nights. The warden wants Old Quiet. You lean toward Undersong. The dark waits through all of it, with something that might be amusement.
events.arc: The First Dark Wants a Name

choices.text: Propose a name with no meaning: Ah

effects.log: The dark ripples, and the name takes. It is the shortest name any god has given, and perhaps the most correct.

choices.text: Ask the dark to choose its own

effects.log: It takes long enough for you to fall asleep. In the morning the warden is weeping with joy: the name is a word in a tongue nobody has spoken.

events.text: Now the first dark sings in the cellars when the lamps are low. {npc} brings it a candle every evening, which it does not extinguish but dims, as a courtesy. Mortals who dream of cellars in your domain wake feeling oddly greeted.
events.arc: The First Dark Wants a Name

choices.text: Send a dream of the cellar to the worshippers

effects.log: They wake knowing a very old friend is below, and they leave small candles at your shrine in thanks.

choices.text: Keep it a household secret

effects.log: The first dark is yours, and the warden's, and it is not for anyone else to know.

events.text: Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars stands at your gate on a ladder that is far too tall, holding a lantern. {npc}, {his} apprentice, apologises for the intrusion. The great god has a star to hang over your lands, and needs to borrow a hook.
events.arc: The Ladder of Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars

choices.text: Lend the hook from your own hall

effects.log: The great god thanks you in a voice like distant weather. The star goes up, small, over your eastern hills, and you find you can see by it.

choices.text: Offer to hold the ladder

effects.log: You hold the ladder steady while the greatest of the Sky's gods climbs to hang a small star on a cloud. {npc} holds the lantern. It is a very quiet job.

choices.text: Ask what the star is for

effects.log: Cheonho says: it is for the person who looks up tonight and has nothing else. That is all, and it is enough.

events.text: A month on, the apprentice returns alone with a thank-you gift: a small jar with a captured star-glow in it, and a note in Cheonho's sweeping hand saying that no one has ever offered to hold the ladder before.
events.arc: The Ladder of Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars

choices.text: Keep the jar at your bedside

effects.log: It glows faintly all night. You sleep better than you have in an age.

choices.text: Hang the glow over the shrine door

effects.log: Pilgrims arriving after dark find the shrine door lit and say it feels like being expected.

events.text: Some years later the ladder leans on your wall again, and Cheonho is tired. The great god is not, today, hanging anything. {He} sits on the lowest rung and looks at the stars that {he} hung, and asks whether any of them still look right.
events.arc: The Ladder of Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars

choices.text: Tell Cheonho they look exactly right

effects.log: The old god nods, satisfied, and sits a little longer in the evening. {npc} brings blankets.

choices.text: Point out the one that hangs a little crooked

effects.log: Cheonho laughs, long and warm, and says that one is on purpose; it is the star for anyone who feels a little crooked.

events.text: Mujin of the Thousand Banners has never lost a battle, and keeps every banner from every one. {npc}, {his} banner-mender, knocks at your door, nervous, with a bundle under {his} arm. One banner has been torn by a sparrow, and no one else in the Hall dares tell the great god.
events.arc: The Banner-Mender of Mujin

choices.text: Offer to tell Mujin yourself

effects.log: You carry the banner to the great war-god in person. Mujin looks at the sparrow-tear for a long moment and laughs, at last, for the first time in an age.

choices.text: Mend it yourself, quietly

effects.log: It is the worst needlework in the history of the Hall. {npc} takes it, wipes a tear, and says that is perfect.

choices.text: Advise the mender to tell the truth

effects.log: The mender goes pale and does it. You are told later that it went well.

events.text: Mujin sends you a thousand-and-first banner: plain white, with a single sparrow stitched in one corner. It is, the note says, the only banner the great god is fond of. {npc} hangs it over your door.
events.arc: The Banner-Mender of Mujin

choices.text: Hang it above the shrine and tell the story

effects.log: Pilgrims come to see the banner and are told the story. The sparrow is, by the next year, a small cult of its own.

choices.text: Keep it inside and say nothing

effects.log: You keep it folded in a chest by your bed. Once a year, on a bad day, you take it out.

events.text: The mender comes by at the year's end, grey and gently teasing, to say that Mujin has taken up needlework. It is, apparently, terrible. The banner room is full of lopsided flags, and the great god is happier than the Hall has ever seen.
events.arc: The Banner-Mender of Mujin

choices.text: Send Mujin a thimble

effects.log: A reply comes with a very formal thank-you. The next lopsided flag is stitched with a pattern of tiny thimbles.

choices.text: Ask the mender to pass on your respects

effects.log: The respects are passed on. Mujin sends back a single stitched sparrow, again.

events.text: The Unmaking, the quiet wearing-away at the borders of the world, took something from your lands overnight: not a thing, but the name of one. A small river is still there, still wet, but no one can say what it was called, and {npc} the river-herald weeps over a dictionary.
events.arc: The Name the Unmaking Took

choices.text: Give the river a new name, now

effects.log: You pick one in a breath, a plain good name. The river carries it on with an air of relief.

choices.text: Search the old songs for the lost name

effects.log: You spend a week among the elder chanters. Not one remembers. The song is gone, and the river sings on without it.

choices.text: Let the river go unnamed a while

effects.log: You let it flow nameless. The herald, to your surprise, begins to sleep better.

events.text: A second name goes in the Unmaking's night: this time the name of a hill. And then the name of a little ford. {npc} is keeping a list in a hand grown frantic. The Unmaking is not hungry; it is, the herald says, merely tidying up what no one says aloud.
events.arc: The Name the Unmaking Took

choices.text: Order your worshippers to say the names aloud each dawn

effects.log: The dawn-recitation begins. In a month the names come back, one by one, spoken by tired people on their doorsteps.

choices.text: Write every name into the stone of your hall

effects.log: The hall's walls fill with names over a season. The Unmaking nibbles at the margins and finds the stone too hard.

events.text: A year on the Unmaking comes for the name of your own domain. {npc} runs into your hall at noon with the news. Outside, the sky is a shade paler where the word used to hang.
events.arc: The Name the Unmaking Took

choices.text: Say the name aloud with every worshipper at once

effects.log: A hundred thousand voices say the name. The pale sky deepens and the word settles back as if it never left.

choices.text: Take a new name, freely, and let the old one rest

effects.log: You accept a new name, and the old one is laid in the river like a boat. It is not erased; it is only finished.

events.text: The Unmaking never comes back to your lands. {npc} keeps the list of lost names in a drawer and recites them at the river on the first dawn of each year. Many of the names have been given to children.
events.arc: The Name the Unmaking Took

choices.text: Name a child after the river

effects.log: The child is named. The river bubbles, in a way that may be gratitude.

choices.text: Let the recitation be the herald's own

effects.log: The herald's voice grows stronger. You never again have to say a word.

events.text: The shrine of a forgotten god burned down long ago in your domain, but its hound still guards the ash. {npc}, a charcoal-burner, says the animal has not eaten in a month and growls at everyone but you, whom it watches from a distance with burning, patient eyes.
events.arc: The Hound of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Go up to the ash and sit down near it

effects.log: The hound does not move. After an hour it lies down, six paces away, with its chin on its paws.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of broth at the edge of the ash

effects.log: It waits until you leave, then drinks. The next day the bowl is clean, and a stone has been placed in it.

choices.text: Ask the charcoal-burner what the shrine was

effects.log: {He} says no one remembers, but the hound used to sing at dusk. It stopped the day the last pilgrim died.

events.text: The hound has followed you home, six paces behind. It sleeps at the foot of the shrine wall of your hall, and at dusk it lifts its head and howls, once, a note as low as an organ. {npc} insists it is a prayer.
events.arc: The Hound of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Learn the howl, and answer it

effects.log: You howl back, badly. The hound tilts its head. After a week your answer is almost right, and the hound's tail thumps the stone.

choices.text: Ask a priest to find out whose prayer it is

effects.log: The priest goes to the archives for a season and comes back pale: the prayer is addressed to no god. It is addressed to the one who is left.

events.text: Mortals from the old shrine's valley start to walk the hills, drawn by the howl. They bring no gifts but ash on their palms. They say their grandmothers prayed here, and they have come to see whether anyone is listening.
events.arc: The Hound of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Rebuild a small shrine from the burned stones

effects.log: The pilgrims lift the black stones with their own hands. The hound sits at the new doorstep as if it had only been waiting for permission.

choices.text: Receive them quietly at the ash and ask nothing

effects.log: You stand with them in the ash. The hound sings, and they listen, and no one prays aloud.

events.text: The hound dies in its sleep one cold dawn, curled at the new shrine's step. {npc} wraps it in a blanket of ash-grey wool. The pilgrims bury it under the threshold, and for a season there is no howl at all. Then, one dusk, a new note.
events.arc: The Hound of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Listen for who sings it now

effects.log: It is a child of seven from the valley, standing at the step, trying out a new voice. The note is exactly right.

choices.text: Leave a blanket on the step for the next one

effects.log: You leave one every autumn. Whoever sleeps there is welcome.

events.text: In the burned shrine's ruin, {npc} the sweeper finds a floor of ash that has taken the print of a thousand knees. Every dusk a wind lifts a line of ash into the air and writes a few words, always the same: please come back.
events.arc: The Prayers Written in Ash

choices.text: Reply in ash, with the same hand

effects.log: You scatter a line of ash on the wind: I am here. The wind carries it up, and next dusk it writes: thank you.

choices.text: Sit with the sweeper and watch it write

effects.log: The ash writes the words over and over, patiently. {npc} says it has been doing so for three hundred years.

choices.text: Record the words and leave

effects.log: You copy them down. They look simpler on paper, which is worse.

events.text: The ash writes a name now, once a week. It is not the burned god's name; it is a mortal's, over and over, a woman who must once have lit the last lamp in this shrine. {npc} thinks it is an apology.
events.arc: The Prayers Written in Ash

choices.text: Find the mortal's grave and light a lamp there

effects.log: It takes months. The grave is under a tree on the far side of the hills. You light a lamp. The ash on the shrine floor writes: that is enough.

choices.text: Leave the ash its own sorrow

effects.log: You do not intrude. The sweeper nods, and sweeps around the letters, careful not to scuff a single one.

events.text: The wind stops writing after the lamp is lit. The ash lies flat. {npc} tidies the floor for the first time in an age and is surprised by how much of it is simply dirt. A weed has begun to grow in a corner.
events.arc: The Prayers Written in Ash

choices.text: Plant something living in the ruin

effects.log: You plant a pear sapling in the old sanctuary. It takes root in the ash and flowers inside two seasons.

choices.text: Let the weed be

effects.log: The weed grows. The sweeper stops sweeping and starts watering.

events.text: Thunder is made by drummers, as every god of the domain knows, and the drummers are tired. {npc}, the chief drummer, has been beating the ninth drum for nine hundred years and reports that {his} wrists are done. Storm season is a month away.
events.arc: The Drummers of the Nine Drums

choices.text: Take the sticks yourself for a day

effects.log: You drum for a day. It is dreadful, and the first honest noise your domain has heard in an age. The chief drummer rests with {his} feet in a bucket.

choices.text: Hire a younger drummer from the pilgrims

effects.log: You send word through the shrines. Three young hopefuls arrive within the week, hands calloused from other drums entirely.

choices.text: Tell {him} to rest until the first storm

effects.log: The chief drummer rests, with a bad conscience, and spends the month teaching the ninth drum to a nephew.

events.text: Your new drumming is passable now, and a rumour has crossed the domain: the thunder has changed its voice. Mortals say the storms sound younger. The chief drummer is torn between pride and an old grudge against anything younger.
events.arc: The Drummers of the Nine Drums

choices.text: Keep the old style, and teach the new ones to match

effects.log: The old pattern returns to the sky by the next season. {npc} says nothing, but starts to hum while {he} works.

choices.text: Let the new voice stand

effects.log: The storms are sharper and quicker now, and the farmers say they sleep better through them.

events.text: On the longest night of storms the ninth drum cracks. A thin, bright crack across the skin, like lightning drawn small. {npc} stands over it, silent, with the sticks in both hands.
events.arc: The Drummers of the Nine Drums

choices.text: Have the drum remade by the old drum-maker

effects.log: It takes a season. The new drum has the same voice as the old, and the chief drummer swears it is better.

choices.text: Leave the crack, and let the drum play with it

effects.log: The crack gives the drum a low rattle under every beat. Mortals call it the voice of the old storm, and love it.

events.text: Every tide in your sea is kept by a keeper, a modest mortal-born spirit with a ledger and a conch. {npc}, the keeper of the grey strand, reports that last night's high tide arrived four minutes late, and begs your pardon with a very formal bow.
events.arc: The Tide-Keepers' Ledger

choices.text: Forgive it and ask the cause

effects.log: The cause is a lost mooring-rope on the bottom that snagged the water. You send a current to pull it free.

choices.text: Tell the keeper the tide is always allowed four minutes

effects.log: The keeper, who has agonised about this for a night, wipes {his} face and says thank you.

choices.text: Inspect the ledger

effects.log: The ledger is a work of art. Every entry for three thousand years is in the same careful hand.

events.text: A dockside cult has formed around the keeper, mortals who think {npc} is the sea. {He} is mortified. They leave offerings of dried fish at the strand, and {his} ledger has to be moved above the wave-line.
events.arc: The Tide-Keepers' Ledger

choices.text: Explain to the cult that the sea is you

effects.log: The cult adjusts quickly and starts leaving dried fish for you instead. The keeper sighs with relief.

choices.text: Let the cult be and bless the keeper

effects.log: The keeper accepts the blessing like an apology. The dried fish continue.

events.text: The oldest keeper on the coast, a spirit as flat and grey as a plate, asks to be allowed to stop. It has kept one tide on one beach for six ages and would like, just once, to see a tide it did not keep. {npc} offers to take the beach.
events.arc: The Tide-Keepers' Ledger

choices.text: Release the old keeper to wander the shores

effects.log: The old keeper walks the coast for a season and sends you a postcard from every beach. {npc} runs the grey strand well.

choices.text: Ask the old keeper to stay and teach

effects.log: It agrees, gruffly. For ten years it sits in a chair on the beach, calling out wrong tides on purpose, to keep the young ones sharp.

events.text: The departed queue at the river each dusk, in the order they died and with the patience that death gives. {npc}, one of the ferry-marshals, reports a small problem: a person near the head of the queue refuses to board, because they have not finished a sentence.
events.arc: The Queue at the Ferry of the Pale Ferryman

choices.text: Go to the head of the queue and hear the sentence

effects.log: The sentence is a half-told story about a goat. You hear it to the end. The goat, it turns out, was clever. The waiting one boards, smiling.

choices.text: Ask the marshal to hold the boat a little

effects.log: The boat waits. The sentence goes on for an hour. No one in the queue complains.

choices.text: Send the waiting one to the back of the queue

effects.log: They shuffle to the back, patiently, to begin again. The marshal looks at you, once, and says nothing.

events.text: A second problem: a person in the queue has been trying to bribe the marshal with a bag of seeds. They want to be buried with them. They say the seeds are a promise. {npc} looks at you; the rules say nothing about seeds.
events.arc: The Queue at the Ferry of the Pale Ferryman

choices.text: Let the seeds ride in the boat

effects.log: They go over the river. On the far bank, years later, a small green shoot is reported from the shore. No one will say whose.

choices.text: Take the seeds and plant them yourself

effects.log: You plant them on the near bank. They grow into a hedge of white flowers that the queue loves.

events.text: On the quietest night of the year the queue runs out. Everyone has crossed. {npc} stands by the empty landing with a lantern, unsure what to do with such an evening. The river lies calm and dark, and the boats rest at their moorings.
events.arc: The Queue at the Ferry of the Pale Ferryman

choices.text: Sit on the landing and share the lantern

effects.log: You and the marshal sit side by side and watch the water. It is the only silence the ferry has ever had.

choices.text: Send the marshal home for the night

effects.log: The marshal goes. You stay on the landing a long time, listening to the river learn what to do with itself.

events.text: Fate's knot-readers sit in rows in the loom hall, reading the knots in the threads of lives with their fingertips. {npc}, the senior reader, brings you a knot that will not read: a thread tied back on itself in a way that is not in any manual.
events.arc: The Knot-Readers of the Loom Hall

choices.text: Feel the knot yourself

effects.log: Under your fingers it is a tiny, tidy loop, a promise someone made in the thread of a life and kept. It is not a knot of fate at all; it is a knot of choice.

choices.text: Ask the Weaver's office for a ruling

effects.log: The Weaver's office replies in five weeks that it is probably nothing, which {npc} reads as an alarming yes.

choices.text: Tell the reader to leave the knot alone

effects.log: The reader leaves it. Nothing happens, which is to say, something happens quietly somewhere else.

events.text: More knots of choice appear. The hall is unsettled. The readers argue about whether to untie them or write them into the manual. {npc} asks you, quietly, which you would prefer.
events.arc: The Knot-Readers of the Loom Hall

choices.text: Write them into the manual as a new kind

effects.log: The manual grows by a chapter. The readers feel clever for a season, and the chapter is read at night by young apprentices.

choices.text: Leave them alone and read around them

effects.log: The readers learn to read the knots by their absence, as a stone is read by its shadow. It makes them gentler.

events.text: The oldest knot-reader goes blind in the autumn and reads the threads by ear now, listening to the little sounds they make. {npc} sits beside {him} to learn. The old reader says every thread hums, a different note, and that yours hums two.
events.arc: The Knot-Readers of the Loom Hall

choices.text: Ask what the two notes mean

effects.log: The old reader smiles. One is the god you are. One is the person you were before. They agree, mostly.

choices.text: Ask nothing and be glad of the compliment

effects.log: You leave the loom hall humming, and cannot tell which note is yours.

events.text: Dreams are not made; they are delivered, every night, to every sleeper. Mongsa the Sleeper runs the night shift in a great hall of lamplit shelves. {npc}, one of the deliverers, is weeping in the corridor: {he} delivered one dream to the wrong sleeper, and the sleeper liked it too much to give it back.
events.arc: The Night Shift of the Sleeper

choices.text: Go and ask the sleeper to give it back

effects.log: You appear in a dream and ask, gently. The sleeper says the dream was lovely and offers a trade: any dream you like, as long as it is theirs.

choices.text: Let the sleeper keep it, and write it off

effects.log: The ledger takes a small hit. The deliverer weeps with relief. The sleeper wakes happy.

choices.text: Tell the deliverer to try harder

effects.log: The deliverer tries harder. It does not make the dream any less misdelivered.

events.text: The night shift is short of hands, as it always is. A great many sleepers lie dreamless on the nights the shelves run bare. The Sleeper asks the shift for a volunteer who will deliver the dreams that no one claims. {npc} looks at you, hopefully.
events.arc: The Night Shift of the Sleeper

choices.text: Deliver the unclaimed dreams yourself for a week

effects.log: You walk the night streets with a lamp and a basket. The dreams you deliver are odd, misshapen, tender. You are told the sleepers loved them best.

choices.text: Hire three more deliverers from the pilgrim shrines

effects.log: The shift grows by three. The shelves are never bare again, and the dreams get a little odder.

events.text: One night the deliverer {npc} stops at a bedside and does not leave the dream. The sleeper is a very old person, awake, who says they are not afraid. {He} asks you what to do. The rule is that dreams are delivered, never watched.
events.arc: The Night Shift of the Sleeper

choices.text: Sit with them both until morning

effects.log: The old sleeper tells the dream aloud, and {npc} listens. By dawn nobody has slept, and the dream was received.

choices.text: Remind {him} that the shift cannot wait

effects.log: The deliverer moves on, grieved. The old sleeper waves.

events.text: The herds cross your domain in their seasons: sky-deer in spring, river-bulls in summer, thorn-boars in autumn, snow-hares in winter. {npc}, the herd-warden, comes to your door with a map of this year's crossings and one problem: two herds are scheduled for the same pass on the same day.
events.arc: The Great Herds Cross the Domain

choices.text: Split the pass: one herd at dawn, one at dusk

effects.log: You adjust the calendar. The herds cross in order, with only a little grumbling. The pass smells of dust and wet fur for a week.

choices.text: Open a second pass through the hills

effects.log: You lift a low ridge, and a second pass appears. Mortal travellers use it too, and give thanks.

choices.text: Let the herds sort it out themselves

effects.log: The herds take an afternoon to argue, and an hour to settle. They are better at it than gods.

events.text: A calf is born mid-pass and the whole herd stops to wait. {npc} watches from a rock, grey with worry. The calf stands, falls, stands again. The herd will not move on until it can walk.
events.arc: The Great Herds Cross the Domain

choices.text: Steady the calf with a hand of warm wind

effects.log: The calf takes three steps. The herd lifts its head as one and moves. {npc} sags onto the rock with relief.

choices.text: Wait with the herd and do nothing

effects.log: You wait with them an afternoon. The calf stands, in its own time. The herd moves on at dusk, in a long unhurried line.

events.text: In the winter crossing, the snow-hares come down the pass in their thousands, white on white, and settle for a night in the garden of your hall. {npc} says it is a custom; you have never heard of it. At dawn the hares have gone, and left a single tuft of fur on every doorstep.
events.arc: The Great Herds Cross the Domain

choices.text: Keep the tufts in a jar

effects.log: A jar of hare-fur sits on your windowsill and keeps the room warm all winter.

choices.text: Sweep the garden and say nothing

effects.log: You sweep the garden clean. The next winter, they come back, and bring a few more.

events.text: Every pantheon asks its gods for small duties: a lamp at the common altar, a word to a young god, a seat kept warm. {npc}, a pantheon clerk, arrives with the list for the season. It is long, mundane, and, as always, unenforceable.
events.arc: The Small Tithe of the Pantheon

choices.text: Do all of it, carefully

effects.log: You light the lamp, speak the word, warm the seat. It takes a week. The clerk is startled and writes a very short note of thanks.

choices.text: Do the lamp and the word, and skip the seat

effects.log: You do two of three. The clerk makes a small mark that will be found in an audit in some other age.

choices.text: Send a polite refusal with a small gift

effects.log: The clerk takes the gift and the refusal with equal grace. The list is not mentioned again.

events.text: The clerk returns with a second list: this one asks for something the pantheon needs and will not say. {npc} leaves it on your table and does not look at it. It is a request for a name to be left out of a report.
events.arc: The Small Tithe of the Pantheon

choices.text: Leave the name out of the report

effects.log: You leave it out. You have done a small wrong for a large loyalty, and you carry the name with you after.

choices.text: Include the name, and stand behind it

effects.log: The report goes up with the name in it. The pantheon is annoyed. The named god sends you an anonymous basket of pears.

events.text: A season later the clerk is gone, replaced by a stern young god who cannot tell you why. You learn that the clerk was sent away for a small kindness. {npc} had left a name out of a report, once, and was found out.
events.arc: The Small Tithe of the Pantheon

choices.text: Write a letter on the clerk's behalf

effects.log: The letter goes unanswered for a year. Then a thin reply: the clerk is well, and reassigned to a lighthouse.

choices.text: Let the pantheon's business be its own

effects.log: You say nothing. Some silences last longer than they should.

events.text: The Silent Hall keeps a vigil on the longest night: every member sits in the dark hall and says nothing until the dawn bell. {npc} has the seat beside yours and, an hour in, begins very quietly to hiccup.
events.arc: The Vigil in the Silent Hall

choices.text: Pass over a cup of water without a word

effects.log: The hiccups stop. {npc} nods gratitude into the dark. The vigil, for you, has become something close to prayer.

choices.text: Ignore it and keep the silence

effects.log: The hiccups go on for an hour and then stop on their own. You keep the vigil clean. The next day, a polite note arrives, thanking you for your composure.

choices.text: Slip out for a moment of air

effects.log: You leave for a breath and return. No one notices; no one admits to it.

events.text: At the third hour a voice breaks the silence: a young god of the Hall, new to the seat, has begun to cry. It is the loudest sound the Hall has heard in a century. Every head turns. {npc} looks at you.
events.arc: The Vigil in the Silent Hall

choices.text: Cross the hall and sit beside the young god

effects.log: You sit. The young god weeps until dawn, and the Hall, for the first time in an age, keeps a vigil that is not entirely silent.

choices.text: Stay in your seat and send a calm breath

effects.log: The calm breath crosses the hall. The weeping ebbs to a sniffle. The vigil survives.

events.text: A decade on, the elders of the Hall add a line to the vigil's rule: weeping is permitted. Some of the old ones are dismayed, some are quietly pleased. {npc} says the rule was changed because of a single night.
events.arc: The Vigil in the Silent Hall

choices.text: Accept thanks for the night

effects.log: You are thanked, formally, at the next feast. The young god you sat beside brings you a flower.

choices.text: Disclaim all credit

effects.log: You say you did nothing. The Hall sees what it sees.

events.text: At the divine courts the gods with no pantheon sit on the last bench, by the door, where the draught comes in. {npc}, the usher, has been told to keep it that way. This season {he} has set out an extra cushion for you, and looks as if {he} expects to be shouted at.
events.arc: The Last Bench at the Court

choices.text: Take the cushion and sit

effects.log: You sit on the draughty bench with a cushion. The god beside you, old and grey, says nothing, but moves over a little.

choices.text: Thank the usher and stand at the back instead

effects.log: You lean against the wall like a guard. The usher seems relieved not to have to find another cushion.

choices.text: Ask why the last bench is the last bench

effects.log: The usher says it has always been so. When pressed, {he} admits that no one has ever written it down.

events.text: A petition is circulating among the masterless: ask the court for a bench nearer the dais. It needs forty signatures, and so far has thirty-one. {npc} puts the scroll in your hand and says nothing, being careful not to hope aloud.
events.arc: The Last Bench at the Court

choices.text: Sign, and canvass the other nine

effects.log: You collect the remaining signatures in a week. The petition goes up. The court receives it in a long, rustling silence.

choices.text: Sign, and quietly lobby three friendly pantheon gods

effects.log: Three gods of rank agree to look at the petition kindly. It may even work.

choices.text: Decline to sign, and wish them well

effects.log: You wish them well and mean it. The petition reaches forty without you.

events.text: The court grants the masterless a bench three rows nearer the dais. It is a small victory and everyone knows it. At the next session the old grey god beside you shakes your hand, hard, and says nothing at all.
events.arc: The Last Bench at the Court

choices.text: Move to the new bench with the others

effects.log: You move your cushion together, a small uneven procession of unaffiliated gods. A pantheon herald coughs in the aisle. Nobody minds.

choices.text: Stay on the old bench a while longer, out of habit

effects.log: The old bench is comfortable, in its own way. You move eventually.

events.text: A god holding a domain is a seat, as well as a person: the seat has hours, petitioners, and a very old chair. {npc}, a lesser god of a nearby brook, arrives at your seat with a petition so humble it apologises in three places for taking up your time.
events.arc: The Petitioner at the Seat of a Domain

choices.text: Receive the petition and read it carefully

effects.log: It asks for a single change: that the brook be allowed to flow downhill on Tuesdays. You read it twice. It is not as simple as it sounds.

choices.text: Receive it with warmth and defer the reply

effects.log: You thank the brook-god. A month later you reply with a small decree. {npc} bows deeper than is needed.

choices.text: Refuse to receive it before noon

effects.log: The seat has hours. You keep them, and the brook-god waits patiently on the step.

events.text: The brook flows downhill on Tuesdays, and the other days of the week it flows uphill, in the old arrangement. The valley below has noticed and holds a small festival every Tuesday. {npc} is somewhat embarrassed at being the cause.
events.arc: The Petitioner at the Seat of a Domain

choices.text: Attend the Tuesday festival

effects.log: You attend. The valley is overwhelmed and delighted. A girl hands you a paper boat to float on the brook.

choices.text: Send a thank-you wind to the festival

effects.log: The wind goes over the valley and stirs a thousand paper boats. The brook-god weeps with joy.

events.text: When you pass the seat to your successor, the petition of the brook is the one thing you leave on the desk with a note. It is the only decree of your whole tenure that you want carried forward.
events.arc: The Petitioner at the Seat of a Domain

choices.text: Write a long note of explanation

effects.log: The note is two pages. The successor reads it and keeps the Tuesdays, and wonders at your fondness.

choices.text: Leave it with a single line: keep this

effects.log: One line. The successor keeps it. The brook never knows how close it came.

events.text: The hunt horn of your domain has gone quiet; a bird has built a nest in its bell. The huntsmaster stands under it holding a ladder and looking at you with the face of someone about to be asked to do something unreasonable.

choices.text: Leave the nest until the chicks fly

effects.log: The horn is silent for a season. The chicks fly. The first hunt after is the loudest in memory.

choices.text: Move the nest, gently, to a nearby bough

effects.log: You move it. The mother accepts a new tree with a clatter. The horn sounds on time.

events.text: A pack of hounds you did not summon is running the moor at dusk, silent, in a long grey line. They are not hunting. They run as if late for something. At the end of the line a very small hound struggles on, looking back at you.

choices.text: Carry the small hound a mile on your shoulder

effects.log: It rides in silence, then barks once and is set down. The pack greets it without remark.

choices.text: Run beside them for the length of the moor

effects.log: You run with the pack till dawn. At the last you find you are laughing. The hounds vanish into a mist.

events.text: The star-stags shed their antlers in the meadow at the turn of the year, and the antlers glow faintly until spring. Pilgrims come with baskets. The shrine-keeper asks if you will bless the gathering, and warns that someone always tries to keep the biggest.

choices.text: Bless the gathering, and the biggest antler too

effects.log: The pilgrims fill their baskets. Someone does take the largest, and bows to the meadow as they leave.

choices.text: Keep the largest antler as your own

effects.log: You hang it over the hall door. It glows through the winter and gets a little dimmer every year.

events.text: A child follows the hunt from the shrine, and is lost on the moor. The hounds find them first and form a circle round them, patient and enormous, until a priest arrives. The child is delighted and wants to name the biggest hound.

choices.text: Let the child name it

effects.log: The hound is called Biscuit for the rest of its long life. The priest sighs.

choices.text: Give the child a bell to ring if lost again

effects.log: The bell hangs in the shrine. It has never been needed, but is rung each year for luck.

events.text: A beast of the hunting moors dies in your domain, old and gently, in a hollow. The other beasts bring it small offerings of moss and stones. A priest asks whether it is blasphemy for animals to worship the dead.

choices.text: Tell the priest it is the oldest worship of all

effects.log: The priest goes away thinking. The moss on the hollow flowers by spring.

choices.text: Add a stone of your own

effects.log: You set a stone on the pile. The animals watch and approve, in whatever way animals approve.

events.text: A minor god has been taking sacred deer from your preserve and selling the antlers at a distant market. When confronted, they put on a very small wounded dignity and explain that their shrine has had no offerings in a hundred years.

choices.text: Forgive, and make them a keeper of the preserve

effects.log: They keep the preserve with the sulky thoroughness of someone caught out. The deer are never safer.

choices.text: Have the antlers returned, and fine them a favour

effects.log: The antlers are returned. The favour is a long boring one involving a ditch.

events.text: The horn of one pantheon sounds over the bounds of another, and a dispute begins at once. The two huntsmasters stand either side of a stream, each pointing at the other's boots. They turn, in unison, to you.

choices.text: Rule that the boundary belongs to the stream

effects.log: Both are insulted equally, which is a good verdict. Both go home.

choices.text: Propose a joint hunt

effects.log: The joint hunt is a disaster, and then, to everyone's surprise, a joy.

events.text: Before the hunt, the horn-bearers wait in a clearing at dawn without speaking. A bird sings. Another answers. It is the best part of the hunt, and no one ever says so. The old huntsmaster nods to you to sit.

choices.text: Sit with them until the sun is high

effects.log: You sit through the dawn chorus. The hunt that follows is uneventful and perfect.

choices.text: Ask them what they listen for

effects.log: Nobody answers. The huntsmaster smiles. After a time you hear it too.

events.text: The wall of a sealed heaven at the foot of your hills breathes out, cold and slow, once a year on the same night. Shepherds bring in their flocks and shut their doors. This year the breath smells, faintly, of baking bread.

choices.text: Stand at the wall with a loaf of your own

effects.log: You hold the loaf up to the wall. Something on the far side seems to approve.

choices.text: Make a note and leave the wall alone

effects.log: The note goes in the register. It is the most appetising entry in it.

events.text: A letter has been pushed through a crack in a sealed heaven's wall, addressed to you, in a hand like a spider on ice. It says only: the weather here has been the same for an age. How is yours?

choices.text: Reply with a long description of your weather

effects.log: The reply is slid through the crack. The next letter thanks you, and asks for the sound of rain.

choices.text: Send a small cloud through the crack

effects.log: The cloud floats in. A faint, delighted shout comes from within.

events.text: The guards of a sealed heaven change on the first of the month, and the old guard hands over the same two keys to the new guard with the same sentence. Today the sentence has an extra word, said by the old guard to the new: sorry.

choices.text: Ask the new guard what the word meant

effects.log: The new guard does not know. The old guard is already gone. You write the word in your own book.

choices.text: Offer the guards a hot meal

effects.log: They accept. The meal is a long, quiet one. The seal feels, for a night, a little lighter.

events.text: Mortal children have found the ruined outer gate of a sealed heaven and have made it a playground. The sealed gate is not worried; the children play and chalk the stones. A priest wants them chased off. The gate, quietly, seems to prefer them.

choices.text: Leave the children to play

effects.log: The children chalk the gate. By autumn it wears a smile.

choices.text: Give them a safe playground nearby and gently move them

effects.log: The children move, grumbling, to a new place that is nicer. The gate stays quiet.

events.text: The sealing-office asks every god to inventory what lies behind the walls of sealed heavens in their domain. Most inventories say unknown. Yours is blank except for one line, written long ago by someone else: do not wake.

choices.text: Honour the line and return the inventory blank

effects.log: The office accepts blank. You are quietly given a small, peculiar badge.

choices.text: Send a mortal scribe to look through the crack

effects.log: The scribe comes back pale and speechless and asks for a week off. The line, now, has a second line under it: please.

events.text: In a field of your domain is a stone older than the domain. It has no name and no shrine and no worshippers, and nothing grows on it. Today it is warm, as if it had been lightly sat on by something that left.

choices.text: Sit where the warmth is

effects.log: The warmth fades slowly. For a moment you feel the stone remember being a mountain.

choices.text: Leave an offering of water

effects.log: The water dries on it in an instant and the stone seems, faintly, to settle.

events.text: A river without a source runs through the oldest wood in your domain. It was there before the domain was cut, and it does not know it has a god. A fisher tells you the fish in it have no fear, and no names.

choices.text: Drink from it

effects.log: The water is cold and tastes of nothing at all, and for a long moment you are quiet inside.

choices.text: Name nothing, and watch

effects.log: You watch the water until dusk. The wood is a good deal older than you, and quite kind about it.

events.text: A tree in a hollow of your hills bears a single fruit every thousand years, and today is the day. The fruit is no colour you have a name for. A crow sits on the branch and watches you with cold interest.

choices.text: Let the crow have it

effects.log: The crow takes it with a croak that sounds, you could swear, like thanks. The tree sighs.

choices.text: Eat it

effects.log: It tastes of the first morning. You will never be able to describe it, and cannot stop smiling.

events.text: At the heart of an old forest is a clearing where nothing makes a sound: no wind, no birds, no step. A wandering priest says the silence is older than the first word, and that you are the first god in an age to listen to it.

choices.text: Stay an hour in the silence

effects.log: You sit. After an hour you hear, very faintly, your own thoughts as if they belonged to someone else.

choices.text: Say a single word and leave

effects.log: You say hello. The silence considers it. Walking out you feel, behind you, a faint politeness.

events.text: Hwarin of the First Hearth has sent a small boy to your door with a coal in a clay pot, and a note: please keep this alight through the winter. The boy will not say why. The boy eats three bowls of rice, sleeps by the stove, and leaves at dawn.

choices.text: Keep the coal alight all winter

effects.log: You feed it a splinter each night. In spring it flares up, rises, and goes out through the chimney with a happy crackle.

choices.text: Ask the First Hearth why

effects.log: The First Hearth answers with a warm wind. You understand nothing, and feel entirely reassured.

events.text: Baekun the Pale Ferryman leaves his boat, unattended, at your riverbank one morning, and nobody knows why. The boat is empty and perfectly dry. It smells of rain and old rope. By dusk the oar is gone, and the boat is just a boat.

choices.text: Row it a little, upstream

effects.log: The oars return after an hour. You came back no wiser, and a good deal calmer.

choices.text: Leave the boat alone

effects.log: By morning the boat is gone. A single pale feather lies on the bank.

events.text: Saengmo Mother of Seeds passes through your domain in a plain shawl, unnoticed, and leaves a single seed in the shrine's offering bowl. The shrine-keeper thinks it is millet. You know better.

choices.text: Plant it in the shrine garden

effects.log: It comes up as a green so deep that the garden looks lit from inside. The keeper stops arguing about millet.

choices.text: Keep it safe and unplanted

effects.log: You keep it in a tin. Once a year you hold it to your ear and hear a very faint spring.

events.text: Haeryong Keeper of Tides arrives at your hall on a wave that stops at the doorstep. The great god asks, with elaborate courtesy, whether you might have a bucket. The tide has gone strange, and a bucket is the only way to bring it home.

choices.text: Bring the bucket

effects.log: Haeryong fills it, drinks half, and walks away across the grass, trailing a faint tide. You never learn what it was for.

choices.text: Offer a cup instead of a bucket

effects.log: Haeryong takes the cup solemnly. A laugh like surf ripples through the hall.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver sends no word, only a single silver thread that arrives on a breeze and ties itself, loosely, round your wrist. It does not pull. It only waits, as if it had someone to meet.

choices.text: Follow the thread, on foot, for a day

effects.log: It leads to a stone bench by a road. You sit. Nothing happens, and it is the most restful hour of your year.

choices.text: Wear it as a bracelet

effects.log: The thread becomes a friend of the wrist. Once a month it tightens a little, as if to check you are still there.

events.text: A lane in your domain has been quietly unmade, not destroyed, just forgotten: the cobblestones are still there and the houses too, but no one remembers where it led. The old woman at the corner says she used to know.

choices.text: Walk the lane to its end with her

effects.log: You walk it together. It leads to a small well. She laughs: of course.

choices.text: Mark the lane with a milestone

effects.log: The milestone gives the lane back its name. The woman pats it, satisfied.

events.text: A page in the archive of your hall has turned blank overnight. It was the page about a minor feast, held on the third day of the third month. No one remembers if the feast was good. A clerk wrings their hands in the corridor.

choices.text: Hold the feast again, on the blank page's day

effects.log: The feast is held, improvised and a little too sweet. By evening, the page has writing on it again.

choices.text: Leave the page blank and put a candle by it

effects.log: The candle burns a year. The page stays blank. Somehow, it feels better.

events.text: A mountain in your domain has lost its echo. Hunters call and nothing returns. It is not eerie; it is just a little lonely. A goatherd asks if you can fetch it back, or at least send a substitute.

choices.text: Answer the goatherd's calls yourself, for a week

effects.log: You call back from behind a rock. The goatherd is satisfied, and does not look behind the rock.

choices.text: Ask the mountain what it did with the echo

effects.log: The mountain, slowly, says it gave it to someone who needed it. It does not say who.

events.text: A bell that survived the burning of a shrine rings in the ash, once a year, on the day of the fire. Mortals have learned to stand around it with caps in their hands. This year the bell rings twice, and everyone looks at each other.

choices.text: Ring a third time, softly

effects.log: The bell answers. The crowd laughs with relief, wet-eyed, and the bell is, for the first time, not the last sound of a death.

choices.text: Let the second ring stand unexplained

effects.log: No one speaks of it. It becomes an annual custom: two rings, one for the burning, one for what is left.

events.text: The threshold of a burned shrine is all that remains of it: a single worn slab with two foot-hollows. A traveller stops there to rest, notices the hollows, and fits their feet in. Their face changes. They look up and thank the air.

choices.text: Greet the traveller from the doorway of nowhere

effects.log: The traveller starts, then bows. You walk with them a mile and say nothing at all.

choices.text: Leave them undisturbed

effects.log: The traveller rests and goes on. Something in the slab warms for a day.

events.text: A pilgrim brings you an ember from a burned shrine in a clay cup. They don't say whose shrine; they say only that they have carried it for six days and it is still alight. They ask that you keep it.

choices.text: Light a lamp from it in your hall

effects.log: The lamp burns low and gold. Over a season it becomes the warmest light in the building.

choices.text: Carry the ember to the shrine's old ground

effects.log: You set it down on the ash, and a thin fire climbs from it for one evening.

events.text: The first clap of thunder each year is sounded by a different drummer in turn. Tthe year it is the chief drummer's youngest nephew, nine years old, in a borrowed apron. The drum is taller than the child is. The whole domain holds its breath.

choices.text: Cheer him on from the front row

effects.log: The clap is crooked, loud, and a little late. The domain roars. It is the best thunder you have heard in an age.

choices.text: Steady the drum with a hand of wind

effects.log: The clap is perfect. The nephew never knows, and neither does anyone else.

events.text: A storm in your domain has a rumble but no lightning, and the valley below is nervous: thunder without light is bad luck. A drummer swears it is only a cough in the third drum. The farmers want you to say so.

choices.text: Tell the valley the third drum has a cough

effects.log: The valley laughs, a bit nervously. The drum is mended. The next storm sparks properly.

choices.text: Send a bolt over the valley, small, for reassurance

effects.log: The bolt falls on a barren field. The farmers cheer.

events.text: The sea delivers bottles to the shore, every tide: letters mortals threw in, years ago, to someone. The tide-keeper asks what to do with the ones that were never answered. There are, apparently, a great many.

choices.text: Answer a handful yourself, by hand

effects.log: You answer five. The people who wrote them are long gone, but the answers are left on the strand in their stead.

choices.text: Let the tide return them to the deep

effects.log: The tide takes them back, gently. The keeper writes: delivered, in the ledger.

events.text: A whale of the deep sings a tune that has no repeats, and the tide-keepers have started to chart it. It has been going three years, and shows no sign of a chorus. A keeper asks whether a song with no repeats is allowed.

choices.text: Allow it, and listen

effects.log: You listen to the whale on a night of low waves. Somewhere past the first hour, you realise it is describing a coastline.

choices.text: Ask the whale to repeat just one line

effects.log: The whale does, lower, in a voice like a door. The keeper is thrilled and pale.

events.text: In the waiting hall of the ferry there is a chair that no one is ever seated in. The marshals sweep around it. This morning a small child is found sitting in it, swinging their legs, and refusing to be moved.

choices.text: Sit down on the floor beside them

effects.log: You sit. The child tells you a long story about a rabbit. The marshal does not interrupt.

choices.text: Ask the marshal what the chair is for

effects.log: The marshal says it is for the next to arrive who has nobody. The child is it, apparently.

events.text: The lamp-keepers of the ferry run low on oil. Gods of Death are not supposed to ask for gifts, but the keeper looks so embarrassed at the shortage that the whole landing seems to hold its breath.

choices.text: Send a barrel of lamp-oil from your own stores

effects.log: The barrel arrives. The lamps burn brighter that night than they have in an age, and the departed notice.

choices.text: Teach the keeper to press oil from the river-reeds

effects.log: The reeds give a pale, steady oil. The keeper has a hobby for life.

events.text: A knot-reader drops a thread on the loom hall floor. It is nobody's thread yet; it is just waiting. The reader stares at it with horror. The thread twitches, then lies still, and something somewhere is slightly different.

choices.text: Pick up the thread and tie it off cleanly

effects.log: You tie it. Somewhere a child is born with a slightly easier life, and nobody ever knows.

choices.text: Leave it where it fell

effects.log: You leave it. The reader is aghast. By evening the thread has been taken by a mouse, which is probably also meant.

events.text: An apprentice reader asks, in a voice so small it could be a mouse, whether it is true that a knot of fate can be untied by the person it binds. The senior readers do not answer. The apprentice looks at you.

choices.text: Tell them the knots may be untied by the stubborn

effects.log: The apprentice nods, with a gleam. The senior readers look at you as at a traitor, and quietly approve.

choices.text: Say it is not mine to say

effects.log: The apprentice nods, disappointed, then smiles: that is an answer too.

events.text: In the dream hall is a shelf of pillows from the sleepers who died in their sleep. They are kept warm, in case. A cleaner is dusting them with the tenderness of a nurse. Today one of them has been taken, and no one will say by whom.

choices.text: Help the cleaner look for it

effects.log: You find it in the hands of an old dreamer, who is holding it and weeping gently. You leave it with them.

choices.text: Ask the dreamer-in-chief for an inventory

effects.log: The inventory shows nothing missing. The cleaner is baffled, and relieved, and a little haunted.

events.text: Nightmares have clerks, too. One arrives at your door in a polite grey coat to ask for a day off. It has been frightening people for four thousand years, and would like, just once, to see a beach.

choices.text: Grant the day off, and lend a sunhat

effects.log: The clerk goes to the beach. It comes back with a sunburn and a seashell. Nightmares are, for a week, notably milder.

choices.text: Ask what it would do on a beach

effects.log: It says: nothing. Just exist, in the sun. You find that reasonable beyond all argument.

events.text: The oldest ewe of the mountain flock has begun to lead the sheep to the same place each evening, a bare rock above the lowest cloud. The shepherds say she is praying. They do not know to whom, and ask whether it is you.

choices.text: Go to the rock at dusk and sit with her

effects.log: You sit among forty sheep on a cold rock. They do not look at you. It is the quietest worship you have had in years.

choices.text: Let her keep her own god

effects.log: You do not go. The ewe keeps up the evening habit till spring, when she is gone and the rock is bare.

events.text: A wolf with a limp has taken to sitting at the edge of the shrine yard each dusk, ears back, as if apologising for something. The shrine-keeper wants to chase it off. The wolf waits, lowering its head very slightly.

choices.text: Leave a bone at the edge of the yard

effects.log: The wolf takes the bone and goes. Next dusk, a rabbit is left on the step in return. You pretend not to see it.

choices.text: Heal the limp with a touch

effects.log: The wolf bounds off into the hills. It never comes back, and you find you were rather fond of the limp.

events.text: It is your night to light the common lamp at the pantheon's altar. It takes a minute and nobody will check. The lamp has been lit every night for four thousand years by someone, and tonight it is you.

choices.text: Light it, and stay a moment

effects.log: The lamp burns. You stay, in the quiet, with four thousand years of other hands.

choices.text: Light it and leave

effects.log: The lamp burns. You leave. It is a small duty, done.

events.text: A young god of your pantheon comes to ask how to behave at the next feast. They have rehearsed the question for a week, and still stumble over it. The pantheon, you remember, did not teach you either.

choices.text: Teach them the three rules you wish you had known

effects.log: They write the rules on their sleeve. At the feast, they use all three, and are noticed in the right way.

choices.text: Tell them to be themselves, within reason

effects.log: The young god looks relieved, then alarmed, then thoughtful.

events.text: An elder of your pantheon asks you to keep their seat warm at an unimportant court session while they nap in the corridor. It is the sort of thing that is asked in every pantheon, of everyone, and never refused.

choices.text: Keep the seat warm, and take notes

effects.log: The notes are good. The elder snores through the whole session and thanks you profusely.

choices.text: Politely pass the seat to a younger god

effects.log: You find someone who wants the experience. The elder wakes up annoyed, then pleased.

events.text: An old Masterless God leaves a cushion on your doorstep with a note: I sat on this for four thousand years at the last bench. It has a dent in the shape of an age. I thought you might like it.

choices.text: Keep the cushion and sit on it, proudly

effects.log: You sit on the dent. It is surprisingly comfortable, and the old god sends back a shy thumbs-up through a window.

choices.text: Return it with a cake

effects.log: The old god is moved. The cake is eaten. The cushion comes back anyway, with the dent deeper.

events.text: At a court break, a pair of pantheon gods talk over your head about the Masterless: no manners, no purpose, no one to answer to. They have not noticed you are right behind them with a cup of tea.

choices.text: Say good afternoon, cheerfully

effects.log: They freeze, then make a mumbled excuse and leave. The tea is excellent.

choices.text: Tell them politely that the tea is unaffiliated

effects.log: The joke lands badly. It lands again an hour later with a stifled laugh.

events.text: A Masterless God of the third hour offers to share a hall with you, for company, as no pantheon has a spare. The hall has one big room, one fire, and a lot of drafts. The offer comes with a plate of biscuits.

choices.text: Accept, and bring your own chair

effects.log: The hall is cold in winter and loud in summer. You are never lonely again, which is its own strange gift.

choices.text: Thank them and decline, kindly

effects.log: The god takes it well. The biscuits stay on your table.

events.text: The chair of your domain is a hard one. Gods of other domains sit in it when they visit and fidget. Every holder, you've been told, leaves a small mark on it. Today you find a note carved under the armrest by your predecessor: sit lightly.

choices.text: Carve your own line under it

effects.log: You carve: sit well. It is all you can think of, and it will do.

choices.text: Leave the note alone and keep it in mind

effects.log: You sit lightly for a month. It is surprisingly useful advice.

events.text: A lesser god of no domain at all comes to see how a true domain-holder spends the day. They take notes. They do not sneer or envy. They ask only: is it lonely? You find that you do not know how to answer.

choices.text: Tell them honestly: sometimes

effects.log: They nod. The honesty seems to be what they came for.

choices.text: Tell them it is mostly paperwork

effects.log: They laugh with relief. The paperwork, they decide, is something they can live without.

events.text: {npc} comes to your shrine eight months along with a child, asking for the birth blessing now, in case the child arrives somewhere without a god in earshot. It is the first time anyone has booked a blessing in advance.
events.arc: The Blessing That Came Early

choices.text: Give it now, in full

effects.log: You lay the blessing on {npc} like a warm shawl. {He} walks home taller, and the child kicks twice in thanks.

choices.text: Give half, keep half for the birth

effects.log: You hold half the blessing back and promise the rest at the true hour. {npc} nods, as one who understands contracts.

choices.text: Send {him} home with a bowl of shrine water

effects.log: It is not a blessing, but {npc} treats it like one, and carries it home in both hands.

events.text: The birth comes in a storm, three roads from any shrine. A midwife sends up the loudest prayer you have heard in a year, and uses your name only as punctuation.
events.arc: The Blessing That Came Early

choices.text: Hold the storm off the roof until it is over

effects.log: You lean on the clouds until the cry of a newborn comes through the rain. The midwife never knows why the thunder waited.

choices.text: Let the storm come, and walk through it as a plain traveller to the door

effects.log: You arrive wet and unannounced, hold a lamp, and say nothing. It is the best you can do with your hands.

choices.text: Listen, and keep the storm out of it

effects.log: The prayer ends in a laugh and a wail, and you realise you had been holding your breath, a thing gods are not supposed to do.

events.text: Years on, the child comes to the shrine and wants to know why the blessing felt like a hand on the shoulder. {npc} told the story wrong, and the child has made it better.
events.arc: The Blessing That Came Early

choices.text: Tell the true version, gently

effects.log: The child listens, solemn, and decides the true version is the better one. {npc} laughs at being corrected by a god and a child at once.

choices.text: Let the better version stand

effects.log: You nod along. A story improved by love is a kind of blessing too, and it does no harm.

events.text: Years on, the child comes to the shrine alone and reports that the walk through the storm to the door was seen. A lamp, a plain coat, and no explanation. The child has told no one but you.
events.arc: The Blessing That Came Early

choices.text: Admit it was you

effects.log: The child grins as if a long argument has been won. You have a secret-keeper for life, and a small, fierce devotee.

choices.text: Say it was a kind stranger, and leave it

effects.log: The child accepts it with the polite scepticism of the very young. The lamp is still lit on the family shelf.

events.text: {npc} has prayed to you for six years about a single person at the next market stall: not for love, only for a good morning. You have, for six years, been quietly rearranging the weather so they pass each other at the well.
events.arc: A Marriage Prayed For

choices.text: Arrange one more meeting, a proper one

effects.log: You send a cart wheel off its axle at exactly the right spot. {npc} comes home with a stranger, a bruise, and a name.

choices.text: Step back and let them manage on their own

effects.log: You leave the well unshaken. Nothing changes for a season, which is also information.

choices.text: Send a good-morning light to the stall

effects.log: The stallholder looks up, startled by the sun, and says good morning first. A small start.

events.text: A betrothal is announced. It is a muddle: two families, one dispute over a goat, and a priest who wants a god to bless the whole mess by name.
events.arc: A Marriage Prayed For

choices.text: Appear at the betrothal feast, unnamed, and smooth the goat

effects.log: The goat is settled over a shared bowl, and you leave before the toasts. {npc} says the god must have been looking after them.

choices.text: Bless it from the shrine, at a distance

effects.log: The blessing falls over the table like a quiet snow, and the elders find, to their surprise, that they like each other.

choices.text: Decline to be named in the vows

effects.log: You send word that gods do not witness vows they have written. The priest is startled, then relieved.

events.text: The wedding falls on a day of rain, and the couple climb to your shrine in wet finery to ask if the rain is a bad omen. It is only rain. You did not send it.
events.arc: A Marriage Prayed For

choices.text: Say so plainly: rain is rain

effects.log: They laugh with relief and kiss on the shrine step, drenched. The priest writes down that the god has no opinion on rain.

choices.text: Take credit, and make it stop for an hour

effects.log: The sun comes out on cue. You have built a story for their grandchildren, though you suspect it will not be told as it was.

events.text: The couple do not come to ask about omens. They come to give you the wedding bread, whole and uncut, and say they will not eat until a god does.
events.arc: A Marriage Prayed For

choices.text: Eat, with them, on the shrine step

effects.log: You eat bread with two mortals in the cold rain, and it is the best meal of the century. They tell it the rest of their lives.

choices.text: Take a crumb, and bless the loaf

effects.log: A crumb is plenty, and the loaf stays warm a week. It is a miracle of the humbler kind.

events.text: A funeral crowd gathers below your shrine and the priest points up, saying a god will explain why the grandmother was taken now. They have all brought questions. They have also brought a very good soup.
events.arc: The Funeral and the Question

choices.text: Appear, plainly, and admit you did not choose it

effects.log: You tell them a god does not ladle out the hour of every life. Some are angry, some are relieved. All eat the soup together.

choices.text: Say that all is arranged, and bless the departed

effects.log: They are comforted, and you carry the lie like a stone in a sleeve. It is a god's old habit.

choices.text: Stay silent, and warm the soup

effects.log: You say nothing and make the soup the best it has ever been. The mourners notice, and no one asks.

events.text: {npc}, the grandmother's eldest, comes alone afterwards and asks the one question the crowd did not: was it painful, and was anyone near?
events.arc: The Funeral and the Question

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth, which is kind

effects.log: Asleep, you say, with a hand held in theirs. {npc} weeps, and then straightens. {He} has what {he} came for.

choices.text: Give {him} a dream of the last evening

effects.log: {npc} wakes knowing the shape of that evening, and writes it down before it fades.

choices.text: Say you do not know, and ask {him} to tell you

effects.log: {npc} tells you, in order, the whole of a long life. You listen until the lamp is empty.

events.text: Years later, {npc} brings a child to the shrine for a naming, and the child has the grandmother's way of tilting the head. {npc} asks whether the dead come back. You are quiet a long time.
events.arc: The Funeral and the Question

choices.text: Say that the dead come back in the small things, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} nods, tears bright, and the child laughs. It is not an answer. It is better.

choices.text: Say that is a matter for the Silent Hall, and you will ask

effects.log: You write a letter to the god of death. A reply, on grey paper, arrives within the year: all is well, and sleeping, and thank you for the soup.

events.text: Years later, {npc} climbs to the shrine and says: you told us all was arranged. It was not, was it? {He} says it without anger, which is somehow worse.
events.arc: The Funeral and the Question

choices.text: Admit it, and apologise to {him}

effects.log: You bow your head. {npc} puts a hand on the shrine stone, as on the shoulder of an old friend, and forgives you slowly.

choices.text: Say that comfort has its own kind of truth

effects.log: {npc} considers, and does not argue. The lie sits between you like a third seat at the table.

events.text: A pilgrim has set out for your shrine from the far end of the world. It will take forty years, because {he} walks only on the days it is not raining, and {he} will not be hurried. {npc} sends no prayer. {He} just walks. You can feel the footsteps.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Walks Forty Years

choices.text: Shorten the road a little

effects.log: You fold the map. A river is a hundred paces narrower. {npc} notices and says nothing, pleased in a stubborn way.

choices.text: Leave the road as it is

effects.log: You let the road stay long. A pilgrimage is the road, and you will not steal it.

choices.text: Send a small wind at the pilgrim's back

effects.log: Not enough to be noticed. Enough to be felt, perhaps, on the worst hill.

events.text: Twenty years in, the pilgrim stops at a river ford and does not cross for a season. No prayer comes; only a whisper: I am not sure I still want to arrive.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Walks Forty Years

choices.text: Appear as a ferryman and cross {him} over

effects.log: You pole the raft in a plain coat. {npc} talks the whole way, and by the far bank {he} has decided to go on.

choices.text: Do nothing: the choice is the pilgrimage

effects.log: You let the river do its quiet work. At last {npc} crosses on foot, wet to the chest and furious, and laughing.

choices.text: Send a dream of the shrine as it will be

effects.log: The dream is a modest hall with a leaking roof. {npc} wakes and finds {he} wants the leak.

events.text: The pilgrim reaches the steps at last, grey and slow. {He} has no petition. {He} climbs the last stair, looks around the empty hall, and asks, without irony: is this all?
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Walks Forty Years

choices.text: Say yes. Isn't it enough

effects.log: A silence, and then {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit. {He} says it is exactly enough, and stays a month.

choices.text: Open the hall's hidden door, the one nobody climbs to find

effects.log: Behind it is a small room with a single window over the whole domain. {npc} sits down in it and does not come out for a day.

events.text: The pilgrim reaches the steps, a little late, and finds a note on the door in your hand. It says: I was not in. Come back in forty years. {npc} reads it twice and bursts into delighted laughter.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Walks Forty Years

choices.text: Be there when {he} returns the next time

effects.log: You wait on the top step in a plain coat, and {npc} does not recognise you until the tea is poured.

choices.text: Send another note: I am always in. Knock.

effects.log: It takes {npc} an hour to knock. When {he} does, the door opens by itself, and the whole hall is warm.

events.text: A child has been sent to your shrine to learn the proper prayers. {npc} lasted four lines before saying: why do you need us to say them if you already know what we mean? The priest has gone grey.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues

choices.text: Answer honestly: I like to hear them

effects.log: {npc} considers that and finds it unexpectedly satisfying. {He} says the prayers after that, rather well, with commentary.

choices.text: Say it is the form of respect, and a god should not be explained

effects.log: {npc} is unconvinced and writes the question on the shrine wall in charcoal. It stays there for decades.

choices.text: Laugh, in the priest's hearing

effects.log: The priest jumps. The child grins. You realise you have not laughed aloud since the second century.

events.text: The child, older now, has found a weak place in your doctrine: if you are kind, why does it rain on the sick? {npc} has brought a list of seventeen items. Items one through four are unfair.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues

choices.text: Argue back, fairly

effects.log: You argue for the better part of an afternoon. {npc} concedes two points, wins five, and storms off pleased with the whole business.

choices.text: Concede everything, and ask for help drafting a better doctrine

effects.log: {npc} is thrown, then fascinated, and the two of you write a page that the priest later bans and then quietly keeps.

choices.text: Say that you do not know, and that it bothers you too

effects.log: {npc} stares. No god has said so. {He} stops arguing and begins to think.

events.text: {npc} has grown, and is now the shrine's youngest priest, still arguing. The elders want {him} removed. A word from you would settle it either way.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues

choices.text: Speak for {him}: let the argument be part of the worship

effects.log: The elders mutter, and then concede. The shrine becomes known as the place where gods can be questioned, and the pilgrims triple.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let them decide

effects.log: The elders keep {npc} by one vote. {He} knows you did not speak, and respects it more than a rescue.

events.text: {npc} comes back to the shrine as a grown stranger with a young child of {his} own, saying the child asks the same questions. {He} is trying not to look pleased.
events.arc: The Child Who Argues

choices.text: Welcome the new questioner with a long cup of tea

effects.log: You pour tea for two generations of argument. The old charcoal line on the wall is still there, and the child finds it and gasps.

choices.text: Give the child the first question to ask you

effects.log: The child asks something so simple it takes you a month to answer. {npc} hides a smile behind a sleeve.

events.text: Every dawn for thirty years {npc} has stood before your shrine and said only: thank you. No requests, no names, no complaints. A god gets used to being asked. Being thanked has become an unsettling habit.
events.arc: The One Who Never Asks

choices.text: Give {him} something {he} did not ask for

effects.log: A bird nests in {his} roof. A well that was dry fills. {npc} accepts all this with the same two words.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} wants

effects.log: You speak to {npc} in a dream, plainly. {He} says: nothing, honestly. Then, after a long moment: perhaps company on the walk home.

choices.text: Just listen, and let it be enough

effects.log: You listen to the thank-you as one listens to a clock in a quiet house. It is oddly restful.

events.text: The thank-you stops. For three dawns there is no one at the shrine, and you discover, with some alarm, that you had been waiting for it.
events.arc: The One Who Never Asks

choices.text: Go looking for {npc} in a plain coat

effects.log: You find {him} in bed with a fever, nursed by a neighbour. {He} stares at you, and says thank you, out of habit.

choices.text: Send a healing wind and wait

effects.log: {npc} gets better on the fourth day and is at the shrine on the fifth, saying thank you as if nothing had happened.

choices.text: Pace the shrine, which is beneath your dignity

effects.log: The priest watches a god pace and says nothing. Gods have strange rituals.

events.text: {npc}, old now, finally asks for something. It is small: that when {he} dies, the thank-you be said to the next dawn by someone, anyone.
events.arc: The One Who Never Asks

choices.text: Promise it, and keep it

effects.log: Every dawn after, a small wind says two words to the shrine step. The priests think it is the wind. It is you.

choices.text: Tell {him} the next dawn will have its own thanks

effects.log: You say it kindly. {npc} laughs, because that is exactly right, and asks for nothing more.

events.text: {npc}, old now, finally asks for something. It is small: for one hour, not to be thanked back.
events.arc: The One Who Never Asks

choices.text: Grant it: sit in silence for the hour

effects.log: You say nothing. {npc} says nothing. At the end of the hour {he} says thank you anyway, laughing.

choices.text: Thank {him} instead

effects.log: The old face goes quite still. Then {npc} bows to a god who has just bowed back. Neither of you has ever done it before.

events.text: A grandmother has been singing a lullaby with your name in it for sixty years. It is not a hymn; it is about a god who loses a sock. You did not lose a sock. You have not been able to stop humming it.
events.arc: The Lullaby With Your Name In It

choices.text: Appear in a dream and ask for the other verses

effects.log: {npc} wakes delighted and writes down all nine verses. Verse six is quite rude about the god of the sea.

choices.text: Find the sock

effects.log: You search the sky for a week, find a lost sock under a cloud, and leave it on {npc}'s windowsill. The grandmother weeps with laughter.

choices.text: Hum it at the next council and see who notices
