effects.log: Two gods turn pale. One hums along. You keep a straight face with effort.

events.text: A rival god hears the lullaby sung in a faraway valley and complains to the courts that it is a trivialisation of your dignity, and therefore of divinity in general.
events.arc: The Lullaby With Your Name In It

choices.text: Defend the lullaby before the court

effects.log: You hum a line in front of the whole bench. Three judges join in by the second verse. The case is dismissed.

choices.text: Let the complaint die of its own pomposity

effects.log: No one answers it. By autumn it is a joke in the copyists' hall.

choices.text: Add a verse about the complaining god

effects.log: The verse spreads in a month. The rival is the only one who does not enjoy it.

events.text: The grandmother is dying, and the family asks that the lullaby be sung at the last. They are not sure whether a god will mind being included.
events.arc: The Lullaby With Your Name In It

choices.text: Sing the first line yourself, into the room

effects.log: The family hears a voice they cannot place, a little cracked, joining. The grandmother smiles and is gone by the end of the verse.

choices.text: Stay respectfully silent and let them have it

effects.log: The family sings, badly, and it is the best you have heard. You hold your peace and your sock.

events.text: The lullaby has outgrown its grandmother. It is sung in five valleys now, in four dialects, and in one of them you are a clumsy god with a sock and in another a stern one with a staff.
events.arc: The Lullaby With Your Name In It

choices.text: Collect all the versions in a book

effects.log: Your shrine-keeper binds the book. It is the strangest scripture on any shelf, and the pilgrims love it.

choices.text: Let it wander unrecorded, as songs should

effects.log: You let it go. In a thousand years some child in some valley will hum it and not know why.

events.text: A worshipper has left your shrine in a public huff and set up a rival: one stone, on a hill, dedicated to You Are Not a God, You Are a Weather. {npc} preaches there on market days. The crowds are small. The wit is large.
events.arc: The Heretic With One Stone

choices.text: Go listen, in a plain coat

effects.log: You stand at the back. {npc}'s sermon is clever and wrong in four places, and there is a joke about you that you laugh at before you can stop.

choices.text: Send the priest to debate {him}

effects.log: The priest returns pale. {npc} won on points. The crowd has doubled.

choices.text: Ignore it, with great and obvious dignity

effects.log: Everyone sees you ignoring it. It is the loudest ignoring in the valley.

events.text: A storm breaks the heretic's one stone in half. The faithful call it a sign. {npc} stands over the pieces looking, for the first time, uncertain.
events.arc: The Heretic With One Stone

choices.text: Mend the stone, quietly

effects.log: You knit it overnight. {npc} comes at dawn, finds it whole, and sits down. {He} does not preach that day.

choices.text: Let it lie, and let the people choose to help

effects.log: A few of the faithful, ashamed, help {npc} lift the pieces. It is a lesson of sorts.

choices.text: Send a plain rain on both shrines alike

effects.log: The rain does not choose. {npc} notices, and takes a long time to say so.

events.text: {npc} comes to your shrine at last, not to recant but to argue properly, with tea. {He} says the stone was not meant to replace you but to test whether you would let a doubter live. You have, for years.
events.arc: The Heretic With One Stone

choices.text: Name {him} the shrine's Honoured Doubter

effects.log: It is a ridiculous title, and {npc} wears it for the rest of {his} life. The shrine is the livelier for it.

choices.text: Take a cup and argue about weather

effects.log: You argue about whether a god can be a weather until the cups are cold. Neither wins. Both are satisfied.

events.text: {npc} grows old on the hill with the one stone, still preaching to the few. A young listener asks you in a dream whether it is wrong to love a heretic. You do not have a rule for that.
events.arc: The Heretic With One Stone

choices.text: Say that love is no heresy, and bid them listen on

effects.log: The young listener wakes and walks to the hill. A second stone is set beside the first.

choices.text: Say that doubt, kindly kept, is a form of prayer

effects.log: The listener thinks about that for years. The sermons on the hill get gentler.

events.text: Two siblings pray to you at the same hour from opposite sides of one fence. One asks for rain for a field; the other, for sun to dry the hay on the next. They know they are praying against each other. They do it anyway, each with a straight face.
events.arc: The Twins Who Pray for Opposites

choices.text: Give rain to the field and sun to the hay, in a narrow band

effects.log: You split the weather along the fence. The two siblings meet at the fence the next day and cannot decide who is more annoyed.

choices.text: Give both the same plain overcast

effects.log: Nobody gets what they asked, and nobody is cheated. The fence is quiet for a week.

choices.text: Wait to see which of them bows first

effects.log: Neither does. You admire the family stubbornness more than you should.

events.text: The siblings come to the shrine together, for the first time in a year, to ask which of them you love more. Both are laughing, but one is not entirely joking.
events.arc: The Twins Who Pray for Opposites

choices.text: Say you love the fence between them most

effects.log: They groan and are delighted. It becomes a family saying.

choices.text: Answer truthfully: they are indistinguishable at this distance

effects.log: This is gravely insulting to both, and they leave arm in arm, united in being wronged by a god.

choices.text: Refuse to choose, and bless the fence

effects.log: You bless the fence. It is a very good fence, thereafter.

events.text: Years on, one twin dies. The other comes to you in the oddest of prayers: asking for the weather the pair always argued over, one more time, as it was. Rain on one side, sun on the other.
events.arc: The Twins Who Pray for Opposites

choices.text: Grant it, along the old fence

effects.log: You split the sky in two for an afternoon. The surviving twin stands in the rain with a laugh and the sun on the left shoulder. It is the best weather you have ever made.

choices.text: Grant it, but only a little, as one honours a memory

effects.log: A thin line of light falls across the fence. The twin sits down on it, quietly, for an hour.

events.text: Years on, the two siblings have both grown stubborn about the fence being rebuilt. They come to you to arbitrate. The fence is the point. It always was.
events.arc: The Twins Who Pray for Opposites

choices.text: Help them rebuild it together

effects.log: You send two poles and the exact right wind to keep both upright. The fence goes up on the second day, and the siblings eat on either side of it.

choices.text: Leave them to it and send a good day

effects.log: The fence falls twice. The third time it holds. They shake on it, grumbling.

events.text: A young apprentice at your shrine confides to the incense that {he} cannot feel anything when {he} prays. The incense, which is you, is listening. {npc} has been going through the motions beautifully for a year.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Doubts

choices.text: Offer a small sign, and see what {he} does with it

effects.log: A single petal falls on the altar. {npc} stares at it for a full minute and then, to your surprise, laughs at {him}self.

choices.text: Let the doubt run its course

effects.log: You say nothing. A doubt tended is a faith with deeper roots, if you are patient, and you are.

choices.text: Remind yourself you once felt that way too

effects.log: You did, in your first century. The memory is oddly tender.

events.text: The apprentice leaves to walk the world for a year and returns more doubtful and, oddly, more steady. {He} says, bluntly, that the people elsewhere are happier without gods. Then: so why is it that {he} still wants to come back?
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Doubts

choices.text: Say that you do not know either, and are glad of it

effects.log: {npc} grins. A god who does not know is a god one can sit beside.

choices.text: Offer a vision of the shrine at dawn, empty and lit

effects.log: {npc} weeps a little at the quiet. It is not an argument, but it is an answer.

choices.text: Pour {him} a cup and ask about the road

effects.log: You hear four hours of road. By the end {he} has talked {him}self to a decision.

events.text: {npc} is made full priest at the next festival. {He} asks that you be absent from the ceremony, since {he} wants to be certain it is {his} own faith and not your presence that carries {him}.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Doubts

choices.text: Stay away, and watch from far off

effects.log: The ceremony goes on without a sign. {npc} takes the vows with a steady voice, and you cry a little into the clouds.

choices.text: Come, but plainly, in the back row

effects.log: You sit at the back as a worshipper. {npc} sees you and does not falter, which says everything.

events.text: {npc} leaves the shrine for good, kindly, to work in a clinic by the river. {He} does not renounce you; {he} says the work is {his} prayer now. The shrine is lonelier.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Doubts

choices.text: Bless the clinic, quietly

effects.log: The river runs clean past the clinic door, and the sick mend a little faster. No one is told why.

choices.text: Visit {him} there from time to time

effects.log: You carry water in a plain coat, and no one knows. {npc} knows. {He} says nothing.

events.text: An old veteran comes to your shrine and asks, in a flat voice, that you stop answering their old prayers. Not remove them. Just stop remembering. They say it is a mercy, for both.
events.arc: The Veteran Who Asks to Be Forgotten

choices.text: Do as {he} asks, and forget the old prayers

effects.log: You let the memory go. A weight lifts from {npc} that you only half understand. A sliver of your past dims with it.

choices.text: Refuse, but promise to hold them gently

effects.log: You will remember, and you will not speak of it. {npc} accepts that, with a nod you can read as thanks.

choices.text: Sit with {him} a while, then decide

effects.log: You sit on the shrine step for an hour while the sun goes down. Nothing is said, and a good deal is understood.

events.text: The veteran begins to appear at the shrine each dusk to do nothing. {He} sweeps the same three stones, hums a tune that is not a hymn, and leaves.
events.arc: The Veteran Who Asks to Be Forgotten

choices.text: Sweep with {him}, in a plain coat

effects.log: You hold the other end of a broom. {npc} says nothing, and after a week hums slightly louder.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice at the end of the stones

effects.log: The bowl is empty at dawn, and washed. {npc} never says a word of it.

choices.text: Let the stones be swept

effects.log: The shrine has never been cleaner, and you have never been so uneasy about its being so.

events.text: The veteran dies in the spring. At the funeral a stranger asks the priest what the old one was famous for. The priest cannot recall. The air in the room is very still.
events.arc: The Veteran Who Asks to Be Forgotten

choices.text: Speak at the funeral, from the roof, in one sentence

effects.log: You say: they kept this shrine swept. The mourners hear it as a gust of wind, and a stranger starts to cry.

choices.text: Let the silence stand, which is what {he} wanted

effects.log: No song, no speech. {npc} is buried with the broom, as asked, and the sweeping goes on by another hand.

events.text: The veteran dies in the spring. Nobody comes to the funeral but the priest, and the old broom, and you, in the back, in a plain coat.
events.arc: The Veteran Who Asks to Be Forgotten

choices.text: Stay for the whole thing

effects.log: The priest finishes the rites, then looks around and asks the empty room if it needs anything. You almost answer.

choices.text: Leave the shrine bell ringing once, for them

effects.log: The bell rings across the domain, once. A far valley goes quiet for a breath.

events.text: A dying worshipper has prepared a list of questions for you. Fourteen of them. {npc} has been carrying the list for forty years and keeps crossing items off. Only three remain, and {he} cannot decide which to ask.
events.arc: The Dying Worshipper's Questions

choices.text: Offer to answer all three

effects.log: {npc} laughs: no, no, a god cannot be asked everything at once. {He} chooses one and puts the others back in the bag.

choices.text: Offer to answer the one {he} would be most afraid to ask

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long time. Then {he} reads the first one on the list aloud, and it is the right one.

choices.text: Say nothing, and wait for {him} to choose

effects.log: You wait for a very long time. It is difficult, and it is the best thing you can do.

events.text: The question, when it comes in a dream, is small: did it matter? {He} does not say what. The whole life, perhaps, or a quarrel with a brother, or a lost letter. You do not know which, and neither does {he}.
events.arc: The Dying Worshipper's Questions

choices.text: Say yes, simply and without hedging

effects.log: {npc} lets out a breath held forty years. The dream ends gently.

choices.text: Say that mattering is not a thing a god can measure

effects.log: {npc} thinks about that in the dream until it fades. {He} wakes, perhaps, a little more at peace with not knowing.

choices.text: Hold {his} hand in the dream

effects.log: There is nothing to say. There is a hand to hold. It is enough.

events.text: {npc} dies in the night, and the list is found on the pillow with every line crossed out in one clean stroke. At the bottom, in a new hand: thank you for the one I asked.
events.arc: The Dying Worshipper's Questions

choices.text: Keep the list in the shrine

effects.log: It is framed beside the bell. Pilgrims read it and some weep, and some write lists of their own.

choices.text: Return it to the family, with a petal

effects.log: The family finds a petal in the folds. They press it in the family book.

events.text: {npc} dies in the night with the list unread. Three questions remain unanswered, and on the pillow is a folded note: if I did not ask, it is because I forgot to be afraid.
events.arc: The Dying Worshipper's Questions

choices.text: Answer them anyway, into the quiet room

effects.log: You answer all three to the empty bed. The room is warmer afterwards, and no one will ever know why.

choices.text: Leave them unanswered, as {he} chose

effects.log: Some questions are better left in the bag. You tuck the note back and let the household find it.

events.text: One family has prayed to you for nine generations, always from the same doorstep, always on the same feast day. The latest, {npc}, has just realised it is a tradition, and is horrified to find it is not meaningful to them at all.
events.arc: Nine Generations at One Doorstep

choices.text: Tell {him} that tradition does not need meaning to be kept

effects.log: {npc} sits down on the doorstep, relieved. {He} keeps the feast, with less guilt and more cake.

choices.text: Appear and tell {him} about the first one who prayed there

effects.log: You describe a starving ancestor on that very step. {npc} is silent, then moved, then hungry. {He} puts on the kettle.

choices.text: Send a small gift to the doorstep

effects.log: A pot of honey appears. The family thinks the neighbours left it. The neighbours think the family did.

events.text: {npc} proposes to end the prayers. {He} says the family has outgrown the custom, and asks if you mind. The custom is nine generations old, and so is your habit of listening to it.
events.arc: Nine Generations at One Doorstep

choices.text: Say you do not mind, and mean only half of it

effects.log: {npc} cancels the feast. The doorstep is empty on the day, and you pace the clouds for it.

choices.text: Say that a feast need not be prayer; it can simply be a feast

effects.log: {npc} considers that, and keeps the day, without the prayer. You find you like the feast better.

choices.text: Say it is theirs to end, and be gracious

effects.log: You are gracious, and a little hurt, and it comes out much the same.

events.text: Twenty years on, a stranger knocks at the old doorstep asking whether this is the house of the nine generations. The family is not sure. The stranger says someone told them it was lucky.
events.arc: Nine Generations at One Doorstep

choices.text: Make it lucky, for the old days

effects.log: The stranger finds work within the week, and the doorstep is mentioned in three taverns. The family does not know why.

choices.text: Leave the doorstep plain

effects.log: The stranger sits on it a while, rests, and goes on. It is a doorstep, after all.

events.text: Twenty years on, {npc}'s grown child climbs to the shrine with a small bag and an apology: they are restarting the nine-generations feast, and it will be the tenth. Would you come?
events.arc: Nine Generations at One Doorstep

choices.text: Come, openly, and sit at the head of the table

effects.log: You sit among the cousins, who cannot help but stare. The food is excellent. A tenth generation is a fine thing to see.

choices.text: Come as the stranger, and take the end seat

effects.log: You eat at the end of the table in a plain coat. No one looks twice. You are, you realise, very happy.

events.text: A pilgrim arrives at a hill where a shrine to you was once marked on an old map. There is nothing here but wind and an ancient wall. {npc} sits, unbothered, and says to the air: I came a long way. I will wait.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Arrives to Nothing

choices.text: Appear, plainly

effects.log: {npc} looks you over. A god in a plain coat on an empty hill. {He} nods: that will do. A shrine is whoever is there.

choices.text: Raise the old shrine for a night

effects.log: The walls stand up around {npc} as a ghost of stone, with a warm hearth. By morning it is gone. {npc} leaves a flower.

choices.text: Let {him} wait, and keep the wind kind

effects.log: The wind keeps the cold off. {npc} dozes, and wakes pleased with a fine day.

events.text: {npc} stays. {He} begins to rebuild the wall, stone by stone, alone, with no permission from any priest or god. A traveller asks what it is for. {He} says: someone should.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Arrives to Nothing

choices.text: Send a quiet hand with the heavy stones

effects.log: A big stone shifts a hand's breadth when no one is looking. {npc} stares at it, then laughs, and does not ask.

choices.text: Leave the work entirely theirs

effects.log: You leave the wall to the pilgrim. A thing built alone is a thing built whole.

choices.text: Bring {him} water, in your plain coat

effects.log: You carry water up the hill for a month. {npc} thanks the kind stranger, over and over.

events.text: A season passes and a shrine stands on the hill, small and crooked. The first pilgrim sends word along the roads: there is a place again. Others arrive.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Arrives to Nothing

choices.text: Name it for the first pilgrim, not yourself

effects.log: It is called the Waiting Step. {npc} is mortified, and cannot stop smiling.

choices.text: Take it as yours, and bless it plainly

effects.log: You bless the crooked walls. They stay crooked on purpose, from then on.

events.text: The pilgrim never finishes the wall. {npc} grows too old, and dies on the hill, content, with the wall half built and a hearth in the middle of it. Someone else will finish it, in time.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Arrives to Nothing

choices.text: Finish it yourself, in a night, and tell no one

effects.log: By dawn the wall is complete. The next traveller finds a perfect shrine and a grave beside it, and wonders at the work.

choices.text: Leave the wall half built, for the next to finish

effects.log: The next to come finds the gap and a pile of stones, and understands the invitation.

events.text: A scribe at your shrine has taken on the work of writing down every prayer ever spoken in the hall. {npc} has forty years of notes, and is now two centuries behind, because the prayers are also remembered from before {he} was born.
events.arc: The Scribe of Every Prayer

choices.text: Help by reading the old prayers aloud in a dream

effects.log: {npc} wakes with an aching hand and fourteen new pages. {He} is delighted, and then disheartened by the arithmetic.

choices.text: Tell {him} the work cannot be finished, and is no less good for it

effects.log: {npc} takes this like a blow and then like a gift. {He} keeps writing, more slowly and with greater care.

choices.text: Bring {him} ink, and nothing else

effects.log: The ink is the best in the domain. {npc} writes a beautiful letter of thanks, which you do not need.

events.text: The scribe finds, in an old prayer, a request that was never answered: a child asking for a mother to come home. It is three hundred years old. {npc} asks you what became of the mother.
events.arc: The Scribe of Every Prayer

choices.text: Search the old records for the answer

effects.log: You find the mother: home at last, a day late, to a house that had moved on. The answer is bittersweet. {npc} writes it in the margin.

choices.text: Admit you do not remember, and are sorry

effects.log: {npc} nods and writes: the god does not remember. Under it: but the god is sorry.

choices.text: Pray the old prayer yourself, to no one

effects.log: You say it into the air. A quiet falls across the hall, and a candle gutters out.

events.text: {npc} completes a volume, the first of nineteen, and brings it to the altar. It is not a scripture: it is a record of everything people were afraid of, and what they asked for, in the order that they asked.
events.arc: The Scribe of Every Prayer

choices.text: Read it aloud at the festival

effects.log: The crowd listens in the dark. When it ends, no one speaks, and then someone quietly starts to sing.

choices.text: Keep it on the altar and let it be read in private

effects.log: The book is read, one at a time, by anyone who asks. It is thumbed to softness within ten years.

events.text: {npc} dies mid-sentence, the pen still wet. The priest finds the page and cannot decide whether to finish the line. It reads: and the god, listening, said nothing, and that was
events.arc: The Scribe of Every Prayer

choices.text: Finish the line, in a dream, for the priest

effects.log: The priest writes: and that was enough. It is, as it happens, the right word.

choices.text: Leave the line unfinished

effects.log: The priest decides it is the better ending. The page is bound in as it is.

events.text: A newly born child, three days old, is carried to your shrine to be named. It sneezes on the altar, which the priest takes as a good sign. You take it as a review.

choices.text: Bless the sneeze

effects.log: The child sneezes again, delighted with its power. The family laughs, and the blessing sticks.

choices.text: Give a quiet name in the dream of the mother

effects.log: The mother wakes knowing it. It is a better name than any the priest had written.

events.text: Someone has been using your shrine to pray for another god's domain, since theirs is a day's walk away. The offerings are for you; the prayers are for the harvest. You are quietly forwarding them.

choices.text: Forward them faithfully, with a note of thanks

effects.log: The harvest god writes back, curtly, to say they are received. A small peace is made.

choices.text: Answer a few yourself, on principle

effects.log: It is not your domain. You do it well anyway.

events.text: A wedding procession reaches your shrine late for the blessing, because the groom lost the way. The bride is composed. The groom is in tears. The priest has gone for tea and will not be back.

choices.text: Give the blessing at once, to save the day

effects.log: You bless them in the middle of the road. The groom stops weeping. The bride says, to the sky, thank you, and laughs.

choices.text: Make the road shorter next time

effects.log: You fold a bend out of the road. The next wedding arrives early, to everyone's alarm.

events.text: A funeral party below your shrine has run out of soup. The mourners have begun to look at each other in the way of the very hungry. A kettle is empty, and a cloud overhead is the right shape.

choices.text: Let it rain gently, onto the kettle

effects.log: The kettle fills. It is oddly good soup. The mourners decide not to ask.

choices.text: Nudge a neighbour to bring bread

effects.log: A baker arrives with an apology and an armful of loaves. A neighbour is a good miracle.

events.text: A pilgrim limps to your shrine door with a blister the size of a coin and asks you, with great politeness, whether suffering is required. You have never actually decided.

choices.text: Say no. Sit down, and heal it

effects.log: The blister closes. The pilgrim looks at you in astonishment, then bursts out laughing.

choices.text: Say the walk was the prayer, and the foot the proof

effects.log: The pilgrim limps off nodding. You are not sure you believe it either.

events.text: A small child asks the shrine-statue, quite loudly, why it never blinks. The statue does not blink. You, in the next valley, find that you have been holding your eyes open for a hundred years.

choices.text: Blink, for the child, through the statue

effects.log: The statue's eyelids shift by a hair. The child shrieks with joy and runs to tell everyone.

choices.text: Let the statue stay still: some things are for looking at

effects.log: The child stares, rapt, for a long while. Nobody ever tells you what was seen.

events.text: A cook prays over a pot every morning, a short prayer, no more than a grunt. The pot is always good. It dawns on you that you have been in on the cooking for twenty years.

choices.text: Keep helping, quietly

effects.log: The pot is better still. The cook never says a word, and nods at the steam.

choices.text: Taste it, in a dream

effects.log: You eat the stew in the cook's dream, and a long-forgotten pleasure rises up. You thank the cook with a good winter.

events.text: A very small child leaves a single acorn on your altar. It is the first offering of their life. They have chosen it with enormous care, and hid it from siblings for a week.

choices.text: Grow an oak from it, somewhere safe

effects.log: In a distant meadow an oak sprouts, wholly unexplained. The child visits it in later life.

choices.text: Keep the acorn on the altar for good

effects.log: The acorn sits in its place for a thousand years. It is the smallest relic you own, and the most precious.

events.text: The priest's prayer book has fallen apart and been rebound so many times that nobody can say which words are the original ones. Some of them are quite wrong. One of them is rude. One of them is lovely.

choices.text: Leave the rude one in

effects.log: It stays in. It is read at every festival, with a particular tone. You are fond of it.

choices.text: Add a better prayer, in a dream, for the next rebinding

effects.log: A new line appears in the margin. In fifty years it is the most-quoted one.

events.text: A homesick worshipper, far from their valley, prays in a tavern. The tavern has no shrine. The prayer finds you anyway: it asks only for one dream of the old kitchen.

choices.text: Send the kitchen, whole, with the smell

effects.log: The worshipper wakes in tears and runs to write a letter home. A dream is a very small thing to give.

choices.text: Send a traveller with news from home

effects.log: A pedlar from the valley arrives the next day with a bundle of letters. It is the cleverer miracle.

events.text: A worshipper has dragged a sick goat to your shrine. It is not clear if the offering is the goat or the cure. The goat seems not to care either way.

choices.text: Cure the goat, and leave the worshipper wondering

effects.log: The goat gets up, eats the altar flowers, and trots away. The worshipper thanks the flowers.

choices.text: Send a veterinarian's dream to a neighbour

effects.log: A neighbour wakes and arrives with the right herb. A god may delegate.

events.text: The festival in your honour has been held on the wrong day for forty years, since a scribe mistook a numeral. Nobody has complained. The harvest, oddly, has been fine.

choices.text: Say nothing; it works

effects.log: The festival goes on, a perfectly adequate wrong day. The scribe, long dead, is silently thanked.

choices.text: Quietly shift the true date to match

effects.log: You nudge the calendar of the domain by a few days. No one notices but the swallows.

events.text: A worshipper at the back of the hall whistles tunelessly through all the hymns. The priest has been trying to stop it for a decade. It is, in fact, the only part of the service you can hear clearly.

choices.text: Whistle along in the air

effects.log: The hall hears a faint extra note in the rafters. The priest has a quiet turn.

choices.text: Let the whistler be

effects.log: The whistling goes on. The hymns, thereafter, are slightly better.

events.text: A pilgrim arrives at your shrine and, in a state of exhaustion, delivers a prayer meant for the god of lost keys. You have no jurisdiction. You also have, in your pocket, a key.

choices.text: Forward the prayer, with the key

effects.log: The lost-keys god writes back with a single raised eyebrow, a stamp, and a receipt.

choices.text: Say nothing, and give the pilgrim a fine afternoon

effects.log: The pilgrim finds the lost key in a pocket they had already searched. It is possible you had a hand.

events.text: A worshipper arrives to ask for a blessing in an openly bad mood. They have been laid off, quarrelled with a sibling, and lost a shoe. They want the blessing, quote, to just be over with.

choices.text: Give it quickly, and without comment

effects.log: The blessing falls plainly. The worshipper leaves with a dry nod, and the shoe is found outside.

choices.text: Ask what is wrong, and listen

effects.log: You listen to the whole list. The blessing, when it comes, is an afterthought, and works better.

events.text: A shy worshipper wants to speak to you but is afraid of the priest's eavesdropping. They whisper into a jar and put it on the altar. The jar is very full of whispers.

choices.text: Open the jar and listen, with care

effects.log: You listen to eleven years of small fears. None is large; all are tender. You answer, in dreams, one by one.

choices.text: Keep the jar sealed and send a general kindness

effects.log: A warm weather falls on the whole valley that week. The shy worshipper is among the happiest.

events.text: A naming feast in your honour is going very well until the host announces that the baby will be named after you. You are, at this point, a tempting name, and there are now four babies in the valley named after you. They are a handful.

choices.text: Bless all four with a lasting good humour

effects.log: The four grow up laughing, sworn rivals in the pretence of being the real one. Fine children.

choices.text: Appear and gently suggest a second name for the next one

effects.log: The host hears you in a dream, and takes the suggestion, and the valley is much improved by it.

events.text: A pilgrim's dog has climbed the whole mountain to your shrine and refuses to leave. The pilgrim is long gone, home, and the dog sits at the altar with great dignity.

choices.text: Keep the dog as a shrine-beast

effects.log: The dog guards the door for eleven years, and bites only the insincere. It is the best shrine-keeper you have ever had.

choices.text: Send the dog home in a gentle dream-wind

effects.log: The dog is on the pilgrim's step the next morning, looking reproachful. They are very happy.

events.text: A worshipper prays to apologise to a sibling who has died. They have not got the words. They have only the shape of the apology, a hard lump, and they leave it on your altar.

choices.text: Carry the lump to the Silent Hall

effects.log: Baekun takes it without remark. A grey reply comes: accepted. Nothing more. It is all that was needed.

choices.text: Give the worshipper a dream of the sibling, smiling

effects.log: They wake with the lump gone. They do not say why. They look younger.

events.text: The baker who makes the festival cake in your honour has burned it, forty minutes before the procession. {npc} stands in the ashes of the oven and prays, in a rush, for a miracle or at least a bigger oven.
events.arc: The Festival Cake That Burned

choices.text: Send a dream of the recipe, plus the right wind for the fire

effects.log: The second cake rises like a sunrise. {npc} credits the oven, the flour, the neighbours, and never once the god.

choices.text: Let the cake burn, and send the crowd a laugh

effects.log: The procession arrives to a charred cake and a baker in tears, and the crowd, to their surprise, applauds the effort.

choices.text: Say nothing; hold the sun a minute longer

effects.log: The procession is delayed by a river-crossing misfortune that was not an accident. The baker gets {his} time.

events.text: The charred cake becomes a tradition. The next year, the baker burns one on purpose for luck. The year after, a rival baker tries to burn a better one.
events.arc: The Festival Cake That Burned

choices.text: Bless the burnt cake as the proper festival fare

effects.log: The charred cake is declared holy by a priest too quick to the point. You smile into your sleeve.

choices.text: Tell the bakers that a god likes a good cake, burnt or not

effects.log: The contest collapses into a general bake-off, and there is no winner but everyone is fed.

choices.text: Eat one in disguise

effects.log: It is terrible. You eat three.

events.text: Years on, a grown child of the baker opens a bakery at the shrine gate and sells only burnt cakes. They are, you must admit, delicious.
events.arc: The Festival Cake That Burned

choices.text: Leave a blessing on the oven

effects.log: The cakes burn at precisely the right degree. The queue winds round the courtyard.

choices.text: Buy one yourself, in a plain coat

effects.log: You pay in the only way you can, with a charm of luck slipped into the till. The child never knows why trade is so good that month.

events.text: Years on, the bake-off is held every year and attended by pilgrims from three domains. {npc}, grey, is asked to cut the first cake and weeps into the cream.
events.arc: The Festival Cake That Burned

choices.text: Bless the knife

effects.log: The first cut is clean as a bell. {npc} laughs, finally, at an old shame.

choices.text: Hold the room in a warm hush for the cutting

effects.log: The crowd feels, for one breath, as if they were all family. It passes, and the cake is eaten.

events.text: A blessing meant for a newly married pair has been delivered, by an overworked wind, to the wrong house, where it settles on {npc}, a lifelong bachelor who has just burned {his} supper. {He} is baffled to be so suddenly lucky.
events.arc: The Blessing Delivered to the Wrong Door

choices.text: Let it stay; the wind knew something

effects.log: {npc} wins a small prize, finds a lost ring, and meets the baker's sibling at the market. The wind is unrepentant.

choices.text: Move it on to the intended pair

effects.log: You retrieve the blessing with an apologetic tug. {npc} feels it leave, and for a day is oddly sad.

choices.text: Send a second blessing for both

effects.log: It costs little, and the world has plenty of room for two.

events.text: {npc} comes to the shrine to give thanks and find out why a stranger like {him} was chosen. {He} asks for nothing. {He} wants to know whether it was a mistake.
events.arc: The Blessing Delivered to the Wrong Door

choices.text: Tell {him} honestly: the wind erred, and it was a happy error

effects.log: {npc} laughs for a quarter hour. {He} says it was the best error that ever happened to {him}.

choices.text: Say that blessings go where they are needed

effects.log: {npc} is quiet, then moved. It is a pretty lie, and it fits.

choices.text: Offer {him} tea

effects.log: You pour tea, and the question goes cold in the cup, forgotten.

events.text: Years on, {npc} has become a famously cheerful person who pays the blessing forward: a thousand small favours across the domain. A rumour says a god arranged it.
events.arc: The Blessing Delivered to the Wrong Door

choices.text: Let the rumour stand

effects.log: The rumour grows. {npc} is a minor local saint within a decade, and is appalled.

choices.text: Quietly whisper that it was all {his} own doing

effects.log: The rumour fades. {npc} is left with the credit, which is the proper place for it.

events.text: Years on, the wind that made the error is old and tired, and comes to the shrine to apologise for the rest of its career. It is, it says, the best thing it ever did wrong.
events.arc: The Blessing Delivered to the Wrong Door

choices.text: Forgive it, and promote it to a gentler route

effects.log: The wind sighs and drifts off to a lovely valley. You have never had a prouder subordinate.

choices.text: Ask it for the story, and write it down

effects.log: The wind tells it in a long breath. You write it as the first entry of a new book of kind mistakes.

events.text: A worshipper has been leaving flowers at your shrine each week to apologise for a quarrel with their mother that you had nothing to do with. The flowers are lovely. The mother has no idea, and neither has the quarrel.

choices.text: Nudge the mother toward the shrine road

effects.log: The mother finds the flowers, understands everything, and goes home to make soup. The quarrel ends over a bowl.

choices.text: Accept the flowers, and keep quiet

effects.log: You hold the apology like a coat borrowed for someone else, and it warms you a little.

events.text: Every seventh day a widow leaves half a loaf at your shrine and takes none home. The widow is lean. The loaf is left anyway. The priest looks away.

choices.text: Return the bread, doubled, by morning

effects.log: The widow finds a whole loaf on the doorstep and decides the neighbours have made a mistake in their favour.

choices.text: Say nothing, and send a grain-wind to the field

effects.log: The next harvest is richer, and the widow takes the credit for it, as is proper.

events.text: A blind pilgrim reaches the shrine by touching the walls, and asks you only to describe the view from the steps. They have heard it is fine.

choices.text: Describe it in detail, for an hour

effects.log: You describe the valley, the morning, the mist on the river. The pilgrim listens with a still face and says, at the end, that it was fine.

choices.text: Send the view as a dream

effects.log: The pilgrim wakes in tears with the whole valley in them and does not ask for it again.

events.text: The shrine's old priest has caught a bad cold and recites the morning prayers in a dreadful honk. The worshippers hold their breath. A god, they say, is wise and kind and should not be asked to endure this.

choices.text: Send a warm broth-wind to the priest

effects.log: The cold breaks the same day. The priest credits the broth. You prefer it so.

choices.text: Listen to the honk with perfect gravity

effects.log: It is, you decide, the most sincere recitation of the century. The priest never knows.

events.text: The children of a valley have started a game where they claim to have dreamed of you the night before, and the grandest dream wins. Nobody is lying. All are exaggerating.

choices.text: Appear in the best-told dream

effects.log: The winner wakes to find the details quite accurate. They do not tell. It is the only fair game in the valley.

choices.text: Appear in the dream of the child who lost, for comfort

effects.log: The loser is woken by a soft warm light, and does not tell anyone. The light has a bit of tea in it.

events.text: Your festival procession is soaked by a rain you did not send, and the neighbouring storm-god is suspected. The worshippers sing louder in protest, and hence the festival is a triumph.

choices.text: Dry the paper lanterns, one by one

effects.log: The lanterns light and the procession cheers. A neighbour god can be forgiven for rain, if not for the smirk.

choices.text: Take the rain as a gift and dance in it

effects.log: You dance in your own festival rain, invisible. It is the best afternoon of a decade.

events.text: A pilgrim arrives with a gift for you that is a rock. It is a nice rock. They found it on the way and thought you might not have one like it.

choices.text: Put the rock on the altar, with honours

effects.log: It is mentioned in the chronicles as the Rock of the Pilgrim. It is the most admired object in the hall.

choices.text: Say it is the nicest rock you have ever been given

effects.log: It is also the first. The pilgrim goes home happy, and you hold it while you think.

events.text: The shrine-keeper has started a guest book. The first entry reads: nice view. The second: god not in. The third: wrote this on the altar, sorry. You sign it, in your own hand, once.

choices.text: Sign it: god was in

effects.log: The shrine-keeper finds the signature in the morning and carries the book about for a month, pale with joy.

choices.text: Add a note: please do not write on the altar

effects.log: The writing on the altar does not stop. It becomes beautiful.

events.text: A worshipper has built a perfectly good shrine to you under the name of a god who does not exist. You find you do not mind. You answer to it.

choices.text: Accept the name, and answer to it

effects.log: You grow into it, a little. It has a rather pleasant ring to it.

choices.text: Correct the name, in a dream, with a kindness

effects.log: The worshipper stares, and then writes the old name beside the new one. Both stay on the lintel.

events.text: A mother prays about a child's nightmares. The prayers are very precise: the monster has seven noses and carries a fish. You have never heard of this monster, and suspect a relative.

choices.text: Send a dream where the monster is tamed with a bun

effects.log: The child wakes laughing, the monster's seven noses all leading to a sweet. The mother is baffled and thankful.

choices.text: Ask the Silent Hall if they are missing a monster

effects.log: Mongsa replies, in a drowsy hand: not mine, probably the cousin. Return when found.

events.text: A family leaves a new baby's first tooth at your shrine, wrapped in a flower, as thanks for a good birth. It is the smallest relic you will ever own.

choices.text: Keep it on the altar until the child is grown

effects.log: The tooth waits, and returns, in a dream, to the grown child, who is amused and moved.

choices.text: Plant it under the shrine tree

effects.log: In a year the tree bears one strange fruit, which the family finds and eats with great ceremony.

events.text: The faithful in the valley keep a fast day in your honour, and by noon the entire valley is cranky. A priest hands out wafers at the temple door against orders.

choices.text: Send a gentle wind of crumbs through the valley

effects.log: The valley eats, unsure why. The priest, unpunished, gives you a long look.

choices.text: Say that a fast kept hungry is a fast kept stupid

effects.log: The priest relays your message exactly, to scandalised laughter. The fast is shortened to dawn.

events.text: The cook who makes your ambrosia has served three gods before you and tells you so at every meal. {npc} has opinions about salt, about steam, and about gods who do not clear their plates. Tonight {he} has served you a bowl of something grey.
events.arc: The Cook of Ambrosia

choices.text: Eat all of it, and ask for the recipe

effects.log: {npc} goes pink to the ears. It is the first time in a century anyone has asked. The grey was a test; the next bowl is gold.

choices.text: Say that grey is not your colour

effects.log: {npc} sniffs, takes the bowl, and sends back a dish of astonishing plainness, with a note: as you wish.

choices.text: Praise the salt, specifically

effects.log: {npc} says the salt is nothing. The next day the salt is better.

events.text: A rival god sends a gift of fine spices and a note suggesting that your cook might like a change of employer. {npc} does not mention it. You find the note in the bin.
events.arc: The Cook of Ambrosia

choices.text: Raise {his} wages, in faith, quietly

effects.log: The shrine-fire burns a shade brighter. {npc} says nothing, and cooks a pie the size of a hillside.

choices.text: Ask {him} openly if {he} is tempted

effects.log: {npc} says: for a century I have been tempted. It is how I know where I want to be.

choices.text: Return the spices with thanks

effects.log: You send them back, politely, with a pie. The rival is silenced for a decade.

events.text: {npc} falls ill from standing too long at the great hearth. The kitchen goes cold for the first time in a thousand years, and the shrine-beasts wander the corridors looking betrayed.
events.arc: The Cook of Ambrosia

choices.text: Cook for {him}, badly, as a gift

effects.log: You make a stew. It is a crime. {npc} eats it with tears of laughter and gets well in the sheer effort of criticism.

choices.text: Send for a healer-god and wait at the bedside

effects.log: The healer comes and prescribes a week of sitting. {npc} sits, scowling, at the head of the kitchen, directing you through every step.

events.text: {npc} announces a retirement, with ceremony, and then a promotion for the scullion who is, you notice, terrified. It is the sort of change you did not expect from an old cook.
events.arc: The Cook of Ambrosia

choices.text: Host a feast in {his} honour, cooked by the scullion

effects.log: The scullion cooks with shaking hands and a perfect result. {npc} tastes it, and lays down the ladle at last.

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach for one more year

effects.log: {npc} agrees, with heavy sighs, and the scullion blossoms. The kitchen goes on.

events.text: Your herald is the finest runner in the sky and the worst announcer. {npc} arrives at every court with breaking news and cannot get past the first word. Your enemies call it a curse. You call it a delay.
events.arc: The Herald Who Stammers

choices.text: Write the announcements down for {him}

effects.log: The scroll is smooth. The courts grumble that it is not as dramatic. {npc} cannot decide whether to be grateful.

choices.text: Send {him} to speak with a patient voice teacher

effects.log: The teacher is an old river-god, who takes it slowly. {npc} improves by a syllable a season.

choices.text: Let {him} stammer, and ask the courts to wait

effects.log: The courts wait, and the news is no worse for being late. The courts are disappointed by this lesson.

events.text: At a council, the herald is called to give a message that matters. The room goes quiet. {npc} takes a breath, and opens {his} mouth, and the whole court hears it.
events.arc: The Herald Who Stammers

choices.text: Stand beside {him}, to say the first word

effects.log: {He} says the rest. It takes a long time. The room, to its credit, does not breathe.

choices.text: Let {him} do it alone

effects.log: {npc} delivers the message, in five hard pieces, and the council applauds when it is done. It is the best day of {his} life.

choices.text: Cough, to cover the pauses

effects.log: It helps. It also gets you a reputation for a cough.

events.text: Years on, {npc} is asked by the other heralds to lead their guild, because {he} is the only one who never garbles a message. Slow is fine, they say, if it is true.
events.arc: The Herald Who Stammers

choices.text: Speak for {him} at the guild hall

effects.log: Your voice is cheered. {npc} becomes guild-master, and the guild's slogan is, by popular vote, Take Your Time.

choices.text: Say nothing, but bring a good scroll

effects.log: {npc} reads it aloud at the ceremony without error. You sit at the back, beaming.

events.text: Years on, {npc} retires to a small shrine of their own: a god of Careful Words. It has three worshippers, all fluent, all patient.
events.arc: The Herald Who Stammers

choices.text: Send a gift of a single good word

effects.log: The word is delivered by a wind on the first day. {npc} puts it in a small frame and says it every morning.

choices.text: Come to the opening, in a plain coat

effects.log: You sit with the three worshippers. {npc} says the opening prayer without a stammer, and stops, startled, and laughs.

events.text: Your shrine-beast is an ember-crane, thin and proud, with a single tail feather that glows in the dark. It has begun to stand at the east wall at dawn and stare. The shrine-keeper, {npc}, says it is homesick. For a nest it left a thousand years ago.
events.arc: The Shrine-Beast That Wanted to Go Home

choices.text: Offer to fly it home

effects.log: The crane considers, then declines to leave the post. But it stops staring at the wall.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to take a message to the old nest

effects.log: {npc} walks for a month to the far hills and returns with a feather and a story. The crane is quiet for days.

choices.text: Sit with the crane at dawn

effects.log: You watch the east wall until it is warm. The crane leans, a very little, against your sleeve.

events.text: The crane finally goes. It leaves at night, without a farewell, with a single feather on the sill. The shrine feels hollow, and the fire burns lower.
events.arc: The Shrine-Beast That Wanted to Go Home

choices.text: Follow it, at a respectful distance

effects.log: You find the nest, long ruined, and the crane sitting in it, patient as a stone. You turn back and let it have the night.

choices.text: Wait for it to return

effects.log: You keep the fire lit and the door open. The crane is a long time gone.

choices.text: Send a wind with directions

effects.log: The wind finds the crane, and the crane, offended, ignores it entirely.

events.text: The crane returns in spring, three feathers lighter and a great deal calmer, and takes up the east wall again. It brought back a stone from the old nest, which {npc} sets by the door.
events.arc: The Shrine-Beast That Wanted to Go Home

choices.text: Put the stone on the altar

effects.log: The stone is warm, with a faint ember-light inside. The shrine-fire answers it, and the whole hall glows for a night.

choices.text: Leave it by the door, as the crane wished

effects.log: Every pilgrim touches it going in. By autumn it is smooth as a river pebble.

events.text: The crane does not return. A letter arrives from a far valley, in a stranger's hand: it has built a nest there and has taken a mate. It is well, the letter says, and sends its regards.
events.arc: The Shrine-Beast That Wanted to Go Home

choices.text: Send a gift for the new nest

effects.log: A pile of ember-straw, delivered by wind. A year later you receive a small feather, burning faintly.

choices.text: Appoint {npc} to look after the east wall in its stead

effects.log: {npc} sweeps the east wall every dawn, and sometimes talks to it. It is the shrine's new custom.

events.text: The god next door, {npc}, has moved the boundary stone between your domains by the length of a goat. It is a very good goat. It was standing on a hill with the best view of your valley.
events.arc: The Boundary Stone

choices.text: Move the stone back, at night

effects.log: The stone is back in the morning. By noon, so is the goat. By evening {npc} has moved the stone again, with a lunch.

choices.text: Send a polite note proposing a boundary walk

effects.log: {npc} replies with a note even more polite and a date three centuries hence. It is the courtesy of a god who has no hurry.

choices.text: Let the goat have the hill

effects.log: The goat bleats, victorious. The valley's view is the goat's, now.

events.text: The boundary quarrel has become a minor court matter. Both of you present maps. Both maps are accurate. They disagree by a hill, a river, and a small blue temple that appears on neither.
events.arc: The Boundary Stone

choices.text: Argue that tradition favours you

effects.log: Your case is long and eloquent. The court nods and does nothing. The quarrel is entered in the register as ongoing.

choices.text: Propose to share the hill

effects.log: {npc} reluctantly agrees. A small footbridge is built. The goat is given both citizenships.

choices.text: Draw a third map, impartially

effects.log: It satisfies nobody, which the clerk takes as a sign of success.

events.text: The small blue temple turns out to belong to a lesser god nobody has heard of, who sits in it quietly eating figs. The hill, they say, has always been theirs. Both of you have been quarrelling over a home.
events.arc: The Boundary Stone

choices.text: Apologise to the fig-god, and fund a roof

effects.log: The fig-god accepts the apology with a nod and a fig. You and {npc} share the roof bill, resentfully, and end up friends.

choices.text: Propose the fig-god as the border-keeper

effects.log: The fig-god, startled, accepts. The border is peaceful for three hundred years, and fig-flavoured.

events.text: The boundary quarrel outlasts the court. It settles into the long, comfortable grievance of old neighbours: nobody wins, and nobody leaves. You fill an entire drawer with letters. Some of them are rather fond.
events.arc: The Boundary Stone

choices.text: Write {npc} a truce letter, signed with a fig

effects.log: {npc} replies in kind. The quarrel continues, but now as a correspondence. You look forward to the post.

choices.text: Burn the drawer and start fresh

effects.log: You burn the old letters with ceremony. The ash rises in a thin column. {npc}, in the next valley, sees it and, after a long time, lights a stick.

events.text: A mortal has written to you every month for nine years to complain about your weather. The letters are numbered. They are courteous. They are also relentless. Today you receive number 112, which begins: I regret to inform you.
events.arc: The Letters of Complaint

choices.text: Reply, formally, with an apology

effects.log: {npc} writes back at once, delighted, and with seven further complaints. A correspondence has begun.

choices.text: Change the weather, quietly

effects.log: The next letter begins: I regret to inform you that you have changed the weather. {npc} complains about the new weather instead.

choices.text: File it with the others, and admire the handwriting

effects.log: The handwriting is lovely. The grievances are a bit shrill. You file it between a love letter and a recipe.

events.text: {npc} writes to say they have been unwell, and that they have had to postpone the complaint about the winds. They hope this is not an inconvenience. You are, at this point, a little worried.
events.arc: The Letters of Complaint

choices.text: Send a healing wind in return

effects.log: {npc} recovers within the week, and the next letter opens with a stern note on healing winds.

choices.text: Write a short, warm note, plain, with no apology

effects.log: The reply is three lines: thank you, I will recover, complaint 113 follows. You laugh in the empty hall.

choices.text: Wait for the next letter

effects.log: It arrives, two weeks late, signed with a shaky hand.

events.text: One day a letter arrives that is not a complaint. It says: I wonder whether you read these. I wonder whether anyone listens. It is the only honest sentence in a hundred and thirty letters.
events.arc: The Letters of Complaint

choices.text: Appear to {him} in a dream and say: always

effects.log: {npc} wakes calm. The next letter is a complaint, as a courtesy. It is also, you suspect, a love letter.

choices.text: Reply with a framed collection of all of them, bound

effects.log: {npc} is stunned to see the letters bound and indexed. {He} stops writing, satisfied, and a month later sends a thank-you.

events.text: The complaints have not stopped. {npc} is old now, and the letters are slower. The last one reads only: the weather has been agreeable this year. It is unsigned.
events.arc: The Letters of Complaint

choices.text: Keep that letter on the altar

effects.log: The altar has a hundred and forty letters of complaint and one of praise, and the praise is the shortest and the best.

choices.text: Reply, in a dream, with a single word: gladly

effects.log: {npc} wakes and writes nothing more. The silence that follows is not unhappy.

events.text: A stranger arrives at your shrine carrying a tin cup. {npc} says it was found in a river-bed, under a stone, and that the name scratched inside it is not any god's. It is the name you had before you were one.
events.arc: The Mortal You Were

choices.text: Take the cup, and hold it a long time

effects.log: The tin is cold and ordinary. A thousand years fold up like a letter. You remember the taste of the water.

choices.text: Tell {npc} to put it back where it was found

effects.log: {npc} shrugs and goes. The cup goes back under the river-stone, where some part of you wanted it.

choices.text: Ask {him} how the name was read

effects.log: {npc} says it was read aloud by an old woman in a ferry, who had known the family. You sit very still.

events.text: The old ferry-keeper is a hundred years old, and still alive, and lives on a small island in a marsh. They do not know you are a god. They only know they once poured water for someone with that name.
events.arc: The Mortal You Were

choices.text: Visit the ferry-keeper in a plain coat

effects.log: The ferry-keeper looks at you for a long moment and says, in a flat voice: you have a look I know. It undoes you. Nothing is asked of you.

choices.text: Send a dream of the old days

effects.log: The ferry-keeper wakes, smiling, and tells a grandchild a story. It is yours, and nearly right.

choices.text: Leave the ferry-keeper be

effects.log: You let the past stay in its marsh. It is, perhaps, the kind thing.

events.text: The ferry-keeper dies in the spring, in sleep, and leaves you a small bundle in the will. Inside: a lock of hair, a comb, and a note in a spidery hand saying: you were a good child. Do not forget to eat.
events.arc: The Mortal You Were

choices.text: Keep the comb, and wear it on festival days

effects.log: It is a plain horn comb. You wear it in your hair at the great feasts, and nobody ever asks.

choices.text: Bury the bundle in the marsh, under the ferry post

effects.log: You say a prayer for the ferry-keeper, which is the first prayer you have said, not heard, in a thousand years.

events.text: Years on, the tin cup resurfaces: someone has cleaned it, and is selling it as a relic of the god's mortal days. The legend attached to it is entirely invented, and very good.
events.arc: The Mortal You Were

choices.text: Let the legend run

effects.log: The cup is sold ten times, and the legend grows with each. You are told, at a feast, that in your youth you tamed a river. You never did.

choices.text: Buy the cup back, anonymously, with faith

effects.log: A pilgrim acting as your agent buys it. It sits on your shelf, and the legend dies a quiet death.

events.text: A community has built you a magnificent temple in the middle of a salt marsh. It sinks an inch a year. The priest, {npc}, is thrilled. The foundation stones are a delight. The bells are sinking at a quarter-tone per decade.
events.arc: The Temple in the Wrong Place

choices.text: Raise the temple, a little, once a year

effects.log: You hoist it from below with a kind of gentle muscle, and {npc} credits the foundations. They are very good foundations.

choices.text: Tell the priest, in a dream, about the marsh

effects.log: {npc} wakes and agrees at once that the temple is in the wrong place. The congregation does not.

choices.text: Say nothing; it is very lovely

effects.log: It is lovely, sinking. You grow fond of the bells.

events.text: A flood comes and the temple stands in a lake. Pilgrims arrive by boat and are astonished. A fisherman sets up a stall at the portico. The priest has stopped apologising.
events.arc: The Temple in the Wrong Place

choices.text: Hold the water steady so the temple is dry inside

effects.log: The inside stays dry. The crowd calls it a miracle. You quietly regret the precedent.

choices.text: Let the temple be a lake-shrine, and enjoy the view

effects.log: It becomes the Water Temple. The boatmen are very pleased. You are told it is picturesque.

choices.text: Send a heron to sit on the roof

effects.log: The heron is photogenic. It also eats the fish in the pews.

events.text: The congregation moves the temple, stone by stone, to higher ground: a labour of seven years, and a quarrel in every year. When the last brick is set, {npc} is too old to climb the new steps.
events.arc: The Temple in the Wrong Place

choices.text: Carry {him} up, in a plain coat

effects.log: You carry the old priest up the new stairs, as one carries a sack of rice. {npc} says nothing, and wets a sleeve.

choices.text: Ease the stairs, so {he} can walk them

effects.log: The steps lengthen and flatten, a hand-width each. {npc} climbs them in peace, and has no notion why.

events.text: The temple keeps sinking, slowly, into the marsh, and a generation later it is a half-sunken ring of arches with water between them. Children paddle through it. It is the most beloved ruin in the domain.
events.arc: The Temple in the Wrong Place

choices.text: Preserve it exactly as it is

effects.log: You halt the sinking at the perfect moment. It is the temple you didn't ask for, and the one you most love.

choices.text: Let it go on sinking, gracefully

effects.log: Over centuries the arches go under, one by one. The marsh becomes a lake. A single bell tolls beneath the surface on windless nights.

events.text: Your oldest servant, {npc}, has served the household for nine hundred years and asks, very quietly, for a day off. The household goes still. Nobody has ever asked. Nobody knew it was possible.
events.arc: The Servant Who Wants to Retire

choices.text: Grant a week, and ask what {he} would like to do

effects.log: {npc} says: sit in the sun. The household is stunned to learn that servants can sit.

choices.text: Grant the day, but ask {him} to train a successor first

effects.log: {npc} bristles very slightly. The successor is trained, and is not as good, and is allowed to fail.

choices.text: Ask what the household needs to make the day possible

effects.log: The household produces a list of seventeen things. You do eleven yourself.

events.text: {npc} comes back from the week unrecognisable: rested, a bit sunburnt, and with opinions. {He} has noticed the household has been run badly for centuries, and politely says so.
events.arc: The Servant Who Wants to Retire

choices.text: Ask for {his} list, and act on it

effects.log: The list is long. Half is wrong. The other half changes the household for good.

choices.text: Make {him} steward and be done with it

effects.log: {npc} accepts with a long sigh. The household runs smoothly. You see a good deal less of {him}.

choices.text: Thank {him} and say nothing more

effects.log: It is the first time a servant has been thanked here. The household stiffens in surprise.

events.text: {npc} announces a plan to leave for a small cottage at the edge of the domain. {He} wants to garden. The household wails; the shrine-beasts leave a pile of offerings at the door.
events.arc: The Servant Who Wants to Retire

choices.text: Give {him} the cottage, and the garden, and a pension of faith

effects.log: The cottage is built in a month. {npc} cultivates tomatoes of astonishing size and sends the household one every week.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay one more year

effects.log: {npc} agrees. At the end of the year there is a farewell feast so grand it is still discussed. {He} leaves with a bag of seeds.

events.text: {npc} serves on, as steward, and the household thrives, and it dawns on you one day that {he} has been running the entire domain without a fuss for a century.
events.arc: The Servant Who Wants to Retire

choices.text: Name {him} the Second Voice of the Shrine

effects.log: It is an honour without a power. {npc} bows, and says: I thought that was already my title.

choices.text: Take the evening meal with {him}, as equals

effects.log: It is awkward, then easy. {npc} tells you the household's gossip, which is spectacular.

events.text: A river-god at the edge of your domain, {npc}, charges a toll of one pebble per crossing. Your pilgrims have begun to complain. {npc} says the pebbles are for the river's upkeep. The river's upkeep is a nap.
events.arc: The Ford Between Two Gods

choices.text: Pay the toll for all your pilgrims, in advance

effects.log: {npc} is baffled and thrilled. The riverbed is now covered in your pilgrims' pebbles, and the water runs a shade bluer.

choices.text: Write a polite request to waive the toll for the pious

effects.log: {npc} replies: the pious are exactly who I charge. They can afford it. You almost respect the logic.

choices.text: Build a footbridge, as a rebuke

effects.log: The bridge stands for one week before {npc} floods it, affably, and sends a bill.

events.text: A drought dries the river to a trickle. {npc} sends an urgent petition to your domain for help. The petition is signed: Your neighbour, very much in need.
events.arc: The Ford Between Two Gods

choices.text: Send rain, with no strings

effects.log: The river swells. {npc} writes a letter of thanks that is mostly an apology. The toll is waived for a year.

choices.text: Send rain, in exchange for the toll's end

effects.log: {npc} agrees with a groan. The ford is free. You are not sure it was your finest moment.

choices.text: Send a modest drizzle and watch what {he} does

effects.log: {npc} spends the drizzle on the pilgrims' pebbles, and the river keeps its balance.

events.text: The river-god comes to your shrine in person, a damp and awkward guest. {He} brings a gift of river stones, and says that {he} has not been to a neighbour's home in six hundred years.
events.arc: The Ford Between Two Gods

choices.text: Host {him} for the evening, with proper hospitality

effects.log: You feed {him} the best the kitchen can offer. {npc} cries a little into the soup. The tide in the next valley rises a handbreadth.

choices.text: Return the visit the next week

effects.log: You arrive at the ford and sit on the bank. The river is quiet, and cold, and rather lovely. {npc} brings a flask of something strong.

events.text: The river-god and you settle into a long and comfortable quarrel, with regular meetings. The pilgrims still pay a pebble. It has become a custom, and then a tradition, and then, to the surprise of both of you, a festival.
events.arc: The Ford Between Two Gods

choices.text: Join the pebble festival in disguise

effects.log: You toss a pebble in the river at the festival and wish for nothing at all. It is surprisingly restful.

choices.text: Declare the festival yours too, jointly

effects.log: The joint patronage is announced at the next council. A small stir results. A bridge is built, finally, with both your names.

events.text: An invitation arrives, scented with something expensive. {npc}, who spent a century trying to ruin your festival, is holding a feast to honour a new age. You are expected. Refusing would be an insult. Attending would be an insult to yourself.
events.arc: The Old Enemy's Feast

choices.text: Go, in your finest, and be gracious

effects.log: You arrive, bow, and say something polite. {npc} is visibly disappointed to find nothing to be annoyed by.

choices.text: Go, in a plain coat, as no one

effects.log: You sit at the far end and eat quietly. {npc} does not notice you for an hour, which is its own delight.

choices.text: Decline with a very formal note

effects.log: The note is two lines. The court reads it aloud for fun. {npc} is, as intended, aggrieved.

events.text: At the feast, your seat is the lowest at the table, beside the kitchen door. {npc} smiles across the room. It is an old joke. It is not funny, but it is old.
events.arc: The Old Enemy's Feast

choices.text: Take the seat and make it the best at the table

effects.log: You turn the kitchen door into a fine entrance. The cooks adore you. The other gods drift over, one by one, to see what the fuss is.

choices.text: Move quietly to a better seat

effects.log: {npc} watches, offended. The seating chart gets muddled and nobody can be blamed.

choices.text: Sit, eat, and smile back

effects.log: A smile in return is the sharpest reply there is. {npc} stops smiling first.

events.text: Late in the night, {npc} approaches you in the garden, away from the guests, and says, after some effort: I did not expect you to come. I have not forgotten why I stopped sending letters. Do you remember why we quarrelled?
events.arc: The Old Enemy's Feast

choices.text: Say yes, and say what it was

effects.log: It was small. It was a misread note, a missed feast. {npc} laughs bitterly, and for a moment looks very old.

choices.text: Say you do not, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} stares. Neither of you can remember. The quarrel has outlived its cause by a thousand years.

events.text: Late in the night, {npc} approaches you in the garden and offers a toast to your festival, in public, at last. The words are polite. The glass is shaking.
events.arc: The Old Enemy's Feast

choices.text: Raise your glass in return

effects.log: The court applauds. A peace, of the long cold kind, begins.

choices.text: Accept the toast, and send a gift in the morning

effects.log: The gift is a plain cup. {npc} drinks from it for a thousand years.

events.text: You have taken up kite-making. It started as a distraction and became a mania. The study is stacked with frames, paper, and thread spun from morning mist. A visiting priest, {npc}, finds you at 3 a.m. gluing a dragon and decides to say nothing.
events.arc: The God Who Makes Kites

choices.text: Invite {him} to try one

effects.log: {npc} makes a lopsided duck and flies it from the shrine roof. It stays up for a day. You are both enchanted.

choices.text: Hide the kites, embarrassed

effects.log: {npc} pretends not to see. A kite pokes out of the wardrobe for the rest of the century.

choices.text: Explain it as a ritual of the sky

effects.log: You say that kites are an old rite. {npc} nods, and builds one for you in the same spirit.

events.text: A kite-festival is arranged in the valley. The god of the sky sends a stiff note: kites are the sky's business. You respond, with an extremely courteous letter, that you have been practising.
events.arc: The God Who Makes Kites

choices.text: Enter a kite of your own in the contest, under another name

effects.log: It wins second place. The winner is the god of the sky's own entry, which is a kite shaped like a scroll of rules.

choices.text: Teach the valley children to fly their own

effects.log: The sky above the valley fills with crooked, joyful kites. The god of the sky gets quite emotional.

choices.text: Fly a kite without telling anyone

effects.log: It floats over the shrine, tied to nothing. Nobody mentions it.

events.text: Your masterpiece is a kite the size of a field. It takes a hundred children and a storm to lift. When it rises, the whole valley goes silent, and then roars.
events.arc: The God Who Makes Kites

choices.text: Let the children fly it, and stay on the ground

effects.log: They fly it for an afternoon and call it theirs. You watch from a hillside and are quite happy.

choices.text: Fly it yourself, to the top of the sky

effects.log: It reaches the edge of the clouds and tugs, like a living thing. You laugh aloud for the first time in an age.

events.text: You are asked to judge the next kite contest. You decline, which is wise, because you have a conflict of interest and a sprained wrist.
events.arc: The God Who Makes Kites

choices.text: Sponsor the prizes instead

effects.log: The prizes are fine thread and good paper. The winners cry. It is a better contest for your absence.

choices.text: Judge it in a plain coat, in secret

effects.log: You award the prize to the worst kite, which was the funniest. The crowd approves.

events.text: {npc} comes to your shrine and asks, in the quietest of voices, for something no god can give: that a dead spouse be returned for a single hour. {He} has brought no gift. {He} has only a worn pair of slippers.
events.arc: The Prayer a God Cannot Answer

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: it cannot be done

effects.log: {npc} nods. {He} knew. {He} wanted to hear it said. {He} sits on the step with the slippers on {his} lap, and you sit with {him}.

choices.text: Offer a dream of the spouse instead

effects.log: {npc} accepts it with a long breath. A dream is not an hour, but it is more than a memory.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let {him} sit

effects.log: You say nothing for three hours. When {npc} rises, {he} says thank you, and means it.

events.text: {npc} returns each spring for a decade. {He} brings the slippers and puts them on the step and sits. Sometimes {he} talks. Sometimes {he} falls asleep. The shrine-keeper has started to leave a blanket.
events.arc: The Prayer a God Cannot Answer

choices.text: Appear in the dream the night after each visit

effects.log: {npc} wakes always a little lighter. The dreams are short. The slippers, one spring, are gone from the step.

choices.text: Keep the slippers warm on the altar between visits

effects.log: The shrine-keeper obliges. The slippers are, after a decade, remarkably well preserved.

choices.text: Let {him} come and go

effects.log: The ritual builds its own quiet strength.

events.text: On the tenth spring, {npc} climbs the step and announces that {he} has come to leave the slippers for good. {He} wants a god to have them. {He} says they are the only thing {he} owns that is not already held by memory.
events.arc: The Prayer a God Cannot Answer

choices.text: Accept them, with a vow to keep them

effects.log: You place them on the highest shelf. {npc} does not weep. {He} thanks you, and walks down the hill more easily than {he} climbed it.

choices.text: Ask {him} to keep them one more year, but promise to be there when it is time

effects.log: {npc} considers, and nods. At the eleventh spring, you are there, and the slippers are placed in your hands together.

events.text: On the tenth spring, {npc} does not come. A grandchild arrives, in {his} place, with the slippers and a note: I have gone to see for myself. Please keep these for me.
events.arc: The Prayer a God Cannot Answer

choices.text: Take the slippers, and bless the grandchild on the road

effects.log: The grandchild accepts the blessing shyly and goes home. The slippers sit beside the bell.

choices.text: Ask the Silent Hall to be gentle

effects.log: Baekun replies that this is always the case. But a ferry lamp is lit a little brighter that night.

events.text: An old friend from before you rose arrives in the hall, aged, bent, and delighted. {npc} has been dead for forty years, apparently, and is here on a short pass from the grey boats. {He} has brought a bag of nuts.
events.arc: The Friend From Before

choices.text: Welcome {him} with full honours

effects.log: The household is thrown into a panic. {npc} sits at your right hand and eats nuts, and tells embarrassing stories from your youth.

choices.text: Sit with {him} alone in the garden

effects.log: You eat nuts. You talk about nothing. For a few hours you are a person with a friend, and not a god with a position.

choices.text: Ask what it is like, over there

effects.log: {npc} says: slow. Very restful. The tea is good. You listen to the details with a sudden stillness.

events.text: {npc} asks, just before leaving, whether you ever think about the old days. {He} is gentle about it. {He} knows what a god is. {He} also knows what you were.
events.arc: The Friend From Before

choices.text: Say yes, often, and give an example

effects.log: {npc} listens to the example, and laughs, and corrects a detail. The memory improves.

choices.text: Say you try not to

effects.log: {npc} nods. {He} says: that makes sense. But do not try too hard. It will come to you anyway.

choices.text: Hug {him} goodbye

effects.log: The household watches a god embrace a ghost in front of the soup. Nobody says a word.

events.text: Years on, a nut-tree grows in the corner of the garden where you sat with your friend. It bears small, dark, delicious nuts. The household has no idea where it came from.
events.arc: The Friend From Before

choices.text: Let the tree stand, and tell no one

effects.log: Each autumn you take a handful and sit under it. The nuts are very good.

choices.text: Put a small plaque on the trunk: from a friend

effects.log: The household reads it, and asks no questions. The tree is declared sacred, in a casual way.

events.text: Years on, you receive a message by grey boat: the friend has moved on beyond the harbour and sends one last line. It reads: they say I may not return. Eat the nuts.
events.arc: The Friend From Before

choices.text: Eat the nuts, with a toast

effects.log: You eat the nuts in the garden, and the household sees a god weeping into a pastry. They bring more nuts.

choices.text: Plant the last nut where the friend sat

effects.log: A small tree will grow there in a hundred years. By then you will have forgotten why you planted it, and that will be fine.

events.text: The shrine's door-keeper counts prayers as they come in and has gone slightly mad. {He} greets every worshipper with a number. Yesterday {he} told a pilgrim: you are four thousand and eleven. The pilgrim was delighted.

choices.text: Keep the count, and ask {him} to stop at a round number

effects.log: The count stops at five thousand. {He} celebrates for a week, then resumes at one.

choices.text: Tell {him} to count only the kind ones

effects.log: The count drops sharply. {He} is quiet for some time and then, sadly, begins to include the rest.

events.text: The household's dust of ages has become an issue. The shrine-maid has been sweeping a layer deposited in the First Century into a pile that now has its own weather. A cloud has formed. It rains soot on Tuesdays.

choices.text: Declare the pile a minor sacred site

effects.log: Pilgrims come to see the Hill of Dust. It is a hit. The maid is promoted to Keeper of the Hill.

choices.text: Blow it out the window in one breath

effects.log: A grey plume crosses three domains. You receive complaints for a decade.

events.text: The shrine mice have held a meeting. They have decided to worship you. They leave tiny offerings of seeds on the altar and chitter in a hymn that is, after consideration, quite musical.

choices.text: Reply with a modest blessing of the larder

effects.log: The mice are ecstatic. The larder is full. The cook is furious.

choices.text: Ask the cook to be kind to them

effects.log: The cook sniffs, and leaves a saucer of milk. A truce is signed on a crumb.

events.text: A goat belonging to a rival god has wandered across the boundary and eaten the flowers on your most important altar. The goat is unrepentant. The rival god is on the way to retrieve it, with a very formal apology.

choices.text: Accept the apology graciously, and keep the goat for tea

effects.log: The goat is returned. The tea, you are told, was lovely.

choices.text: Send the goat back with a bouquet

effects.log: The rival god is moved, and the rivalry cools by a degree.
