events.text: A letter of thanks arrives, addressed to Whoever Has Been Doing This. It is from a family that has been quietly benefited by your weather for forty years and has finally worked out whom to thank.

choices.text: Reply with a modest, unsigned note

effects.log: The family frames the note and thinks it came from the previous owner of the farm.

choices.text: Send the weather a little further, unannounced

effects.log: The family writes again, unsettled by your reticence.

events.text: It is the anniversary of the day you rose to godhood. Nobody remembers. You buy yourself a small pastry and sit on the roof and watch the stars for an hour.

choices.text: Light a lamp for who you were

effects.log: The lamp stays lit all night. A moth finds it and does not leave until morning.

choices.text: Tell the shrine-keeper, quietly, and share the pastry

effects.log: The shrine-keeper is moved, and says nothing, and cuts the pastry exactly in half.

events.text: The neighbour god keeps a rooster that crows exactly on the boundary line. It crows at three in the morning. You have mentioned this three times. The neighbour says it has no jurisdiction over its own rooster.

choices.text: Send the rooster a bad dream about hawks

effects.log: The rooster sleeps in, and you sleep in. You feel slightly guilty. Not very.

choices.text: Offer to buy the rooster a clock

effects.log: The neighbour is offended, then touched, then delighted. The rooster is retrained to crow at seven.

events.text: A cartographer from the court arrives to draw a new map of your domain, and spends a month drawing a perfectly accurate map that leaves out the small valley where you sit when you want to be alone. You ask them why.

choices.text: Thank the cartographer, and leave it off

effects.log: The valley stays unmarked on every map. It is the only secret you have kept in a thousand years.

choices.text: Have it added, and pretend you do not mind

effects.log: The valley is on the map. Tourists arrive. You never sit there again.

events.text: A pilgrim, confused, has left a bowl of soup at your door rather than the shrine. It is a perfectly good soup. It would be rude to refuse it. You are, you realise, a god who has been left a soup.

choices.text: Eat it, and send back the bowl

effects.log: The bowl returns with a fresh coat of glaze. The pilgrim thinks the shrine-keeper did it.

choices.text: Send the pilgrim a warm night and a full pantry

effects.log: The soup was not an offering. The pilgrim finds, in the morning, they have a larger one.

events.text: The shrine-hound has chosen to nap on the altar, and has done so for a week. The pilgrims lay offerings around it. The priest is trying to find a rule against dogs on altars and has not found one.

choices.text: Let the hound sleep

effects.log: It sleeps. Its dreams, you notice, are about you. It is a very devoted hound.

choices.text: Nudge it onto a cushion, kindly

effects.log: It wakes, yawns, takes the cushion, and puts it on the altar. The cushion is now an altar.

events.text: The household has a room for the memories of previous gods who held your domain. It is full of dust, grudges, and one very good chair. A previous god's portrait watches you from the wall. It has a mildly sarcastic expression.

choices.text: Sit in the good chair and ask the portrait what went wrong

effects.log: The portrait does not answer, as you expected, but the room feels attentive. You leave better informed.

choices.text: Hang a new picture beside it, of yourself, grinning

effects.log: The portrait looks, if possible, even more sarcastic. You get on beautifully.

events.text: The toll collector at the pass to your domain has retired, and the new one is overzealous. Pilgrims are being asked to declare their prayers. A man was fined for a sneeze.

choices.text: Have a quiet word with the new collector

effects.log: The collector turns red. By the weekend the pass is open, and the fine is waived.

choices.text: Dissolve the post and let travellers pass

effects.log: The pass is free. A tavern opens in its place within the month.

events.text: The priest's sermon on Humility has run for two hours. The congregation is asleep. The shrine-beasts are asleep. The sermon is, oddly, getting better with every minute you listen to it.

choices.text: Stay for the whole thing

effects.log: The ending is superb. The priest, glowing, never knows who the stranger was who clapped.

choices.text: Send a small breeze to wake the front row

effects.log: The front row starts, and applauds, thinking it is over.

events.text: The household has a pot of tea that has been brewing since the Second Century. Nobody dares touch it. It has developed, according to the cook, a personality. It is, apparently, quite strong.

choices.text: Pour a cup

effects.log: The tea is astonishing. Your sinuses clear. A forgotten memory blooms, and fades.

choices.text: Leave it to its personality

effects.log: The cook nods. The pot sits on, brewing.

events.text: A visiting god is staying in the guest chamber, and has been staying for three years. Nobody wants to ask when they are leaving. They have started to do the shrine's accounts. They are good at it.

choices.text: Give them the accounts as a formal role

effects.log: The guest is thrilled to have a title, and stays another century.

choices.text: Throw a leaving feast, with a hint

effects.log: The guest takes the hint and leaves with a tearful speech. A letter arrives a month later: may I come back?

events.text: A god of one stream, a very small god indeed, lives at the edge of your domain and has been shyly leaving you gifts for eight hundred years: a pebble, a feather, a lost button. You have never replied.

choices.text: Reply at last, with a letter of thanks

effects.log: The small god goes silent for a year, then sends back a whole stone. It is the most beautiful stone you have ever seen.

choices.text: Visit, in a plain coat, to sit by the stream

effects.log: The stream is a stream. The god is a delight. You come away lighter.

events.text: A neighbouring god has sent you an enormous gift: a gold statue of themselves. It is, to be frank, hideous. It must be displayed, or the neighbour will be wounded. The shrine-keeper has found a corner.

choices.text: Display it in the cloakroom

effects.log: It is admired by all coats. The neighbour is told it is in the place of honour. This is, strictly, true.

choices.text: Send a gold statue of yourself in return, equally hideous

effects.log: The two statues stare at each other across the border. A friendship grows from a shared joke.

events.text: A pilgrim arrives at the altar, kneels, and sits there for an hour in complete silence, asking for nothing. When they rise, they bow, and say: that was nice. They leave.

choices.text: Return the bow

effects.log: The pilgrim is startled to see the altar bow back. They tell no one, because no one would believe them.

choices.text: Send a small star-glow to light the road

effects.log: The road home is gently lit. The pilgrim does not look up.

events.text: You find the old pantry of your mortal days, preserved as a relic in the oldest wing of the household. Jars of plums, a loaf, a wooden spoon. The plums are, impossibly, still good.

choices.text: Eat one plum

effects.log: It tastes of a summer you had forgotten. You sit on the pantry floor for a long time.

choices.text: Seal the pantry and mark it a shrine

effects.log: The household adopts it at once. A pilgrim wonders why the plums are so important.

events.text: A scholar from the court visits to take notes on your household for a treatise on domestic divinity. They have already been told off by the cook, the maid, and the hound. They have made a friend of the mice.

choices.text: Give them a tour, and show them the tea

effects.log: The scholar writes four pages on the tea. It is the best chapter of the treatise.

choices.text: Let them wander

effects.log: They wander for a month. The treatise, when published, praises the household as a model of confusion.

events.text: A neighbouring valley has thanked you for a rain that was in fact sent by the god of the next domain. The neighbour is very tired of it. You have written, apologetically, to correct the record. The valley has not changed its mind.

choices.text: Forward the thanks, and take a modest cut

effects.log: The neighbour accepts the thanks, wearily, and sends you a dried fig as commission.

choices.text: Accept the rain graciously, and send a little more

effects.log: The valley is satisfied. The neighbour sulks for a month, and then forgets.

events.text: The servants have split into two factions over who gets to carry the great chair. Both have a case. Both have a grandmother. The chair is not, in fact, particularly heavy.

choices.text: Have both carry it, one on each side

effects.log: The chair is carried by both factions, awkwardly. They are friends by evening.

choices.text: Replace the chair with a lighter one

effects.log: The factions turn, together, on the new chair. A truce is called on the grounds of its ugliness.

events.text: The great festival in your honour ends with the burning of a straw effigy of you, a custom older than you are. This year the effigy refuses to burn. It smoulders, hisses, and stands up in the ash. {npc}, the festival-marshal, goes grey.
events.arc: The Effigy That Would Not Burn

choices.text: Let it stand, and bow to it

effects.log: The crowd goes quiet, and then bows back. The effigy stands until dawn, perfectly upright, and then crumbles to warm dust.

choices.text: Quietly finish the burning with a breath

effects.log: A breath of flame, and the effigy goes up. The crowd cheers, relieved, and the marshal wipes a brow.

choices.text: Walk through the crowd in disguise to hear what they say

effects.log: They say it is a sign. Half say it means good fortune. The other half have brought extra bread, just in case.

events.text: Next year the marshal builds a stronger effigy, with a frame of green wood and wet straw, and it burns like a candle. The crowd is quiet. Something about it feels wrong. They liked the one that stood.
events.arc: The Effigy That Would Not Burn

choices.text: Send the effigy a small sign of life, a stir of the arm

effects.log: The crowd gasps. The effigy lifts one straw arm, and the festival is made. The marshal weeps with relief.

choices.text: Tell the marshal in a dream: let them choose whether it burns

effects.log: {npc} wakes and decides to ask the crowd. The vote is held in the square. It takes four hours, and it is the best festival in years.

choices.text: Let it burn, and say nothing

effects.log: The effigy burns. The crowd goes home subdued. A year later they ask for the stubborn one back.

events.text: The Effigy That Stands becomes a festival tradition: it is built, lit, and left to stand, and children are told to bow to it. Rival priests call it blasphemy. The faithful call it Tuesday.
events.arc: The Effigy That Would Not Burn

choices.text: Let the priests argue it out

effects.log: The argument lasts a decade. Both sides write long treatises, which are shelved side by side in the archive.

choices.text: Declare it a good custom, in a dream to the high priest

effects.log: The high priest wakes and writes an edict: the effigy may stand. Everyone is a little disappointed it was so simple.

events.text: The crowd votes, in the end, to let the effigy burn or stand by the feel of the evening. Some years it burns. Some years it stands. {npc} keeps a ledger and a cheerful temper.
events.arc: The Effigy That Would Not Burn

choices.text: Send a quiet hand to settle each year's choice

effects.log: You nudge it gently, just enough. The festival is never boring and never wrong.

choices.text: Leave it to the crowd, entirely

effects.log: The crowd learns what they like. The effigy burns on the fourth year, to a great cheer, and stands on the fifth.

events.text: At your festival, a thousand paper lanterns are released into the night, each carrying a prayer. A wind you did not send takes the lot, not up to you, but sideways, over a hill and into a neighbouring god's orchard. {npc} the lantern-maker stares in horror.
events.arc: The Lanterns That Drifted Wrong

choices.text: Gather them back, one by one, with a hush of wind

effects.log: You coax the lanterns home. A few are scorched. The neighbour god, woken, grumbles and returns to sleep.

choices.text: Let them settle in the orchard and send an apology

effects.log: The neighbour finds a field of prayer-lanterns among the apple trees and is, to everyone's surprise, charmed.

choices.text: Say nothing, and pretend it was intended

effects.log: It is accepted as a new custom. The lantern-maker is baffled to be called inspired.

events.text: The neighbour god, whose orchard it was, sends a basket of apples with a note: please do it again. The apples are the best you have ever tasted. The note is signed with an unmistakable flourish.
events.arc: The Lanterns That Drifted Wrong

choices.text: Do it again, deliberately, next year

effects.log: The lanterns drift over the hill by design. The orchard blooms in the wrong season, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Send the lantern-maker to the orchard as an ambassador

effects.log: {npc} is nervous, and then enchanted. The apple-god gives {him} a seedling. The festival has a new tradition.

choices.text: Eat the apples quietly

effects.log: They are as good as the note suggested.

events.text: A decade of shared festivals later, the two valleys are one in everything but name. Their children play in each other's orchards. A boundary stone is left to the moss.
events.arc: The Lanterns That Drifted Wrong

choices.text: Propose a joint festival at the old border

effects.log: The joint festival is the loudest in either domain. The boundary stone is wreathed in paper flowers.

choices.text: Let it grow naturally, without a name

effects.log: No one calls it a festival. It is just what the two valleys do in autumn. The lanterns drift as they please.

events.text: {npc} grows old and passes the lantern-making to a grandchild, who makes the lanterns slightly larger each year. By the third year, a lantern lifts a whole cat.
events.arc: The Lanterns That Drifted Wrong

choices.text: Catch the cat, softly, on a cloud

effects.log: The cat is delivered to a rooftop, unharmed and affronted. The grandchild is mortified.

choices.text: Send a wind to guide the lanterns downward in good time

effects.log: The lanterns stay low, and the cat remains grounded. The crowd grumbles. The cat purrs.

events.text: A small child has wandered away from the crowd at your festival and is sitting on the shrine steps, unbothered, eating a honey cake. {npc} does not seem to be lost; {he} seems to be waiting for someone, and has chosen the right place.
events.arc: The Child Lost at the Festival

choices.text: Sit beside {him} and share the cake

effects.log: {npc} explains, with the gravity of the very small, that {his} grandmother said to wait here for the god. You take a bite of honey cake.

choices.text: Send the shrine-keeper to find the family

effects.log: The shrine-keeper returns with a flustered parent, who apologises to everyone in sight. {npc} finishes the cake.

choices.text: Watch from a distance, in case of trouble

effects.log: No trouble. The child makes four friends in ten minutes and a rival of a pigeon.

events.text: {npc} asks you a question you have never been asked: what do gods do all day? It is a fair question, and you have no ready answer.
events.arc: The Child Lost at the Festival

choices.text: Tell the truth: mostly we listen

effects.log: {npc} considers that. {He} says that sounds boring. Then {he} says it sounds like a grandmother. You cannot disagree.

choices.text: Make something up, about a dragon

effects.log: You describe a day of dragon-wrangling. {npc} listens, wide-eyed. You will have to live up to it.

choices.text: Ask {him} what {he} does all day

effects.log: {npc} gives a precise and thrilling account of a puddle. You listen, rapt.

events.text: Years later, {npc} is grown and arrives at the shrine with a scroll: {he} has been writing down what gods do, and would like you to check the facts. The first chapter is on dragons.
events.arc: The Child Lost at the Festival

choices.text: Correct the facts gently

effects.log: You correct what you can. The dragon chapter stays: it has become so beloved it would be a crime to remove it.

choices.text: Leave a margin note: this is nearly right

effects.log: {npc} frames the note. The scroll is bound and sent to the great library, where it is, to your dismay, shelved under Authorities.

events.text: Years later, a grown {npc} runs the festival cake stall. The honey cakes are, by general agreement, the best in three domains. {He} saves the first one every year for the shrine steps.
events.arc: The Child Lost at the Festival

choices.text: Appear on the steps and eat it

effects.log: You eat it in a plain coat and say it is good. {npc} puts a hand over {his} mouth and says nothing at all.

choices.text: Bless the stall

effects.log: A thin gold dust of luck falls on the cake counter. The stall is never short of customers.

events.text: {npc}, a litigious mortal, has filed a lawsuit against you at the lowest court of the heavens, for failing to prevent a hailstorm. The summons arrives by sparrow. The charge is Negligence of a Sacred Duty. The sparrow wants a tip.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Sued the God

choices.text: Appear in court, in person

effects.log: The clerks are in a state of shock. A god in the dock. {npc} reads the charges for forty minutes. You listen with perfect gravity.

choices.text: Send the shrine-keeper as your advocate

effects.log: The shrine-keeper, terrified, reads a statement that says: the god regrets the hail. The court accepts this at once.

choices.text: Pay the sparrow, and ignore the summons

effects.log: The sparrow leaves, aggrieved, and returns with a second summons. The sparrow is going to be a recurring figure.

events.text: The case turns on a technical point: the hail fell on the border of two domains, and nobody can prove whose it was. {npc} presses on, passionately. The judge, a tired old judge of the domains-god, has fallen asleep.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Sued the God

choices.text: Admit it was probably yours, and offer a repair

effects.log: {npc} blinks. Nobody has ever admitted anything to {him}. The court is thrown, and the case settles with a pile of roof tiles.

choices.text: Argue the border dispute at length

effects.log: You argue beautifully. The judge wakes, confused, and rules that hail belongs to the clouds. {npc} is outraged.

choices.text: Wait for the judge to wake

effects.log: The judge wakes, asks what the case was, and starts again from the beginning.

events.text: {npc} is moved by your honesty and withdraws the suit. {He} says no god has ever said sorry to {him}, and {he} is not sure what to do with it. {He} asks for a recipe for roof tiles instead.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Sued the God

choices.text: Give {him} the best recipe in the domain

effects.log: {npc} goes home with a recipe and a new respect. A hundred roofs in the valley are better for it.

choices.text: Send {him} a tile-maker to work with

effects.log: The tile-maker and {npc} become unlikely partners and fiercely feuding friends. Roofs are rebuilt across the district.

events.text: {npc} wins the argument over the border and is awarded a symbolic coin from the god of hail, who feels left out. The ruling is entered in the archive, to the great pride of the litigant.
events.arc: The Mortal Who Sued the God

choices.text: Congratulate {him}, wholeheartedly

effects.log: {npc} accepts it stiffly, and then cries. It was never about the hail. It was about being answered.

choices.text: Send an official letter of recognition, with a fig

effects.log: {npc} frames the letter and eats the fig. The litigation stops for good.

events.text: A child with no family has taken to sleeping on your shrine's porch. {npc} is small, quiet, and good at stealing offerings, which are then secretly given to the other children. The priest has noticed. The priest has said nothing.
events.arc: The Orphan at the Shrine Door

choices.text: Warm the porch at night

effects.log: The porch stays warm in the worst of the frost. {npc} wakes, suspicious, and checks the floor for tricks.

choices.text: Leave extra offerings where they can be taken

effects.log: The offerings multiply on the altar. {npc} takes them with a puzzled expression, and the other children eat well.

choices.text: Watch, and wait

effects.log: You watch the child for a week. {npc} steals only what is needed. It is a kind of ethics.

events.text: The priest takes {npc} in as an acolyte, grumbling. The child proves to be impossible: sharp-tongued, unafraid of gods, and brilliant at arithmetic. The shrine's accounts have never been better.
events.arc: The Orphan at the Shrine Door

choices.text: Give {him} a gift: a small bell, tuned to {his} voice

effects.log: The bell rings once at dawn. {npc} calls it a nuisance and wears it on a cord.

choices.text: Appear to {him} and say plainly that {he} is welcome here

effects.log: {npc} stares, shrugs, and says: obviously. But {he} is quieter all week.

choices.text: Say nothing; let the priest do the work

effects.log: The priest does the work admirably. You are proud, and invisible, and fine with it.

events.text: {npc} comes of age and is offered the title of high priest of another shrine. {He} refuses, citing the porch. {He} has a plan to rebuild it as a school for the unwanted.
events.arc: The Orphan at the Shrine Door

choices.text: Support the school with a stream of luck

effects.log: The school opens in the spring with fourteen children. It is run on a shoestring, and a remarkable amount of luck.

choices.text: Send a wise old teacher-god in disguise

effects.log: The teacher arrives with a bundle and a limp. {npc} knows at once, and does not say. The school thrives.

events.text: {npc} leaves the shrine for a life of wandering and sends a postcard each year: drawings of the places visited. You pin each to the shrine wall. The wall is nearly full.
events.arc: The Orphan at the Shrine Door

choices.text: Add a small flourish to each, in a dream

effects.log: Each postcard gains a tiny bright detail by morning: a bird, a star. {npc} puzzles over them in some far inn.

choices.text: Send a postcard back, to the next address

effects.log: The postcard reaches {npc} in a distant city and is read in the rain. It says: come home when you like.

events.text: You have started a garden in a corner of the hall, and it has gone badly. Your roses are the colour of mud. Your beans do not climb. A young gardener-priest, {npc}, watches from the door with the careful politeness of someone swallowing a laugh.
events.arc: The Garden of an Idle God

choices.text: Ask {him} to teach you

effects.log: {npc} is appalled, then delighted. The first lesson is on soil. It takes four hours and you take notes.

choices.text: Insist you know what you are doing

effects.log: {npc} bows. The roses wilt further. The beans, out of what seems like spite, begin to climb in the wrong direction.

choices.text: Let the garden go wild

effects.log: The weeds are surprisingly beautiful. A snail takes up residence.

events.text: The garden recovers. The beans climb. A rose, small and unscented, blooms in the corner. It is the first thing you have ever grown. You find you are rather moved.
events.arc: The Garden of an Idle God

choices.text: Share a bloom with {npc}

effects.log: {npc} puts it in a cup on the sill of the gardener's hut. It lasts a month, which is unheard of for roses.

choices.text: Keep the rose for yourself

effects.log: It sits on your desk. You find yourself talking to it. It does not answer, which is why you like it.

choices.text: Plant more of them

effects.log: The garden fills with small unscented roses. The household calls it the Quiet Corner.

events.text: A grand god visits and condescends to the garden. It is, they say, rustic. They are offered a rose, and they take it, and sit very still, and do not say another word for an hour.
events.arc: The Garden of an Idle God

choices.text: Let the grand god sit

effects.log: The grand god leaves at dusk, wiping one eye, and sends you a rare seed the following week. A friendship begins.

choices.text: Offer the grand god a seat and a cup of tea

effects.log: They stay for supper. The garden is mentioned at the next council, with respect.

events.text: Your mud-coloured rose is the only thing that survives a hard winter. {npc} calls it a miracle of stubbornness. You call it a relative.
events.arc: The Garden of an Idle God

choices.text: Name the rose after your mortal self

effects.log: The rose keeps the name. Every spring it flowers a little redder.

choices.text: Take a cutting for every shrine in your domain

effects.log: A hundred small roses bloom in a hundred shrines, all unscented and all stubborn. The pilgrims love them.

events.text: At the market a stall is selling charms with your name on them, at a price and in a quality you cannot approve. {npc} the stallholder has a smooth pitch and a sad charm: blessed by the god, guaranteed, absolutely your own.
events.arc: The Stall That Sold Your Name

choices.text: Confront {him}, in a plain coat

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and offers you a discount. You are shocked to find you like {him}.

choices.text: Send the shrine-keeper with a stern letter

effects.log: {npc} replies with a bow and a free charm. The shrine-keeper is not sure what to do with it.

choices.text: Buy a charm and examine it

effects.log: It is a lopsided wooden disc with a face on it. The face is not your face. It is, in its way, a better one.

events.text: The charms, to your annoyance, start to work. A few. A sprain mends. A lost coin returns. The luck is real, small, and entirely unauthorised. You did not arrange it. You are not sure who did.
events.arc: The Stall That Sold Your Name

choices.text: Investigate quietly

effects.log: You trace the luck to the faith of the buyers, which, you realise, is yours by right of name. It is a small and modest miracle.

choices.text: Confront {npc} again, and ask for a share of the profits

effects.log: {npc} smiles. We are partners, {he} says, and you do not correct {him}. A modest cut goes to the shrine fund.

choices.text: Let it be

effects.log: A stall full of unlicensed luck is a harmless thing. It is one of the pleasures of the world.

events.text: {npc} comes to you in a dream, ashamed, and confesses that the charms are nothing but wood and hope. {He} has been selling hope for forty years, and it has begun to weigh on {him}.
events.arc: The Stall That Sold Your Name

choices.text: Tell {him}: hope is the oldest relic

effects.log: {npc} wakes lighter. The stall sells charms for another twenty years, and the face on them changes to yours.

choices.text: Tell {him} to stop selling luck and start selling honesty

effects.log: {npc} takes this to heart. The stall becomes a bookshop of cheap, honest proverbs, and the best-loved in the market.

events.text: {npc} retires, handing the stall to a nephew who sells worse charms at higher prices. The luck thins. The nephew, perplexed, comes to the shrine to ask what {he} is doing wrong.
events.arc: The Stall That Sold Your Name

choices.text: Tell the nephew to listen to {his} customers

effects.log: {He} does, over time. The charms improve, the prices drop, and the luck returns.

choices.text: Let {him} fail, and learn

effects.log: The stall closes within the year. The nephew opens a bakery and is much happier.

events.text: A hard winter has fallen on the domain and the great bell of your shrine has frozen mute. Pilgrims come to find it silent and, assuming the worst, whisper that the god has gone. {npc}, the bell-ringer, hangs from the rope in dismay.
events.arc: The Winter of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Warm the bell with a breath

effects.log: The bell rings, a rough, low, golden note. The valley hears it and weeps with relief. {npc} falls off the rope.

choices.text: Ring it yourself from the heavens, soundlessly, as a feeling

effects.log: The valley feels a deep note in the chest. Nobody quite hears it. The frost thins on the shrine roof.

choices.text: Send a message through the shrine-keeper: the god is here

effects.log: The word spreads. The pilgrims gather, mutter, and light candles. A silent bell is a patient bell.

events.text: The winter drags on. The food stores shrink, and the priest begins to ration the offerings. {npc} asks, in a low voice, whether gods can send grain. You can, a little. It is against the courts' guidance.
events.arc: The Winter of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Send the grain, discreetly

effects.log: Sacks of grain appear in the shrine storehouse. The priest suspects a neighbour. The courts never find out.

choices.text: Ask the god of the harvest for a loan

effects.log: Pungnyeon replies with a stiff note, three sacks, and a bill. The valley eats. You owe a favour.

choices.text: Send a thaw, and hope

effects.log: The thaw comes a week early. It is not enough, but it is the right direction.

events.text: Spring comes. The valley survives, thinner and humbler. {npc} rings the bell at dawn, with a smile. The first crocus appears by the door. You find you have been holding your breath all winter.
events.arc: The Winter of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Send the first warm wind of the year, on purpose

effects.log: The wind passes over the valley, and every roof gives up its snow at once. A hundred children run out of doors and shout.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} by the bell at dawn

effects.log: {npc} says: I thought you might be gone. You say: so did I. The bell rings anyway, and neither of you is sorry.

events.text: Spring comes. The valley, which borrowed grain from the god of the harvest, holds a festival to repay the debt, and by accident turns it into a feast for a whole district.
events.arc: The Winter of the Silent Bell

choices.text: Thank Pungnyeon, publicly

effects.log: The god of the harvest, startled by the attention, sends a basket of ripe fruit and a rare smile.

choices.text: Quietly settle the debt with a favour

effects.log: The god of the harvest never mentions it again. A friendship stays on the books.

events.text: The priest of your largest shrine has seven children and a wife who runs the festival committee. {npc}, the eldest, wants to be a god. Not a priest: a god. {He} has drawn up a plan. It is detailed.
events.arc: The Priest's Large Family

choices.text: Read the plan, seriously

effects.log: The plan is thirty pages. Page eleven is a request for a domain. Page twelve is for a rank. You go through every line with care.

choices.text: Tell {him} gods are not made with plans

effects.log: {npc} is deflated, then rebellious. {He} burns the plan on the altar, which turns out to be an acceptable offering.

choices.text: Appear in a dream, and ask why {he} wants it

effects.log: {npc} answers with a speech about justice, hunger, and a goat. It is a good speech.

events.text: {npc} sets off to prove {him}self, in secret, and gets into a quarrel with a minor deity who is not amused. The deity writes to you for compensation. The sum is one pig.
events.arc: The Priest's Large Family

choices.text: Pay the pig, and send a dream of caution

effects.log: {npc} learns that quarrels with minor gods are the most dangerous kind, since they have the most time.

choices.text: Send {npc} to apologise in person, with the pig

effects.log: {npc} delivers the pig, a bit green. The deity, mollified, offers tea. A grudging friendship forms.

choices.text: Let the pig matter resolve itself

effects.log: The pig is delivered by a neighbour. The matter is dropped.

events.text: {npc} comes back years later, humbled, and asks for something modest: to be allowed to serve a small shrine at the edge of your domain. A god of a single hill, who has been alone for a century.
events.arc: The Priest's Large Family

choices.text: Grant it, and watch with interest

effects.log: {npc} tends the hill-shrine with an obsessive devotion. The hill-god, astonished, begins to bloom.

choices.text: Make {him} the keeper of your own shrine instead

effects.log: {npc} accepts, eyes shining. {He} keeps the books, the bells, and the peace for sixty years.

events.text: {npc} never does become a god. {He} becomes a legend among the priests: the one who wrote a plan that was too long to be answered. The plan, framed, hangs in the archive hall.
events.arc: The Priest's Large Family

choices.text: Send a short reply, in the plan's own margin

effects.log: It says: noted. The priests read it as a blessing. It may be one.

choices.text: Add a quiet blessing to the framed plan

effects.log: The plan acquires, on dark nights, a faint warmth. Visitors say it feels like being listened to.

events.text: A pilgrim in a worn coat has been at your shrine for a week, praying with great energy and no skill. {npc} gets every gesture wrong, bows to the wrong side, and recites a hymn from an old, discontinued liturgy. You recognise the handwriting.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Was a God

choices.text: Greet {him} by name

effects.log: {npc} flinches, and drops the act. {He} is a god of another domain, tired and ashamed. {He} says: I wanted to know what it was like.

choices.text: Let the act stand, and play along

effects.log: You deliver a sermon on humility to the visiting god, with a straight face. {npc} nods like a model student.

choices.text: Pour tea and say nothing

effects.log: The pilgrim drinks the tea and says nothing. It is the most honest conversation of the week.

events.text: {npc} confesses that {he} is tired of being worshipped, and wants to know whether the quiet life of a pilgrim is any good. {He} has had a week of sore feet and cold soup, and loves it.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Was a God

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: it is a lovely thing, and not a way to live

effects.log: {npc} nods. {He} says: I know. But I would like to do it once a decade.

choices.text: Teach {him} the proper bows

effects.log: You teach {him} the proper bows, and {he} practises them in the courtyard with a monkish seriousness.

choices.text: Share a bowl of cold soup

effects.log: It is terrible. You both finish it.

events.text: Years on, the visiting god sends a gift: a pilgrim's staff of a fine, unknown wood. A note says: I take it up once a decade. I thought you might like to borrow it.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Was a God

choices.text: Take the staff on a walk of your own

effects.log: You walk the length of your own domain with the staff, unrecognised, and eat cold soup in a plain tavern. It is wonderful.

choices.text: Hang the staff in the hall as a memento

effects.log: It becomes the hall's most beloved decoration. Pilgrims ask where it came from and are told: from a friend.

events.text: Years on, you meet the visiting god at a council. They pretend not to know you, as agreed. Under the table, a foot taps yours, twice. It is the signal for a pilgrim's blessing.
events.arc: The Pilgrim Who Was a God

choices.text: Tap back, three times

effects.log: It is the answer: all is well. The council goes on, grave and dull. The two of you share a secret.

choices.text: Raise a glass, silently, across the table

effects.log: The visiting god raises a glass and hides a smile. Nobody else sees.

events.text: {npc} comes to your shrine at night, in tears, and confesses something small and terrible: {he} broke a promise to a dying friend. {He} does not ask for forgiveness. {He} asks whether it is possible.
events.arc: The Worshipper Who Needs Forgiving

choices.text: Say that forgiveness is not the god's to give here

effects.log: {npc} nods, wiping {his} face. {He} says: then to whom? You tell {him} the friend would have known.

choices.text: Forgive {him}, plainly, as a god

effects.log: {npc} breathes, and sits down. It is not what {he} needed, but it is something.

choices.text: Sit with {him} until dawn

effects.log: The night is long. Neither of you speaks. At dawn {he} says thank you, and you say nothing, and it is the same thing.

events.text: {npc} spends a year trying to keep the broken promise in other ways: tending the friend's garden, caring for the friend's old dog. It is not the promise. It is what a person can do.
events.arc: The Worshipper Who Needs Forgiving

choices.text: Send a dream of the friend, smiling, in the garden

effects.log: {npc} wakes and does not weep. The garden is already in bloom.

choices.text: Bless the dog with a long life

effects.log: The dog lives another twelve years and sits on {npc}'s feet each evening. It is the best blessing {he} ever receives.

choices.text: Let {him} work it out

effects.log: The garden flourishes. The dog gets fat. {npc} says, once, softly: I think it is enough.

events.text: {npc} comes to the shrine on the anniversary and lights a candle for the friend. {He} says, simply: I think the promise was never what I thought. It was the keeping of company. You nod.
events.arc: The Worshipper Who Needs Forgiving

choices.text: Light a candle beside it

effects.log: The two candles burn together until morning. The shrine-keeper, finding them, extinguishes neither.

choices.text: Say that it is the oldest promise there is

effects.log: {npc} smiles, a real one. {He} leaves the shrine lighter than {he} came.

events.text: {npc} never quite forgives {him}self, but learns to live in the company of the broken promise, as one lives with a limp. {He} tells the story, years on, to a young worshipper in the same trouble.
events.arc: The Worshipper Who Needs Forgiving

choices.text: Appear to the young worshipper too, in a dream

effects.log: The young worshipper wakes calmer. {npc} would not know why. It is the sort of kindness that is its own proof.

choices.text: Leave the telling to {npc}

effects.log: The telling is clumsy and perfect. The young worshipper cries, and thanks {npc}, and a chain is begun.

events.text: A very old mortal sits on your shrine step every afternoon with a board of black and white stones and plays against no one. {npc} says that the opponent is always late. You sit down across the board.
events.arc: The Game on the Shrine Step

choices.text: Play white, and play badly

effects.log: {npc} wins in forty moves, politely. {He} says it is the best loss {he} has ever had to watch.

choices.text: Play well, and see what happens

effects.log: The game runs for a week. {npc} sits perfectly still, and moves like a landslide. It is a draw.

choices.text: Just watch the stones

effects.log: You watch the stones for an hour. The patterns are lovely. {npc} does not look up.

events.text: {npc} begins to treat you as the regular afternoon opponent. {He} talks of nothing: tea, a bad knee, a dream about a pony. The games are slow and the talk is slower. It is the best hour of your day.
events.arc: The Game on the Shrine Step

choices.text: Bring tea to the afternoon

effects.log: You bring tea in a plain jar. {npc} accepts it without remark. The tea is better than usual.

choices.text: Tell {him} a secret over the board

effects.log: {npc} nods. {He} says: I knew. It is nice of you to say so. The next move is a good one.

choices.text: Say nothing, and play

effects.log: The silence is companionable. The stones click. It is a kind of prayer.

events.text: One afternoon {npc} does not come. The board is on the step, set mid-game, with a white stone beside it. A note: your move.
events.arc: The Game on the Shrine Step

choices.text: Make the move, and leave the stone

effects.log: You move. In the morning, a black stone has answered. The game goes on, with a ghost, for years.

choices.text: Finish the game for {him}, with both colours

effects.log: You play both sides to a draw. It takes a month. At the end, you leave the stones in a pattern, and the shrine-keeper does not touch it.

events.text: {npc} grows old, and the games get shorter. At the last one, {he} resigns early, and says: I am tired of winning against someone who lets me.
events.arc: The Game on the Shrine Step

choices.text: Admit it, with an apology

effects.log: {npc} laughs for a quarter hour, and then says: let me win properly next time. The next game is the finest of your life.

choices.text: Say you did not, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} looks at you. {He} says: then I am better than I thought. {He} leaves quite pleased.

events.text: A new apprentice has been put in charge of the festival lights and has set off all the fireworks at once. The sky is a single white flash. The shrine-beasts are hiding under the altar. A rain of sparks falls on a vegetable stall.

choices.text: Catch the sparks in a cloud and rain them softly

effects.log: The sparks fall as warm glitter. The crowd gasps and claps, taking it for the finale.

choices.text: Let the apprentice take the blame, and send a blessing

effects.log: The apprentice is mortified and forgiven. The vegetable stall sells out.

events.text: The procession carrying your statue has stopped at a crossroads. The two bearers disagree about the route. The statue, sitting on its palanquin, is quietly annoyed. The crowd is looking at you.

choices.text: Nudge the palanquin toward the right road

effects.log: The bearers feel the weight shift, and take it as a sign. The procession proceeds, and the argument is settled by a statue.

choices.text: Let them argue; it is a festival

effects.log: They argue for an hour and take the third road. It is the best route.

events.text: The festival feast has run out of food forty minutes early. The stewards are panicking. A hush has fallen over the great tables. A wise old cook announces that gods have always provided.

choices.text: Provide, modestly, from the larder

effects.log: The stewards find more food in the back, unexpectedly. The cook says: I told you so.

choices.text: Tell them to share what is left

effects.log: The feast turns into a picnic of shared plates. The best festival in years.

events.text: Two drum guilds have come to blows over who plays first at your festival. The drums are in the square. The guild-masters are nose to nose. A very small child is banging a pot.

choices.text: Let the child play first

effects.log: The child plays. The crowd falls silent, then laughs. The guilds shake hands over the pot.

choices.text: Send a clap of thunder to settle the order

effects.log: The thunder claims first place. The guilds are awed and slightly insulted.

events.text: A thief has stolen a small idol of you from the market and left a note: sorry, I need the money. The idol is hardly worth a coin. The thief is clearly desperate.

choices.text: Let the thief keep it, and send a good meal

effects.log: A meal appears at the thief's door. The idol is returned, in a week, with a bunch of flowers.

choices.text: Find the thief and ask what else is needed

effects.log: The thief is a young person with a sick parent. You send a healer in a dream.

events.text: A pilgrim at the market haggles for a lower price on candles to light at your shrine. The stallholder haggles back. You listen to the exchange for an hour. It is an art.

choices.text: Pay the difference, in a quiet way

effects.log: A coin appears on the stallholder's counter. Both are satisfied. The pilgrim leaves with a candle and a grin.

choices.text: Let the haggling go on

effects.log: It ends in a tie and a handshake. The candle is lit with extra ceremony.

events.text: The priest has fallen asleep in the middle of the evening prayer, on the altar steps. The congregation is too polite to wake {npc}. A worshipper begins, hesitantly, to continue the prayer, and does it well.

choices.text: Bless the stand-in prayer

effects.log: The stand-in prayer is beautiful. The priest wakes at the end and says amen, with great confidence.

choices.text: Send the priest a pleasant dream and let {him} sleep

effects.log: The priest smiles in sleep. The congregation tiptoes out.

events.text: The choir has begun a hymn at the wrong tempo, and cannot get back. It has become a dirge. The priest is making a slashing gesture. A small child is humming the correct tune from the back row.

choices.text: Hum the correct tune, for the choir to follow

effects.log: The choir finds the tempo. The child grins, and the hymn ends beautifully.

choices.text: Let the dirge run; it has a certain gravity

effects.log: The dirge is the most-remembered hymn of the year. It is requested again.

events.text: Half a valley dreams on the same night of a flock of sheep with your face. It is a mild, fluffy nightmare and a certain comic hit. The morning after, everyone is whistling.

choices.text: Look into it, with some concern

effects.log: It is a stray dream from the Silent Hall, mislaid. Mongsa sends an apology and a basket of figs.

choices.text: Enjoy it, quietly

effects.log: The sheep with your face are the talk of the market. A sheep-seller does very well.

events.text: A worshipper coughs through the whole of their prayer and apologises at the end. You have sat through it feeling oddly invested. You find you hope the cough clears.

choices.text: Send a warm wind, and a spoon of honey

effects.log: The cough eases the same week. The worshipper credits the honey.

choices.text: Pray, in return, for the worshipper

effects.log: A god's prayer is an odd thing. It goes up and finds itself, with a small bow.

events.text: An inn has been built on the road to your shrine and named The Pilgrim's Rest. Its owner has painted your likeness on the sign. It looks like a duck. The beer is excellent.

choices.text: Stay for a night in a plain coat

effects.log: The inn is warm and the bed is soft. The duck looks down from the sign and approves.

choices.text: Bless the cellar

effects.log: The beer is better yet. The owner credits the water.

events.text: Your statue in the main hall has a crack in it, running from the nose to the chin. The priests argue about whether to repair it. Some say it adds character. Some say it adds a scandalous expression.

choices.text: Seal the crack, quietly, in the night

effects.log: The statue is whole by morning. The priests are baffled and a little disappointed.

choices.text: Leave it as it is

effects.log: The crack becomes known as the Smile. Pilgrims touch it for luck.

events.text: Someone prays to you at midnight every night, in a whisper, in the rain, under a hedge. It is not a prayer for anything. It is a list of the day's small events. It is, you realise, a diary.

choices.text: Listen to the diary, nightly

effects.log: It is the kindest thing you do all year. You learn the names of everyone in the hedge-dweller's life.

choices.text: Reply with a single, small sign each week

effects.log: A leaf lands on the hedge-dweller's shoulder. It is a modest reply, and it is received.

events.text: A child has made a flower crown for your statue, and cannot reach. They are standing on tiptoe on an overturned bucket, wobbling. The statue is twice as tall.

choices.text: Lower the statue's head, gently, by a hand's breadth

effects.log: The crown is placed. The child shouts. The priest has seen nothing, and will say so.

choices.text: Keep the bucket steady

effects.log: A wind holds the bucket still. The crown is placed. The child never knows.

events.text: Snow has covered the shrine steps and nobody has come to sweep them. The keeper is ill. A small crowd of pilgrims stands at the foot of the stairs, looking up at your door with patient hope.

choices.text: Melt the snow with a warm breath

effects.log: The steps are clear in a moment. The pilgrims climb, thank the keeper they have not seen, and light candles.

choices.text: Send the keeper a dream of broth

effects.log: The keeper wakes with a hunger. Someone leaves a pot of soup by the bed.

events.text: The shrine bell has begun to whisper before it rings. It says: soon. It says it very softly. The shrine-keeper has stopped sleeping in the hall. The bell, you note, is not wrong.

choices.text: Ring the bell yourself, once

effects.log: The bell rings, and the whisper stops. The keeper returns to bed.

choices.text: Listen to the whisper

effects.log: It says soon, and then, after a long pause, thank you. You are not sure which of you it was meant for.

events.text: A worshipper prays to you to be reminded of a dream they cannot recall. It was warm, they say. There was a river. They woke up crying and happy and do not know why.

choices.text: Return the dream, softly

effects.log: The worshipper wakes smiling, and is silent all day. By evening they have written a poem.

choices.text: Leave it forgotten; send a warm morning

effects.log: A warm sun on the sill. The worshipper does not need to know.

events.text: The festival costume of your festival-giant has been borrowed by a rival valley and returned with a stain and a sheepish note. The giant is made of cloth, wire, and the tireless pride of three hamlets.

choices.text: Let it be; a stain is a story

effects.log: The stain becomes part of the costume. It is explained to children, for centuries, as a divine hiccup.

choices.text: Clean it in the night with a breath of mist

effects.log: The costume is spotless. The valley thanks the rival valley for their care, ironically.

events.text: A trader is selling a second-hand portable shrine of you, with a handwritten certificate. The certificate is spelled badly. The shrine is dented. The trader is honest about both.

choices.text: Buy it, as a gesture

effects.log: It sits on your shelf. The dent has character. The certificate is framed.

choices.text: Bless the shrine in the market, unseen

effects.log: It sells that afternoon, to a family who hang it by the stove. It is warm for years.

events.text: The shrine-keeper falls asleep standing up. Not a lapse; a way of life. {He} sweeps in {his} sleep. The floors are cleaner than they have ever been. {He} wakes to find the hall spotless and is baffled.

choices.text: Take the broom for a night, as a favour

effects.log: The keeper wakes rested, and decides {he} is a marvel. You do not correct this.

choices.text: Let {him} sleep-sweep

effects.log: The shrine floor shines. The keeper is quietly proud, and suspects a miracle.

events.text: A stack of petitions from the lower courts has arrived on your desk. The top one reads: Re: the Matter of the Goat, continued. You remember none of it. A note on the second: urgent. The third: please ignore the second.

choices.text: Read them all, in order

effects.log: The Matter of the Goat resolves itself on page nine. You sign the last petition with a flourish.

choices.text: Delegate the stack to the shrine-keeper

effects.log: The keeper answers each, tidily. The goat is returned, and the court is silenced.

events.text: A cousin of yours, a god of a smaller domain, drops by unannounced and stays for dinner. They talk non-stop of their troubles. You listen to forty minutes of drainage problems before you realise you are enjoying yourself.

choices.text: Offer practical advice on drainage

effects.log: Your advice is sound, to your mild astonishment. The cousin leaves with a plan and a basket of eggs.

choices.text: Just listen

effects.log: The cousin leaves lighter, and you have a slightly clearer head. It is what cousins are for.

events.text: A child arrives at your shrine with a riddle, and will not leave until a god answers it. It is: what is heavier, a cloud or a lie? The child does not wait for your answer. {npc} has already decided.

choices.text: Say a cloud, because it is honest about its weight

effects.log: The child nods, solemn. {He} says: I thought so. {He} leaves with a bag of sweets.

choices.text: Say a lie, because it needs carrying

effects.log: The child is silent for a long moment, then says: that is a very sad answer. It is also correct.

events.text: A snail has made its way across the entire shrine courtyard over the course of three years, and has just reached the altar. The priest stops the service. The congregation waits in respectful silence.

choices.text: Bless the snail with a long and quiet life

effects.log: The snail lives another decade, on the altar, and is known as the Pilgrim of the Lintel.

choices.text: Lift the snail to the offering plate

effects.log: The snail is delighted, or perhaps bewildered. The congregation applauds.

events.text: Once a year every sheaf in your domain is brought to the great scales and weighed against a sheaf of the first harvest. {npc}, the scale-keeper, has done it for a thousand years. This year a mortal farmer has brought a sheaf so light it will not sink the pan, and stands there with a fierce face.
events.arc: Weighing Day in the Golden Field

choices.text: Weigh it anyway, and say the number aloud

effects.log: The pan barely stirs. The farmer nods: that is what the year gave. The crowd, to its credit, is quiet.

choices.text: Add a quiet grain of luck to the pan

effects.log: The pan dips. The farmer does not know. {npc} knows, and says nothing, and looks at you a long moment.

choices.text: Ask the farmer to tell the story of the sheaf

effects.log: The farmer tells it: a hailstorm, a lost child, a field half-sown. The crowd claps. The scale stays honest.

events.text: A merchant-god of the market quarter offers to buy the lightest sheaves in the domain and sell them as a delicacy, under the name of Golden Whisper. The farmers are flattered, and a little hungry. {npc} frowns at the contract.
events.arc: Weighing Day in the Golden Field

choices.text: Allow it, with a fair share to the farmers

effects.log: The farmers see coin for the first time in a bad year. The scale-keeper adds a column for it.

choices.text: Forbid it; the light sheaves are fed to the poor

effects.log: The merchant-god is offended and tells everyone. The poor eat well that winter and remember you.

events.text: The scale cracks in the hundredth year of {npc}'s service. The great pan splits clean in two and the sheaves of the whole domain tip to the ground. {He} stands there with the pieces in {his} hands, and says very quietly that it was always going to.
events.arc: Weighing Day in the Golden Field

choices.text: Commission a new scale from the mountain-smiths

effects.log: The new scale takes a year. It is cold and exact and a little cruel, and {npc} learns to love it.

choices.text: Weigh the next harvest by hand, in the old way

effects.log: The farmers weigh each other's sheaves in their own arms. It takes three days and is the loudest, kindest weighing in memory.

events.text: Each year since, a small child carries the first sheaf to your shrine on weighing day, and it is never heavy, and never light. {npc} says that this is the thing the scale was for.
events.arc: Weighing Day in the Golden Field

choices.text: Receive the sheaf in your own arms

effects.log: It weighs exactly what a sheaf weighs. You are surprised by how much that matters.

choices.text: Bless the child, not the sheaf

effects.log: The child goes home hungry and proud and cannot say why.

events.text: The mountains hold a council every century, and a council of mountains is slow: the first speaker has not finished their opening sentence in forty years. {npc}, the council's clerk, is a quick little spirit with a pen, and is losing hope of ever writing anything.
events.arc: The Slow Council of the Mountains

choices.text: Sit in the council for a decade, and listen

effects.log: A decade passes. You learn that a long sentence is, if you listen, a very short story told patiently.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to summarise and read it to the mountains

effects.log: The summary takes the mountains a generation to absorb. They approve, in principle.

choices.text: Send a brisk wind through the council hall

effects.log: The council pauses. Several mountains register a mild complaint. It takes them six years.

events.text: The council has reached its first decision in a century: a ridge should move two hand-widths east. The ridge has agreed. Mortals in the valley below will find their well a little dry in thirty years, and will be baffled.
events.arc: The Slow Council of the Mountains

choices.text: Ask the council to move the ridge back

effects.log: The council deliberates for sixty years and says no. But the clerk sends a note: they appreciated being asked.

choices.text: Prepare the valley with a new well, long in advance

effects.log: You dig a deep well that will outlast the valley's children. The mountain does not notice; the valley does, in time.

events.text: The oldest mountain speaks at last, a few words: a question, in a voice like sliding scree. It asks what the little ones are doing in the valley, running about in such a hurry. {npc} writes it down, stunned.
events.arc: The Slow Council of the Mountains

choices.text: Answer the mountain with a day-long description

effects.log: You talk till dusk. The mountain says nothing until a century later, when it sends a single boulder to the valley with a flower growing on it.

choices.text: Say they are living, and leave it at that

effects.log: The mountain considers this for twenty years. Then: yes. That is the whole reply, and it is exactly enough.

events.text: The drill field of your domain is where the dead of old wars are said to march, and the living are not usually invited. {npc}, an old drill-sergeant spirit with one boot, reports that the line is short of a member and asks you to fall in for the evening.
events.arc: The Drill Field of Old Soldiers

choices.text: Fall in at the end of the line

effects.log: You march until dark, shoulder to shoulder with ghosts. No one speaks. You feel the rhythm settle into you like a second heart.

choices.text: Watch from the fence and count the steps

effects.log: You count three hundred. The line is perfectly in time. The sergeant salutes the fence.

choices.text: Decline, with thanks and a flask of tea

effects.log: The ghosts have tea at the break. They cannot drink it. They hold the cups, and that is enough.

events.text: A mortal soldier has wandered onto the field in the dark, lost, and joined the line without noticing. The ghosts do not mind. {npc} asks whether to wake the soldier or let the night run, as the line has not had a new recruit in an age.
events.arc: The Drill Field of Old Soldiers

choices.text: Wake the soldier gently and walk them home

effects.log: You lead them out by the elbow. They remember nothing but a rhythm and wake humming it for years.

choices.text: Let the soldier march till dawn

effects.log: At dawn they stir, and stand blinking, with the ghosts dissolving in the light. They salute the empty field.

events.text: The old sergeant asks, very formally, for a discharge. {He} has marched on the drill field for nine hundred years, and the last war {he} fought in has been forgotten by every living mouth. {He} would like to go home, wherever that is.
events.arc: The Drill Field of Old Soldiers

choices.text: Grant the discharge, with full honours

effects.log: The ghosts form two lines. The sergeant walks between them, with one boot, and does not look back. The field is a little quieter after.

choices.text: Ask the sergeant to stay and train the young ghosts

effects.log: The sergeant stays, gruffly pleased. The line has never marched better.

events.text: Once a year every cloud in the Sky must be counted, and each is a person in a small way. {npc}, the cloud-census taker, arrives with a ladder and a very long list. This year there is one cloud too many, and none of the others will own up to it.
events.arc: The Census of Clouds

choices.text: Find the extra cloud yourself

effects.log: It is a small grey cloud, sitting in a corner of the sky, alone, shy. It says it was a fog once, and does not know how it got up here.

choices.text: Ask the clouds to count themselves

effects.log: They count themselves off with a rumble. The extra cloud is the only one that falls silent.

choices.text: Leave the count as it is, uneven

effects.log: The census-taker records one too many. A footnote is added: unexplained, and welcomed.

events.text: The little fog-cloud has been given a place in the census and a name, Wisp, and wants to be useful. It offers to carry messages. The only trouble is that it rains whenever it is nervous, which is always.
events.arc: The Census of Clouds

choices.text: Give it the shrine-to-shrine postal route

effects.log: Wisp delivers the post for a year. Every letter arrives damp, and the recipients forgive it.

choices.text: Teach it to be still before it speaks

effects.log: Wisp learns, slowly. It stops raining on cue and begins to appear only when it is needed.

events.text: In the autumn, the census-taker comes back with news from the ladder's top: Wisp has been seen over the mountains, huge, a proper storm-cloud now, trailing the first lightning of the year. The other clouds are astonished.
events.arc: The Census of Clouds

choices.text: Congratulate Wisp with a rainbow

effects.log: The rainbow holds for an hour. A few mortals below weep without knowing why.

choices.text: Let the cloud have its moment, in silence

effects.log: You say nothing. The thunder is its own thanks.

events.text: Every dusk the lamplighters of the Hearth Road walk the long highway of your domain and light a lamp at each milestone. {npc}, the senior lamplighter, is slow now and says the road has grown longer in the night, a joke {he} tells every dusk.
events.arc: The Lamplighters of the Hearth Road

choices.text: Walk a stretch of the road with the lamplighters

effects.log: You walk four miles with a taper, lighting lamps behind a silent crowd. At the end, your shoulders ache pleasantly.

choices.text: Light every lamp from a distance, in a single stroke

effects.log: A line of fire runs down the road. The lamplighters stand under it in the dusk, a little bereft.

choices.text: Hire two more lamplighters from the shrines

effects.log: Two apprentices arrive. They get the dusk wrong twice, then right.

events.text: A single lamp on the road goes out every night at the same milestone, however carefully it is lit. {npc} has relit it eleven thousand times. Tonight the old lamplighter sits down beside it and says {he} is done relighting.
events.arc: The Lamplighters of the Hearth Road

choices.text: Sit with the lamp and find out why

effects.log: A draught from a crack in the old stone, an unnoticed little breath. You seal it, and the lamp burns all night.

choices.text: Let it go dark and mark the stone

effects.log: You carve a small mark in the stone: a lamp that is allowed to go out. Travellers pause there, and some pray.

events.text: The Hearth Road is lit end to end for the festival of the first fire, and a pilgrim in a grey coat walks all of it, from the first lamp to the last, with a tin cup. At the end the pilgrim blows out one candle in the cup and nods.
events.arc: The Lamplighters of the Hearth Road

choices.text: Join the pilgrim at the last lamp

effects.log: You sit with them as the final lamp burns. They say nothing. It is the best festival of the year.

choices.text: Let them go unremarked

effects.log: They walk on into the dark with the cup. The road, behind them, glows a little brighter.

events.text: Every birth in your domain has a small midwife-god in attendance, invisible, to give the first breath its push. {npc}, the chief of them, is hoarse. A hard season has brought forty births in a night, and the midwife-gods are short of breath themselves.
events.arc: The Midwife-Gods of the First Cry

choices.text: Join the night shift, at the bedsides

effects.log: You attend nine births in a night, unseen. By dawn you are exhausted and cannot stop smiling.

choices.text: Send breath from the domain's winds to the midwives

effects.log: A gentle wind runs through the bedrooms of the domain. The midwives straighten and go on.

choices.text: Praise them in a dream and let them rest

effects.log: They sleep for the whole next day. The births continue, as they will.

events.text: A child is born who does not cry. The midwife-god tries every trick of the trade. The room is still. {npc} looks at you across the bed, stricken, and mouths a word that is not in any rule: please.
events.arc: The Midwife-Gods of the First Cry

choices.text: Breathe the first breath into the child yourself

effects.log: The child coughs, gasps, and wails. Mother and midwife-god weep together. It will cost you something, and you cannot yet tell what.

choices.text: Call the nearest healer-god, quickly

effects.log: A healer-god arrives in a heartbeat and does the thing. The child cries. You stand in the corner and are grateful.

events.text: Years later the child from the quiet room comes to your shrine, grown, with a basket of bread, and says they have been told a god gave them breath. They do not ask for anything. They just wanted, they say, to see the one who did it.
events.arc: The Midwife-Gods of the First Cry

choices.text: Show yourself and sit down to bread

effects.log: You eat bread together. They tell you they have become a midwife. It is the best news you have had in a century.

choices.text: Accept the basket and stay unseen

effects.log: You let them leave the basket and go. You eat the bread alone, and it is a good deal better than ambrosia.

events.text: The Throne of Storms hunts once a generation, and the quarry is a white whale that crosses the whole sea and back and has never been caught. {npc}, the hunt's herald, asks if you will take the stern oar of the lead boat. It is an honour, and a dangerous one.
events.arc: The Storm Throne's Hunt of the White Whale

choices.text: Take the stern oar

effects.log: You steer the lead boat through a storm of your own making. The whale shows once in the spray and is gone. The crew cheers you hoarse.

choices.text: Ask to sail as a hand, not a leader

effects.log: You haul line with the crew, wet to the bone. A grizzled sailor-god hands you a flask without a word.

choices.text: Decline and wave them off from the shore

effects.log: The fleet sails. You stand on the quay till the last sail is gone, a little wistful.

events.text: On the ninth night the whale surfaces beside the lead boat, vast and pale, and looks at the crew. It does not flee. It is old, and tired, and seems to be waiting to be asked something. The harpooner stands frozen.
events.arc: The Storm Throne's Hunt of the White Whale

choices.text: Lower the harpoon and bow to the whale

effects.log: The crew bows. The whale sinks beside the boat, slowly, giving each of them an eye, one at a time.

choices.text: Ask the whale where it is going

effects.log: It tells you in a song you cannot follow, but all of you weep at the end. It dives and is gone.

events.text: The Throne of Storms is furious with the hunt for failing, and then quiet, and then, to everyone's surprise, a little relieved. The white whale becomes a sacred sight, not a quarry. {npc} writes a new rite for the hunt: they now sail to see it, and sail home.
events.arc: The Storm Throne's Hunt of the White Whale

choices.text: Join the new rite each generation

effects.log: You sail again a generation later. The whale is waiting in the same spot, and you sit on the deck and say hello.

choices.text: Let the hunt's new rite be the herald's own

effects.log: You send a bottle of wine to the herald, who weeps on opening it.

events.text: The Will of Heaven flies falcons, great golden birds trained to hunt the shadows of clouds. {npc}, the falconer, comes to you with a hooded bird on a thick glove and a request: the bird will fly for no one but a god in their first year of service. It is your year.
events.arc: The Falcon Hunt of the Will of Heaven

choices.text: Take the glove and release the falcon

effects.log: It rises into the noon with a cry. It does not come back until sunset, and when it does it brings you a cloud-shadow in its talons, folded like a handkerchief.

choices.text: Take the glove, but hold the bird a little longer

effects.log: You hold the falcon quiet. The falconer nods: it is the right instinct. The bird flies at dusk instead, and does better.

choices.text: Hand the glove back

effects.log: The falconer shrugs, takes it, and the bird goes unflown that year.

events.text: The falcon has taken a shadow that was not a cloud's. In its claws, wrapped like a scarf, is the shadow of a god who died long ago. The falconer says, quietly, that it happens once a century.
events.arc: The Falcon Hunt of the Will of Heaven

choices.text: Return the shadow to the grave of the dead god

effects.log: You carry it across the hills to a barrow of dry grass. The shadow settles into the earth like a sigh.

choices.text: Keep the shadow at your shrine for a night

effects.log: It spreads across the floor of the shrine, a long soft tall shape. At dawn it is gone, and the stone is warm.

events.text: The falcon never comes down to anyone else's glove again. It perches on your shrine roof, hooded or not, and watches the sky. {npc} says it will be the only bird of its kind to refuse a master and keep a friend.
events.arc: The Falcon Hunt of the Will of Heaven

choices.text: Give the falcon a name

effects.log: You name it Noon. The falconer rolls their eyes, and adds the name to the book.

choices.text: Let it be a bird without a name

effects.log: It goes on being a bird. You feel, absurdly, honoured.

events.text: A dream has escaped the Silent Hall: a plump, glowing, ill-mannered dream about a lost beach, which has taken up residence in a sleeping mortal's head and will not leave. {npc}, from the Hall's office of strays, asks you to help catch it before the mortal begins to like it.
events.arc: The Hunt for a Dream That Got Loose

choices.text: Enter the mortal's sleep and chase the dream down

effects.log: You run along a long beach of gold sand. The dream is quick, and laughs. The mortal sleeps on, smiling.

choices.text: Set a trap of warm milk and a lullaby

effects.log: The dream wanders to the cup, curious. It is a very easy dream to catch, as it turns out, if you offer it hospitality.

choices.text: Tell the office the dream is not worth the trouble

effects.log: The office writes it down as a stray and moves on. The mortal keeps the beach.

events.text: The dream pleads: it does not want to go back to the Hall. It says the shelves are cold, and that it has been delivered to a thousand sleepers who all woke up and forgot it. The mortal, it says, remembered.
events.arc: The Hunt for a Dream That Got Loose

choices.text: Let it stay for a season, then return

effects.log: It stays. The mortal keeps a diary of the beach. In spring the dream goes home, still glowing.

choices.text: Take it back and arrange a better shelf

effects.log: You arrange a warm shelf by a window. The dream is content, and the office is faintly embarrassed.

events.text: The mortal wakes one morning in their old age and writes a poem about a beach they have never seen. It is read at their funeral. {npc} brings you a copy, without comment, and the dream sits on its shelf, softly bright.
events.arc: The Hunt for a Dream That Got Loose

choices.text: Place the poem on the dream's shelf

effects.log: The dream glows brighter than it ever has. It has something, at last, that remembers it.

choices.text: Read the poem aloud to the hall of dreams

effects.log: The hall is quiet. The dreamers weep, in the way dreams do.

events.text: A school of the old gods was walled off with its pupils inside, in a war whose cause is forgotten. {npc}, a retired warden, tells you the bell of the school has begun ringing again, faintly, from behind the seal, for morning class.
events.arc: The School That Was Sealed With Its Pupils

choices.text: Go to the seal and listen at the wall

effects.log: You hear the shuffle of feet, the clatter of slates, and a thin young voice reciting the old creed. They think no time has passed.

choices.text: Knock and say good morning

effects.log: The recital pauses. A clear voice asks if you are the new master. You say yes, and are alarmed to find you mean it.

choices.text: Report to the sealing-office and wait

effects.log: The office takes a season. The bell rings in the meantime.

events.text: The pupils behind the seal are young gods and lesser spirits, and they are well. They have taught themselves, and each other. They ask only two things: news of the war, and whether they may be given a master who is not a ghost.
events.arc: The School That Was Sealed With Its Pupils

choices.text: Tell them the war is long over, and offer to teach

effects.log: You teach through the crack for a season. The class is the keenest you have ever had.

choices.text: Tell them the war is over and ask the seal to open

effects.log: The sealing-office, shamed, agrees. The seal comes down in a long soft sigh.

events.text: The pupils walk out of their school into a world that has changed beyond naming. They blink in the light. A pupil of nine hundred years reaches for your hand, as for a rail, and does not let go until she is sure of the ground.
events.arc: The School That Was Sealed With Its Pupils

choices.text: Take them all in as your own students

effects.log: Your hall fills with pupils. The noise is joyous and awful. You have never been so tired.

choices.text: Find each of them a place among the pantheons

effects.log: It takes a decade. By the end, every pupil sits at some table, and many send you letters.

events.text: The school's bell still rings, from behind a seal that was never lifted, for morning class. {npc} goes there each morning with a bag of chalk and a stool, and says it is the best work of {his} retirement.
events.arc: The School That Was Sealed With Its Pupils

choices.text: Send chalk, slates, and a new bell-rope

effects.log: The supplies are slid through the crack. The class thanks you in unison. The bell rings, brighter.

choices.text: Visit on feast days only

effects.log: You visit on feast days and bring cake. The class fights over it and learns a lesson in sharing.

events.text: Behind the seal of one old heaven a market has been going for ten thousand years. {npc}, the fishmonger of the seal's mouth, trades through a slot with the outside world once a decade, and has a request: they need a replacement for a worn-out scale.
events.arc: The Market Inside the Seal

choices.text: Send a scale through the slot

effects.log: The scale slides in. A cheer goes up from within. Next decade, a jar of pickled lotus comes out.

choices.text: Ask what else the market lacks

effects.log: The list is long and surprising: salt, thread, and news. They would give anything for news.

choices.text: Wait and trade with them next decade

effects.log: You wait. When the slot opens again, you have a better offer.

events.text: You send news through the slot: a page a year for ten years, with the winners of the feasts, the new gods, the changes in the weather. The market reads it aloud in the square. Within a year it is their only newspaper.
events.arc: The Market Inside the Seal

choices.text: Include a column of gossip

effects.log: The gossip is the part they love best. The market pays you in an array of dried fruit and a hat.

choices.text: Keep it strictly to facts

effects.log: The market takes the facts seriously. A debate begins about whether it was true.

events.text: The market sends you a gift from inside: a woven cloth, a rich dark blue, that was made by a hundred hands over a hundred years. {npc} says it is the best thing the seal has ever produced. It is a map, but of no place you know.
events.arc: The Market Inside the Seal

choices.text: Study the map until you find the place

effects.log: It is the market itself, drawn from above, with a gap in the south wall. They are telling you where they could be reached.

choices.text: Hang it in your hall unstudied

effects.log: The cloth hangs for years and is admired. No one asks what it shows.

events.text: In a hollow of the world is a pool that has never moved: no ripple, no wind, no fish. It is the water from before the tides, and gods avoid it. {npc}, a wandering hermit, asks if you would stand at its edge with {him}, because {he} has never dared go alone.
events.arc: The Water That Has Never Moved

choices.text: Stand at the edge with the hermit

effects.log: You stand. The water holds your reflection perfectly, and for a long time neither of you speaks.

choices.text: Throw a small stone in

effects.log: The stone makes a ring, and the ring does not end. It spreads, and spreads, and the hermit gasps.

choices.text: Go home and think about it

effects.log: You go home. For a week you are very quiet, and your servants tiptoe.

events.text: The pool has begun, faintly, to move. A ring, no larger than a thumbnail, moves outward, and the hermit goes pale. {npc} says it is the first change since the cutting of the domains. Something wants out, or wants in.
events.arc: The Water That Has Never Moved

choices.text: Speak to the water, softly

effects.log: The ring stops. The water, you realise, has been waiting to be spoken to for an unimaginable time. It says nothing; it simply listens.

choices.text: Back away and let it settle

effects.log: You and the hermit retire. The ring crosses the pool slowly, and fades.

events.text: The hermit builds a hut at the pool's edge and sits there for thirty years. The water slowly learns to move, a ripple at a time, by echoing {npc}'s breathing. The tides of the oldest sea are said to have begun in much the same way.
events.arc: The Water That Has Never Moved

choices.text: Visit the hut every spring

effects.log: You bring {him} tea and listen to the pool breathe. It is the quietest friendship you have ever had.

choices.text: Send a small gift of salt

effects.log: The salt goes into the water. The water, for the first time, tastes of something.

events.text: A road of unknown age crosses the border of your domain, laid before the domains had borders. It leads from nowhere to nowhere. {npc}, a travelling tinker, says every god in history has walked it once, and that no god has yet reached the end.
events.arc: The Road Older Than the Domains

choices.text: Walk the road for a day

effects.log: You walk. The road is smooth and warm underfoot, and it is hard to tell whether you are going forward or being carried.

choices.text: Walk it with the tinker, talking

effects.log: The tinker's stories fill the miles. At evening you turn back together, tired and cheered.

choices.text: Mark its crossing with a stone

effects.log: The stone is quietly accepted by the road. A weed grows at its foot.

events.text: On the road you meet a traveller coming the other way, a stranger with a long stride, who nods and says the end is not very far, if you keep to the left. They look entirely ordinary. They cast no shadow.
events.arc: The Road Older Than the Domains

choices.text: Ask which left they mean

effects.log: The stranger smiles, says left of whatever you are carrying, and walks on. You carry nothing, and wonder.

choices.text: Wish them well and turn back

effects.log: You turn back with a light heart. Some roads are for those who finish them; some are for those who start.

events.text: The tinker mends a pot at the roadside and gives it to you as a gift: a plain iron pot, dented, that boils water at once. {npc} says it came from the road, and that anything made there will always find its way home.
events.arc: The Road Older Than the Domains

choices.text: Keep the pot on your hearth
