effects.log: It boils, and boils well. Guests remark on it, and so does the pot, in its way.

choices.text: Pass the pot on to a pilgrim in need

effects.log: The pilgrim weeps. The pot, you hear, found its way back to the road.

events.text: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field arrives at your door, in a dusty straw hat, and asks if there is any tea. The great god of the harvest is accompanied by {npc}, a young steward who looks as if {he} has been told to behave. You are not entirely sure how to treat a god who is also a field.
events.arc: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field Comes to Tea

choices.text: Serve tea in your best cups

effects.log: Pungnyeon drinks it carefully, and sets the cup down with a clink like a seedpod. Your tea garden, you notice, is blooming out of season.

choices.text: Serve tea in your plainest cups

effects.log: Pungnyeon grunts with pleasure. This is the sort of cup, the great god says, that a field has been dreaming of.

choices.text: Ask what the tea is meant to fix

effects.log: Pungnyeon looks, for a moment, much older. Nothing, says the great god. I just want to be somewhere I am not needed.

events.text: The steward writes to you a month after: the great god has taken to sitting in the margins of fields in your domain, in an old coat, unrecognised. The farmers are puzzled by a stranger who sits and grunts approvingly at their furrows.
events.arc: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field Comes to Tea

choices.text: Send the steward a map of your quietest fields

effects.log: The map is received. Pungnyeon takes it and sits in them all, one season at a time.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the great god be

effects.log: You say nothing. A quietly-cut hay bale appears on your step the next autumn.

events.text: When the great god leaves your domain, there is one field that has not been planted, and it is the best one. A single stalk grows in it, golden, taller than the gate. The steward says it is for you.
events.arc: Pungnyeon of the Golden Field Comes to Tea

choices.text: Cut it at harvest and share the grain

effects.log: The grain feeds a town for a winter. Nobody knows where it came from, and it is the best bread anyone has tasted.

choices.text: Leave it standing, and let the wind sing in it

effects.log: The stalk sings a low note all winter. In spring it is gone, and a seed sits in your palm.

events.text: Daeak of the Unmoving Peak does not travel. Today, a very small cart has arrived at your gate, pulled by four goats, with {npc} on the box and in the back a single boulder, wrapped in blankets. {He} says the great god would like to visit your hall, and that this is how.
events.arc: The Visitor Who Does Not Move

choices.text: Welcome the boulder and give it a place by the fire

effects.log: The boulder is set by the hearth. It says nothing for a week, and then, in a voice like a landslide, asks for more fire.

choices.text: Place it in the garden, in the sun

effects.log: The garden suits it. Birds nest in the blankets. The cart-driver naps beside it happily.

choices.text: Ask what the great god would like to see

effects.log: A pause of an afternoon. The answer: a lake, any lake, from above.

events.text: You carry the boulder to the top of a hill at dawn and set it by a lake. Daeak, in the boulder, gazes at the water for the whole day. At dusk, a single word: thank you. It echoes down the valley for a month.
events.arc: The Visitor Who Does Not Move

choices.text: Stay with the boulder, until it has seen enough

effects.log: You stay three days. At the end, the great god says the lake is very small and very good.

choices.text: Leave the boulder in peace and return at dusk

effects.log: You return at dusk. The great god says it was a long day, and quite enough.

events.text: The goats and cart return a year later with a polite small gift: a stone the size of a walnut, grey, plain, impossibly heavy. {npc} says it is a piece of the peak, and is yours to keep, if you can stand it.
events.arc: The Visitor Who Does Not Move

choices.text: Keep the stone in your pocket

effects.log: You carry it. It grows heavier by the day, and then lighter, and then you stop noticing it. Your steps become unhurried.

choices.text: Set it by your shrine door

effects.log: Pilgrims touch it and go quiet. It is the most popular object in your shrine.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper is sleeping in your guest room. No one invited the great god; {npc}, a worried dream-attendant, explains that Mongsa wandered in, lay down, and will wake in perhaps a month or a century. The attendant's job is to keep the dreams from leaking.
events.arc: Mongsa the Sleeper Naps in Your Hall

choices.text: Give the attendant the east wing and a stipend

effects.log: The attendant sets up in the east wing with a kettle. Your hall gets strange, gentle dreams all through the long nap.

choices.text: Learn to keep the dreams from leaking yourself

effects.log: It takes weeks to learn the trick. Your hall stays dreamless, and you never sleep as well again.

choices.text: Close the guest room door softly and carry on

effects.log: You carry on, on tiptoe, for a month. It is the quietest month of your reign.

events.text: In the second month the dreams leak anyway, one by one: a dream of a field of silver grass, a dream of a mother singing in another tongue, a dream of falling upward. Servants wake up weeping and refuse to say why, but ask for more.
events.arc: Mongsa the Sleeper Naps in Your Hall

choices.text: Gather the dreams in jars and keep them for the great god

effects.log: You keep a hundred jars on a shelf. When Mongsa wakes, the jars are untouched, and the god smiles.

choices.text: Let the servants dream and take notes

effects.log: The notes are strange and lovely, and by autumn you have a small book of them.

events.text: Mongsa wakes on a morning in spring and wanders to the kitchen, hair wild, asking for something sweet. The dream-attendant bursts into tears. The great god eats three buns, thanks you vaguely, and says it was the best sleep in four thousand years.
events.arc: Mongsa the Sleeper Naps in Your Hall

choices.text: Give the great god the jars of dreams

effects.log: Mongsa opens one, and goes still. Then, with great care, opens them all. It takes the day. At dusk the great god thanks you with a hug that smells of rain.

choices.text: Offer a room for the next nap

effects.log: Mongsa says yes. The room is kept ready ever after, with a bun on the sill.

events.text: Your neighbour in the next valley is a god of ferns, and is being unmade very gently: no one has prayed to them in a century, and they grow translucent at the edges. {npc}, their last follower, brings a bowl of fern-tea and asks you for ideas.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Is Being Forgotten

choices.text: Visit the fern-god and bring a few of your worshippers

effects.log: Your worshippers sit in the ferns and say a few polite prayers. The fern-god flickers, and takes a little colour.

choices.text: Write the fern-god into your own litany

effects.log: Your priests add a line. A hundred voices say the name in the dawn. The fern-god reappears, startled.

choices.text: Listen to the follower's account of the god

effects.log: The account is long and tender and full of small details. You carry it away to think.

events.text: The fern-god regains a modest outline but is stuck there. They are tired. They tell you in a dry whisper that they would rather be forgotten than kept alive by a charity. They would, they say, like to be remembered for something.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Is Being Forgotten

choices.text: Help them find something to be remembered for

effects.log: You ask the fern-god what they love. A tiny ravine, shaded and quiet. You help them make it a place to rest.

choices.text: Honour their wish and let them fade

effects.log: You sit with them. They fade over a season, quietly, calmly, with a nod. Their follower plants a fern.

events.text: Years later the ravine is full of travellers resting in the shade. The fern-god sits at the lip of it each dusk, not worshipped, but visited, and finds it a good deal better. {npc} has become the ravine's keeper, and cries when it rains.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Is Being Forgotten

choices.text: Visit at dusk and sit at the ravine's lip

effects.log: You and the fern-god share the silence. It is more than most gods get.

choices.text: Send fern-tea each autumn

effects.log: The tea is always returned with a leaf pressed in a letter.

events.text: A priest of a burned shrine, very old, arrives at your door on foot with an ash-stained bundle. {npc} says their god was burned out of the world long ago and they have prayed to the ashes ever since. They have come to ask whether any god will take the prayers.
events.arc: The Priest of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Take the prayers, and read them one by one

effects.log: The bundle holds eighty years of devotion. Reading them takes weeks. You feel more known than you have in an age.

choices.text: Take the priest in, and leave the prayers for later

effects.log: The priest eats and sleeps like someone who has been walking for decades. The bundle sits by the stove, warm.

choices.text: Say the prayers are not yours to take

effects.log: You say it with regret. The priest nods, and walks on, with a lighter step and a heavier bundle.

events.text: In the bundle is a single page in a different hand: a letter from the burned god to the priest, left on the night of the fire. It says only: do not carry me, carry yourself. The priest has never opened it, fearing the ash would crumble.
events.arc: The Priest of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Read it aloud to the priest

effects.log: The priest weeps like a child. After a long hour, the old shoulders drop. It is the lightest they have felt in eighty years.

choices.text: Seal the letter and keep it safe for them

effects.log: You keep it in a stone box. The priest visits yearly, and does not ask to open it.

events.text: The priest dies at your threshold on a quiet autumn night, hands folded, bundle empty. {npc} was ninety-one. At the funeral, a handful of ash from the old shrine is scattered in your garden, and by spring a new, unknown green shoot is growing there.
events.arc: The Priest of the Burned Shrine

choices.text: Tend the green shoot

effects.log: It grows into a tree with white bark. Its leaves smell of smoke, in the best way.

choices.text: Leave it wild

effects.log: The shoot becomes a thicket. Children play in it. Nobody asks why it smells of old prayers.

events.text: Your pantheon sends an envoy: {npc}, a smooth minor god, who asks nothing large. A word in the right ear. A seat kept at a banquet. A gift to a rival at the proper hour. Each favour is small. The list of favours is long.
events.arc: The Envoy Who Asks Small Favours

choices.text: Do the favours, all of them

effects.log: It takes a month. At the end the envoy hands you a receipt, signed by an elder, that says only: noted.

choices.text: Do the ones you can do cleanly

effects.log: You do two of five. The envoy marks the list with a small, careful hand.

choices.text: Decline, and offer a plain gift of your own

effects.log: The envoy is startled and takes the gift. Nothing is said, which is a message in itself.

events.text: A favour arrives that you cannot do cleanly: a quiet word to a rival god, designed to cost them a seat. The envoy says it is only a word, and nothing a god would remember. You would remember.
events.arc: The Envoy Who Asks Small Favours

choices.text: Say the word, as asked

effects.log: The rival loses the seat. Nobody traces it to you. You feel, afterwards, a little smaller.

choices.text: Warn the rival in a dream

effects.log: The rival keeps the seat and sends you a thank-you in the form of a very expensive flower. The envoy never asks you for anything again.

choices.text: Say you cannot, and give no reason

effects.log: The envoy bows and takes it up the chain. The pantheon notes it and, for now, goes quiet.

events.text: A decade later the envoy comes to your door again, diminished, in a plain coat. The pantheon has retired them. They ask for nothing, only a seat by the fire, and say they always liked your hall.
events.arc: The Envoy Who Asks Small Favours

choices.text: Give the envoy a room and a place at the table

effects.log: The envoy becomes a friend, which is a quiet and unexpected result. Their stories are good.

choices.text: Give them a meal and see them on their way

effects.log: They eat. They thank you. They go. You find you have done everything right and feel a little sad.

events.text: A god with no pantheon cannot borrow a shrine from anyone; they must build their own. {npc}, a carpenter who has just converted to your cause, comes to you with a plan of a small hall and a bucket of nails, and a promise: the hall will be built without a debt to any court.
events.arc: A Masterless God Builds a Shrine

choices.text: Build with the carpenter, on weekends

effects.log: You work with a hammer on a hillside. The hall is crooked, and holds. At the end of a season there is a roof.

choices.text: Fund the hall with a modest gift of your own

effects.log: You give a purse of faith from your store. The carpenter is moved to silence.

choices.text: Wish them well and draft a prayer for the lintel

effects.log: The prayer is carved over the door, in your own hand. The carpenter is quietly overcome.

events.text: A pantheon god arrives at the finished hall with a tape measure and an official air, to check that the building is not a nuisance to the neighbourhood. {npc} stands in front of the door with the nails still in {his} apron, and says nothing.
events.arc: A Masterless God Builds a Shrine

choices.text: Welcome the inspector with tea and let them look

effects.log: The inspector walks round twice, finds nothing wrong, and takes a second cup of tea. The matter is dropped.

choices.text: Quote the old law that lets any god raise a roof

effects.log: The law is real and obscure. The inspector takes it up the chain; nothing more is heard.

events.text: The first worshippers arrive at your hall a year later: five of them, a family from a distant valley, with a basket of bread. They kneel on the plank floor and say your name. Nobody has ever told them they should not.
events.arc: A Masterless God Builds a Shrine

choices.text: Receive them, and promise to keep the door open

effects.log: You promise. The family weeps. The hall is quiet and warm and has no pantheon behind it at all.

choices.text: Listen to their prayers and say nothing

effects.log: You listen to every word. When they leave, you sit in the empty hall a long time.

events.text: The god who held your domain before you left a drawer of notes on the desk: lists of petitioners, stray debts, a recipe for fish. {npc}, the old seat's steward, says that every holder of this seat leaves a drawer, and that the previous holder's was the thickest.
events.arc: The Seat You Were Handed

choices.text: Read every note, slowly

effects.log: It takes a month. The previous holder's voice comes through: patient, funny, a little lonely. You feel less alone in the seat.

choices.text: Read the first and last notes only

effects.log: The first is a welcome. The last is a farewell. In between, you decide, is for you to write.

choices.text: Put the drawer aside for later

effects.log: You close it. The steward gives you a look that says drawers do not wait.

events.text: In the drawer is a debt: the previous holder promised a mortal village below a spring that would never run dry, and never delivered. The mortals have been waiting two hundred years. {npc} lays the note in front of you and does not say anything.
events.arc: The Seat You Were Handed

choices.text: Honour the debt, and open the spring

effects.log: You open the spring. The mortals below weep, pray, and build a shrine. The previous holder, wherever they are, must be at peace.

choices.text: Ask the mortals what they now need instead

effects.log: They need a road. You build it. The promise is honoured in a different form.

events.text: When your own time at the seat grows long, you start a drawer of your own. The first note is a recipe. The second is an apology to a god you once wronged. The third is blank, and you leave it blank on purpose.
events.arc: The Seat You Were Handed

choices.text: Write a long final note, for whoever comes next

effects.log: It is the best thing you have written. You seal it in the drawer and feel unexpectedly light.

choices.text: Leave the blank page as the last note

effects.log: The blank page says more than you could. The steward, reading, smiles.

events.text: A younger god of a neighbouring pantheon has begun to petition the court for a domain like yours, claiming it has been poorly kept. {npc} is clever, patient and polite, and has all the paperwork in order. At the next session, {he} bows to you with exact courtesy.
events.arc: The Rival Who Wants Your Domain

choices.text: Invite {him} to see the domain for a season

effects.log: The rival visits. After a month {he} sees how much work the place needs, and looks at you differently.

choices.text: Answer the petition in court, with a long and careful reply

effects.log: The reply takes an afternoon. The court is impressed. The rival is cooler towards you after.

choices.text: Ignore the petition

effects.log: The petition is read. The court looks at your empty seat. It is noted.

events.text: The rival makes an offer, privately: swap, for a century, domains. {npc} will keep yours while you keep theirs, and they will see which of you does it better. It is either an insult or an invitation, and from {him} probably both.
events.arc: The Rival Who Wants Your Domain

choices.text: Accept the swap for a century

effects.log: The domains swap. By decade ten you have learned a great deal and been quietly humbled. The rival has done the same.

choices.text: Decline politely, with a counter-offer to share the work

effects.log: The rival, to your surprise, accepts the share. You become allies, not equals.

events.text: A century later the rival comes to dine with you. The old grievance has become a shared joke. {He} says the petition was never about wanting your domain; it was about wanting to be taken seriously. {npc} raises a cup.
events.arc: The Rival Who Wants Your Domain

choices.text: Raise a cup in return

effects.log: The two of you drink late into the night. It is the best court-business ever conducted.

choices.text: Give them a seat at your council

effects.log: You offer a seat. They accept. You are not sure who has gained more.

events.text: The third hour of the afternoon has a goddess, who is small, dull, and almost entirely unvisited. {npc} is a young herald of the goddess, and comes to ask you, nervously, for a favour: the hour needs a festival, and nobody remembers how to hold one.
events.arc: The Goddess of the Third Hour

choices.text: Design a festival for the third hour

effects.log: You design a festival of afternoon light: tea, long shadows, a pause. It is held the next month, and goes oddly well.

choices.text: Teach the herald to design it

effects.log: The herald works for weeks with chalk on a slate. The festival is clumsy and sincere.

choices.text: Attend as a guest, not a planner

effects.log: You attend. It is dull, kind, and exactly the festival the third hour deserved.

events.text: The goddess herself, tiny and drowsy, appears at the festival's end and tells you she has not been remembered in three thousand years. She brings a single gift: the right to one extra minute of afternoon, whenever you wish.
events.arc: The Goddess of the Third Hour

choices.text: Use the minute to sit in the garden

effects.log: The minute is as long as you need. The sun does not move. It is the quietest rest you have ever had.

choices.text: Give the minute away to a tired worshipper

effects.log: The worshipper has an extra minute at their dying mother's bed. They do not know why, and never forget.

events.text: The third hour has become a custom among your worshippers: they put down their tools at the third bell and drink tea. A mortal poet writes that the afternoon is a small god, kindly, and that it is best not to hurry past.
events.arc: The Goddess of the Third Hour

choices.text: Send the poet a cup of the third-hour tea

effects.log: The poet drinks it and writes the best verse of their life. The goddess blushes.

choices.text: Keep the custom unchanged and unspoken

effects.log: It spreads quietly through three domains. Nobody can say who began it.

events.text: Once a century each pantheon renews its oath: every member stands in a circle and swears the old words aloud. {npc}, the oath-keeper, reminds you that you have not yet spoken them since you joined, and that tonight the circle will go round in your direction.
events.arc: Oath Night at the Pantheon

choices.text: Swear the oath fully, as written

effects.log: The words are old and slightly absurd. You say them with a steady voice, and mean about two thirds.

choices.text: Swear it, but add a line of your own

effects.log: The line is a small one: and may we be kind. A few gods hide a smile. The keeper lets it pass.

choices.text: Stand in the circle and say nothing

effects.log: You stand silent. A moment passes, and the circle moves on, politely.

events.text: After the oath the pantheon feasts, and tradition requires the newest member to give a toast. {npc} hands you a cup and a piece of paper with a toast on it, written by a long-dead member, and warns that it rhymes.
events.arc: Oath Night at the Pantheon

choices.text: Read the rhyming toast with feeling

effects.log: The toast is dreadful. You read it with full conviction, and by the last line the hall is cheering. You are asked to read it every century.

choices.text: Throw it away and speak from the heart

effects.log: The speech is short and clumsy and true. It is not the toast anyone expected. It is remembered.

events.text: A century passes. Oath night comes round again, and this time you are one of the old hands, and the newest member is a nervous youngster with a stammer. The keeper looks at you, gently, and pushes the cup in your direction.
events.arc: Oath Night at the Pantheon

choices.text: Stand beside the youngster and say the words with them

effects.log: You say them together, half a beat out of step. The pantheon claps. The youngster nearly faints.

choices.text: Pass the youngster the toast and a glass of water

effects.log: The toast is read, the voice gains strength, and the hall forgives the stammer.

events.text: The first loaf of the new harvest is carried up the shrine steps by a child, and the steps are steep. The child's face is so serious that the whole procession slows to match. At the top, the child sets the loaf down, and looks at you.

choices.text: Take the first bite, and share the rest with the child

effects.log: The loaf is warm and rough and the best you have had. The child nods and eats the other half with great ceremony.

choices.text: Bless the loaf and let the child carry it home

effects.log: The loaf is carried home. A family is fed that night with a god's blessing, and a very serious expression.

events.text: A scarecrow in your fields has been wearing the same hat for forty years, and the farmers, who have grown fond of it, ask if it can be blessed. They will not say whether they want the scarecrow to be lucky or the crows.

choices.text: Bless the scarecrow

effects.log: The scarecrow stands a little straighter. The crows, who had been planning a raid, go away.

choices.text: Bless the crows, quietly

effects.log: The crows take the field's edge and leave the middle. The farmers are baffled and pleased.

events.text: At the end of the harvest, the gleaners come into the stripped fields to pick up what the reapers missed. They are the poorest in the domain, and quiet. One of them hums a song you made up in your youth.

choices.text: Leave a few extra sheaves behind

effects.log: The gleaners find them and say nothing. The song stops, and begins again.

choices.text: Sing the second verse, unseen

effects.log: The gleaner stops mid-line, listens, and sings the verse back, wondering.

events.text: A mountain in your domain has sent a landslide into a small valley by accident. It is mortified, in the slow way of mountains. A boulder the size of a house rolls up to your door the next week, wrapped in flowers, to apologise.

choices.text: Accept the apology and ask the mountain to help rebuild

effects.log: The mountain lends its stones. The valley has a new wall and a fine view, and the mountain is much cheered.

choices.text: Remind the mountain gently to be careful

effects.log: The mountain grumbles. It is careful for the next three centuries.

events.text: Every mountain has a snow cap, and every autumn the mountains argue over who has the best one. This year the quarrel has come to you for judgment. There are three entrants, and none of them will wear their caps lower than the others.

choices.text: Rule in favour of the oldest, with honour

effects.log: The oldest mountain accepts with a small avalanche of satisfaction. The others sulk, then cheer.

choices.text: Declare a three-way tie

effects.log: The three mountains are insulted equally. A diplomatic success.

events.text: A bench in your war domain is reserved for veterans who have no one to sit with. Today it is occupied by a young recruit who has no right to it, and who is crying. The veterans have politely stopped sitting down.

choices.text: Sit beside the recruit and say nothing

effects.log: You sit. After a time the veterans, one by one, sit down too, forming a quiet line of old men and women, each nodding.

choices.text: Move the recruit to a softer seat and sit with them

effects.log: The recruit is grateful. The veterans take back their bench, and nod to you, approvingly.

events.text: In the hall of your war domain are banners of battles lost and won. A cleaner finds that one has been dusted so many times it has gone blank. Nobody knows which battle it recorded. They ask you what to do with a flag with nothing on it.

choices.text: Hang it in the place of honour

effects.log: It hangs in the hall: the banner of the battle that no one recalls. Veterans pause beneath it with bowed heads.

choices.text: Embroider it with something new

effects.log: You stitch a small plain dove. The flag is something again.

events.text: On the day of the kites, the mortals below fly every kite they have to the Sky, and the Sky holds them. Thousands bob at the ends of their strings. This year one kite is a very small one, very red, and pulling with unusual stubbornness.

choices.text: Hold the red kite steady for a minute

effects.log: It stills. Far below, a child lets out a cry of triumph. You let go, and the kite soars.

choices.text: Send a gust to carry it higher

effects.log: The kite goes up, up, past the clouds. The string snaps. Somewhere, a child learns what it means to let go.

events.text: A lost cloud has wandered into your Sky and cannot find its way home. It is small and sad and rains softly on all the wrong fields. A passing sailor-god points out that it came from the sea.

choices.text: Send a warm wind to carry it back to the sea

effects.log: The wind carries it. It bobs in the air, grateful, and goes.

choices.text: Give it a corner of your own sky to live in

effects.log: The cloud settles above your hall and is no trouble at all.

events.text: At the first forge of your fire domain an apprentice has been working the bellows for nine hours without stopping, out of pride. The master smith is too stubborn to tell the apprentice to rest. They both look at you, trapped.

choices.text: Order a break for everyone, with soup

effects.log: The break is taken. The apprentice sleeps in the ashes. The master pretends not to have asked.

choices.text: Take the bellows for an hour yourself

effects.log: You pump the bellows. The apprentice watches wide-eyed. When you hand them back, the apprentice makes a fire you could have wept at.

events.text: A mortal child lights a candle at your fire-shrine and makes a wish, aloud, as children do. It is a very small wish: for the cat to stop being cold. You have several thousand much larger wishes in the queue.

choices.text: Warm the cat

effects.log: The cat curls up in a patch of sun that was not there before. The child never knows.

choices.text: Warm the cat and the whole house

effects.log: The house is warm. The child's family thinks it is the stove. You are content.

events.text: A cart of seed arrives at your life-domain shrine, pulled by a donkey who knows more than the driver. The driver is a young priest delivering the first planting of the year. They ask you to say a word over the seeds before they are sown.

choices.text: Say a quiet word over each sack

effects.log: You say a word over every sack. Some of the seeds will grow into things you did not intend.

choices.text: Say nothing; bless the donkey

effects.log: The donkey is blessed, and visibly pleased. The seeds grow well anyway.

events.text: The first snowdrop of the year has pushed up through the ice outside your shrine, and a crowd of small mortals has come to look at it. It is the only green thing for ten miles. The crowd is silent, and the snowdrop trembles.

choices.text: Warm the ground around it by a degree

effects.log: The ice softens. The snowdrop bows, and the crowd cheers, quietly.

choices.text: Leave it exactly as it is

effects.log: The snowdrop stands in the snow alone, and the crowd takes in the sight, and goes away changed.

events.text: A pack of mist-hounds drifts across the lowlands at dawn, hunting nothing, and the mortals call it a ghost-pack. The hunt-master of your domain wants to follow them. The master cannot say why; it is simply what one does.

choices.text: Follow the mist-hounds with the hunt-master

effects.log: You follow them through a low white morning. They stop at a stream, drink, and dissolve. The hunt-master nods.

choices.text: Stay home and watch from the window

effects.log: You watch the mist roll past. It is, in its way, a hunt.

events.text: The star-stag you let go three years ago has come back to the meadow, with a fawn. The huntmaster stares. They do not hunt, but they track, and the track has led to this. The fawn comes up to your hand without fear.

choices.text: Stroke the fawn

effects.log: The fawn blinks. Its fur is full of stars. The stag watches, calm, from the hill.

choices.text: Keep your distance and watch

effects.log: The fawn wanders off with the stag. The huntmaster writes: still here, in the book.

events.text: Before the great hunt of the year, the nets must be mended, and the whole hall sits in rows with needles. It is the part of the hunt that nobody sings about. An old netter in the corner shows you the right knot, and the netter is very patient.

choices.text: Mend nets with the hall until dusk

effects.log: You mend sixty feet of net. Your fingers ache. The hall approves and offers you soup.

choices.text: Ask about the nets' history

effects.log: The history is long and includes a goat. You will never forget the goat.

events.text: A bell hangs in the hunting-lodge of your domain, to be rung only when a beast has been taken, and it has not been rung for a hundred years. The lodge-keeper dusts it every morning anyway. Today a child asks what it is for.

choices.text: Tell the child the bell is for a day that is still to come

effects.log: The child nods and goes away thinking. The keeper gives you a look of deep approval.

choices.text: Tell the child the bell is for the animals to hear

effects.log: The child stares. They ring the bell by accident. Every animal in the valley looks up.

events.text: At the gate of a sealed heaven is a visitor log, which no one has signed in an age. A wanderer has just added a line: came, looked, left, was not afraid. A second line follows, in another hand: nor were we.

choices.text: Add your own line to the log

effects.log: You write: also here. Next morning there is a third line beneath it: good.

choices.text: Read the whole log by lamplight

effects.log: The log is an odd diary of a thousand visitors. Reading it takes the night and is gently funny.

events.text: There is a light in a window of a sealed heaven where no one has lived for ages. It is lit at dusk and out at dawn, like clockwork. A shepherd swears it has been doing this since their grandmother's time. You can see the window from your garden.

choices.text: Wave to the window every evening

effects.log: You wave. After a month, the curtain moves. Only once.

choices.text: Leave a lamp in your own window in reply

effects.log: Two lights, two windows, across a valley. It is, you decide, a sufficient conversation.

events.text: A sealed heaven leaks ink: black, slow, harmless, running out of a crack in the gate to form a small pool. A scribe collects it each week to write letters. The ink writes slightly better than any other, and the letters are always a little more honest.

choices.text: Write a letter in the leaked ink

effects.log: The letter says things you meant to leave out. You send it anyway. The answer is kind.

choices.text: Ask the scribe to stop collecting

effects.log: The scribe stops. The pool dries. The scribe misses the honesty of it, and does not say so.

events.text: Snow falls only on the sealed heaven in your hills, though the rest of the country is dry. It falls inward, from nowhere, and melts at the seal. A family of mortal fox-keepers sits at the edge each winter to watch it.

choices.text: Sit with the fox-keepers and watch the snow

effects.log: The snow falls on nothing in silence. The foxes sleep in your lap. You stay till the frost.

choices.text: Bring a flask of warm wine to the family

effects.log: The family accepts with startled gratitude. The snow melts at the seal, as ever.

events.text: In a cave in your domain is a smooth round stone of unknown age, warm to the touch, which the ancient hermits call the egg. It has never hatched. A visiting scholar wants to open it. The hermits stand in a row at the cave mouth, silent.

choices.text: Tell the scholar to leave it

effects.log: The scholar, offended, leaves. The hermits bow. The egg warms, a very little.

choices.text: Sit by the egg for a night yourself

effects.log: The egg hums low. You do not understand it, and are glad to have heard it.

events.text: A single footprint in hard stone marks the oldest place in your domain, and no one has ever claimed it. The print is plain: one bare foot, set down firmly, going nowhere. It is the right size for you.

choices.text: Place your foot in the print

effects.log: It fits. For a moment you feel the whole weight of whoever stood there, and then it passes.

choices.text: Leave a flower beside it

effects.log: The flower wilts by evening. Another is left by someone else, and soon there is a small garden.

events.text: Before the Sky had a dawn, there was only a slow brightening, and your domain has a hill from which it can still be seen, on one day a year. A few ancient birds come to watch it. This year it is your turn to stand on the hill.

choices.text: Stand on the hill and watch it all

effects.log: The brightening takes three hours. When it is over, you feel entirely new.

choices.text: Share the hill with the birds

effects.log: They roost on your shoulders. It is the most peaceful dawn you have had.

events.text: A tall ladder has been left against your hall by Cheonho Who Hangs the Stars, with a note: back soon. It has been there a month. A stray star hangs from a rung, as if forgotten, humming softly.

choices.text: Hang the star somewhere useful

effects.log: You hang it above the crossroads. Travellers find their way by it, and the ladder is finally collected.

choices.text: Leave the star where it is

effects.log: The star hums for a season and then, quietly, rises. The ladder disappears the next morning.

events.text: Noegong of the Nine Drums sends a messenger with a very small drum, just a hand-span wide, wrapped in a silk cloth. A note reads: tap it if you are lonely. The drum, you find, is very quiet, and very old.

choices.text: Tap the drum once

effects.log: A far-off thunder answers, kindly. You are not alone.

choices.text: Keep it in a drawer, unplayed

effects.log: You know it is there. Some comfort is the knowledge of it.

events.text: Horang Lord of the Wild is seen crossing your lands in the shape of a lame fox, limping, with a patch of white on one ear. The beasts of the domain pay no attention, which is how you know. You step aside and let the fox pass.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of milk by the gate

effects.log: The fox drinks it, looks at you with a very old eye, and goes on. Next morning, the hens lay doubly.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the Wild pass

effects.log: The Wild passes. The woods are quiet behind it, and listening.

events.text: A song that every mortal in your domain used to know has been unmade, a verse at a time, by the quiet wearing away. Only the tune remains, hummed without words. An old singer tries to remember, frowning, and cannot.

choices.text: Write new words to the tune

effects.log: The new words are simple. By the next spring a whole valley is singing them, and the old verses are forgotten.

choices.text: Hum the tune with her, and say nothing

effects.log: You hum together. It is enough.

events.text: A cup that has been on your table since your first day as a god, plain and chipped, has slipped away into the Unmaking: you can see it, hear it rattle, but when you reach for it your fingers close on air. A tiny, polite absence sits in its place.

choices.text: Pour tea into the absence

effects.log: The tea pools in a shape that is not a cup. You drink it. It tastes, faintly, of the first day.

choices.text: Buy a new cup, and call it the same name

effects.log: The new cup is chipped by the end of the year. The name holds.

events.text: The lintel stone of a burned shrine has been used by a farmer as a doorstep for a barn for sixty years. A scholar tells the farmer its history. The farmer says nothing, and in the morning the lintel is back where the shrine used to stand.

choices.text: Visit the lintel and sit on it a moment

effects.log: It is just a stone. And yet you feel for a moment that you are on a threshold.

choices.text: Send the farmer a new doorstep

effects.log: The farmer gets a new doorstep and a better barn door, and never asks why.

events.text: A band of pilgrims passes through your domain singing a mourning song for a shrine that burned a thousand years ago. They sing it every year on the anniversary, and walk three hundred miles to do it. They do not ask for anything.

choices.text: Walk beside them for a day, unseen

effects.log: You listen. The song is a good one, and the pilgrims are cheerful for people in mourning.

choices.text: Leave a table of bread and water at their way

effects.log: They take the bread and say a short prayer for you, whoever you are.

events.text: Once a year, the lesser gods of your pantheon go on a picnic in a field with no shrine. It is meant to build solidarity. It builds mostly sunburn and arguments about a very small dog. You are invited.

choices.text: Go, and bring a hamper

effects.log: The hamper is a hit. The small dog follows you home. Solidarity, in its way, is achieved.

choices.text: Go, and sit under a tree

effects.log: You sit under the tree and speak with a shy god of ladders. It is the best conversation of the year.

events.text: A feud between two gods of your pantheon has lasted six thousand years over a matter nobody can remember. Both have asked you, separately, to take their side at the next session. Each says the other started it.

choices.text: Refuse both, and host them at the same table

effects.log: They sit at your table. They do not speak. They both ask for the salt. It is a start.

choices.text: Choose neither side, and say so openly

effects.log: Both are insulted. Both quietly come around.

events.text: At the bridge to a pantheon's court, a toll-keeper charges Masterless Gods double. They don't explain; it is simply listed. A pantheon god behind you in the queue winces and offers to cover the difference.

choices.text: Pay the double toll, without a word

effects.log: You pay. The keeper looks away. The pantheon god behind you remembers your face.

choices.text: Accept the offer, and thank them

effects.log: The pantheon god pays. A small kindness passes between you that neither will forget.

events.text: You receive a letter from a pantheon, inviting you to join. It is carefully worded and very friendly, and says nothing about what it would cost. You turn it over; the back of the page is blank.

choices.text: Write back that you are honoured, and not yet ready

effects.log: The reply is polite. A basket of fruit arrives, and a second letter, shorter.

choices.text: Put the letter in the fire without reply

effects.log: The letter burns. The pantheon does not write again for a century.

events.text: The petitions to your seat arrive by the cartload each morning: for rain, for a lost ox, for an end to a feud. A clerk sorts them into piles. One pile, tiny, is marked, in the clerk's hand: those that only want to say thank you.

choices.text: Read the thank-you pile first

effects.log: The pile is short and warm and takes ten minutes. It makes the rest easier.

choices.text: Read the oxen pile first

effects.log: The oxen are found by noon. The pile of thanks keeps for another day.

events.text: The map of your domain in the council hall is a hundred years out of date, and the cartographer-spirit has taken to redrawing it in the margins. It shows, in a corner, a small island that you do not remember. A note says it was made by the domain itself.

choices.text: Go and look at the island

effects.log: It is a small knoll with one tree. The domain seems rather proud of it.

choices.text: Approve the new map, island and all

effects.log: The map is hung. The island, for reasons of its own, blooms.

events.text: Your domain turns a thousand years old this season. The mortals have decided to celebrate, in a muddle of banners, cakes, and a procession led by a child on a donkey. They have asked you to say a few words. They are afraid of what you will say.

choices.text: Say the shortest speech of your reign

effects.log: You say: thank you. The crowd roars. The child on the donkey falls off.

choices.text: Say nothing and eat a cake

effects.log: You eat a cake. The crowd is delighted by your approachability.

events.text: The old keeper of a hill shrine of yours has died, and the child comes home to close it: {npc}, now a physician in the lower towns, who has not prayed in twenty years and says so politely. {He} has a satchel, a cart and one week.
events.arc: The Keeper's Child Who Studied Medicine

choices.text: Show {him} the valley's fevers, in a dream

effects.log: {npc} wakes in the keeper's bed with the whole winter's sickness behind {his} eyes, every cough in the valley counted.

choices.text: Ask {him} to light one candle before closing

effects.log: {npc} lights it without a word and watches it burn down to the wick.

choices.text: Let {him} close the shrine, kindly

effects.log: The shutters go up. You watch from the lintel and are not offended. {He} was not asked to believe.

events.text: {npc} stays a fortnight past the week. Pilgrims come up the hill with sore feet and worse, and {he} treats them in the shrine yard, grumbling that this is not prayer. One pilgrim asks whether {he} is the new keeper.
events.arc: The Keeper's Child Who Studied Medicine

choices.text: Let the pilgrim's thanks reach {him}

effects.log: A warm word carries across the yard. {npc} looks round for who said it and finds only a hen.

choices.text: Send a fine dry week for the work

effects.log: The yard stays dry and the cart wheels turn. {npc} credits the season.

events.text: {npc} reopens the shrine as a house of healing, and writes to you in plain words: 'I do not believe in you, but I believe in a roof.' It is the best prayer you have had in years, and it comes with a ledger of the sick.
events.arc: The Keeper's Child Who Studied Medicine

choices.text: Bless the roof

effects.log: The thatch never leaks again, and the sick sleep better under it for a hundred years. (+faith)

choices.text: Send herbs in a dream, each with its use

effects.log: The physician keeps a notebook of dreamed herbs, and tells nobody where they came from.

events.text: {npc} leaves for the lower towns in the morning, the candle burned out. A year later a letter arrives: a clinic in the lower town has a small sign over the door, in your colour, and no explanation. {He} has not changed {his} mind, only {his} habits.
events.arc: The Keeper's Child Who Studied Medicine

choices.text: Send the clinic a quiet luck

effects.log: The clinic's first winter is a good one. {npc} thinks it is the new stove.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the sign be

effects.log: The sign weathers. Patients come, and do not ask for whom it is.

events.text: The old chanter of your lake shrine left the chant to two heirs. {npc}, the elder, sings it as taught, slow and plain. The younger sings it faster, with a flourish the old chanter never allowed. The congregation cannot tell which of them is yours.
events.arc: The Heirs of the Chant

choices.text: Favour the elder's plain chant

effects.log: A low note rolls over the lake and the plain chant carries. {npc} sits straighter at the next dawn.

choices.text: Favour the younger's flourish

effects.log: A bright run of notes rolls over the water. The flourish catches. {npc} says nothing, and sings plainer.

events.text: At the lake festival both heirs sing the chant together, a beat apart. The congregation, delighted, begins to clap at the gap. {npc} goes red to the ears and keeps singing.
events.arc: The Heirs of the Chant

choices.text: Send a little echo across the water to bridge the beat

effects.log: The lake sings back and the gap closes for a verse. Pilgrims call it a miracle of the middle.

choices.text: Let the gap stand

effects.log: The gap becomes the festival's favourite part.

events.text: The younger heir leaves for a town shrine and sings your hymn with the flourish there. {npc} keeps the plain chant at the lake. Two shrines now sing you in two ways, and each calls the other the lesser, fondly.
events.arc: The Heirs of the Chant

choices.text: Bless both, and tell neither which is the better

effects.log: The two chants carry in two valleys. (+faith)

choices.text: Visit the lake in a plain coat and hum along

effects.log: {npc} catches you humming off the beat, and says nothing, to the end.

events.text: {npc} gives up the lead to the younger heir after a hard winter of comparisons, and sits at the back as the best listener the lake has had. {He} is never seen to sing again. Some mornings the lake does it for {him}.
events.arc: The Heirs of the Chant

choices.text: Send {him} a quiet dawn song of your own

effects.log: A single note drifts across the water, only for {npc}. {He} bows, and eats breakfast for the first time in months.

choices.text: Praise the listener at the next festival

effects.log: {npc} is named Keeper of the Quiet. {He} has never been so proud.

events.text: Each time you send your valley a small kindness, the god across the ridge sends the same. You send rain; {npc} sends rain. You send a rainbow; a bigger one arrives from over the ridge. The valley has begun keeping score on a wall.
events.arc: The Rival Who Matches Your Rain

choices.text: Send a kindness {he} cannot match: a late snow on the first blossom

effects.log: The orchard goes white and gold at once, and the valley goes silent with delight.

choices.text: Send word across the ridge: let the valleys share a festival

effects.log: A note goes over the ridge, polite and short. The answer is a single word: 'Gladly.'

events.text: In the hamlet on the ridge where the two valleys meet, a wedding falls on a day both of you want to bless. Rain comes from one side and sun from the other, and the couple stands under a double sky, looking up with their mouths open.
events.arc: The Rival Who Matches Your Rain

choices.text: Yield the sun to {npc}

effects.log: The sun goes to the far side, and the couple is married in gold. {npc} sends no reply, but the rain stops at once.

choices.text: Share the one rainbow between you

effects.log: A bow of light spans both valleys. The couple names their first child for the sky.

events.text: {npc} answers the snow with a hush: a thaw so gentle that not one petal falls, and the blossom holds three weeks past its time. The valley wall is wiped clean. A note arrives under your door: 'Well played.'
events.arc: The Rival Who Matches Your Rain

choices.text: Send a note back, in the same hand

effects.log: A flower is pressed in it. The two valleys are friends from that day, in the slow way of rivals.

choices.text: Pin the note above your door

effects.log: It hangs there for a century, and travellers ask who won.

events.text: The shared festival fills the ridge: two shrines, one table, a rain that falls half on each side and a sun that does the same. {npc} gives the opening speech, and for once does not try to outdo yours. The wall of scores comes down.
events.arc: The Rival Who Matches Your Rain

choices.text: Bless the table the valleys share

effects.log: The table is never moved, and the ridge becomes a pilgrim road. (+faith)

choices.text: Ask {npc} to open the next festival, too

effects.log: {He} agrees. A rival becomes a host, and the habit holds.

events.text: Pilgrims leave offerings on a cairn at a crossroads without saying which god it is for. {npc}, a god of the neighbouring road, has begun to leave a competing marker on top: a flat stone with a mark scratched on it. The offerings go on piling up.
events.arc: The Cairn at the Crossroads

choices.text: Add a marker of your own beside it

effects.log: A second flat stone goes on the cairn. The offerings do not stop for either.

choices.text: Leave the offerings unlabelled, to the road

effects.log: You take down your hand and the offerings stay, and the road is simply the road.

events.text: A storm washes both markers away in the night. At dawn the cairn stands, and the offerings on it, and nobody knows whose they are. {npc} stands on one side of it and you on the other, both a little wet.
events.arc: The Cairn at the Crossroads

choices.text: Offer {npc} a dry cloak

effects.log: {He} takes it with a scowl, then wears it all morning. It is the closest to peace the crossroads has had.

choices.text: Say nothing and wait

effects.log: The two of you wait together by the cairn, saying nothing, until the sun comes.

events.text: Two fresh markers are set on the cairn side by side, and pilgrims touch both. The crossroads becomes known as the Twin Stones. {npc} and you keep a courteous distance, a stone's throw apart, like old neighbours.
events.arc: The Cairn at the Crossroads

choices.text: Bless the Twin Stones for the road

effects.log: Travellers leave the crossroads safe and rested, and say a word to both. (+faith)

choices.text: Nod to {npc} across the cairn each spring

effects.log: A nod is returned. It is the whole of the treaty, and enough.

events.text: Without a god's mark, the cairn gathers a road-keeper of its own: a small, shy god of the way itself, who sweeps the crossroads each dawn. {npc} departs with a grunt. You lose the crossroads and the road gains a friend.
events.arc: The Cairn at the Crossroads

choices.text: Leave the road-keeper a small gift

effects.log: A lantern hung from the cairn lights the crossroads till morning. (+faith for the road)

choices.text: Walk the road in a plain coat, once a year

effects.log: You are greeted by a sweeper with a broom, and no questions.

events.text: After a fire, your shrine at the river-mouth was rebuilt on a loan of faith from a neighbouring god's reserve. {npc}, the neighbour's steward, arrives with a folded paper and many apologies. The loan has fallen due.
events.arc: The Shrine That Owed Faith

choices.text: Promise a season of good fishing

effects.log: You promise, and you must now deliver. {npc} writes it down in a very small hand.

choices.text: Offer to read the terms aloud together

effects.log: You read every clause with {npc}, at the shrine step, over bread. It takes the afternoon.

events.text: {npc} stays to see the debt honestly settled and proves a good lodger: {he} mends the thatch, learns the bell-ringer's name, and takes the morning bread at the shrine step. The neighbouring god sends a note asking when {he} will be home.
events.arc: The Shrine That Owed Faith

choices.text: Tell {him} the shrine can spare {him} a while

effects.log: {npc} stays another month, and no one minds.

choices.text: Send {him} home with a loaf and a fair copy of the terms

effects.log: {He} goes, and comes back by the next full moon with a hammer.

events.text: The season of fishing is a fat one. The river-mouth boats come home heavy and the debt is paid in full in the neighbour's own coin of gratitude. {npc} leaves the receipt framed on the shrine wall, at your request.
events.arc: The Shrine That Owed Faith

choices.text: Thank the neighbour god in a dream

effects.log: The neighbouring god wakes pleased, and sends a gift of nets. (+faith)

choices.text: Send the extra fish upstream, unasked

effects.log: A feast is held three valleys away by people who do not know why.

events.text: The terms prove to say the faith is repaid in kind: one kindness for each prayer borrowed. {npc} and you spend a year on small kindnesses, a mended net, a warm word, a lantern, and the book fills line by line. At the end the debt is gone, and a friend is gained.
events.arc: The Shrine That Owed Faith

choices.text: Record the kindnesses in the shrine book

effects.log: A long page of small deeds hangs in the shrine. Pilgrims add to it. (+faith)

choices.text: Keep the account closed and private

effects.log: {npc} and you share a last cup of tea and burn the paper.

events.text: Each pantheon keeps a roster of small duties: who holds the lamp at the dawn procession, who counts the cushions at the feast. {npc}, the roster-keeper, has given you the lamp for the entire coming year, with the apologetic air of one handing out a plague.
events.arc: The Roster of Small Duties

choices.text: Take the lamp with good grace

effects.log: {npc} is so relieved that {he} nearly drops the scroll. The lamp is yours.

choices.text: Ask to swap with a god who loves lamps

effects.log: {npc} gives you a look of pure betrayal, and writes a name down in the margin.

events.text: The dawn procession is long and cold. You hold the lamp at the front and see everything: who is late, who is sulking, who walks arm in arm with whom. A good lamp-bearer, it turns out, is the pantheon's quiet witness.
events.arc: The Roster of Small Duties

choices.text: Remember it all, kindly

effects.log: A hundred little things are kept in your head, and none of them used.

choices.text: Slow the pace for the oldest god at the back

effects.log: The line eases to a stroll. The oldest god nods, once, in thanks.

events.text: At the year's end the elders thank you by name for the lamp. It is not a grand honour, a line in the minutes, but it is read aloud. {npc} brings you a new, finer lamp and asks in a small voice whether you would keep it another year.
events.arc: The Roster of Small Duties

choices.text: Keep the lamp another year

effects.log: Another year of cold dawns. The pantheon now thinks of you as dependable. (+loyalty)

choices.text: Hand it on to a younger god with a speech

effects.log: The younger god nearly faints. The line in the minutes is yours all the same.

events.text: The swap costs you a favour: the god who loves lamps asks a small thing in return, a word with an elder, and you must pay. {npc} marks you in the margin as one who bargains. The pantheon notices, mildly.
events.arc: The Roster of Small Duties

choices.text: Pay the favour in full, cheerfully

effects.log: The elder is spoken to, and the lamp-lover smiles. The books balance. (+loyalty)

choices.text: Admit the swap was a mistake, to {npc}

effects.log: {npc} laughs at last, and tells you what everyone says of the lamp. It is not kind, and it is true.

events.text: The pantheon's choir sings at the founding anniversary, and every god must stand in it. You cannot sing. {npc}, the choirmaster, has heard you try, and asks, with great delicacy, whether you might stand at the back and move your mouth.
events.arc: The Pantheon Choir

choices.text: Stand at the back and move your mouth

effects.log: You mouth the words with great solemnity. {npc} gives a small, grateful nod.

choices.text: Practise in secret until you can carry a line

effects.log: You practise in an empty hall. The echo is not kind. You carry on.

events.text: At the dress rehearsal your voice, or its absence, is noticed. An elder in the front row turns round slowly. The whole choir stops, mid-note, and looks at the back. {npc} presses both hands to {his} face.
events.arc: The Pantheon Choir

choices.text: Bow, and carry on regardless

effects.log: You carry on to the end of the verse. The elder turns round again, slowly.

choices.text: Ask the elder what the verse should sound like

effects.log: The elder demonstrates, in a voice like a cracked bell, and the choir cannot look at each other.

events.text: The elder, it turns out, had noticed years ago, and declares the anniversary hymn the best-sung in memory. The silence at the back, the elder says, was the warmest note. You are asked to stand there every year. (+loyalty)
events.arc: The Pantheon Choir

choices.text: Accept the place of honour in the quiet

effects.log: You stand at the back every founding day. The pantheon calls it the Hush. (+loyalty)

choices.text: Thank the elder, and keep it private

effects.log: A warm word passes, and the matter ends.

events.text: On the day your voice cracks on the highest note, loud as a shutter. The hall freezes. Then the pantheon laughs, all of it, gods of war with gods of dew, and {npc} sings the next line twice as loud to cover for you. It is, everyone agrees, the best anniversary in years.
events.arc: The Pantheon Choir

choices.text: Sing the next line with {npc}, flat and proud

effects.log: The two of you finish together, a mile off the key. (+loyalty)

choices.text: Bow at the end and take the laughter as a gift

effects.log: The laughter follows you out into the corridor like a friend.

events.text: The Masterless gods at the court sit on the last bench, which the marshals keep dim to save oil. {npc}, an old Masterless god, has brought a lantern, a plain tin one, and set it on the end of the bench, saying the bench has been dark for four hundred years.
events.arc: The Lantern on the Back Bench

choices.text: Add oil to the lantern from your own store

effects.log: You pour a measure of your own light into the tin. It flares, and then settles into a steady glow.

choices.text: Sit beside it and say nothing

effects.log: You sit in the circle of light, shoulder to shoulder with {npc}, and watch the marshals look anywhere else.

events.text: A marshal approaches the bench, politely, with an extinguisher on a pole, and asks whether the lantern is strictly necessary. {npc} says it is not strictly necessary, only true. The marshal considers this for some time.
events.arc: The Lantern on the Back Bench

choices.text: Add that the lantern harms nobody

effects.log: The marshal admits it harms nobody. The extinguisher is lowered an inch.

choices.text: Let {npc} speak for the bench

effects.log: {npc} makes a short plain speech, and the marshal bows to it, a little.

events.text: The lantern is lit at every council. Soon other Masterless gods bring one each, and the back bench becomes a row of small lights, like a street at dusk. The court's gods find themselves looking back at it, and none will say why.
events.arc: The Lantern on the Back Bench

choices.text: Bless the row of lights

effects.log: The lights never go out in a draught. The Masterless gods call it the Street. (+faith)

choices.text: Add a light of your own at the end

effects.log: Your lantern is the last and the brightest. {npc} says it looks well.

events.text: The marshal relents with a rule: the lantern is allowed, under a cloth, at council. {npc} calls it a victory, and you sit together in the cloth-dimmed gold, two Masterless gods on a bench at the back, entirely content.
events.arc: The Lantern on the Back Bench

choices.text: Accept the cloth as a start

effects.log: The cloth is lifted by a degree each year, and in a century it is gone. (+faith)

choices.text: Thank the marshal personally

effects.log: The marshal is nonplussed, and unbends enough to nod.

events.text: At the feast the servants carry the pantheons' leftovers to the Masterless table in a heap and leave them with a bow, as if it were a charity. {npc}, a Masterless cook who has eaten nothing else for three hundred years, looks at the heap and at you.
events.arc: The Leftovers at the Masterless Table

choices.text: Make a proper meal of the leftovers

effects.log: You and {npc} sort, season and re-fire them. By the second bell the heap is a supper.

choices.text: Decline the heap and bring your own dish next time

effects.log: The servants take the heap away with visible relief. {npc} looks at the empty table, and nods.

events.text: The supper's smell reaches the high tables. A god of war sends a servant for a second plate, and then a god of dew sends two. By dessert a small line of the pantheon's youngest is passing the Masterless bench with an air of casual hunger.
events.arc: The Leftovers at the Masterless Table

choices.text: Serve them with a nod and no remark

effects.log: The youngest eat, and there is no remark. It is the nicest dinner of the season.

choices.text: Let {npc} take the compliments

effects.log: {npc} stands behind the bench, hands in apron, enjoying it.

events.text: The Leftover Supper becomes famous. Pantheon gods sneak to the back bench to eat, and the high tables send over the better cuts, openly, for the Masterless to work on. No one says it is charity any more.
events.arc: The Leftovers at the Masterless Table

choices.text: Keep the supper a Masterless custom

effects.log: The supper is held at every feast, and it is the best table in the hall. (+faith)

choices.text: Invite the high tables to bring a dish

effects.log: They do, sheepishly. The back bench fills.

events.text: Every Masterless god brings a dish to the next feast, and the bench groans. The marshal quietly stops sending scraps, and sends a proper course instead, hot, with a napkin. It is a small thing and it is entirely the whole matter.
events.arc: The Leftovers at the Masterless Table

choices.text: Thank the marshal with a dish of your own

effects.log: A dish goes to the marshal's table with no card. It is eaten, and the plate is returned clean.

choices.text: Accept the course in silence

effects.log: You eat. {npc} eats. A small silence falls over the bench, a good one.

events.text: {npc}, a warden of your sky, reports that a small cloud has begun to follow the same road every day and sulk when it rains. It has lost two sisters to a squall. It will not go home. The warden has run out of ideas and ginger biscuits.
events.arc: The Cloud That Wanted a Name

choices.text: Give the cloud a name

effects.log: You whisper one, softly. The cloud brightens like a face. {npc} writes the name on the day's roll.

choices.text: Tell the warden to leave it alone

effects.log: {npc} takes up a seat on a wall, and watches the cloud with a flask of tea.

events.text: The little cloud drifts over a dry hill where the herders have been praying for rain for two years. It trembles, and lets go a thin, silver shower. The herders stand with their faces up, utterly silent.
events.arc: The Cloud That Wanted a Name

choices.text: Let it rain a little longer

effects.log: The shower holds for an hour. The herders sing without words.

choices.text: Watch with {npc}, without a word

effects.log: You and {npc} watch from the wall as the cloud thins. It is the best rain of the age.

events.text: The hill celebrates a named cloud. A festival is held on its road each year, with paper cloud-kites and a cake shaped like a raindrop. The cloud, flattered and shy, brings a drizzle on the right day, every year.
events.arc: The Cloud That Wanted a Name

choices.text: Bless the cloud's road

effects.log: The road is never dry again, and the herds grow fat. (+faith)

choices.text: Attend the festival in a plain coat

effects.log: You eat the cake. It is excellent. A child asks whether you are a cloud.

events.text: At the end of summer the cloud drifts away over the ridge, and does not return. The next spring a flock of small clouds comes over the same ridge instead, all with its shape. {npc} says nothing, and takes off {his} hat.
events.arc: The Cloud That Wanted a Name

choices.text: Let them rain on the old hill

effects.log: The flock sheds a gentle rain, one cloud after another, down the old road. (+faith)

choices.text: Name the first of them, too

effects.log: The flock has a leader, then. The warden writes the name down.

events.text: In the evening, when the ferry-lamps are lit in your domain, an old gardener named {npc} sits at the edge of {his} own plot, knowing it is {his} last. {He} asks for nothing at all, only to finish the row of beans.
events.arc: The Gardener's Last Evening

choices.text: Hold the dusk a little longer

effects.log: The sun hangs a hand's breadth above the hill. {npc} looks up, nods once, and takes up the hoe.

choices.text: Let the evening run its hour

effects.log: The light fades in its usual order. {npc} works by the last of it, steadily.

events.text: The neighbours hear and come to the fence one by one, carrying nothing, saying little. They stand with their hands on the rail and watch the old gardener work. Somebody brings a stool. {npc} refuses it.
events.arc: The Gardener's Last Evening

choices.text: Stand at the fence with them, in a plain coat

effects.log: You stand shoulder to shoulder with a dozen neighbours. No one asks who you are.

choices.text: Send a mild wind to cool the rows

effects.log: The wind lifts the bean-leaves, and {npc} smiles.

events.text: The row is finished before the lamps burn low. At sunrise every bean on it is in flower, and the old gardener sits against the fence with the hoe in {npc}'s lap, gone gently in the night. The ferry-lamp at the plot's edge is lit for a day longer than the rest.
events.arc: The Gardener's Last Evening

choices.text: Let the row bloom for a season more

effects.log: The beans flower out of season and the whole street comes to see. (+faith)

choices.text: Say a quiet word at the fence

effects.log: You say one word, a name you were given, and the lamp flickers.

events.text: {npc} falls asleep with the trowel in hand while the light is still gold, and does not wake. The neighbours finish the row in the dark, and no one says a word. The beans are the sweetest in the street that year.
events.arc: The Gardener's Last Evening

choices.text: Carry the first beans to the ferry

effects.log: The ferryman receives the basket with a bow. A small smoke goes up. (+faith)

choices.text: Let the neighbours keep the plot

effects.log: A neighbour's child takes up the hoe the next morning. No one told them to.

events.text: In the loom-room a young apprentice named {npc} has pulled a thread before its hour. A traveller in a far town is about to meet an old friend years too soon. {He} comes to you at dusk, as white as the thread, hands knotted in {his} apron.
events.arc: The Thread Pulled Too Early

choices.text: Tie the thread back, slowly, with {him}

effects.log: You hold the ends and {npc} ties the knot, with a trembling thumb. It holds, nearly.

choices.text: Let the meeting come, and soften it

effects.log: You send a small mist to the town road. The two will meet in it, and not be sure it is true.

events.text: Unmyeong the Weaver passes through the loom-room that night and stops at the repaired place, and looks at it for a long time. {npc} stands very still. The Weaver says nothing, and moves on, and a single thread in the room stirs.
events.arc: The Thread Pulled Too Early

choices.text: Say that the fault is yours, not the apprentice's

effects.log: The Weaver does not turn round. The thread stirs again, a little.

choices.text: Stay silent, and let the work speak

effects.log: The work speaks. The Weaver's footsteps do not return.

events.text: The knot is tied true, and the old friends meet at the right hour, years later, on a bridge in the rain. {npc} learns to knot well, and is soon the room's best at it. The Weaver sends a spool of silver thread as a mark of regard.
events.arc: The Thread Pulled Too Early

choices.text: Keep the silver spool for the apprentice

effects.log: The spool is given to {npc} in your hall, unwrapped, for the work. (+faith)

choices.text: Thank the Weaver in a dream

effects.log: A grey figure bows, in a dream, and walks off with the spool of thanks.

events.text: The two meet in the mist and cannot decide whether it is true. They spend a week together, anyway, in a town whose inn has one room, and part as friends. Unmyeong, told of it, laughs once, and leaves the thread loose a while longer.
events.arc: The Thread Pulled Too Early

choices.text: Take the credit with {npc}, as a pair

effects.log: The pair of you are named on the loom-room wall, in small letters. (+loyalty)

choices.text: Let {npc} keep the credit alone

effects.log: {He} blushes to the roots. The room hums.

events.text: A young thunder in your sky stutters: it cannot get its roll out in one go, only a series of small cracks like a dropped tray. {npc}, the thunder's tender, has coaxed it for a year. The valley below has begun to mistake it for a spill of gravel.
events.arc: The Thunder That Stuttered

choices.text: Teach the thunder a long low breath

effects.log: You breathe with it in the clouds. The next roll is longer, if not quite whole.

choices.text: Let it stutter, and give the stutter a name

effects.log: You name it the Tumble, and the valley is charmed.

events.text: A parent in the valley tells the child it is the sky laughing, in small bits. The child laughs back. The thunder, hearing, tries a laugh too, and for a moment the whole valley shakes with a tiny, delighted rumble.
events.arc: The Thunder That Stuttered

choices.text: Answer with a warm gust over the roofs

effects.log: The valley turns a hundred faces up. {npc} claps both hands to {his} mouth.

choices.text: Keep still and listen

effects.log: The sky laughs in bits. You have rarely heard a better sound.

events.text: The thunder learns, at last, a long roll, and uses it on the night of the first harvest. The whole valley feels it in its bones. Then it stutters once, on purpose, at the end, like a signature. {npc} weeps with pride.
events.arc: The Thunder That Stuttered

choices.text: Bless the signature

effects.log: The valley counts the roll and its small final stutter as a blessing. (+faith)

choices.text: Praise the thunder in a dream

effects.log: The thunder dreams it is a bell, and wakes gentle.

events.text: The Tumble becomes the valley's festival sound. Children drum on pots when the sky stutters, and the thunder, encouraged, stutters more. Visiting gods of storm find it unseemly, and stay for the cakes. {npc} keeps a tally on the shed wall.
events.arc: The Thunder That Stuttered

choices.text: Accept the pot-drumming as a hymn

effects.log: The children drum for you each storm. (+faith)

choices.text: Defend the Tumble to the visiting storm-gods

effects.log: You say it is a local custom. The storm-gods nod gravely and ask for the recipe.

events.text: It is the custom that the last sheaf in the last field is left standing for you. This year the field belongs to {npc}, an old reaper whose back will not bend. {He} stands at the edge of the final row with the sickle, looking at the one sheaf, and does not cut it.
events.arc: The Last Sheaf

choices.text: Give the old reaper a breeze at the back

effects.log: A warm wind steadies {npc}'s spine. {He} cuts the whole field but the last sheaf, and straightens with a grunt.

choices.text: Take the last sheaf yourself, and let {him} rest

effects.log: You cut it in a plain coat, as a stranger who stopped to help. {npc} thanks you without knowing.

events.text: The neighbours bring the harvest supper to the field's edge, since the reaper cannot walk far. The table is laid on the stubble. Somebody has put the last sheaf in the middle, tied with a red cord, like a guest of honour.
events.arc: The Last Sheaf

choices.text: Sit at the table in a plain coat

effects.log: You eat with the neighbours and are asked for no name.

choices.text: Make the sheaf glow, faintly

effects.log: The sheaf glows. The neighbours think it a trick of the sunset.

events.text: The reaper dies in the winter, and the field passes to a grandchild who has never held a sickle. In spring {npc}'s last sheaf is found sprouting in the barn, a pale stalk of green. The grandchild plants it by the gate and does not ask why.
events.arc: The Last Sheaf

choices.text: Let the gate-plant grow for a century

effects.log: The plant stands by the gate for a hundred years. Every harvest a sheaf of it is left for you. (+faith)

choices.text: Whisper the reaper's name to the wind

effects.log: The wind carries it across the stubble. The grandchild looks up.

events.text: {npc} gives you the last sheaf by the old rite, on the day of the harvest feast, at the shrine step. You hold it for a moment in both hands, and then it goes to ash, a clean grey ash that smells of bread. {He} has spent a life on that sheaf.
events.arc: The Last Sheaf

choices.text: Scatter the ash on the next year's field

effects.log: The field is richer for a lifetime. (+faith)

choices.text: Keep a pinch, and say nothing

effects.log: A pinch of grey ash on a shelf, for a good year.

events.text: A hunter named {npc} sets an orphaned wolf-cub on your shrine step at dawn and says nothing about it. The cub is grey, hungry and unimpressed. {He} wants you to decide, {he} does not say how, whether it should go back to the wild or stay among people.
events.arc: The Wolf-Cub at the Shrine Gate

choices.text: Tell {him} the wild is where it belongs

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, takes the cub up in a basket and starts for the hills.

choices.text: Say it may stay at the shrine

effects.log: The cub is fed. It sleeps behind the altar and chews the corner of a cushion.

events.text: The cub grows. By winter it hunts the shrine's mice, by spring it hunts the pilgrims' hats. {npc} visits often, and sits on the step with a pipe and says very little. The wolf-cub follows {him} wherever {he} goes, and growls at the dog.
events.arc: The Wolf-Cub at the Shrine Gate

choices.text: Send the cub a quiet dream of a long run

effects.log: The cub dreams of pines, and wakes with its legs running.

choices.text: Feed it a scrap at dusk, secretly

effects.log: The cub is grateful and does not show it.

events.text: {npc} leaves the cub in the high woods, as the shrine's blessing, and for years a grey wolf watches the shrine from the ridge each dusk, and does not come down. The hunter sends a note once a year: 'Still there.' It is a perfect prayer.
events.arc: The Wolf-Cub at the Shrine Gate

choices.text: Send the grey wolf a clear night each year

effects.log: The ridge is lit by the full moon on the right night, every year. (+faith)

choices.text: Answer the hunter's note with one of your own

effects.log: A line goes back, anonymous. {npc} keeps it in a pipe.

events.text: The wolf stays at the shrine until it is old, a grey presence who walks pilgrims to the gate. When it dies, behind the altar, {npc} comes down from the hills to bury it. The shrine acquires a small tombstone, and a custom of bringing bones.
events.arc: The Wolf-Cub at the Shrine Gate

choices.text: Bless the grave of the shrine-wolf

effects.log: Wolves of the high woods are known to pass the shrine on their roads. (+faith)

choices.text: Sit at the grave with the hunter

effects.log: You sit in the dusk, two figures on a wall, and say nothing for an hour.

events.text: The grandchildren of a long-dead pilgrim climb to your hall, dusty and polite, in a party of six. {npc}, the eldest, says the old pilgrim walked here for forty years and never said what {he} prayed for. They have come to ask.
events.arc: The Pilgrim's Grandchildren

choices.text: Tell them the truth: nothing, only to be there

effects.log: {npc} takes it in. The younger ones are quiet. Then the smallest laughs, and the rest follow.

choices.text: Say the old pilgrim asked after them, by name

effects.log: You name the six, one by one. {npc} puts a hand to {his} mouth.

events.text: The six stay a week and fill the guest hall with sound. They fix the broken stair, mend the bell-rope, and ask you a hundred questions, none of which you can answer well. They leave a small clay lamp on the sill, unasked.
events.arc: The Pilgrim's Grandchildren

choices.text: Light the lamp each evening

effects.log: The lamp burns steady, and the guest hall feels less empty.

choices.text: Send each of them a small luck for the road

effects.log: Six small luck-threads leave the hall with six grandchildren.

events.text: {npc} returns every ten years, and every ten years brings more of the family. The hall becomes a stop for a line of travellers who do not pray to anyone in particular, and sit on the stair. You are, by common consent, the family's god.
events.arc: The Pilgrim's Grandchildren

choices.text: Accept the family as your own

effects.log: A branch of worshippers who ask for nothing, and give a great deal. (+faith)

choices.text: Keep it quiet; let them think of you as a host

effects.log: A guest-hall god is a fine thing to be.

events.text: The grandchildren take the names you spoke home, and name their own children for them. A family of children called after your guests grows up in a far valley, and each of them, one day, makes the climb. {npc} comes first, and is the first to say your name.
events.arc: The Pilgrim's Grandchildren

choices.text: Receive the new children by name

effects.log: You name every child who arrives. They look at you as at a miracle. (+faith)

choices.text: Let {npc} introduce them

effects.log: {npc} presents each, with a speech, and the hall hums.

events.text: {npc}, who was for sixty years the chief priest of the god across the ridge, appears at your gate with a bundle, retired, bent, and furious about it. The rival god has sent a younger priest to do the work. {He} asks for a corner in your shrine and a bowl of soup.
events.arc: The Rival's Retired Priest

choices.text: Give {him} a corner and the soup

effects.log: {npc} eats, glaring, and sleeps the sleep of the dispossessed. The rival god sends no word.

choices.text: Send {him} back with a letter to the rival god

effects.log: The letter is polite and unmistakable. {npc} reads it on the road and weeps for an hour.

events.text: Word reaches the rival god, who sends a stiff message across the ridge about poaching. {npc} reads it aloud from the shrine step, flat and loud, so that the whole valley can hear what is being said of {him}.
events.arc: The Rival's Retired Priest

choices.text: Answer the message with a bowl of soup, sent across
