effects.log: The bowl comes back washed. That is a reply.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the valley judge

effects.log: The valley judges, mostly in {npc}'s favour.

events.text: {npc} lives out {his} years in your shrine, and teaches your priests the rival's old hymns, which are better than yours. The rival god never asks for {him} back. On {his} last evening {he} asks to be buried facing the ridge, and you grant it.
events.arc: The Rival's Retired Priest

choices.text: Grant the grave on the ridge

effects.log: The grave faces the rival's mountain. Both gods bring flowers. (+faith)

choices.text: Send the rival god a dream of the old priest, content

effects.log: The rival wakes, and a gift of incense arrives at dawn.

events.text: The rival god's answer to your letter takes ten years, and comes in the person of the younger priest, nervous and grateful, to say the old one was right to ask. The two shrines trade hymns that year, and an old quarrel loses its edge.
events.arc: The Rival's Retired Priest

choices.text: Trade a hymn, and a priest, for a season

effects.log: A priest crosses the ridge each way, and both shrines are the better for it. (+faith)

choices.text: Thank the young priest, and send them home with soup

effects.log: The young priest goes down the road with a flask and a lighter heart.

events.text: On the drill field of your war domain a child with a stick drills three goats in the evening light. The goats are unmoved. The child's commands are very firm. A sergeant in the distance has stopped to watch, and is saluting, very gravely, with his hat held over his heart.

choices.text: Make the goats stand to attention for one moment

effects.log: The goats stand in a perfect row for the length of a breath. The child shrieks. The sergeant weeps.

choices.text: Let the child have the field

effects.log: The child marches the goats home, a general in a short coat.

events.text: In a household of your hearth domain, the fire has been let go out on purpose: the family is moving house in the morning, and the grandmother has said that a hearth should die at home, not be carried. The cold ashes are swept clean. Nobody sleeps.

choices.text: Carry one ember to the new hearth in the dark

effects.log: At dawn a spark is found in the ash of the new house. The grandmother pretends not to see it.

choices.text: Let the old hearth rest, as asked

effects.log: The hearth lies cold and the move goes on. The new fire is lit by hand, and it takes.

events.text: A seed in a sill-pot has not sprouted in nine years. A child waters it every day and calls it Grandfather, after nobody in particular. Your domain of life counts it among the least of its charges, and the most faithfully tended.

choices.text: Wake the seed, a little, on the child's birthday

effects.log: A white thread of root uncurls in the pot. The child's scream is heard three streets away.

choices.text: Let the child go on watering, and wait

effects.log: The seed does not sprout. The child waters it all the same, which is the whole of the miracle.

events.text: A dreamer in your dream domain dreams only of doors: green doors, painted doors, doors in the sea. They try the handle of each one and never open it. It is the most peaceful dreaming you have seen in a century, and the dreamer wakes refreshed.

choices.text: Open one door, a crack, and show a garden

effects.log: The dreamer's next dream has a garden in it, and stays there for years.

choices.text: Leave the doors shut; they are theirs

effects.log: The doors stay closed. The dreamer sleeps on, content.

events.text: A fisher in your sea domain talks to the third wave of every set, and has done for forty years. The wave, you notice, has begun to answer, in small gurgles at the boat's edge. The fisher has not noticed, and has never caught fewer fish.

choices.text: Let the wave tell the fisher what it has been saying

effects.log: The fisher hears at last, and laughs so hard the boat rocks.

choices.text: Keep the secret between the wave and the boat

effects.log: The conversation goes on, unnoticed and warm.

events.text: The echo in a deep valley of your mountains has begun to arrive late: a cry from the shepherd comes back after a full minute, in the shepherd's own voice, slightly amended. The shepherd has begun asking it for advice, and taking it.

choices.text: Make the echo wiser, a little

effects.log: The echo returns the shepherd's cry with a gentler turn. The flock prospers.

choices.text: Leave the echo to its own opinions

effects.log: The echo is wrong about the weather, and right about everything else.

events.text: Among the prayers at your gate there is one written in the large, shaky hand of a child who has just learned letters. It says, in full: I CAN WRITE NOW. THIS IS FOR YOU. The rest of the page is a drawing of a dog.

choices.text: Send the child a good word for the dog

effects.log: The dog gets a bone that afternoon, and the child is certain it was the prayer.

choices.text: Keep the page on the wall of your hall

effects.log: The page hangs among the great hymns. It is, by some distance, the best.

events.text: At the pantheon's dawn roll-call every god answers to their name in turn, and the roll takes an hour. You answer 'present' on time, as you have for four hundred years. The clerk, for the first time, looks up and says: 'Thank you.' It is startling.

choices.text: Answer the clerk's thanks with a bow

effects.log: The clerk goes pink, and the roll moves on faster that day.

choices.text: Say 'Always', quietly

effects.log: It is the pantheon's oldest answer, and the clerk writes it down.

events.text: By the door of the feast hall there is a row of coat-hooks, each with a god's name above it in gilt. At the end hangs a plain hook with no name at all. A Masterless god's coat hangs on it, and the coat is damp. Nobody has dried it. You take it to the fire.

choices.text: Dry the coat by the fire

effects.log: The coat is dry and warm when its owner comes for it. They look at you and say nothing, which is thanks.

choices.text: Ask the marshal for a hook with a name on it

effects.log: The marshal writes a name in chalk on the plain hook, and says it is a start.

events.text: A note from a rival god is pushed under your door: 'Your hedge is crooked.' You step outside to look. It is crooked. You have been meaning to straighten it for nine hundred years. The rival has taken three hundred of them to say it.

choices.text: Straighten the hedge, and send a thank-you

effects.log: The hedge is true by the evening. A short reply arrives: 'About time.' It is warm.

choices.text: Leave it crooked, and send a pot of tea

effects.log: The tea is returned empty, and a second note says: 'Crooked is acceptable.'

events.text: A bell rings at your shrine once a month with no one pulling the rope. The keeper says it is the debt-bell, rung by the shrine itself on the day its loan of faith falls due. It has been ringing for sixty years. The last coin of the debt is a single prayer.

choices.text: Answer the bell with one prayer of your own, for the shrine

effects.log: The bell rings a last time, long and sweet, and then stops for good.

choices.text: Let the shrine keep its debt a while longer

effects.log: The bell rings on. A shrine in debt, you decide, is a shrine that is still trying.

events.text: A child who once rang your bell every morning comes back grown, with a city accent and a bag of ledgers. They do not kneel. They ask if the bell is still there. It is, a little more green. They ring it once, hard, grinning like the child they were.

choices.text: Make the bell's note the same as the day they left

effects.log: They stop, hand still on the rope, and wipe their eyes with the other.

choices.text: Let the green bell speak for itself

effects.log: The note is low and a little hoarse, and they like it better.

events.text: At the gods' market, the Masterless stalls are put in the last row, behind a wall, where the foot-traffic does not reach. Today the wall has been moved a hand's breadth by a prankish wind, and a trickle of customers has found the row. Several have bought something.

choices.text: Move the wall another hand's breadth

effects.log: More customers find the row. The marshals sigh.

choices.text: Leave the wall to the wind

effects.log: The wall stays where the wind put it, and the stalls are busier than they have been in years.

events.text: {npc} is the herald who announces you at court, and does it beautifully, with a little extra music in the vowels. Today {he} asks to be transferred to the Office of Verse. {He} has written forty-one odes to doorways and has no one to read them to.
events.arc: The Herald Who Wanted to Be a Poet

choices.text: Read an ode, honestly, and say what moved you

effects.log: {npc} listens to your verdict with {his} eyes shut, then nods once. It was the first honest word {he} has had about the odes in a century.

choices.text: Promise a transfer and speak to the Office

effects.log: A note goes to the Office of Verse on your seal. It will take eleven years to be answered, which in the courts is promptly.

events.text: The announcing goes on while the request travels. {npc} begins to slip verse into your titles at court, a rhyme here, a rising line there. The Master of Ceremonies frowns at the rhymes and the courtiers, quietly, start arriving early to hear them.
events.arc: The Herald Who Wanted to Be a Poet

choices.text: Let the verses go on

effects.log: The courtiers hush when {npc} draws breath. You are the only god whose entrances are applauded.

choices.text: Ask {him} to keep the rhymes for feast days

effects.log: {He} agrees, bowing, a little crestfallen and a little proud of being told it was a problem of excess.

events.text: The Office of Verse answers at last: {npc} is accepted as a junior reader of odes. {He} stands at your door with the letter, unable to speak, and the court for once is the quiet one. Someone will have to announce you tomorrow.
events.arc: The Herald Who Wanted to Be a Poet

choices.text: Announce yourself, plainly, and let {him} listen

effects.log: You walk in and say your own name to an unamazed court. At the door, {npc} is weeping and taking notes.

choices.text: Borrow a stammering page and enjoy the hush

effects.log: The page stumbles through your titles, the court holds its breath, and you realise how much music {npc} gave you.

events.text: The transfer goes through and {npc} leaves with a cart of odes. Years on, a bound volume arrives with your name on the dedication page and a single line inside: 'For the god who said it was only fair.' It has gone into three editions.
events.arc: The Herald Who Wanted to Be a Poet

choices.text: Keep the volume by your bed

effects.log: You read an ode to a doorway every night and begin to notice doorways. (+faith)

choices.text: Send a copy to every shrine-keeper

effects.log: Keepers in forty valleys read verse aloud at dusk. The faithful take it for a new rite.

events.text: Not every prayer arrives on time. {npc} carries the late ones, delayed by distance, by illness, by wars between the prayer and its god. {He} lays today's bundle at your gate: forty-one prayers, the oldest nine hundred years old, all wanting rain for a harvest long since eaten.
events.arc: The Courier of Late Prayers

choices.text: Answer them, late, with a rain in the right valley

effects.log: The old valley wakes to a soft rain on bare soil. The farms are gone but the grass comes up green and nobody there knows why.

choices.text: Read each aloud before you decide

effects.log: You read them in the voice of their senders. By the thirtieth you know the valley better than any god alive.

events.text: {npc} has a rule: a late prayer is delivered to the god it was addressed to, never to the one who happens to be nearest. Today {he} asks you, politely, whether you accept a bundle addressed to a god you have never met and who may no longer exist.
events.arc: The Courier of Late Prayers

choices.text: Accept it as the nearest address

effects.log: You hold it for a week, uneasy, and then {npc} nods: it is a fair place to leave it.

choices.text: Refuse and ask where the addressee went

effects.log: {npc} makes a note. Asking where a god went is, apparently, rarer than anything {he} carries.

events.text: A prayer in the bundle is your own, from the days you were mortal, sent up to nobody. {npc} found it in a crevice of the sky and has carried it three thousand years looking for the right god. {He} says, shyly, that you were the right god after all.
events.arc: The Courier of Late Prayers

choices.text: Open it in front of {him}

effects.log: It is a child's prayer for an easier winter. You read it twice and find you are not quite steady. {npc} gives you a cup of water.

choices.text: Take it and keep it unopened

effects.log: It goes in a drawer. Some prayers, you decide, are for the one who sent them.

events.text: When the last bundle is done {npc} asks to be released from the late route: it is lonely, and {he} has begun to reply to prayers in {his} own head. You hold the route in your gift. There is no one else who would take it so gently.
events.arc: The Courier of Late Prayers

choices.text: Release {him}, and carry the late route yourself for a season

effects.log: You learn the long stairs and the wind that blows the wrong way. {npc} sends a postcard from a place with a harbour.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stay one more year and promise a companion

effects.log: A young runner is found for {him}. The late route has two lamps now.

events.text: On the morning of your pantheon's festival, the herald {npc} cannot find {his} voice. It is not a cold. It left in the night, as voices sometimes do, and it has been seen on the roof, according to the pigeons, trying to look dignified.
events.arc: The Herald Who Lost the Proclamation

choices.text: Search the roof with {him}

effects.log: You climb together and find the voice sulking behind a chimney. It will not come down for a lecture, but it will for a small joke.

choices.text: Proclaim the festival yourself, badly

effects.log: You proclaim it with great seriousness and no technique. The court is moved to laughter, then to a vague respect.

events.text: The voice is back, but changed. It has taken to humming between the titles, a low note under every announcement, like a bell underwater. Courtiers say it makes their teeth feel important. The Master of Ceremonies has asked for it to stop.
events.arc: The Herald Who Lost the Proclamation

choices.text: Defend the hum in the Master's hearing

effects.log: The hum is declared 'a regional accent'. {npc} bows, hum and all, and the court nods as if it had always been so.

choices.text: Ask {npc} whether {he} wants it gone

effects.log: {He} thinks, and says the hum is the first thing that has been entirely {his} own. It stays.

events.text: A year on, {npc} is asked to proclaim at a far court, and the hum goes with {him}. Gods who never listened to a proclamation in their lives stand on their chairs to hear it. A letter comes back thanking you for lending the voice.
events.arc: The Herald Who Lost the Proclamation

choices.text: Reply that the voice was never yours to lend

effects.log: The letter comes back with a gift: a bell tuned to the hum. {npc} hangs it over your door.

choices.text: Take the credit in silence

effects.log: It costs you nothing and you feel faintly worse for it.

events.text: In time {npc} is offered the post of First Herald. {He} hesitates: the First Herald proclaims for the whole pantheon and may not hum. You are asked, by someone, to advise. The hum has become something people travel for.
events.arc: The Herald Who Lost the Proclamation

choices.text: Advise taking the post, hum and all

effects.log: The pantheon accepts the hum. The festival that year is the first where nobody checks the clocks.

choices.text: Advise staying where {he} is happy

effects.log: {npc} turns down the post. The court is a little poorer, and {he} is much louder at home.

events.text: {npc} has carried notes for the Silent Hall for six thousand years and announces, over tea, that {he} will retire at the next new moon. {He} wants a garden and a long afternoon. There is a vacancy on the route that nobody wants.
events.arc: The Retiring Messenger of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Offer to find a successor

effects.log: You start asking around. The answer, mostly, is polite horror. A young godling in the kitchens has been seen reading the route map for fun.

choices.text: Offer to walk the route yourself, once

effects.log: You walk it: forty doors, nine bridges, one very old tea-stall. It takes all night and you come back with a respect for sore feet.

events.text: On the last week, {npc} shows you the habits of the route: which door sticks, which clerk hates mornings, which stair counts its own steps. None of it is written down. It is the sort of knowledge that vanishes when someone leaves.
events.arc: The Retiring Messenger of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Offer to write it down with {him}

effects.log: It takes three evenings. {npc} dictates and corrects. The result is a small book that makes the route sound like a person.

choices.text: Listen and keep it only in your head

effects.log: You carry it like a bird. Some of it will be gone by spring.

events.text: The successor, a nervous godling, takes the route with the book in {his} pocket. {npc} sends a note from the garden: tomatoes. In the whole six thousand years it is the first thing {he} has ever grown and {he} wants you to be told.
events.arc: The Retiring Messenger of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Send a seedling of your own domain's best

effects.log: It arrives and thrives in the wrong soil. {npc} sends back a tomato the size of a fist. (+faith)

choices.text: Send nothing, but visit on a long afternoon

effects.log: You sit in the garden and say nothing for an hour. It is the finest gift either of you has had.

events.text: The route is broken: a door has been bricked up in a feud between two clerks. {npc}, in {his} garden, hears of it, puts down {his} trowel and comes back for one night. The Silent Hall has never been so grateful for an old man's irritation.
events.arc: The Retiring Messenger of the Silent Hall

choices.text: Walk the route with {him} and fix the door

effects.log: The two of you reopen the door at dawn. The clerks, ashamed, share a pot of tea.

choices.text: Leave it to {him} and keep the kettle hot

effects.log: By evening the route is whole. {npc} goes home to the tomatoes satisfied.

events.text: {npc} is the fastest runner your pantheon has trained, and has one flaw: {he} arrives before the message is sent. Notes you have not yet written are received, thanked for, and answered. The court clerks have stopped trying to explain it.
events.arc: The Runner Who Arrives Before the Message

choices.text: Write the note you were about to write

effects.log: The note is delivered, thanked for, and filed under the day before it was written. {npc} considers this a normal Tuesday.

choices.text: Ask {him} to slow down, for a day

effects.log: {npc} does, and finds the world strangely long. {He} comes back with a pebble picked up on the road, astonished.

events.text: A rival god sends word that your runner is stealing the pleasure of surprise from the court. The word is carried, as it must be, by {npc}, who delivers it to you before the rival has finished writing it.
events.arc: The Runner Who Arrives Before the Message

choices.text: Answer it in advance, politely

effects.log: You send a gracious reply before the complaint exists. The rival, reading both together, is puzzled and then flattered.

choices.text: Tell the rival to try keeping up

effects.log: The rival sends a very short note back. {npc} brings it before you finish the sentence.

events.text: {npc} outruns something this season: a plague of idle prayers that were threatening to stall the whole route. {He} delivers them in a flash, before they pile up, and is found on the last step, laughing in the dust, entirely out of breath.
events.arc: The Runner Who Arrives Before the Message

choices.text: Honour {him} at the next feast

effects.log: A seat of honour is set for {npc}, who arrives after dessert, early.

choices.text: Give {him} a day of rest, enforced

effects.log: {npc} sleeps for twelve hours and wakes with a better sense of time.

events.text: The day {npc} learns to slow, {he} stops arriving early, and for the first time in a hundred years misses a message by a minute. {He} is mortified. The court cheers. A message that is only on time is, to a god, a sort of miracle.
events.arc: The Runner Who Arrives Before the Message

choices.text: Teach {him} how a slow day tastes

effects.log: {npc} learns to walk, and finds a stall that sells pears, and a stair with a view.

choices.text: Say nothing; let it be {his} secret

effects.log: {He} keeps the pebble on a shelf. It is a very small thing to hold a whole afternoon.

events.text: {npc} is a courier of the Sun pantheon who will only carry good news. Disasters are rephrased into opportunities, losses into 'changes of ownership'. The whole court knows it, and half of it has begun to dread the arrival of cheerful letters.
events.arc: The Messenger Who Carries Only Good News

choices.text: Ask {him} to deliver one bad piece of news plainly

effects.log: {npc} takes a breath, delivers a flood in your valley as a flood in your valley, and goes pale, but the court listens and acts.

choices.text: Let {him} carry on, and read between the lines

effects.log: You learn to read {his} letters like a weather glass: the brighter the tone, the worse the matter.

events.text: A real disaster comes: a drought in a valley you share with a neighbour. {npc}'s letter says only that 'the harvest looks light, and the sky is generous with sun'. The neighbour's court takes it as a blessing. Nobody sends water.
events.arc: The Messenger Who Carries Only Good News

choices.text: Send water yourself, quietly

effects.log: Springs rise in the valley. Nobody knows who to thank, and that is enough.

choices.text: Write to the neighbour, plainly, asking for help

effects.log: A reply arrives within the hour with a promise of rain and a grudging respect.

events.text: {npc} comes to you after the drought, grey in the face. {He} says {he} has never been able to carry sorrow, because carrying it means being the one to say it. {He} asks, humbly, whether it is possible to learn.
events.arc: The Messenger Who Carries Only Good News

choices.text: Teach {him} to sit with a bad letter first

effects.log: You sit with {npc} while {he} reads a grief aloud, once, and again, until it can be said steadily.

choices.text: Give {him} a post carrying only celebrations

effects.log: {npc} is happy and relieved. The court sighs, and goes on reading between the lines.

events.text: {npc} is promoted, at last, for something nobody expected: {he} reads the court the worst news of the century in the most gentle voice anyone has heard, and the court, to its astonishment, does not break. The gentleness was the point all along.
events.arc: The Messenger Who Carries Only Good News

choices.text: Stand beside {him} while {he} reads

effects.log: You are in the front row, hands folded. {npc} sees you and does not falter. (+faith)

choices.text: Send a gift of plain paper for honest letters

effects.log: The stationery becomes a custom: a plain page for a plain word.

events.text: The heralds of the divine courts have gathered in the cloister and announced that they will no longer carry insults between gods. {npc}, their elder, reads out the demand in a voice worn smooth by ten thousand polite sentences. A feud is due this week and no one will carry it.
events.arc: The Heralds Who Refuse to Carry Insults

choices.text: Side with the heralds in open court

effects.log: You stand and say the heralds are not letters. The room is cold, and then, grudgingly, nods.

choices.text: Offer to carry the week's insult yourself

effects.log: You carry the feud's first insult across the hall in your own voice, which makes it so awkward that both parties apologise at once.

events.text: The strike is a quiet one: heralds sit on the stairs of the cloister with their sashes folded on their knees. Messages pile up. A council of senior gods has been called to settle the matter, and no one has been able to find the agenda.
events.arc: The Heralds Who Refuse to Carry Insults

choices.text: Bring the heralds tea

effects.log: The tea gets round the whole cloister, and a few of the senior gods, hearing of it, send biscuits.

choices.text: Sit among the heralds for an hour

effects.log: {npc} makes room for you without comment. It is, you realise, the first time a god has sat on those stairs.

events.text: The council agrees, narrowly: heralds will carry what is true and civil, and will return anything else with a note of regret. {npc} is hoisted in the cloister, embarrassed, and carried to the kitchens on a tray, since there is no chair.
events.arc: The Heralds Who Refuse to Carry Insults

choices.text: Propose a day of thanks for the heralds

effects.log: A yearly day is set where gods carry their own messages. The cloister is festooned with sashes.

choices.text: Send a case of good ink

effects.log: The heralds write beautiful regrets for a decade.

events.text: A year after the strike, the great feud is finally settled, and not by insults. {npc} reads out the peace treaty in person, having carried every earlier draft, and every unkind word, back and forth, and refused to deliver the worst of them.
events.arc: The Heralds Who Refuse to Carry Insults

choices.text: Thank {him} publicly for the words that were never sent

effects.log: The hall is hushed. {npc} bows, and says it was the best work of the century to be unemployed in the matter of cruelty.

choices.text: Raise a glass to the unsent letters

effects.log: A toast to everything that was not said runs round the hall twice.

events.text: {npc} is a wind-courier with a reputation for shortcuts. Today {he} arrives with your letter a day early, flustered, with a feather of cloud in {his} hair, and admits {he} came through a mortal's dream to save time. The mortal has not yet noticed.
events.arc: The Courier Who Took a Shortcut Through a Dream

choices.text: Ask whose dream it was

effects.log: {npc} names a woman in a lowland town. In the dream, {he} says, there was a long table, a dog and a letter. You will want to look in on the dreamer.

choices.text: Tell {him} the shortcut is forbidden

effects.log: {npc} bows, shaken. The shortcut is closed, and the roads take twice as long.

events.text: The mortal in the lowland town has begun to dream of the courier: a figure in a grey coat who leaves a letter on a table and does not stay. She writes it down in a notebook, with the date, and has started to wait for the next.
events.arc: The Courier Who Took a Shortcut Through a Dream

choices.text: Leave a letter on her table yourself

effects.log: She wakes with the sense of having been thanked. She writes the date in the notebook and underlines it.

choices.text: Ask the courier to stop the visits

effects.log: The dreams stop. She stays up the next night, waiting, then goes to bed disappointed.

events.text: Years later the woman gives birth to a child who runs very fast. The child's grandmother says it is in the blood, and tells no one about the grey coat. {npc} hears of it and comes to you, white to the ears, to ask whether this is {his} doing.
events.arc: The Courier Who Took a Shortcut Through a Dream

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: probably, and gladly

effects.log: {npc} sits for a long time. Then {he} asks whether a courier may send a present to a child.

choices.text: Say the world is large and much is accident

effects.log: {npc} takes comfort in it, though not quite enough.

events.text: The shortcut stays closed, and the lowland dreams never return. But the notebook is kept, and on the day the dreamer dies the pages are laid on the dreamer's chest. {npc} reads the last entry, out of curiosity, and finds one word: 'Thanks.'
events.arc: The Courier Who Took a Shortcut Through a Dream

choices.text: Let {him} keep the notebook

effects.log: {npc} hangs it in the courier house, between a map and a bell.

choices.text: Have the notebook copied for the archive

effects.log: The archive files it under 'courtesies'. It is the only entry there.

events.text: {npc} stands at your gate in a faded sash, with a scroll and the stiff posture of a servant whose master has been forgotten for eight hundred years. {He} says {he} still has messages to deliver, and no one to deliver them to.
events.arc: The Herald of a God Who Is Gone

choices.text: Take the scrolls and read them

effects.log: They are small, tender notes of a long-vanished god's daily business: a favourite pear, a word for the harvest. You are the first to read them in centuries.

choices.text: Offer {him} a place in your household

effects.log: {npc} bows and shifts the scrolls from one hand to the other, as if unsure which to put down.

events.text: Among the scrolls is a list of the dead god's worshippers, ten thousand names long. {npc} has kept them in order, and every year {he} reads them aloud, alone, in an empty courtyard. No one has been there to hear it since the second century.
events.arc: The Herald of a God Who Is Gone

choices.text: Join the reading this year

effects.log: You stand in the courtyard and hear ten thousand names. It takes the whole night and you do not leave.

choices.text: Ask whether any names are still alive

effects.log: {npc} blinks. No one has asked that before. {He} spends a month checking.

events.text: Of the ten thousand names, three still pray. They have long forgotten whom, but light a lamp on a certain day for a god whose name has worn off the wall. {npc} has found them, and begs you to let the old god be remembered, even in you.
events.arc: The Herald of a God Who Is Gone

choices.text: Take the old god's lamp-day into your own calendar

effects.log: Your calendar grows by a day. Three households light lamps, and think nothing odd about it. (+faith)

choices.text: Let the lamps burn unaltered, and send a quiet blessing

effects.log: A blessing falls on three households who will never know it.

events.text: {npc} grows lighter as the lamps are lit. At the third year's lamp-day {he} is not at the gate, only the sash, folded on the step, and the last scroll on top of it, unrolled to a note: 'Thank you for hearing it.' The note was written, you realise, in {his} own hand.
events.arc: The Herald of a God Who Is Gone

choices.text: Hang the sash in your hall

effects.log: It hangs beside your banner, faded and quiet.

choices.text: Add the name to the lamp-day, and the herald's with it

effects.log: Four names are said at the lamp-day now.

events.text: A courier named {npc} arrives with a sealed letter addressed to 'the god of whatever is happening at the time of delivery'. It is not for you, yet it is: whatever is happening to you today will be its subject. {He} refuses to leave it unopened.
events.arc: The Letter Nobody May Open

choices.text: Open it at once

effects.log: Inside, in a patient hand, is a single sentence: 'This is the day you will be tested by something small.' The courier looks relieved.

choices.text: Wait until evening to open it

effects.log: Nothing happens all day, which is itself the test. The letter, unopened, sits on the table like a patient cat.

events.text: The test arrives in a form no one planned. A shrine-keeper's goat wanders into your hall during an audience, eats a petition, and sits down in front of your seat with the manner of a minor god. The court looks to you.
events.arc: The Letter Nobody May Open

choices.text: Hear the goat's case

effects.log: You hear it, gravely. The goat is, on the whole, justified. The court is delighted.

choices.text: Have the goat escorted out with honours

effects.log: The goat leaves in procession. A petitioner follows, weeping from laughter.

events.text: {npc} returns the next season to ask how the day went. {He} does not know who wrote the letter, only that it was found on a stair, and that many such letters are circulating, each addressed to no one in particular and each right about the day.
events.arc: The Letter Nobody May Open

choices.text: Ask to see the other letters

effects.log: A stack of letters is brought, each a gentle prediction. They are in your handwriting, from a time you have not lived yet.

choices.text: Ask {him} to stop carrying them

effects.log: {npc} agrees. The letters, you learn, continue to arrive by other means.

events.text: On a calm morning a letter arrives with no courier at all, addressed to 'the god who waited until evening'. Inside is a single line: 'Thank you for the patience, it was the right test.' You have not heard from the sender since.
events.arc: The Letter Nobody May Open

choices.text: Keep the letter in your sleeve

effects.log: It stays with you a long while. Patience, after that, comes a little easier.

choices.text: Frame it above the door

effects.log: Visitors read it and nod as if it were addressed to them, which, in a way, it was.

events.text: {npc} keeps the Rolls of Precedence, and knows to the inch where each god stands in a procession. Yours has just moved up two places, quietly, in a recopying of the rolls. {He} comes to explain it, which is how you learn that nobody had asked.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Keeps the Order of Precedence

choices.text: Ask what you did to earn it

effects.log: {npc} consults a ledger for an hour. The answer is: a small kindness to a minor god, seven hundred years ago, recorded and then forgotten.

choices.text: Ask to be moved back

effects.log: The clerk turns a delicate shade of green. No one has ever asked to move back in the Rolls.

events.text: Word of the change reaches the other gods. One, two places below you now, writes to {npc} in a fury of capitals. The clerk answers every letter in a style so courteous that the writer apologises, unprompted, in the next.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Keeps the Order of Precedence

choices.text: Send the rival god a small gift

effects.log: The god accepts, reluctantly, and falls silent for a decade.

choices.text: Stay out of it

effects.log: The storm passes without you. Courtesy, in the courts, is a form of weather.

events.text: {npc} summons you to the Hall of Rolls to see the book at last. The pages are old, the ink older, and the last margin carries a note in an early hand: 'Order is a kindness. Do not let the rolls grow cruel.' {He} asks if you will help keep them gentle.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Keeps the Order of Precedence

choices.text: Offer a seat on the committee that revises the Rolls

effects.log: You join the committee. Its first act is to add a footnote to every demotion. (+faith)

choices.text: Offer a small sum of attention each year

effects.log: A visit each year, a cup of tea, a question. It is enough.

events.text: In the end the Rolls are rewritten as a circle, with no first place and no last, and {npc} oversees the copying in the finest hand of a long career. The old gods grumble. The young gods, who have never been given a seat in their lives, are said to weep.
events.arc: The Clerk Who Keeps the Order of Precedence

choices.text: Sign the new Rolls first

effects.log: Your signature sits on the circle, no higher than the others.

choices.text: Hold the ink for {him} as {he} writes

effects.log: You hold the ink pot for a whole afternoon, a god serving a clerk, and no one objects.

events.text: {npc} runs the lowest archive of the heavenly court: the room where petitions go that no god answered. It is vast, quiet and smells of paper. {He} has read every one and says it is the most hopeful library in existence, because everyone in it is still asking.
events.arc: The Archivist of Unanswered Petitions

choices.text: Ask to read a petition at random

effects.log: You draw one: a girl asking for a kite to come back. It is eleven hundred years old, and the kite is mentioned twice more in other files.

choices.text: Ask which petition {he} would answer first

effects.log: {npc} does not hesitate: a tradesman asking for one good winter. It is, {he} says, the smallest and the oldest.

events.text: {npc} has a request. The archive has a rule that no petition may be answered once filed, and {he} has begun to wonder who made it. You are asked to look into it. The rule, it turns out, was made by a god who was tired and wanted the files to be quiet.
events.arc: The Archivist of Unanswered Petitions

choices.text: Ask the court to revisit the rule

effects.log: A motion is entered. It will take a century, and the court will call it brisk.

choices.text: Answer one petition quietly, and see what happens

effects.log: Nothing happens, except that in the archive a petition goes warm in {npc}'s hand.

events.text: The kite is answered at last: a gust, a field, a woman of forty with a grey braid, looking up. Nobody knows why the woman looks. The woman bends down, picks up a small paper kite from the grass, and laughs for a long time.
events.arc: The Archivist of Unanswered Petitions

choices.text: Let the memory of it reach the archive

effects.log: {npc} adds a note to the petition: 'Answered, though late.' The file glows for a week.

choices.text: Keep it a secret between you and the kite

effects.log: The kite is the woman's own. You are not mentioned.

events.text: One good winter is granted to the tradesman's descendants, a hundred and forty of them, spread across three valleys. {npc} writes the grant into the archive and, for the first time, closes a file. {He} sits for a while with it closed.
events.arc: The Archivist of Unanswered Petitions

choices.text: Stay with {him} while the file stays closed

effects.log: You stay. The archive is very quiet, and a little less sad.

choices.text: Tell the court that one of its files is finished

effects.log: The court is faintly alarmed, and then pleased. There is a motion about it.

events.text: {npc} copies the court's chronicles, and has been caught altering them. A battle is a little less bloody, a quarrel a little more gracious. {He} admits it without shame: the old gods, {he} says, deserved better than the way they were remembered.
events.arc: The Copyist Who Corrects History

choices.text: Ask to read the changes

effects.log: You read the originals and the copies side by side. The copies are better writing, kinder, and entirely untrue in small ways.

choices.text: Tell {him} to stop at once

effects.log: {npc} stops, with great reluctance, and spends a month copying the plain truth. It is the worst writing of the century.

events.text: A visiting scholar notices the changes and brings it to the court. The court is in an uproar. Half of it wants the copyist expelled; the other half confesses, in whispers, that it has been reading the corrected versions to children for years.
events.arc: The Copyist Who Corrects History

choices.text: Speak for {npc} in front of the scholar

effects.log: The scholar listens, nods, and leaves with a note to be quieter about it in future.

choices.text: Say the truth must stand, and offer to help {him} write footnotes

effects.log: The footnotes become a joint work of record and mercy.

events.text: The compromise is a new kind of book: a chronicle in two columns, the old facts on one side and the gentler telling on the other. {npc} oversees the printing and takes, for once, no credit. The book sells out in a day.
events.arc: The Copyist Who Corrects History

choices.text: Write a preface for it

effects.log: Your preface is short: 'Both columns are true. They are true of different things.' It is quoted for centuries.

choices.text: Buy twenty copies for the shrines

effects.log: The shrines read both columns on feast days.

events.text: Years later the copyist is asked to correct the chronicle of your own deeds. You are given the pen. {He} watches, quietly, as you write the true version without a single kindness, and gently takes the pen back for the last line.
events.arc: The Copyist Who Corrects History

choices.text: Let {him} soften it

effects.log: The last line is kinder than the facts and truer than the rest. You read it twice.

choices.text: Insist on the plain version

effects.log: The plain version stands. {npc} bows, respectfully disappointed, and fixes the margins.

events.text: The court's archivists have discovered that a year is missing from the records: the five hundred and ninth of the third age. Not erased, just absent, like a tooth. {npc}, the head archivist, asks for your help, since it was a year in which you were, officially, nowhere.
events.arc: The Year the Archive Lost

choices.text: Search your own memory of the year

effects.log: You recall a long quiet, a river, an argument about nothing. It is a pleasant memory and not at all helpful.

choices.text: Go through the lower stacks with {him}

effects.log: You wander the stacks for a week and find a door that has not been opened since the year that was lost.

events.text: Rumours spread through the court: the year was hidden on purpose, by a god who had something to be ashamed of. Gods begin to look at one another with a new narrowness. {npc} begs you to find the truth before it turns into an accusation.
events.arc: The Year the Archive Lost

choices.text: Calm the court with a short speech

effects.log: You speak on the value of not knowing. It is not what they came for, and it works.

choices.text: Promise a full inquiry

effects.log: The court settles, somewhat. An inquiry is a kind of lullaby.

events.text: The door opens on a small room with a single table and the missing year laid out on it, folded like a letter: a year in which the whole pantheon, exhausted, agreed to do nothing. The entry is signed by every god. They forgot, in the end, because they were happy.
events.arc: The Year the Archive Lost

choices.text: Leave the year closed, and tell the court only that it was peaceful

effects.log: The court takes the news quietly. A faint wistfulness settles over the next festival.

choices.text: Read it aloud to the court

effects.log: The court listens, and sits very still, and then begins to laugh. Some of them cry.

events.text: The year is entered in the records at last, in {npc}'s careful hand: 'The year of rest.' It is a single line. The archivist closes the book as one might close the lid of a music box, and the room smells, for a moment, of rain.
events.arc: The Year the Archive Lost

choices.text: Propose a yearly day of rest in its honour

effects.log: The first Day of Rest is observed the following spring. Nobody quite knows what to do with it. (+faith)

choices.text: Thank {npc} for the patience of the search

effects.log: {He} accepts the thanks with the air of one who has been reading backwards for a century.

events.text: {npc} is compiling an index of every god's name, in every language it has ever been spelled. It has taken four thousand years. {He} arrives with a question: your name appears twice in the index, in two different hands, as two different gods.
events.arc: The Indexer of Names

choices.text: Ask to see both entries

effects.log: One is your name as the faithful say it, the other a variant from a valley that thought you were a different god. They have been praying to the variant for six centuries.

choices.text: Merge the entries on the spot

effects.log: {npc} winces and does it, with a flourish. A valley's god is silently absorbed into you, with all its debts.

events.text: The valley that prays to the variant is told, by a visiting priest, that its god is the same as yours. The valley refuses. It likes its god, who is shy, answers promptly and has a different favourite colour. The priest is almost cheerful about it.
events.arc: The Indexer of Names

choices.text: Send the valley a word of thanks

effects.log: A warm wind goes through the valley's temple, addressed to the variant, from you. The shy god, wherever it is, is grateful.

choices.text: Ask the valley what the shy god is like

effects.log: A shepherd tells you in detail. It sounds, a little, like you on a good day.

events.text: The index finds a third entry, and a fourth: a pilgrim's nickname for you, a child's drawing labelled with your name, a joke from a feast that stuck. {npc} adds them all, delighted. The index is not a list of gods, {he} says, but a list of the ways you are loved.
events.arc: The Indexer of Names

choices.text: Read the new entries aloud

effects.log: You read them in the quiet of the archive. Each is odd, small and undeniable.

choices.text: Ask {him} to add a column for the ones who do not love you

effects.log: {He} adds it, and the column is shorter than you feared.

events.text: The index is finished at last, eleven volumes long, and {npc} places the final page with trembling hands. Then {he} lifts the first volume and asks you to hold it: a god's weight, {he} says, is the sum of the names it has been given.
events.arc: The Indexer of Names

choices.text: Hold the volume for the length of a breath

effects.log: It is lighter than you expected and warmer. {npc} lets out a breath.

choices.text: Add your own name, in your own hand, as the last entry

effects.log: It is the shortest entry in the index. {npc} frames the page.

events.text: {npc} supplies the court's scribes with ink, and brews it from dawn: the pale gold that pools on the plateau at first light. {He} comes to ask for a favour. The dawn has been thin this year, the ink watery, and the scribes are grumbling.
events.arc: The Scribe Who Makes Ink of Dawn

choices.text: Make the dawn brighter over {his} plateau

effects.log: The sun comes up thick and amber. {npc} fills forty jars before breakfast and weeps a little.

choices.text: Ask the scribes to be patient with a thin ink

effects.log: A season of pale, honest writing follows. The court's letters grow shorter, and kinder.

events.text: A rival ink-maker sells a cheaper black made from soot and claims it will last longer. The court tries it. It does last longer, and the letters written in it are curiously cold. {npc} shrugs, brews on, and says the dawn will outlive the soot.
events.arc: The Scribe Who Makes Ink of Dawn

choices.text: Order a bottle of each, and compare

effects.log: The soot ink is clear and flat; the dawn ink warms the page. You keep both for different letters.

choices.text: Praise the dawn ink at court

effects.log: Three scribes switch back. The rival sulks, but is invited to the next feast.

events.text: The court's highest decree of the century is written in dawn ink, at {npc}'s own bench, in the pale gold light of the plateau. As the scribe signs the last line the whole page glows, and the ink, for a moment, tastes of morning.
events.arc: The Scribe Who Makes Ink of Dawn

choices.text: Sign it in dawn ink yourself

effects.log: Your name goes on in gold. The decree is read aloud in three courts and carried, by common consent, as a very warm one.

choices.text: Hold the lamp while {he} writes

effects.log: You hold the lamp for an hour, and it is the quietest hour of the year.

events.text: In {npc}'s last year at the bench, {he} bottles a final jar of the thin pale dawn, and labels it with your name. It is the ink of the honest year. {He} asks you to write one letter in it, to whomever you most owe the truth.
events.arc: The Scribe Who Makes Ink of Dawn

choices.text: Write to the mortal you were

effects.log: The letter is short. It is read by no one, and it is the most honest page you have written.

choices.text: Write to a god you have wronged

effects.log: The reply comes in a week, in the same pale ink.

events.text: {npc} keeps the Ledger of Oaths, in which every vow a god has sworn is written, and its fulfilment noted. Yours is a short entry, made when you were new: 'To hear the smallest prayer.' {He} asks, with perfect politeness, whether you intend to keep it.
events.arc: The Clerk of Oaths

choices.text: Say you have, and name three small prayers

effects.log: {npc} checks the three against the ledger and makes a tick in the margin. The tick takes a long time.

choices.text: Admit you have not, always, and ask for a chance

effects.log: {npc} marks a note in pencil rather than ink, which is, you gather, a kindness.

events.text: The ledger is audited each century, and the auditors are never kind. A visiting god of the Hall has been sent to examine your page. {npc} reads it for an hour in perfect silence, then asks what, precisely, you consider the smallest prayer.
events.arc: The Clerk of Oaths

choices.text: Say it is a child asking for the dark to go away

effects.log: The auditor nods and writes a line you cannot read.

choices.text: Say you are still finding out

effects.log: The auditor allows this, grudgingly, as an answer.

events.text: The smallest prayer arrives that spring: a sparrow, if a sparrow prayed, asking for a crumb. You send a loaf the size of a house and the entire sparrow family weeps with astonishment. {npc} records it in ink, with a flourish.
events.arc: The Clerk of Oaths

choices.text: Send the sparrows a nest of gold thread

effects.log: They nest in your hall for a century. (+faith)

choices.text: Send nothing more; one loaf is a vow kept

effects.log: The vow is marked fulfilled. {npc} dusts the page.

events.text: At the next audit the page is read again. This time the ledger holds two entries for you: the old oath, and below it, in {npc}'s hand, 'Kept, imperfectly, and with love.' You are told this is the highest mark the ledger allows.
events.arc: The Clerk of Oaths

choices.text: Ask to keep a copy of the page

effects.log: A copy is made. You keep it where you can see it, and it humbles you daily.

choices.text: Ask {him} to leave the word 'imperfectly'

effects.log: {He} does. It is, {he} says, the truest word on the page.

events.text: The great archive is staffed by day. By night it is dark, silent and, according to rumour, quietly tidied by someone nobody has seen. Tonight you stay late and meet {npc}, shelving scrolls by lantern, who says {he} is only a night clerk and will be gone by dawn.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Works Only at Night

choices.text: Ask what {he} reads when no one is looking

effects.log: {npc} confesses to a fondness for lost-property lists: the beautiful, sad catalogues of things gods have mislaid.

choices.text: Offer to help shelve

effects.log: You shelve for an hour and discover how much you do not know about the filing of sorrow.

events.text: The day clerks complain that the shelves are sometimes tidier than they left them, and that books return to the wrong place for the right reasons. They suspect a ghost. {npc} suggests to you, shyly, that a ghost would at least be punctual.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Works Only at Night

choices.text: Keep the night clerk's secret

effects.log: The day clerks remain mystified. Mysteries, in a library, are a kind of warmth.

choices.text: Introduce {him} to the head archivist

effects.log: The head archivist stammers, shakes {npc}'s hand, and offers a day contract. {He} declines it, kindly.

events.text: On the longest night of the year you find {npc} at the back of the archive, reading by a small flame. {He} is reading your own file, slowly, with the care of someone who has been through it many times and likes a good number of the pages.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Works Only at Night

choices.text: Ask if you may read it with {him}

effects.log: You read it together. It is a very odd experience to be a story in someone else's hands.

choices.text: Leave {him} to finish it in peace

effects.log: You leave a lantern burning and a cup of tea. In the morning the cup is empty and washed.

events.text: {npc} is discovered at last, by a young apprentice who walks in early. The night clerk is promoted, against {his} will, to day duties. {He} is miserable. You hold a quiet word with the head archivist: the night is {his} proper hour.
events.arc: The Archivist Who Works Only at Night

choices.text: Win {him} back the night shift

effects.log: The night shift is restored, with an honorarium of one candle a week.

choices.text: Let {him} try the day for a season

effects.log: {He} tries. In spring {he} asks, sheepishly, to go back.

events.text: A notice arrives from the court archive: a scroll borrowed in your name is nine hundred years overdue. {npc}, the lending clerk, signs the notice with a stern flourish. You do not remember borrowing it. You do not remember what it was.
events.arc: The Scroll Nine Hundred Years Overdue

choices.text: Search your hall for it

effects.log: You turn out chests and shelves and a very old shoe. Nothing. {npc} adds a note: 'Search noted. Fine remains.'

choices.text: Visit the archive and ask what the scroll was

effects.log: {npc} consults a card index. The scroll is a collection of lullabies, borrowed by a younger version of you, and never returned.

events.text: The fine is nine hundred years of interest. {npc} calculates it with relish and a pencil. The sum, converted to the court's currency of favours, comes to a small number of dinners, a poem and an apology to a minor goddess you do not recall insulting.
events.arc: The Scroll Nine Hundred Years Overdue

choices.text: Pay in dinners

effects.log: Three dinners are held in your hall, to which {npc} comes with a very small appetite and a ledger.

choices.text: Write the poem and skip the dinners

effects.log: The poem is read aloud. {npc} is moved, against protocol, and fines you an extra line.

events.text: The lullabies turn up in the least likely place: a nursery. A shrine-keeper's child has been singing them to a wooden horse. They are in your own voice, learned from nobody, handed down the generations of a family that never knew they had them.
events.arc: The Scroll Nine Hundred Years Overdue

choices.text: Return the scroll's words to the archive, and leave the lullabies to the family

effects.log: You copy the words and leave the tune where it lives. {npc} stamps the notice 'Discharged, with love'.

choices.text: Sit by the nursery window and listen

effects.log: The song comes through a keyhole of stars. The child is asleep before the second verse.

events.text: {npc} presents the discharge in person, and shyly asks whether a lullaby might be added to the archive's collection. The clerk who fined you has, you learn, been awake for ten years with nothing to sing. You teach {him} one, softly, in the lending room.
events.arc: The Scroll Nine Hundred Years Overdue

choices.text: Stay until {he} has it by heart

effects.log: The lending room, that night, holds the sound of a very stern clerk singing.

choices.text: Send {him} the tune on a scroll, properly lent

effects.log: The scroll is returned within a week, with a ribbon.

events.text: A petition lands on your desk stamped twice, once approved and once refused, by two different clerks on the same day. {npc}, the junior who carried it, wants to know which stamp is binding. The petitioner is a widow asking for a winter's roof.
events.arc: The Petition Stamped Twice

choices.text: Honour the approval

effects.log: You tear the second stamp from the page and send the roof. {npc} watches, wide-eyed, as law is made out of kindness.

choices.text: Call the two clerks to explain themselves

effects.log: The clerks arrive, reluctant. One had misread the widow's name; the other had not. The mistake is neither's alone.

events.text: The two clerks, shaken, begin to quarrel over who is to blame. Their quarrel spreads: soon the whole floor is divided into the Approvers and the Refusers, each with a ribbon. {npc} comes to you with the ribbons in {his} hands, helpless.
events.arc: The Petition Stamped Twice

choices.text: Declare a day on which all ribbons are swapped

effects.log: The day of swapped ribbons is a farce, a relief and a lesson. The quarrel loses its edge.

choices.text: Ask both sides to list what they have in common

effects.log: The list is longer than anyone expected. It includes, at the bottom, the widow.

events.text: The widow's roof stands that winter. {npc} visits to confirm it. The widow offers {him} tea, and asks what the stamps meant. {He} cannot explain. The widow nods, and says that was the guess: all the courts are made of tea and stamps.
events.arc: The Petition Stamped Twice

choices.text: Send the widow a lamp in thanks

effects.log: The lamp burns blue and low and brightens the cottage for years.

choices.text: Send {npc} back with a better answer

effects.log: {He} explains: the stamps mean someone looked. The widow seems satisfied.

events.text: The double stamp becomes, in time, a rule: a petition marked both ways is always read as yes, until a god says otherwise in person. {npc} is the first to apply it, and the first to be thanked. {He} learns that law can be a kindness with a form to fill.
events.arc: The Petition Stamped Twice

choices.text: Draft the rule's preface yourself

effects.log: Your preface is brief, and the rule is cited in a thousand cases.

choices.text: Let {npc} sign it alone

effects.log: {He} signs, trembling, in a hand that steadies halfway down the page.

events.text: The clerks of your pantheon's records office run on tea, and a rota that no one has ever seen written down. {npc}, its keeper, is retiring and asks you to keep the rota safe. It lives, {he} says, in a teapot on the third shelf.
events.arc: The Clerks' Tea Rota

choices.text: Take the teapot home

effects.log: The rota is a list on the inside of the lid, in four hands, with a stain from every century. You make tea in it, carefully.

choices.text: Leave the pot where it is and promise to look after it

effects.log: The third shelf becomes, by quiet understanding, a shrine of sorts. Clerks bow to it on the way to their desks.

events.text: A dispute arises: the new head of records wants the tea replaced with a printed schedule of 'hydration intervals'. The clerks go quiet in a way that makes the corridors feel colder. {npc} writes you a note from retirement, three words long.
events.arc: The Clerks' Tea Rota

choices.text: Defend the tea in the head's office

effects.log: You speak for the pot. The head listens, flushes, and lets the matter drop.

choices.text: Propose a trial of both systems

effects.log: The trial ends in a week. The schedule is quietly retired to a drawer.

events.text: On the day of {npc}'s farewell the whole office brews at once, and the rota is read aloud: four centuries of names, each one a clerk who made tea for the rest. It ends on {npc}, and a blank. The blank, the clerks tell you, is for whoever carries it on.
events.arc: The Clerks' Tea Rota

choices.text: Write your own name in the blank

effects.log: You write it in plain ink. The clerks applaud, quietly, with teaspoons.

choices.text: Ask a young clerk to fill it

effects.log: A shy girl in the corner writes a name and goes pink. The pot is the girl's now.

events.text: A year on, the tea rota is mentioned in the court's annual report as a model of administration. The head of records reads out the passage. The clerks, at the back, exchange the faintest of smiles. {npc}, in a garden somewhere, is said to have sneezed.
events.arc: The Clerks' Tea Rota

choices.text: Send {him} a tin of the office's tea

effects.log: A tin arrives with a handwritten label: 'From the shelf.' {He} puts it on the mantel and does not open it.

choices.text: Visit the office in a plain coat and stand in the queue

effects.log: You wait your turn like anyone. The tea is very good.

events.text: A clerk named {npc} finds a judgment misfiled for two thousand years: a minor god, Seoran of the Reeds, condemned to silence for a quarrel Seoran did not start. The record shows a page missing. Seoran has been silent since. Someone, {he} says, ought to do something.
events.arc: The Judgment That Was Misfiled

choices.text: Take the case to the court

effects.log: The court agrees to reopen it, reluctantly. A hearing is set for the next quarter.

choices.text: Find Seoran yourself

effects.log: You walk the reed-beds at dusk. A pale shape sits among them, listening to the wind, and does not look up.

events.text: The missing page is found in a drawer under another god's lunch. It records that the accuser admitted the false charge and was told to say nothing. The accuser is a respected elder of your pantheon. {npc} lays the page before you, shaking.
events.arc: The Judgment That Was Misfiled

choices.text: Take the page to the elder privately

effects.log: The elder reads it, goes pale, and asks for a day. A day is granted.

choices.text: Read it in open court

effects.log: The court is horrified. The elder rises, bows, and does not argue.

events.text: Seoran's silence is lifted. Seoran stands among the reeds and for a long minute says nothing, then says one word, which is your name, and then, to your embarrassment, the word 'tea'. {npc} weeps openly. The reeds hush and then, in a body, whisper.
events.arc: The Judgment That Was Misfiled

choices.text: Ask Seoran what could have been said all those years

effects.log: There is a great deal to say. It takes the afternoon. Most of it is about weather.

choices.text: Take Seoran to the court's table, to a seat of honour

effects.log: The seat is Seoran's. Seoran sits, a little unsure what to do with both hands.

events.text: The elder resigns the seat in the end, with grace, and retires to a mountain. The court votes Seoran a seat. In the first speech Seoran thanks the clerk who found the page, then thanks the drawer, then the lunch. The hall is delighted. {npc} is promoted to chief of records.
events.arc: The Judgment That Was Misfiled

choices.text: Propose a rule that every judgment be copied thrice

effects.log: Triple copies become law. {npc} writes the first.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the misfiled

effects.log: The toast is long and sweet. The misfiled are many.

events.text: The herald at your door clears their throat, and nothing comes out but a small, apologetic squeak. The court is waiting. They look at you with panic in their eyes and a scroll in their hand.

choices.text: Take the scroll and read your own title

effects.log: You read it, with a bow, to the delighted court. The herald recovers by dessert.

choices.text: Mime the proclamation

effects.log: You mime it so well that the court gives you applause in lieu of title.

events.text: The post for prayers has been sorted by a temp clerk who files them by smell. Prayers for harvest are all together; prayers for love are in a tidy pile that smells of pear. You admire the system and cannot find the prayer you were waiting for.

choices.text: Ask the clerk how the smell system works

effects.log: It turns out to work remarkably well. The clerk is hired for good.

choices.text: Sniff for it yourself

effects.log: You find it under the pears. It was a small, shy one.

events.text: On the stairs to the council hall you meet a herald carrying a tray of cups from the kitchens, each with a name on it. The cups are for gods who will not attend. The herald lays them out anyway, every time, in case.

choices.text: Ask for one of the cups to be yours

effects.log: A cup with your name is set aside for the days you are not there.

choices.text: Tell the herald it is a kind habit

effects.log: The herald looks as if no one had ever said it.

events.text: A pigeon of the courier service has been delivering your letters to a statue of you in a distant city, which has begun to answer them in a gruff voice. The statue's replies, by common consent, are sound.

choices.text: Read the replies

effects.log: The statue is right about a boundary dispute and wrong about a wedding. You send it a pigeon of your own.

choices.text: Let the correspondence continue

effects.log: A statue and a god write to each other for a century.

events.text: In the archive, a clerk spills a bottle of ink across a century of minutes. The ink spreads, the pages swell, and for a moment the whole record reads as a single black sentence. The clerk looks at you, aghast.

choices.text: Help dry the pages

effects.log: You spend the afternoon blotting. The minutes of the century are slightly improved by the stain.

choices.text: Declare it an abridged edition

effects.log: The abridged edition is the most readable the archive has ever produced.

events.text: It is a junior clerk's thousandth birthday and nobody knows. The clerk sits at the desk, small and unremarked, with a single candle brought from home. You pass the open door, with a plate of cake that was meant for someone else.

choices.text: Offer the cake

effects.log: The clerk takes it, wordless. The whole office turns out to sing, an hour later, when the news gets round.

choices.text: Leave a note on the desk

effects.log: The note says 'Many happy returns'. It is the only note the clerk has ever kept.

events.text: A young runner arrives breathless at your door with a bundle of prayers and the confession that they are lost, have never been lost before, and do not know which of the nine valleys is whose.

choices.text: Walk them home through the valleys

effects.log: You show them the valleys by name. By the ninth, they know them by heart.

choices.text: Give them a lantern that points to home

effects.log: The lantern leans toward the courier house. They go away, reassured.

events.text: The minutes of last night's council record that you proposed a motion you do not remember, in terms you would never use, to great applause. The clerk who took them is very pleased with it.

choices.text: Let the minutes stand

effects.log: The motion is passed in your name. It turns out to be a good one.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to read it aloud once more

effects.log: It is a lovely speech. You promise to give it, next time.

events.text: A scribe from the Hall slips a folded note into your sleeve and hurries off. It reads: 'You have been very kind to my cousin, who is an archivist. Please accept nothing, and be well.' It is unsigned and has been blotted lovingly.

choices.text: Keep the note

effects.log: It sits in your sleeve for a century, a small dry thing.

choices.text: Send an answer to the Hall, unsigned in return

effects.log: A note comes back: 'Received.'

events.text: A messenger of the Sea pantheon delivers a thunderous declaration of war to your door. It is addressed to a neighbour who has moved. The messenger, red-faced, offers to deliver it again to the right door and take the blame.

choices.text: Offer to forward the declaration yourself

effects.log: You forward it with a kind note. The neighbour is delighted by the courtesy, and declines the war.

choices.text: Send the messenger home with a pie

effects.log: The messenger stumbles off bearing a pie. The war is quietly forgotten.

events.text: The oldest archivist in the court has stopped reading and begun to hum. Visitors ask for the file on the harvest god; the archivist hums a tune, and the file appears. The system works better than before.

choices.text: Ask for the file on yourself

effects.log: The archivist hums. A thin, kind file is placed in your hand.

choices.text: Hum back

effects.log: The archivist nods approvingly and gives you a ribbon.

events.text: A bench outside the lending room has a long row of scrolls waiting for pickup, each tied with the ribbon of a different god. Yours is at the end, tied with a ribbon you do not recognise. It is warm.

choices.text: Untie it and read

effects.log: A short note in a hand you almost know: 'We are well. Come when you can.'

choices.text: Carry it home unopened

effects.log: You hold it all the way home. It stays warm.

events.text: A prayer-sorter in the lower office shows you the shelf of prayers marked 'cannot be sorted'. They are prayers addressed to everyone and no one: to the weather, to the dead, to anybody awake. The sorter keeps them near the window, where there is light.

choices.text: Take one and answer it

effects.log: It is a plain thank-you for a bowl of soup. You send the soup's maker a good year.

choices.text: Leave them by the window

effects.log: You open the window a little wider. The prayers rustle.

events.text: Two clerks come to you to settle a dispute: whose seal is bigger. The seals are the size of walnuts. The dispute is two hundred years old. They have each brought a lawyer, and a ruler.

choices.text: Measure them with the ruler, gravely

effects.log: The seals are exactly the same. The clerks are crushed, relieved and friends.

choices.text: Declare a third seal, bigger, for yourself

effects.log: The clerks, outraged by the tyranny, unite against you.

events.text: In the dead-letter office you find a shelf of messages that were sent but never wanted: apologies refused, offers declined, good news nobody believed. The clerk there says they are the most honest letters in the building.

choices.text: Read one aloud

effects.log: It is an apology for a harvest. The harvest was good. The clerk smiles.

choices.text: Ask the clerk to deliver a few again

effects.log: Three are delivered. Two are accepted this time.

events.text: The heralds of your pantheon have been given new hats, tall and green with a plume. Your own herald wears it with the dignity of someone who has been asked to carry a small bird on their head all day.

choices.text: Say the hat suits them

effects.log: The herald stands a little taller. The plume trembles.

choices.text: Ask the plume's purpose

effects.log: It is, you learn, a unit of rank. This one is four plumes high, and the herald is very proud.

events.text: A decree of yours from a thousand years ago is rediscovered by a clerk and read out in full. It forbids the sale of sunsets. You do not remember it. The market gods have been quietly breaking it for centuries.

choices.text: Repeal it with a flourish

effects.log: The repeal is celebrated. A sunset is auctioned the same evening.

choices.text: Enforce it, just once, for the fun

effects.log: A single sunset is confiscated and returned. The merchants applaud.

events.text: The courier-house horn sounds at the wrong hour. It is not an emergency: a young horn-blower has simply learned a new tune and cannot wait to play it. Heads pop out of every window, wondering which festival they have forgotten.

choices.text: Tell them it is a festival of the new tune

effects.log: The festival is declared. The horn-blower, thunderstruck, plays it again.

choices.text: Ask the horn-blower to teach you

effects.log: Your first note is dreadful. The horn-blower consoles you at length.

events.text: A leak in the roof of the archive has dripped on the ledger of favours owed. Several debts have run together. You are now owed a hat by a god you have never met, and owe a song to a mountain.

choices.text: Honour the new debts

effects.log: A hat arrives in a week. A mountain receives a song and hums back.

choices.text: Ask the clerks to redraw the ledger

effects.log: They do, protesting. The debts are now a clean, boring, correct list.

events.text: A herald hides a letter inside a loaf of bread to avoid a certain rival's inspector. The inspector eats the bread. The letter is delivered, in a way, and so is the inspector, to the nearest privy, in a hurry.

choices.text: Pretend not to have noticed

effects.log: The incident is never recorded. You and the herald share a smile.

choices.text: Send the inspector a basket of peaches

effects.log: The inspector never suspects. The peaches are eaten with care.

events.text: A herald school opens in the lower courts and invites you to give a lecture on 'the dignity of the proclamation'. The students are three hundred small godlings who have never been quiet. You are expected to speak for an hour.

choices.text: Speak for five minutes and then ask for questions

effects.log: The questions are better than the answers. The hour is spent happily.

choices.text: Teach them a single short proclamation, to be shouted together

effects.log: The hall shakes. The school bell is rung, in alarm, from the next district.

events.text: A headman named {npc} has driven forty goats to your shrine as a sacrifice, to thank you for a good spring. The goats are loud, bewildered and healthy. {He} stands among them, grave and proud, with a knife {he} plainly does not want to use.
events.arc: Forty Goats at the Gate

choices.text: Accept the offering by blessing the goats alive

effects.log: The goats stop bleating at once and stand in a respectful ring. {npc} lowers the knife with a breath that is nearly a sob.

choices.text: Refuse the sacrifice and ask for the milk instead

effects.log: {npc} blinks. No god has ever asked for milk. Within a week every household is leaving a cup at the shrine step.

events.text: The goats stay. They wander the hill, eat the flowers off the altar and become, by degrees, a flock of the shrine. One has taken to standing on the roof. Pilgrims arrive to see the goats as often as the god.
events.arc: Forty Goats at the Gate

choices.text: Let the roof-goat be

effects.log: The roof-goat is named for you by the third day. It has not once fallen.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to build them a fold

effects.log: The fold is built in a day and the goats move into it with great ceremony.

events.text: A hard winter. {npc} arrives at the shrine at dusk, thin and quiet, to say the household has nothing left to eat but the goats, and will not eat them without leave. The goats watch from the fold, chewing, unconcerned.
events.arc: Forty Goats at the Gate

choices.text: Give leave, and thank the goats

effects.log: The goats are eaten at midwinter with great gratitude and not a single wasted bone. {npc} says the grace in your name.

choices.text: Send a warm wind and a good thaw

effects.log: The thaw comes in a week. The goats survive, and so do the people.

events.text: The cup at the shrine step has grown into a custom: each household's milk is poured into a stone trough, and what is left over feeds the foxes. {npc}, now an old keeper, confides that you were the first god who asked for less than {he} offered.
events.arc: Forty Goats at the Gate

choices.text: Tell {him} that less was all you ever wanted

effects.log: {He} nods, slow and grateful. The trough is never empty again.

choices.text: Pour a little from the trough on the roof-goat

effects.log: The goat looks at you, offended, then drinks.

events.text: A tradesman, {npc}, lays a purse on your altar: a year of savings, every coin, wrapped in a handkerchief. {He} asks for nothing. {He} says {he} has had a good year and it would be shameful to keep it all. The altar looks overburdened.
events.arc: The Offering That Was a Whole Year

choices.text: Return it quietly, and bless the trade

effects.log: The purse is found on the doorstep the next morning with a ribbon. {npc} understands, slowly, and cries a little in the shop.

choices.text: Accept the purse and make it grow

effects.log: You turn the purse into a seed. In a year it is a cherry tree in {npc}'s yard, heavy with fruit, and no one knows how.

events.text: Word of the offering spreads. Pilgrims arrive carrying purses, jars and heirlooms, and lay them on the altar until the keeper begins to look worried. The altar groans. Offerings have a way of becoming a pressure.
events.arc: The Offering That Was a Whole Year

choices.text: Declare a day on which only flowers are accepted

effects.log: The Day of Flowers fills the shrine with every bloom in the valley. The keeper weeps with relief.

choices.text: Send the surplus to the lowest house in the valley

effects.log: The surplus arrives in the night. The lowest house wakes to find itself, briefly, the richest.

events.text: {npc}'s shop prospers in a quiet way. There is no miracle in it, only a trade that has become kinder. At the year's end {he} lays a single copper coin on the altar, and says it is the most honest thing {he} has ever given.
events.arc: The Offering That Was a Whole Year

choices.text: Take the copper and set it in the shrine wall

effects.log: The coin glows faintly for a century. It is the smallest relic you own.

choices.text: Return it with a note saying thank you

effects.log: {npc} keeps the note and spends the coin on bread.

events.text: The cherry tree has become a landmark. In summer, children climb it; in autumn, the keeper dries the fruit for the sick. {npc} sits under it, evenings, and tells nobody that it was once a purse.
events.arc: The Offering That Was a Whole Year

choices.text: Send a bird to nest in it

effects.log: A pair of finches nests there for a hundred years. {npc} names the first chick for you.

choices.text: Leave the tree be

effects.log: It stands in the yard, quiet and fruitful.

events.text: At the harvest festival a proud steward, {npc}, has a whole banquet laid on a pyre as your portion: roasted birds, honey cakes, a full orchard's worth of fruit, all set alight. The smoke rises in great fragrant columns. The hungry crowd watches in silence.
events.arc: The Feast That Was Burned for You

choices.text: Take the smoke, and send the feast back whole

effects.log: The pyre cools. The banquet is untouched and warm. The crowd falls on it in tears. {npc} sits down heavily on the steps.

choices.text: Let the pyre burn, and ask {him} for a lesson in humility next year

effects.log: The feast is lost. Next year {npc} hosts a feast for the poor, with you as unnamed guest.

events.text: Whispers follow: that the god of the valley is hungry for fire, that a feast not burnt is a feast wasted. A priest rises to preach it. The valley, uneasy, starts to wonder if it has been getting you wrong for years.
events.arc: The Feast That Was Burned for You

choices.text: Appear in a dream of the preacher and eat a pear

effects.log: The preacher wakes with pear juice on the chin and a newly modest sermon.

choices.text: Say nothing and watch what the valley decides

effects.log: The valley, left alone, decides on kindness. It takes a decade.

events.text: {npc} comes to your altar on the third night after the feast, hollow and apologetic, to confess that {he} did it to be seen by the pantheon: a grand gesture for a grand god. {He} asks whether you can forgive a showman.
events.arc: The Feast That Was Burned for You

choices.text: Forgive {him}, and ask for a smaller gift

effects.log: {He} offers one small seed cake. You accept. The pantheon notices nothing and the valley everything.

choices.text: Say you will think about it, for a few years

effects.log: The years pass gently. {He} grows humble in the waiting.

events.text: Years later, the steward gives a feast for the whole valley at no one's expense but {his} own. No pyre, no smoke, just long tables under the stars. You attend in a plain coat. {npc} serves you pie without knowing who you are, and asks if you want more.
events.arc: The Feast That Was Burned for You

choices.text: Accept a third helping, gladly

effects.log: {He} beams. It is the most you have ever been fed.

choices.text: Leave a leaf of your domain on the table

effects.log: {He} finds it in the morning and recognises it with a start.

events.text: A scholar-priest, {npc}, has declared that the finest way to honour you is to give up what {he} loves most. {He} stands at the head of a long line of porters carrying the contents of a library to the altar. Every scroll {he} ever copied is here.
events.arc: The Library Given in Your Name

choices.text: Stop the porters and ask {him} to read to you instead

effects.log: {npc} sits on the step and reads for three days. You listen to every word, and the library goes back to its shelves.
