choices.text: Accept the gift as a loan, with thanks

effects.log: The scrolls are laid in your hall, and {npc} is given a key. It is the most generous loan in the history of the valley.

events.text: The scholar's students begin to arrive at the shrine, one by one, asking to read what their teacher gave you. They sit in the cool of the hall, copying quietly. The keeper grumbles, then brings them tea.
events.arc: The Library Given in Your Name

choices.text: Hire the keeper as librarian

effects.log: The keeper is delighted, and terrified, and takes to it at once.

choices.text: Send a lamp that never smokes

effects.log: The hall is lit, evenings, with a steady clean light.

events.text: A fire breaks out in the lower town, and the porters rush to rescue the shrine library, as if it were a child. They carry the scrolls into the open and sit on them until the fire is out. {npc} wakes the next day to find the library intact and the porters asleep in a heap.
events.arc: The Library Given in Your Name

choices.text: Send a fine dry week to let the scrolls air

effects.log: The sun is warm and gentle, and the scrolls dry in their hundreds. (+faith)

choices.text: Bless the porters with a restful night

effects.log: The porters sleep soundly and wake refreshed and a little embarrassed.

events.text: In {npc}'s last year, the old scholar asks to be buried in the library, between two shelves. You grant it. A modest tomb is built, and at its door a lamp is lit that has never gone out. Students read there still, and say it is the quietest room in the valley.
events.arc: The Library Given in Your Name

choices.text: Stand at the tomb's door for a night

effects.log: The lamp burns steady, and you read one line from each shelf by its light.

choices.text: Send a spring to run beside it

effects.log: A thin bright stream runs past the door. Students drink from it and are unaccountably cheerful.

events.text: The potter {npc} cannot speak, and has never prayed in words. Every year {he} leaves a single bowl at your shrine, glazed the colour of a certain evening. The keeper stacks them in a corner. There are now thirty-one, and none of them match.
events.arc: The Potter Who Gave a Bowl

choices.text: Drink from this year's bowl

effects.log: A cup of water from the shrine well, in a bowl the colour of dusk. You are certain, afterwards, it was the best water you have had.

choices.text: Visit the potter's kiln in a plain coat

effects.log: {npc} is shaping a bowl as you arrive. {He} gestures you to the bench, hands you a lump of clay and does not ask who you are.

events.text: The bowls have begun to sing, very faintly, when the wind is right. A pilgrim reports hearing a low note from the corner of the shrine. The keeper tests it by flicking a bowl with a finger. It answers with a pitch that makes the cat leave.
events.arc: The Potter Who Gave a Bowl

choices.text: Tune them with a breath

effects.log: The thirty-one bowls ring a single quiet chord. Pilgrims weep and cannot say why.

choices.text: Let them sing as they will

effects.log: They sing differently each year. The keeper starts to take requests.

events.text: The potter's hands begin to fail. {He} brings a final bowl, and for the first time a note in a shaky hand: 'For whoever listens.' It is the first thing {he} has written for you. {He} sits on the step, looking at your door.
events.arc: The Potter Who Gave a Bowl

choices.text: Come out and sit beside {him}

effects.log: You sit with {npc} on the step in plain clothes. Neither of you says anything. The sun goes down on both.

choices.text: Send a small wind to turn the bowl gently

effects.log: The bowl turns in the light, and the note on it can be read by all.

events.text: After {npc} is gone, a hundred bowls arrive in a year, from every potter in the valley, all in the dusk colour. The glaze is called by {his} name. In the shrine corner the thirty-two original bowls hum together, a low steady note that no one else can make.
events.arc: The Potter Who Gave a Bowl

choices.text: Keep the first bowl on your altar

effects.log: It sits where you can see it. It is your favourite.

choices.text: Give the valley a day for potters

effects.log: The Day of the Dusk Bowl becomes a feast of clay and quiet.

events.text: The leaking roof of your largest temple has produced a committee of seven worshippers, who cannot agree on a roof. {npc}, the chair, wants copper. The others want slate, thatch, tile, a different kind of tile, and a roof of living vines. You are asked to settle it by sign.
events.arc: The Committee of Seven for the Roof

choices.text: Send a sign for copper

effects.log: A copper-coloured dawn lights the hall. {npc} bows in triumph. The other six go to bed in ill temper.

choices.text: Send a sign for the vines

effects.log: A creeping green light falls on the hall and the committee falls silent. Vines, it is agreed, are mysterious.

events.text: The committee splinters into two committees, each with a roof. For a season there are two sets of scaffolding, two sets of builders and a long wooden wall between. The temple is nearly impassable. The keeper starts to lock the back door.
events.arc: The Committee of Seven for the Roof

choices.text: Bless the builders on both sides equally

effects.log: Both roofs rise at the same pace. They meet, awkwardly, at the ridge.

choices.text: Ask the committees to dine together

effects.log: The dinner lasts all night. It is not a success, but it is a start.

events.text: At the ridge, the copper meets the vines, and to everyone's surprise the join is lovely: green creeping over bronze, a roof that looks like an old coin left in a garden. {npc} stands under it, tolerant, as if it had been the plan.
events.arc: The Committee of Seven for the Roof

choices.text: Tell {him} it was the best of both

effects.log: {npc} agrees with dignity. The committee votes to dissolve itself and form a society.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the roof speak

effects.log: The roof speaks. It is thrown by rain.

events.text: The vines, as vines will, take over. In a hundred years the temple is a green hill with a door, and the committee's record is housed in a hollow log. {npc}'s great-great-grandchild is chair. The agenda has not changed.
events.arc: The Committee of Seven for the Roof

choices.text: Send a gentle rain to feed the vines

effects.log: The temple blooms in every colour. The agenda is changed to include 'blossom'.

choices.text: Leave the committee to its work

effects.log: It works, as committees do, for a very long time.

events.text: The faithful of a mountain town want to gild the lintel of your temple. {npc}, who runs the fund, has raised a tower of gold leaf from every household. {He} asks, shyly, whether you would prefer it gilded in a pattern or plain.
events.arc: The Gilding of the Lintel

choices.text: Ask for a pattern of the town's own people

effects.log: The lintel is gilded with a long line of small figures, a procession of everyone who gave.

choices.text: Ask for it plain, with a single line of verse

effects.log: The lintel is gilded in plain gold, with a verse: 'All who come in are welcome.' It is spelled correctly.

events.text: The gilders arrive from the lowlands, a family of six, bickering about leaf and gum. They scaffold the lintel and work through a spring of mist. The temple smells of gold size and a generous tolerance for noise.
events.arc: The Gilding of the Lintel

choices.text: Dry the mist for them in the afternoons

effects.log: The gilders work with the sun on their hands. They sing as they lay the leaf.

choices.text: Send a warm lunch to the scaffold

effects.log: The family eat on the planks, thanking an unseen kindness.

events.text: When the scaffold comes down the lintel is dazzling, and a child in the town asks why the little figures have no faces. {npc} has no answer; the gilders were told to leave them blank, so that anyone could be inside.
events.arc: The Gilding of the Lintel

choices.text: Give each figure a face, in a dream, to the child who asked

effects.log: The child dreams every face and wakes up and draws them all. The drawings hang in the school.

choices.text: Leave them blank, and let the town look for itself

effects.log: The lintel becomes a mirror in a quiet way. Townspeople point out their own.

events.text: A hundred winters on, the verse over the door has softened, and a stranger has scratched a line below it: 'And so are you.' The keeper thinks it was a child. The scratch is left. Pilgrims touch it as they enter, and say it is the best line of the lot.
events.arc: The Gilding of the Lintel

choices.text: Add a gold dot beside it

effects.log: A single gold dot appears next to the line, so small it might be a mistake. It never tarnishes.

choices.text: Pretend not to have noticed

effects.log: The line stays. It is sufficient.

events.text: A temple repair was begun on your hill and abandoned for lack of funds, leaving a great scaffold of lashed bamboo around a half-mended wall. {npc}, a mason's widow, has taken to hanging charms on it. There are forty already, and the scaffold hums.
events.arc: The Scaffold That Became a Shrine

choices.text: Bless the scaffold, bamboo and all

effects.log: The bamboo roots in the hillside and puts out green shoots. The scaffold is alive.

choices.text: Send funds, quietly, to finish the wall

effects.log: A stranger arrives at the quarry with a purse and a letter in your hand. The wall is finished in a month.

events.text: Pilgrims begin to pray at the scaffold itself, saying it brought them luck. A lamp is hung. A bell. A very small altar. The wall, half-mended, is considered holier than the whole. The keeper is exasperated.
events.arc: The Scaffold That Became a Shrine

choices.text: Leave the scaffold up, by decree

effects.log: The decree is read at the next festival. The scaffold stands, and a rope-swing is added.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the charms mean

effects.log: {He} laughs. They are mostly wishes for the mason, who liked the view.

events.text: {npc} grows too old to climb. A pair of children take over the charm-hanging, and begin to add to the scaffold in odd ways: a small bridge, a ladder to nowhere, a platform for watching the sunrise. It has become a sort of hamlet of its own.
events.arc: The Scaffold That Became a Shrine

choices.text: Strengthen the lashings, so no one falls

effects.log: The scaffold holds. Children climb it for a hundred years without a scratch.

choices.text: Let the children build as they will

effects.log: A tower rises. It leans a little and is much loved.

events.text: The wall behind the scaffold is finally rebuilt, long after, by the descendants of the mason, who recognise the work as their own. They keep the scaffold up around it out of respect, and call the whole structure 'the Widow's Shrine'.
events.arc: The Scaffold That Became a Shrine

choices.text: Add a stone with {npc}'s name

effects.log: The stone is set, quiet and plain, at the base of the wall. (+faith)

choices.text: Come in the evenings to watch the children climb

effects.log: You sit on the hillside. It is the best seat for an easy mind.

events.text: The renovation committee has hired an architect, {npc}, who looks at your high dome and announces that it should be lower. 'Worshippers should not need to crane,' {he} says. Half the committee is outraged. The other half, privately, has had a stiff neck for years.
events.arc: The Architect Who Wanted the Dome Lower

choices.text: Side with the architect

effects.log: The dome is lowered by a third. The hall feels intimate, like a room in a house, and the stiff necks recover.

choices.text: Side with the old dome

effects.log: The dome stays high. {npc} is gracious and sulks a little. The committee buys cushions.

events.text: A visiting god of the Sky comments that a lowered dome makes the temple feel less like a place for gods, more like a place for people. He means it as an insult. The committee takes it as a compliment and adds it to the brochure.
events.arc: The Architect Who Wanted the Dome Lower

choices.text: Invite the Sky god to dinner and show him the cushions

effects.log: He sniffs, sits, and falls asleep before dessert.

choices.text: Ignore the comment

effects.log: The comment fades, as comments do.

events.text: {npc} is asked to design your next temple, in a hill town where the people are short and the winters long. {He} proposes a dome so low that you must bend to enter, and a door at the back, facing the sunrise. The town's elders are puzzled. The children adore it.
events.arc: The Architect Who Wanted the Dome Lower

choices.text: Bless the low dome, and the bowing it asks

effects.log: Every entrant bows without noticing. The elders, bowing, forgive the novelty.

choices.text: Walk in through the back door at dawn

effects.log: The sun lands on your shoulder as you enter. You have never been so welcome.

events.text: Many years later {npc} returns to the high temple to see what has become of it. The high dome is cracked, and the cushions are in rags. {He} says nothing, but stays to repair the plaster all afternoon, and the committee, ashamed, helps.
events.arc: The Architect Who Wanted the Dome Lower

choices.text: Thank {him} for the repair and ask for the plans for a new dome

effects.log: {He} sketches by the light of the clerestory. Your next dome is the best of either kind.

choices.text: Say nothing, and leave a dry week

effects.log: The plaster dries, and the dome holds.

events.text: The god of the next domain sends a child to stay with you for a season, 'to learn a little from a different weather'. {npc}, a young godling, arrives with a trunk, a cold and an enormous idea of {his} own importance. The cold, at least, is real.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Eldest Comes to Stay

choices.text: Put {him} to bed with broth and a hot stone

effects.log: The cold breaks by morning. {npc} is mortified to have been nursed and then, cautiously, grateful.

choices.text: Show {him} the shrine and let {him} be bored

effects.log: {npc} sulks for a week, then discovers the shrine cat, and is not heard of until supper.

events.text: The godling has opinions about your domain. The rain is too gentle, the thunder too polite, the sunsets 'a bit domestic'. {He} recommends improvements. The shrine-keeper notes them all, solemnly, in a ledger headed 'Visitor's Remarks'.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Eldest Comes to Stay

choices.text: Try one improvement

effects.log: A very large sunset follows. {npc} is thrilled and the keeper exhausted.

choices.text: Ask {him} to try it on a smaller scale

effects.log: {He} makes a lovely, modest rainbow over a pond. It is the first thing {he} has made.

events.text: At the season's end {npc}'s parent comes to collect {him}, and finds a changed child: thinner, browner, humbler and fond of cats. The parent looks at you with a mixture of gratitude and alarm. 'What did you do to them?' 'Nothing,' you say. 'I fed them.'
events.arc: The Neighbour's Eldest Comes to Stay

choices.text: Offer to host the next child as well

effects.log: The parent agrees, stiffly. A tradition of exchange begins between the two domains.

choices.text: Send the godling home with a cat

effects.log: The cat is a hit. A second cat follows, then a third.

events.text: Decades later the godling sends a letter, now a god of some small hill in the neighbour's domain. 'I make sunsets,' {he} writes, 'but always the domestic kind. It turns out they were the right ones.' A cat's paw is stamped at the bottom.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Eldest Comes to Stay

choices.text: Reply with a sketch of your own best sunset

effects.log: The sketch travels and is hung in a hall of the neighbour. Two domains share a sky at dusk.

choices.text: Keep the letter on your shelf

effects.log: It is kept with other things you do not like to lose.

events.text: Your neighbour, a thunder-god of long temper, has twin children who keep running across the boundary stone into your domain. {npc} is the louder twin. {He} has just thrown a stone at a heron, missed, and is looking at you with the particular defiance of a small god.
events.arc: The Next Valley God's Twins

choices.text: Return the stone to the twin, politely

effects.log: {npc} takes it, startled. No god has ever returned a thrown thing.

choices.text: Teach {him} to skim it across a lake

effects.log: The stone skips nine times. {npc} stares at the water, silent, then demands a bigger stone.

events.text: The twins have begun to play a game on the boundary: whoever crosses the stone loses a piece of the other's territory. The game is a hundred years old in the telling. Neither child knows that their parents quarrelled over the same game.
events.arc: The Next Valley God's Twins

choices.text: Join the game, on the losing side

effects.log: The twins are delighted by a god who loses. The game ends in laughter and a draw.

choices.text: Tell the parents about the game

effects.log: The parents are embarrassed and, in the evening, cautiously pleased.

events.text: A storm breaks over the boundary stone, from the neighbour's domain, loud and furious. {npc} appears in your hall at the height of it, white to the lips, saying the storm is {his} fault, and {he} does not know how to stop it. {He} has lost control of a wild temper.
events.arc: The Next Valley God's Twins

choices.text: Sit with {him} until the storm blows out

effects.log: You sit and talk of nothing. The thunder grows hoarse and then, in time, tired. {npc} sleeps in your best chair.

choices.text: Guide {his} hand to the cloud

effects.log: The storm answers, grumbling. {npc} learns what it means to be listened to by weather.

events.text: Many years on, the twins hold a festival at the boundary stone, with a banquet of both domains and a game in which everyone loses a little. {npc} proposes a toast to the neighbour who did not shout. The thunder-god, red in the face, joins in.
events.arc: The Next Valley God's Twins

choices.text: Raise your cup to both twins

effects.log: The toast rings over the valley, and the stone is garlanded.

choices.text: Slip away early and leave them to it

effects.log: They are happier without a witness.

events.text: The heir of the next domain, {npc}, arrives at the boundary with a tin pail, and announces that your rain is better than {his} own and that {he} would like to borrow some. The pail is very small. The heir's own valley has dried out, and nobody has mentioned it.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Wanted Your Rain

choices.text: Fill the pail, and fill a few more

effects.log: The pail is filled and a dozen more follow. {npc} flushes, and says nothing, and carries them home on a pole.

choices.text: Ask what happened to the heir's own rain

effects.log: {npc} shuffles. The valley's rain was promised to a quarrel nobody remembers, and {he} was too proud to say.

events.text: A messenger from the neighbour's court arrives with a cold note: please do not feed the heir's habits. The valley must learn to make its own weather. The pail, in the messenger's hand, is empty. {npc} stands behind, wearing the look of a child caught stealing apples.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Wanted Your Rain

choices.text: Answer the note with an invitation

effects.log: The neighbour's court reads it twice, then sends an honest reply.

choices.text: Ask whether the heir is allowed to learn

effects.log: The court, a little stung, concedes.

events.text: {npc} stays for a season to learn your rain: how it is gathered, folded, loosed. {He} is a slow learner and a stubborn one. By midsummer {he} can make a shower the size of a garden. It is crooked and lovely. The keeper hangs a flag over it.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Wanted Your Rain

choices.text: Praise the shower, truthfully

effects.log: {He} glows. The flag flaps. {He} sends a small shower to every house in the valley.

choices.text: Send {him} home with a seed of cloud

effects.log: The seed opens over the home valley in a week. It rains for a day, and the rain is {his} own.

events.text: When {npc} returns to the home valley the dry spell breaks, and not by your hand. It is {his} own rain, in a clumsy, joyful downpour. The heir stands in it, hatless, and the neighbour god, watching, finally puts down the quarrel and lets the valley have its weather.
events.arc: The Neighbour Who Wanted Your Rain

choices.text: Send a rainbow over both valleys

effects.log: A bow spans the boundary. The two courts agree, for once, on a colour.

choices.text: Stay away, and let them celebrate alone

effects.log: The rain falls, and it is not yours, and you are glad.

events.text: A child, {npc}, is discovered asleep behind your altar, with a satchel and a note from the god of the next domain: 'If found, please feed.' The note is apologetic and a little desperate. The child is a godling of about a thousand years, which in the courts is nine.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Child Who Ran to Your Shrine

choices.text: Feed {him}, and say nothing of the note

effects.log: {npc} wakes to soup and sits at the keeper's table in silence. By the third bowl {he} is talking about the parent {he} left.

choices.text: Send a gentle word to the parent

effects.log: A reply comes in an hour: 'Thank you. We were frightened. Please keep the child as long as the child needs.'

events.text: {npc} takes a job at the shrine, sweeping, and is discovered to be very good at it. The step is clean to the point of gleam. The keeper tries to teach {him} to light the lamps; {he} lights them with a snap of a finger and a silent expression of triumph.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Child Who Ran to Your Shrine

choices.text: Give {him} a small broom of your own

effects.log: The broom is a gift of the hearth. {He} cradles it like a puppy.

choices.text: Teach {him} the names of the lamps

effects.log: Each lamp has a name. {He} learns them all in a night.

events.text: The parent arrives at last, in a plain coat, trembling with the effort of looking calm. {npc} is on the step with the broom. The parent stands in front of {him}, speechless. The child looks up. 'I swept,' {he} says. The parent sits on the step and takes the broom.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Child Who Ran to Your Shrine

choices.text: Leave them alone on the step

effects.log: You go indoors. Through the door, for an hour, there is the sound of a quiet apology, and a quieter one back.

choices.text: Bring them a tray of tea

effects.log: They drink it without looking up, and the child leans on the parent's arm.

events.text: {npc} goes home, but visits every spring, and sweeps your step before leaving. In time the sweeping becomes a rite among the godlings of both domains: a day of brooms and a day of gifts. The parent always comes, and is always asked to hold the dustpan.
events.arc: The Neighbour's Child Who Ran to Your Shrine

choices.text: Join the broom day

effects.log: You sweep the step with the others. It is a good way to see how quickly a step gets dirty.

choices.text: Send each sweeper a ribbon

effects.log: The ribbons are tied to the broom handles. They are still tied.

events.text: The family of {npc} are leaving your valley for a distant coast, where the soil is rumoured to be kind. They come to say goodbye at the shrine, with a cart. {He} asks whether a god may follow a family across a sea. The question is not rhetorical.
events.arc: The Family That Took You Overseas

choices.text: Say yes, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} nods, and then, shyly, takes a pinch of shrine soil in a handkerchief. The cart rolls away down the hill.

choices.text: Say a god's reach is only as long as its faithful

effects.log: {npc} goes quiet. Then {he} lays a hand on the altar and says, 'Then we shall be long.'

events.text: A letter, slow as a snail, arrives from the new coast: the family has built a hut, planted a field and set a stone for you at the field's edge. The stone is small and crooked. No priest has blessed it. Prayers arrive from it every morning.
events.arc: The Family That Took You Overseas

choices.text: Bless the stone from here

effects.log: The stone grows warm. Another family, passing, stops to kneel.

choices.text: Send a seed of your own valley's grain

effects.log: The grain arrives in a wind-borne packet and grows in the foreign soil.

events.text: A stranger on the coast begins to pray at the family's stone. Then another. In ten years there is a small chapel to you, built of driftwood, among people who never saw your valley and who pray in a language you have to learn. {npc} serves as keeper, and says the grace slightly wrong.
events.arc: The Family That Took You Overseas

choices.text: Learn the new tongue, and answer in it

effects.log: The first answer startles the whole coast. {npc} laughs until {he} weeps.

choices.text: Let the grace stay a little wrong

effects.log: The wrong grace becomes the right one in that country.

events.text: In {npc}'s old age, the grandchildren ask to be taken to see the first valley. They cannot; the sea is wide and the world is full of other business. So {he} describes it, evening after evening, and at last you come in a dream to describe it with {him}. The children see a hill they have never touched.
events.arc: The Family That Took You Overseas

choices.text: Show them the shrine as it is today

effects.log: They see it, small and warm, with a cat on the step. They wake up crying and cheerful.

choices.text: Show them the valley as it was

effects.log: They see a younger shrine, a green hill and a lost summer.

events.text: A sailor, {npc}, prays to you on the deck of a ship on a dark sea, holding a pinch of your shrine's soil. {He} grew up in your valley and left at sixteen. It is the first prayer you have received from a boat, and the first in three years that did not ask for anything.
events.arc: The Pinch of Soil

choices.text: Answer by making the sea a little calmer

effects.log: The swell eases. {npc} looks at the soil, then at the horizon, and does not tell anyone.

choices.text: Send a dream of the valley in spring

effects.log: {He} sleeps in the swaying hammock and sees the hill in bloom. {He} wakes with soil under {his} nails.

events.text: Years pass and the sailor prays at every port, with the same pinch of soil, at every dawn. {He} has begun to leave a tiny grain of it at each harbour. A string of crooked little shrines now runs along the coast, each with a dot of your valley under it.
events.arc: The Pinch of Soil

choices.text: Bless each one in passing

effects.log: A line of faint blessings runs along the coast like a lit fuse. Sailors speak of a lucky shoreline.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to count them

effects.log: There are sixty-one. The sailor knows each by smell.

events.text: {npc} sails home at last, with a pocket empty of soil and a heart full of ports. {He} climbs the hill to your shrine on tired legs, and puts a pinch of salt on the altar, from the sea, as a return. The keeper does not know what to do with it, and you do.
events.arc: The Pinch of Soil

choices.text: Sprinkle the salt on the field of the shrine

effects.log: The field is sweeter that year. The sailor sits on the step and falls asleep in the sun.

choices.text: Keep the salt in a small jar on the altar

effects.log: The jar is known thereafter as the Sea's Reply.

events.text: The sailor's coast shrines continue after {npc}'s death. Each year a handful of salt is brought up the hill by travellers, who do not know why, only that it is traditional. The shrine keeps a trough of salt in the yard, and a trough of soil, side by side.
events.arc: The Pinch of Soil

choices.text: Bless the exchange

effects.log: The soil and the salt are swapped on feast days. A brisk custom grows from it. (+faith)

choices.text: Come to the exchange in a plain coat

effects.log: You hand a pinch of soil to a stranger who weeps without knowing why.

events.text: A letter arrives at your shrine addressed in a hand you cannot read, from a place you cannot find. The keeper tells you it is from {npc}, who left for a new land twenty years ago. It says: 'We are well. We have a daughter. We do not pray here, because we are afraid of the wrong god.'
events.arc: The Emigrants' Letter Home

choices.text: Send a dream in which you are very clearly yourself

effects.log: {npc} wakes and writes to say that the god of home has appeared, in a coat, with a cup of tea.

choices.text: Send nothing, but pray for them yourself

effects.log: Praying is an odd feeling for a god. Something in the sky shifts to receive it.

events.text: The keeper, a literal woman, asks whether a god can be homesick. You say you are not sure. The keeper says she is, for a place she has never been, and then puts the kettle on. It is a very long afternoon.
events.arc: The Emigrants' Letter Home

choices.text: Spend it with the keeper

effects.log: You drink tea. It is possible to be homesick together.

choices.text: Walk the hill alone

effects.log: The hill is as you left it. Something in it is very far away.

events.text: A second letter, from the daughter of {npc}, now grown, arrives in a clumsy child's script: the writer wants to know who the god of the valley was, and what the god liked. The keeper reads it aloud. It takes a long time to decide what to say.
events.arc: The Emigrants' Letter Home

choices.text: Write back, as yourself, with three true things

effects.log: You write that you liked rain, pears and the sound of the keeper's cat. The daughter writes that all three are liked there too.

choices.text: Let the keeper answer for you

effects.log: The keeper's letter is short and warm. It is signed with a paw print.

events.text: The daughter comes at last, in the autumn, to see the valley. A visitor walks the hill with a notebook, and finds the shrine, the cat and a plain coat that looks vaguely familiar. The visitor asks whether you are the gardener. You say you are, in a way. {npc}'s daughter laughs, and stays for pears.
events.arc: The Emigrants' Letter Home

choices.text: Show the visitor the oldest tree

effects.log: The tree is a hundred feet tall and older than the shrine. A palm is pressed to the bark, and is quiet.

choices.text: Give a pear and let the visitor keep the secret

effects.log: The pear is eaten, and declared to taste like a mother's letters.

events.text: The oracle of your shrine, {npc}, announces from the tripod that the god of the valley is a wolf: lean, grey and dangerous, with a hunger in the eyes. The pilgrims go pale. You are, in fact, a god of small streams. You like the sound of water on a stone.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Saw a Wolf

choices.text: Appear to the oracle as a stream, and let {him} see

effects.log: {npc} sits for an hour by a brook, listening, and amends the vision on the spot: a wolf who drinks.

choices.text: Let the wolf stand, and see what the valley does

effects.log: The valley buys wolf amulets and leaves out bones. A shaggy dog adopts the shrine.

events.text: The wolf is now an established fact in the valley. The children howl at the moon. A local poet writes a ballad called 'The Grey Lord'. You begin to feel that it is a better description of you than the truth, and feel faintly rude about it.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Saw a Wolf

choices.text: Listen to the ballad, all the way through

effects.log: It is long and sad and rather good. You send the poet a wolf-cub in a dream.

choices.text: Ask the oracle to correct the vision

effects.log: {npc} refuses, politely: the vision has taken on a life.

events.text: A real wolf is seen on the edge of the valley, thin and shy, hunted down from the hills by a hard winter. The valley, which now believes in you as a wolf, feeds it. The wolf, unnerved, eats everything left at the shrine and sleeps on the step.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Saw a Wolf

choices.text: Bless the wolf with a long peace

effects.log: The wolf lives to a great age on the step, and sires nothing but good-tempered dogs.

choices.text: Appear to the valley as a stream and a wolf both

effects.log: You appear in the shrine pond as a stream and in the brush as a wolf. The valley is quietly thrilled.

events.text: {npc} dies in {his} sleep, and the new oracle, a girl of twelve, announces from the tripod that the god of the valley is a stream that remembers a wolf. The valley nods, relieved. The vision has become, with time, correct.
events.arc: The Oracle Who Saw a Wolf

choices.text: Thank the new oracle with a clear spring

effects.log: A spring rises beneath the tripod. The oracle drinks and giggles.

choices.text: Send a dream of the old oracle to the new one

effects.log: The dream is short and kind. It ends with a nod.

events.text: The young apprentice {npc} reads the smoke at your shrine and says, in a small voice, that the old oracle is wrong: you are not angry about the late harvest, only tired. The old oracle huffs. The pilgrims side with the old oracle, who has a beard.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Read It Right

choices.text: Appear in a dream to the apprentice and confirm it

effects.log: {npc} wakes with a shout. {He} says nothing of the dream but stands a little straighter.

choices.text: Stay quiet and let the contest run

effects.log: The old oracle proclaims fury; the apprentice, tiredness. The pilgrims watch your face for clues.

events.text: The old oracle sets a trial: each shall read the same dawn, and the pilgrims will vote. The old oracle reads an omen of fire. {npc}, with trembling hands, reads a yawn. The pilgrims laugh, and then, a moment later, yawn too.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Read It Right

choices.text: Yawn, conspicuously, from the sky

effects.log: The yawn comes down as a gust over the valley. A hundred pilgrims blink and nod.

choices.text: Stay awake and give no sign

effects.log: The vote is close. You find that you are rather moved.

events.text: The apprentice wins the vote by a handful. The old oracle storms off to a hill, declaring the valley will be sorry. The valley, pleased, throws a feast. {npc} spends the whole feast apologising to the old oracle, in absentia, to a bowl of pickles.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Read It Right

choices.text: Send a message to the old oracle on {npc}'s behalf

effects.log: The old oracle sits on the hill and reads it twice, and sends back a pot of honey.

choices.text: Leave the old oracle to the hill

effects.log: The old oracle sulks for ten years and then comes down to be useful.

events.text: Years later the old oracle reads a true omen at last, in a fit of honesty, and weeps. {npc} comforts the old oracle with the words once used for {him}. The two read the smoke together through the next winter. The valley calls it the Year of Two Hands.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Read It Right

choices.text: Warm their tripod with a quiet glow

effects.log: The tripod shines. The two oracles read in perfect agreement for once, and note it.

choices.text: Send the pair a pot of tea

effects.log: The tea steams in the cold. They toast the smoke.

events.text: The oracle {npc} has foretold a great flood that will drown the lower fields. The valley has moved its stores to the hills, cancelled the festival and begun building boats. You have, at present, no flood in mind. You would not, in fact, know how to arrange one.
events.arc: The Prophecy of the Wrong Flood

choices.text: Correct the oracle in a dream

effects.log: {npc} wakes and insists the dream was a test. {He} refuses to alter the prophecy by a syllable.

choices.text: Send a modest flood, to spare the oracle's credit

effects.log: A single polite tide rises in the lower fields and recedes. The valley cheers. {npc} is vindicated.

events.text: The boats built for the flood have nowhere to go. The valley turns them into houses for chickens, planters, and a rather splendid hall. A boat-shaped feast hall rises in the square. The oracle is its patron, and does not enjoy the irony.
events.arc: The Prophecy of the Wrong Flood

choices.text: Attend the feast hall's opening

effects.log: The hall is warm, absurd and full of chickens. You find it the best-built hall in the valley.

choices.text: Send a gentle wind to set the hall's flag

effects.log: The flag is a boat in a blue field. It flaps with some dignity.

events.text: The oracle comes to you, ashamed, and admits that the prophecy was a wish: {he} wanted the valley to need someone. {He} had a hard youth and has never forgiven the ordinary. {He} asks whether a false prophecy can be undone by a true prayer.
events.arc: The Prophecy of the Wrong Flood

choices.text: Say that a true prayer answers any prophecy

effects.log: {He} prays. It is a short, ugly, honest prayer, and you answer with something very like love.

choices.text: Say the valley already forgave {him}, in the hall

effects.log: {He} gazes at the boat-hall, and begins to laugh, helplessly.

events.text: A real flood comes at last, a century on, and the boats are ready. They are chicken coops and planters and a hall, but they float. The valley rides the water through a night of rain, and in the morning the oracle's statue is the only thing above the waterline.
events.arc: The Prophecy of the Wrong Flood

choices.text: Send the water down gently by dawn

effects.log: The flood goes down by morning. The statue, wet and smiling, is carried through the streets.

choices.text: Hold the water at the hall's step, and nothing further

effects.log: The hall is a harbour, and every cat in the valley comes aboard.

events.text: For three years the prayers have thinned. Not because the valley is unhappy, but because it is prosperous and busy. The altar is a quiet place. {npc}, the keeper, sweeps it daily with the grave air of a person tending an empty nest.
events.arc: The Famine of Prayer

choices.text: Visit the town in a plain coat and ask what it needs

effects.log: The town needs nothing and says so politely. It is the polite kind of forgetting.

choices.text: Rest, and let the quiet teach you

effects.log: You sit through the quiet. It is longer than you expected, and surprisingly instructive.

events.text: {npc} confides that the town's young people have stopped coming to the shrine. They do not disbelieve; they are simply elsewhere, in the lower cities, in the barges, in the new factories. The keeper sets out a bench in case, and no one sits.
events.arc: The Famine of Prayer

choices.text: Send a small, plain miracle: a warm bench in winter

effects.log: The bench stays warm all winter. A few old people sit on it and talk.

choices.text: Ask the keeper to hold a festival for the absent

effects.log: The festival is held for the faces that are not there. The old people sing for them.

events.text: A letter arrives from one of the young, in a lower city: 'We still pray, but on trains, where there is no altar.' {npc} reads it aloud on the step. The keeper wonders whether the shrine should be moved onto a train. You seriously consider it.
events.arc: The Famine of Prayer

choices.text: Send your blessing along the line

effects.log: A thin glow runs along the railway. Passengers look up from their newspapers, and are briefly quiet.

choices.text: Ask for a small chapel to be added to the station

effects.log: A tiny shrine is built in the station corner. It is used by the late-shift workers.

events.text: The famine ends without a sound. One evening a child leaves a flower on the altar, then another, then a whole family. It is not a revival, only the old quiet tide turning. {npc} counts nine prayers at dusk, and weeps, and counts them again.
events.arc: The Famine of Prayer

choices.text: Answer all nine, one by one, with small kindnesses

effects.log: Nine kindnesses fall across the valley like stars. The keeper writes them in a book.

choices.text: Let the quiet be a gift

effects.log: You leave the nine unanswered, out of gratitude, and they feel heard anyway.

events.text: A rumour has gone round the lower cities that your shrine answers every prayer. By midsummer, forty thousand pilgrims have arrived and are sleeping in the fields. {npc}, the overwhelmed keeper, has run out of bowls. The altar is a wall of paper.
events.arc: The Flood of Prayer

choices.text: Answer the nearest hundred, and let the rest wait

effects.log: The hundred are answered. The waiting pilgrims are patient, as it happens, and take it for a blessing in itself.

choices.text: Send word that you cannot answer them all

effects.log: A letter is read at the gate: 'I am one god. I hear you.' The pilgrims go quiet, and many weep.

events.text: The fields are trampled. The keeper's cat has been seen on a roof, eyeing the crowd with contempt. A food shortage looms. {npc} comes to your door at midnight and asks, hoarsely, whether the gods have any rule about declining to be popular.
events.arc: The Flood of Prayer

choices.text: Send bread to the fields in the night

effects.log: Loaves appear in baskets at dawn. The pilgrims whisper of a miracle and are right.

choices.text: Ask the lowland shrines to take in half the pilgrims

effects.log: Word goes round. The lowland keepers throw their doors open.

events.text: Half the pilgrims go home with a smaller prayer than they came with. The other half remain, and build a town. {npc} writes you a note: 'We have a market, a school and a cat. We are in your debt.' The town has a name, taken from a prayer.
events.arc: The Flood of Prayer

choices.text: Bless the school

effects.log: The school flourishes. Its first pupils learn to read from a primer of prayers.

choices.text: Ask for the market to give a share to the keeper

effects.log: The share is agreed. The keeper buys a larger kettle.

events.text: Years on, the town is large and busy, and the old shrine is an island of calm in the middle of it. {npc}, old and cheerful, leads visitors up the steps and says: 'Once, forty thousand prayed here. Now they pay rent.' You find, listening in a plain coat, that this pleases you.
events.arc: The Flood of Prayer

choices.text: Ask {him} for a tour, as a visitor

effects.log: You are shown around your own shrine by one who has no idea. It is a very good tour.

choices.text: Send the town a wind, once a year, to carry the memory

effects.log: Every spring a warm wind goes through the streets. The shopkeepers call it the Pilgrims' Breeze.

events.text: The faith of the valley turns with the seasons, like a tide. In spring it is bright and frivolous; in summer, busy; in autumn, thankful; in winter, deep. {npc}, a senior priest, has kept a graph of it for two hundred years and brings it for you to see.
events.arc: The Season Faith Turned

choices.text: Study the graph with {him}

effects.log: The graph is an odd, gorgeous wave. You find that your own mood follows it, a little behind.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the graph does not show

effects.log: {He} thinks, and says: the people who pray and leave no mark. They are, {he} says, the majority.

events.text: Spring brings a flush of prayers for love, weather and exams. The altar is covered in small notes. {npc} sorts them with a patient smile, and, as in every spring, finds one addressed to 'the god who is probably busy'. This one is for you.
events.arc: The Season Faith Turned

choices.text: Answer it first

effects.log: A shy student passes an exam and does not know why. You decide it is the best use of the morning.

choices.text: Read the rest of the notes before choosing

effects.log: There are four hundred. You read them all, and feel faintly responsible for the valley's heart.

events.text: Autumn sends the thankful. Winter sends the deep. {npc} has been telling you for a century that the winter prayers are the true ones, and this year you listen. They are plain and quiet and unadorned, and they say, over and over, a single word: 'still'.
events.arc: The Season Faith Turned

choices.text: Answer every winter prayer with a lit window

effects.log: The valley's windows glow a little brighter that night. It is the gentlest answer you have ever made.

choices.text: Say the word back, once, from the hills

effects.log: The valley hears a low 'still' in the wind. It carries a long way.

events.text: When {npc} dies, the graph is extended by a student, who continues it with a shaky hand. The last point on it is a small dot labelled 'a good winter'. You keep a copy. In the margin you write, with some embarrassment, 'Thank you for counting me.'
events.arc: The Season Faith Turned

choices.text: Bless the student's hand

effects.log: The next hundred years of the graph are drawn in a steady line.

choices.text: Put the copy in your sleeve

effects.log: It stays there. It is warm.

events.text: A goat has been crowned with a wreath at the harvest festival, and now believes itself a minor deity. It stands on the shrine step and glares at pilgrims. The priest tries to persuade it down with a carrot, and you with a thought.

choices.text: Send the goat a very small blessing

effects.log: The goat is pacified and falls asleep in the sun. The priest sighs with relief.

choices.text: Let the goat reign for the day

effects.log: The goat accepts offerings of apples until sunset.

events.text: A merchant lays a heap of gold on your altar and asks for nothing. He seems quite terrified. The coins are warm as if from a pocket. The keeper whispers that the man has cheated his partner and is trying to buy peace.

choices.text: Return the gold with a dream of the partner's face

effects.log: The merchant wakes sweating, and by noon has paid his partner back with interest.

choices.text: Take the gold and spend it on a roof for the partner's family

effects.log: The roof goes up that week. The merchant weeps with relief, a little more.

events.text: A grandmother has lit a hundred candles on your altar, one for each year of a long life. The wax is running onto the floor. She is happy and entirely oblivious to the fire risk. The keeper has taken to standing nearby with a bucket.

choices.text: Make the flames cool and steady

effects.log: The candles burn without a single drip. The grandmother says it is a miracle, and goes home.

choices.text: Add one candle of your own

effects.log: One more candle burns, bright as a star. She counts a hundred and one, puzzled.

events.text: The renovation committee is on its fourth day of debate about the colour of a door. The tea has gone cold. A junior member whispers that the door is lovely as it is. Everyone turns to look at the junior. The junior goes red.

choices.text: Say the door is fine

effects.log: The committee exhales. The door stays as it is. The tea is renewed.

choices.text: Call for a vote on the colour of the tea

effects.log: The vote is a tie. The committee begins to laugh.

events.text: A mason carves the name of a god on the wrong pillar, and the committee panics. The name is yours, spelled correctly, on the pillar of another god's shrine. The mason confesses with tears. The pillar looks very good.

choices.text: Let it stand, with a note

effects.log: The pillar becomes a shared monument. The other god is touched and a little amused.

choices.text: Ask the mason to carve a second name, beside it

effects.log: Two names on a pillar. The mason's chisel is steady.

events.text: A small child of the next domain's god is lost on your hill, and the whole valley turns out to find them. They are discovered an hour later, asleep in the shrine cat's basket, with a thumb in the mouth and a firm grip on the cat's tail.

choices.text: Carry the child home yourself

effects.log: The neighbour god opens the door and is silent for a while. Then, thickly, thanks you.

choices.text: Leave the child with the keeper to be returned at dawn

effects.log: The child goes home at dawn with a bun and an opinion of cats.

events.text: A note comes over the boundary from the neighbour's heir: 'Your rain was wet. Mine is wetter. Come and see.' A small hand-drawn map is attached, with an X. It is the first invitation from that quarter in four centuries.

choices.text: Accept the invitation

effects.log: The rain over there is damper than yours and a touch cheerful. You go home with an umbrella and a smile.

choices.text: Send a modest reply and a seed

effects.log: The seed comes up in a week as a small cloud over the neighbour's pond.

events.text: A postcard arrives at the shrine from a faraway coast: a picture of a harbour, a hurried note and a pressed flower from a plant that does not grow in your valley. It is addressed to 'the old hill'. The keeper pins it above the altar.

choices.text: Smell the flower

effects.log: It smells of salt and a strange green sap. You send a seed of the hill's own in return.

choices.text: Add the card to the keeper's wall of thanks

effects.log: The wall has a hundred such cards and they are all, in their way, prayers.

events.text: The oracle at your shrine has a cough, and every prophecy comes out punctuated. 'The harvest will be... *cough*... plentiful, though the... *cough*... frost shall come on the third day.' The pilgrims are baffled and write down the coughs as well.

choices.text: Send a warm tea in a dream

effects.log: The oracle wakes with a mug of honeyed tea on the bedside table. The cough eases.

choices.text: Interpret the coughs yourself, solemnly

effects.log: You interpret the coughs as a sign of a fair spring. It is, as it happens, a fair spring.

events.text: An oracle reads the flight of a heron as a sign you are wroth, and calls a three-day fast. The heron, annoyed, circles back to the river to eat a fish. The valley, hungry, begins to doubt the fast and, pointedly, the heron.

choices.text: Send the heron to the oracle's window with a fish

effects.log: The heron drops a fish on the sill. The fast ends at once, with a feast.

choices.text: Let the oracle learn from it

effects.log: The oracle learns, with some humility, that herons eat.

events.text: The prayers come in on the evening tide, as they always do at the turn of the season: thousands at once, soft and eager, wanting everything. It is like being poured into. You hold on to a chair until it passes.

choices.text: Answer the first, plainest prayer

effects.log: The plain prayer is for a good night's sleep. The sender gets it, and so do you.

choices.text: Wait for the tide to ebb before answering any

effects.log: The tide ebbs. You answer the quiet ones that remain, and find them the best.

events.text: In the dry season the shrine fountain falters and then stops. The keeper looks at you as if you had personally withheld the water. You have only forgotten, for the moment, to be generous with it.

choices.text: Let the fountain run again

effects.log: The water leaps up and the keeper's face clears.

choices.text: Sit by the dry basin and think about why

effects.log: You think about it for a day and a night. In the morning you remember to be generous.

events.text: The festival has gone wrong. The lanterns will not light, the musicians are in a sulk, the cakes have fallen. The crowd stands in a loose, patient circle waiting to be pleased. You are, in a sense, the host.

choices.text: Light the lanterns with a breath

effects.log: They bloom all at once. The musicians take it as a cue and begin, a little sourly, to play.

choices.text: Tell the crowd a true and funny story

effects.log: The crowd laughs. The cakes are eaten as they are.

events.text: Some dawns no prayer comes. The silence is not hostile, just empty, like a dish. You eat your breakfast with an odd sense of fasting. At noon a small voice says: 'Hello?' and then, 'Is anyone there?' and then a laugh.

choices.text: Answer the small voice, once

effects.log: A child, hidden in the shrine bushes, has been testing if you exist. You do.

choices.text: Hold the silence a little longer

effects.log: The silence deepens, and becomes a kind of company.

events.text: The renovation committee wants to add a bell tower. A lively debate ensues about the bell. Should it ring on the hour, the half or the quarter? The committee splits into three factions, each insisting on a different number of chimes.

choices.text: Suggest a bell that rings when it feels like it

effects.log: The bell is approved, to general confusion. It is rung by the wind.

choices.text: Let the committee argue

effects.log: They argue until the bell is finally cast. It rings once and is declared perfect.

events.text: A pilgrim has rubbed your statue's nose for luck and worn it flat. The sculptor is summoned to restore it; instead, the sculptor sits and looks at it for an hour, and then gives it a second, slightly different, flat nose.

choices.text: Approve the flat nose

effects.log: You are known thereafter as the god of the flat-nosed statue. It is a fond title.

choices.text: Ask the sculptor to leave the old one alone

effects.log: The sculptor nods. The nose is left worn. It is lucky.

events.text: The neighbouring god's household arrives at your boundary stone for an unannounced picnic. They have brought three baskets and a very tall hat. They spread a cloth over the stone, and lay out pastries with the air of long practice.

choices.text: Join the picnic

effects.log: The pastries are excellent. The tall hat is passed round and everyone wears it in turn.

choices.text: Bring a jug of your own rain-water

effects.log: The water is declared sweeter than their wine. Politely.

events.text: You find an answer you wrote to a prayer long ago, never sent. It says: 'Yes.' The prayer, filed beneath it, is a little girl's, asking for a puppy. Seventy years too late, but the yes has the tone of someone who meant it.

choices.text: Send the yes anyway

effects.log: A puppy appears in a grandmother's lap, tail wagging. She weeps with laughter.

choices.text: Frame the pair and hang them in your hall

effects.log: The frame is plain wood. Visitors read it and are quiet.

events.text: The oracle's latest prophecy has a message folded in it, a little ribbon of paper tucked into the knot. It reads: 'This is a guess.' You find you are fond of the oracle for the first time in a century.

choices.text: Send a quiet thanks

effects.log: The oracle's next prophecy is gentler, and wrong in a better way.

choices.text: Keep the ribbon

effects.log: The ribbon goes in your sleeve. It is the most honest thing on the premises.

events.text: The pilgrims have gone home. The stalls are folded, the lamps are out and the lanes are littered with petals. You walk down the middle of the street in the quiet. A single stall still stands, tended by an old woman who has not noticed it is over.

choices.text: Buy a paper fan from her

effects.log: She sells it with enormous dignity. The fan is plain and perfect.

choices.text: Sit with her until she is ready to pack up

effects.log: You sit. At last she folds the awning, and you carry it for her.

events.text: A pair of swallows has built a nest in the hollow of your altar bell. Every time the bell is rung, the swallows protest. The keeper, who is fond of birds, has stopped ringing it. The valley has gone without a dawn bell for a month.

choices.text: Ask the swallows to move, politely, in a dream

effects.log: The swallows shift to the eaves. The bell is rung again, and they sing along.

choices.text: Let the bell rest until the chicks fledge

effects.log: The chicks fledge in a fortnight. The bell is rung in their honour.

events.text: Two priests of yours, {npc} of the upper shrine and a colleague of the lower, both claim the well at the hill's foot. Each says it was blessed for their shrine. Both have written to you at length, and both letters smell of lilac, which is suspicious.
events.arc: Two Priests and One Well

choices.text: Go down in a plain coat and draw a bucket

effects.log: The water is sweet. You meet both priests at the well and neither recognises you. Each tells you, with great fairness, that the other is a liar.

choices.text: Summon both to your hall and hear them out

effects.log: They arrive within a minute of each other, in clean robes, and take a very long time to say very little.

events.text: The dispute spreads. The upper shrine's pilgrims will not drink from the lower buckets, and the lower shrine's pilgrims will not climb the hill. A hole in the road is blamed on the other side. A festival day has been moved twice to avoid the meeting.
events.arc: Two Priests and One Well

choices.text: Send a quiet drought to both shrines

effects.log: Both wells go low. The priests, appalled, find themselves hauling water together.

choices.text: Ask the keeper of the road to mend the hole

effects.log: The road is mended by the third week. Both sides take credit.

events.text: You rule. The well belongs to neither shrine and to both, and is a gift of the hill to the valley, with a rota. {npc} receives it stiffly, bows, and says, 'The lower priest is still a liar.' The lower priest, passing, says the same. Both look at you for agreement.
events.arc: Two Priests and One Well

choices.text: Declare the well a shared shrine, with a keeper from each

effects.log: The two keepers share a hut and a kettle and a grudge. The well is the best-kept in the valley.

choices.text: Say you cannot find fault in either, and make them both sit down

effects.log: They sit. The silence lasts an hour. Something small and long-overdue is said.

events.text: In later years the two priests are discovered by pilgrims to be old friends, bickering at a bench by the well each evening. 'It is the best part of the day,' {npc} says, unprompted. You were, it seems, judging a habit rather than a quarrel.
events.arc: Two Priests and One Well

choices.text: Add a bench with a canopy

effects.log: A canopied bench is built by the well. The pair claim opposite ends and meet in the middle.

choices.text: Leave them to it

effects.log: They bicker on for fifty years. Each outlives the other by a week.

events.text: Two of your priests keep different calendars: {npc} counts by the moon, the other by the harvest. As a result they celebrate your feast on days a fortnight apart, and each calls the other's a fraud. The pilgrims, unsure, attend both and are fat.
events.arc: The Priests Who Disputed the Calendar

choices.text: Back the moon calendar

effects.log: {npc} is vindicated and insufferable for a decade. The harvest priest sulks in a barn.

choices.text: Back the harvest calendar

effects.log: {npc} is mortified, and then, to everyone's surprise, relieved. The moon is a difficult thing to keep a feast by.

events.text: The pilgrims, who like feasts, begin to push for both. A pamphlet circulates: 'Why not two?' The priests, outraged, issue a joint statement for the first time in years, defending the single feast, and are laughed at by the whole valley.
events.arc: The Priests Who Disputed the Calendar

choices.text: Read the pamphlet with a smile

effects.log: It is well written. You tuck it behind a candlestick for later.

choices.text: Ask the printer to put out a second edition

effects.log: The second edition sells out in a week.

events.text: At the next double feast you appear in person, in a plain coat, and eat at both tables. {npc} sees you from across the hall and goes grey. The other priest does likewise. You are, you realise, the only guest who has ever been to both.
events.arc: The Priests Who Disputed the Calendar

choices.text: Declare the two feasts a pair, and bless the fortnight between

effects.log: The fortnight becomes a season of small feasts. It is the happiest the valley has been.

choices.text: Say nothing, eat the pudding, leave a leaf

effects.log: The leaf is found by both priests and framed by one.

events.text: {npc} writes to you late in life, penitent: the feasts never mattered, only that someone showed up. You decide that was the whole of the dispute. In the margin of the letter, in a hand you hardly use, you write: 'We all knew.'
events.arc: The Priests Who Disputed the Calendar

choices.text: Send the letter back with a pressed flower

effects.log: The flower is kept in the shrine for a century.

choices.text: Keep the letter

effects.log: It goes in the same drawer as the pamphlet.

events.text: The old keeper of the hill shrine has died and left two keys: one to the front door and one to the vault of offerings. {npc} has the front, the keeper's niece has the vault, and neither will give way. Each claims the old keeper meant them to hold both.
events.arc: The Two Keys to the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Visit the shrine unseen and ask the dead keeper's cat

effects.log: The cat leads you to a note under a flowerpot: 'Let them share. They will grow up.' You read it, and decide not to mention that it is in the cat's paw print.

choices.text: Call both to the altar and hold the keys yourself, for the night

effects.log: Both arrive with their pride. You hand each the other's key. The silence that follows is a very productive one.

events.text: The swap leaves them locked out of their own halves of the shrine. {npc} and the niece are forced to ask each other politely for the door, and to wait in each other's presence. It takes a week for either to say 'please'.
events.arc: The Two Keys to the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Leave them to it

effects.log: The word 'please' is eventually said by both, simultaneously, to a locked door.

choices.text: Send a cold rain to push them into the porch together

effects.log: The porch is cramped. The conversation is brief and unexpectedly warm.

events.text: A year on, the shrine is run by the pair with a single jangling ring of keys that they pass back and forth. {npc} confides that the vault was never full of treasure, only of letters the old keeper wrote to the gods every year, unsent. The two read one a night.
events.arc: The Two Keys to the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Answer a letter, with a small kindness for each

effects.log: A small kindness lands in the valley for each unsent letter. The pair watches for them and writes them down.

choices.text: Let the letters stay unanswered, a gift of their own

effects.log: They go back in the vault, in order, sealed with ribbon.

events.text: When the niece marries, the wedding is held at the hill shrine, and {npc} gives the bride away with the vault key on a ribbon. The key becomes a keepsake of the family. The front door, ever after, is left unlocked at night.
events.arc: The Two Keys to the Hill Shrine

choices.text: Bless the unlocked door

effects.log: The door stays unlocked for a thousand years, and nothing is ever taken but a few apples.

choices.text: Attend the wedding in a plain coat and catch the bouquet

effects.log: You hold it all through the feast, politely, for want of anywhere to put it down.

events.text: {npc} accuses a fellow priest of stealing a sermon. The sermon, on the virtue of patience, has been given at both shrines, word for word, in the same week. Both priests are in tears, and both swear they wrote it. The congregations have started to compare notes.
events.arc: The Sermon That Was Stolen

choices.text: Ask each to deliver the sermon in your hall

effects.log: The two deliver it in turn. They have the same pauses. The same joke. The same moment where the voice breaks. Whoever wrote it, you realise, is not in the room.

choices.text: Treat it as a joke and ask them to swap sermons for a month

effects.log: They swap. A month of surprising insights follow, and an equal number of crises.

events.text: A third voice enters the quarrel: a small sweeper at {npc}'s shrine, who says that the sermon is in a book on the shelf. Both priests read from it at night, the sweeper reports, with candles. The sweeper is not thanked, has crumbs on the chin and is delighted.
events.arc: The Sermon That Was Stolen

choices.text: Find the book

effects.log: It is an old one, with no author. The title page says 'For whoever needs it'. You take it, delighted.

choices.text: Give the sweeper a ribbon

effects.log: The sweeper takes it in both hands, quite sure it is a medal.

events.text: The book is a gift of an older god, long gone, who left it on a hillside for the first priest to find. The sermon is common property. {npc} reads the note on the flyleaf in silence, and then goes across the valley to apologise to the other priest, on foot, in the rain.
events.arc: The Sermon That Was Stolen

choices.text: Send a gentle sun to dry them on the way

effects.log: The sun breaks as {npc} reaches the door. The other priest opens it with an umbrella, and then, seeing, laughs and drops it.

choices.text: Wait in the book, so to speak

effects.log: You wait and watch. The apology takes ten seconds and the supper after it takes ten hours.

events.text: The two priests start a school on the sermon, with the sweeper as its first pupil. 'The Patience School', they call it. It teaches nothing but how to wait for a thing to grow. It has been going for four hundred years and is the quietest school in the realm.
events.arc: The Sermon That Was Stolen

choices.text: Bless the school with long afternoons

effects.log: The afternoons grow slightly longer in that valley. No one has ever complained.

choices.text: Enrol as a visiting student, unannounced

effects.log: You sit at the back and learn, with some embarrassment, how much you do not know about patience.

events.text: The healer-priests of your two shrines, {npc} and another, offer rival cures for the winter cough: one a tea of pine and honey, the other a poultice of onions. The valley is divided in nose and throat. Both beg you to bless their cure and curse the other's.
events.arc: The Two Healer-Priests

choices.text: Bless the tea

effects.log: The tea acquires a faint golden glow. {npc} sniffs and writes a pamphlet about onions.

choices.text: Try both cures yourself, at the same time

effects.log: You emerge from a night of onion and honey greatly improved. Both healers are astonished that you chose to be a patient.

events.text: A particularly bad winter arrives and the cough spreads. Neither cure is enough. The healer-priests, exhausted, tour the valley in opposite directions, passing each other on the road without a word. They have both stopped sleeping.
events.arc: The Two Healer-Priests

choices.text: Send a warm spell to the worst-hit houses

effects.log: The cough relents in a week. The valley credits the cures, both.

choices.text: Order the two healers to share a cart

effects.log: They are forced into the same cart, a day's ride, and emerge with new respect for each other's feet.

events.text: A third cure emerges: both, in a cup, with a spoonful of honey. It tastes appalling and works. {npc} and the other healer, who invented it together on the cart, name it after you, which is embarrassing, and put your name in the margin of the recipe.
events.arc: The Two Healer-Priests

choices.text: Accept the name with good grace

effects.log: The cure is sold throughout the valley, with a modest ribbon on each jar. (+faith)

choices.text: Ask that it be named for the cart instead

effects.log: It is called the Cart Cure. It sells better.

events.text: {npc} is sent to a lower city for a conference on coughs, and stands on a podium to present the Cart Cure to a room of grim physicians. They try it. They cough. They confer. They add it to the book. {He} writes to tell you, in the tone of one who has been trusted.
events.arc: The Two Healer-Priests

choices.text: Send {him} a word of pride

effects.log: A word of pride reaches {him} on the train home, where {he} reads it twice.

choices.text: Send a sprig of pine and a sprig of onion in a pot

effects.log: The pot sits on {his} windowsill and thrives, to everyone's confusion.

events.text: A young godling, {npc}, is sent to your hall by the pantheon to be apprenticed. {He} is the god of puddles, and makes puddles in the wrong places: on your carpet, in your boots, at the exact height of your ankle. {He} stands very straight, dripping, and offers a bow.
events.arc: The Apprentice God of Puddles

choices.text: Show {him} how to make a puddle where it belongs

effects.log: A puddle appears in the courtyard, in perfect reflecting stillness. {npc} stares at it for an hour and cannot stop smiling.

choices.text: Give {him} a bucket and a quiet corner of the garden

effects.log: {He} fills the corner with puddles, small and vain. A frog arrives, and then a second.

events.text: The apprentice grows. The puddles are better, rounder, more consistent. But {he} is lonely, and the puddles, like all things made in loneliness, tend to arrive in sets of one. You find yourself speaking to them. One answers back, in a tiny, damp voice.
events.arc: The Apprentice God of Puddles

choices.text: Sit with the apprentice and talk about puddles

effects.log: You talk about puddles for three hours. You learn a great deal about reflection.

choices.text: Introduce the apprentice to the young goddess of rivers

effects.log: The two sit on the steps and splash their feet. It is the best afternoon of the year.

events.text: The pantheon sends an inspector to see whether the apprentice is making progress. The inspector arrives in a downpour and falls into a puddle, not amused. {npc} offers a hand, and a towel, and an apology, in that order. The inspector is disarmed.
events.arc: The Apprentice God of Puddles

choices.text: Vouch for the apprentice in the inspector's report

effects.log: The report is glowing. 'A god of puddles, thoroughly reflective.' The inspector never visits again, for fear of the carpet.

choices.text: Give the inspector a towel and a cup of cocoa

effects.log: The inspector leaves damp and contented, with a pocket of cocoa powder.

events.text: When the apprenticeship ends, {npc} leaves for a small domain of {his} own: a crossroads in a lowland town, where puddles are plenty. {He} sends you a note on the first rainy day, with a drawing of a puddle in which you appear, small, in a coat, smiling.
events.arc: The Apprentice God of Puddles

choices.text: Frame the drawing

effects.log: It hangs in your hall, damp-looking, forever.

choices.text: Send back a bucket as a gift

effects.log: The bucket is installed in the crossroads shrine. It is always full.

events.text: A strong young godling, {npc}, is placed with you to learn gentleness. {He} arrives with enormous hands and an apology already prepared. By the second week {he} has broken a small mountain, by accident, while stretching, and stands before the rubble with a face like wet paper.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Broke a Small Mountain

choices.text: Help {him} put the mountain back, rock by rock

effects.log: It takes a month. The mountain is a little different afterwards, with a neat shelf where the summit was. {npc} is proud of the shelf.

choices.text: Declare the rubble a new feature of the landscape

effects.log: The rubble becomes a famous scree, popular with goats. {npc} is mortified, then gradually pleased.

events.text: You start to teach the apprentice slow things: how to hold an egg, how to lift a cup of water, how to open a door without taking it off the hinge. {He} cries at the egg. {He} is very good at the water. The door takes a year.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Broke a Small Mountain

choices.text: Celebrate the door

effects.log: The door is opened, slowly, with a ribbon, in front of the whole hall. {npc} bows to it.

choices.text: Give the apprentice a sparrow to hold

effects.log: The sparrow sits still for an hour. {npc} does not breathe for the entire time.

events.text: A real landslide threatens a valley town, and {npc} is the only one close enough to stop it. {He} looks at you, shaking, and asks whether it is allowed to use all of {his} strength just once. 'Gently,' you say. {He} nods, and goes.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Broke a Small Mountain

choices.text: Follow at a distance and stay out of the way

effects.log: {npc} holds the hill like an egg until the town is clear, and sets it down so softly that not a stone rattles.

choices.text: Send a wind to steady {him}

effects.log: The wind is not needed, but {he} feels it, and it helps.

events.text: The landslide is the making of the apprentice. A small shrine to {him} rises in the valley town, and {he} accepts it with an expression of severe, speechless gratitude. The shrine has a shelf where the summit would be, and a vase of flowers on the shelf.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Broke a Small Mountain

choices.text: Congratulate {him}, with a cup of cold water, gently held

effects.log: {He} takes the cup in both hands. Not a drop spills.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the flowers speak

effects.log: The flowers are replaced weekly. The apprentice is quietly moved.

events.text: The young apprentice {npc} is placed with you for the god of dusk's training. {He} is promising, careful and terrified of the dark. Dusk, {he} explains, is only the dark arriving. {He} sleeps each night with a lamp, a cat and one eye open.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Feared the Dark

choices.text: Walk with {him} through the dusk, hand in hand

effects.log: You walk the long dusk with {npc}, naming each shade of blue as it comes. By the end, {he} is humming.

choices.text: Give {him} a small lamp of your own

effects.log: The lamp burns a soft gold, and {npc} carries it everywhere, like a pet.

events.text: {npc} improves. The dusk deepens under {his} hand, becomes velvet, even kind. But something in the dark is watching {him}; {he} says so, quietly, one evening, and you realise {he} is right. It is not a monster. It is only very old.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Feared the Dark

choices.text: Greet the old dark, politely

effects.log: The dark, which has never been greeted, is awkward and tries to curtsy.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to introduce you

effects.log: {He} does it with trembling hands. The dark is a shy acquaintance.

events.text: A night comes when the lamp goes out. {npc} is alone in the dusk garden, and there is a long silence. When you arrive {he} is sitting on the grass, quite calm, talking aloud to the dark about {his} day. 'It listens,' {he} says. 'It never interrupts.'
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Feared the Dark

choices.text: Sit and listen with {him}

effects.log: The dark is a very patient listener. You find yourself telling it something you have not told anyone. (+faith)

choices.text: Slip away and leave them to it

effects.log: You leave. In the morning {npc} is asleep on the grass with a smile.

events.text: In later years, {npc} becomes the god of the dusk that comforts: a dim and generous hour that mortals walk home in. The lamp {he} carried is lit in every window at that hour. They say it began with a godling who feared the dark and made friends with it.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Feared the Dark

choices.text: Give {him} your blessing on the day of the first lamp

effects.log: The first lamp is lit across the valley at dusk. It is the most beautiful sunset of the century.

choices.text: Keep your own lamp lit as a reminder

effects.log: Your lamp burns beside the door, small and gold.

events.text: {npc}, your apprentice, has learned a mortal song from a ferryman, and cannot stop singing it. It has seven verses, a dreadful tune and a chorus about a goose. The other gods find it unbearable. {He} sings it at your feast. A silence descends.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Learned a Mortal Song

choices.text: Join the chorus on the second verse

effects.log: You join in, in a rich and tuneless baritone. The whole hall, relieved by the sight of a god being undignified, joins in. It is a triumph.

choices.text: Ask {him} to sing it more quietly, and later

effects.log: {He} complies, hurt. The song retreats to the kitchen, where the cooks pick it up.

events.text: The song spreads. Gods hum it in the corridors. The goose becomes a symbol of the pantheon's lower court. A senior god declares it vulgar, then is overheard singing it in the bath. The apprentice is invited, without warning, to the Hall of Song.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Learned a Mortal Song

choices.text: Accompany {him} to the Hall of Song

effects.log: You sit in the back row. {npc} sings the song for the Hall's choirmasters, who weep openly at the goose.

choices.text: Ask the ferryman to come as a guest

effects.log: The ferryman arrives in an old coat, astonished, and leads the Hall in the chorus.

events.text: The ferryman is brought up to the divine realm for a single night, and sings the song in the Hall to a thousand gods. The ferryman does not understand the place and thinks it a very large tavern. At dawn the ferryman goes home. {npc} stands on the quay, waving, until the boat is gone.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Learned a Mortal Song

choices.text: Return the ferryman with a gift

effects.log: The ferryman wakes in the boat with a new oar. It is never lost, and never leaks.

choices.text: Let the ferryman remember the night as a dream

effects.log: The ferryman tells the tale for forty years, and nobody believes it.

events.text: The goose song is still sung at the divine feasts, and still in the lower courts, and in the mortal taverns, where it has grown extra verses. {npc}, a mature god now, is asked to write down the original. {He} writes it with care and gives it to you. It is seven verses long, and the goose is, in the last, quite dead.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Learned a Mortal Song

choices.text: Add a verse of your own, in gratitude

effects.log: The new verse is accepted into the canon. It is, a scholar notes, the weakest.

choices.text: Keep the manuscript in your hall

effects.log: It sits beside your best books and a feather.

events.text: The apprentice {npc} has been sitting in your chair when you are away. At first it was a joke. Now {he} has had a nameplate made. The pantheon is watching with interest, and the kitchen with open speculation. {He} stands in the doorway, chin up, waiting for you to say something.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Wanted Your Seat

choices.text: Offer {him} the chair for a day, and watch

effects.log: {npc} sits, and hears fourteen petitions, and gives fourteen answers. By evening {he} is grey, and has found the chair is not a throne but a duty.

choices.text: Remove the nameplate and say nothing

effects.log: {npc} sulks for a season. The nameplate is found in the garden, rusting, with a note: 'Too soon.'

events.text: The pantheon whispers that you are being outflanked. Some of the whispering is encouraged by {npc}, who has taken to speaking about 'a new generation'. The kitchen is horrified. The cat has begun to sit in {his} lap, which is the final humiliation.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Wanted Your Seat

choices.text: Ask {him} to chair the next council

effects.log: The council meets. It is long and ragged and {npc} runs it well. Something in {him} has settled.

choices.text: Go away for a month and see what happens

effects.log: You return to find the domain intact and {npc} a little hollow-eyed. A cup of tea is waiting.

events.text: At the next feast {npc} stands to propose a toast. Everyone expects a challenge. Instead {he} says: 'To the one who let me sit in the chair, and did not stop me.' The hall is silent. Then it roars. {He} sits down, scarlet, and glares at the soup.
events.arc: The Apprentice Who Wanted Your Seat

choices.text: Return the toast with grace

effects.log: You raise your cup. 'To the one who can run it, and knows what it costs.' The hall roars again.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let {him} have the moment

effects.log: The moment is entirely {his}. The soup is excellent.

events.text: Years on, {npc} is the god of a minor but respected valley, and writes on the anniversary of the chair: 'I still think it should be mine. But not yet. Not before you are tired.' It is signed with a flourish. You frame it, without telling anyone.
