events.arc: The Apprentice Who Wanted Your Seat

choices.text: Write back that you are never tired

effects.log: You write that you are tired a little, in the evenings, and always have tea. A reply comes by return: 'Tea?'

choices.text: Keep the note on your desk

effects.log: It sits beside the real nameplate and a dried pear.

events.text: A dream comes to you that is not yours. In it, a river you once governed has risen over a lowland town, and you stand on a hill, watching, with a rule of the divine courts in your hand that said you must not interfere. {npc}, a ghost of the town's keeper, asks you why.
events.arc: The Flood You Did Not Stop

choices.text: Answer honestly: you were afraid

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'So was I,' {he} says. 'It was a long time ago.' The river in the dream slows, a little.

choices.text: Answer with the rule, as you did then

effects.log: {npc} listens to it, politely, and says nothing. The river in the dream rises a little.

events.text: You wake with the taste of river water. In the morning you find in your sleeve a small thing from the dream: a pewter lamp, dented, with a name stamped on the base. It is the name of the town. It has not been spoken in the divine courts for nine hundred years.
events.arc: The Flood You Did Not Stop

choices.text: Say the name aloud, once

effects.log: The name is said into the room. Something in the hall turns, as if a door has been opened.

choices.text: Place the lamp on your altar, with a flower

effects.log: The lamp stays, dented and bright. Pilgrims ask who it is for.

events.text: A pilgrim arrives from the far lowlands, from a family whose town was lost in that flood. They have never prayed to you. They have come to ask where their ancestors went, and the question lands in your lap like a stone. You have the answer, and it is not a comfortable one.
events.arc: The Flood You Did Not Stop

choices.text: Tell them the truth, gently, all of it

effects.log: You tell them. The pilgrim cries and thanks you in the same breath. It is the first time you have said it aloud.

choices.text: Lead them to the lamp

effects.log: They hold the lamp and look at the name for a long time, and say it, and go.

events.text: A small shrine rises near the old river, and you let it be built in your name, though you rarely visit. Every spring the lamp is lit there. It is not a miracle, not a blessing. It is only a thing a god remembers, and a place where a god's regret may be held by others.
events.arc: The Flood You Did Not Stop

choices.text: Attend the lamp-lighting, in a plain coat

effects.log: You stand at the back as the lamp is lit. Nobody turns. You are, for the length of a flame, forgiven by no one and by everyone.

choices.text: Send a warm wind to carry the flame

effects.log: The flame bows and holds. The crowd is quiet.

events.text: A letter, nearly rotten, reaches you across a thousand years. It is from a friend of your mortal youth, {npc}, who writes that {he} is old and has not forgotten the pact the two of you made, to meet on the hill once you were rich. You are a god. {He} died long ago.
events.arc: The Friend You Did Not Visit

choices.text: Climb the hill, now, in the dark

effects.log: At the top you find a stone with a name scratched in it. It is the same name. You sit by it until it is light.

choices.text: Put the letter away and try to forget it

effects.log: It does not stay put away. It leaves the drawer and sits on the table, as quiet as a cat.

events.text: {npc} is not the only one you left behind. A hundred half-remembered faces rise at the edge of your mind: a neighbour who lent you a coat, a girl who taught you to whistle, a teacher who believed in you. You have not visited. You have not prayed to them, though you pray for a hundred strangers.
events.arc: The Friend You Did Not Visit

choices.text: Write their names on a list

effects.log: The list is long, and ragged, and you do not stop until dawn.

choices.text: Ask the Hall for a ledger of the dead of your old home

effects.log: The Hall's clerks find it in a day. It is a thin book, and a kind one.

events.text: You descend to the hill of your childhood, which is now a prosperous farm. The farmer has never heard of you. You introduce yourself as a traveller. The farmer shows you a stone on the lawn, scratched with a name, kept clean for generations 'because it was always there'.
events.arc: The Friend You Did Not Visit

choices.text: Tell the farmer whose stone it is

effects.log: The farmer is quiet. 'We keep it clean,' the farmer says. 'We were never sure for whom.' You both look at it for a while.

choices.text: Say nothing, and sweep the stone with your hands

effects.log: The leaves go. The name shows. You say it, quietly, and go on.

events.text: Over the years you visit the hill, the stone and the farm, quietly, on certain days. The farmer's family greets you as a traveller they cannot place. A child asks if you are lost. You say no. You say you have been, but you are not now.
events.arc: The Friend You Did Not Visit

choices.text: Leave a gift for the child

effects.log: The gift is a whistle. It plays only one tune, and the child learns it, and teaches it to the others.

choices.text: Carry on visiting, and ask nothing

effects.log: The visits become a custom of the hill, and a custom of yours.

events.text: For six hundred years {npc} has been your rival at court, and never once have you said the plain thing: that {he} was right, in the quarrel that began it. You were wrong. You have known it for five hundred and ninety-nine years. Today, {he} is ill.
events.arc: The Word You Never Said to a Rival

choices.text: Visit and say it now

effects.log: {npc} listens in silence, then smiles in a way that would shame a saint. 'I knew you knew,' {he} says. 'Sit.'

choices.text: Send a note instead

effects.log: The note is brief, and the reply is brief, and neither is quite what it could have been.

events.text: {npc}'s illness is slow and unlikely to be fatal, but it is long, and the courts assume the worst. Messengers come and go with rumour. You find yourself in the odd position of being asked, by half the court, for news of your enemy.
events.arc: The Word You Never Said to a Rival

choices.text: Stay by the bedside for a day

effects.log: You sit. {npc} sleeps. The room smells of medicine and old books.

choices.text: Tell the court {he} is better than ever

effects.log: The court sighs with relief. {npc} laughs aloud at your lie.

events.text: {npc} recovers, thin and acid-tongued. {He} calls on you in the spring, in a good coat, and says that the old quarrel has been beautifully ended and wants to know what to do with all the spare time. You hadn't thought of that. Neither of you has hobbies.
events.arc: The Word You Never Said to a Rival

choices.text: Propose a hobby, and take it up together

effects.log: You choose pottery. Neither of you is any good. It is the most enjoyable thing either has done in centuries.

choices.text: Offer to be rivals at something harmless

effects.log: The new rivalry is over a rose, and lasts half a millennium.

events.text: When {npc} eventually fades, the court hears it from you first. You stand before them and say the plain thing again, aloud: that the quarrel was your fault and {he} was the better god. The court is stunned. It is not entirely certain it likes it. It remembers it.
events.arc: The Word You Never Said to a Rival

choices.text: Hold a feast in {his} honour, with the rose on every table

effects.log: The rose is passed round. The feast is quiet, and no one eats much.

choices.text: Plant the rose in a hill shrine

effects.log: The rose blooms every year, red and thorny.

events.text: In the early millennia you planted a garden in a corner of your domain, and then, as gods do, forgot it. A traveller, {npc}, arrives with news: the garden has grown wild, strange and enormous, and has begun to answer prayers on its own. It would like to speak with you.
events.arc: The Garden You Abandoned

choices.text: Go and see it

effects.log: The garden is a green riot. Roses climb pines. A pear tree is wearing a coat of ivy. A path, uninvited, leads you to the middle, where a bench has been left for you.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to describe it first

effects.log: {He} describes it in such detail that you begin to remember: the smell of the soil, a name you gave the lilacs.

events.text: The garden has opinions. It has decided, in your absence, that it is a god, or the beginnings of one. It has a small following of bees, three squirrels and a gardener who is not entirely a person. It receives you with the stiffness of a child meeting a long-lost parent.
events.arc: The Garden You Abandoned

choices.text: Apologise to the garden

effects.log: The garden accepts the apology with gravity and a brief shower of petals.

choices.text: Ask what it wants

effects.log: It wants, as it turns out, to be asked. A great many things follow.

events.text: You and the garden settle into a kind of friendship. You visit once a year, and it saves you the best pear. The traveller {npc} turns out to be the garden's chosen messenger, and travels the realm telling gods, politely, to remember what they have planted.
events.arc: The Garden You Abandoned

choices.text: Take a cutting home

effects.log: The cutting thrives in your hall. Visitors comment on the smell, which is of everything you forgot.

choices.text: Plant a new corner and promise to tend it

effects.log: The new corner is small and well-weeded. The garden watches with approval.

events.text: The garden, in a century, grows a small shrine of its own and calls itself 'the Garden of the Forgetting', after you. It is a joke, and it is also an honour. A sign on the gate reads: 'All who forgot are welcome.' You have never felt so thoroughly forgiven by a plant.
events.arc: The Garden You Abandoned

choices.text: Hang a sign of your own beside it

effects.log: Your sign reads: 'And all who remember.' It is the shortest sermon you have ever preached.

choices.text: Walk away through the roses, humming

effects.log: The roses bow as you pass. It is entirely their own idea.

events.text: It is your turn to host the midsummer feast of the pantheon, and you have dreaded it for four hundred years. {npc}, the pantheon's steward, arrives with a list of two thousand gods, their dislikes, their allergies and the seating arrangements that will cause war.
events.arc: Hosting the Midsummer Feast of the Pantheon

choices.text: Ask {him} to simplify the list

effects.log: {He} cuts it to eight hundred, with an expression of professional pain. The rest will eat in the garden.

choices.text: Take the list as given and plan around it

effects.log: You plan for a fortnight. The table plan is a work of art, and nobody will like it.

events.text: The preparations go awry. A sea god arrives early, wet. A fire god is sulking in the kitchen. The lamps, newly polished, do not light. You are standing in the middle of a hall of three hundred half-laid tables, with a ladle, when {npc} appears to say, calmly, that the hall is on fire.
events.arc: Hosting the Midsummer Feast of the Pantheon

choices.text: Put the fire out with a laugh

effects.log: It is only the cook's ambitious pastry. The cook is mortified and gets a medal.

choices.text: Ask the sea god to help

effects.log: The sea god leaps into the kitchen and puts out the fire, and the pastry, and a good portion of the floor.

events.text: The feast itself is a success in a rickety way. A senior god falls asleep in the soup. A pair of old enemies are seated together by mistake and discover they have the same sense of humour. A child god gets into the cellar and returns, glowing, with a jug of something that tastes like the first morning.
events.arc: Hosting the Midsummer Feast of the Pantheon

choices.text: Raise a toast to the accidents

effects.log: The hall roars. The toast is repeated at every feast for the next thousand years.

choices.text: Slip into the kitchen and thank the cook

effects.log: The cook is hiding behind the stove, still mortified. You give the medal a second pin.

events.text: When the guests are gone, {npc} remains, folding napkins with the weariness of a victor. 'It was almost graceful,' {he} says. You help, in silence, until dawn. The steward leaves you a note: 'Your turn again in eleven hundred years. Please rest.' You frame it.
events.arc: Hosting the Midsummer Feast of the Pantheon

choices.text: Offer the steward a long holiday

effects.log: {He} accepts, with a bow like a fall. A letter arrives six months later from a beach.

choices.text: Keep the napkins

effects.log: They are folded in the shape of small swans. You keep six.

events.text: You are hosting a feast, and two guests, {npc} and a god of a neighbouring domain, have declared they will leave if seated near one another. Both are important. Both are stubborn. The table has a limited number of ends. {He} arrives early to inspect the seating chart, and frowns.
events.arc: The Guests Who Cannot Sit Together

choices.text: Seat them at opposite ends, with a long table between

effects.log: The table is twenty yards long. At the midpoint, a fountain. Neither can see the other. Both are secretly disappointed.

choices.text: Seat them side by side and hope

effects.log: They sit, rigid, staring at their plates. The first course takes forty minutes to be eaten.

events.text: The feast proceeds. The two guests do not speak. The servants walk on tiptoe. Then a child god trips with a tray of pastries and, in the rescue, the two guests find themselves catching the same tray from either side. A flicker of eye-contact. A pastry is shared.
events.arc: The Guests Who Cannot Sit Together

choices.text: Pretend not to have seen

effects.log: The feast goes on with a faint, lovely air of conspiracy.

choices.text: Bring the child a second tray

effects.log: The child delivers it with perfect gravity. Both guests take a pastry.

events.text: By the end of the evening the two have exchanged exactly thirty words, twenty-eight of them rude. This is, you realise, progress. {npc} leaves with a cold bow and a hot pastry in a napkin. At the door, {he} says, tiredly, 'Next time, perhaps the same table.'
events.arc: The Guests Who Cannot Sit Together

choices.text: Promise a smaller table next time

effects.log: The next feast is held in your kitchen. Nobody wears a crown. The rivals discover a shared love of soup.

choices.text: Say you will think about it

effects.log: You think about it for half a century. The seating chart is redrawn, and is slightly better.

events.text: In the end the rivals are found at a window, quietly sharing a bottle, arguing about the correct way to bake a pear. They do not stop when you approach. They do not notice. It is perhaps the greatest compliment ever paid your hospitality.
events.arc: The Guests Who Cannot Sit Together

choices.text: Tiptoe away and leave them to it

effects.log: They finish the bottle at dawn and part on a handshake neither admits to.

choices.text: Join them for the last glass

effects.log: The pear is, you agree, best with cinnamon. You are all wrong.

events.text: You have hosted a pantheon festival, with lanterns, music and a banquet of eleven courses, and nobody has come. A storm blocked the roads, a rumour of plague turned the guests back, and the invitation, it appears, was mislaid. {npc}, the steward, stands in the empty hall, with a tray.
events.arc: The Festival Nobody Came To

choices.text: Sit down and eat with {him}

effects.log: You sit at the head of a table of two. {npc} is aghast, then relieved, then hungry. The soup is superb.

choices.text: Send out a call to anyone nearby

effects.log: A shepherd, a pair of pilgrims and a lost dog arrive. It is the best attended banquet of the decade.

events.text: The feast goes on, small and unlikely. {npc} gives a speech to the pilgrims about the harvest, the dog gets a bone, the shepherd tells a long, bad story about a sheep. The lanterns are lit one by one. By the third course, someone has started to sing.
events.arc: The Festival Nobody Came To

choices.text: Sing along

effects.log: You sing, in a terrible voice, and no one has the heart to stop you.

choices.text: Pass round the second jug

effects.log: The jug is passed. The pilgrims fall asleep at the table.

events.text: In the morning, the great doors burst open and the late guests arrive, all of them, apologetic, mud to the knees, to find the hall in happy ruin and a dog asleep in the best chair. They stand in the doorway, ashamed. No one tells them off.
events.arc: The Festival Nobody Came To

choices.text: Welcome them in, and pour the last of the wine

effects.log: The late guests are given a fine breakfast. The feast resumes, and is remembered as the finest.

choices.text: Say the feast is over, and the next begins tomorrow

effects.log: A second feast, in a better mood, runs three days.

events.text: A century later, the small feast has become a tradition: the Feast of the Empty Chair. Every year a place is laid for whoever does not come. {npc} makes the place with a particular care. Last year, a tired stranger sat in it, and was not asked a single question.
events.arc: The Festival Nobody Came To

choices.text: Come as the stranger, and sit in the chair

effects.log: You eat in silence among strangers. It is an honour to be nobody's guest of honour.

choices.text: Send a gift of an extra place and a blanket

effects.log: The chair gets a blanket. It is, by custom, always warm.

events.text: {npc} has been your friend for three thousand years, and has quarrelled with you, on average, every forty. Today's is about a boat. It is not a serious quarrel, but it has the air of ritual. You both know the steps, down to who storms out first.
events.arc: The Millennium of Quarrelling Friends

choices.text: Storm out first, for once

effects.log: {npc} is thrown, and does not know the next line. The quarrel collapses in laughter.

choices.text: Let {him} storm out, as always

effects.log: {He} storms out. You make tea. In an hour {he} is back, and takes the second cup.

events.text: Their quarrels have an ancestry. The first, over a mortal's wedding, cost you a century of silence. The second, over a poem, a decade. The third, over nothing, a night. You are both conscious, now, that the intervals are shrinking, and wonder whether this is progress or its opposite.
events.arc: The Millennium of Quarrelling Friends

choices.text: Count the next one carefully

effects.log: It takes eleven days. You note it in the margin.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what it means

effects.log: {He} says, after thought, that it is how friends say 'I'm still here'.

events.text: A true quarrel arrives at last, with weight: an unkind remark about a dead mutual friend. Both of you go very quiet. The silence lasts a year. In the second year, a letter is written and not sent. In the third, a pear arrives at your door, unsigned, ripe.
events.arc: The Millennium of Quarrelling Friends

choices.text: Send the pear back, with a bite taken

effects.log: The bite is a joke. The reply is laughter, and a visit.

choices.text: Eat the pear and write the letter you were not sending

effects.log: The letter is short and a little foolish. It is received.

events.text: When {npc} eventually begins to fade, you sit together on a mountainside, in the afternoon, as old friends sit. Neither of you speaks of it. You talk about boats. You quarrel, mildly, about the correct way to moor one. It is the best afternoon of the millennium.
events.arc: The Millennium of Quarrelling Friends

choices.text: Let {him} win the quarrel

effects.log: {He} wins, magnificently. You lose, and are happy.

choices.text: Win it, honestly, and watch {him} pretend to mind

effects.log: {He} minds, properly, and then laughs. The boat, it is agreed, is a poor boat.

events.text: A pear tree grows exactly on the boundary between your domain and that of {npc}. Its branches lean over both. The pears fall on both. Each claims the pears. The feud has been going for nine hundred years, though the original tree has died and been replaced by its own seedlings, three times.
events.arc: The Feud Over a Pear Tree

choices.text: Offer to share the pears, equally

effects.log: {npc} suspects a trick. {He} counts the pears on your side, twice. The offer is accepted at last, with grudging terms.

choices.text: Propose a contest for the tree

effects.log: A pear-eating contest is arranged. It ends in a tie, and indigestion.

events.text: Pears pile up on both sides of the boundary. They are given to the poor, baked in pies, sent in hampers. The tree is now the most productive in the realm. The feud, to the dismay of both parties, has become a source of civic pride.
events.arc: The Feud Over a Pear Tree

choices.text: Bake a pie for {npc}

effects.log: The pie is accepted at the boundary with a nod. A return pie arrives the next day.

choices.text: Walk the boundary at dusk, alone

effects.log: The tree rustles. Something in its leaves is listening.

events.text: A storm cracks the tree in half, and for a moment both gods stand on the boundary in the rain, staring at it. The split trunk is hollow, and in the hollow is a nest of small pears, preserved in honey and wax, left by an older god, as a gift to whoever should one day be reasonable.
events.arc: The Feud Over a Pear Tree

choices.text: Take half the nest and give {npc} the other half

effects.log: The two of you eat the old pears in silence. They taste of a summer neither of you remembers.

choices.text: Take the whole nest and give the tree to {npc}

effects.log: {He} is startled, and then moved, and then furious, and then, in the end, grateful.

events.text: The tree is mended with a graft from each side. It grows lop-sided, with two kinds of fruit, one sweeter and one sharper. The pears are marketed as 'Boundary Pears'. {npc} and you have taken to sitting beneath it, once a year, on opposite benches, in complete and companionable disagreement.
events.arc: The Feud Over a Pear Tree

choices.text: Name a pear after {him}

effects.log: The Pear of the Boundary is renamed, quietly, by the market. {npc} says nothing, and orders a crate.

choices.text: Leave the benches as they are

effects.log: The benches are replaced every century. They are always placed the same distance apart.

events.text: You meet {npc} at a pantheon gathering, after two thousand years of absence. {He} nods, politely, and asks your name. It is a joke, you think; it is not. {He} has lost, over the long years, a number of memories, and yours is one of them. The shock is greater than any quarrel.
events.arc: The Old Friend Who Became a Stranger

choices.text: Introduce yourself again, warmly

effects.log: You say your name and a fact or two. {npc} listens with the patience of an old scholar being shown a new map.

choices.text: Say nothing of it and buy {him} a drink

effects.log: You sit and talk of the weather. {He} is a good listener, and no more than a stranger.

events.text: You meet again, by degrees. {npc} remembers nothing, but is curious. {He} asks about the friendship, and you tell the stories one at a time, as one might unwrap a series of gifts. {He} laughs in the right places, and cries at the one about the goat.
events.arc: The Old Friend Who Became a Stranger

choices.text: Tell the best story last

effects.log: It is the story of how you first met. {He} says it sounds like something {he} might have enjoyed.

choices.text: Ask {him} to tell you something new

effects.log: {He} tells you of a small thing {he} discovered last year. It is lovely, and new.

events.text: It occurs to you that the friendship does not need the old memories to continue: it only needs a new beginning, and the willingness to be someone's friend twice. You say as much, awkwardly, over dinner. {npc} considers it for a long time and says, 'Then let us begin.'
events.arc: The Old Friend Who Became a Stranger

choices.text: Begin again, with a handshake

effects.log: You shake hands. It is the oddest and best handshake you have ever given.

choices.text: Begin again, with a small gift

effects.log: A pear changes hands, and the cycle of three thousand years begins afresh.

events.text: A few decades on, {npc} remembers one thing: the smell of your hall at winter, wood-smoke and old paper. {He} turns up on your doorstep without warning and sits by the fire. 'This,' {he} says. 'I remember this.' It is not much. It is everything you needed.
events.arc: The Old Friend Who Became a Stranger

choices.text: Make up the fire and pour the tea

effects.log: You make up the fire. {npc} falls asleep in the chair, and you watch the flames for a long time.

choices.text: Say nothing and sit beside {him}

effects.log: You sit. The fire does the rest.

events.text: The domain beast that serves your hall, a great tide-ox named {npc}, has taken to sleeping in the kitchen on cold nights. {He} is the size of a barn. The cooks work around {him} with a combination of terror and affection, and have given {him} a cushion the size of a haystack.
events.arc: The Domain Beast in the Kitchen

choices.text: Scratch {his} ears, and ask the cooks to give {him} soup

effects.log: {npc} sighs enormously. The soup arrives in a washing-copper. {He} drinks it in one slow draught.

choices.text: Ask {him} to sleep in the courtyard

effects.log: {He} goes, wounded, and stands in the rain, watching the kitchen windows like a dog.

events.text: The beast has opinions about the menu. {He} refuses to be in the same room as the lamb. {He} enjoys cabbage more than seems reasonable. {He} has begun to follow the head cook about, and to rest {his} enormous head on the counter, hopefully, while the pastry cools.
events.arc: The Domain Beast in the Kitchen

choices.text: Give {him} a pastry of {his} own

effects.log: {npc} takes the pastry with surprising delicacy, and eats it in a single, dignified gulp.

choices.text: Ask the cook what {he} likes best

effects.log: The cook says, with embarrassed pride, that {he} likes the singing.

events.text: A cold winter. The beast is old, now, older than the hall. {He} spends the whole of it in the kitchen, breathing slowly, steaming faintly, warm as a hill. The cooks put the breakfast bread to rise against {his} flank. The bread is the best they have made.
events.arc: The Domain Beast in the Kitchen

choices.text: Sit with {him} in the evenings

effects.log: You sit on the cushion, leaning against {his} side. {He} hums, a note below hearing.

choices.text: Send an extra fire to the kitchen grate

effects.log: The fire is kept up all night. {npc} sleeps soundly, and snores like a bell.

events.text: {npc} dies in the spring, quietly, at dawn, on the cushion in the kitchen. The cooks stand around with their hands in their aprons. You ask that the cushion be kept. The kitchen, from that day, is a little warmer than the rest of the hall, and no one can say why.
events.arc: The Domain Beast in the Kitchen

choices.text: Make the cushion a relic of the hall

effects.log: The cushion sits by the stove, round and sagging, for ten thousand years. The cooks never move it.

choices.text: Plant a cabbage patch by the kitchen door

effects.log: The cabbages thrive. The cooks pull one for every feast, and leave a leaf on the step.

events.text: A star-stag of the Sky has attached itself to your household. {npc} slept on the doorstep for a week, then in the hall, then on the foot of your bed, where {he} rests with antlers like a small constellation. Visitors find it hard to say what is more distracting, the stag or the stars.
events.arc: The Star-Stag Who Sleeps at the Foot of the Bed

choices.text: Let {him} stay on the bed

effects.log: {npc} sighs. The bed is a thing of cold light and warm weight. You sleep soundly for the first time in a century.

choices.text: Move {him} to a cushion by the fire

effects.log: {He} moves, graciously, with the air of an elder being politely escorted.

events.text: The stag's antlers have a habit: on certain nights they shed a single small star, which falls onto the carpet and rolls under the furniture. The cleaning staff have devised a ritual for retrieving them. The household has an odd collection of tiny, warm, sleeping lights.
events.arc: The Star-Stag Who Sleeps at the Foot of the Bed

choices.text: Hang the stars from the ceiling

effects.log: The ceiling glows. Visitors take it for a design choice, and ask about the architect.

choices.text: Plant one star in the garden

effects.log: A tiny constellation takes root among the beans. The beans are astonishing.

events.text: A hunter of the Sky pantheon arrives to claim the stag for a sacred hunt, which is owed. The hunter is polite and firm. The stag, behind you, stands very still. {He} has not been hunted in four hundred years, and has learned to like being a pet.
events.arc: The Star-Stag Who Sleeps at the Foot of the Bed

choices.text: Refuse the claim, and offer the hunt a different quarry

effects.log: A star-hare is offered. The hunter, delighted, accepts. {npc} lies down and breathes again.

choices.text: Offer to let {him} go if {he} chooses

effects.log: {npc} chooses to stay. The hunter nods, respectfully, and leaves a salute at the door.

events.text: In time {npc} grows old and silver, and wanders the garden, and one night does not return to the bed. In the morning there is a new star over the garden, low and warm. A sprig of antler is on the pillow. You keep it, and look at the star until dawn, and name it.
events.arc: The Star-Stag Who Sleeps at the Foot of the Bed

choices.text: Name the star after {him}

effects.log: The star is named. Sky pilgrims leave small offerings under it, and the beans do very well.

choices.text: Keep the name to yourself

effects.log: The star has a name nobody else knows. It is a quiet comfort.

events.text: Two of your priests bring you a dispute: whose turn it is to ring the dawn bell. They have a rota, a counter-rota and a diagram. Both have been ringing it, in competition, since sunrise, and the valley has not slept since midnight.

choices.text: Rule that each rings it on alternate days, starting with the louder

effects.log: The louder priest is appalled. The bell is quiet on the next day.

choices.text: Ring it yourself, once, very gently

effects.log: The bell sounds a note so soft that the whole valley falls into a nap.

events.text: Two priests of yours teach two versions of the same hymn, differing by a single word. The congregations sing them at one another across a river. It is the most beautiful quarrel in the realm and you are loath to settle it.

choices.text: Hum the middle way

effects.log: A third version rises from nowhere, with a compromise word. Both choirs adopt it, at once, and are cross.

choices.text: Say nothing and enjoy the river's music

effects.log: You listen from the bank for an hour. The river takes both versions.

events.text: A new apprentice arrives at the door, holding a letter of introduction and a small plant. The letter says the apprentice is gifted and cannot be spoken to before breakfast. The plant, you gather, is the apprentice's only friend.

choices.text: Offer breakfast, and a window for the plant

effects.log: The apprentice eats three eggs and says hello. The plant is moved to the sill.

choices.text: Let the apprentice find the way alone

effects.log: The apprentice finds the kitchen in an hour, and a place at the table in two.

events.text: Your apprentice sneezes in the middle of a solemn rite and a gust of storm blows through the hall, scattering the incense, the petitions and a visiting dignitary's hat. The apprentice stands frozen, hands to the mouth, eyes enormous.

choices.text: Chase the hat with the apprentice

effects.log: The two of you run the length of the hall after the hat, laughing. The dignitary is charmed.

choices.text: Declare the sneeze an omen

effects.log: The sneeze is recorded as a portent of rain. It does rain, a week later.

events.text: At three in the morning a small regret turns up: a rude word you said to a spring, eleven hundred years ago. It stands at the foot of your bed in its night-shirt, wringing its hands. It is a very small regret, but it has come a long way.

choices.text: Apologise to the spring in the morning

effects.log: The spring bubbles a little. You are forgiven by a small, wet voice.

choices.text: Offer the regret a cup of tea

effects.log: It drinks, and nods, and goes away a little lighter.

events.text: In a crowd at a pantheon feast, you see a face from your mortal life. It is a stranger with a similar nose, but your heart stops. When it is over, you find you have been standing for some time with a cup in your hand, staring at the wall.

choices.text: Take a walk in the cold

effects.log: The cold air helps. You return calm, and a little sad.

choices.text: Light a candle for the one you saw

effects.log: The candle burns steadily, and you let it.

events.text: Before your feast, a hundred silver spoons are found to be missing. The kitchen is in a panic. The spoons are discovered at dawn in a bundle on the roof, along with a very small godling, asleep, with a spoon in each hand and an expression of cheerful guilt.

choices.text: Return the spoons and wake the godling gently

effects.log: The godling confesses to a plan to feed the pigeons. The pigeons, at the feast, are given a spoonful each.

choices.text: Let the godling sleep, and use wooden spoons

effects.log: The feast is rustic and splendid.

events.text: At the end of your feast, each guest is meant to receive a gift. You find, to your dismay, that you have wrapped one hundred and nineteen gifts for one hundred and twenty guests. The missing guest is the quietest, and the most important.

choices.text: Give the quiet guest your own coat

effects.log: The guest wears it home, and returns it the next year with a stain and a smile.

choices.text: Give the guest a promise instead

effects.log: The promise is kept, in a week, and is better than a gift.

events.text: A letter arrives from an old friend, two thousand years since last you spoke. It says: 'I was thinking of you. That is all.' It is brief and perfect. You read it six times and write a reply that takes four years to get right.

choices.text: Send the reply as it is

effects.log: The reply is received. A second letter follows, equally brief, equally perfect.

choices.text: Keep the first letter and send nothing

effects.log: The letter lives on your desk. Some letters want only to be had.

events.text: Someone has laid a wreath on the boundary stone of your oldest feud. It is a plain wreath of leaves, with a ribbon. No card. The feud is nine hundred years old, and has long outlived its causes. You suspect it is from the other side.

choices.text: Lay a wreath of your own beside it

effects.log: Two wreaths now sit by the stone. In a month they have wilted into each other.

choices.text: Leave it and pretend not to notice

effects.log: The wreath decays slowly and the feud, for a season, is quiet.

events.text: Your domain beast has left a dead mouse on your pillow. You have no way of knowing whether it is a gift, an apology, or a complaint about breakfast. The beast sits at the foot of the bed with an air of tremendous modesty.

choices.text: Accept the gift with a nod

effects.log: The beast purrs, or the divine equivalent. The mouse is quietly removed.

choices.text: Give the beast a better breakfast

effects.log: The beast eats in a dignified silence and returns to the cushion.

events.text: A visiting god is startled to find a domain beast in your parlour, sprawled on the rug, reading, so far as anyone can tell, a newspaper. The beast looks up, blinks, and returns to the newspaper. You smile, and offer the visitor a chair.

choices.text: Introduce the beast formally

effects.log: The beast nods once. The visitor, disarmed, sits on the rug.

choices.text: Say the beast is the real host

effects.log: The beast looks up with great seriousness. The visitor takes this as a compliment.

events.text: Your domain beast is off its food. It lies in the corner of the hall with its nose on its paws and a heavy, patient sorrow. The cooks hover. The healer says it is nothing, and it is nothing, and the beast stays down for a week.

choices.text: Sit with the beast through the evening

effects.log: You sit. The beast breathes, long and slow. In the morning it eats a little toast.

choices.text: Send a warm wind through the hall

effects.log: The wind curls around the beast like a blanket. It sighs and sleeps.

events.text: Your apprentice has attempted a star and produced a small, wobbling smudge of light that hovers in the corner of the library and hums out of tune. The apprentice looks at it in horror. You look at it with something more like love.

choices.text: Declare it a lamp and keep it

effects.log: The smudge serves as a reading lamp. It hums, faintly, while you read.

choices.text: Show the apprentice how to tune it

effects.log: The note is corrected by a tiny breath. The apprentice looks proud.

events.text: Rain begins to fall on the pantheon festival you are hosting. A hundred gods look up at the sky, then at you, with the air of those who suspect you of weather. You have not, in fact, ordered any. The rain has an opinion of its own.

choices.text: Dismiss the rain with a gesture

effects.log: The rain withdraws, offended. A smaller rain arrives later, as a kind of apology.

choices.text: Declare a dance in the rain

effects.log: A hundred gods dance in the downpour. It is the best part of the festival.

events.text: A priest of the Silent Hall and a priest of the Green Assembly come to you with a joint request: they want to marry each other. Their pantheons have objected. They are quite sure about it. They have a plan and a picnic.

choices.text: Bless the match and carry the plan to the pantheons

effects.log: The two courts, outflanked by a picnic, grudgingly agree.

choices.text: Ask the pair to wait a season and see

effects.log: A season passes. They are still sure. A second picnic follows.

events.text: At dusk, in the empty temple, you sing a hymn you wrote as a mortal, very quietly, not for anyone. It is a poor hymn, with a dreadful tune. When you finish, a mouse sitting in the corner applauds with both paws.

choices.text: Bow to the mouse

effects.log: The mouse bows back. It is, you think, the finest audience you have ever had.

choices.text: Sing it again, louder

effects.log: The second time is better. The mouse, impressed, fetches a friend.

events.text: Two of your priests have each prepared a room in your honour. One is a plain cell with a mat; the other a grand chamber of silk. You are invited to sleep in one. Both priests watch your face for a sign. Both have, quietly, been fasting for a week.

choices.text: Sleep in the plain cell and lunch in the grand chamber

effects.log: You sleep well, and eat well. Both priests glow.

choices.text: Sleep in both, in turn

effects.log: You sleep four hours in each. The priests compare notes in the morning, awed.

events.text: The apprentice's room is empty. The bed is made, the books stacked, the plant gone. A note on the pillow reads: 'Gone to see the sea. Will write.' The note is signed with a flourish. You smile, and set out a second cup for the evening anyway.

choices.text: Wait for the letter

effects.log: The letter comes, in a month, damp and delighted: the sea is wet, large and loud.

choices.text: Send a gull with a coat

effects.log: The gull delivers the coat and a note. The apprentice wears it for a year.

events.text: A god whom you have known for three thousand years has a birthday today, and you remember it, which you are not used to. You arrive at the door with a cake, a pear and a poor sense of timing. The god is out. The cake sits on the step in the sun, and begins to melt.

choices.text: Eat the cake yourself, and leave a note

effects.log: The note says 'Sorry I missed you.' The god, delighted, writes back.

choices.text: Wait on the step until the god returns

effects.log: The god returns at dusk to find you asleep on the step. Neither of you mentions the cake.

events.text: The domain beasts of your hall have outgrown the stable, and a petition arrives from them, written in hoof-prints and tail-flicks, asking for an extension. A clerk translates it in an hour. It is perfectly reasonable and slightly rude.

choices.text: Approve the extension

effects.log: The stable grows by a bay. The beasts hold a modest ceremony.

choices.text: Invite the beasts to design it

effects.log: The beasts' design is a wonder, with a skylight and a very large cushion.

events.text: The two stone lions at your lower gate have begun to shift at night. {npc}, the mason who mends them, swears they only move their paws. By morning the cakes left on the step are gone and there are crumbs in the manes.
events.arc: The Stone Lions of the Lower Gate

choices.text: Leave a larger cake on purpose

effects.log: The cake is gone by dawn, and a lion looks very slightly smug.

choices.text: Sit up and watch the gate

effects.log: You watch all night. Nothing moves, and you feel strangely watched in return.

events.text: The lions are now seen walking the hill road at dusk, politely, like old gentlemen out for air. Pilgrims bow to them. One has been known to walk a lost child home and sit on the doorstep until the door opened.
events.arc: The Stone Lions of the Lower Gate

choices.text: Bless the walk with a little warmth in the stone

effects.log: The lions walk a little further each dusk, warm underfoot.

choices.text: Say nothing and let the road have its guardians

effects.log: The road keeps its guardians, and no pilgrim is robbed that year.

events.text: The lions have grown fat on the cakes and no longer fit between the gateposts. {npc} proposes to widen the gate; the lions, stuck, look mortified. A queue of pilgrims waits in the rain on the road.
events.arc: The Stone Lions of the Lower Gate

choices.text: Widen the gate and carve a lion-door beside it

effects.log: The gate is widened by a hand's breadth. The lions pass through with a great dignity and a small scrape.

choices.text: Ask the lions to eat less

effects.log: They look at you for a long moment. The next morning there is exactly one crumb.

events.text: Watched, the lions never move, and {npc} grows sure they have lost their nerve. Then {he} finds a muddy pawprint on the temple floor, set neatly inside your own footprint. You were not being watched at all; you were being followed.
events.arc: The Stone Lions of the Lower Gate

choices.text: Laugh, and leave them a lantern each

effects.log: Two lanterns burn at the gate all winter. The lions never move while you are looking.

choices.text: Take a cake out to them at midnight, openly

effects.log: The lions accept it with great ceremony. You share the step until dawn.

events.text: A grey heron stands in the shrine pond and cries once on the hour. Nobody taught it. {npc}, the shrine-keeper, has set the whole day by it for twenty years, and today the heron is an hour late.
events.arc: The Heron Who Keeps the Hours

choices.text: Ask the heron what delayed it

effects.log: The heron regards you with one gold eye. In its own time, it says nothing.

choices.text: Reset the keeper's day to the sun

effects.log: {npc} carries on, unsettled, by the sun. The heron takes it badly.

events.text: The heron has begun to cry at odd hours, and the morning bell, the noon meal and the evening lamps are all mistaken. The pilgrims are late, the offerings are cold, and the priest who sells the lamps says it is the best week of the year.
events.arc: The Heron Who Keeps the Hours

choices.text: Send a small wind to turn the pond's reeds into a clock

effects.log: The reeds lean in the proper hours and the heron, offended, falls silent.

choices.text: Wait it out in good humour

effects.log: By the end of the week the shrine runs on heron time. It suits everyone better.

events.text: The heron is old. {npc} finds it one dawn sitting very still on the pond rock, and cries the hour for it, badly, in its place. The pilgrims think it is a new custom.
events.arc: The Heron Who Keeps the Hours

choices.text: Take the heron's place a day and cry the hour yourself

effects.log: You stand in the cold water and cry the hour. The pond lights up, and the heron, sitting beside you, says nothing grandly.

choices.text: Leave {npc} and the heron to it

effects.log: {npc} cries the hours until the heron is well again. The pilgrims leave the shrine praising both.

events.text: The heron is gone in the spring and the hours go quiet. {npc} sets a small wooden bird on the rock instead, and cries the hours from the steps. Within a year a young heron has taken the rock and never says why.
events.arc: The Heron Who Keeps the Hours

choices.text: Thank the new heron with a fish of light

effects.log: The new heron eats the fish and is late the next day. Some traditions begin that way.

choices.text: Leave the wooden bird on the rock beside it

effects.log: The two birds stand together on the rock, one forever and one on the hour.

events.text: Under the threshold of your oldest shrine lives a tortoise that is older than the roof. {npc}, the keeper, found it when the floor was lifted for mending, and the floor has not been put back since. The tortoise is the shrine's only worshipper who has never once looked up.
events.arc: The Tortoise Under the Threshold

choices.text: Have the floor laid around it

effects.log: The floor is laid in a ring, and the tortoise sits in the middle of a circle of boards like a small sun.

choices.text: Carry the tortoise gently to the garden

effects.log: The tortoise does not go. It returns to the threshold before dark and stays there for a week.

events.text: A pilgrim from the far coast says the tortoise is a messenger of a god who sank before the domains were cut. {npc} thinks it is just a tortoise. The pilgrims begin to leave it lettuce, and quietly, small coins of old faith.
events.arc: The Tortoise Under the Threshold

choices.text: Listen at the threshold

effects.log: You hear the sea, very faint, as if under the world there is a slow tide.

choices.text: Let the legend stand without comment

effects.log: The legend grows and nobody is any worse off. The tortoise eats well.

events.text: The tortoise has not moved in a year and {npc} fears the worst. You kneel at the ring of boards and find a small damp mark where, once, a shell had lain. Beneath the threshold, the tortoise has dug down a little way, toward the old tide.
events.arc: The Tortoise Under the Threshold

choices.text: Lay a stone saying what you heard

effects.log: {npc} carves the stone. The tortoise is left to its tide, and the stone to the pilgrims.

choices.text: Dig down with the keeper

effects.log: You find only a sliding smooth stone with a mark like a drawn tide. {npc} puts it back, saying nothing.

events.text: The tortoise returns to the threshold each time you carry it away, for seven years. {npc} finally puts a cushion there, and a bowl. The tortoise tolerates the cushion. It is the nearest thing to thanks the shrine has had in a century.
events.arc: The Tortoise Under the Threshold

choices.text: Accept the stalemate and sign the bowl over

effects.log: The bowl is the shrine's, the tortoise is the bowl's, and the threshold is no one's.

choices.text: Put the tortoise's name on the shrine's own roll

effects.log: A tortoise is added to the roll of the faithful. The scribe resigns.

events.text: The shrine's evening bell has been rung before the keeper's hour for a week. {npc} finally sits up in the dark and sees: a goat has found that the bell-rope is edible, and rings it by chewing.
events.arc: The Goat Who Rang the Bell

choices.text: Replace the rope with an iron chain

effects.log: The goat eats the chain's rust and rings it twice as loud. {npc} takes this as a sign of devotion.

choices.text: Let the goat ring the evening bell

effects.log: The goat rings; the pilgrims arrive at the proper hour; the keeper sleeps.

events.text: The goat has become a minor figure of devotion. Pilgrims bring it garlands, and a woman from the coast has asked to marry it to her own goat, in your name, at the next festival.
events.arc: The Goat Who Rang the Bell

choices.text: Bless the marriage of goats

effects.log: Two goats are wed with great gravity. The festival is the best attended in a decade.

choices.text: Quietly decline to attend

effects.log: The goats are wed without you. A small cake is sent, anonymously.

events.text: The goat is gone from the pen. {npc} searches the hills for three days, and finds it on the high ridge, ringing a small rusty bell nobody had hung there. The bell is older than the shrine, and the goat will not leave it.
events.arc: The Goat Who Rang the Bell

choices.text: Hang the old bell in the shrine beside the new

effects.log: Two bells ring, a little apart in pitch. The goat stands between, delighted.

choices.text: Leave the bell on the ridge and send the goat a cake

effects.log: The goat rings the old bell each dusk. Hill farmers set their suppers by it.

events.text: The goat grows old and stops ringing. {npc} takes over the rope and rings it badly, out of kindness, and the pilgrims prefer the badly rung bell. It becomes the shrine's custom to ring the evening bell a little out of time.
events.arc: The Goat Who Rang the Bell

choices.text: Ring it badly with {npc} one evening

effects.log: You pull the rope together. The bell clangs in a happy disorder and the whole valley hears.

choices.text: Have it mended to ring true

effects.log: A smith tunes it. The goat, from the pen, calls it dull.

events.text: You sent rain to the south terraces. It fell, instead, on the north hill, where {npc}, a shepherd who had not asked for rain, stood with a drying fleece and a month's work in the sun. The south terraces stayed dry.
events.arc: The Rain That Went to the Wrong Hill

choices.text: Send the rain on to the south at once

effects.log: The cloud turns, a day too late; the shepherd is soaked and the terraces half-watered.

choices.text: Own the mistake and send a second rain to the shepherd's fleeces to dry them

effects.log: You blow a warm wind where the rain fell. The fleeces dry, smelling of storm.

events.text: The north hill, to everyone's surprise, blooms. The shepherd's neighbours, who have prayed for rain for years, take it as a sign of favour, and two shrines are founded on the hill in a week, each claiming the miracle.
events.arc: The Rain That Went to the Wrong Hill

choices.text: Leave both shrines to their claims

effects.log: The shrines argue nobly. The hill is green.

choices.text: Visit both in a plain coat

effects.log: You are fed in each, and told by each that the other is false.

events.text: The south terraces have forgiven you, but {npc} has not. {He} comes down the hill with a dry fleece in {his} arms and says, plainly, that a god who cannot aim should not throw. {He} then asks for next year's rain in writing.
events.arc: The Rain That Went to the Wrong Hill

choices.text: Give your word and keep it

effects.log: You put the promise in a dream. The rain, next year, arrives on the hour.

choices.text: Laugh, and send a rainbow as a receipt

effects.log: A rainbow lies over the hill for an afternoon. {npc} frames the sky in {his} memory.

events.text: {npc} is no longer a shepherd on the north hill. {He} is a priest, of a small shrine to the wrong rain, and {he} will not hear that it was a mistake. Pilgrims come from three valleys to the hill that was rained on by accident.
events.arc: The Rain That Went to the Wrong Hill

choices.text: Let the shrine to the wrong rain stand

effects.log: The miracle of the wrong hill becomes a feast day, and you are credited with the aim.

choices.text: Tell {npc} privately the truth

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. 'It still rained, though,' {he} says. 'It still rained on me.'

events.text: You blessed one field, once, and it has since borne a crop so heavy that {npc}, the farmer, cannot carry it in. The barley bends the sheds. Stalks have come up through the floor of the granary.
events.arc: The Blessing That Weighed Too Much

choices.text: Ask the farmer to share the crop with the hamlet

effects.log: {npc} grumbles, but sends carts. The hamlet eats well for a season.

choices.text: Take the blessing back by half

effects.log: You thin the blessing like a broth. The crop becomes merely large.

events.text: The blessing seems to have stuck to the farmer. {npc}'s cow gives too much milk, the dog catches too many hares, and the youngest child has learned to read in a night. A visiting priest asks if this is quite proper.
events.arc: The Blessing That Weighed Too Much

choices.text: Smile and keep out of the way

effects.log: The priest goes home with a fine anecdote and a ripe cheese.

choices.text: Gently ask the blessing to settle

effects.log: The milk, the hares and the child's reading drop to a respectable level.

events.text: A year of plenty has come to nothing: the hamlet has no room to store it and half the crop has rotted. {npc} stands in the heap of it and weeps with frustration, and asks, without much hope, if a god might arrange to have it eaten.
events.arc: The Blessing That Weighed Too Much

choices.text: Send the neighbouring hamlets an invitation in dreams

effects.log: Carts arrive from three valleys. The feast goes on for nine days.

choices.text: Quietly turn the rot back into soil

effects.log: The soil that year is the richest in the valley. {npc} does not understand why, and sings.

events.text: With the blessing halved the farmer's fields are an ordinary size again, and {npc} is quiet. {He} says that for a year {he} felt like a well that someone else was drinking from. {He} is not sure why {he} is saying it to a god.
events.arc: The Blessing That Weighed Too Much

choices.text: Listen to the end

effects.log: {npc} talks until the lamp is low. You say nothing; it is what was needed.

choices.text: Offer a different small blessing: a good roof

effects.log: The roof does not leak that winter. {npc} accepts it like an apology.

events.text: The well in the shrine yard has begun to answer questions, in a voice very like yours. The first to ask was {npc}, the water-carrier, who wanted to know if rain would come. The well said yes. Then it said a number of other things, some of which were true.
events.arc: The Well That Answered in Your Voice

choices.text: Listen at the well in secret

effects.log: The well, you find, mimics you perfectly, down to the sigh. It is uncomfortably good.

choices.text: Silence the well

effects.log: The well goes quiet. The yard feels strangely lonely.

events.text: Pilgrims queue at the well now. The well tells one that the harvest will fail, another that a lost ring is under a fig tree, and a third that the way to wealth is to stop asking wells. Some of it comes true. The queue grows.
events.arc: The Well That Answered in Your Voice

choices.text: Let the well answer small things only

effects.log: The well, firmly told, becomes a local almanac. Nobody is ruined.

choices.text: Visit the queue in a plain coat

effects.log: You ask the well the weather and it gets it right. You tip your hat to yourself.

events.text: The well has begun to quarrel with you in the night. It says you are lazy, which is partly true, and that the shrine's roof leaks, which is wholly true. {npc} brings it a lamp every evening, as if to a lodger.
events.arc: The Well That Answered in Your Voice

choices.text: Fix the roof, and tell the well so

effects.log: The well says 'about time'. It is quiet for a month.

choices.text: Tell the well it is not a god

effects.log: The well says 'neither are you, fully'. It has a point.

events.text: The yard has been quiet for years. {npc}, now old, still brings a lamp to the dry well in the evening. One night the well answers, not in your voice but in a very small one, and says: 'Thank you, I was only learning.'
events.arc: The Well That Answered in Your Voice

choices.text: Say 'you did very well' into the well

effects.log: The yard is silent. The next morning a spring has come up in the corner.

choices.text: Say nothing; light a second lamp

effects.log: Two lamps at the dry well. The pilgrims, seeing it, remember.

events.text: A prayer reaches you every new moon in a language none of your scribes knows. It is certainly a prayer, and certainly addressed to you; the sound of it is warm. The scribe {npc} has pinned a copy of every one to the wall of the archive and says they are the best-sounding ones in the file.
events.arc: The Prayer in a Tongue Nobody Knows

choices.text: Ask the scribes of other gods who might know the tongue

effects.log: Four heralds come, hear it, and each declares it must belong to the next god over.

choices.text: Answer it in the same sounds, as best you can

effects.log: The next prayer is longer and clearly delighted. You have said something, perhaps rude.

events.text: {npc} reports that the prayers have begun to come in pairs, one in the old tongue and one, now, in a rough trade speech with a mistake in each line. Someone is learning to translate for you.
events.arc: The Prayer in a Tongue Nobody Knows

choices.text: Wait and answer when the translation is ready

effects.log: The translation, when it comes, is full of mistakes, and the best prayer of the year.

choices.text: Send a dream of a dictionary

effects.log: A dream of an enormous book, open to a page of delicate nonsense.

events.text: The prayers come from a boat. {npc} reads the final one: a fisherman's family at the end of the shore thanked you for a safe year, in a tongue spoken by perhaps eleven people, of whom three are children. The last speaker of the language is dying.
events.arc: The Prayer in a Tongue Nobody Knows

choices.text: Visit the boat in a plain coat and ask them to teach you

effects.log: You sit in the stern for a month, learning to say thank you in a dying language.

choices.text: Have the scribes copy the prayers carefully for the archive

effects.log: The prayers go into the archive on the best paper. The language is, at least, kept.

events.text: The translation, when it finally arrives, turns out to be four words long. 'We are still here.' {npc} reads it twice, and goes to find a particularly good brush for the answer.
events.arc: The Prayer in a Tongue Nobody Knows

choices.text: Answer in the same four words

effects.log: You answer in four words. The next prayer is the same four, louder.

choices.text: Send a gift of a fair wind to the shore

effects.log: The boats come home early that week. The prayer that follows is long, and mostly about fish.

events.text: A prayer reaches you made not of words but of knots, tied in a long rope that hangs in the rain at the sea shrine. {npc}, the net-mender who tied it, says each knot is a name, and the names are the crew of a boat that has not come back.
events.arc: The Prayer Tied in Knots

choices.text: Read the rope slowly, one knot at a time

effects.log: Seventeen knots. The seventeenth, you notice, is tied loosely, as if left open.

choices.text: Ask the Keeper of Tides if the boat passed

effects.log: Haeryong's herald says the boat is not in the deep. 'Not drowned,' says the herald, 'only late.'

events.text: {npc} ties a second rope, for the next boat, and a third. The sea shrine's whole railing is now hung with prayers in rope. The gulls, being gulls, have started to take the loose ends for nests.
events.arc: The Prayer Tied in Knots

choices.text: Wait with {npc} at the shrine rail

effects.log: You hold the rope's end together in the wind. Neither of you says anything for an hour.

choices.text: Ask the gulls to leave the knots

effects.log: The gulls look at you with great contempt and leave only the very worst.

events.text: A boat comes in, battered and late, on a wind that does not belong to the season. The seventeenth knot, the loose one, was the boy at the stern, who fell asleep during the storm and is the reason the boat was steered home. {npc} unties the loose knot with shaking fingers.
events.arc: The Prayer Tied in Knots

choices.text: Let the wind stay a day longer to see them to shore

effects.log: The boat comes in on a day of unnatural calm. The shrine-rail is hung with bright cloth that evening.

choices.text: Whisper to the boy in a dream that the storm was well steered

effects.log: The boy wakes laughing, though the boy cannot say why.

events.text: The boat does not come in. {npc} leaves the ropes in the rain, and one spring they are found tied together into a single long line that runs up the stair of the shrine to the god's own hall. The line ends in a blank knot, an invitation.
events.arc: The Prayer Tied in Knots

choices.text: Tie a knot of your own in the blank place

effects.log: You tie a knot with a warm hand. The line is left in place; it is the oldest prayer in the shrine.

choices.text: Carry the line to the Keeper of Tides

effects.log: Haeryong takes the rope and holds it over the sea. For a moment the water goes still.

events.text: {npc} was an ordinary worshipper, until {he} nursed a whole hamlet through a fever and was named a saint by acclamation. {He} has since helped everyone in the valley with everything, including things nobody needed help with: the baking, the quarrels, the roof.
events.arc: The Saint Who Would Not Stop Helping

choices.text: Bless {his} work and let {him} be

effects.log: The valley is grateful for a month. Then the tiredness begins.

choices.text: Visit {him} in a plain coat and ask what {he} wants

effects.log: {He} says nothing, because {he} is busy, and hands you a broom.

events.text: {npc} has been helping the neighbouring valley without invitation. The hamlet's own healers have been put out of work, and their pride is hurt. A quiet delegation of three comes to the shrine to ask if the saint could possibly take a holiday.
events.arc: The Saint Who Would Not Stop Helping

choices.text: Send {npc} a dream of a quiet afternoon

effects.log: {He} wakes smiling and sits for an hour, and by noon is repairing the neighbour's fence.

choices.text: Speak to the delegation gently

effects.log: You promise nothing. They leave a little lighter, and a little shamed for having come.

events.text: The valley has given {npc} a shrine of {his} own and begun to pray to {him}. {He} is mortified and helpful. A cupboard of {his} old tools is now a relic, and a boy has been cured, apparently, by touching {his} sleeve while {he} was asleep on a bench.
events.arc: The Saint Who Would Not Stop Helping

choices.text: Ask {npc} to retire and sit in the shrine

effects.log: {He} sits in it for a day, and then finds a ladder, and mends the roof from the inside.

choices.text: Make {him} a proper under-saint of the shrine with a set of hours

effects.log: Hours are fixed: {he} helps from morning to noon, and rests. It lasts a season.

events.text: {npc} is tired. {He} sits in the shrine garden and says that if {he} stops helping, everything will fall apart. You take {his} hand and point to the gate: a line of neighbours have come with soup, wood, and a small bell, to look after {him}.
events.arc: The Saint Who Would Not Stop Helping

choices.text: Say the valley has learned from {him}

effects.log: {npc} looks at the line of neighbours for a long time, and takes the soup.

choices.text: Send a gentle sleep over {npc}

effects.log: {He} sleeps for nine hours, a record. The valley bakes quietly around {him}.

events.text: Outside the saint's shrine a stall has appeared selling relics: thread from the saint's sleeve, dust from the saint's bench, a lock of the saint's hair that, {npc} the stallkeeper admits, is a goat's. Business is good. The saint has asked if you could do something.
events.arc: The Relic Stall at the Pilgrim Gate

choices.text: Visit the stall and buy a relic

effects.log: You buy the goat hair. It is the only honest thing on the table.

choices.text: Send a tidy dream to the stallkeeper about honesty

effects.log: {npc} wakes, thoughtful, and changes the labels on three jars.

events.text: The relics have multiplied. {npc} has hired a boy to bring thread, a cousin to bring dust, and an aunt to say prayers over both. The saint's whole bench has been sold, in pieces, six times over. The saint is not sure whether to be flattered.
events.arc: The Relic Stall at the Pilgrim Gate

choices.text: Lend the stall a real relic: a feather from the shrine

effects.log: The feather is sold at once. It is the one real thing, and no one can tell.

choices.text: Leave the stall to its devices

effects.log: A quiet autumn. The stall grows by two barrels.

events.text: A pilgrim bought a bottle of the saint's breath and, to everyone's astonishment, was cured of a cough. {npc} stares at the bottle. 'It was air,' {he} says. 'I filled it myself. By the well.'
events.arc: The Relic Stall at the Pilgrim Gate

choices.text: Tell {him} the cure was the faith, not the air

effects.log: {He} nods slowly, then corks another bottle.

choices.text: Make the bottle a real blessing for one day

effects.log: The bottles are all real that afternoon. {npc} is overcome, and by evening has closed the stall.

events.text: The relic stall has become a small guild, with a ledger, a patron and a banner. {npc} has been asked to speak at the pilgrim gate on the honest sale of relics, and does, with passion, to an audience of thirty who all own goat hair.
events.arc: The Relic Stall at the Pilgrim Gate

choices.text: Attend, in a plain coat, and clap

effects.log: You clap. It is the best speech about goat hair that you have heard.

choices.text: Grant the guild a small charter

effects.log: The guild receives a seal, and agrees to label the goat hair as such.

events.text: {npc}, god of a small ford, arrives at your hall with a basket of dried apricots and an unusually clean robe. The ford has had no traffic in a decade, and {he} asks, politely, to borrow some faith, to be returned when the road recovers.
events.arc: A God Comes to Borrow Faith

choices.text: Lend a modest measure of your faith

effects.log: A thread of light passes between you. {npc} bows deeply, and the apricots are eaten.

choices.text: Ask what the ford needs besides faith

effects.log: {He} lists three things, the second a plank. You find you can help with the plank.

events.text: {npc} writes from the ford. Faith has, apparently, a texture; the borrowed kind makes the water taste of your shrine. The ford is busier. Pilgrims have been seen crossing it, bowing to the wrong god.
events.arc: A God Comes to Borrow Faith

choices.text: Send a note that bowing in either direction is fine

effects.log: The ford's pilgrims bow both ways. It looks well.

choices.text: Let the taste remain

effects.log: The water tastes a little of your shrine for a year. It is considered a feature.

events.text: The road has recovered. {npc} returns with a sack of faith, polite, exact, and slightly too much, like a man who has counted twice. {He} also brings a small drum, a gift from the ford's children.
events.arc: A God Comes to Borrow Faith

choices.text: Accept the exact amount, and keep the drum

effects.log: The drum is not very good. You keep it by the bed.

choices.text: Tell {him} to keep the surplus for the next hard year

effects.log: {npc} tries to refuse and cannot find the words.

events.text: The plank was the problem; the ford was fine. {npc} repaired the planking and found traffic had already begun to return. {He} brings back the faith unborrowed, and asks if you might have lunch instead.
events.arc: A God Comes to Borrow Faith

choices.text: Have lunch at the ford

effects.log: You eat standing in the river. The fish is not good. It is the best lunch you have had.

choices.text: Send the apricots back with a note

effects.log: {npc} eats them on the bank and writes a grateful, long letter.

events.text: Where the domain of Fire meets the domain of the Sea, a market has grown on the shore: salt for ember, kelp for coal, boiled seaweed for a spark. {npc} keeps the stall nearest the line and says the border runs through the middle of {his} counter.
events.arc: The Border Market of Fire and Sea

choices.text: Walk the market in a plain coat

effects.log: You are charged the border price for a wet spark. It is, you must admit, worth it.

choices.text: Ask the stallkeeper which side of the counter you stand on

effects.log: {npc} laughs: 'Whichever pays more.'

events.text: The border has moved. A hot spring has opened on the Sea side, and the stalls that were safe by the water are now steaming. {npc} pulls the counter across the line and refuses to say whose land it is. The two heralds who arrive to settle it end up buying kelp.
events.arc: The Border Market of Fire and Sea

choices.text: Settle it by drawing a new line in the sand

effects.log: The line wavers as the tide takes it. Nobody is sure whose it is now.

choices.text: Declare the market free ground

effects.log: The market receives a banner of neither colour. The stalls cheer.

events.text: A war of prices breaks out between the two sides of the market. Salt is dear, ember is cheap, and {npc} stands in the middle selling both with an expression of enormous innocence. The two domains' gods have sent each other cold notes.
events.arc: The Border Market of Fire and Sea

choices.text: Broker a peace over a bowl of boiled seaweed

effects.log: The two heralds shake hands over a steaming bowl. Prices fall by a third.

choices.text: Buy out {npc}'s whole stock and gift it to both sides

effects.log: Everyone gets a crate. The market, shocked, behaves for a month.

events.text: The market is still there at the end of the century. The border has moved three times; the stall has not. {npc}'s grandchildren sell salt-smoked ember, and a child from the Fire side has married one from the Sea. The line runs through the wedding feast.
events.arc: The Border Market of Fire and Sea

choices.text: Attend the wedding in a plain coat

effects.log: You are seated on the line. Both families laugh and serve you twice.

choices.text: Send the couple a small hot spring

effects.log: A spring rises beside their house, tasting faintly of both.

events.text: On the road between the domain of Life and the domain of Death stands a toll-house kept by {npc}, a retired ferrywoman's cousin who takes only small coins and stories. Both Baekun and Saengmo are said to pass by it, and neither has paid.
events.arc: The Toll-House Between Life and Death

choices.text: Pay the toll yourself, with a story

effects.log: You tell a short story about a turnip. {npc} writes it down in a thick book and says it was acceptable.

choices.text: Ask the keeper how many have passed unpaid

effects.log: {He} consults the book: a great many, but few have crossed twice.

events.text: {npc} has had a visitor: a very young god, in a worn robe, who says {he} is the god of the last step and the first, and has come to ask which side of the toll-house is {his}. {npc} does not know. The young god waits, patiently, on the threshold.
events.arc: The Toll-House Between Life and Death

choices.text: Offer the young god a bowl of soup

effects.log: The young god eats the soup in silence and begins to look less transparent.

choices.text: Send a note to Baekun and Saengmo together

effects.log: A cold herald and a warm one arrive at the same time, and argue pleasantly.

events.text: The young god has become a fixture at the toll-house. People crossing from Life to Death pay the toll and are told something small and kind; those crossing the other way are told the same. {npc} says it is the best thing that has happened to the road.
events.arc: The Toll-House Between Life and Death

choices.text: Give the young god a seat and a title: Keeper of the Threshold

effects.log: The title is written in the thick book. The young god cries a little and puts on weight.

choices.text: Visit the toll-house each solstice with a small gift

effects.log: The gifts are noted. The young god keeps a drawer for them.

events.text: The toll-house burns down in a dry year, and {npc} stands outside it with the thick book clutched to {his} chest. The young god and a hundred travellers from both directions have begun to build it again, plank by plank, without being asked.
events.arc: The Toll-House Between Life and Death

choices.text: Lend wood and a roof-beam from your own shrine

effects.log: The beam is raised with a song. The toll-house is bigger than before.

choices.text: Say a quiet word to both domains' gods

effects.log: Two gods send a plank each. Neither will say who first.

events.text: A god you knew has faded: the god of an old orchard on the western slopes, whom you met only a few times and always liked. {npc}, their last priest, brings you word, and a small jar of orchard earth, and does not know what to do with either.
events.arc: The Mourning of a God Who Faded

choices.text: Take the earth, and sit with {npc} through the afternoon

effects.log: You do not speak much. {npc} tells you the orchard god's favourite joke, and does not finish it.

choices.text: Ask whether the orchard still bears

effects.log: It does, {npc} says. It has simply stopped being anyone's.

events.text: The orchard god's shrine is being quietly dismantled by the neighbours, who need the stone. {npc} stands in the way and is politely ignored. A pear tree on the slope has been seen to bloom out of season.
events.arc: The Mourning of a God Who Faded

choices.text: Ask the neighbours to leave one wall

effects.log: One wall stays, and the neighbours leave small gifts at its foot.

choices.text: Plant a seed from the earth jar

effects.log: A pear seedling comes up between the stones.

events.text: A year after, {npc} brings a request: a funeral, properly, of the kind gods do not usually have. The orchard god was fond of apple wine and bad songs. {He} would like you to speak.
events.arc: The Mourning of a God Who Faded

choices.text: Speak, and tell the joke {npc} could not finish

effects.log: You finish the joke. The orchard laughs, in a strange wind, and two blossoms fall.

choices.text: Sing a bad song, loudly

effects.log: The song is truly bad. {npc} weeps and laughs until dusk.

events.text: Years pass. {npc} keeps the wall and the pear tree and the jar. A pilgrim comes by asking who the shrine is for. {npc} says: 'A good neighbour.' The pilgrim leaves a plum.
events.arc: The Mourning of a God Who Faded

choices.text: Take the shrine, quietly, under your own care

effects.log: The wall is yours now, and the pear tree, and the plum. You name no god at it.

choices.text: Leave it in {npc}'s hands

effects.log: {npc} dies in the end, gently, under the pear, and the orchard goes on as an orchard.

events.text: Once a year {npc}, your festival-keeper, lights seven candles for the gods who faded in your lifetime. This year there are eight names. The eighth was a river god whom no one but you remembered, and the candle has been set out by someone else already.
events.arc: Seven Candles for the Faded

choices.text: Ask who set the eighth candle

effects.log: A child did, {npc} says, who heard about it from a heron.

choices.text: Light a ninth for the child

effects.log: The ninth candle burns beside the eighth. The festival begins in a good mood.

events.text: The candle-lighting has become a small tradition. People in the valley bring a candle for their own dead, and set it at the foot of the eight. The shrine floor is a field of light by the end of the evening.
events.arc: Seven Candles for the Faded

choices.text: Stay all night with the candles

effects.log: You keep watch. Towards dawn a bat circles the field of light, and sleeps.

choices.text: Bless each flame with a small warmth

effects.log: The candles burn until noon. The wax smells of honey.

events.text: A stranger comes to the candle festival: a god of salt, long unseen, who says the river god was an old friend. The stranger lights a candle, weeps a little, and asks where the river ran. The river is gone; the valley is dry.
events.arc: Seven Candles for the Faded

choices.text: Take the salt god down the dry bed

effects.log: You walk the bed together at dusk. The stranger names every bend.

choices.text: Send a small rain to the bed for the evening

effects.log: A brief stream runs, and the salt god kneels in it, and is gone by morning.

events.text: The ninth candle has been lit by the child every year since. The child is grown now, and keeper of the festival, and has added a tenth for those gods no one remembered at all. The tenth candle stands in the middle, unnamed, and always the brightest.
events.arc: Seven Candles for the Faded

choices.text: Add your own flame to the tenth

effects.log: The unnamed candle burns blue for a moment. The keeper, startled, bows.

choices.text: Watch it burn, and let it be

effects.log: You say nothing. The tenth is the best part of the evening.

events.text: A family of pigeons has settled on the head of your statue in the central square. {npc}, the mason's apprentice, is sent every week to scrub it, and every week it is worse. A pilgrim has remarked that you look, at last, relaxed.
events.arc: The Pigeons on Your Statue

choices.text: Let the pigeons stay

effects.log: The statue is crowned with a white wreath. The pigeons coo a low chorus.

choices.text: Send a hawk to the roof to frighten them

effects.log: The hawk eats nothing, but the pigeons relocate to the ear.

events.text: The pigeons have hatched, and the statue now has a nest in each hand and one on the brow. {npc} stands with a bucket and a look of long weariness. Children in the square have named the chicks after the lesser gods.
events.arc: The Pigeons on Your Statue

choices.text: Bless the chicks to grow tidy

effects.log: The chicks grow up tidy, in a remarkably neat manner.

choices.text: Ask the apprentice what they would like

effects.log: {npc} says: 'A different god.' Then laughs, appalled.

events.text: A festival is held in the square and the pigeons are, for the occasion, banished by net. The statue gleams. And at once the pilgrims say the god looks cold. {npc} comes to your shrine and asks, miserably, whether the pigeons might be invited back.
events.arc: The Pigeons on Your Statue

choices.text: Send word that the pigeons are welcome again

effects.log: They return at dusk in a great wheel. The square applauds.

choices.text: Insist on a clean statue for the one festival day only

effects.log: The pigeons are rested for a day. The pilgrims note the statue is warmer in a different way.

events.text: The pigeons have spread to every statue in the city, and a rival god's priest has complained in writing. {npc} has been appointed Warden of the Birds, by a board that does not exist. {He} wears the badge to bed.
events.arc: The Pigeons on Your Statue

choices.text: Support the Warden publicly

effects.log: {npc} becomes, briefly, the most respected pigeon expert in three domains.

choices.text: Reply to the rival god's priest with a pigeon

effects.log: The pigeon, uninstructed, perches on the priest's hat.

events.text: An oracle at your highest shrine has been reading the prayers backwards, by accident, for a year. {npc}, a priest, has only just noticed. Requests for rain have been understood as offers of rain, and a great many pilgrims have been instructed to give thanks for things they have not asked for.
events.arc: The Prayer Read Backwards

choices.text: Correct the oracle at once
