effects.log: The oracle is mortified and begins reading at the right end. It reads a great deal more slowly.

choices.text: Wait and see whether the mistake helps

effects.log: To your mild surprise, the pilgrims have been happier thanking before asking.

events.text: The oracle's backwards reading has taken on the air of a school. A few young priests have taken to reading prayers from the end, 'for balance', and a book has been published: Gratitude Before Hope.
events.arc: The Prayer Read Backwards

choices.text: Read the book through, and enjoy it

effects.log: It is in fact quite good. You mark a passage.

choices.text: Send a gentle warning to the school

effects.log: The school hears the warning backwards and is delighted.

events.text: The oracle is old now, and ashamed. {npc} brings a small tray of tea. The oracle asks, quietly, whether all the years of the backward reading made any difference, and whether the dead ones were comforted, or only confused.
events.arc: The Prayer Read Backwards

choices.text: Tell the oracle that the dead were comforted

effects.log: The oracle nods, reaches for the tea, and spills it, laughing.

choices.text: Tell the oracle the truth: some were confused, and some were helped

effects.log: The oracle says: 'That is fair.' Then the oracle falls asleep, peacefully.

events.text: The backwards school has outgrown the shrine. {npc} runs it now, and teaches that gratitude is a kind of asking. The old forward reading is kept by one stubborn priest in the corner, who winks at you every feast day.
events.arc: The Prayer Read Backwards

choices.text: Visit the school at the festival

effects.log: The students recite a prayer backwards. It is oddly beautiful.

choices.text: Sit with the stubborn priest and have tea

effects.log: The priest says nothing. The tea is excellent.

events.text: Every winter a small shrine on the north slope fills with hedgehogs. They shelter in the offerings and under the altar cloth. {npc}, the winter-keeper, has been told to remove them and has not. {He} says they are the shrine's most reliable congregation.
events.arc: The Hedgehogs of the Winter Shrine

choices.text: Visit the winter shrine in a plain coat

effects.log: A hedgehog sits on your boot for an hour.

choices.text: Order the shrine cleared to spare the cloth

effects.log: {npc} sighs and sweeps them out. They return by morning, in pairs.

events.text: A hard frost arrives and the hedgehogs do not wake. {npc} watches them pile together on the altar steps, breathing slowly, in a heap of grey bristle. A harsh wind blows through the open door. The keeper has covered them with every cloth in the shrine.
events.arc: The Hedgehogs of the Winter Shrine

choices.text: Send a small warmth to the heap

effects.log: The heap breathes easier. The cloths are ruined.

choices.text: Close the door with a wind of your own

effects.log: The door shuts. The shrine is warm all night.

events.text: Spring. The hedgehogs wake and leave, and the shrine is quiet. {npc} sweeps the stone floor and finds a tiny pile of acorns left in the corner of the altar. The shape of it is a small offering: a thank-you in the only way a hedgehog could.
events.arc: The Hedgehogs of the Winter Shrine

choices.text: Take one acorn and plant it

effects.log: A small oak comes up at the shrine door within a season.

choices.text: Leave the acorns where they lie

effects.log: They sprout by themselves in the cracks of the stone.

events.text: The winter shrine is rebuilt, and the new one has a hedgehog door at the base, a small arch, and straw by the altar. {npc} says the old ones had their door by custom; the new one is by law. The hedgehogs treat the new one with distrust.
events.arc: The Hedgehogs of the Winter Shrine

choices.text: Bless the little door with a stone's warmth

effects.log: The hedgehogs test the door and accept it by morning.

choices.text: Declare the shrine a refuge for the winter creatures

effects.log: A board is posted. A hedgehog reads it, or looks at it.

events.text: In a small shrine to the god of weavers, moths have eaten the altar cloth so thoroughly that only a lace of holes remains. {npc}, a weaver, has come to ask you to mend it. {He} says the holes make a pattern, and cannot decide whether to say so.
events.arc: The Moths of the Thread-Altar

choices.text: Look at the pattern with {npc}

effects.log: The holes make a map of the valley, with the river wrong.

choices.text: Mend the cloth with a thread of light

effects.log: The cloth is whole, and a little less interesting.

events.text: The moths have started to follow {npc} about the loom house. They settle on finished cloth and, at night, rearrange the threads into tiny blunt patterns. The weaver's customers are charmed and a little frightened.
events.arc: The Moths of the Thread-Altar

choices.text: Ask the moths to stay out of the best wool

effects.log: The moths comply for one week. The patterns come back as border lace.

choices.text: Let the weaver sell the moth-lace as a speciality

effects.log: The lace sells out. The weaver buys a new loom.

events.text: Pilgrims come from three valleys to buy a scrap of moth-lace for luck. {npc} makes a modest fortune, and gives half of it to the shrine. The moths, apparently ignorant of the trade, continue their work in the dark.
events.arc: The Moths of the Thread-Altar

choices.text: Bless the lace, once, for those who buy it fairly

effects.log: The lace brings a little luck to honest buyers. The cheats find it rather itchy.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: The lace goes on selling well. The moths work on.

events.text: {npc} is old. The last of the moth-lace goes into {his} shroud, as {he} wished, and the moths follow the cloth up to the hall of the god of weavers and settle on the altar. The altar, for a night, glows.
events.arc: The Moths of the Thread-Altar

choices.text: Let the moths settle in your hall

effects.log: They fill the ceiling like a slow snow. You leave them undisturbed.

choices.text: Escort them back to the thread-altar

effects.log: They sit on the altar and sleep. The weaver's loom is silent.

events.text: The offering bowl at the east shrine has a crack that has been mended with gold seven times. A new priest asks whether it ought to be replaced. The bowl is not valuable. It has been mended, more than anything else, by affection.

choices.text: Tell the priest to mend it an eighth time

effects.log: The bowl is mended, and the priest finds the gold weight pleasing in the hand.

choices.text: Say a bowl that has been loved this long can stay

effects.log: The priest nods and sets it on the altar. The offerings seem to fill it more easily.

events.text: A pilgrim has left a single child's slipper at your shrine door, with a note: 'for the god who walks at night'. There is no other offering. The slipper is small and has been worn at the toe.

choices.text: Keep it on the altar

effects.log: The slipper sits among the great offerings, the smallest and the most looked-at.

choices.text: Send a warm night wind to wherever the child is

effects.log: Somewhere a child sleeps unusually well that night.

events.text: A prayer reaches you that is mostly cough. The words, when you listen through them, say: 'Not for me. For the hens.' The hens, it turns out, are in a shed a long way from the shrine, and have gone quiet.

choices.text: Send the hens a warm morning

effects.log: The hens begin, noisily, to lay again.

choices.text: Send the coughing worshipper a cup of something hot in a dream

effects.log: The cough eases and the prayer is a little longer the next night.

events.text: A man comes to the shrine every dawn to apologise to you. He has done nothing to you; he has quarrelled with his brother. He apologises to you because he cannot bring himself to apologise to the brother. The words are all correct.

choices.text: Send the brother a dream of the same apology

effects.log: The brothers meet at the shrine gate the next week and say nothing at length.

choices.text: Accept the apology and say nothing

effects.log: You accept it, and he leaves lighter, if not wiser.

events.text: One of your priests has taken to keeping bees in the shrine eaves, and the honey is now the best thing the shrine produces. The bees treat the altar as a front door. The pilgrims leave offerings of sugar water.

choices.text: Bless the hive

effects.log: The honey takes on a warm, grave sweetness. Pilgrims buy it by the jar.

choices.text: Ask for a jar

effects.log: The priest sends a large one. It is excellent.

events.text: A new priest has taken to writing the prayers on the shrine wall in very small, very neat letters. By midsummer the wall is covered and the old prayers have been written over. Nobody has objected. Nobody has read them.

choices.text: Read them, slowly, in the evening

effects.log: They are good. They are, in places, better than the ones you are used to.

choices.text: Have a second wall built

effects.log: A second wall is built. The priest begins at once.

events.text: Someone has put a straw hat on your statue. It sits at an angle. The priests are scandalised and the pilgrims are delighted. In the evening a small queue forms to be photographed, in the manner of the realm, beside the god in the hat.

choices.text: Leave the hat

effects.log: The hat stays through the summer. It is replaced, each year, by a fresh one.

choices.text: Quietly straighten it

effects.log: The hat sits properly for a day. The next morning it is crooked again.

events.text: Moss has grown on the north side of your statue, in the shape of a beard. The priests wish to scrape it. A boy of eight says it makes you look kind. You have never been told that you looked kind.

choices.text: Let the moss grow

effects.log: The beard fills in over the year, soft and green.

choices.text: Trim it to a neat point

effects.log: The beard is trimmed, and the boy approves of this too.

events.text: A thin white fog has stood in one valley of your domain for a week, and nobody has asked you for it. The valley folk are keeping to their houses. A child has been seen, leading a goat into the fog, humming.

choices.text: Clear the fog with a warm wind

effects.log: The fog lifts to show the goat, the child, and a surprising number of mushrooms.

choices.text: Walk into it yourself

effects.log: You walk in the fog for an hour and hear a great many small things, none of them urgent.

events.text: The swallows have come back to your domain three days early, in a great skein. The valley folk take it as a sign. You have no idea what of. The swallows seem proud of themselves.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the sign be a sign

effects.log: A feast is held for the early swallows. You are credited with the foresight.

choices.text: Make the spring match the swallows

effects.log: The spring arrives early in a rush. The valley folk are baffled and pleased.

events.text: The first thaw of the year runs down your domain in a thousand small streams, each with its own opinion. A herald of the Sea has complained that your water comes down very fast. You tell the herald it is only excited.

choices.text: Slow the thaw a little for the neighbours

effects.log: The streams slow, murmuring. The Sea's herald sends a thank-you.

choices.text: Let the thaw run

effects.log: The streams race down. Children sail small boats on them all week.

events.text: A dragonfly the size of a hand lands on your table at breakfast and will not move. It is, it says, a minor envoy of a pond god. The pond is drying. It would like a word, and then a small rain.

choices.text: Send the rain

effects.log: The pond fills overnight. A hundred dragonflies stand on the roof, to say thanks.

choices.text: Hear the envoy out and offer breakfast

effects.log: The envoy takes a crumb and talks for an hour on the dignity of ponds.

events.text: A boy arrives at your hall with a paper lantern and an unreasonable amount of courage. He has walked from the coast to ask whether the lantern, which he made himself, might be allowed to hang in the god's hall. He does not ask for anything else.

choices.text: Hang it in the middle of the ceiling

effects.log: The lantern is crooked and bright. The boy goes home with the largest grin of his life.

choices.text: Hang it in the hall's doorway for everyone to see

effects.log: Visiting gods stop to admire it. A herald asks who the maker is.

events.text: A stall at the border market sells prayers by the weight. A scale, a jar of dried words, and a stallkeeper who looks you directly in the eye and says, brightly, that the prayers are very fresh. Several are your own.

choices.text: Buy a prayer addressed to you

effects.log: You read it at the stall. It is a wedding prayer, and you weep a little over the sweets.

choices.text: Ask where the stall gets its prayers

effects.log: The stallkeeper says: 'From the wind.' It may be true.

events.text: A stall at the Fire and Sea border offers a jar of the first spark of a fresh hearth, sealed with wax. The stallkeeper swears it has never been used. You are fairly sure it is a jar with a candle in it. The jar is warm, however.

choices.text: Buy it

effects.log: You keep the jar by the bed. It warms the room, a little, on cold nights.

choices.text: Tell the stallkeeper you know, and compliment the craft

effects.log: The stallkeeper grins. 'The best are the ones you can't tell,' they say.

events.text: You dream, for one night only, of a ceiling you do not know. It is a plain ceiling, painted blue, with a long crack running the length of it. In the morning a messenger tells you that someone, somewhere, is dreaming your dreams by mistake.

choices.text: Look into the matter

effects.log: The ceiling belongs to a sleeping girl in a nearby hamlet. She dreams of your hall in return.

choices.text: Leave the dreamer in peace

effects.log: The ceiling fades. You find that you miss the crack.

events.text: In a dream a stranger gives you the last pear of a tree that no longer grows. It tastes of a summer you were never at. You wake with the taste in your mouth and no idea who the stranger was, but you are glad.

choices.text: Ask the Sleeper's heralds to look into it

effects.log: The heralds find nothing. They give you a small cup of dream-tea.

choices.text: Plant a pear tree in your garden

effects.log: The tree takes root at once. It will not bear for many years.

events.text: At the court a minor god has taken to carrying a very large fan, to cool the air around those they like. You are, so far, not cooled. You are not sure whether to take offence. The god fans the pillar next to you, thoughtfully.

choices.text: Ask for a fan of your own

effects.log: A fan is brought. It is lighter than it looks and has your seal on it.

choices.text: Pretend you are very warm

effects.log: A servant comes at once. You are fanned until the end of the feast.

events.text: A feast is served in which every dish is a pear: pear soup, pear dumplings, pear in wine, pear in the shape of a swan. The host is a god of orchards, and beams. It is delicious and slightly alarming. You eat all of it.

choices.text: Compliment the host warmly

effects.log: The host is overjoyed. A basket of pears is sent to your hall.

choices.text: Quietly ask for something that is not a pear

effects.log: A single bowl of rice is brought. The host is stricken.

events.text: A game of throwing flat stones across the pond is held before the feast. A very old god of ponds has never lost. This year a boy from the kitchens skips a stone eleven times. The old god bows, sincerely, and the court applauds.

choices.text: Offer the boy a small blessing for his arm

effects.log: His arm gets a little better. He drops the stone anyway, from nerves.

choices.text: Challenge the old god to a rematch

effects.log: You skip four. The old god skips nine. It is a good afternoon.

events.text: An elder god, so old that they stopped speaking some time ago, walks the length of your hall at dawn, once a year, without a word. It is regarded as an honour. This year they pause at your hearth and put a hand briefly on the mantel.

choices.text: Bow, and say nothing

effects.log: The elder nods, a hair's breadth. In the mantel's stone a faint warmth remains for years.

choices.text: Offer a cup of water

effects.log: The elder drinks it, slowly, and leaves the empty cup on the mantel.

events.text: The council is stuck on a matter of boundaries, as always, and a herald brings in a tray of biscuits. The mood changes. By the end of the biscuits the boundary has been quietly settled. Nobody mentions the biscuits in the minutes.

choices.text: Mention the biscuits in the minutes

effects.log: The minutes record 'a plate of biscuits' as a contributing factor. The clerk is moved.

choices.text: Quietly send a second tray to the next council

effects.log: The next council goes better.

events.text: You lie on the roof of your hall and count the stars, as you did when you were new. There are more than you remember, and one that is not where it was. You say its name aloud, the way an old friend says a name.

choices.text: Ask Cheonho about the star

effects.log: Cheonho says the star has simply moved to a better seat. 'It is quite common,' says Cheonho.

choices.text: Keep counting until dawn

effects.log: At dawn you have the same number, and a stiff neck, and a good mood.

events.text: In the middle of an ordinary afternoon a very small bell rings somewhere in your hall. You cannot find it. It rings once, clearly, and stops. Every god you ask has heard it too. Nobody knows what it announced.

choices.text: Keep the afternoon quiet in case it rings again

effects.log: It does not ring again. The afternoon is very still.

choices.text: Ring a bell of your own in answer

effects.log: Your bell echoes somewhere far off. A second small bell answers, once.

events.text: A new priest arrives at the shrine with two bags, a clock and an enormous opinion about the state of the floors. Within a day the floors are bright, the clock is on the wall, and three older priests have been politely overruled.

choices.text: Welcome the new priest with a blessing

effects.log: The priest receives the blessing as a due. The floors gleam all season.

choices.text: Quietly ask the older priests how it is going

effects.log: They say it is going very well and look slightly pale.

events.text: Somewhere in your domain a goat bell rings in the dusk, patient and slow. Everything else is quiet. You listen to it for a long while, and find it is the nicest sound you have been sent all year.

choices.text: Send a warm evening to the hill

effects.log: The hill glows a little. The goat continues.

choices.text: Just listen

effects.log: The bell fades with the light. You feel unaccountably rested.

events.text: Pilgrims at the lower shrine have discovered that incense, burned on a still evening, makes rings. A boy has taught the whole step to do it. The shrine rises in the dusk like a mist of small halos, each with a wish in it.

choices.text: Send a gentle updraft to carry the rings higher

effects.log: The rings rise past the roof, one by one, lit gold by the last of the sun.

choices.text: Make a ring yourself, and let it float to the boy

effects.log: The boy catches it in a cupped hand and looks up with a very serious face.

events.text: Two priests of your hill shrines once quarrelled over where the dawn bell should hang. Both are long dead. Now their grandsons, {npc} and a cousin, quarrel over the same bell with the same words. Nobody remembers why, and everybody takes a side.
events.arc: The Grandsons of the Two Priests

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the quarrel is about

effects.log: {He} explains for an hour and ends by admitting {he} does not know.

choices.text: Move the bell to a third hill, quietly

effects.log: The bell is found on the third hill. Both sides blame each other for stealing it.

events.text: The feud has outgrown the bell. The two shrines refuse to share a lamp-oil seller, a ferry or a festival day. Children of the two sides throw acorns at each other on the road and are scolded, in identical words, by their grandmothers.
events.arc: The Grandsons of the Two Priests

choices.text: Declare a feast day on which the two sides must dine together

effects.log: The feast is stiff, silent, and long. The pudding is shared.

choices.text: Let the acorns fly

effects.log: The acorns fly. Two children fall in love before the season ends.

events.text: {npc} and the cousin are old men now, and the bell is cracked from age. Both, separately, ask you to mend it, each to the other's disgrace. You see that the quarrel is all that either of them has had to talk about for fifty years.
events.arc: The Grandsons of the Two Priests

choices.text: Mend the bell, and ring it for both at once

effects.log: The bell sounds a fine mournful note. The two old men stand on their hilltops and listen.

choices.text: Leave the bell cracked; the crack is theirs

effects.log: The crack becomes the sound of the dawn. Travellers think it is a local custom.

events.text: On the third hill the bell has been rung by a wandering boy for three years, and the valley has quietly settled on it. {npc} hears it at dawn and grudgingly climbs the hill. The cousin is already there. They stand side by side, pretending not to.
events.arc: The Grandsons of the Two Priests

choices.text: Send a mist to hide their faces

effects.log: In the mist the two old men speak a long while. Nobody hears what.

choices.text: Let them be seen

effects.log: The valley sees them stand together. The first murmur is soon a cheer.

events.text: Your priests wear red on the east hill and blue on the west. Two hundred years ago the colours were a matter of dye prices. Now {npc}, a young priest of the blue, has fallen in love with a young priest of the red, and neither family will speak of it at table.
events.arc: The Red Robes and the Blue

choices.text: Bless the love quietly

effects.log: A sparrow lands on both shoulders at once. It is not a miracle, merely suggestive.

choices.text: Leave it to the families

effects.log: The families are left to themselves, and do it badly.

events.text: The colours have become a matter of honour. Red priests will not dine with blue, and blue will not bless red; the wedding fees have collapsed. In the middle, {npc} has stopped wearing any colour at all and goes about in plain grey, to everyone's horror.
events.arc: The Red Robes and the Blue

choices.text: Declare grey a priestly colour for a season

effects.log: Grey sells out in three days. Both sides take offence.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to carry a message between the two hills

effects.log: {He} carries it, cheerfully, and is stopped three times on the road.

events.text: A wedding is held in grey at the foot of the hill where the two roads meet. Neither family attends in colour. The priest who marries them is a very old one, who has no colour left, only the shape of one. {npc} weeps and smiles at once.
events.arc: The Red Robes and the Blue

choices.text: Attend in a plain coat and stand at the back

effects.log: You are given a plate of cake. Nobody notices you are not a guest.

choices.text: Send a pair of swallows to circle the wedding

effects.log: The swallows, red-breasted and blue-backed, fly over twice. A child points.

events.text: Years later the robes on both hills are striped, red and blue, a fashion that began at no one's order. {npc}'s own children wear them to the festival and are quite unaware there was ever a quarrel. The old priests mutter and are ignored.
events.arc: The Red Robes and the Blue

choices.text: Add a stripe of your own colour to the festival banner

effects.log: The banner is accepted. The stripes proliferate.

choices.text: Say nothing, and enjoy the stripes

effects.log: The festival is one of the best you have seen.

events.text: Your priests of the high shrine have a chant they sing at dawn. {npc}, a priest from the lower shrine, was found writing it down in the bushes. Both shrines now claim the chant as theirs and the verses as their own. The first accusation has been laid.
events.arc: The Chant Stolen and Stolen Back

choices.text: Call both to the hall to sing it at once

effects.log: They sing, and the high shrine finds it has the second verse wrong.

choices.text: Say the chant belongs to whoever sings it best

effects.log: A contest is announced. The chant improves at once.

events.text: Each shrine has started adding verses. The high shrine's now has six, one mildly insulting to the lower. The lower has seven and a chorus. Pilgrims arrive at one and are sent, in a respectful hush, to the other, where it is sung differently.
events.arc: The Chant Stolen and Stolen Back

choices.text: Gather the verses into one book

effects.log: The book is compiled by a patient scribe. Seven verses are cut.

choices.text: Pick your favourite verse and hum it for a week

effects.log: The valley hums it back. It becomes the third chant.

events.text: Three generations on, {npc} is the last singer who knows the original. The two shrines have long since forgotten who stole what. {He} asks you, plainly, which version was true, and whether it matters.
events.arc: The Chant Stolen and Stolen Back

choices.text: Tell {him} the true version was the one sung with a cold

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. The cough, you notice, is in tune.

choices.text: Sing the original to {him}, once, quietly

effects.log: {He} listens with eyes shut, nods, and sings the second verse.

events.text: The contest produced a new chant, shared, and the old ones are sung by the elderly out of love. {npc} has taken on the task of teaching the new chant to the children, in both shrines on alternate days, and carries a stool between.
events.arc: The Chant Stolen and Stolen Back

choices.text: Provide a second stool

effects.log: A second stool is carved. {npc} sits on it with great relief.

choices.text: Attend a lesson in a plain coat

effects.log: You are asked to hold the pitch. You do it badly. Everyone is kind.

events.text: A child of the valley, {npc}, has painted your portrait on the shrine wall with the red clay of the riverbank. In it you have three arms, a hat and a moustache. The priests are appalled. Pilgrims are enchanted. The child is nowhere to be found.
events.arc: The Portrait Painted by a Child

choices.text: Look at the portrait carefully

effects.log: It is bad, and it is very much you. You have never looked so cheerful.

choices.text: Ask the priests to leave it

effects.log: They agree, grudgingly. A rope is hung to keep the damp off.

events.text: The child has been found, hiding under the temple steps with a pot of clay. {He} says {he} painted what {he} saw in a dream. The priests ask if you would like it painted over by a proper artist. The proper artist has already arrived.
events.arc: The Portrait Painted by a Child

choices.text: Hold a contest between the child and the artist

effects.log: The child wins by acclamation. The artist stays for cake.

choices.text: Ask the artist to teach the child

effects.log: The artist agrees, and by the next season the child has a better brush.

events.text: The portrait grows. {npc} now paints new gods on the walls, in time with the feasts: Mujin in a pink hat, the Pale Ferryman holding a goose. The priests have given up. Visiting gods stop in the lane to see themselves, with varying humour.
events.arc: The Portrait Painted by a Child

choices.text: Commission a portrait of the whole pantheon

effects.log: {npc} paints them all in one mural, kindly, with a goose in the corner.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to paint something plainly beautiful, for once

effects.log: {He} paints the dawn on the hill. It is unforgettable.

events.text: {npc} has grown, and no longer paints your hat. The shrine wall has been whitewashed by a diligent new priest. {He} comes back, years on, to see the empty wall, and sits under it for a long afternoon with a small pot of clay.
events.arc: The Portrait Painted by a Child

choices.text: Appear in a plain coat and ask for a portrait

effects.log: {He} paints it, a little shyly, a good deal better than before. The moustache remains.

choices.text: Send the wind to carry a flake of old red to {his} hand

effects.log: {He} looks at it, and starts, again, with a fingertip.

events.text: The children's school in the valley has drawn a gallery of gods on its wall: every god in the realm, drawn from rumour. You are a long, thin man with a kettle. The Pale Ferryman is a duck. {npc}, the teacher, is mortified and cannot afford to whitewash.
events.arc: The Gallery of Children's Gods

choices.text: Look through the gallery and take notes

effects.log: There is more insight in the duck than in some theology.

choices.text: Tell the teacher the gallery is fine

effects.log: {npc} relaxes. The children cheer without understanding why.

events.text: Pilgrims have started visiting the school to see the gods. The children give tours, in the mornings, in high clear voices, with great error. A visiting god of boundaries has complained that his portrait has no borders. The children add a fence.
events.arc: The Gallery of Children's Gods

choices.text: Fund the school's lunches in a quiet way

effects.log: The school's cupboard is full, and no one asks why.

choices.text: Add your own captions to the wall

effects.log: A caption appears under your portrait: 'He is tall. He says nothing.' It is accurate.

events.text: A child asks {npc} whether the gods can see the wall. {npc} says, hesitantly, that perhaps they can. The child says: 'Then I should like to say sorry to the duck.' The next day there is a new, rather better duck.
events.arc: The Gallery of Children's Gods

choices.text: Accept the apology on behalf of the duck

effects.log: The duck, you assure the child, forgives everyone.

choices.text: Send a real duck to the school

effects.log: A duck arrives, aghast, at the school door. It is adopted at once.

events.text: The gallery has grown out of the schoolroom into the road. {npc} has added a section for gods who have faded, drawn very carefully from the descriptions of the eldest valley-folk. A pilgrim cries at it. The children are proud.
events.arc: The Gallery of Children's Gods

choices.text: Add a quiet candle in front of the faded

effects.log: A candle burns there all week. The children guard it.

choices.text: Add a new portrait to the faded section: yourself, as a joke

effects.log: The children laugh, and then do not, and then redraw the portrait with more care.

events.text: The pilgrim road to your high shrine is yours to keep, by an old law: a god must see that the road is fit. This year the spring floods took a stretch of it. {npc}, the roadman, brings a tally of the damage and a pile of stones, and asks what the god proposes.
events.arc: The Road You Must Keep

choices.text: Mend the road yourself, in a plain coat, beside {npc}

effects.log: You carry stones all day. You are told, by a passing pilgrim, that you are slow.

choices.text: Send the roadman stone from the hill, and a good wind

effects.log: The stones arrive, and the road is mended in a week. {npc} is baffled.

events.text: The mended road is lovely, and it floods again, three miles on. Pilgrims arrive muddy and not at all put out. {npc} reports that a hostel has opened at the muddy stretch and is doing very well.
events.arc: The Road You Must Keep

choices.text: Build a stone causeway across the mud

effects.log: The causeway holds. The hostel loses half its custom, and gains a better one.

choices.text: Visit the hostel

effects.log: You are served a stew and told that the god ought to do something about the road.

events.text: The old law is read out at a council of the roadmen: that a god's road must be walked by the god once in a generation. It has been four generations. {npc} gently reminds you that the pilgrims have grown suspicious. You say you are a very busy god.
events.arc: The Road You Must Keep

choices.text: Walk the whole road, from the sea to the shrine

effects.log: It takes nineteen days. You are fed by strangers, and recognised by none.

choices.text: Walk the last mile, and send the rest as a dream

effects.log: You walk a mile, and the pilgrims count it, generously.

events.text: The road is now so well kept that pilgrims complain it is too easy. {npc} proposes to leave a rough stretch on purpose, to preserve the merit. You are of two minds, and so is the whole council of roadmen.
events.arc: The Road You Must Keep

choices.text: Leave the rough stretch

effects.log: The rough stretch becomes a point of pride. Pilgrims weep on it with relish.

choices.text: Smooth it to a gentle slope

effects.log: The slope is lovely. The complaints stop. The pilgrims weep elsewhere.

events.text: The pilgrim road crosses a gorge on a rope bridge, kept by {npc}, whose family has mended it for nine generations. Last night a plank cracked under a pilgrim's foot. Nobody was hurt. {npc} stands over it, speechless with shame.
events.arc: The Bridge on the Pilgrim Road

choices.text: Mend the plank with the keeper

effects.log: You work the plank into place. {npc} corrects your knot twice.

choices.text: Tell {npc} that no plank is eternal

effects.log: {He} thanks you, and sits down on the bridge for a good while.

events.text: A council of the pilgrim road proposes a stone bridge. {npc}'s family has fought it for three centuries on grounds of tradition. The council, clever, offers the family the post of Keeper of the Stone Bridge and a pension. {npc} is torn.
events.arc: The Bridge on the Pilgrim Road

choices.text: Support the stone bridge

effects.log: The stones arrive in spring, slow and good. {npc} grumbles at every one.

choices.text: Back the rope bridge

effects.log: The old bridge stays. The stone bridge's stones are given to the hostel.

events.text: The stone bridge is done and the rope bridge hangs beside it, empty, swaying in a breeze. {npc} comes to you with a request: that the rope bridge not be cut down, only left, to please the families. It is a small, odd request.
events.arc: The Bridge on the Pilgrim Road

choices.text: Declare the rope bridge a shrine of its own

effects.log: The bridge becomes a place of prayer. Pilgrims cross it once, for luck, in single file.

choices.text: Leave it in place, no ceremony

effects.log: The bridge stays. A child crosses it, daily, for years.

events.text: The rope bridge remains the pilgrim road's road. A hundred years on, {npc}'s descendants still knot each rope by hand. Crossing it, you meet the youngest, a child of nine who asks if the god is afraid of heights. You say: 'Always.' The child nods, as one professional to another.
events.arc: The Bridge on the Pilgrim Road

choices.text: Cross hand in hand with the child

effects.log: You cross the gorge with the child. Half way, the child laughs.

choices.text: Leave the child a small token on the far side

effects.log: A tiny knot of light sits on the post. The child finds it at once.

events.text: On the pilgrim road, at the third milestone, {npc} keeps an inn so small that it has one room and a hen. Pilgrims arrive hungry, pious and very slightly frightened. {He} keeps a loaf for each, and a story. {He} has never once been paid in faith.
events.arc: The Inn at the Third Milestone

choices.text: Stay a night in a plain coat

effects.log: The room is clean, the hen is rude, the loaf is warm.

choices.text: Send {npc} a quiet gift of firewood

effects.log: A stack of wood appears at the door. {npc} counts it twice and asks no questions.

events.text: {npc}'s inn is full this season: seven pilgrims, two goats and a travelling singer of ballads. The hen has been ejected and sulks in the rafters. A rival innkeeper in the next town has begun to spread rumours that the loaves are stale.
events.arc: The Inn at the Third Milestone

choices.text: Visit the rival in disguise and eat the rival's loaves

effects.log: The rival's loaves are worse. You pay the full price and say nothing.

choices.text: Send the ballad singer a verse in praise of the loaves

effects.log: The ballad is sung in three towns. The rumour dies.

events.text: A hard winter closes the road. {npc} keeps the inn open for pilgrims who cannot move on, rationing the loaves and the hen's eggs. By the end, the pilgrims have fallen to arguing about the hen's name. The hen is called three things.
events.arc: The Inn at the Third Milestone

choices.text: Send a thaw a day early

effects.log: The road opens. The pilgrims leave in tears, and an argument over the hen's name.

choices.text: Send a hamper of provisions through the snow

effects.log: The hamper arrives. {npc} wonders aloud whether the hen has friends in high places.

events.text: Years on, the inn is a hostel with two floors and a famous loaf. {npc} still sleeps in the little room. A young priest asks what {npc} would like from the god. {He} says: 'The hen, back.' The hen, one assumes, is dead.
events.arc: The Inn at the Third Milestone

choices.text: Send a hen of the same kind and manner

effects.log: A grey hen walks up the road at dawn. {npc} laughs and cries.

choices.text: Tell {him} the hen is well, wherever the hen is

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. 'I thought so,' {he} says.

events.text: A wedding is to be held in the Sun pantheon's great hall between a minor god of wells and the daughter of a god of orchards, and you have been asked to attend. {npc}, the herald in charge of seating, is distraught. You have been placed beside the god of a river you quarrelled with in the third age.
events.arc: The Seating of the Wedding

choices.text: Accept the seat with grace

effects.log: You sit beside the river god. Neither says a word until the third course.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to move the river god to the next table

effects.log: {He} does, with great relief, and two other gods are moved at once.

events.text: The seating plan has spread to the whole feast. The god of the first frost cannot sit within three seats of the god of summer. Two goddesses of the moon cannot be seen in the same room. {npc} has retired to a back room with a pot of tea and a diagram.
events.arc: The Seating of the Wedding

choices.text: Lend a hand with the diagram

effects.log: You help with the diagram and find a solution on a napkin.

choices.text: Leave the herald to it

effects.log: The herald, undisturbed, produces a plan so complicated nobody dare question it.

events.text: The wedding feast is a triumph. The river god, seated beside you, eventually says, stiffly, that the third age is long ago. You agree. Then you both laugh at a poor joke the groom makes, and the old quarrel quietly dissolves into the gravy.
events.arc: The Seating of the Wedding

choices.text: Raise a cup to the old quarrel

effects.log: The cup is raised, and the quarrel, honoured at last, is declared over.

choices.text: Pass the river god the salt

effects.log: The river god takes it, thanks you, and talks for an hour about trout.

events.text: The new seating, at the other table, works too well. You spend the feast in excellent company and learn that the god of lost keys has a marvellous tenor. {npc} comes to your table at last, grey with exhaustion, and is made to sit. You pour {him} the best wine.
events.arc: The Seating of the Wedding

choices.text: Toast the seating plan

effects.log: The table toasts the diagram. {npc} faints with joy.

choices.text: Make {npc} the guest of honour for one dessert

effects.log: The dessert is shared. {He} is brought a plate of honeyed figs.

events.text: The god of a great river is to marry the goddess of a hill. The ceremony requires the bride to be present, and {npc}, the herald, has just realised that the bride is a river and cannot be present anywhere else. The groom has not yet been told.
events.arc: The Bride Who Was a River

choices.text: Suggest the wedding be held on the riverbank

effects.log: {npc} sighs with relief. Nobody has thought of the riverbank.

choices.text: Suggest a dream wedding with a ribbon for the water

effects.log: A ribbon is arranged. It floats downstream, and the bride is moved.

events.text: The riverbank wedding is arranged and the river is high. Guests arrive in boats, muddy and scandalised. The groom is a god of a hill and has never been in a boat. The groom stands at the water's edge, pale, with an enormous bouquet.
events.arc: The Bride Who Was a River

choices.text: Lend the groom a wind to steady the groom's feet

effects.log: The wind steadies the groom, who crosses the little pier like a very large cat.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to carry the bouquet for the groom

effects.log: {He} does, and drops half of it. The river is delighted.

events.text: The wedding is held in a downpour. The bride speaks as a long low murmur of water, and the herald has to translate each vow. {npc} speaks the final words aloud for the river: 'Where you run, I shall stand.' The hill wipes its eyes.
events.arc: The Bride Who Was a River

choices.text: Stand witness at the water's edge

effects.log: You sign the register with a drip of rain. The ink is bright.

choices.text: Send a rainbow to close the vows

effects.log: A rainbow stands across the river. The gods applaud wetly.

events.text: Years later the couple have a child, a spring on the hill that runs down to the river. {npc}, retired, is invited to the naming. The spring is named by splashing; {npc} writes down the sound with great care.
events.arc: The Bride Who Was a River

choices.text: Give the spring a gift of smooth stones

effects.log: The stones are laid in the spring's bed. It sings on them.

choices.text: Visit the spring and sit quietly with {npc}

effects.log: The two of you sit by the little spring until dusk.

events.text: A wedding has ended and left a mountain of gifts that the couple cannot keep: three live cranes, a sealed jar of north wind, a tiger-sized urn, and a note that reads only 'with gratitude, from a former rival'. {npc}, the couple's steward, wants guidance.
events.arc: The Wedding Gifts Nobody Could Return

choices.text: Read the notes with the steward

effects.log: The notes are all warm. Two are quietly apologies.

choices.text: Send the gifts to the shrine for safekeeping

effects.log: The cranes settle on the roof. The jar of wind is placed carefully on a high shelf.

events.text: The jar of north wind has cracked. A thin cold current runs through the shrine all winter and puts out the lamps. The cranes huddle on the altar. {npc} tries to mend the jar with wax and is given a very cold look by a goddess of frost.
events.arc: The Wedding Gifts Nobody Could Return

choices.text: Seal the jar with a warm breath

effects.log: The wind goes quiet. The lamps are relit.

choices.text: Let the wind blow itself out

effects.log: It blows for a week and leaves the shrine remarkably clean.

events.text: The cranes have become guests rather than gifts. {npc} wants to return one to the river god who sent it. The river god sends back a polite note: they would feel hurt. The cranes dance in the courtyard, and the pilgrims come to watch.
events.arc: The Wedding Gifts Nobody Could Return

choices.text: Declare the cranes shrine birds

effects.log: The cranes are enrolled. Their dance is added to the festival.

choices.text: Quietly send a thanks to each giver

effects.log: Letters go out. Six reply the same week.

events.text: The note from the former rival turns out to be an invitation, in disguise, to talk. {npc} sets down the whole pile of gifts and says: 'You might see them.' You do. It is the slowest, politest lunch of your life, and the beginning of a thaw.
events.arc: The Wedding Gifts Nobody Could Return

choices.text: Accept the rival's lunch invitation

effects.log: The lunch lasts four hours. It is not unpleasant.

choices.text: Send an answering gift: a single plain stone

effects.log: The rival sends a single plain stone in return, with a smile drawn on it.

events.text: It is a bad year. The first rain came late, the second came early, and a goat ate your ceremonial robe. {npc}, your steward, brings in the morning post: seven complaints, an eviction notice for a minor shrine, and a fish that is not for you.
events.arc: The Year Nothing Went Right

choices.text: Face the post one letter at a time

effects.log: You read all of it, which is its own kind of courage.

choices.text: Take the day off in a plain coat

effects.log: You walk by the river. Somebody's goat nibbles your sleeve. It is a fair day.

events.text: It does not improve. A flood takes the lower shrine's fence. Three pilgrims bring identical colds. A rival god, at a feast, says kindly that they hope you are 'resting'. {npc} has taken to leaving the post at the door and running.
events.arc: The Year Nothing Went Right

choices.text: Ask {npc} to run the post to the Silent Hall instead

effects.log: The Hall acknowledges receipt. Nothing else.

choices.text: Write one letter of your own, to an old friend

effects.log: The friend writes back at once, with a recipe for plum soup.

events.text: By autumn something turns. A bumper crop in the lower valley, a calm sea, a feast without incident. {npc} sits down at the foot of your steps and says, in the quiet, that the bad year was, after all, a year in which no one gave up on the shrine.
events.arc: The Year Nothing Went Right

choices.text: Hold a small feast for the faithful who stayed

effects.log: The feast is small and loud. The soup is plum.

choices.text: Send {npc} a quiet word of thanks

effects.log: {He} bows, goes pink, and goes to wash the ceremonial cups.

events.text: The bad year is over and a small tradition is born: on its anniversary, you and {npc} go for a walk to the river in plain coats, and are bitten by midges. Pilgrims, hearing, begin to take a walk on the same day. It becomes the Day of the Midge.
events.arc: The Year Nothing Went Right

choices.text: Bless the Day of the Midge

effects.log: The midges, blessed, bite less. The pilgrims are entirely unsurprised.

choices.text: Leave the day to the midges and the walkers

effects.log: The day is kept as a day of quiet complaint, which is a kind of rest.

events.text: The great bell of your hall cracked on the first morning of the year, mid-stroke, and has sounded like a goose ever since. {npc}, the bellman, is inconsolable. The omens are bad. The omens, as {he} puts it, honk.
events.arc: The Year of the Cracked Bell

choices.text: Declare the goose-note a blessing

effects.log: The pilgrims love it. The bellman is not sure whether to be flattered.

choices.text: Order the bell recast

effects.log: A founder is sent for. The bell is carried off in a cart.

events.text: Without the bell the hall is quiet, and the quiet turns out to be unbearable. Pilgrims arrive at the wrong hour, the cook oversleeps, and a visiting god mistakes the afternoon for evening. {npc} paces with a wooden clapper and a tragic expression.
events.arc: The Year of the Cracked Bell

choices.text: Borrow a bell from the sea shrine

effects.log: A bell arrives, tuned to the tides. The whole hall rings in slow swells.

choices.text: Ring a pair of cooking pots at the hours

effects.log: The pots are surprisingly adequate.

events.text: The recast bell is hung, and it is excellent, and nobody loves it. The pilgrims miss the goose. {npc} confesses, in a low voice, that {he} does too, and has kept a fragment of the old bell in {his} pocket as a charm.
events.arc: The Year of the Cracked Bell

choices.text: Hang the fragment on the new bell's tongue

effects.log: The bell now rings true, with a faint honk at the end. Everyone is happy.

choices.text: Let {npc} keep the fragment

effects.log: {He} keeps it. The bell sounds out clearly all winter.

events.text: The goose-note bell becomes the hall's emblem. Pilgrims arrive for the sound, and {npc} is promoted to Master of the Honk. A school of bell-ringers forms around it, specialising in cracks. The bell is, on the whole, doing very well.
events.arc: The Year of the Cracked Bell

choices.text: Visit the school of cracked bells

effects.log: You are taught to ring a bell badly. You are pleased by how much you improve.

choices.text: Grant the school a banner

effects.log: The banner shows a bell and a goose. It is much copied.

events.text: A year of golden luck has fallen on your rival, the god of the next valley. Their harvest is huge, their shrines are full, and at the court feast they are seated higher than you for the first time in three ages. {npc}, your herald, whispers the news with some delicacy.
events.arc: The Year a Rival Prospered

choices.text: Congratulate the rival warmly

effects.log: The rival is so startled by the warmth that they drop their cup.

choices.text: Say nothing, and eat your soup

effects.log: The soup is excellent. The silence is not.

events.text: It continues. The rival's shrines bloom, and a small procession of your own worshippers has crossed the ridge to pay respects to the more fashionable god. {npc} counts them with a sorrowful face and gets to nineteen.
events.arc: The Year a Rival Prospered

choices.text: Let them go with a blessing for the road

effects.log: They go, and they wave. One returns, later, with a basket of cherries.

choices.text: Ask the nineteen what they were seeking

effects.log: They say, awkwardly, that the rival's festivals have better cakes.

events.text: The rival visits, unannounced, in a plain coat, to look at your shrines. They stand a long time in your garden and say, at last: 'It's quieter than mine.' It is the first honest thing they have said to you in three ages.
events.arc: The Year a Rival Prospered

choices.text: Offer them tea and a bench

effects.log: You sit on the bench together. Neither of you is winning anything.

choices.text: Show them the oldest of your shrine cats

effects.log: The cat sits on the rival's lap and refuses to move.

events.text: The rival's luck turns, as it must, and the bloom of their shrines fades. {npc} reports that the rival's pilgrims are arriving again, shyly, at your gates with nowhere else to go. You take them in, and the rival takes it well, to your surprise.
events.arc: The Year a Rival Prospered

choices.text: Send a cake of thanks to the rival

effects.log: The rival writes back: 'Better than mine.' You keep the note.

choices.text: Quietly send half the pilgrims back with a good word

effects.log: The pilgrims go back. The rival's luck, which had been wobbling, steadies.

events.text: You sent a dream of warning to a farmer whose roof would soon fall. The dream was received by {npc}, the farmer's neighbour, a dealer in fish, who is not in any danger but now knows a great deal about roofs. {He} has begun to measure the neighbours' rafters.
events.arc: The Dream Sent to the Wrong Sleeper

choices.text: Send the right dream to the right sleeper at once

effects.log: The farmer's roof is saved with a night to spare. {npc} continues to measure rafters.

choices.text: Let the fishmonger's warning do the work

effects.log: {npc} knocks on the farmer's door, politely, and warns the farmer. The farmer is bemused and stays out of the house.

events.text: {npc} has begun to dream of roofs, nightly, with a precision that unsettles the neighbourhood. A carpenter hires {him} as an assessor. The farmer pays {him} in cheese. The dreams were meant to stop after the warning; they have not.
events.arc: The Dream Sent to the Wrong Sleeper

choices.text: Send {npc} a dream of the sea to wash the roofs away

effects.log: {He} dreams of fishing boats, wakes pleased, and sells a very large cod.

choices.text: Let the roof dreams run their course

effects.log: They run for a month and fade, leaving {him} a decent carpenter.

events.text: A messenger of the Silent Hall arrives about the mistake. Dreams are the Sleeper's province, and misdirected ones are, it seems, reportable. The messenger holds up a long form, with a space for 'sleeper intended' and one for 'sleeper received'. You fill both in carefully.
events.arc: The Dream Sent to the Wrong Sleeper

choices.text: Take full responsibility on the form

effects.log: The messenger stamps it and smiles, which is unusual. The form is filed under 'resolved'.

choices.text: Describe the circumstances in detail, with some humour

effects.log: The messenger laughs aloud and has to be given water.

events.text: Years on, {npc} is the valley's best finder of weak roofs, and a minor local legend: the man who had someone else's dream. Pilgrims come to ask for dreams by post. {He} politely tells them that it cannot be arranged, and to buy some good rope.
events.arc: The Dream Sent to the Wrong Sleeper

choices.text: Send {npc} a quiet thanks, in a dream, to the right address

effects.log: The dream arrives properly this time. {He} wakes and weeps, briefly, for no reason.

choices.text: Leave {him} to it

effects.log: {He} continues, for forty years, to inspect roofs, and never has a dream again.

events.text: A dream you sent to a dying shepherd landed in the wrong ear, a young woman's, {npc}, who is not dying at all. It was a gentle one: a green slope, a warm sun, a dog. {He} woke in tears. {He} is now trying to find the green slope on the map.
events.arc: The Sleeper Who Kept the Dream

choices.text: Tell {npc} in a dream where the slope is

effects.log: {He} sets off the next morning with a bag of bread and the dog.

choices.text: Let {him} look, and not tell

effects.log: {He} looks for a month and learns every hill in the region.

events.text: {npc} has found a slope, but not the slope. The shepherd for whom the dream was meant has since died in bed, and was comforted by another dream, a plainer one. {npc}, on the wrong hill, is not unhappy. {He} has met a dog.
events.arc: The Sleeper Who Kept the Dream

choices.text: Visit {npc} on the hill, in a plain coat

effects.log: {He} offers you bread. You sit with the dog.

choices.text: Send a dream of thanks to the dead shepherd

effects.log: The shepherd's sleeping smile is wider the next morning.

events.text: {npc} builds a hut on the hill, a small one, and plants a garden. {He} says the dream belongs to {him} now, and that the god should know. {He} says it politely, but firmly. The hut is on land in your domain, in the shadow of a ridge.
events.arc: The Sleeper Who Kept the Dream

choices.text: Grant {him} the hill in your name

effects.log: A deed is written, in light, on the nearest stone.

choices.text: Accept that it was a gift, and not a lease

effects.log: {He} nods. The garden flowers before the winter.

events.text: {npc} lives to be old on the hill, tending a small flock and the dog's descendants. In the last hour, {he} asks to dream the dream again. You send it, the right way this time, to the right address. {He} walks into the green, without any hurry.
events.arc: The Sleeper Who Kept the Dream

choices.text: Walk the first part with {him} in the dream

effects.log: You walk the green slope together, in plain coats, and part at the crest.

choices.text: Send the dream, and keep out of it

effects.log: {He} sleeps. The dog sits at the door for a week.

events.text: Mongsa the Sleeper has sneezed. The dreams of a whole valley are crossed: a baker dreams a general's battle, a general dreams of bread, and {npc}, a dreamer by trade, dreams all of them at once and has stopped speaking in sentences.
events.arc: The Night the Dreams Crossed

choices.text: Visit Mongsa's hall and ask for the sneeze to be undone

effects.log: Mongsa, half-asleep, says sorry and promptly sneezes again.

choices.text: Help {npc} to sort the dreams one at a time

effects.log: You sit by {npc}'s bed and hand each dream to its owner. It takes a night.

events.text: The crossed dreams have mixed into small odd gifts. The baker now bakes battle-shaped loaves, the general draws up a fine recipe for rye, and {npc} has rejoined the world with a sentence: 'I should like to buy a hat.'
events.arc: The Night the Dreams Crossed

choices.text: Buy {npc} the hat

effects.log: {He} wears it everywhere. It does not suit {him}.

choices.text: Let the valley keep the dreams as a curiosity

effects.log: A small fair is held to display the odd gifts. The loaves sell fast.

events.text: Mongsa wakes, finally, and sends a bag of fresh dreams as an apology, each tied with a ribbon and labelled. {npc} is asked to deliver them. The bag has a note: 'Please do not read the blue ones.' You read a blue one. It is about a lake. It is lovely.
events.arc: The Night the Dreams Crossed

choices.text: Deliver the blue dream personally to someone who needs it

effects.log: A lonely old man gets the lake and wakes to a damp pillow and a very good mood.

choices.text: Seal the bag and return it unread

effects.log: Mongsa is touched. The Sleeper's seal is on your next invitation.

events.text: A year on, the hat has become the symbol of the Day of the Crossed Dreams, kept by the valley on the anniversary. Everyone wears an ill-fitting hat. {npc} leads a small procession and mistakes the baker for the general twice.
events.arc: The Night the Dreams Crossed

choices.text: Wear a hat to the procession

effects.log: You wear a straw one, three sizes too large. You are mistaken for the general.

choices.text: Bless the procession with a pleasant dream for all

effects.log: The valley sleeps on the evening of the day in perfect, odd peace.

events.text: {npc}, the old bell-founder of the foothill shrines, comes to you with a request: one last bell, the best {he} has ever cast, for the shrine where {he} was first a boy. {He} is not well. {He} asks for a flame hot enough to melt the metal in one night.
events.arc: The Bell-Founder's Last Bell

choices.text: Lend a warm flame from the First Hearth

effects.log: The furnace runs with a pure gold light. The metal flows like cream.

choices.text: Send help in the shape of a young apprentice

effects.log: A bright-eyed girl arrives at the foundry door the next day, asking for work.

events.text: The casting is a success, but {npc} is tired. The bell sits in the mould for two days, cooling slowly, while the old man sleeps in a chair by the furnace. The apprentice waits at the door with a lamp and does not speak.
events.arc: The Bell-Founder's Last Bell

choices.text: Watch the mould with the apprentice

effects.log: You keep the lamp lit. The mould ticks as it cools.

choices.text: Send a deep sleep to the old man so that {npc} might rest

effects.log: {npc} sleeps eleven hours and wakes with the morning light and the bell undamaged.

events.text: The bell is broken free of its mould and rung. It sounds a long low note that quiets the whole valley. {npc} listens with closed eyes. 'That is the one,' {he} says. 'I have been trying to cast that note for sixty years.'
events.arc: The Bell-Founder's Last Bell

choices.text: Say the note is the best you have ever heard

effects.log: {He} smiles, and does not say anything for a minute.

choices.text: Ring the bell yourself, once

effects.log: It rings again, deeper still. The founder weeps.

events.text: {npc}'s apprentice casts the bell for the shrine's twin, from the same pattern, and the two bells ring together for the first time. The valley says it is like hearing two old friends talk. The founder, in {his} last year, is carried out in a chair to hear it.
events.arc: The Bell-Founder's Last Bell

choices.text: Attend the dual ringing in a plain coat

effects.log: You stand at the back. The two bells speak. The old man hums the bass.

choices.text: Grant the apprentice a small blessing for the craft

effects.log: The apprentice casts a better bell the next year, and tells nobody why.

events.text: Each spring the people of the high valley dress your sacred spring in flowers, a custom nobody remembers starting. This year {npc}, who leads the dressing, has noticed that the water is slightly less clear. It is not much. It is a shade of a shade.
events.arc: The Dressers of the Spring

choices.text: Look into the spring itself

effects.log: You find a stone fallen into the source. The water finds its way round.

choices.text: Say nothing, and trust the valley to clear it

effects.log: The valley dresses the spring with extra care, and clears it by hand.

events.text: The dressers are out in force: garlands, ribbons, a great arch of willow. A child falls into the spring, and the fuss that follows nearly ruins the festival. The child emerges delighted. {npc} hauls up the offending ribbon and holds it like a fish.
events.arc: The Dressers of the Spring

choices.text: Bless the child who fell

effects.log: The child is blessed with a sneeze and a lucky day.

choices.text: Send a gentle breeze to dry the child

effects.log: The child, dried, begs to fall in again.

events.text: The stone has been lifted, and the spring runs clean. The dressers, to celebrate, hold a feast by the water. {npc} gives the first cup to the stone, which is placed upright in the garden as a small guest of honour.
events.arc: The Dressers of the Spring

choices.text: Toast the stone

effects.log: You raise your cup to the stone, solemnly. It is a very good stone.

choices.text: Make a small shrine of it

effects.log: The stone is given a hat of moss and a cup of water daily.

events.text: Over the years the dressing has become a grand affair, with a procession, a dance and a prize for the best arch. {npc}'s great-granddaughter wins it with a wreath of pure white. The girl tells you afterwards, politely, that the wreath was copied from a dream.
events.arc: The Dressers of the Spring

choices.text: Tell the girl the dream was yours

effects.log: The girl laughs, says that was known all along, and thanks you in an oddly adult voice.

choices.text: Let the girl keep it

effects.log: The girl wins the prize again the next year, and again, by the girl's own hand.

events.text: Your shrine on the island is reached by a ferry, and the ferryman, {npc}, has rowed it alone for forty years. Pilgrims pay in coin, fish or prayers. This season {he} has asked, for the first time, for a day off, having had none since the lake froze in {his} youth.
events.arc: The Ferryman of Your Shrine Lake

choices.text: Take the oars yourself for a day

effects.log: You row badly. Pilgrims look mildly alarmed. You arrive eventually.

choices.text: Send a fair wind so the crossing is easy for anyone

effects.log: The ferry, empty, moves of its own accord. Pilgrims are bemused.

events.text: The ferryman's day off was spent sitting in the reeds, doing nothing. {npc} returns refreshed and unsettled, and tells the pilgrims in a low voice that {he} saw a heron stand on one leg for six hours and does not think {he} wants to go back to rowing.
events.arc: The Ferryman of Your Shrine Lake

choices.text: Offer to find a second ferryman

effects.log: A young man steps forward, awkward and eager, and is shown the oars.

choices.text: Tell the ferryman the oars may be left

effects.log: {npc} thanks you, then picks them up again, as if to test their weight.

events.text: The young ferryman rows well, but the pilgrims miss {npc}'s silence. They ask to be rowed by the old one, and {he} agrees, on alternate days. They notice that they are quieter on {his} days, and sleep better after.
events.arc: The Ferryman of Your Shrine Lake

choices.text: Declare the old ferryman's days a season of silence

effects.log: The pilgrims keep a silent crossing and find the island more beautiful.

choices.text: Add a bench at the stern for the quiet crossings

effects.log: A bench is carved. Pilgrims sit on it like owls.

events.text: The old ferryman rows his last crossing at dusk, with a single passenger, a child asleep in the stern. At the island he sets the oars in the boat and stands a long time in the water. 'I should like to be rowed,' he says, to the evening.
events.arc: The Ferryman of Your Shrine Lake

choices.text: Row him across yourself, in a plain coat

effects.log: You row him a slow circle round the island. He closes his eyes.

choices.text: Send the lake a calm so smooth that the boat floats on its own

effects.log: The boat drifts around the island, once, without a ripple.

events.text: {npc}, a lamp-seller's daughter of eleven, has taken to sitting on the shrine step each evening, telling the wind what it should do. The wind, to everyone's mild alarm, has begun to listen. A pilgrim reports a gale that stopped for a whole sentence.
events.arc: The Lamp-Seller's Daughter

choices.text: Listen to what the girl tells the wind

effects.log: The girl tells it to be kind to the old roof, and the roof thanks the girl.

choices.text: Leave the girl to the work

effects.log: The girl continues, with the wind's full attention.

events.text: The girl is talked of in the valley, with some unease. The shrine priests wish to make her an oracle; her father wishes her to mind the shop. The wind, in the meantime, has become oddly obedient, and the weathercock does not know what to do.
events.arc: The Lamp-Seller's Daughter

choices.text: Ask the girl what she wants

effects.log: 'To mind the shop on Tuesdays,' she says. 'And the wind on the others.'

choices.text: Send a note to her father

effects.log: He reads it twice, folds it, and gives her Tuesdays off.

events.text: {npc} is grown. {He} minds the shop and the wind, and has a small reputation for fair weather. {He} comes to the shrine one evening with a lamp and a tiny cough and asks if the god might recommend a successor for the wind.
events.arc: The Lamp-Seller's Daughter

choices.text: Recommend the next child on the step

effects.log: A boy of nine is found who tells the wind what to do, badly. {npc} nods in approval.

choices.text: Say the wind will choose its own

effects.log: The wind, as ever, does.

events.text: The lamp-shop passes to {npc}'s daughter, and the wind stays, politely, with the shop. On the anniversary of the first gale-stop, the wind brings a bundle of leaves to the step, tied with a thread. The leaves spell, in a very uncertain hand, 'thank you'.
events.arc: The Lamp-Seller's Daughter

choices.text: Leave a lamp for the wind on the step

effects.log: The lamp burns steadily all night. The wind circles it, humming.

choices.text: Send a quiet reply on a breeze

effects.log: The leaves rise up and spin once in the air. A child claps.

events.text: The priest of the east shrine sweeps the dust off the altar every dawn, and every dawn it comes back. He has done this for thirty years, and says it is not dust but the shrine's breathing. You have no opinion. You have never been sure.

choices.text: Sweep the altar with him one dawn

effects.log: You sweep side by side. The dust is oddly golden.

choices.text: Tell him it is dust, and he may stop

effects.log: He nods, and sweeps on. 'It is nice to be told,' he says.

events.text: A donkey has taken up residence at the shrine's lower door. It is not anyone's. It brays at pilgrims, ignores priests, and eats the offerings of barley with a calm that borders on the devotional. The keepers have given it a name.

choices.text: Bless the donkey's patience

effects.log: The donkey brays in a lower, more thoughtful note.

choices.text: Bring the donkey a carrot yourself

effects.log: It eats the carrot and considers you with one soft eye.

events.text: At midnight a woman comes to the empty shrine and prays in a whisper for ten minutes about nothing in particular: her mother's soup, a mule she liked, the weather in her youth. Then she goes home. You are not sure she wants anything at all.

choices.text: Listen to the whole prayer

effects.log: It is the most restful quarter hour of your week.

choices.text: Send her a warm dream of her mother's soup

effects.log: She wakes, smiling, and sits very still for a while.

events.text: The boys of the lower town have a custom of throwing pebbles at your shrine roof for luck. The priests find it a nuisance, and the tiles a ruin. This year the pebbles have started to arrange themselves, in lines, as if for a message.

choices.text: Read the pebbles

effects.log: They spell, with difficulty, 'hello'. You are touched.

choices.text: Send a handful of small smooth stones in reply

effects.log: The boys find them at dawn, and are quiet for a week.

events.text: A young priest has caught a cough from the damp of the shrine, and refuses to leave her post. Her superiors are away. She continues to chant, hoarsely, and the worshippers make a point of coughing along out of solidarity. It is a strange sound.

choices.text: Send a gentle warmth through the shrine

effects.log: The cough eases in the room. The chant is clear again.

choices.text: Send her a dream of rest

effects.log: She wakes and, for the first time, sleeps in.

events.text: The priests of the shrine have a rota for the kettle, which is of no great age but of enormous consequence. A dispute has arisen over whose week it is. The matter has been referred to the god. It is a very small kettle.

choices.text: Rule that the kettle belongs to all

effects.log: The kettle is declared common property and promptly polished by three people.

choices.text: Rule that it is the youngest priest's week, always

effects.log: The youngest priest is overjoyed and slightly alarmed.

events.text: A crack has appeared across the cheek of your statue. The mason wants to repair it. A visiting grandmother says that it makes you look like someone who has been through a bit, and asks that it be left. The mason stands with his hammer raised.

choices.text: Let the crack stay

effects.log: The crack stays. The grandmother brings a flower each Thursday.

choices.text: Have it mended with a seam of gold

effects.log: The mended crack catches the light. The grandmother approves of that too.

events.text: Every year the children of the lower school weave a wreath for your statue. This year's is so large that the statue cannot be seen behind it. Only your nose is visible, and one hand. The children are very proud. The priests are not sure where to look.

choices.text: Accept the wreath with a warm breeze

effects.log: The wreath trembles and holds. The children cheer.

choices.text: Quietly add a second layer of petals

effects.log: A rain of blossoms falls on the wreath. The statue vanishes entirely, and that is fine.

events.text: Lambing season in your domain: three thousand lambs in a week, each of them a small determined catastrophe. The shepherds are exhausted and in love. A lamb has been named after you at every farm, and they are all, without exception, rather stupid.

choices.text: Bless the nights with a little more light

effects.log: The nights are shorter, if only by a candle. Shepherds sleep an hour more.

choices.text: Walk the hills in a plain coat, carrying lambs

effects.log: You carry a lamb to a barn. It falls asleep on your shoulder.

events.text: The first snow of the year falls on your domain at dusk and nobody has asked for it. It falls softly, without wind, on every roof. The valley comes out to look at it. You find that you are very pleased with yourself.

choices.text: Let it fall all night

effects.log: By morning the valley is a new place, and children run through it.

choices.text: Sprinkle a few stars into the snow

effects.log: The snow glitters faintly. Pilgrims say it is a sign.

events.text: Spring mud has taken the lower road to the shrine. Pilgrims arrive with their boots in their hands, and a few without their boots at all. They are cheerful about it. A boy has made a small fortune carrying people across on a door.

choices.text: Dry the road in a night

effects.log: The road is dry by dawn. The boy is out of work and takes it well.

choices.text: Let the mud stay one more day

effects.log: The boy has the best day of his life. The road is dry the next morning.

events.text: A snail the size of a cart arrives at your hall, at the pace of a very small cart, and turns out to be the envoy of a god of moss. The envoy took nine years to arrive. The message, delivered in a soft slow voice, is a greeting.

choices.text: Receive the greeting with ceremony

effects.log: The ceremony lasts an afternoon. The snail enjoys it.

choices.text: Send a reply by the quickest cloud

effects.log: The reply arrives at the moss god's threshold three seconds later. The envoy is astonished at the speed.

events.text: A widow arrives at your hall with a small cart and an enormous pie. She does not want anything. She has made the pie for her husband's anniversary and thought the god, being alone, might like some. You are, in truth, quite alone today.

choices.text: Share the pie with her

effects.log: You eat the pie together. It is the best you have had in a century.

choices.text: Thank her and have a table set for her

effects.log: The kitchens send out a full meal. She is delighted, and a little afraid.

events.text: At the market of the twelve domains a stall sells clocks that run on the hour of the shrine they were made at. Each is different. A seller lets you choose one, and you find the one that runs to your own temple's hours. It is a good clock. It runs a little slow.

choices.text: Buy it

effects.log: The clock ticks on your mantel, never quite right.

choices.text: Ask the seller to set it to the heron's hour

effects.log: The seller, who has heard of the heron, nods with delight.

events.text: A cook at a stall in the border market is making a dish you remember from a thousand years ago, a stew of leeks and river-fish, from a hamlet that no longer exists. You eat it standing, and say nothing. The cook watches you eat.

choices.text: Ask the cook where they learned it

effects.log: 'My grandmother,' says the cook. 'She was from a place that isn't any more.'

choices.text: Pay double and say it is the best in the realm

effects.log: The cook turns pink and gives you a second bowl.

events.text: You dream of a snow house in which a family is having an argument about a goat. It is a very small argument. In the end the goat is brought inside and the argument ends. You wake in a good mood, with no idea whose dream you were in.

choices.text: Send the family a goat-blessing in thanks

effects.log: Somewhere a goat is unusually healthy this year.

choices.text: Keep the dream as it is

effects.log: The dream is a comfort on a grey afternoon.

events.text: In a dream the Sleeper's hall has a flight of stairs that goes down and down. At the bottom is a small door. You do not open it. You wake, and the door is still in your mind, ajar, with a light behind it, very faint and not at all alarming.

choices.text: Tell Mongsa's heralds about the door

effects.log: The heralds look at each other. 'We will tell the Sleeper,' they say.

choices.text: Say nothing, and keep it for another night

effects.log: The door is there the next night. You do not open it then either.

events.text: At court the rumour is that a certain god keeps a great fish in their bath, and speaks to it. You attend a reception and are, by chance, shown into the bathroom. The fish is enormous and regards you with some courtesy.

choices.text: Greet the fish

effects.log: The fish blows a bubble. You feel obscurely approved of.

choices.text: Pretend you did not see it

effects.log: You leave quietly. The god in question, on the stairs, gives you a slow wink.

events.text: The council is divided, evenly, six to six, on whether the harvest festival should be held before or after the first frost. The deciding voice is yours. Nobody will look at you. A herald brings in a cup of tea and sets it carefully in front of you.

choices.text: Vote for before the frost

effects.log: The festival is held before the frost. It is warm and noisy.

choices.text: Vote for after the frost

effects.log: The festival is held after the frost. It is cold and, in a way, better.

events.text: The pantheon dines at a long table with a single pot at the centre, from which everyone must eat. It is a hot pot, and there is a protocol for who dips first, who stirs, and who may quietly take the last mushroom. You are the last mushroom's guardian.

choices.text: Give the last mushroom to the youngest god present

effects.log: The young god takes it, pink with gratitude, and chews it very slowly.

choices.text: Eat the last mushroom with relish

effects.log: It is excellent. You are watched by the entire table.

events.text: A game of knots is held in the shrine yard. Each player ties a rope according to a pattern and the others try to untie it. A girl of ten ties a knot no one can undo. The best untiers of three domains have been defeated. She is eating a plum.

choices.text: Offer to untie it yourself

effects.log: It takes you an hour. You are awarded second place.

choices.text: Declare the girl the winner and give her a rope of light

effects.log: The girl accepts it gravely and ties it, at once, into a bow.

events.text: A contest of choirs is held among the shrines of the valley, and judges are needed. You are one, in a plain coat. The best choir is the small one from the lowest shrine, whose members cannot sing in tune but know all the words, and mean them.

choices.text: Vote for the lowest shrine's choir

effects.log: The lowest shrine wins by a hair. The choir wept with joy and sang worse for it.

choices.text: Vote for the technical winners

effects.log: The best-trained choir wins. The lowest shrine is not upset, and is invited to sing for lunch.

events.text: An elder god, famous for silence, keeps a small garden of plain herbs and speaks of nothing else. You visit, on the pretext of a question about the festival, and instead end up weeding. You do not ask the question. It is not important.

choices.text: Weed until dusk

effects.log: The elder says, at last, 'You do it well.' It is the longest speech you have heard from them.

choices.text: Ask the question anyway

effects.log: The elder answers in a single word, and it is correct.

events.text: The yearly hunt of the wild geese of your domain is held in the high marsh, with horns and flags, and nobody has ever caught a goose. This is understood. This year a young hunter, by mistake, catches one by the neck, and is mortified. The goose looks astonished.

choices.text: Let the goose go with an apology

effects.log: The goose waddles off, offended, and returns with its whole family to honk at the hunter.

choices.text: Declare the goose the hunt's champion

effects.log: The goose is crowned with a ribbon and given a bowl of barley. It is outraged and eats it.

events.text: On the longest night the star-gods hang paper lanterns in the sky, one for each of the faithful dead of the year. Yours is a small one this time. It is yellow. It sways in a high wind. You watch it for the whole night and are not sad.

choices.text: Light a second lantern beside it

effects.log: The two lanterns sway together, and the sky is a little brighter.

choices.text: Keep watch alone

effects.log: At dawn the lantern is gone, as it should be.

events.text: At the edge of your domain a flock of herons rises from the marsh at dusk, ten thousand at once, and turns the whole sky grey with their wings. They do not sound. The sound arrives a moment late, like a breath. You stand in it, entirely still.

choices.text: Stand in the sound until it passes

effects.log: The sound passes. Something in you has been rearranged, very slightly, for the better.

choices.text: Send a warm updraft to lift them higher

effects.log: The herons spiral up through the dusk and are gone.

events.text: A small bell is delivered to the shrine in a sack, with no note, from a place far away. It rings with a sound like a spoon on glass. The priests do not know whether to hang it or return it. It is, at least, very clear.

choices.text: Hang it by the gate
