effects.log: The bell rings in the wind. Pilgrims stop to listen, and then forget why they were hurrying.

choices.text: Keep it by your bed

effects.log: It rings once, softly, in the night. You sleep very well.

events.text: At dawn, the temple sweepers come out in a line with long brooms and sweep the courtyard in silence, a slow arc, left to right. It is the most dependable beauty in your shrine. You have watched it for four thousand mornings. You will watch it again.

choices.text: Watch from the roof, as always

effects.log: The courtyard is clean in the first light. It is enough.

choices.text: Sweep one arc with them

effects.log: You sweep one arc. The line adjusts without a word and carries on.

events.text: From the kitchens of the lower shrine comes the sound of a kettle singing, a high thin note that rises as the water boils. The cook is unaware that the note is a good one. You listen to the kettle the whole time it takes to boil, and a little after.

choices.text: Send a faint warmth to the kitchen

effects.log: The note holds a moment longer than it should. The cook looks puzzled and pleased.

choices.text: Wait for the kettle to stop

effects.log: It stops. The silence is fine too.

events.text: {npc}, a hill priest, preaches that the river will rise this autumn and the lower shrines must move. The orthodoxy of the valley is that you have promised the river to keep within its banks. {He} is shouted down at the festival, and put out of the shrine with a loaf.
events.arc: The Heretic Who Was Right About the Flood

choices.text: Hear {him} out in a plain coat on the hill road

effects.log: {He} shows you cracks in the old weir, and the colour of the clay. {He} is quite serious.

choices.text: Let the valley's priests settle it

effects.log: The priests settle it by a show of hands. {npc} loses by forty.

events.text: Autumn nears. {npc} has started to carry stones, alone, to the high ground, to build a small refuge nobody asked for. A few children help. The priests call it a scandal. The river, listening, murmurs a little louder at night.
events.arc: The Heretic Who Was Right About the Flood

choices.text: Send a dream of the weir cracking to the head priest

effects.log: The head priest wakes, sweating, and orders a small, private inspection.

choices.text: Lend {npc} a gentle strength for the stones

effects.log: The stones move more easily. The refuge rises.

events.text: The river rises. The lower shrines are moved, at the last minute, to {npc}'s refuge, half-laughing, half-in-tears. The weir breaks at midnight. Nobody drowns, and the valley, for once, is silent. The head priest comes up the hill and does not know what to say.
events.arc: The Heretic Who Was Right About the Flood

choices.text: Declare {npc} a true priest of the valley

effects.log: {He} is given a bell, a robe, and a seat at the head table. {He} gives the robe to a child.

choices.text: Say nothing in public, and send {him} a quiet blessing

effects.log: {He} finds the blessing in the morning, in a bowl of fresh milk.

events.text: The river rises, the lower shrines are lost, and {npc} is found to have been right. By then, however, the valley has dispersed, and {npc} is left to keep a hill shrine of the survivors. {He} does not gloat. {He} puts a stone on the wall for each name.
events.arc: The Heretic Who Was Right About the Flood

choices.text: Help {npc} carve the names

effects.log: You work through the night. By dawn the wall is full.

choices.text: Send a gift of seed to the hill

effects.log: The hill is green by the next spring. {npc} sows with a tired smile.

events.text: {npc}, a former priest of yours, was expelled for teaching that gods need not be thanked, only understood. {He} now holds classes in a barn. Seven students attend. The barn smells of hay and doctrine. The old priests have written you a lengthy letter.
events.arc: The Heretic's Disciples

choices.text: Attend a class in a plain coat

effects.log: {npc} lectures on the gods as weather, and is a better speaker than you expected.

choices.text: Reply to the old priests with a polite silence

effects.log: Nothing is done. The barn fills.

events.text: The barn has become a school. Thirty students now, some of them well-born, and a boy who asks questions so sharp that the lecturer has taken to writing the answers down at night. A cousin of yours at court says the Hall is asking after the barn.
events.arc: The Heretic's Disciples

choices.text: Invite {npc} to dine at your hall

effects.log: {He} attends in a borrowed robe and talks all through the soup.

choices.text: Send a gentle warning that the Hall is watching

effects.log: {npc} sends a gentle reply: 'Let it watch.'

events.text: A messenger from the Silent Hall comes to the barn, and sits at the back of a class, and says nothing for six hours. After, the messenger tells {npc}: 'You are mostly wrong. The Hall is interested in the part where you are right.' {npc} faints into a haystack.
events.arc: The Heretic's Disciples

choices.text: Take {npc} under your wing as a lecturer of the shrine

effects.log: A seat is made for {him}. The barn becomes the shrine's school.

choices.text: Leave the barn alone, and send hay

effects.log: The barn is left alone. It thrives.

events.text: {npc} is old and the school is large. The old doctrine, that gods must be understood, is taught to the children as a matter of course. One of the students, now a priest, sits at your threshold one evening and asks whether the gods understand themselves. You say: 'No.' The student laughs.
events.arc: The Heretic's Disciples

choices.text: Sit with the student and talk until dawn

effects.log: The conversation is the most honest of your year.

choices.text: Send the student a book from your own shelves

effects.log: The student reads it in a week and returns it, with notes.

events.text: Four hundred years ago your temple burned the treatise of a heretic named Pyeon, who wrote that the stars were not gods but lamps lit by gods. A copy has surfaced in a trunk, and the scribe {npc}, who found it, wants permission to read it. The trunk smells of smoke.
events.arc: The Burned Book Returned

choices.text: Let {npc} read it first

effects.log: {He} reads for a night and a day, and comes out silent, with ink on {his} fingers.

choices.text: Read it yourself, privately

effects.log: The prose is sharp, rude, and very good. You are annoyed to find it correct on one point.

events.text: News has spread. The old priests wish to burn the book again. A younger set wishes to read it aloud at the next feast. {npc} is torn between them and has built a small fort of cushions in the archive to read in peace.
events.arc: The Burned Book Returned

choices.text: Declare a sitting in which both sides may speak

effects.log: The sitting is long and shrill. A pie is thrown.

choices.text: Make a fair copy before anything else is done

effects.log: The copy is made in the night by three scribes. The original is hidden in a jar.

events.text: The treatise, read aloud, turns out to be partly right and partly delightfully wrong. The stars, it argues, are lamps. The Sky god Cheonho, asked, says only that they are 'also that'. {npc} is moved to have lived to see a book come out of smoke.
events.arc: The Burned Book Returned

choices.text: Publish the treatise at the shrine's cost

effects.log: The book is bound and set in the library, with a preface by {npc}.

choices.text: Lay the book on the altar for a year

effects.log: It lies there, open, and the pilgrims read it a page at a time.

events.text: The book is read, argued with, and loved. A young hand has written beneath one of its lines: 'You were right about the lamps.' {npc} traces the line with a finger and asks, softly, if the old heretic is anywhere to be thanked. You say that you will look.
events.arc: The Burned Book Returned

choices.text: Look for Pyeon among the faded

effects.log: In a ledger of the faded you find the name, and a small stone beside it. You leave a lamp.

choices.text: Send a star to the grave of the book's first burning

effects.log: A small bright star hangs low over the old fire-pit for a week.

events.text: An auditor of the Heavenly Court has arrived at your hall with a ledger and an unreadable expression. {npc} has come to count your answered prayers against your unanswered, and to compare the figure with the average. The auditor has brought their own lamp.
events.arc: The Audit of Answered Prayers

choices.text: Receive the auditor with a cup of tea

effects.log: {npc} drinks it without a word and writes down 'tea: adequate'.

choices.text: Hand over your own records, tidy as they are

effects.log: The records are accepted with a flicker of suspicion.

events.text: The audit proceeds. {npc} is tireless, polite, and entirely without humour. Prayers for rain that were answered with drizzle are marked 'partial'. Prayers for love answered with a stray dog are marked 'under review'. The dog is brought as evidence.
events.arc: The Audit of Answered Prayers

choices.text: Defend the dog

effects.log: You argue that the dog was a splendid answer. The auditor makes a note.

choices.text: Let the auditor draw their own conclusions

effects.log: The auditor draws several and underlines them.

events.text: The audit concludes. You have answered two prayers in five, which the Court finds acceptable and, in some respects, remarkable. {npc} says, formally, that the figure is the best in this part of the realm. Then, quietly, that it is the best {he} has seen in a hundred years.
events.arc: The Audit of Answered Prayers

choices.text: Thank {npc} and ask what the unanswered ones were

effects.log: {He} produces a short list of the saddest prayers of the year. You read them all.

choices.text: Offer the auditor a seat at your feast

effects.log: {npc} attends, stiff and astonished, and eats three helpings of pie.

events.text: The audit finds a fault: sixty prayers, a decade back, were answered in the wrong order, to the lasting disadvantage of a minor worshipper. {npc} requests a correction in writing. Your hand shakes slightly as you sign. The worshipper has long since died, in comfort.
events.arc: The Audit of Answered Prayers

choices.text: Add a note of regret to the ledger

effects.log: The ledger carries your note of regret. It is the only one in its pages.

choices.text: Send a dream of apology to the worshipper's grandchildren

effects.log: A dream goes out. The grandchildren wake, puzzled and warm.

events.text: An auditor of the Heavenly Court, {npc}, proposes a new method: to count not the answered prayers but the silences. A silence, {he} explains, is a prayer a god chose not to answer, and every god has a number. {He} would like to examine yours.
events.arc: The Auditor Who Counted Silences

choices.text: Agree, and offer your records

effects.log: {He} thumbs through them with a thin smile. There are a great many silences.

choices.text: Ask what the silences would prove

effects.log: {npc} says: 'That a god is a person.' You are not sure how to take this.

events.text: The count of silences is long, and {npc} goes through them slowly. Some are marked 'by mercy', others 'by oversight', a few 'by temper'. The temper silences make you blush. One is marked simply 'by cowardice'. You ask which.
events.arc: The Auditor Who Counted Silences

choices.text: Ask to see the cowardice entry

effects.log: It is from nine hundred years ago. A mother asked you for a thing you could not give.

choices.text: Ask the auditor to be gentle

effects.log: {npc} says {he} is always gentle. {He} is, truly, though it is not a comfort.

events.text: {npc} gives the verdict: your silences are chiefly mercy. A few are failures, and {he} marks them as such. 'It is the failures,' {he} says, 'that make a ledger worth reading.' You are not sure if this is praise.
events.arc: The Auditor Who Counted Silences

choices.text: Take the failures to the altar and name them aloud

effects.log: You name them. The shrine is very quiet. A priest cries in the back.

choices.text: Thank the auditor and burn nothing

effects.log: {npc} nods. 'Good,' {he} says. 'The Court will want to see them again.'

events.text: The method spreads through the Court. Within a decade every god is asked to account for their silences, and an entire floor of the Heavenly Court is given to the task. {npc} is promoted and made miserable by it. {He} writes to you for advice on how to bear praise.
events.arc: The Auditor Who Counted Silences

choices.text: Reply with a cup of tea and a short note

effects.log: 'Drink the tea,' it says. {He} does.

choices.text: Visit {npc} in a plain coat and eat with {him}

effects.log: You eat noodles at the Court canteen. {He} laughs for the first time in years.

events.text: While reviewing your answered prayers the Court's clerk, {npc}, finds that eleven were credited to you and answered by another: a neighbour, a stray cart, a saint in the next valley. {He} must note the discrepancy. {He} apologises, at length, for the discrepancy.
events.arc: The Prayers Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Ask who answered them

effects.log: {He} names a cousin, a miller, and a saint who is very annoyed.

choices.text: Let the credit stand, if it is useful

effects.log: {npc} writes 'noted' and 'with reservations'.

events.text: The saint of the next valley, who answered four of the prayers, arrives to ask for credit. A modest request, formally made. The saint has brought a small pie. The pie is persuasive.
events.arc: The Prayers Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Grant the saint the credit and share it

effects.log: The saint is overjoyed and eats the pie alone.

choices.text: Say that credit is a poor currency anyway

effects.log: The saint takes this with a nod, then eats the pie, and nods again.

events.text: The ledger is corrected. Eleven prayers move from your column to others'. Your figure drops. The Court notes that the corrected figure is more honest and the miller, who answered three, has been named in the Court's rolls for the first time in a long life. {npc} brings you the miller's thanks.
events.arc: The Prayers Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Receive the miller's thanks and keep them in the hall

effects.log: A bag of flour sits beside the altar all year. It is the best flour in your realm.

choices.text: Send the miller a favourable wind for the mill

effects.log: The mill turns twice as fast. The miller says the wind is a very good neighbour.

events.text: The credit stands. For years your figure is the envy of the region. Then, one night, the cousin who answered two prayers comes to confess, in tears, that they should have been named. {npc} is sent to take the confession. The cousin cries into a handkerchief.
events.arc: The Prayers Answered by Someone Else

choices.text: Take the cousin's part and thank them privately

effects.log: The cousin leaves lighter and more embarrassed.

choices.text: Correct the ledger yourself, the next morning

effects.log: You write the corrections in your own hand. {npc} is visibly relieved.

events.text: A shrine in the south has built a carved panel celebrating a miracle of healing as the work of the god of fire. The miracle, you remember, was yours. {npc}, a southern priest, has come to your hall to say that the panel is finished and the record, regrettably, not.
events.arc: The Miracles Credited to the Wrong God

choices.text: Ask to see the panel

effects.log: It is beautiful. The fire god is drawn as a kindly man with ash on a sleeve.

choices.text: Say it matters little

effects.log: {npc} looks at you, long, then bows.

events.text: The fire god, hearing of the panel, writes to ask whether you might share the credit. The letter is polite, and a little too long. {npc} waits at your door for your reply with the face of a messenger in a very bad story.
events.arc: The Miracles Credited to the Wrong God

choices.text: Write back that the panel may stand, and the credit is shared

effects.log: The fire god answers with a feast invitation.

choices.text: Write back a detailed account of the healing

effects.log: The fire god responds with a long, slow, grudging 'quite'.

events.text: At the fire god's feast the matter comes up again, to the delight of the whole table. The fire god tells the story, with a few embellishments, as their own, and you tell it as yours, with fewer. {npc} goes round the table with the ledger, taking notes, red with laughter.
events.arc: The Miracles Credited to the Wrong God

choices.text: Let the stories be both true

effects.log: The ledger records: 'Healing: two gods, one fire, one patient.' It is accepted.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the shared miracle

effects.log: The cup is raised. A third god at the table claims the cup.

events.text: The matter lingers. Years later a pilgrim to the panel falls ill and prays to the fire god. The fire god, a good fellow, sends the prayer on to you. You answer it. The panel is given a small plaque at the bottom, in {npc}'s hand: 'Also by the neighbour.'
events.arc: The Miracles Credited to the Wrong God

choices.text: Visit the panel and read the plaque

effects.log: You read it twice. It is a small thing and it pleases you more than it ought.

choices.text: Send a note of thanks to {npc}

effects.log: {He} frames it above the shrine door.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has sent an inspector, {npc}, to your shrines. The inspector arrives unannounced, in a clean grey coat, with a measuring rod. Your priests, forewarned by pigeon, have swept the floors twice and hidden the cat.
events.arc: The Inspector of Shrines

choices.text: Accompany the inspector in a plain coat

effects.log: {npc} measures your doorways and notes that the lintel is crooked. You agree it is.

choices.text: Leave the priests to receive the inspection

effects.log: The priests hold, and offer the inspector biscuits.

events.text: The inspection continues for a week. {npc} finds the roof leaking, a candle unlit, and a door ajar. The cat, uncovered, sits on the inspector's feet and refuses to move. The report is stalled by a fur-covered boot.
events.arc: The Inspector of Shrines

choices.text: Offer the inspector a seat by the fire

effects.log: {He} sits. The cat purrs. The report is not written that day.

choices.text: Remove the cat gently

effects.log: The cat is removed. It returns, and gets a biscuit.

events.text: The report is generous. Three faults, all mended in a week; one commendation, for the garden. {npc} reads it aloud in the hall, solemnly, and adds a final remark off the record: that it is the first shrine in a century where {he} has felt welcome.
events.arc: The Inspector of Shrines

choices.text: Invite the inspector back in the spring

effects.log: {He} returns with a basket of seed.

choices.text: Send a copy of the report to the neighbouring shrines

effects.log: Six shrines clean their floors and hide their cats less.

events.text: A harsher report follows a year later from a different inspector, after a complaint by a rival. {npc} is sent to check, and quietly rewrites the finding in your favour. {He} will not say why. It is, {he} says, within the margin.
events.arc: The Inspector of Shrines

choices.text: Thank {npc} and decline any further favour

effects.log: {He} nods. 'The margin is mine to use,' {he} says.

choices.text: Send {npc} a quiet gift of dried plums

effects.log: The plums are received with a flush and a smile.

events.text: The Heavenly Court has laid a tax on incense, a pinch in twelve to be sent upward each season as a tithe. {npc}, the tax-clerk, arrives at your shrine with a small silver scale and the gloomy air of one who knows the likely reception.
events.arc: The Tax on Incense

choices.text: Pay at once, with a smile

effects.log: The scale is balanced. {npc} is so astonished that {he} weighs it twice.

choices.text: Ask what the tithe is for

effects.log: {He} says it is for the upkeep of the Hall of Smoke. You have never heard of it.

events.text: The tax is resented. Priests burn less incense to avoid paying, and pilgrims complain of smokeless shrines. A thin grey winter settles over the valley. {npc} comes back, looking worried: the Hall's fires are getting low.
events.arc: The Tax on Incense

choices.text: Declare a feast of smoke to restore the levy

effects.log: The shrines blaze for a day. The tax is paid in a great fragrant heap.

choices.text: Quietly pay the shortfall yourself

effects.log: A fragrant parcel is sent. The clerk does not ask.

events.text: You visit the Hall of Smoke in a plain coat. It is a long low building at the edge of the Court, kept by a hundred old women who spend their days sorting incense by smell. They say the hall keeps the memory of every prayer ever burned. They offer you tea.
events.arc: The Tax on Incense

choices.text: Sit with the old women and be taught to sort

effects.log: You sort for an afternoon. They tell you the smell of each god's shrine.

choices.text: Pay the hall a year's tithe in advance

effects.log: The old women nod. A small bundle of herbs is pressed into your hand.

events.text: The tax is never repealed but becomes a custom: a pinch in twelve, with a bow. {npc}'s apprentices collect it in clean aprons and are given tea. The hall's fires are bright. The pilgrims note the sweetness of the incense on the road, and know where it goes.
events.arc: The Tax on Incense

choices.text: Attend a collection day in a plain coat

effects.log: You are weighed, solemnly, and found correct.

choices.text: Offer the clerks a better scale

effects.log: A new scale is brought from the hill. It is a work of art.

events.text: Beneath the Heavenly Court is an office where lost prayers are kept: prayers that were misaddressed, mistimed or whispered into a well. {npc} keeps it, in a cloud of dust and string. A prayer addressed to you has been there for four hundred years, and {he} would like to return it.
events.arc: The Lost-Property Office of Prayers

choices.text: Collect the prayer in person

effects.log: It is a small grey thing in a tin box, warm as a pocket.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read it aloud

effects.log: {He} clears {his} throat and reads. It is a single sentence about a lost goat.

events.text: The goat prayer was never answered. {npc} offers to look into whether the goat can be found. After a week the office has found a descendant of the goat, grazing on a hill nobody has visited in ages. The goat is large, and indifferent to all of it.
events.arc: The Lost-Property Office of Prayers

choices.text: Send the descendant a small blessing

effects.log: The goat gives a single suspicious bleat. It seems to approve.

choices.text: Visit the hill and bring the goat a loaf

effects.log: You sit with the goat. It eats the loaf and walks off.

events.text: {npc} shows you the office's back room: shelves of lost prayers, thousands, each in its tin, each labelled with a date. Some are four thousand years old. {He} says that the office has not had a visitor in a hundred years, and that you may take any you like.
events.arc: The Lost-Property Office of Prayers

choices.text: Take one at random and answer it

effects.log: The prayer is a boy's wish for a pony. The pony, long dead, is answered in a dream of a field.

choices.text: Take none, and offer to fund a second clerk

effects.log: The office is given a second clerk and a lamp. {npc} weeps into the string.

events.text: The office has become your pastime. Each year you answer a few of the oldest prayers, with a long delay, and the replies reach the descendants of the praying, who do not know why they feel suddenly lucky. {npc} keeps the tally in a green notebook.
events.arc: The Lost-Property Office of Prayers

choices.text: Send {npc} a new notebook

effects.log: The notebook is a deep green with a gold spine. {He} sheds a tear on the first page.

choices.text: Answer one more, and then rest

effects.log: The prayer is answered. You sleep very deeply afterward.

events.text: {npc}, a priest at one of your quieter shrines, has begun to tell pilgrims the truth. When asked if the god will answer, {he} says: 'Probably not.' When asked if the god cares, {he} says: 'I think so.' Attendance has doubled.
events.arc: The Priest Who Told the Truth

choices.text: Visit incognito and ask a question

effects.log: {He} answers you with a cautious honesty that is disarming.

choices.text: Ask the other priests what they think

effects.log: They say it is unseemly, and very popular.

events.text: The honest priest draws a following. Pilgrims arrive with hard questions: Why did the harvest fail? Why did my mother die? {npc} says: 'I do not know.' The pilgrims weep with relief. A rival shrine puts up a sign saying 'Full Answers'.
events.arc: The Priest Who Told the Truth

choices.text: Send {npc} a quiet courage

effects.log: {He} stands straighter. The next pilgrim cries on {his} shoulder.

choices.text: Say nothing

effects.log: {npc} carries on without a sign, and without a mistake.

events.text: A grieving father comes to {npc} demanding to know whether the god ever listens. {npc} brings the father to you in a dream. The father shouts. You listen to every word. When the father is done you say: 'I heard you.' It is all that you have.
events.arc: The Priest Who Told the Truth

choices.text: Add: 'I am sorry'

effects.log: The father weeps, and sleeps, and wakes with the anger gone grey.

choices.text: Say nothing more

effects.log: The father wakes with a feeling of having been listened to.

events.text: {npc}'s honesty reaches the Court, where it is called either heresy or a fine example. The matter is debated for a decade. In the end {npc} is given a medal and a warning, in equal parts, and asked to say less. {He} keeps the medal and says what {he} must.
events.arc: The Priest Who Told the Truth

choices.text: Wear the medal at the next feast, beside {npc}

effects.log: You stand together at the end of the table, a god and a priest, both slightly out of place.

choices.text: Send {npc} a bottle of good wine

effects.log: {He} drinks it with the other priests, honestly.

events.text: {npc}, a researcher in the Court's archive, claims there is a thirteenth domain that was never assigned: the Domain of Small Hours, the minutes between one thing and the next. No one holds it. {He} has been writing to every god in the realm to ask whether any would like to try.
events.arc: The Thirteenth Domain Nobody Holds

choices.text: Read {npc}'s proposal with an open mind

effects.log: The proposal is modest, learned, and moving. You mark a passage.

choices.text: Decline politely

effects.log: {He} thanks you, and adds your name to the list of the courteous.

events.text: The domain is unclaimed, but the hours have begun to misbehave. Meals arrive late, and an afternoon was lost entirely in the east. {npc} reports that the minutes are, in a manner of speaking, wandering. Several gods have asked whether it is their fault.
events.arc: The Thirteenth Domain Nobody Holds

choices.text: Offer to mind a quarter-hour of the day

effects.log: A quarter-hour is yours. Nobody notices, and everything runs a little better.

choices.text: Ask the Weaver where the minutes are going

effects.log: Unmyeong says: 'Into the gaps.' Which is accurate.

events.text: A candidate steps forward: a clerk of the Court, quiet, modest, with a very good watch. The clerk is made a minor god of the Small Hours, with a shrine the size of a cupboard and a seat at the bottom of the table. {npc} weeps at the confirmation.
events.arc: The Thirteenth Domain Nobody Holds

choices.text: Be the first to leave an offering

effects.log: You leave a clock. It does not tick, for the offering is the pause between ticks.

choices.text: Attend the cupboard-shrine's opening

effects.log: The opening takes four minutes. It is the most punctual ceremony of the century.

events.text: The Small Hours are put right over some years. {npc} retires to a cottage and the clerk-god, shy and busy, is generally well liked. At the next feast, however, you notice a place laid for a fourteenth domain, with no name. {npc} winks, from the servants' door.
events.arc: The Thirteenth Domain Nobody Holds

choices.text: Sit in the empty place for the length of a soup

effects.log: The seat is warm. A faint voice hums beside you.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the fourteenth domain is

effects.log: {He} says: 'Not yet. Perhaps after your time.'

events.text: Beyond your northern hills a hermit god lives in a hut with a shut door. {npc}, a goatherd, has taken them bread for thirty years and has never seen the door open. Today the bread is untouched, and there is a note on the step. The note says only: 'Not yet.'
events.arc: The Hermit God Who Will Not Open

choices.text: Knock at the door yourself

effects.log: No answer. The bread is warm, as if someone had just taken it in.

choices.text: Leave the hermit to it

effects.log: {npc} sits on the step with the goats and waits.

events.text: {npc} has given up waiting and now simply visits. The goats treat the step as their own. A year passes. In spring a small flower pushes through the threshold of the shut door, and then another. {He} brings you a blossom in a cup.
events.arc: The Hermit God Who Will Not Open

choices.text: Look at the flower and admire it

effects.log: It is a plain thing, white, with a hint of salt.

choices.text: Plant a seed beside the step

effects.log: A shoot comes up. It leans toward the door.

events.text: The door opens a hand's breadth on a quiet night. A voice says, out of the dark, 'Is the world still going?' {npc} replies, trembling: 'Yes.' The voice is silent for a while, then says, 'Good.' The door closes. It has been three hundred years.
events.arc: The Hermit God Who Will Not Open

choices.text: Add: 'It is much the same, but kind'

effects.log: The door does not open again, but the bread is taken in.

choices.text: Stay quiet, and let {npc} speak for the world

effects.log: {npc} speaks until dawn. In the morning the step is swept.

events.text: {npc} is gone and the goats are many. The hermit's door stands open. Inside there is a chair, a lamp, and a heap of dust that was, perhaps, a god. On the table lies a half-finished letter, addressed to nobody: 'Dear, I have been thinking about—'.
events.arc: The Hermit God Who Will Not Open

choices.text: Finish the letter in the hermit's hand

effects.log: You add one sentence. It is the kindest you can find.

choices.text: Leave the letter and close the door softly

effects.log: The door is closed. The goats lie down on the step.

events.text: The lesser gods of your valley have no school for their children, and the children of the god of one puddle are, as a result, playing with the children of the god of one stile, with predictable disaster. {npc}, a retired teacher-priest, volunteers to start a school if the god will provide the roof.
events.arc: The School for Lesser Gods' Children

choices.text: Provide a roof of living thatch

effects.log: A thatch roof grows from nothing. {npc} nods approvingly.

choices.text: Provide the old stable, newly swept

effects.log: The stable has a charm. The children bring their own stools.

events.text: The school opens with eleven pupils, three of them dangerous. A child god of storms has sneezed over the schoolhouse twice, and one of the little gods of frost has frozen a classmate's boots. {npc} is firm, kind and soaked. Lessons begin in earnest.
events.arc: The School for Lesser Gods' Children

choices.text: Visit as a guest teacher on the weather

effects.log: You teach for an afternoon. The storm child asks the sharpest question.

choices.text: Send a bag of dry boots

effects.log: The boots are accepted by the whole class, shouting.

events.text: The first term ends with a small examination. The youngest, a tiny god of the doorstep, recites the entire list of the twelve domains without a single mistake, and then bursts into tears. {npc} holds the child and says the tears are marked correct.
events.arc: The School for Lesser Gods' Children

choices.text: Award the doorstep god a little blessing for the future

effects.log: The child sits up straighter. A doorstep somewhere is permanently dry.

choices.text: Present the school with a shelf of books

effects.log: The books arrive and are read to ruin in a week.

events.text: Years on, the school's pupils are minor gods in their own right. The god of the doorstep is the Warden of Thresholds. At a feast, the Warden finds you and bows gravely, saying only: 'The roof is still green.' You would like to be less moved than you are.
events.arc: The School for Lesser Gods' Children

choices.text: Ask the Warden to sit with you

effects.log: You eat together and talk of {npc}, who is old and still correcting essays.

choices.text: Send {npc} the Warden's thanks, with a hamper

effects.log: The hamper reaches {npc} the next day. {He} claims it is too much and eats it all.

events.text: {npc}, a mapmaker, has been commissioned by the Court to draw a true map of the twelve domains. {He} has a great deal of ink, three assistants, and a growing despair: the borders will not stay still. Rivers of one domain run into the next, and the map is already wrong.
events.arc: The Cartographer of the Domains

choices.text: Lend {npc} a clear day for surveying

effects.log: The day is cloudless and the horizon exact. {He} surveys until the light fails.

choices.text: Invite {npc} to leave the borders loose

effects.log: 'A map can breathe,' you say. {He} stares at you, then draws a very faint line.

events.text: The map grows. {npc} has found that each domain has an edge that moves in the course of the day: War's border is firmer at dawn; Dreams' edge dissolves at noon. The map is being drawn in layers. A deputy of the Court asks for a single sheet.
events.arc: The Cartographer of the Domains

choices.text: Suggest several sheets, one for each hour

effects.log: The map becomes a book. The deputy is satisfied and bewildered.

choices.text: Suggest a map that is mostly rivers

effects.log: {He} tries. The result is nearly beautiful.

events.text: The map is finished and hung in the Hall of the Court. It is a vast sheet of delicate lines, and the gods crowd round to find their own homes on it. {npc} stands in the corner, blinking. A minor god finds an error and is thanked profusely for it.
events.arc: The Cartographer of the Domains

choices.text: Praise the map, and find an error of your own

effects.log: The error is that your shrine is a little to the left. {npc} is delighted.

choices.text: Mark your own shrine with a small gold star

effects.log: A gold star is drawn. Six other gods ask for one.

events.text: The loose-lined map is the favourite of the pilgrims. The borders are clouds and rivers, and a traveller can read the whole realm in a glance and be right enough. {npc} is old now and signs copies for the pilgrims. {He} gives each a small tip: 'Go by the river.'
events.arc: The Cartographer of the Domains

choices.text: Buy a copy from {npc} and have it signed

effects.log: {He} signs with a flourish. 'Go by the river,' {he} says.

choices.text: Send a river to the map's heart

effects.log: A small stream runs through the Court. The map is amended with delight.

events.text: In a gully on the western edge of your domain a shrine has woken. Its lamp is lit. Its altar is warm. It has no priest and no worshippers, and it is addressed to nobody. {npc}, a traveller who stumbled on it, has sent a hurried message to you and then sat down to wait.
events.arc: The Shrine Woken After a Thousand Years

choices.text: Go to the shrine in a plain coat

effects.log: It is clean, small, and humming. {npc} is eating a pear on the step.

choices.text: Send a priest to keep it

effects.log: A priest sets out and is back in a week with news that the shrine is already kept.

events.text: The shrine is kept, but by whom? Fresh bread appears on the altar each dawn. Pilgrims, a few, find their way. {npc} has taken to sleeping on the step and says that the shrine does not mind. In the night, someone is heard sweeping.
events.arc: The Shrine Woken After a Thousand Years

choices.text: Wait at the shrine one night

effects.log: You sit until dawn. The broom sweeps. You see nobody.

choices.text: Leave a loaf and a note

effects.log: In the morning there is a loaf in return, with a note: 'Thank you.'

events.text: A voice speaks from the altar on the shortest day, softly: it is the shrine's god, long faded, remembered only by the shrine itself. The voice asks whether it may be kept. It does not ask for faith. It asks for company.
events.arc: The Shrine Woken After a Thousand Years

choices.text: Promise to visit on every shortest day

effects.log: The voice thanks you. The lamp burns a little brighter.

choices.text: Make the shrine a part of your own, with its god named at the altar

effects.log: The shrine's god gets a name again. It is the first in a thousand years.

events.text: The shrine's voice has faded again. {npc} stays, as keeper, and sweeps the altar on the shortest day. The shrine remembers a few pilgrims at a time. On the last day of the old year you find yourself there, and the lamp is lit, and no voice speaks, and it is enough.
events.arc: The Shrine Woken After a Thousand Years

choices.text: Sit with {npc} until the lamp burns low

effects.log: You sit in silence. The lamp lasts exactly as long as you do.

choices.text: Leave a flower on the altar and go

effects.log: The flower is still fresh at the next solstice.

events.text: Long ago, before you were a god, you knew a mortal named Seoro, a boatman, who taught you to whistle. {npc}, one of Seoro's descendants, has come to the shrine to ask whether the god knows where the old man is buried. The grave has been lost. {He} says it matters to the family.
events.arc: The Grave of a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Say you will look, and mean it

effects.log: {npc} brightens. 'No hurry,' {he} says. 'We have waited a hundred years.'

choices.text: Admit that you knew Seoro

effects.log: {npc} stares. You are given a chair, and tea, and asked a hundred questions.

events.text: You find a likely place, on a bank above a river, by a stone shaped like a boat. The earth there is sweet. It is so quiet that you can hear the river thinking. {npc} comes out to see the spot and stands for a long time without a word.
events.arc: The Grave of a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Whistle the old tune

effects.log: A long, thin note on the wind. The river answers a moment late.

choices.text: Leave a smooth pebble on the stone

effects.log: The pebble lies where it falls. It looks as if it had always been there.

events.text: The family holds a small ceremony at the grave. They do not know a god is present. {npc} reads the old man's name aloud, and a child says a line of a boatman's song, off key. You stand at the back, in a plain coat, and join the chorus.
events.arc: The Grave of a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Sing the whole song

effects.log: You sing it all, to the last verse. The family look around, puzzled, then join in.

choices.text: Hum it quietly

effects.log: No one notices. It is enough.

events.text: The grave is tended. Every year on the same day a boat of the family drifts past with a lamp. You, a god, take the oars on the evening of the hundredth year, in a plain coat, as the boat drifts past. {npc} does not look up, and you do not mind.
events.arc: The Grave of a Mortal Friend

choices.text: Row the family's boat through the dusk

effects.log: The river is calm. You row the whole way and no one knows.

choices.text: Send a following breeze to the boat

effects.log: The boat glides. A child in the bow says it feels like being carried.

events.text: At the foot of your hill there is a house for orphans, kept by {npc}, a gruff old cook, and the children there sing at the dawn bell, loudly, out of tune, with great spirit. The priests find it exhausting. The pilgrims drop coins in a bowl.
events.arc: The Orphan Choir

choices.text: Listen from the gate, in a plain coat

effects.log: The children sing the morning hymn with real feeling and a different tune each.

choices.text: Ask the priests to be patient

effects.log: The priests agree, with a sigh, and take to wearing earplugs of wax.

events.text: The orphan choir is invited to sing at a pantheon feast, by mistake or by malice; nobody knows. {npc} leads them up the hill in two rows and a cart. The children are overawed by the gods' hall. The youngest sings first, and falls over.
events.arc: The Orphan Choir

choices.text: Catch the child, gently

effects.log: You catch the child before the fall. The hall laughs in a warm way.

choices.text: Start the song for them

effects.log: You sing the first line, flat. The children, delighted, correct you.

events.text: The choir sings, and the gods fall silent. The song is out of tune and enormous with joy. A very old god in the corner of the hall, who has not smiled for centuries, is seen to smile. {npc} stands stiff with pride, and crying. The feast gives each child a plate of sweet buns.
events.arc: The Orphan Choir

choices.text: Toast the choir with your cup

effects.log: Every cup in the hall is raised. The children eat the buns, shyly.

choices.text: Quietly endow the house with a year of firewood

effects.log: The firewood arrives with the first frost. {npc} grumbles, and cries.

events.text: Years later the orphan choir is the chief singer of the valley, and its old members return in turn as cooks, priests, mothers. {npc} is gone. The house stands on the hill with a new roof and a bell, which the children ring, badly, at dawn.
events.arc: The Orphan Choir

choices.text: Visit on a dawn in a plain coat and listen

effects.log: You are given a seat on the step. The bell rings, and they sing.

choices.text: Send a bell of silver to the house

effects.log: The silver bell is hung. It rings a good deal sweeter than the old one. The children keep ringing both.

events.text: Once a year the shrines of the valley hold a festival of bad poems. Each priest reads out one, as dreadful as can be arranged, and the winner is crowned with a wreath of nettles. {npc}, last year's champion, is nervous. {He} has a sequel.
events.arc: The Festival of Bad Poems

choices.text: Attend the festival in a plain coat

effects.log: You are seated among the nettles. The first poem is about a turnip. It is dreadful.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read you the sequel in advance

effects.log: It is worse than the original. You find yourself in tears of laughter.

events.text: The festival is a rout. A young priest rhymes 'altar' with 'faltered' and 'psalter' and is applauded for fifteen minutes. A goat eats the judges' scorecards. {npc} reads the sequel, and a respectful hush is followed by a roar.
events.arc: The Festival of Bad Poems

choices.text: Award {npc} a wreath of nettles with your own hands

effects.log: The nettles sting. {He} wears them proudly.

choices.text: Ask for an encore

effects.log: {He} gives one. It is, remarkably, even worse.

events.text: A rival god complains that the festival is a mockery of poetry. They arrive in a flutter of silk, with a scroll, and ask to compete. The poem they read is unbearably beautiful. {npc} and the priests stare. After a long pause, the rival says: 'It is bad, isn't it?' and the whole yard falls about.
events.arc: The Festival of Bad Poems

choices.text: Declare the rival's poem the worst of the festival

effects.log: The rival bows, delighted. A wreath of nettles is placed on the silk.

choices.text: Defend the rival's poem as truly bad

effects.log: You argue it with perfect gravity. The rival is wounded and honoured.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and the festival has become a fixture of the realm: gods send their own bad poems, anonymously, and a panel in the Court reads them aloud once a year. {He} is invited to chair it. {He} accepts, in a poem so poor that the Court weeps.
events.arc: The Festival of Bad Poems

choices.text: Contribute a poem of your own, anonymously

effects.log: Your poem is read out, and placed second worst. You feel obscurely proud.

choices.text: Sit in the audience and clap for {npc}

effects.log: You clap for the whole length of the evening.

events.text: {npc}, a priest of the weather, writes an almanac each year, predicting the seasons of your domain. {He} is nearly always wrong, and the pilgrims love it. This year the almanac says it will rain on the feast of the autumn lamps, and you had intended otherwise.
events.arc: The Weather-Priest's Almanac

choices.text: Make the rain fall on the feast day

effects.log: The rain falls. {npc} is overcome with a sense of destiny.

choices.text: Keep the feast dry and let the almanac fail

effects.log: The feast is dry. {npc} laughs at {him}self and sulks for a day.

events.text: The almanac is now half a joke and half a scripture. Pilgrims quote its failures with affection: 'The frost that never came' and 'The year of the lost sun'. {npc} has begun to write footnotes explaining each error, and the footnotes are longer than the text.
events.arc: The Weather-Priest's Almanac

choices.text: Read the footnotes aloud at the feast

effects.log: The footnotes are better than the almanac. The crowd cheers each one.

choices.text: Send {npc} a pencil of good luck

effects.log: The pencil writes true for a week. {He} is horrified and hides it.

events.text: A year comes when {npc}'s almanac is right in every particular. The rain falls on the proper day, the frost comes on the hour, the sun returns as promised. {He} is delirious. The pilgrims are offended; the almanac has broken a tradition.
events.arc: The Weather-Priest's Almanac

choices.text: Admit that you helped

effects.log: {He} laughs until {he} weeps, then pins the confession to the wall.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let the year stand

effects.log: The year stands. The next almanac is back to nonsense, to general relief.

events.text: {npc} writes a last almanac and predicts nothing. The pages are blank, with a note: 'This year let it come as it comes.' It is the best-selling almanac in the history of the valley. Pilgrims buy it as a charm. The year it describes is gentle and strange.
events.arc: The Weather-Priest's Almanac

choices.text: Make the year a gentle one

effects.log: A mild year follows. The blank almanac is laid on the altar.

choices.text: Make it entirely ordinary, as the almanac asks

effects.log: The year is ordinary, and unremarkable, and everyone says it was the best.

events.text: Along the salt road that crosses the border of three domains, a shrine on wheels travels with the caravans: a painted cart with a bell and a tiny altar. {npc}, the cart-priest, asks permission to dedicate the cart to you, since your domain is the one the road crosses most.
events.arc: The Caravan Shrine on the Salt Road

choices.text: Accept the dedication in a plain coat, at a crossroads

effects.log: You are anointed with a smear of salt. {npc} is moved.

choices.text: Send a blessing to the cart's axle

effects.log: The axle never squeaks again. The mules are suspicious.

events.text: The caravan shrine becomes famous along the road. Merchants pay a coin to ring the bell at dusk. {npc} keeps a ledger of what is asked: safe roads, fair prices, a dry night. The ledger grows heavy. The cart groans.
events.arc: The Caravan Shrine on the Salt Road

choices.text: Lend a mule from the shrine's herd

effects.log: A sturdy mule arrives, named after a theologian.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to read the ledger aloud one evening

effects.log: It is a record of ordinary fears, and ordinary hopes. You are quietly moved.

events.text: A storm closes the road. The caravan shelters at a ruined inn, and the cart-shrine's bell tolls through the night to guide the stragglers. {npc} rings until {his} hands are raw. By morning the last wagon has found its way in out of the dark.
events.arc: The Caravan Shrine on the Salt Road

choices.text: Hold the storm back a little with a shouldering wind

effects.log: The storm turns, grumbling. The last stragglers arrive.

choices.text: Send a light to the bell, to help it be seen

effects.log: A faint gold glow stands over the ruined inn. The stragglers steer by it.

events.text: The cart is rebuilt as the years wear it out, plank by plank, until nothing is original but the bell. {npc} hands the reins to a younger priest, who asks, doubtful: 'Is it still the same cart?' You say, from the roadside, in a plain coat: 'Does the road mind?'
events.arc: The Caravan Shrine on the Salt Road

choices.text: Walk the next stage of the road beside the cart

effects.log: You walk with the cart for a day, and ring the bell at dusk.

choices.text: Leave the bell a gift of tone

effects.log: The bell rings truer. Muleteers on the road stop and listen.

events.text: A spider has spun a web across the altar of the north shrine, a miracle of geometry, and the new priest wants to sweep it away. The old priest says the spider was here first. The web, in the morning dew, catches the first light like a lamp.

choices.text: Leave the web

effects.log: The web stays, and the dew is lovely. The priest learns to dust around it.

choices.text: Ask the spider's opinion

effects.log: The spider says nothing, and spins a small new square in the corner.

events.text: Wasps have built a nest in the shrine bell, so it rings a little muffled and sounds, to the pilgrims, rather holy. The priests are afraid to remove it. A child offers to ask the wasps politely, and does, and they leave an hour later in a neat column.

choices.text: Thank the child with a small blessing

effects.log: The child grows a little braver that year, and a little stung.

choices.text: Send the wasps a gift of honey in the next valley

effects.log: The wasps nest elsewhere, and forgive the bell.

events.text: A worshipper comes to your shrine every dawn and whistles a tune he made up in his youth. It is a plain little tune. He says it is not a prayer, only a thing to do with the morning. You find that you wait for it.

choices.text: Whistle it back, once, on the wind

effects.log: He stops mid-note, looks up, and laughs, and carries on.

choices.text: Listen and keep still

effects.log: The tune is the best part of the morning.

events.text: A washerwoman prays to you each morning as she beats the cloth on the river stones. The prayers are mostly about the cloth. You have come to know the cloth quite well. Today she asks only for a dry afternoon, for a wedding dress.

choices.text: Send a dry afternoon

effects.log: The dress dries in an hour. The wedding is held in sunshine.

choices.text: Send a breeze that smells of lavender

effects.log: The dress smells of lavender for years, to the bride's confusion.

events.text: A priest has fallen off a ladder while hanging the festival lanterns. He is not hurt, only embarrassed, and lies on the grass with a red lantern on his chest, laughing. The other priests, appalled, stand around him with their hands out.

choices.text: Send a soft wind so he lands lightly next time

effects.log: He lands lightly next time. Nobody can say why.

choices.text: Let him laugh

effects.log: He laughs for a long time. The lanterns are hung by the others, crookedly.

events.text: A priest of the south shrine has gone on a retreat, and the shrine is run by an apprentice and a goose. The apprentice is nervous. The goose is not. The pilgrims leave their offerings under the goose's eye, and the goose accepts them with an air of great seriousness.

choices.text: Visit and congratulate the goose

effects.log: The goose hisses. It seems to accept the compliment.

choices.text: Send the apprentice a quiet confidence

effects.log: The apprentice leads the evening prayer without a stammer.

events.text: A swallow has built its nest in the crook of your statue's arm. The arm is raised in blessing, and the nest has made it a little lopsided. The priests are cross; the pilgrims are charmed; the eggs are blue. You have been holding one pose for a century.

choices.text: Hold the pose until the chicks fledge

effects.log: The chicks fledge in June. The arm is, forever after, slightly more relaxed.

choices.text: Ask the swallow to take the other arm next time

effects.log: The swallow chooses the same arm. It is a very good arm.

events.text: Snow has fallen on the statue's head and shoulders in the night and given it a white cap. The children of the school come out in the morning and add a carrot, a scarf and a pair of stones. It is a very fine god of snow. They bow to it, and then to you.

choices.text: Let the snowgod stand for a day

effects.log: The snowgod stands until noon. The children bring it tea.

choices.text: Keep the snow from melting until nightfall

effects.log: The snowgod holds. The children are overjoyed and soaked.

events.text: A white mist has settled on the fields at dawn, and all the farmers are standing in it, to the waist, smoking their pipes and looking at nothing. It is the only hour of the day on which they are all quiet at once. You stay out of it.

choices.text: Hold the mist for an extra quarter-hour

effects.log: The farmers do not notice. They are slightly kinder at breakfast.

choices.text: Let the sun burn it off at the usual time

effects.log: The sun takes the mist. The pipes are tapped out, the day begins.

events.text: A skein of late geese passes over the shrine at night, heard but not seen: a long creaking song and the beat of wings. Every priest in the yard stops what they are doing. Nobody says a word. Then someone laughs, and the yard goes back to its work.

choices.text: Send the geese a clear sky

effects.log: The geese go south under a canopy of stars. You hear them for an hour.

choices.text: Stand in the yard until they have gone

effects.log: They go. The yard smells of the first frost.

events.text: The ford below the shrine has risen overnight and a family of pilgrims is stranded on the near bank, with a cow. They are not worried; they are picnicking. The cow looks at the water, then at you. It seems to have an opinion.

choices.text: Lower the ford for the cow

effects.log: The ford falls to a trickle. The cow crosses first and does not look back.

choices.text: Send a boat of mist to ferry the family

effects.log: A boat of white mist carries the family across. They think nothing of it.

events.text: A mole, polite and short-sighted, surfaces in your hall at tea-time. It is the envoy of the god of the deep soil. It brings a small gift of worms and a greeting. It also asks, with grave courtesy, whether you might keep the carpet a little lower.

choices.text: Receive the gift with thanks

effects.log: You do not eat the worms. The mole is not offended.

choices.text: Lower the carpet, as requested

effects.log: The carpet is lowered. The mole nods, and disappears into the floor.

events.text: An elder goddess of the fields who calls you kin arrives unannounced at your hall with three trunks and a parrot. She stays for the season. She corrects your table manners, your altar and your posture. You find yourself, secretly, a little glad of her.

choices.text: Accept her corrections with grace

effects.log: You sit straighter for a month. She nods and leaves a pie.

choices.text: Show her the new shrine garden

effects.log: She prunes it. It is better. You would not say so.

events.text: At the market a stall sells thread spun on the Weaver's own wheel, in lengths of a few hand-spans. The stallkeeper does not know whose thread it is. It is faintly warm to the touch. You buy a length, and tie it round your wrist, and feel, for a moment, accounted for.

choices.text: Keep it on your wrist

effects.log: The thread stays warm for a season, then fades.

choices.text: Take it to the Weaver to ask whose it is

effects.log: Unmyeong says: 'Yours, I think.' And says no more.

events.text: At the market of the winds a stall sells kite-string by the mile. The seller says it is spun from morning, which is why it never breaks. You buy a mile and fly a kite with it from your roof for an afternoon. It is one of the best afternoons of the year.

choices.text: Fly the kite high

effects.log: The kite goes out of sight. The string hums.

choices.text: Give the kite to a child in the square

effects.log: The child runs with it across the square, shrieking.

events.text: You dream of an orchard in a country you have never visited. Each tree bears a different year of your life. You pick one, an ordinary spring from long ago, and bite into it. It tastes of plain bread and good company. You wake hungry.

choices.text: Have bread and tea for breakfast, and nothing else

effects.log: You eat it slowly. It tastes of that spring.

choices.text: Write the dream in your book of dreams

effects.log: The book has a great many dreams. You file this under 'pleasant'.

events.text: In a dream, a cartwheel rolls down a hill with no cart behind it. It rolls for a whole night and into the day. When it stops, it falls over very slowly, like a tired person lying down. You wake feeling you have witnessed something.

choices.text: Tell Mongsa about the wheel

effects.log: Mongsa nods. 'That one has been rolling a long time,' says the Sleeper.

choices.text: Look for a wheel on the hill the next morning

effects.log: You find none. You find a good place to sit.

events.text: At court, a minor god has lost their seal and cannot sign any document. They have been ghosting the corridors for three days, apologetic, holding a blank paper. You find the seal in your own sleeve, where it has been since the feast. You do not know how.

choices.text: Return the seal quietly

effects.log: The god is overcome. A bowl of dried plums arrives at your hall the next day.

choices.text: Announce the discovery with a flourish

effects.log: The court applauds. The god is mortified and delighted.

events.text: A muddy pair of boots has been left in the corridor of the Court, and no god will own them. They are enormous, and ancient, and smell faintly of the sea. The matter has been referred to three offices. The boots are quietly there each morning.

choices.text: Claim the boots as your own

effects.log: You wear them home. They fit, to your surprise.

choices.text: Place a flower in each boot

effects.log: The boots become a minor shrine. The Court sweeps around them.

events.text: The council has recessed for tea, and the tea has taken three hours. Matters of state stand untouched on the table. The assembled gods have discovered that the Sea's herald makes extraordinary scones. A motion to adjourn in favour of scones is carried unanimously.

choices.text: Second the motion with feeling

effects.log: The motion carries. The scones are eaten in a reverent hush.

choices.text: Take a scone to the youngest clerk

effects.log: The clerk accepts it with both hands, and a start.

events.text: At every pantheon feast there is a chair left empty for the god who is not there. Nobody remembers whose it was. This year a small child sits in it, by chance, and is not removed. The child eats three helpings of rice. The whole table is conscious of her.

choices.text: Raise a cup to the child in the chair

effects.log: The table follows. The child is startled and beams.

choices.text: Pass her the best dish

effects.log: She takes it in both hands and says thank you, with perfect manners.

events.text: At a festival game, a frog is entered into the wrestling by a mischievous child. The frog loses to everyone but wins the crowd. At the final bout it wrestles a large, grave god of war, and loses with a dignified squeak. The god of war carries it out like a hero.

choices.text: Present the frog with a crown of clover

effects.log: The frog sits on the clover and takes the cheers.

choices.text: Compliment the god of war on his manners

effects.log: He turns pink, and bows, with the frog on his shoulder.

events.text: A pie contest is held among the shrines, with a god of the harvest as judge. A priest of the lowest shrine enters a pie made by his grandmother, which has a crust like a cobblestone. It tastes of her kitchen, and the judge weeps, and gives it the prize.

choices.text: Congratulate the priest on his grandmother's behalf

effects.log: He accepts it, in tears. The grandmother cannot be found, being at home.

choices.text: Ask for a slice

effects.log: You eat it in the yard. It is the best thing you have had all year.

events.text: An elder god, who has outlived all their friends, sits on the shrine bench and recites a list of names, steadily, under their breath. They have done this each evening for a thousand years. You sit beside them one night and listen. You do not recognise a single name.

choices.text: Add one name of your own to the list

effects.log: The elder pauses, nods, and says it with the rest.

choices.text: Listen until the list is done

effects.log: It takes two hours. When they stop, the elder gives your hand a single pat.

events.text: On a hunt for the star-stag you find only tracks in the frost, a mile of them, leading nowhere. At the end of the line is a single bronze bell, newly dropped. The stag is gone. The bell, warm, rings once at your touch, and the hounds fall silent.

choices.text: Keep the bell and call off the hunt

effects.log: The hunt is called off. The stag, you are fairly sure, watches from a ridge.

choices.text: Hang the bell on a branch and leave

effects.log: The bell stays on its branch all winter, ringing in the wind.

events.text: On the night of the lamps the star-gods light the orchard of the sky, one lamp to a tree. You stand with the lamplighters on a high roof and hold the ladder. A small god falls off it and is caught by the one at the bottom. They laugh until the lamps flicker.

choices.text: Offer to hold the ladder for the next lamp

effects.log: You hold it for six lamps. The small god wobbles beautifully.

choices.text: Light one lamp yourself

effects.log: Your lamp burns with a slightly different colour. Nobody comments.

events.text: You stand at the edge of a lake so still that the sky has fallen into it, stars and all. Not a ripple. You can see the whole of the Court reflected in it, upside down, tiny, bright. You have never seen your own realm from below before.

choices.text: Stay until the reflection fades

effects.log: It fades with the dawn. Something remains with you, small and clear.

choices.text: Skip one stone and break it

effects.log: The ripples spread across the sky. The stars come back together, slowly, laughing.

events.text: The smell of fresh bread reaches your hall from the kitchens of the lower shrine. It is unmistakable and extraordinary and it drifts through the long corridors, calling everyone to it. Even the elder gods are seen walking in the direction of the oven.

choices.text: Follow the smell yourself

effects.log: You are given a heel of the loaf, and a stool, and a cup of milk.

choices.text: Send a warm wind to carry it further

effects.log: The smell reaches the far hills. Shepherds sniff and are hungry.

events.text: Rain on the shrine roof, steady, from dusk to midnight. The priests have gone to bed. The lamps burn low. You sit in your hall and listen to it, and for the first time in a while you are not responsible for any of it, and are content.

choices.text: Listen until it stops

effects.log: It stops at the third hour. The silence after is delicate.

choices.text: Add a faint thunder, far away

effects.log: A thunder rolls in the hills, kindly. The priests sleep sounder.
